SLIIT Codefest 2026 - AI Competition Document Corpus
=====================================================

An entirely fictional fantasy franchise archive ('the Ashen Era').

  chronicles/  Narrative novels (PDF/DOCX), long chapters.
  wiki/        Fan-wiki articles (Markdown) with images.
  codex/       Official lore codexes and annals (PDF/DOCX) with plates.
  ephemera/    In-world letters, ledgers, transcripts (mixed formats,
               including scanned pages). WARNING: in-world authors are
               not always reliable.
  images/      Standalone figure plates.

The Ashen Chronicles, Volume III: A Crown of Cinders
Chapter 1
The blood on Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed’s hands had dried black by the time the bells began.
They rang from the dark beyond the walls, slow and hollow, each note passing through the stone like a fist through rotten cloth. He sat beneath a broken arch with his back against the cold, listening to the sound descend into him.
A bell meant surrender once.
A bell meant warning after.
Tonight it meant nothing that could save anyone.
“Captain.”
The voice came from the stairwell. A figure climbed into the ruined chamber, carrying a hooded lamp and a leather case beneath one arm. The flame trembled across the iron fittings of the walls, across the blackened dust, across Brannoc’s hands.
The stranger stopped when he saw them.
Brannoc looked down at his fingers. The blood had gathered in the creases and beneath the nails. It was not all his.
“Say what you came to say,” Brannoc told him.
The stranger swallowed. “You were not meant to be here.”
“I have been told worse by men with better knives.”
Below them, something collapsed. Stone grated against stone. A gust of ash rose through the stairwell, carrying the bitter reek of burned grain and old smoke. Brannoc breathed it in. Hollowvale had smelled like that before the Accord came to it. Not smoke then. Wet earth. Horse dung. Boiled onions from the market vats.
The Accord of Mournthrone had devastated Hollowvale in 301 AS.
The sentence had been written in the leather case before the ink was dry.
The stranger opened it now and removed a folded sheet. His hands shook as he unfolded it.
Brannoc watched the paper rather than the man. “Who wrote that?”
“No name.”
“Then it was written by a coward.”
“It bears the seal of the recorders.”
“There are no recorders left.”
The stranger’s mouth tightened. “There are always recorders.”
Brannoc gave a low laugh. It hurt beneath his ribs. Pain had become a patient animal, lying curled inside him, opening one eye whenever he moved. He had been born in 255 AS, when the realm still pretended its ruins were foundations. He had spent his life learning the price of that pretense.
The stranger held out the sheet.
Brannoc did not take it.
“Read.”
“The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS and ended in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
The bells continued below.
“Again,” Brannoc said.
The stranger’s eyes flicked toward the stairwell. “Why?”
“Because you read it like a prayer.”
“It is a record.”
“Records are prayers for men who expect the dead to answer.”
The stranger read it again. His voice grew flatter the second time, and the words lost their shape in the chamber.
Brannoc closed his eyes.
He saw Mournthrone without seeing it: its shadow over the war, its weight in every bargain, its name carried from mouth to mouth by men who had never stood beneath its walls. The Accord had begun as all such things began, with wax, knives hidden in sleeves, and promises poured into cups. It had become mud, famine, and the sound of gates giving way.
“What else?” he asked.
“The Accord’s collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.”
“A decade,” Brannoc murmured. “The realm has grown fond of long punishments.”
The stranger lowered the sheet.
“There is more.”
“There is always more.”
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.”
For a moment, Brannoc heard only the rain ticking against the broken roof.
Then he smiled.
The stranger stared at him. “You knew?”
“I suspected.”
“You said the retreat was madness.”
“I have called many sane men mad. It is one of the privileges of being a Sellsword Captain.”
The phrase sounded too formal in the ruined chamber. Major Sellsword Captain, the ledgers called him. As though a title could make a wall around a man. As though a rank could keep a blade from finding the seam in his armor.
The stranger glanced at Brannoc’s hands again.
“Is it true,” he asked, “what they say about you?”
“Which lie?”
“That you are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
The blood on Brannoc’s right hand cracked when he flexed it.
Somewhere beneath the rubble, a wounded man began to moan. The sound rose and fell with the bells.
Brannoc had heard the claim in taverns, under banners, beside graves. He had heard it spoken with contempt, with fear, with the hungry softness of men measuring a future throne. The Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged him. That was the word that mattered. Not denied. Not named. Unacknowledged.
A door left closed could still have someone standing behind it.
“Does the Crown know?” the stranger asked.
“The Crown knows what crowns always know.”
“Which is?”
“That a head is beneath them.”
The stranger’s fingers tightened around the sheet. He had come expecting confession, perhaps. A dying man made useful by the nearness of death. Brannoc knew the look. Men believed a final hour stripped the lies from a tongue. They did not understand that death gave a man fewer reasons to be kind.
“What do you want?” Brannoc asked.
“Safe passage.”
“For whom?”
The stranger looked toward the stairwell.
A soft scrape answered him from below.
Brannoc’s hand went to the sword at his side. The motion pulled hot fire through his ribs, but the weapon came free a finger’s breadth. Steel whispered.
The stranger went pale.
“Korvath Nightbrook,” he said.
The name passed through the chamber like a rat slipping beneath a door.
Korvath Nightbrook emerged from the stairwell without a lamp. He wore the unobtrusive shape of a man accustomed to concealed trade: hood, dull cloth, boots darkened by mud. His face remained half-hidden, but his eyes held the wary patience of a smuggler who had survived by noticing what others missed.
“You brought him here?” Brannoc asked.
“I brought the case,” said the stranger.
“Korvath brought himself.”
“That is why he is alive,” Korvath said.
His voice had the quiet scrape of a whetstone. He looked at Brannoc, then at the blood, then at the sword.
“Are you dying?”
“Not quickly enough to satisfy you.”
Korvath moved nearer. “Then listen quickly.”
Brannoc sheathed the sword. The bells had ceased. Their silence seemed louder than the ringing.
Korvath reached inside his coat and drew out a narrow bundle wrapped in grey cloth.
The stranger took one step back. “That was not part of the bargain.”
“No,” Korvath said. “It was part of the danger.”
He laid the bundle on a slab of fallen masonry and unwrapped it.
The object beneath was a grimoire bound in dark material that seemed to drink the lamp’s light. Its cover bore the name Edge of Gloamreach. The letters were shallow and precise, like wounds made by a careful hand.
Brannoc felt the air tighten around it.
“Attunement cost?” he asked.
“Forty-six,” said Korvath.
The stranger whispered something that might have been a curse.
Brannoc did not touch the grimoire. He had learned that some things demanded skin before they demanded blood.
“And the other?”
Korvath’s gaze shifted to the leather case.
The stranger flinched. “There is no other.”
Brannoc saw the lie arrive before the words finished leaving him.
“Open it,” he said.
“I already did.”
“Open it properly.”
The stranger looked at Korvath. Korvath gave no answer. After a moment, the stranger set down the paper and reached into the case’s inner lining. His fingers found a hidden catch. The leather gave with a small, damp click.
Inside lay a blade in a sheath of tarnished metal.
Even wrapped in darkness, it seemed bound by something more than leather. Thin cords crossed its hilt and vanished beneath the guard, three times knotted, each knot blackened as if by ancient fire.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge,” Korvath said.
Brannoc stared at it.
“Regalia,” the stranger murmured. “Forged in 123 AS.”
“No attunement cost is recorded,” Korvath said.
The stranger looked offended by the omission, as though the absence itself were a threat. “That does not mean there is none.”
“No,” Brannoc said. “It means whoever made it did not care to warn us.”
His hand hovered over the sheath.
For an instant, the chamber changed. The ash became snow. The broken arch became a hall of black pillars. He saw banners hanging without wind, and beneath them the five powers that had fed upon the Ashen Era: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown.
No faces. No promises.
Only the understanding that every power in the realm wanted the same thing from a crown.
A throat beneath it.
Brannoc withdrew his hand.
Korvath watched him closely. “You cannot carry both.”
“I carry what I choose.”
“You carry a wound.”
“And you carry contraband. We all have burdens.”
“The Ashen Vanguard will be named victor,” the stranger said, almost pleading now. “The record says so. The Accord will end. The reprisals will follow. If you take that blade, they will say you sought the Crown.”
“They already say it.”
“They will believe it.”
Brannoc turned toward the broken wall.
Far beyond the ruin, the road ran toward the high country. Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. It had been rebuilt, though rebuilding was a word used by men who did not sleep beneath roofs that might fall. Its garrison was 1004, and still it remained outside the core holdings. Brannoc had seen its crooked defenses, its hard-edged towers gripping the mountain like clenched teeth. A wary place. A resilient place. The kind that survived by expecting betrayal from the weather as well as from men.
Further still lay Fenspire, standing in the Gloaming Reach. Founded in 57 AS, it was a core location, garrisoned and disciplined, with a garrison of 3,742 beneath its stark spire. A fortress pretending to be a city. A city pretending it had not become a fortress.
Every road led somewhere armed.
Every gate had learned the shape of hunger.
“Captain,” the stranger said.
Brannoc looked back.
The man had drawn a knife. It was a small thing, made for letters or throats. His hand shook around it.
Brannoc felt the old danger gather in the room—not anger, not fear, but the cold arithmetic beneath both. He had been called the Red-Handed because blood found him wherever men gathered in numbers. The name had outlived the battles that earned it. It would outlive him.
He wondered whether the ledgers would record that.
He wondered whether they would record his death in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone, or merely mark the place where a name stopped being useful.
“Put it down,” Brannoc said.
The stranger’s eyes filled with tears. “You cannot let him leave.”
“Who?”
“Korvath.”
Korvath’s hand disappeared beneath his coat.
Brannoc rose.
The wound beneath his ribs opened. Warmth spread beneath his clothes. The stranger made a frightened sound and backed into the wall. Korvath moved at the same time, swift and silent, but Brannoc’s sword was already in his hand.
Below them, the bells began again.
Not slow now.
Not hollow.
A frantic peal burst through the ruin as flames climbed somewhere in the dark, and from the stairwell came the heavy tread of men ascending—closer, closer, while Brannoc stood between the grimoire, the bound regalia, and the two living men who had mistaken his last hour for an opportunity.
The first man broke the stairwell’s darkness with a shield raised before him. Firelight crawled over its rim. Behind him came another, then another, their boots striking the stone with the blunt certainty of men who believed the room already belonged to them.
Brannoc shifted his weight.
Pain opened under his ribs, wet and intimate. He felt it travel through him in a slow red thread, as though some patient hand were pulling him apart from within. His sword remained level. The point hovered between Korvath Nightbrook and the stranger pressed against the wall.
“Move,” Brannoc said.
The stranger stared at him.
“Not you,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s hand emerged from beneath his coat. Empty.
That was almost worse.
The smuggler’s face had gone still. He wore concealment like another man wore a cloak: not to vanish, but to make every eye slide elsewhere. Now the mask had cracked. Fear showed through it, narrow and bright.
“You heard him,” Korvath said to the stranger. “Go.”
The stranger looked toward the stairwell. The ascending men were close enough that Brannoc could hear the leather creak of their harness and the drag of breath behind metal. Somewhere below, flame consumed timber with a hungry, snapping roar.
“I can’t,” the stranger whispered.
“You can,” Brannoc said.
A blade appeared above the stair’s broken lip.
Brannoc moved.
His sword struck the man’s wrist before the shield could clear the opening. The blade rang against a vambrace. The man cried out, and the shield fell sideways, wedging itself across the narrow stair. The second man crashed into him. The third cursed. Their formation became a knot of iron, cloth, and flesh.
Brannoc kicked the fallen shield.
It struck the first man in the throat.
The sound he made was small. He folded backward into the men behind him, and for one precious breath the stairwell was blocked.
“Now,” Brannoc said.
Korvath did not run.
His eyes had gone to the table.
To the grimoire.
To the regalia bound in black cord.
Brannoc saw the calculation enter him and despised the clarity of it. Korvath was measuring weight, value, escape. A smuggler’s arithmetic. Not courage. Not loyalty. Only what could be carried through a closing door.
Brannoc seized him by the front of his coat and slammed him against the wall.
The wound beneath his ribs flared. His vision whitened at the edges.
“Take one,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s gaze flicked toward the grimoire.
“No.”
“The book or the blade. Not both.”
“The Edge of Gloamreach is worth—”
“I did not ask what it was worth.”
The men on the stairs began to wrench the shield free. Wood groaned. Iron scraped stone.
Korvath’s mouth tightened. “You know what the thing is?”
“I know enough.”
“You know nothing.”
“That is why you are still breathing.”
Korvath glanced at the sword between them. “And the stranger?”
The stranger had not moved. He stood beneath the blackened archway, one hand clamped over his mouth, staring at the gore beginning to shine on Brannoc’s blade. His face seemed bloodless in the furnace-glow. He looked less like a conspirator now than a man who had walked into a room and found the world’s teeth waiting.
Brannoc kept his eyes on Korvath.
“Take the Edge of Gloamreach,” he said. “Leave him.”
A tremor went through the smuggler—not fear this time. Anger.
There it was. The thing beneath the caution.
“You don’t get to decide that.”
“I command Blackford.”
The words came out harder than he intended, and the room seemed to hear them. Even the bells, shrilling above the ruin, could not drown the old authority in his voice.
“Since 285 AS, Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed has commanded Blackford.”
Korvath stared at him.
Brannoc had said the words to men who needed a banner before they needed a name. He had said them in rain, in ash, in halls where the floor had been scrubbed clean and the walls had not. Command was not a title. It was the space that opened when other men decided their lives were safer inside your shadow.
The stairs buckled under another impact.
Korvath’s expression altered. Not submission. Recognition.
Then he laughed once, without humor.
“Blackford,” he said. “You drag that old claim behind you like a chain.”
“It is not a claim.”
“No?” Korvath glanced at the bound regalia. “Then why are you bleeding for it?”
Brannoc looked down.
Blood had reached his glove. It shone dark across the knuckles, gathered in the creases, and made the old epithet seem freshly earned. The Red-Handed. Men had given him that name for reasons that no longer mattered. Names survived their causes. They clung like burrs.
“Because men who come for it usually mean to use it.”
“And you don’t?”
“I mean to keep it from them.”
“That is not the same.”
“No,” Brannoc said. “It is worse.”
The shield tore loose.
The first man surged into the chamber on one knee, one hand at his throat. Brannoc turned and drove his sword down through the gap beneath the raised arm. The blade passed into the shoulder with a thick resistance. He wrenched it free before the man fell fully, using the collapsing body to foul the next advance.
The second man tried to step over him.
Brannoc caught the descending sword on his own. The impact jarred his wound. His knees nearly gave. Steel grated against steel. The other man leaned into him, visor dark, breath harsh within the helm.
Brannoc smelled hot iron and old smoke.
He smelled his own blood.
The stranger made a broken noise and fled toward the far side of the room.
Not toward the door.
Toward the table.
Brannoc saw him reach for the cord around The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The regalia did not move.
The stranger’s fingers closed over it. His face twisted. He made no sound this time, but his arm sagged as if the object had become heavier than stone. The black cord drew taut beneath his hand.
“Leave it!” Brannoc roared.
The man looked up.
Something in his eyes had changed. Not wonder. Not greed. An awful pleading, as though he had touched a buried thing and found it awake beneath the earth.
Korvath saw it too.
He drove his shoulder into Brannoc’s back.
The swordsman staggered. The armored man’s blade slid from his guard and opened a line along Brannoc’s sleeve. Heat followed. Brannoc turned with the stumble, let the pain carry him, and struck low.
The armored man’s knee gave.
Brannoc seized the back of his neck and brought his forehead down against the broken stone. Once. The helm rang. Again. The man collapsed, sword slipping from his hand.
A third man entered behind him.
Brannoc kicked the fallen blade across the floor. It struck the stranger’s ankle. The stranger cried out and fell beside the table, releasing The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The cord lay still.
The grimoire lay beside it, its cover dark beneath a skin of dust and ash.
Korvath had reached the table.
His fingers closed around the Edge of Gloamreach.
“Don’t,” Brannoc said.
Korvath lifted it.
The room seemed to draw inward.
No wind moved. No flame guttered. Yet the darkness beneath the table deepened, gathering around the smuggler’s wrist. The grimoire’s pages stirred beneath its cover, one after another, though no hand touched them. A smell rose from it: damp stone, extinguished candles, something bitter enough to taste.
Korvath’s face tightened.
“What did you do?” the stranger whispered.
“Nothing,” Korvath said.
That was a lie. Brannoc knew the shape of lies. This one had been spoken before the question.
The armored man behind Brannoc raised his sword.
Brannoc turned too slowly.
The blade descended.
Korvath thrust the grimoire between them.
Steel struck its cover.
A sound moved through the chamber—not a crack, not a cry, but the distant murmur of countless voices speaking from behind a closed door. The impact threw the armored man backward. His sword spun away. He struck the stairwell wall and slid down among the bodies.
Korvath stared at the grimoire in his hands.
The Edge of Gloamreach had opened.
Its pages were blank.
Then ink began to spread across them.
Black veins crawled from the binding, branching over the pale paper in crooked strokes. Brannoc watched the marks gather into shapes he could not read and understood, with the instinctive certainty of a man recognizing a drawn bow, that the book was not waiting for a reader.
It was waiting for an answer.
The bells faltered above them.
One peal.
Silence.
Then another, lower and slower, traveling through the foundations.
The stranger crawled backward. “Put it down.”
Korvath’s knuckles had gone white around the cover.
“Put it down,” the stranger said again.
“What is it writing?”
“I don’t know.”
“You brought me here.”
“I brought you to the room.”
“And you knew.”
“I knew enough to be afraid.”
Brannoc stepped toward them. His sword felt heavier now, not from the blood on it but from the weight gathering in the air. The room had become a held breath. The grimoire’s pages turned faster. Ink spilled in thin rivers, running over the edges and dripping onto Korvath’s coat.
Brannoc reached for the book.
Korvath jerked away.
Behind him, the stranger whispered, “It remembers the hand.”
Brannoc stopped.
The phrase found some locked chamber in him. Not memory. Something older than memory, a pressure behind the eyes. He looked at his own hand—the red-streaked glove, the fingers curled around the hilt—and saw the ink on the page arrange itself.
A single word.
Not a name.
A command.
The stone beneath them trembled.
From below came the muffled crash of a door breaking open.
More men were coming.
Korvath shut the grimoire.
The darkness vanished.
For an instant, nothing moved except the blood slipping from Brannoc’s wound and pattering softly onto the floor.
Then the stranger lunged for The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Brannoc caught him by the throat.
He lifted him just enough to take his feet from the ground. The man clawed at Brannoc’s wrist, eyes bulging, while Korvath backed away with the grimoire clutched to his chest.
“You have one breath,” Brannoc said.
The stranger’s hands beat against him.
“One.”
The stairwell filled with voices.
“Two.”
Korvath looked toward the rear passage, where the ruin had split open into a narrow black cleft.
The stranger’s face purpled.
“Three.”
Brannoc threw him aside.
He struck the floor beside the regalia and lay there gasping. Korvath moved at once, not toward the passage but toward him, and that choice—small, involuntary, revealing—cost them both the moment they had left.
Brannoc stepped between them.
The first of the new men appeared at the stair.
And from the darkness beyond the table, something answered the bells.
The answer came again, closer.
Not a voice. Not an animal. The stone itself seemed to draw breath, and the cleft behind the table narrowed as though some vast throat had begun to swallow the ruin.
The first man on the stair raised a hooded lantern. Its light slid over a hooked blade, a mailed shoulder, the pale gleam of teeth.
Brannoc struck him before the man could descend.
His fist met the lantern. Glass burst. Oil sheeted over the stranger’s arm, and the darkness took fire in a sudden blue flare. The man screamed, but the stair behind him was already crowded. Bodies pressed forward. Steel rasped against stone.
Brannoc caught the burning sleeve and dragged its owner down three steps. The man’s skull struck the edge of one. The blue fire went out.
“Move,” Brannoc said.
Korvath did not move. He knelt beside the fallen stranger, one hand still clamped around the Edge of Gloamreach. The grimoire’s black cover drank the firelight that remained. Its clasps trembled beneath Korvath’s fingers.
“The passage,” Korvath said.
“I saw it.”
“Then use it.”
Brannoc looked past him. The rear cleft had become a seam of absolute dark. No rubble had fallen into it. No dust drifted from its mouth. Darkness gathered there with intention.
The bells began again.
One note from beneath the floor.
One from inside the walls.
One from the grimoire.
Korvath flinched at the third. Brannoc saw it and understood that the smuggler had not stolen the book. He had been carrying it because the book had chosen a pair of hands, and those hands had belonged to a coward until Brannoc had made the coward desperate.
The stair disgorged another man. Then another.
“Who sent you?” Brannoc demanded.
The nearest attacker came at him with a short sword.
Brannoc turned aside, caught the man’s wrist, and drove an elbow into his throat. The man folded. A second blade cut the air where Brannoc’s neck had been. He seized the fallen sword and flung it backward. It struck the third man in the chest with a wet, muffled sound.
“Who sent you?”
No answer. Only boots. Too many boots.
Korvath rose at last. The Edge of Gloamreach hung from his hand, its spine flexing like something alive.
“Those are not cartel men,” he whispered.
Brannoc shoved him toward the cleft. “You know every lawful channel in this district?”
“I know the unlawful ones.”
“Then name them.”
“Not while they are trying to kill us.”
A blade glanced from Brannoc’s forearm. Pain opened bright and clean. He answered with the pommel, crushing the attacker’s mouth. Blood painted his knuckles. The sight steadied him. Men called him the Red-Handed for reasons that had once been useful and later become inconvenient. He had never cared which version of the truth frightened them most.
The stairwell filled with smoke and the smell of hot oil. Somewhere above, someone shouted for the doors to be barred.
The ruin had become a trap. The men below were driving them toward the dark, while whatever waited in the cleft had begun its patient reply.
Korvath backed toward it.
Brannoc caught his collar.
“Do not go in blind.”
“I have gone in blind all my life.”
“You have gone in paid.”
Korvath’s eyes flicked to the regalia lying near the table. The Thrice-Bound Edge rested where it had fallen, its surface dull beneath the smoke. It had been forged in 123 AS, long before either of them had been born, long before the realm had learned to mistake surviving ruins for ruling them.
The stranger Brannoc had thrown aside stirred on the floor.
“Do you know what you’re holding?” Brannoc asked him.
The stranger’s gaze fixed on the regalia.
“The price,” he said.
“For what?”
The man smiled through split lips. “For the crown.”
The word passed through Brannoc like a hand laid upon an old wound.
He had heard it whispered in rooms where the lamps were low and the doors watched. He had seen men kneel to an empty chair. He had learned early that blood could be a chain even when no one acknowledged the shackle.
He was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
The knowledge had never made him feel chosen. It had made every oath taste rotten.
A spear thrust down the stair. Brannoc caught the shaft under his arm, wrenched it sideways, and hauled the spearman over the steps. The man came down hard. Brannoc drove his heel into the man’s ribs and felt something give.
“Korvath,” he said.
The smuggler was staring into the cleft.
Within that darkness, shapes moved without making space for themselves. A shoulder. A hand. The suggestion of a face turned toward them, though no features held long enough to be seen.
“The Edge of Gloamreach has an attunement cost of 46,” Korvath said.
Brannoc looked at him.
“What?”
“It is written inside. Forty-six.” Korvath’s voice had gone thin. “I thought it meant coin. I thought—”
“You thought a grimoire was merchandise.”
“I am a Smuggler.”
The admission came without shame. It was almost a prayer.
The men on the stair surged together. Brannoc seized the fallen spear and swept it low. Ankles broke. Bodies tumbled. One attacker fell headfirst and took another with him. The stair became a knot of armor, limbs, and curses.
“Read the rest,” Brannoc said.
Korvath opened the book.
The pages turned by themselves.
A cold wind rushed from the cleft. The flames guttered toward it. Brannoc felt the temperature leave his skin, felt the old ache in his joints sharpen as though winter had found the marrow.
Letters surfaced on the page, black at first, then red.
Korvath bent over them.
“‘The bound hand opens the way.’”
“Whose hand?”
The bells stopped.
Every man on the stair froze.
The silence afterward was worse than the sound. Brannoc heard the drip of oil. Heard Korvath swallow. Heard, beneath the floor, a slow pressure gathering against the stones.
The stranger on the floor began to laugh.
Brannoc turned and stamped on his wrist. Bone cracked.
“Speak.”
The stranger’s laugh broke into a sob.
“You cannot outrun the accord.”
“What accord?”
But Korvath had found another line.
“The Accord of Mournthrone,” he murmured.
The name seemed to darken the ruin. It belonged to a conflict that had begun in 297 AS and would end in 301 AS, with the Ashen Vanguard named victor. Brannoc had heard the declaration in advance, as men heard all victories before they were won: through paid tongues, sealed letters, and the trembling confidence of those who had already sold their allegiance.
The stranger whispered, “When it collapses, the roads will burn.”
Korvath read on. “‘A decade of guerrilla reprisals follows the broken accord.’”
The page shuddered beneath his hand.
Brannoc saw it then—not as a vision, but as a certainty lodged behind the eyes. Blackford’s walls under moonless rain. A crown split by a sword. Men who had fought beneath one banner turning their blades upon every village that had fed them. The Ashen Vanguard’s victory reduced to another word for occupation.
And behind it all, a losing commander accepting a bribe to withdraw.
Not defeated. Purchased.
The truth had the coldness of a knife held against the throat.
“Who was paid?” Brannoc asked.
The stranger’s face had gone slack.
Korvath’s finger stopped on the page. “It doesn’t say.”
“It says enough.”
“No. It says someone will withdraw. It says the Accord of Mournthrone collapses. It says—”
A hand emerged from the cleft.
It was not flesh. It resembled a hand only because the darkness had learned the shape and was practicing it. Long fingers pressed against the edge of the passage. The stone groaned.
Korvath shut the grimoire.
The hand withdrew.
The men on the stair began to retreat.
That frightened Brannoc more than their assault. They had come expecting prey. Now they were looking over their shoulders at something that had not yet entered the room.
“Hold the stair,” Brannoc said.
No one obeyed.
He stepped into the narrow throat of it himself.
The first fleeing man collided with him. Brannoc caught him by the jaw and slammed him against the wall.
“Who sent you?”
The man stared at Brannoc’s bloodied hand.
“The Crown.”
“Which?”
The man’s mouth worked.
The name would not come.
Brannoc tightened his grip until the man’s boots scraped stone. The phrase rose in him again, bitter as bile: unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown. A hidden son for hidden wars. A claim preserved by those who needed a knife and denied by those who feared the hand holding it.
“The Bleeding Crown?” he asked.
The man’s eyes filled with terror.
“Not yours,” he said.
Behind Brannoc, Korvath whispered a word from the book.
The cleft opened.
Not widened. Opened.
The darkness peeled apart from floor to ceiling, revealing no passage beyond, no buried chamber, no foundation stones. It revealed a depth filled with pale drifting ash. Within that ash stood distant silhouettes, each crowned, each bound, each facing away.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lifted from the floor.
It did not fly. It rose with the solemn reluctance of something remembering an order. Its regalia gleamed once, and three bands of dull metal wound around its length like restraints.
Korvath dropped the Edge of Gloamreach.
The grimoire struck the floor and opened.
The pages showed a line of writing neither man had read before.
Brannoc saw his own name.
BRANNOC IRONMERE THE RED-HANDED.
Beneath it:
BORN IN 255 AS.
Beneath that, written in a hand so dark it seemed cut into the world:
DIED IN 300 AS DURING THE ACCORD OF MOURNTHRONE.
His breath stopped.
For the first time that night, he forgot the men on the stair.
He forgot the crown, the regalia, the ruin, the thing waiting beyond the cleft.
Korvath made a sound behind him. “Brannoc.”
The letters began to bleed.
The hand of darkness reached through the opening.
And somewhere beyond the ash, something wearing a crown turned its head.
Chapter 2
Rain worried the shutters like a beggar with a knife.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed sat alone beneath the unlit brazier, listening to the weather spend itself against the stone. The chamber smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the iron tang that clung to every place where men had argued too long. A single candle guttered on the table before him. Its flame leaned whenever the wind found a crack in the walls, as if even fire wished to escape.
He had removed his gloves.
That was the first mistake.
His hands rested flat upon the table, broad and scarred, their knuckles darkened by old blood beneath the skin. The epithet had followed him across ruined roads and salt-black fields, but names were only chains made of sound. Men called him the Red-Handed because they needed a shape for the violence they feared. They called him a Sellsword Captain because a title was easier to stomach than a man who could be hired to decide the fate of a province.
They did not call him heir.
Not aloud.
Across from him, the door remained shut. Behind it waited the soft scrape of boots, the mutter of guards, the careful silence of men paid to hear nothing. He knew that silence. It belonged to courts, camps, and graves.
On the table lay a strip of black cloth, folded around a shard of bone.
Brannoc had not touched it since it arrived.
He had received messages sealed with blood, wax, ash, and once with a child’s milk tooth. He had learned to distrust every seal. The more elaborate the warning, the cheaper the lie beneath it. But this cloth bore no crest, and the bone had been cut cleanly enough to suggest a hand without tremor.
That troubled him.
A knock sounded.
Two taps. A pause. One tap.
Brannoc reached for the knife at his belt. The familiar weight settled his thoughts, though the hilt was slick from the damp in the room. He did not draw it.
“Enter.”
The door opened only as far as necessary. A figure slipped through and closed it with care.
Korvath Nightbrook wore the plain, forgettable clothes of a man who wished to become part of a wall. Rain shone along his sleeves. His hood remained raised, though there was no one in the chamber to deceive but Brannoc, and Brannoc had never mistaken concealment for invisibility.
Korvath glanced at the candle.
“Extinguish it,” he said.
Brannoc did not move. “You came through a guarded corridor to give orders about a candle?”
“Not orders.”
“No?”
“Advice.”
“Then it is worth less.”
Korvath’s mouth tightened. He carried himself like a smuggler: shoulders turned inward, gaze forever measuring the space between exits. Nothing about him invited trust. That, at least, made him useful.
Brannoc leaned back. “You’re late.”
“I was watched.”
“By whom?”
Korvath looked toward the shutters. “Everyone who matters.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one that survives the night.”
The rain thickened. For a moment the chamber became a sealed vessel, the two men listening to the roof endure.
Brannoc tapped the bone with one finger. “You sent this.”
“I carried it.”
“From whom?”
Korvath’s eyes moved to the knife, then to Brannoc’s hands. He had heard the stories. Most men had. They expected some visible deformity from an epithet such as the Red-Handed—a claw, perhaps, or a stain that no washing could lift. Brannoc offered them nothing. His hands were only hands. That disappointed them more than blood would have.
“From a man who will not be alive by dawn,” Korvath said.
“Then he should have spoken before now.”
“He did.”
“And?”
“And he spoke to the wrong people.”
Brannoc picked up the cloth. It was cold and wet, though Korvath had not seemed to touch the rain for long. The bone inside was narrow, pale, and ridged.
“Whose?”
“Not a finger.”
“That was not my question.”
Korvath’s gaze dropped.
Brannoc unfolded the cloth. A sliver of dark metal lay against the bone, thin as a fish spine. Marks had been scratched into it. Not letters. A pattern of three angled cuts bound by a fourth.
His breath slowed.
The mark was familiar, but familiarity could be bait. He had seen the sign pressed into wax on orders that sent men into ravines, painted beneath bridges, carved into the underside of a captain’s chair. It belonged to a language that had outlived those who claimed to speak it.
Korvath said, “The account is true.”
“What account?”
“The one that says the Accord of Mournthrone was never decided in the field.”
Brannoc’s thumb stopped upon the metal.
Outside, something struck the shutters. A branch, perhaps. Or a thrown stone. Neither man looked toward the sound.
“Careful,” Brannoc said.
“I have been careful since birth.”
“And yet you are here.”
“Yes.”
“Which proves the gods are either blind or amused.”
Korvath gave no sign that he heard the bitterness. “The Accord of Mournthrone has been fed to armies as a victory, to nobles as a negotiation, and to the desperate as proof that men can still bind themselves to words. It was none of those things.”
“Every accord is a bargain.”
“This one had a price concealed inside it.”
Brannoc rose.
The chamber seemed to contract around him. He did not need to threaten Korvath. Threats were for men uncertain of their strength. He crossed to the shutters and placed one hand against the wood. The rain trembled through it. Beyond lay the dark bulk of the stronghold, its roofs and towers erased by weather. Somewhere below, soldiers were sleeping in their armor. Somewhere beyond them, envoys waited beneath banners they believed still possessed meaning.
“Say it,” Brannoc said.
Korvath remained by the table. “The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.”
The words did not echo. They sank.
Brannoc stared into the black seam between the shutters. The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.
Not defeated.
Not outmaneuvered.
Bought.
He had watched men die for that retreat. He remembered the sound of it: iron dragged over stone, horses screaming in the rain, a line breaking where no line should have broken. He remembered orders passed from mouth to mouth until they became nonsense. He remembered commanders standing beneath covered lanterns, their faces hollow with disbelief.
He had believed in the wrong thing.
That was the wound. Not the dead. The dead were clean of it.
“What was the price?” he asked.
Korvath’s answer came softly. “A promise of safety. Gold. Passage. Perhaps a title.”
“Perhaps?”
“The ledger does not say.”
“Then it is not a ledger. It is a rumor dressed for court.”
“It names the payment.”
“Names what?”
Korvath reached inside his coat and produced a folded square of oilskin. He placed it on the table, beside the strip of cloth.
Brannoc did not return. “You said the man who carried it would not live by dawn.”
“He was not the man who wrote it.”
“Who was he?”
“A clerk.”
“Whose clerk?”
“The sort who belongs to whoever is holding his throat.”
Brannoc turned. “You are wasting my patience.”
Korvath’s expression hardened. “Your patience is a blade you keep pointing at the wrong throat.”
The candle flame bent low.
For an instant Brannoc saw the table as a battlefield map. The oilskin became a standard. The bone became a marker. The thin shard of metal became a road leading somewhere no army could safely march. He had spent years learning how men moved when they believed themselves free. He knew the twitch before a charge, the pause before betrayal, the moment a hired sword realized the purse had been emptied.
The accord had felt wrong from the beginning.
Too many solemn faces. Too much reverence for ink. Men who had butchered villages speaking of restraint as though restraint were a garment they could put on for witnesses and remove after dark.
He thought of the Bleeding Crown.
The words rose unbidden, dangerous as smoke beneath a door. His claim to it had never been acknowledged. That was the shape of his life: a truth kept beneath the tongue until it tasted like metal. He had been born in 255 AS, into a world that had no use for the child he was and too much use for the weapon he became.
No crown had ever been placed upon his head.
Still, crowns cast shadows.
“What do they want from you?” Brannoc asked.
Korvath blinked. “Who?”
“The people who gave you this.”
“They want it carried.”
“By you?”
“By someone not yet dead.”
“That is not the same as being trusted.”
“No one trusts me.”
“Then why give you the message?”
“Because I can cross a border without belonging to it.”
Brannoc returned to the table. He unfolded the oilskin.
Inside was a page of cramped writing, the ink blurred in places by damp. He read the first line, then the second. The handwriting was disciplined, almost elegant. It listed provisions, withdrawals, sealed instructions, and a transfer of coin described without sentiment. The sum was written clearly.
He did not say it aloud.
Numbers were hooks. Speak them and they lodged in memory.
At the bottom, beneath a smear of black, appeared the mark cut into the metal.
Three angled strokes bound by a fourth.
Brannoc read the page again.
“Where did you get this?”
Korvath lowered his hood. His hair was plastered to his brow. “From a room beneath the eastern quarter.”
“That place is watched.”
“It was.”
“By whom?”
“Men who are now dead.”
“Yours?”
“Some.”
Brannoc folded the page. “You killed them.”
“I moved past them.”
“Do not mistake my contempt for ignorance.”
Korvath’s eyes sharpened. “You think this changes the accord?”
“It changes what men believe it was.”
“Belief is all that keeps most fortresses standing.”
“Stone keeps them standing.”
“Until men decide to open the gates.”
The words settled between them.
Beyond the door, boots passed. Slow. Then slower. The guards were listening, or pretending not to. Brannoc imagined the corridor: damp flagstones, hooded lamps, hands near sword hilts. He imagined the message leaving this chamber in another man’s pocket, then another’s, until the truth became a weapon with no owner.
Korvath said, “There is more.”
“There is always more when a smuggler begins with a warning.”
“The withdrawal was not the end of the payment.”
Brannoc looked up.
Korvath placed both hands upon the table, mirroring Brannoc’s earlier posture. “The losing commander was bribed to withdraw. That was the first bargain. The second was made afterward.”
“With whom?”
“I do not know.”
“Who does?”
Korvath swallowed. “The man who keeps the names.”
“And where is he?”
A shape moved beneath the door.
Not a shadow. A pause.
Brannoc’s hand closed around the knife.
Korvath saw it and stepped back, but too late to hide his fear. The candle shuddered. The rain pressed its many fingers against the shutters. Somewhere in the dark beyond the chamber, metal whispered free of a sheath.
Brannoc lifted the strip of cloth and slipped the bone into his palm.
“Stand behind me,” he said.
Korvath gave a humorless smile. “I have survived this long without standing behind anyone.”
“Then tonight will be an education.”
The latch began to turn.
The latch rose.
Brannoc moved before the door opened. He caught Korvath by the collar and drove him behind the bedstead, where the darkness was thickest and the damp straw gave no room for protest. The smuggler’s breath struck his knuckles, hot and sour with fear.
“Quiet,” Brannoc said.
“I was not—”
“Quiet.”
The door eased inward.
Rain breathed through the gap. A figure stood beyond it, wrapped in a cloak that had drunk the weather black. No face showed beneath the hood. One hand remained outside, hidden by the fold of the garment. The other held a narrow blade with no shine upon it.
Brannoc kept the knife low beside his thigh. The bone lay concealed in his palm, its edges biting into the old scars there. He had expected an assassin. He had not expected the room to feel as if the assassin had been expected by the room itself.
The stranger stepped inside.
Water fell from the cloak in patient drops. The candle flame bent away.
“Brannoc Ironmere,” the figure said.
The voice was neither young nor old. It had been scraped clean of every quality that might later be remembered.
Brannoc’s thumb passed over the knife’s hilt. “You know my name.”
“I know several names.”
“Then you are the man who keeps them.”
Behind him, Korvath stopped breathing.
The stranger shut the door. The latch settled with a soft click, as final as a stone placed over a grave.
“Who sent you?” Brannoc asked.
“Does the question matter?”
“It matters to the man deciding whether to kill you.”
“Then I was sent by the man who understands that decision.”
A small answer, shaped to waste time. Brannoc had heard its like in war tents, at gates before dawn, in the mouths of captains who had mistaken delay for command. He shifted his weight. The floorboards creaked beneath his boot.
The stranger’s blade angled toward the sound.
Fast, then. Not merely careful.
Brannoc glanced at the hood. No ornament. No seal. A strip of gray cloth had been wound twice around the stranger’s wrist, its end stiff with wax. The Silent Choir favored silence as other powers favored iron or blood, but silence alone proved nothing. The Iron-Ring Cartel bought disguises by the cartload. House Morvain had servants who could enter a room as if they had been born there. The Ashen Vanguard called secrecy a vice until secrecy became useful. And the Bleeding Crown—if the crown still possessed anything worth concealing—had made a religion of hidden knives.
“Take off the hood,” Brannoc said.
The stranger did not move.
“Or I take it off for you.”
“Your hand is already occupied.”
Brannoc felt the bone against his palm.
Korvath made a noise behind the bedstead. Not a word. Not quite a sob.
The stranger’s head turned toward it.
Brannoc crossed the room in one step.
His knife struck the stranger’s wrist. Not deep. Deep enough. The narrow blade clattered across the floor as the cloaked figure recoiled, and Brannoc seized the front of the garment with his free hand. He drove the stranger backward into the door. Wood shuddered. The candle gave a weak flare.
The hood fell.
The face beneath it was pale and ordinary. That was its first horror. Brannoc had killed men with faces made for songs, men whose scars proclaimed whole campaigns, men whose eyes burned with the private madness of those who believed the gods had chosen them. This face offered nothing. It could have belonged to a clerk, a pilgrim, a grave-robber, a servant carrying ash from one hearth to another.
Blood threaded from the cut at the wrist.
“Who sent you?” Brannoc said again.
The stranger smiled with only one side of the mouth.
“Not sent.”
Brannoc tightened his grip.
“Then what are you?”
“Late.”
Something struck the shutters from outside.
Korvath surged up. “They’ve found us.”
Brannoc shoved the stranger aside and seized the fallen blade. Its metal was cold enough to numb his fingers. He crossed to the window and lifted the shutter a finger’s width.
The street below was a wash of rain and black stone. No lanterns. No figures. Beyond the crooked roofs, the highland night descended in layers, each darker than the last. He saw movement near the alley mouth: a shape passing between walls, then another. They did not hurry. Hurrying belonged to fear.
Korvath stood beside the bed, clutching the bone as if it had grown there.
“How many?” Brannoc asked.
“I do not know.”
“Who does?”
“The man who keeps the names.”
Brannoc turned. “You said you did not know where he was.”
“I said I did not know who did.”
The stranger had recovered the knife. Blood ran down the hand, but the fingers held steady.
“Put it down,” Brannoc said.
“You have one already.”
“I have yours.”
“You have what you think is mine.”
The stranger looked at the bone in Korvath’s grip. For the first time, something altered in that empty face. Not fear. Recognition, perhaps. Or hunger.
Brannoc saw it and understood that the piece of bone was not a token, not a message, not merely proof of an old bargain. It was a door that could be carried.
“Give it to me,” he said to Korvath.
The smuggler stared.
“Now.”
“You said—”
“I have changed my mind.”
Korvath’s hand closed around it. “That is a dangerous habit.”
“So is surviving.”
A second impact struck the shutters. This time the iron latch jumped.
The stranger moved toward the room’s only other exit.
Brannoc barred the way.
The stranger’s eyes flicked to him. “If they enter, they will not ask questions.”
“Neither will I.”
“That is why you are useful.”
“I am not useful to anyone.”
The words came harder than he intended. They hung between them, larger than the room. Brannoc had spent years making himself into a weapon without a maker, a blade with no crest upon the hilt. Men called him the Red-Handed because they preferred an epithet to an explanation. They saw the blood and invented the rest.
The stranger studied him as though reading a line written beneath the skin.
“You were born for a throne,” they said.
Korvath’s face changed.
Brannoc felt the old wound open—not in flesh, but somewhere behind the ribs where no surgeon could reach. The Bleeding Crown had never spoken his name. It had not needed to. Crowns had ways of denying their own blood while profiting from it.
“Careful,” Brannoc said.
“You are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
The rain seemed to retreat from the shutters.
Korvath whispered, “Brannoc.”
Brannoc struck the stranger across the mouth.
The blow snapped the head aside. A red line appeared at the lip. The stranger laughed once, softly, without pleasure.
“Say it again,” Brannoc said.
“You will have to kill me.”
“That was not the question.”
The door trembled beneath a fist from the other side.
Korvath backed toward the wall. “We need to leave.”
Brannoc did not look at him. “There is nowhere to go.”
“There is always somewhere.”
“That is a smuggler’s prayer.”
“It has kept me alive.”
“For how long?”
Korvath’s gaze slid to the stranger. “Long enough to know when a room is already buried.”
The fist struck again. A splinter jumped from the door.
The stranger wiped blood from their mouth and touched it to the strip of gray cloth around the wrist. Wax softened beneath the warmth. A seal emerged, not pressed into the cloth but hidden within it: a mark of three lines bound together, each line broken before it reached the next.
Brannoc had seen the sign before, scratched into crates that carried grain through Crookvale, carved beneath a table in Fenspire, burned into the dead eyes of a courier found in a ditch. It belonged to no single power. That was what made it feared.
“The names are not kept in a book,” the stranger said.
Brannoc raised the blade.
“Where, then?”
“In the Edge of Gloamreach.”
The title entered the chamber like a breath from a crypt. Korvath flinched.
Brannoc had heard of the grimoire in the mouths of men who wished to sound wiser than death. A book for twilight bargains. A book that demanded an attunement cost of 46. A book whose pages were said to remember what the living had paid to forget.
“You expect me to believe that?”
“No.”
“Then why tell me?”
“Because belief is not required.”
The door cracked.
A blade came through the split, searching blindly.
Korvath cried out and threw himself aside. Brannoc caught the stranger by the throat and hauled them toward the window. The blade in his hand remained poised beneath the jaw.
“Open it,” he said.
“To the rain?”
“To the drop.”
The stranger looked down. The ground waited below in darkness.
“Your grip is not strong enough.”
Brannoc pressed harder.
The stranger’s smile returned. “Not yet.”
The door burst inward.
Rain blew across the room. A shape entered low, armored in dark leather, followed by another behind it. Brannoc saw only fragments: a wet sleeve, a hooked weapon, the pale glimmer of teeth. Korvath shouted something lost beneath the thunder.
Brannoc shoved the stranger through the window.
For an instant the hooded figure hung outside, one hand gripping the sill. The other caught Brannoc’s wrist.
The touch was cold.
“Come to the place where the Thrice-Bound Edge was forged,” the stranger said.
Brannoc looked into that empty face.
“Where?”
But the fingers released him.
The stranger fell.
Brannoc turned as the first intruder crossed the room. He cut upward, felt the blade bite cloth and flesh, and stepped inside the attacker’s reach. The second came at him from the side. Korvath seized a stool and smashed it against the figure’s knees. Wood broke. The attacker buckled.
Brannoc drove his elbow into the first assailant’s throat.
Someone screamed.
The candle went out.
In the dark, hands found him. One closed around his coat. Another scraped across his back. Brannoc fought by pressure and breath, by the wet sound of bodies colliding, by the old arithmetic of violence. He felt the bone slip from Korvath’s grasp. It struck the floor and rolled beneath the bedstead.
“Brannoc!” Korvath shouted.
A new voice answered from the doorway.
“Give us the heir.”
Brannoc stood amid the dark with blood warm on his knuckles and the stolen blade rising in his hand.
“No,” he said.
Then the voice outside spoke his secret name.
The word entered him more cleanly than the blade.
For one breath Brannoc forgot the room, the men crouched within it, the open door breathing cold upon his face. The secret name belonged to a place of ash and locked doors, to a voice that had never risen above a whisper. It had been spoken over him before he could understand speech. Spoken again when he learned that some bloodlines were knives best kept sheathed.
No living tongue had used it since.
Korvath made a sound behind him—not fear. Recognition.
Brannoc turned his head by a fraction. “You knew?”
“I knew a name,” Korvath said. His voice had gone thin. “Not who carried it.”
The man in the doorway stepped through the dark. A shutter shifted somewhere beyond him, admitting a blade of moonless grey. It touched the edge of his face, then failed to reveal anything useful: a hood, a scarf, hands hidden in dark gloves. There were others behind him. Brannoc heard their breathing, disciplined and patient.
The men on the floor began to move.
He stamped on one wrist. Bone cracked beneath his heel.
The man did not cry out. That frightened Brannoc more than any scream.
“Leave Korvath,” said the hooded stranger. “He is not the purpose of this.”
Korvath laughed once, without humor. “A comforting distinction.”
Brannoc kept the stolen blade angled toward the doorway. Its edge trembled—not from fear, but because his hand had taken too many blows in too little time. Blood ran from his knuckles and darkened the hilt.
“Who sent you?”
“The question is already answered.”
“House Morvain?”
The hood gave no sign.
“The Ashen Vanguard?”
Nothing.
“The Silent Choir?”
At that, one of the hidden men shifted. Cloth brushed leather. A small sound, but the dark was full of small betrayals.
Brannoc saw the movement and filed it away.
“Or the Iron-Ring Cartel,” he said. “They buy quieter men than you.”
“Names are a luxury for those with time.”
“Then you’ve come poorly supplied.”
The stranger tilted his head. “You have the temper of the Bleeding Crown.”
The words did not strike as the secret name had struck. They sank deeper.
Korvath swore under his breath.
Brannoc felt the old pressure in his chest, the one he had spent his life mistaking for anger. It was the body’s memory of a door barred from the inside. A cradle emptied before anyone could ask whose child had slept there. A hand withdrawing from his hair. A woman’s voice saying, Never let them see what you are.
The Bleeding Crown had been a story told by enemies and courtiers, by drunk soldiers and dying men. It was a power, a wound, a thing that wore gold only when gold could not be refused. Brannoc had carried its shadow without ever touching its throne.
“I have the temper of a starving dog,” he said. “You should not confuse the two.”
The stranger looked past him toward Korvath. “The heir must come with us.”
“Which heir?” Korvath asked.
The hooded face turned slightly.
Korvath’s courage had always possessed the brittle quality of glass. It shone until pressure found it. Now the smuggler stood among overturned furniture and broken bodies, his hands raised, his mouth wet with blood, and tried to make a shield of mockery.
“You’ve entered a rented room,” he said. “You’ve broken half the furniture. You’ve failed to kill the captain you came for. If you mean to conduct a kidnapping, perhaps begin by identifying the merchandise.”
The stranger lifted one gloved hand.
The men on the floor rose.
The first came at Brannoc low. He caught the man by the collar and drove him into the bedstead. The frame groaned. The second struck from the side. Brannoc turned, took the blow along his ribs, and answered with the hilt of the stolen blade.
The man’s teeth clicked together.
A third entered through the doorway.
Too many.
Brannoc felt the room narrowing around him. He had fought in alleys, stairwells, courtyards slick with rain and courtyards slick with worse. A room could be conquered if it had corners. This one had only bodies, shadows, and Korvath breathing behind him like a man trying not to drown.
“Get the bone,” Korvath said.
Brannoc did not look at him.
“It’s under the bed.”
“I heard you.”
“It may be useful.”
“Then fetch it.”
“I am occupied.”
The third attacker swung. Brannoc ducked, seized the wrist, and twisted until the shoulder came loose with a soft, hideous pop. He shoved the man backward into another. They fell together, snarling.
Korvath lunged for the bed.
The hooded stranger crossed the room with impossible calm.
Brannoc saw him only at the edge of sight: a dark shape passing through violence as if violence had agreed to make way. He moved toward Korvath, not quickly, but without hesitation. That was the mark of a trained killer—not speed, but the certainty that speed would not be required.
Brannoc went after him.
The stolen blade caught the stranger beneath the ribs.
Or should have.
Something turned the point aside. The impact jarred Brannoc’s wrist. Beneath the stranger’s coat, metal rang with a note too pure for ordinary armor.
Regalia.
The Thrice-Bound Edge, forged in 123 AS, had been described to Brannoc by men who lied for coin and by one woman who had not. They had called it regalia, though no one agreed whether it was worn, carried, or endured. He had never seen it. Yet the sound beneath his blade was the sound of an old promise refusing to break.
The stranger seized Brannoc’s forearm.
Pain flashed white.
Brannoc head-butted him.
The hood snapped back. For an instant Brannoc saw a mouth, bloodless and narrow, and eyes that seemed to hold no reflection of the room.
Then Korvath shouted.
Brannoc wrenched free and turned.
Korvath had the bone in one hand. He held it as though it were a key. The men nearest him had stopped. Even the hooded stranger had gone still.
The bone was not large. It was not beautiful. Age had yellowed it, and one end bore a dark stain that no washing had lifted. Yet the air around it seemed to draw inward. The candlewick, though extinguished, smoked toward Korvath’s fist.
“What is that?” Brannoc demanded.
Korvath’s eyes remained fixed on the bone. “You told me it was yours.”
“I told you to hide it.”
“You did not tell me what it opened.”
“Put it down.”
The hooded stranger extended his hand. “Give it to me.”
Korvath’s fingers closed.
A sound came from the walls.
Not a voice. Not a groan of settling timber. It was the faintest susurrus, a pressure against the ear, as though unseen mouths had begun to sing beneath the stone.
The Silent Choir.
Brannoc had heard tales. Every captain heard tales. The Choir moved through cities without banners, without drums, without even the courtesy of leaving corpses where they could be counted. Their prayers were said in rooms where names had been scraped from the walls. Their silence was not the absence of speech. It was speech stripped of mercy.
The room seemed to listen.
Korvath looked at Brannoc. “You should have told me.”
“I should have killed you when I met you.”
“Perhaps. But you did not.”
The words landed between them with the weight of a confession neither man intended.
The hooded stranger moved.
Brannoc threw himself sideways. A thin blade whispered through the space where his throat had been. He seized a chair and broke it across the attacker’s arm. The stranger staggered. Korvath slipped behind the bed, clutching the bone.
“Window,” Brannoc said.
Korvath glanced toward it. “We are above the ground.”
“Then pray.”
“I have never found it reliable.”
A blade struck the shutters. Wood split. Cold air entered, carrying the smell of wet stone and distant ash.
Brannoc drove one attacker into the wall and took his knife. The knife was narrow and badly balanced, meant for the ribs rather than the fight. He used it anyway. A cut opened along the man’s sleeve. Blood shone black in the dimness.
“Who is the heir?” Brannoc demanded.
The stranger did not answer.
Brannoc caught the next blow on his forearm. The impact numbed his hand. He drove his knee upward, felt something tear, and shoved the man aside.
“Who is the heir?”
The stranger raised his face.
“The one who survives this room.”
Beyond the doorway, more feet gathered.
Brannoc heard armor. He heard the scrape of iron rings. He heard someone outside give a low command, and the men within shifted to obey.
The Iron-Ring Cartel, then—or men who wished to be mistaken for them. It hardly mattered. In the Ashen Era, allegiance was often only the name a blade gave its owner before it entered you.
Korvath reached the broken shutters.
He looked down.
Brannoc saw calculation move through him: distance, darkness, the likelihood of bones breaking, the greater likelihood of being taken alive. The smuggler’s face tightened.
“Go,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s gaze cut back. “And you?”
“I am the merchandise.”
“That is not what they said.”
“No. It is what they believe.”
The hooded stranger stepped over the fallen men. “Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
Hearing the full name spoken there, in that cramped room with blood beneath his boots, was worse than hearing the secret one. The epithet had always belonged to other mouths. Soldiers had given it to him. Enemies had polished it. Now it sounded like a summons.
The stranger spoke again, and this time the name beneath the name passed through the room.
Brannoc felt the old door open.
He remembered a hand pressing two fingers to his brow. Remembered the smell of smoke. Remembered being told that if anyone ever called him by that name, he must run—not toward safety, but away from everyone who offered it.
The men surged.
Korvath leapt through the shutters.
Brannoc seized the nearest attacker by the throat and dragged him into the path of the others. Steel struck steel. Someone cursed. The secret name still rang inside him, opening chambers he had buried beneath years of hired blood and cold campfires.
He could not run.
Not yet.
The hooded stranger came through the confusion, reaching not for the blade, not for Brannoc’s throat, but for the place beneath his collar where the old scar lay hidden.
Brannoc caught his wrist.
For the first time, the stranger’s composure broke.
“You know what I am,” Brannoc said.
“I know what you will become.”
The room fell silent around those words.
Far below, Korvath struck the ground. Wood shattered. Then came the sound of him running.
Brannoc tightened his grip until the stranger’s glove creaked.
“And what is that?”
The stranger leaned close. His breath smelled of bitter herbs and old iron.
“The last crown before the ashes take it.”
A shape moved beyond the broken doorway. Not a man. Not quite. A book opened somewhere in the dark, its pages turning though no wind entered.
On the floor, beneath the bedstead, something answered with a dull metallic pulse.
Brannoc looked down.
The bone was no longer in Korvath’s hand.
It lay beside his boot, warm as living flesh.
Chapter 3
I died in 300 AS with iron in my mouth and the Accord of Mournthrone still gnawing at the realm.
The dead did not sleep.
They waited beneath the weather.
At Vharencrag Fortress, the snow fell upward.
It lifted from the broken courtyards in pale threads, dragging ash and splinters with it, and vanished into the low black clouds. Brannoc watched from the gatehouse where no living sentry stood. He had been standing there since the bells stopped. Or since his heart stopped. The difference had become difficult to keep.
Below, the fortress endured its own ruin. Towers leaned toward one another like conspirators. The walls were split by old sorcery, their stones fused into glass along the seams. In the yard, men of the Ashen Vanguard carried lengths of chain through the snow. Their victory had been named, though victory seemed a poor word for a place where the dead still shouted from under the flagstones.
The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS and ended in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.
Brannoc had heard the sentence spoken by a clerk with clean hands.
He had heard it in a chamber where the walls were warm and the wine was red, while the clerk’s quill scratched across a page. The words had possessed the smug finality of a sealed tomb. Yet the fighting had waged at Vharencrag Fortress in 301 AS, and the fortress had not learned that it was finished.
Neither had he.
“Captain.”
The voice came from below.
Brannoc looked down through the arrow slit. A man stood in the courtyard with a hood drawn low over his face. He carried no sword that showed itself, no badge, no banner. His boots were too clean for a soldier and too worn for a courtier.
Korvath Nightbrook, a Smuggler.
Even in death, Brannoc recognized the careful shape of a man who expected every door to be barred and every guard to be bought.
“You are late,” Brannoc said.
His voice descended without sound. Korvath lifted his head all the same.
“Dead men are difficult to find.”
“I was not difficult. I was here.”
“You were a rumor.” Korvath glanced toward the western wall. “Rumors do not open gates.”
“They do when the gate has no hinges.”
Korvath’s mouth tightened. He had brought a narrow case beneath his cloak. Brannoc smelled wax, old leather, and the faint mineral stink of magic. The case had been sealed three times. The seals bore no crest that Brannoc knew.
He knew the weight of certain secrets. They settled in the hand like knives.
“Bring it up,” Brannoc said.
Korvath did not move.
The dead had no authority over the living. That was one of the first lessons Brannoc had learned after the iron entered him. The living continued to obey banners, coin, hunger, lust, and fear. The dead possessed only memory, and memory could not close a fist.
Below, a torch guttered. The men of the Ashen Vanguard passed through the yard without seeing him. Their armor was gray with salt and snow. Their banner hung limp from the ruined keep, its cloth blackened by the Sundering’s old weather.
“Who sent you?” Brannoc asked.
Korvath looked at the fortress.
“Everyone who wants the war to end.”
“Then you have been sent by no one.”
“Not no one.”
“House Morvain?”
Korvath’s silence was answer enough to make the dead colder.
Brannoc turned from the slit. The chamber behind him had no roof. Snow drifted across the floor and through the place where his body had once fallen. He remembered the body clearly: the leather torn at the shoulder, the blood soaking the stones, the hand that had made him famous lying open beside him.
The Red-Handed.
They had called him that before they knew whose blood had marked him. They had called him that after. The name had served better than any sigil. A Sellsword Captain required little more than a blade, a company, and men willing to believe he would be the last one standing.
He had been born in 255 AS.
He had been the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Neither fact had purchased him a father’s name.
Korvath climbed the stair. His steps made no echo. At the top, he stopped before Brannoc, and for a moment the living man’s face seemed to lose its edges.
“Your blood has been hidden,” Korvath said.
“Not well.”
“Better than you think.”
“The Crown has never wanted me.”
“The Crown does not want. People want. The Crown merely gives them a shape to kill for.”
Brannoc looked at the case.
“Open it.”
Korvath drew a small blade and cut the wax. Within lay a dark volume wrapped in oilskin. Its cover was ridged, its corners worn smooth by handling. No title had been written across it, yet Brannoc knew the name before the wrappings came away.
Edge of Gloamreach.
The grimoire breathed once.
Brannoc felt the pull of it through the empty place where his ribs had been. Attunement cost: 46. The number had been written in a margin by a hand too frightened to finish its sentence. He had never touched the book while alive. Now its pages stirred toward him as though they remembered a hand that had not yet claimed them.
“Why bring this to me?” he asked.
Korvath’s gaze remained on the grimoire. “Because the living have begun to fear what the dead know.”
“I know that men lie.”
“You know who paid.”
The wind moved through the chamber. Snow gathered in the shape of a shoulder beside Brannoc, then collapsed.
He remembered the commander.
Not the face. Faces were treacherous things in memory. He remembered the commander’s glove resting on a map. He remembered a purse placed beside the inkpot. He remembered the soft sound of coin shifting against coin while men died beyond the walls.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
That hidden truth had survived beneath the official account, buried under speeches and ash. The Accord’s collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals, and every reprisal carried the taste of that payment.
Korvath reached for the grimoire.
Brannoc caught his wrist.
The living man cried out.
His fingers closed on nothing, yet Korvath’s arm jerked as if seized by iron. Brannoc felt warmth rush through the contact, the fierce, bright animal of a pulse. It angered him. It reminded him of all the things death had taken without asking.
“Do not touch it,” Brannoc said.
Korvath stared at his own wrist. A red mark had appeared there, five narrow lines pressed into the skin.
“The Red-Handed,” he whispered.
“Names are ropes. Be careful what you hang from them.”
Below, the gates groaned.
Brannoc released him.
Voices rose in the courtyard. The Ashen Vanguard had found the lower passage. Their soldiers shouted to one another, and the sound climbed the fortress in waves. Somewhere beneath the stone, something answered with a slow scraping.
Korvath wrapped the grimoire again.
“You cannot carry that through the garrison.”
“There is no garrison here.”
“Not now.”
Brannoc looked toward the east, beyond the shattered walls and the white emptiness. The Gloaming Reach lay there, dim beneath a sky without dawn. Fenspire stood within it, founded in 57 AS, a core location held under permanent military occupation. Its garrison strength was 3742.
He had once received the figure from a quartermaster who would rather have swallowed a nail than speak it aloud. Three thousand seven hundred and forty-two soldiers beneath one stark spire, watching the dark as if discipline could hold back the night.
“Take the book to Fenspire,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s guarded expression hardened. “That is not a smuggler’s road.”
“It is not a road at all.”
“Then why send me?”
“Because you are a Smuggler.”
“I have a name.”
“Korvath Nightbrook.”
The name seemed to trouble the air. Brannoc had no right to know it, and yet the dead kept what the living discarded.
Korvath tucked the case beneath his cloak. “What will I find there?”
“Men who believe the war ended.”
“The war ended.”
“No.”
“The Accord ended.”
“Words end. Hunger does not.”
A figure moved beyond the arrow slit.
Brannoc turned.
For one breath, the chamber filled with regalia: a blade suspended in black cloth, three bindings circling its hilt, each one tighter than the last. The Thrice-Bound Edge, forged in 123 AS. Its defining record contained no attunement cost. It did not glow. It did not sing. It merely waited with the patient silence of a vow.
Then the vision was gone.
Korvath had seen it. His face had become bloodless.
“What was that?”
“Something that does not belong to you.”
“Does it belong to you?”
Brannoc looked at his hands.
The epithet had outlived the flesh that gave it meaning. He could still see the blood there, though no blood remained. He had no canonical features to offer the world, no face for statues or painted histories. Only the red hands. Only the station. Only the claim that had never been spoken before the Bleeding Crown.
“It belongs to whoever survives the binding,” he said.
The lower door burst inward.
Ashen Vanguard soldiers flooded the stairwell. Their steel flashed. Korvath stumbled backward, clutching the case. Brannoc stepped between them, though he knew the living could not see him.
The first soldier raised a crossbow.
Brannoc remembered the moment before death: the shape of the bolt, the silence inside his chest, the knowledge that no banner would bend for him. He remembered dying during the Accord of Mournthrone in 300 AS. He remembered the world continuing without permission.
Now the crossbowman fired.
The bolt passed through Brannoc and struck Korvath in the shoulder.
Korvath fell against the wall. The case dropped. Its seals broke.
The Edge of Gloamreach opened by itself.
Every flame in Vharencrag Fortress went out.
From the courtyard came a roar—not of men, but of stone tearing loose from stone. The fortress lurched beneath them. Somewhere far below, a bell began to ring, though no hand remained to pull its rope.
Brannoc seized the grimoire as the pages turned.
On the first page, ink crawled into a single line.
The Accord of Mournthrone was waged at Vharencrag Fortress in 301 AS.
The letters darkened.
Behind him, the soldiers screamed. Korvath dragged himself toward the fallen case. Beyond the broken wall, the snow was rising higher, carrying voices from every road that led toward Fenspire, Crookvale, the High Spires, the Bleeding Crown, the Iron-Ring Cartel, the Silent Choir, House Morvain—
And beneath them all, beneath the Ashen Vanguard’s shouted commands, another voice spoke from the opened book.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
He bent over the page.
The dead fortress drew breath.
“Choose,” it said, and the stones beneath his feet began to—
move.
Not the stones beneath his boots. The fortress.
Its walls leaned inward with the slow, dreadful patience of a man listening at a door. Mortar sifted from the joints. Snow spilled through the broken roof and vanished before touching the floor, each flake taken by the dark beneath the flagstones.
Brannoc kept one hand on the open book.
The leather was cold enough to burn. Its cover bore no title, but the page before him named it in a thin, crowded hand.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Below that, in a smaller script:
Attunement cost: 46.
The number trembled.
“Choose what?” Brannoc asked.
The voice came from the grimoire, though its lips were ink and its breath was the smell of wet ash.
“Blood.”
His fingers tightened against the page. Behind him, Korvath made a wet sound and tried to rise. The smuggler’s boots scraped uselessly over the stone. He had lost his blade somewhere in the snow. One hand clutched his side; the other reached toward Brannoc with the blind insistence of a drowning man.
“Don’t touch it,” Korvath said.
Brannoc looked back. The broken wall had sealed itself with darkness. No snow came through now. No soldiers screamed. The fortress had swallowed every sound except Korvath’s breathing and the slow grinding of its foundations.
“You know the book?”
“I know enough.”
“You serve at Fenthrone,” Brannoc said. “You know enough to tell me what it wants.”
Korvath’s eyes widened. Fear made them bright, almost childlike. “Korvath Nightbrook serves at Fenthrone,” he whispered, as if the words were a password that might open the world again. “That’s all. That is all I am.”
The stone shifted beneath him. His palm slid across the floor, leaving a dark smear.
Brannoc turned back to the page.
A second line had appeared.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed. Born in 255 AS.
The ink gathered at the final mark and ran downward like blood from a nail.
He had heard men speak his epithet in taverns, at campfires, in the muttering silence before a charge. They had made the Red-Handed into a warning, a blessing, a jest for those who had never seen what a captain became when the work was done and the dead still looked up at him.
The book knew his name without being told.
That was worse than any blade.
A third line formed.
Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
The words did not lie. That was their cruelty.
Brannoc felt the old wound open beneath his ribs, though no sword had entered him. The claim had lived in him like a second spine, hard and secret. Men had died for less than a rumor of it. Others had offered him banners, promises, sealed letters whose wax bore no mark he could trust. He had burned them all. A crown was only a collar with better language.
Korvath crawled another handspan.
“The Crown?” he said. “You knew?”
“Knew what?”
“That it would call you.”
“I have been called by better things.”
The fortress groaned. A seam split the floor between them. Pale light shone below—not firelight, not moonlight, but the color of old metal held beneath water.
The book’s pages began to turn without wind.
One page showed a sword bound three times in black cord.
The Thrice-Bound Edge. Regalia forged in 123 AS.
The image was so precise Brannoc could see the grain of the grip, the small nicks along the guard, the dark binding drawn tight as sinew. It conveyed no promise of power. No hunger. Only restraint.
The next page was a map, though the roads crawled as he watched.
The High Spires rose in serrated strokes. Crookvale crouched among them, rebuilt in crooked lines, its hard walls bristling above a garrison of 1004. Beneath the name, the book wrote:
Founded in 295 AS. Outside the core holdings.
Brannoc pressed his thumb into the margin. The map recoiled from his touch.
A distant horn sounded.
Korvath flinched. “They’re coming.”
“Who?”
The smuggler glanced at the sealed wall. “All of them.”
The words stirred the fortress. The map darkened, and a spire appeared in the Gloaming Reach, stark against a field of gray.
Fenspire. Founded in 57 AS. Garrisoned.
The number beneath it remained black and unchanging.
3742.
Brannoc saw the walls of Fenspire in his mind: disciplined ranks, watchfires burning without warmth, gates that opened only to those already expected. A core holding. A place that had made vigilance into stone.
Then the page tore itself down the middle.
On one half, the Ashen Vanguard marched beneath a sky the color of bruised iron.
On the other, House Morvain’s shadow stretched across a field of dead snow.
The Silent Choir stood where the horizon should have been, faces hidden beneath pale veils. The Iron-Ring Cartel’s mark appeared as a circle of black links. The Bleeding Crown burned without flame.
Five powers. Five hungers. None of them had room for a man who belonged to all their histories and none of their tables.
“Close it,” Korvath said.
Brannoc tried.
The cover would not move.
The voice rose from the binding. “The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.”
The stones beneath Brannoc’s boots rolled like a living back.
“The Accord ended in 301 AS.”
A crack opened near Korvath’s knee. He caught its edge with both hands.
“The Ashen Vanguard was named victor.”
The words struck the fortress, and the fortress remembered.
For an instant Brannoc saw Vharencrag Fortress whole: towers unbroken, banners stiff in the wind, the black teeth of its battlements rising above ranks of men. He saw no faces. The vision denied him faces. It showed only hands signing, hands counting, hands passing sealed pouches beneath a table while a losing commander stood beyond a curtain and turned away.
The truth had no trumpet. It had the quiet sound of coin settling into a palm.
Then the vision collapsed.
Brannoc was on one knee.
Korvath stared at him. “What did you see?”
“An accord.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“It is what you received.”
