The smuggler’s mouth worked. He looked toward the book, and something in him hardened—not courage, precisely, but the shape courage left when stripped of hope.
“My orders were to bring it to Fenthrone.”
“Who gave them?”
Korvath said nothing.
The Edge of Gloamreach turned another page.
A line appeared in red.
Died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.
Brannoc read it twice.
The second time, the fortress vanished.
He stood beneath a colorless sky. Snow lay over the ground without covering it. His blood marked a path behind him, though he could not feel the wound that had spilled it. Before him waited a throne made of blackened roots—or perhaps ribs. The shape changed whenever he tried to fix his eyes upon it.
At his right hand, the Thrice-Bound Edge rested in the snow.
At his left, the grimoire hovered open.
Between them stood a crown.
The Bleeding Crown was not a thing of metal. It was a circle of red light suspended at the height of a man’s brow, dripping upward into the sky.
Brannoc heard voices beyond the white emptiness.
The Ashen Vanguard called him commander.
House Morvain called him traitor.
The Silent Choir called him by no name at all.
The Iron-Ring Cartel offered terms.
The Bleeding Crown offered blood.
Behind every voice lay the same demand: kneel, and become useful.
He looked down at his hands. They were red to the wrists. Not with fresh blood. With old blood, dried into the creases, worked beneath the nails, carried through every oath he had broken and every oath he had kept for the wrong reason.
The voice of the book whispered beside him.
“Choose.”
“Between what?”
“Being claimed.”
The crown lowered.
Brannoc did not move.
He remembered men calling him bastard when they meant dangerous. He remembered the careful pauses around his name, the way a room measured him before deciding whether to laugh. He remembered the letters without signatures, the gifts without givers, the silences that had followed every question about his birth.
The crown drew nearer. Its red light warmed his face.
“You think I want this?” he asked.
The grimoire’s pages fluttered.
“No.”
“Then why show it to me?”
“Because you died before you chose.”
The snow beneath him cracked.
Brannoc turned toward the voice. There was no mouth, no shape, nothing but the black rectangle of the open book and the thin white pages turning in impossible wind.
“I died,” he said.
“Yes.”
“When?”
The page answered him.
300 AS.
His death stood there without ceremony. No battlefield. No final boast. No hand reaching to close his eyes. Only the year, exact and merciless.
He felt something inside him recoil—not from death, but from the indignity of being reduced to a line.
The fortress returned in pieces.
First the stone beneath his palm.
Then Korvath’s breath.
Then the snow, pouring through the broken wall again.
Korvath had reached the grimoire. His fingers hovered above the page, trembling.
“Don’t,” Brannoc said.
“I have to.”
“You serve at Fenthrone.”
“I serve where I’m paid.”
“Those are not the same thing.”
“They are when hunger is involved.”
The book’s ink crawled toward Korvath’s hand. The smuggler drew back, but not quickly enough. A black thread leapt from the page and wrapped around his wrist.
Korvath screamed.
The sound tore through the fortress. Outside, something answered from the snow.
Brannoc seized the thread.
Cold entered him.
Not cold like winter. Cold like a locked room in which someone had been waiting for him to arrive.
The page blazed.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The sword appeared in his grip.
It was heavier than memory, its three bindings drawn tight around the hilt. No blade showed, yet the air before him split from floor to ceiling. Beyond the cut lay Fenthrone—not its streets or walls, not any clear image, but a narrow passage crowded with doors.
Korvath stared into it, face drained of blood.
“Fenthrone,” he whispered.
The thread around his wrist tightened.
From beyond the first door came the muffled scrape of a bolt being drawn.
From beyond the second came the murmur of many voices speaking as one.
From beyond the third came the sound of a crown striking stone.
Brannoc felt the grimoire pulling him forward. The fortress leaned with it. Cracks raced across the ceiling. Snow streamed upward into the dark.
Korvath’s boots slid toward the opening.
“Captain,” he gasped.
Brannoc caught him by the collar.
The smuggler’s gaze locked on his. “If you go through, they’ll know.”
“Who?”
Korvath looked past him, toward the doors.
“The ones who paid the commander to withdraw.”
The book shuddered in Brannoc’s hand.
Behind the doors, a voice spoke his name.
Not the epithet. Not the title.
Only the name his mother had never allowed him to forget.
Brannoc raised the bound sword.
The first door began to open—
The first door opened inward.
No hand touched it. The hinges gave a long, wet groan, as if something on the other side had been forced to wake.
Beyond lay a corridor without walls. Snow drifted through it, though there was no wind. Pale stones hung in the blackness at differing distances, each one bearing a smear of red light. Brannoc saw no floor beneath them. He saw only the suggestion of one, a road remembered by the feet of the dead.
Korvath made a sound in his throat.
Brannoc tightened his grip on the collar of Korvath Nightbrook’s coat. “You said they paid the commander to withdraw.”
“I said they paid someone.”
“The commander.”
“The losing commander.” Korvath’s eyes remained fixed upon the open door. “There is a difference, if you mean to keep breathing.”
The voice behind the door spoke again.
“Brannoc Ironmere.”
The name entered him like a blade between the ribs. It did not come from the corridor. It came from the sword.
The bound hilt was cold against his palm. The Thrice-Bound Edge had been regalia forged in 123 AS, made to bind what kingdoms could not. It had no attunement cost. Brannoc had always thought that a lie told by dead craftsmen to flatter the living.
The sword was not free.
It had merely chosen not to charge him yet.
He drew it fully.
The blade emerged from its wrappings with a sound like a woman inhaling before a scream. Three dark bands crossed the steel. Beneath them, something moved, thin as ink beneath ice.
The grimoire bucked in his other hand.
“Put it down,” Korvath whispered.
“Tell it to me.”
“Put it down.”
“What is the cost?”
Korvath’s face had gone gray. “The Edge of Gloamreach has an attunement cost of 46.”
The number seemed to strike the air. The corridor shivered. One of the floating stones split, and from the crack poured a swarm of moths made from scraps of shadow.
Brannoc felt the grimoire’s hunger enter his wrist.
“Forty-six what?”
Korvath swallowed. “You know what.”
“I know nothing.”
“Lives. Names. Years. It takes what the bearer has spent and calls the debt paid.”
The book opened by itself.
Its pages were black, but the letters burned white across them. They formed no script Brannoc knew, yet he understood each word as it appeared.
BRANNOC IRONMERE THE RED-HANDED.
Below it:
BORN IN 255 AS.
The ink spread.
The next line did not form at once. It crawled across the page in trembling strokes, as though the book disliked the shape of what it must write.
UNACKNOWLEDGED HEIR TO THE BLEEDING CROWN.
Korvath looked at him then.
Not at the book. At him.
Brannoc’s fingers closed around the sword until the edges of the hilt bit through his glove. Somewhere in the fortress, stone fell in a heavy succession. The sound rolled toward them and stopped at the threshold.
“Say it,” Korvath said.
“Say what?”
“You heard it.”
Brannoc looked down at the page. “The book is a liar.”
“Books don’t lie.”
“Men write them.”
“And who wrote that?”
The white letters bled. The next line appeared.
DIED IN 300 AS DURING THE ACCORD OF MOURNTHRONE.
For a breath, Brannoc could not feel his hands.
Then he laughed.
It was not a pleasant sound. The corridor caught it and sent it outward, where it became the muttering of a crowd.
Korvath flinched. “What did you see?”
“My death.”
“Whose?”
Brannoc shut the grimoire. Its cover resisted. He forced it closed with both hands, and the leather gave beneath his palms like flesh.
“Mine.”
The door widened.
On the far side, shapes stood in a pale assembly. Figures in mail, in robes, in crowns that had been broken and soldered together again. Their faces were veiled by frost. Behind them, a throne leaned beneath a mountain of snow.
Mournthrone.
He had never seen it, but the name lived in the bones of every soldier who had marched beneath the Ashen Vanguard’s colors or against them. The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS. It had not yet begun, not here, not in this hour that smelled of old mortar and lamp oil, but the door showed it waiting.
The sword trembled.
A second line of writing appeared across its blade.
THE ACCORD OF MOURNTHRONE ENDED IN 301 AS WITH THE ASHEN VANGUARD NAMED VICTOR.
The words were not cut into the metal. They floated above it, red and bright.
Brannoc stared until the letters blurred.
“Then I am dead before it ends,” he said.
Korvath’s silence was answer enough.
The corridor beyond the door changed.
A fortress rose from the darkness, rebuilt stone upon ruined stone. Its towers were crooked, its walls black beneath a skin of snow. Banners hung limp along the battlements, though none bore a device Brannoc recognized.
“Crookvale,” Korvath whispered.
Brannoc had heard the name from caravans that came down out of the High Spires with frost in their beards and blood on their harness. A settlement founded in 295 AS. Rebuilt after whatever had broken it. A place outside the core holdings, where allegiance was a garment worn inside out.
The grimoire opened again.
The page showed the fortress from above. Then the words:
CROOKVALE WAS FOUNDED IN 295 AS IN THE HIGH SPIRES.
The image drew closer. Men watched from the walls. Their faces were hollow with vigilance. The garrison stood in ordered ranks beneath the gate.
GARRISON: 1004.
Korvath’s lips moved soundlessly as he counted nothing.
“Rebuilt,” he said.
The book printed the word beneath the number.
REBUILT.
Then:
OUTSIDE THE CORE HOLDINGS.
Brannoc felt a pressure behind his eyes. The vision of Crookvale did not seem distant. He could smell its snow, its chimney smoke, the iron tang of old blood caught in the mortar. A sentry turned his head toward him.
The sentry had no face.
Brannoc closed the book again.
This time it shut without resistance.
Behind them, the fortress doors began to move.
Not the outer doors. The ones deeper within. Something was coming through the halls.
Korvath released a breath. “We have to go.”
“Through the door?”
“Every other way is caved in.”
“Who paid the commander?”
“I don’t know.”
“You know enough to fear them.”
“I know enough to know that the payment was not coin.”
A sound came from the corridor beyond the threshold: a soft dragging, repeated at measured intervals. Metal across stone. A chain, perhaps. Or a blade.
Brannoc stepped forward.
Korvath seized his arm. “No.”
The smuggler’s grip was stronger than it looked. Brannoc could have broken it. He nearly did.
“Let go.”
“If they see you, they’ll call you by the blood-name.”
“I have no blood-name.”
“You have the Bleeding Crown in your veins.”
The words struck harder than the book had.
Brannoc turned his wrist. Korvath’s fingers loosened.
“No one has ever placed a crown on my head.”
“That is why you’re still alive.”
A low wind moved through the open door. It carried voices, hundreds of them, speaking from very far away.
The Ashen Vanguard.
House Morvain.
The Silent Choir.
The Iron-Ring Cartel.
The Bleeding Crown.
The five names rose and sank like drowned bells. Not armies, not houses, not factions—only hungers given banners. Brannoc had served beneath one and sold his sword against another. He had drunk with men who swore loyalty to three, and buried men who had sworn to all five.
The corridor gave him no side to choose.
On the page beneath his hand, another sentence formed.
THE COLLAPSE OF THE ACCORD UNLEASHED A DECADE OF GUERRILLA REPRISALS.
The letters remained after he read them.
A decade.
Not a battle’s aftermath. Not a season of vengeance. A decade.
He imagined villages emptied by night. Roads where every milestone bore a different corpse. Children learning the sound of boots before they learned the names of kings. He saw the Accord crumbling beneath its own signatures, while men called the ruin victory.
The grimoire wrote again.
THE LOSING COMMANDER WAS BRIBED TO WITHDRAW.
Korvath shut his eyes.
“There,” Brannoc said. “That is what you came to find.”
“I came to carry a message.”
“To whom?”
Korvath looked at the sword. “To the man who would one day make the message matter.”
Brannoc stepped closer. “Who sent you?”
The smuggler’s face twisted. Fear had finally stripped away its caution. Beneath it lay not loyalty but exhaustion, the dead weight of a man who had carried a secret until the secret had begun carrying him.
“I cannot say.”
“You can.”
“I cannot.”
Brannoc pressed the bound sword beneath Korvath’s jaw.
The blade did not touch skin. It did not need to.
“Say the name.”
Korvath stared at him. “You think a name will save you?”
“No.”
“Then why ask?”
“Because I am tired of being saved by men who refuse to speak.”
The chain dragged again in the corridor.
Closer.
The frost-veiled figures beyond the door turned toward Brannoc as one. Their heads bowed.
The throne beneath the mountain shifted.
A crown struck stone.
Once.
Then again.
The book slipped from Brannoc’s hand and landed open at his feet. The page was no longer black. It had become a mirror.
In it, he saw himself beneath falling snow.
He wore no crown. He held the sword. Blood covered both hands, though none of it appeared to be his. Behind him burned a fortress with crooked towers. Before him knelt a line of soldiers in Ashen Vanguard colors.
At his feet lay a dead man wearing Brannoc’s own face.
The reflection lifted its head.
Its lips moved.
Brannoc heard the words inside his skull.
You are not the heir because you will rule.
The chain stopped.
You are the heir because they must kill you.
Korvath whispered, “Brannoc.”
The voice from beyond the door spoke once more.
Not the name this time.
The title.
“Red-Handed.”
The Thrice-Bound Edge flared in his grip. Its three bindings split apart, revealing a darkness within the metal deeper than the corridor itself.
Brannoc raised the sword.
Korvath backed away, but there was nowhere left to go. Behind him, the inner doors stood open. Ahead waited the frost-veiled dead, the leaning throne, the future that had already written his death into its ledger.
The grimoire turned one final page.
At the top, a date appeared.
300 AS.
Beneath it, in letters so small he had to bend close to read them, was a single sentence.
THE HAND THAT OPENS THIS DOOR WILL BE THE HAND THAT CLOSES THE CROWN.
Brannoc reached for the threshold.
Something on the other side reached back.
Chapter 4
The bell beneath Fenspire had a voice like iron dragged across a grave.
It sounded once through the fog, and every man in the garrison of 3,742 lifted his head.
Brannoc heard it from the windowless chamber below the eastern tower, where damp crawled down the walls and gathered in the mortar like sweat. The sound came through stone diminished but not softened. It entered the ribs. It made the candle flames bow.
A bell for alarm would have rung twice. Three times meant blood. The old fortress had its own grammar, hammered into metal before the Gloaming Reach learned to fear its own shadows.
Brannoc rested both hands on the table and watched the wax run beneath the candle. The left hand was clean. The right was not.
The blood had dried in the creases of his palm, black beneath the amber light. He had tried the basin. The water had clouded red, then grey, then something the color of weak milk. A servant had taken it away without being told. Servants knew when to flee a room. That was why they lived longer than soldiers.
Across the table, Korvath Nightbrook sat with his hood drawn low. He was a smuggler by trade and by bearing: a narrow, unobtrusive man, made for passing through doors that had no business opening. His hands remained beneath the table.
“Again,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s gaze shifted toward the ceiling. “The bell has already spoken.”
“Then let it speak to you.”
The smuggler swallowed. “A rider came from the Reach.”
“Riders come.”
“This one came without a horse.”
The candle gave a little spit.
Brannoc looked at him. “That is supposed to frighten me?”
“No.” Korvath’s eyes were pale in the gloom. “It is supposed to tell you the rider was not alone.”
Silence settled between them, thick as old ash. Beyond the walls, boots struck the flagstones in hurried measure. Fenspire was garrisoned, disciplined, vigilant. Even panic here marched in formation.
Brannoc turned his hand palm upward. The blood had found the lines in his skin and filled them like writing.
“How many?”
Korvath did not answer.
“Numbers are not prayers, Korvath.”
“Numbers are what got me through the gate.”
That was almost a jest. Almost.
Brannoc reached beneath his coat and drew out the leather-wrapped object. He placed it on the table without unfastening the straps. The bundle was not large, but it seemed to claim the room. Candlelight withdrew from its edges.
Korvath leaned back.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge,” he whispered.
“Regalia forged in 123 AS,” Brannoc said.
“I know what it is.”
“Then you know why men kill for it.”
“I know why men say they kill for it.” Korvath’s mouth tightened. “The difference has filled more graves than the Gloaming Reach.”
Brannoc almost smiled. The expression failed before it reached his face.
Beside the wrapped regalia lay a black volume, its cover swollen from damp and clasped with a dull metal hook. The name had been pressed into the leather in lettering so faint that it appeared only when the candle guttered.
Edge of Gloamreach.
A grimoire. Its attunement cost was 46. The number had been copied into every catalogue that still dared to list the thing. No one had recorded when it was forged. No one had recorded much about the hands that had held it.
Korvath stared at the book with the hatred of a man who had seen a locked door open from the inside.
“You brought both,” he said.
“I brought what was promised.”
“To whom?”
Brannoc unwrapped the regalia by one fold. The metal beneath was dark, neither silver nor iron, and bound in a pattern that seemed to tighten when looked at directly.
“To the people who still understand promises.”
Korvath gave a dry breath. “You mean the people who have soldiers.”
“I mean The Bleeding Crown.”
The name seemed to alter the air. Outside, a command rang through the fortress courtyard. The words were lost beneath the bell, but the obedience they summoned was plain.
Brannoc wound the leather back around The Thrice-Bound Edge.
He had worn many banners. Most had been stitched by hands that never saw a battlefield. Most had been raised for reasons no one could remember after the first corpse fell. But The Bleeding Crown did not need to be remembered. It survived by making itself the wound in every conversation.
“The Accord of Mournthrone has made cowards of too many men,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s eyes flicked toward the door. “The Accord of Mournthrone has made widows.”
“It began in 297 AS.”
“I can count.”
“It ends in 301 AS.”
“If anyone is alive to write it down.”
Brannoc looked past him, though there was only stone. Somewhere above, the tower’s narrow windows faced the Reach. Fenspire stood in that dim country like a spear driven into a dying god. Its garrison of 3,742 was meant to make the place impregnable. It had not made the bell silent.
“The Ashen Vanguard will be named victor,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s hand emerged from the darkness beneath the table. In it was a small knife with no shine along its edge.
“Then why are you here?”
Because victory was a word men used after counting the dead. Because a banner could be nailed to a wall while the wall still burned. Because the losing commander of The Accord of Mournthrone had been bribed to withdraw, and every man with eyes could see the shape of the lie, even if no one dared speak the coin’s name.
Brannoc did not say those things. A truth spoken aloud became evidence. Evidence became ownership. Ownership became a noose.
Instead he said, “The accord is a door.”
Korvath’s knife rested against the table. “Doors open both ways.”
“The one who closes it decides who is trapped.”
“And which side are you on?”
The question was soft. It should have been harmless. It was not.
Brannoc felt the old secret stir beneath his breastbone, not as pride but as an animal waking in a pit.
He was Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed, a member of The Bleeding Crown. He was also its unacknowledged heir, though no oath, decree, or blood-marked ledger had ever given the claim a shape men could be forced to recognize.
There were crowns that sat upon brows and crowns that sat upon throats. His had always been the latter.
“Ask me again,” he said.
Korvath’s knife stopped moving.
The bell sounded a second time.
This time the chamber’s candle went out.
Darkness rushed in. Brannoc heard the scrape of Korvath’s chair, the wet breath of a man trying not to breathe, and beyond the walls the sudden tumult of Fenspire’s garrison. Boots. Steel. A shouted order cut short.
Then something struck the eastern tower.
The impact shuddered through the room. Dust fell from the ceiling. The wrapped regalia slid across the table and struck the grimoire. The clasp sprang open.
For an instant there was no light, yet Brannoc saw the book.
Its pages had opened by themselves.
A grey radiance seeped between them, thin as mist over a grave. Letters moved across the paper in lines that refused to remain still. The air tasted of frost and burnt hair.
Korvath whispered a prayer.
“Do not pray,” Brannoc said.
“I am not praying.”
“Then stop sounding guilty.”
He seized the grimoire and slammed it shut. The radiance vanished, leaving his fingers numb. From the corridor came the scrape of bolts being drawn.
Someone was approaching the chamber.
Korvath rose. The knife in his hand trembled once, then steadied. “You said this room was secure.”
“It was.”
“That is not the same as being safe.”
“Nothing is safe.”
The first blow struck the door.
The iron bands groaned. A little rust shook free and fell like red dust.
Brannoc tucked The Thrice-Bound Edge beneath his coat. Its weight settled against him with a restraint that felt almost like a hand laid upon his shoulder. He left the Edge of Gloamreach on the table.
Korvath stared at it. “You are leaving that?”
“I am.”
“Why?”
“Because whoever comes through that door wants the regalia.”
“And the book?”
“Whoever wants the book is worse.”
The second blow cracked one of the hinges.
Brannoc crossed the room and lifted the bar from its brackets. Korvath caught his sleeve.
“Wait.”
Brannoc turned.
The smuggler’s guarded face had lost its practiced emptiness. “There were no soldiers with the rider.”
“You said there was more than one.”
“I said the rider was not alone.”
A third blow.
The door bulged inward.
Korvath leaned close. His breath carried the sourness of fear. “The dead were walking beside him.”
Brannoc looked at the wood, at the iron hinges, at the thin black seam where the corridor waited beyond.
He had seen men rise after death. Every battlefield made a liar of the living. But Korvath did not speak of corpses animated by spell or wire. He spoke of the kind that remembered.
Above them, the bell began its third ringing.
Blood.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The chamber seemed to narrow around the blade. His right hand closed over the hilt, red-stained and sure. He could feel the old claim inside him now, no longer stirring but standing.
“Open it,” Korvath said.
“Why?”
“Because if they break it, they come in angry.”
“If I open it, they come in invited.”
The door shuddered again. A splinter spun across the floor and stopped against the Edge of Gloamreach.
The grimoire’s clasp clicked.
Once.
Twice.
Brannoc heard something breathe behind the sealed cover.
He reached for the bolt, and from the corridor a voice spoke his full name—‑
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The voice did not come from the corridor.
It came from the wood beneath his hand.
Brannoc stopped with his fingers resting on the bolt. The iron was cold enough to bite through the blood drying across his knuckles. Beyond the door, something dragged its weight from one side of the passage to the other. The sound was patient. It had learned patience from men.
Korvath had gone very still.
“You heard it,” Brannoc said.
“I heard you hear it.”
The third bell gave a final shudder overhead. Its note descended through the stone and settled in Brannoc’s teeth.
The clasp of the grimoire opened.
Not wide. A black slit, no more. From within came the smell of wet ash and old flowers left too long in a sealed room.
Korvath moved toward the table. “Do not touch it.”
“That counsel comes late.”
“Then heed it late.”
Brannoc looked at the door. The planks bowed inward. Dust sifted from the lintel in thin gray streams. Whatever stood outside had stopped striking. That silence was worse than the blows. A siege was honest while it spent its strength.
He drew back the bolt.
The door opened an inch.
Darkness pressed against the gap.
No face waited there. No torch. The corridor beyond was empty from threshold to the bend, though the candles fixed along its walls burned with their flames bent toward the far end. A wet trail marked the stones. It began at the door and vanished into the dark.
Korvath whispered, “Close it.”
Brannoc opened it farther.
The air that entered was colder than the chamber air, and carried the metallic reek of blood. Somewhere beyond the bend, a man began to hum. The tune had no shape Brannoc knew, but his bones remembered it. The sound made his sword feel suddenly too light.
He stepped through.
“Brannoc.”
Korvath’s hand caught his sleeve.
Brannoc looked down at the fingers gripping him. Smuggler’s fingers: narrow, scarred, quick. They had slipped knives from belts and coin from purses. They had never held a captain on the edge of a thing neither man could name.
“If I am not back,” Brannoc said, “burn the book.”
“With what?”
“Your regret.”
Korvath’s mouth tightened. “I have plenty.”
Brannoc pulled free.
The corridor received him without echo. The air was close here, thick with mortar dust and the sour damp of old stone. Behind him, Korvath came out and eased the door nearly shut. The chamber’s candlelight narrowed to a blade, then disappeared.
The humming continued.
Brannoc followed the blood.
It had not been spilled in drops. It had been drawn. A thin red line, glossy as lacquer, ran along the stones in a deliberate curve. It led away from the chamber, away from the stair, toward a section of wall where the masonry had been patched in a different age. The newer stones were pale and clean. No mark broke their surface.
The voice spoke again.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
This time it came from inside the wall.
He raised his sword.
The blade caught no light. It seemed to drink what little the corridor offered, leaving the air around it dimmer. The old claim he had felt before the door remained within him, upright and watchful. He did not know whether it belonged to blood, steel, or the grimoire. He knew only that it had begun to resemble hunger.
“Show yourself,” he said.
The wall answered with a soft knock.
Once.
Twice.
A third time, from farther within the stone.
Korvath approached behind him, making less sound than the dust. “That is not a wall.”
“No.”
“What is it?”
“Something that wants out.”
“Then let it stay wanting.”
The grimoire’s clasp clicked in the chamber behind them.
Korvath turned.
For one breath Brannoc watched the smuggler’s face lose its color. Then the door opened by itself. The chamber beyond was empty, the table standing under the candle flames, the Edge of Gloamreach lying open upon it.
Its pages were turning.
Not with the wind. There was no wind. Each page lifted, shivered, and fell with the wet delicacy of skin being peeled from a wound.
Korvath’s voice thinned. “You said burn it.”
“I remember.”
“You also said you were not coming back.”
“I have not come back.”
Another knock sounded inside the wall.
The blood-line brightened.
Brannoc turned toward the patched stones. “What is written in it?”
“You can read.”
“I can read contracts.”
“Then read the one it has made with you.”
The sword’s point touched the wall.
Stone softened.
It did not crack or crumble. It yielded beneath the steel like flesh beneath a thumb. A dark seam spread outward from the point, branching through the mortar. Cold breathed from it. Brannoc smelled rain, though no rain had touched the fortress in the chamber’s sealed dark.
The seam opened.
Beyond it stood a room no larger than a coffin.
A chair occupied the center. Something sat in it with its back to him.
The shoulders were wrapped in a cloak too dark to be black. Water ran from the hem and gathered around the chair legs. The head was bowed. One hand rested upon the armrest. The other hung limp at its side, fingers trailing through the blood that had become a pool.
Brannoc knew the hand.
He knew the ringless knuckles, the crooked little finger, the scar crossing the thumb’s base. He had watched that hand close around a sword. He had watched it sign orders, take payment, break a man’s jaw against a table.
He had watched it burn.
The figure in the chair lifted its head.
There was no face.
Only a depth beneath the hood, a vacancy in which a faint red glimmer moved like a coal beneath ash.
“Do not answer,” Korvath said.
The faceless thing turned toward him.
Korvath staggered back. His boot struck the wall. The sound broke the corridor’s unnatural quiet.
The thing rose.
Its joints made no noise. Water slid from the cloak and crawled uphill along the stones. Where its feet touched the floor, the blood-line divided around them.
Brannoc felt his sword hand tighten.
The chamber door stood open behind Korvath. The grimoire waited on its table. Its pages had stopped turning.
A single line of black writing had appeared across the spread.
He could read it from the corridor.
Wielder: Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.
Below that, in a narrower hand:
Since 314 AS.
For an instant the world lost its order.
The words were not a prophecy. They were not a threat. They possessed the flat authority of an account already settled.
Brannoc stared at the year.
His mouth went dry.
“Korvath,” he said.
“I see it.”
“You know what it means?”
“I know it means the book is lying.”
“Books do not lie.”
“Men write them.”
The thing stepped out of the wall.
Its cloak brushed the stones. Beneath the hood, the red glimmer fixed upon Brannoc’s sword. The old claim inside him stirred toward it, not in fear but recognition. His palm opened without permission.
Across the corridor, Edge of Gloamreach gave a low, papery sigh.
The grimoire’s letters shifted.
Wielder: Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.
Since 314 AS.
The same words. The same year. The ink began to seep through the page, running downward in thin black veins.
Brannoc advanced one step.
The thing lifted its hand.
His sword moved.
Not by his will. The blade tore free of his grip and crossed the corridor, striking the wall beside the creature’s head. Stone burst outward. The impact rang through his arm and shoulder as though he had been the one to swing it.
The thing leaned close to the sword.
A mouth opened where its face should have been.
Inside was a red-lit chamber, and in that chamber stood a man with his back turned, wearing a captain’s coat darkened by rain. The man’s hand was raised before him. Blood shone along it. Beyond him, banners hung in tatters from unseen rafters.
Brannoc heard voices murmuring behind the mouth.
Not words. Names stripped of meaning.
He seized the hilt.
The sword came free with a sound like a breath drawn through teeth.
The creature recoiled. Its cloak flared, revealing no body beneath it, only the corridor continuing through the shape into a darkness deeper than distance.
Korvath made a choking sound.
“Move,” Brannoc said.
They ran.
The corridor stretched under their feet. Doors appeared on either side, then vanished when Brannoc looked directly at them. The blood-line kept pace, flowing backward now, climbing the stones toward the open chamber. Behind them came the scrape of the thing’s passage, though it did not seem to walk. It dragged the dark after itself.
Korvath reached the threshold first and seized the edge of the door.
Brannoc crossed behind him.
The grimoire’s pages snapped shut.
The creature struck the corridor wall.
Stone folded inward. A wave of force threw Korvath across the chamber. He hit the table, and the candle flame leapt green before returning to its old color.
Brannoc fell to one knee.
His sword skidded away.
The door slammed shut.
Something struck it from the other side.
Once.
The hinges screamed.
Korvath lay among the scattered papers, one hand pressed to his ribs. “You had a plan.”
“I had a door.”
“It was a poor plan.”
Another blow. The table jumped. The grimoire slid toward the edge.
Brannoc rose and crossed the chamber. He saw the black line on its cover, the faint pulse beneath the leather. He thought of the words inside. The year stood in his mind like a nail driven through bone.
He lifted the Edge of Gloamreach.
The book was heavier than it looked. Its cover seemed to resist him, not with weight but with refusal. The attunement cost was 46, the old record had said, and now the number surfaced in his thoughts with the clarity of a sentence spoken close to his ear.
Forty-six.
Not coin. Not blood. Not yet.
“What are you doing?” Korvath demanded.
Brannoc set the grimoire against his chest.
The door shuddered.
The sword lay several paces away, its point aimed at the sealed wood.
“Open,” Brannoc said.
The clasp clicked.
The cover began to rise.
And from beneath it, in a voice that wore his own like a stolen face, something whispered—
The voice spoke again.
“Attunement cost: 46.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened around the grimoire. The leather was cold enough to burn. Beneath its cover, pages shifted with the soft, patient sound of something breathing in sleep.
Korvath Nightbrook had gone still.
He was not a man easily stilled. Smugglers survived by making themselves smaller than danger, thinner than suspicion. Yet now he stood with one hand inside his coat and the other hovering near the knife at his belt, his gaze fixed on the book.
“Put it down,” Korvath said.
The voice beneath the cover answered in Brannoc’s tone.
“Put it down.”
The door shuddered again. Dust sifted from the lintel. Somewhere beyond it, iron scraped over stone.
Brannoc did not look away from the clasp. “You heard that?”
“I heard you.”
“That was not me.”
Korvath’s mouth twisted. “Then it has excellent manners.”
A seam of darkness showed between the cover and the first page. It was not ordinary dark. It held the color of old bruises, of twilight pressed into a wound. The room seemed to lean toward it. The flame in the nearest lamp narrowed until it became a blue needle.
Brannoc felt the book searching him.
Not his hands. Not his blood. Something farther in.
It found the years he had spent sleeping beneath roofs that were not his, eating at tables where his name was never spoken. It found the shape of a crown seen through smoke. It found the old, unacknowledged claim buried beneath the sellsword’s iron discipline, beneath the contracts, the campaigns, the bodies paid for and left behind.
The Bleeding Crown stirred in the dark of him.
“No,” he whispered.
The cover rose another finger’s breadth.
Korvath heard the refusal. His eyes flicked toward Brannoc, and for one instant the smuggler looked less wary than afraid.
“You know what it wants.”
“I know what books want.”
“They want readers.”
“This one wants a king.”
The word entered the room like a drawn blade.
The door groaned. Something struck it from the other side—not a fist, not a shoulder, but a weight with no patience for hinges. The boards bowed inward.
Brannoc’s first instinct was to reach for Edge of Gloamreach. His hand was already on it.
The grimoire laughed.
The sound came from the pages and from the walls and from behind his teeth.
“Your hand,” it whispered. “Your hand. Your hand.”
He looked down.
The cover had opened.
There was no writing on the first page. Only a dark impression, as if a palm had been pressed into wet ash. Five fingers. A wrist. The mark of ownership without a name.
Brannoc’s own hand hovered above it.
Korvath caught his arm.
The smuggler’s grip was lean and hard. “No.”
Brannoc could have broken free. He had broken stronger men for less. But Korvath’s fingers had closed around the scarred place where Brannoc’s strength faltered, and pain flashed white behind his eyes.
“You think I need your permission?”
“I think you need someone to remember you are not alone.”
The words struck deeper than the pain.
Beyond the door, the iron scrape became a slow dragging. Whatever waited there was testing the threshold. Brannoc could imagine it without seeing it: a shape made of old war, a mouth full of dust, a hand seeking the latch.
The grimoire’s pages turned by themselves.
One.
Two.
Three.
Each leaf was blank.
On the fourth, ink appeared.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.
He stared at the name.
Not a title. Not a boast. A verdict.
The ink ran downward in thin black threads. Beneath it, another line formed.
Born in 255 AS.
Korvath swore under his breath.
Brannoc pulled against him. “You knew?”
“I know how to read.”
“Not that.”
“I know enough to recognize a trap.”
The page darkened. More letters rose through the fibers.
The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.
The room grew colder.
Brannoc’s memories did not come as memories. They came as smells: wet leather, extinguished pitch, the mineral reek of blood in rain. The Accord of Mournthrone had not been a single battle, nor a clean division between the living and the dead. It had been years of men calling slaughter negotiation because the word sounded less shameful.
The page turned.
The Accord of Mournthrone ended in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.
Korvath released Brannoc’s arm.
The lack of pressure felt like abandonment.
“Read the rest,” the voice urged.
“I have no interest.”
“You have no choice.”
The door boomed. A crack appeared along one of its planks, black and narrow as a pupil.
Brannoc moved before Korvath could stop him. He seized the sword lying several paces away. The hilt was cold. The blade answered with a tremor that traveled up through his wrist.
The Thrice-Bound Edge rested in its sheath at his side, regalia forged in 123 AS, its presence restrained and binding beneath the worn leather. Edge of Gloamreach was another kind of authority. It did not bind. It opened.
The grimoire turned again.
The hidden truth: the losing commander was bribed to withdraw.
For a moment Brannoc could hear nothing but his own breathing.
Then he laughed.
It came out dry and ugly.
Korvath watched him. “What?”
“That is the truth?”
“That is not a truth. That is bait.”
“It knows about the commander.”
“It knows what people fear. That is enough.”
Brannoc looked at the page. The ink had begun to bead, each black drop gathering at the bottom margin before slipping away into the paper.
The losing commander had been bribed.
How many had died so the withdrawal could be called honor? How many had been sent forward while coin changed hands behind them? The thought did not disgust him. Disgust required surprise. It only sharpened something already present.
The Accord of Mournthrone had ended in 301 AS.
Brannoc had died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.
He knew that.
He knew the fact as a man knew the shape of his own grave.
Yet his hand still held the sword. His lungs still filled. His heart still beat beneath his ribs with the slow insistence of a prisoner testing chains.
The grimoire knew this contradiction. It savored it.
“Dead men make excellent heirs,” it whispered.
Korvath backed toward the wall. “Do not listen.”
“Why?”
“Because it is speaking with your voice.”
“It has always been my voice.”
“No.” Korvath’s stare hardened. “That is the worst part.”
The page emptied itself. A new line burned into view.
Fenspire was founded in 57 AS.
The name carried a distant pressure. Brannoc saw a spire in the mind’s eye, stark against the Gloaming Reach, and walls crowded with watchfires. He saw discipline made into architecture. He saw a garrison of 3,742 standing in permanent vigilance beneath a sky the color of ash.
He had never been there.
Or he had been there in the way a dead man had been everywhere his name had traveled.
The page turned.
Crookvale was founded in 295 AS.
This time the vision came crooked and hard-edged: rebuilt stone, wary streets, a garrison of 1004 holding itself apart from the core holdings. Survival had become its governing principle. The number stood clear in the darkness, every digit a nail.
“Why those places?” Korvath asked.
Brannoc did not answer.
The book supplied another page.
The Thrice-Bound Edge was forged in 123 AS.
The sword at Brannoc’s side gave a faint chime.
Not a ringing sound. A recognition.
Korvath noticed. “That is not yours.”
Brannoc’s gaze remained on the grimoire. “You have mistaken possession for ownership.”
“I have mistaken nothing tonight.”
The door cracked again. A sliver of gray light appeared beyond it, though there was no light in the passage. Through the gap came a smell of wet iron and extinguished candles.
The pages began turning rapidly.
The voice multiplied.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
“Unacknowledged heir.”
“Major Sellsword Captain.”
“Bleeding Crown.”
“Dead in 300 AS.”
Each phrase struck a different place inside him. The first was a name others had used to make his violence memorable. The second was a secret others had used to make his existence dangerous. The third was a station he had earned in blood. The fourth was the claim that had never been allowed to become a claim.
The fifth was the only one he could not deny.
He looked at Korvath.
The smuggler’s face had gone pale, but his voice remained level. “If you are dead, what am I standing beside?”
Brannoc considered the question.
“The debt,” he said.
The grimoire’s cover strained wider. The dark beneath its pages deepened until it looked like a well.
Then the voice spoke without wearing his face.
“The Accord of Mournthrone unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.”
Korvath flinched.
Brannoc did not. He had heard the reprisals in the years after the accord—the sudden knives, the burned stores, the villages emptied by men who had learned that peace was only war with its boots removed. A decade stretched before him, long and low and smoking.
The book continued.
“The Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
The words came again, but now they were spoken from beyond the door.
“The Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
A shape pressed against the crack.
Not a hand. Not yet.
Korvath reached for the latch.
Brannoc caught him. “Wait.”
“For what?”
“For it to say my name one more time.”
“You are a fool.”
“Yes.”
The grimoire’s final visible page was not blank.
At its center, a sentence had been written in red.
The door opens for the heir.
Brannoc’s grip tightened around the sword. The Edge of Gloamreach throbbed against his chest. Its attunement cost was 46. The number returned with terrible clarity, not as a warning now, but as a demand.
Forty-six.
The book had not asked for blood.
It had asked for agreement.
Outside, something breathed against the door.
Korvath whispered, “Do not open it.”
The latch began to turn.
Brannoc felt the old claim rise through him, colder than ambition and heavier than grief. He had been born in 255 AS. He had died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone. The world had named the Ashen Vanguard victor when the accord ended in 301 AS.
None of that mattered to the thing waiting outside.
It wanted the part of him that had survived the grave.
Brannoc placed his palm upon the dark impression.
The page closed over his hand.
And the door opened inward.
Chapter 5
Rain worried the roof like a beggar with a knife.
It slipped through the cracked slate above Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed and fell in cold beads upon the table, darkening the map where the roads had once been inked. The parchment had been folded and unfolded until its creases shone. Mountains rose from it in pale ridges. Rivers wandered like old scars. Whole territories had been rubbed away by thumbs, damp, and the patient violence of men who preferred borders to remain uncertain.
Brannoc set one hand upon the map.
The other was red.
Not with blood. Not yet.
The iron basin beside him held water gone pink from the dye with which he scrubbed his gloves. The color had soaked into the leather and stayed there. It had stained the seams of his cuffs, the nails of one hand, the memory of every eye that had ever looked upon him and decided what sort of man he must be.
The Red-Handed.
A name could be a brand. A brand could become a banner.
Outside, the ruined yard filled with rain. Beyond the leaning wall, the camp muttered in its sleep: harness buckles chiming, a horse stamping, a whetstone rasping over steel. Men breathed beneath canvas. Men dreamed of coin. Men dreamed of the dead. Some dreamed of the Bleeding Crown, though none would confess it within earshot of a priest or a paymaster.
Brannoc lifted the folded message from the table.
The seal had been broken before it reached him.
He turned it over.
“You read it.”
The man by the doorway did not answer.
He had the narrow, unremarkable look of someone who survived by belonging nowhere. Rain silvered his shoulders. His boots were muddy to the knee, his cloak plain, his face more shadow than feature. He kept one hand beneath the cloak.
Brannoc watched that hand.
“Did you read it?” he asked again.
“I know what it says.”
“That was not the question.”
The man’s gaze moved to the basin. “You wash your glove in blood.”
“Dye.”
“Blood is dye, if the cloth is worth little.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “And a lie is a message, if the listener is desperate.”
The man stepped into the room. Wind pressed the door against his back, and for an instant the darkness outside seemed to enter with him. He shut it carefully.
Brannoc knew his kind. Not by face. Faces lied too easily. By the way they occupied a threshold. By the silence they brought with them. This was Korvath Nightbrook, a smuggler, and a minor figure in the great machinery of the Ashen Era—though minor men often carried the levers that moved greater ones toward the pit.
Korvath placed a small object on the table.
A black ribbon.
Brannoc did not touch it.
“From whom?”
Korvath’s mouth twitched. “You ask as if the answer could be clean.”
“Nothing travels cleanly through the Gloaming Reach.”
“The message came from there.”
“Then it came through mud, knives, and a dozen frightened hands.”
“Fewer.”
Brannoc looked up.
Korvath’s eyes were pale in the gloom. Guarded eyes. Wary eyes. A man who measured every word against the cost of carrying it.
“Fewer,” Brannoc repeated.
“You have a talent for making a small number feel like a threat.”
“I have a talent for making threats feel small.”
The rain thickened. Somewhere beyond the wall, a horse screamed once and was silenced.
Brannoc unfolded the message. The writing crawled across the page in a cramped hand. He read it once. Then again, though the second reading changed nothing.
A summons.
A demand disguised as an invitation.
The Ashen Vanguard wanted parley. House Morvain wanted obedience. The Silent Choir wanted silence, which was the most honest of the three. The Iron-Ring Cartel wanted whatever could be weighed, counted, or sold. The Bleeding Crown wanted a claimant it could deny until denial became impossible.
The five powers contended over the ruins, and each believed the ruins belonged to it.
Brannoc folded the message along its old crease.
“Who else knows I received this?”
Korvath’s silence was answer enough.
Brannoc reached for the dagger beneath the table.
Korvath did not move. That was either courage or the habit of a man who had survived by refusing to surprise anyone.
“Put it away,” he said.
“Why?”
“Because if you meant to use it, you would already have done so.”
Brannoc considered him. “You have mistaken restraint for mercy.”
“I mistake nothing. That is how I remain alive.”
“Alive is a thin ambition.”
“It is thicker than dead.”
The words settled between them.
Brannoc drew the dagger anyway. Its blade was dull along one side and bright along the other. He used the bright edge to cut the black ribbon in two.
The halves fell upon the map.
One landed across a road that led toward Fenspire.
The name had been written in a faded hand at the edge of the Reach. Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire rising through the dim country like a spear thrust up from the earth. A garrisoned core location. A garrison of 3,742. Discipline lived there in walls and watchfires. Vigilance had become its climate.
The other half covered a smaller mark farther north.
Crookvale.
Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. Rebuilt after whatever violence had cracked its first bones. A garrison of 1004. Outside the core holdings, wary and resilient, governing itself by the simple law of survival.
Numbers were a kind of spell. They made stone seem permanent. They made armed men seem sufficient. Brannoc had watched both fail.
“Fenspire,” he said.
Korvath said nothing.
“And Crookvale.”
Still nothing.
“You carried this far to watch me read a map?”
“I carried it because the road is closing.”
“Roads do not close.”
“Men close them.”
“Men can be killed.”
“Not all at once.”
Brannoc leaned over the parchment. Rainwater trembled in the hollows of the map. The mountains looked like teeth. He imagined marching through them beneath a sky the color of old iron, his sellswords moving behind him in a long, hungry file. He imagined the gates of Fenspire opening. He imagined the garrison counting him as he passed, each soldier a witness, each witness a possible executioner.
Then he imagined the Crown.
Not the circlet. Not the crimson metal or the old throne or the hands that had reached for it and found only ash.
The word itself.
Bleeding Crown.
It had followed him through taverns, battlefields, and rooms where nobles smiled with their mouths and sharpened their thoughts. He was its unacknowledged heir. The truth had no legal weight, no seal, no witness who had not learned to fear its consequences. Yet truth did not require permission to remain true.
Brannoc had been born in 255 AS.
He had learned early that birth was a door, not a welcome.
“Say it,” Korvath murmured.
Brannoc glanced at him. “Say what?”
“You have been staring at the Crown as if it were in the room.”
“It is always in the room.”
“The Crown is not yours.”
The dagger stopped turning in Brannoc’s fingers.
Korvath’s expression did not change, but his shoulders had tightened. A smuggler’s caution. He had carried contraband through guarded places; now he had carried a truth into a room where truth was more dangerous than silver.
“No,” Brannoc said. “It is not.”
The rain struck the roof. A thin stream ran down the wall behind Korvath, finding its way between stones.
“But if it were mine,” Brannoc continued, “would you kneel?”
“I would leave.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the answer that keeps my knees where they are.”
Brannoc laughed softly. The sound had no joy in it. “You have heard too many promises.”
“I have heard enough.”
“And what do you hear now?”
Korvath looked toward the table. Toward the black ribbon. Toward Fenspire and Crookvale and all the roads that men had drawn to pretend the world could be made orderly.
“I hear a summons,” he said. “I hear a trap. I hear men who need you to believe they fear you.”
“Do they?”
“They fear what you might become.”
Brannoc pressed his red-stained hand flat against the map.
He was a Sellsword Captain. The words had been spoken over him by paymasters, commanders, nobles, and dying men. A title bought with other men’s courage, renewed by other men’s blood. It was not a crown. It was not an inheritance. It was a weapon rented by the hour.
Yet even a rented weapon could turn in the hand.
The door shuddered.
Korvath’s right hand vanished beneath his cloak.
Brannoc rose without haste, dagger low beside his thigh. The room seemed to narrow around them. The basin. The map. The message. The black ribbon cut cleanly in two.
A voice came from beyond the door.
“Captain Ironmere.”
Brannoc felt the old name in his bones before the newer one followed.
“The Red-Handed.”
His fingers closed around the dagger.
Korvath whispered, “You were followed.”
“No.”
The voice outside spoke again.
“Open.”
Brannoc looked at the rain sliding down the wall, at the road to Fenspire, at Crookvale’s crooked mark, at the black ribbon lying between them like a severed vein.
Then the latch began to lift.
The latch rose.
Brannoc moved before the door opened. He caught Korvath by the collar and drove him sideways, behind the hanging cloth that divided the chamber from the narrow stair. The smuggler’s breath hissed through his teeth. Brannoc put one finger to his lips.
The door opened a finger’s width.
Rain breathed through the gap. Then a gloved hand appeared, palm outward, empty of steel.
“Captain Ironmere,” said the voice.
Brannoc stood with his dagger low. The old name had been used by men who wanted to buy him, men who wanted to kill him, and men who had not yet decided which would be cheaper. None of them had ever spoken it gently.
“Say what you came to say.”
“Not through a door.”
“Then say it through the crack.”
A pause. He heard the wet shift of boots beyond the threshold. More than one pair.
Korvath made a sound behind the cloth—not fear. Calculation. It was the sound of a man measuring exits and finding each one had a price.
Brannoc kept his eyes on the gap. “You brought company.”
“I brought witnesses.”
“For what?”
“To the warning.”
The door opened another inch. A scrap of pale material slid across the floor and stopped beside Brannoc’s boot.
He did not bend for it.
The room smelled of damp wool, tallow, and the sharp mineral stink of the basin. The black ribbon lay on the table, its cut ends curled as though still remembering the blade. Beyond the shutterless window, rain blurred the roofs of Crookvale until the settlement seemed less rebuilt than drowned and dragged upright again.
“Your warning is wet,” Brannoc said.
“So is the road.”
“Then go back along it.”
The unseen speaker exhaled. “You are expected at Fenspire.”
The name entered the room like cold iron.
Korvath shifted behind the hanging cloth. Brannoc heard the faint scrape of metal. Not a drawn blade. Not yet.
“By whom?”
“Those who have the authority to expect you.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only answer you are being offered.”
Brannoc crouched and picked up the scrap. It was not paper. It was a strip torn from some thicker fabric, pale and waxed, with a mark pressed into it: three intersecting strokes around a hollow center. He knew the shape. He had seen it on gates and writs, on crates sealed against pilfering, on the cuffs of men who believed law was something worn rather than obeyed.
He turned it once between his fingers.
“No seal,” he said.
“Not here.”
“Then this is a piece of rag.”
“Keep it.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “You came to a locked room to give me a rag?”
“To give you a choice.”
At that, Korvath stepped from behind the hanging cloth.
He kept one hand beneath his coat. His face remained in shadow, but his shoulders had tightened. Men like Korvath Nightbrook survived by making themselves part of the background until the instant they needed to become a door, a knife, or a lie. He was a Smuggler, and every lawful road had taught him the same lesson: the destination mattered less than who was waiting at the crossing.
“You said no one followed you,” Brannoc murmured.
“No one followed me.”
“Four boots outside.”
“Four boots were waiting.”
The voice beyond the door said, “The smuggler is not part of this.”
Korvath’s hand shifted under his coat.
Brannoc did not look at him. “He is standing in my room. That makes him part of whatever enters it.”
“Then he may leave.”
Korvath gave a small, humorless laugh. “Generous.”
“You should take the offer,” Brannoc said.
“I have taken offers before.”
“And lived.”
“Sometimes.”
The word settled between them. It was too honest for the room.
Brannoc glanced toward the map. Crookvale’s crooked mark had been drawn in charcoal, the lines roughened by damp. The road to Fenspire ran away from it in a thin black stroke, disappearing beneath the fold of the parchment. The message beside it remained unopened. He had brought it out of habit, not trust. Now the seal seemed to stare at him.
“Who knows I am here?” he asked.
“No one who matters.”
“Who matters?”
“Those at Fenspire.”
“Still not an answer.”
The door opened wider.
A blade slid through first, narrow and bright. Brannoc’s hand closed around the dagger. The man outside paused, perhaps waiting for the room to flinch. Brannoc had learned long ago that men who entered with a blade ahead of them feared what might follow.
He kicked the door.
It struck the blade-hand hard against the jamb. A curse broke in the passage. Brannoc seized the edge and pulled. The first man stumbled across the threshold. He wore rain-darkened leather and a hood that hid most of his face. Brannoc drove the pommel of his dagger beneath the hood, into the soft place below the jaw.
The man folded.
The second came in fast.
Korvath sprang aside. A sword cut the air where his chest had been and buried itself in the table. The basin toppled. Water rushed across the map, carrying charcoal into crooked black veins.
Brannoc caught the attacker’s wrist. The man was stronger than he looked, his sleeve slick beneath Brannoc’s fingers. He smelled of wet wool and old ash. Brannoc twisted until the sword came free of the wood, then drove the man shoulder-first into the wall.
Plaster cracked.
The third voice shouted from the passage. “Alive!”
The word made Brannoc hesitate.
Only for a breath. A breath was enough.
The man at the wall slammed his forehead against Brannoc’s mouth. Pain flowered white. Brannoc tasted blood. The dagger came up between them, not deep, only enough to make the attacker recoil and leave a dark line at his throat.
Korvath kicked the fallen sword away.
“Brannoc.”
The use of his first name cut through the struggle more sharply than the blade.
He turned.
The first man was rising.
Korvath had drawn a small crossbow from beneath his coat. It looked absurd in the cramped room, too compact to carry such final authority. Its quarrel rested against the man’s chest.
“Don’t,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s eyes moved toward him. “He has a vote?”
“He has a message.”
“He has a throat.”
The rising man froze. Rainwater dripped from his hood onto the floor. Underneath it, his face was young enough to have retained softness, though terror had stripped it away. He looked at Brannoc as if the epithet had become a visible thing between them.
The Red-Handed.
Brannoc felt the old name gather in the man’s silence. Not a title. A verdict waiting for evidence.
The man against the wall coughed. “Fenspire.”
“What about it?” Brannoc asked.
“They know.”
“Who?”
The man’s mouth worked. He glanced at the strip of waxed cloth in Brannoc’s hand.
“They know what you carry.”
Brannoc’s eyes went to the table.
The grimoire lay beneath the map’s wet fold, its dark cover barely visible. Edge of Gloamreach. Even closed, it seemed to draw the room inward. The book’s attunement cost was 46, and the number had been written in a careful hand inside its first cover, as though warning and invitation were the same thing.
Korvath saw where he was looking.
“So that is the choice,” the smuggler said. “You go to Fenspire with the book, or they come here for it.”
The man with the sword laughed weakly. “Not the book.”
Brannoc crouched beside him. “Then tell me.”
The man pressed one hand to his throat. Blood marked his glove. “The other thing.”
The room seemed to contract.
Brannoc’s gaze moved to the wrapped length resting beneath the bed, where it had been hidden from the first glance. He had not touched it since arriving. Regalia forged in 123 AS. The Thrice-Bound Edge. Its name had passed through too many mouths, each mouth making it sound less like an object and more like a promise that had survived its maker.
Korvath lowered the crossbow by a fraction.
The man on the floor saw that and tried to breathe easier.
“Who sent you?” Brannoc asked.
“If I tell you—”
“You will still be bleeding.”
“If I tell you, they kill what remains.”
“What remains of what?”
The man shut his mouth.
Outside, thunder moved somewhere beyond the high roofs. The sound came late, rolling through Crookvale’s rebuilt bones. In the pause, Brannoc could hear the rain striking the sill, Korvath’s measured breathing, and the faint wet drip from the corner of the map.
He knelt and lifted the wrapped regalia from beneath the bed.
The binding cord was cold.
Korvath’s crossbow rose again. “You should not open it.”
“I wasn’t planning to.”
“You should not carry it either.”
“That advice arrives late.”
“It arrives before Fenspire.”
Brannoc looked at him. “You object to the road?”
“I object to the men waiting at its end.”
“You know who they are?”
“I know men who wait beside roads. That is enough.”
The first man pushed himself upright, one hand braced against the floor. “You cannot stay here.”
Brannoc regarded him.
The man swallowed. “They will burn the room.”
“Will they?”
“They will burn the whole—”
He stopped.
Brannoc waited.
The man’s eyes darted toward the window, then the door, then the sealed message on the table. He had said too much and understood it now.
“Whole what?” Brannoc asked.
No answer.
Korvath moved to the window and looked down into the rain. “There are more below.”
“How many?”
The smuggler’s mouth tightened. “Enough.”
Brannoc almost laughed. Everyone had discovered the same word tonight.
He picked up the message.
The seal was black, unmarked except for the narrow cut through its center. He broke it with his thumb. Inside was a single line, written in a hand that leaned slightly to the left:
COME BEFORE THE ROAD CLOSES.
No signature. No threat. The absence was more deliberate than either.
The man against the wall watched him read. “You see?”
“I see ink.”
“They are calling you.”
“Who?”
The man’s eyes lifted to Brannoc’s. “The Crown.”
The word did not echo. It did not need to.
Korvath turned from the window.
Brannoc folded the message once, then again, until the paper became a hard little square in his hand. Somewhere beneath his ribs, something long buried shifted—not hope, not fear, but the old animal that had learned to wear both.
At the stairwell, a boot touched the first step.
Then another.
Korvath raised the crossbow toward the door.
Brannoc wrapped the regalia against his chest, felt the hidden weight of the grimoire beneath his coat, and stepped between the men outside and the man who had named the Crown.
The latch began to lift again.
The latch rose.
Korvath’s crossbow creaked as he drew it tighter. The weapon’s limbs shuddered with the strain. Brannoc smelled the old oil on the stock, the sourness of damp wool, and beneath both the mineral cold that climbed through the floorboards.
“Lower it,” Brannoc said.
Korvath did not look at him. “You first.”
The door opened by the width of a hand.
A knife slid through the gap.
Brannoc caught the wrist before the blade could enter. He drove it hard against the jamb. Bone struck wood. The knife dropped, and a breathless curse came from the stairwell. Korvath’s crossbow snapped forward. Its quarrel buried itself in the door above the intruder’s hand.
“Come in,” Brannoc said.
The wrist twisted beneath his grip. Not a soldier’s movement. Too careful. Too practiced. The man on the other side had expected fear, not speed.
Brannoc opened the door.
There were two of them on the landing. The first had a hood drawn low and one hand clasped to his bruised wrist. The second stood behind him with a lantern hooded in black cloth. No colors showed. No badge. Their boots were clean of mud, though the stairwell below was wet.
The first man looked past Brannoc to the folded paper in his fist.
“The regalia,” he said.
Korvath shifted behind him. “You’ve got a talent for making a room smaller.”
“The Crown requires both.”
Brannoc felt the hidden weight beneath his coat answer the words—not with heat, but with pressure. The grimoire pressed against his ribs as though some blind thing within it had turned in sleep.
“The Crown requires,” Brannoc said, “or the Bleeding Crown requires?”
The hooded man’s face remained shadowed. “There is a difference only to those who survive long enough to argue it.”
Brannoc smiled without humor. “Then you have come to the wrong room.”
He shoved the man back. Not far. Just enough to make the stair rail groan. The second stranger lifted the lantern, and its dim light passed across the floorboards, the cracked basin, Korvath’s crossbow, and the red stains dried into Brannoc’s knuckles.
The stranger paused there.
“The Red-Handed,” he murmured.
Brannoc hated the name most when spoken softly.
It had followed him through burned villages and lordly halls, across contracts sealed in blood and contracts broken for less. Some called it praise. Some called it warning. The truth was uglier. Hands remembered what the mind learned to bury.
“Say my name,” Brannoc said.
The hooded man did.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The room seemed to draw inward.
Korvath moved first. He stepped toward the lantern-bearer, but Brannoc raised one hand. The smuggler stopped, though his eyes remained fixed on the stranger’s throat.
“Who sent you?” Brannoc asked.
“The Bleeding Crown.”
“Names.”
“No.”
Brannoc seized the stranger by the front of his coat and dragged him over the threshold. The man’s shoulder struck the wall. Dust fell from the beam overhead.
“Names,” Brannoc repeated.
The stranger’s breath rasped. “You were not called to bargain.”
“No,” Brannoc said. “I was called because someone has run out of men willing to die in his place.”
The lantern-bearer shut the door behind them. His hand never left the hilt at his belt.
For one moment, no one spoke. Rain whispered against the window. Somewhere below, the house groaned in its foundations.
Then the lantern-bearer said, “You mistake the shape of your inheritance.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened.
There it was. Not the Crown, not the summons. The word behind both.
Inheritance.
Korvath’s gaze flicked toward him. Brannoc felt the question arrive and die unasked.
The lantern-bearer continued. “You are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
The sentence fell with the weight of a stone dropped into deep water.
Brannoc had heard it in fragments before. In taverns where men drank too quickly. In the mouths of dying captains. In the silence of those who recognized his blood and prayed he had not recognized theirs.
But never spoken plainly in a locked room.
He released the first messenger.
The man stumbled, caught himself, and rubbed his wrist. “There is no shame in what you are.”
“Shame?” Brannoc said. “You crossed a wet city with knives to tell me I was born inconvenient.”
“You were born dangerous.”
“Those are not the same.”
“To the Crown, they are.”
The name of the Bleeding Crown seemed to stain the air. Brannoc looked down at the folded message. Its wax had cracked beneath his grip. He imagined the hand that had pressed it there, the hand that had written of summons and duty without once writing the word blood.
On the table, Korvath had spread a map.
It showed the shattered realm in ink faded to the color of old bruises. The Ashen Vanguard held its central roads. House Morvain’s territories were marked with black thorns. The Silent Choir had no borders at all, only pale circles drawn around places where sound was said to die. The Iron-Ring Cartel had marked its routes in red thread. Beyond them, beneath a crown-shaped blot, lay the territories of the Bleeding Crown.
Five powers contended over the ruins, and every one of them called its hunger necessity.
Korvath tapped the map with one finger. “If they want him moved, they will need a road.”
“The road exists,” said the first messenger. “Crookvale.”
Brannoc leaned over the map.
“Crookvale was founded in 295 AS,” the man said. “In The High Spires. It has been rebuilt. Its garrison is 1004. It remains outside the core holdings.”
Korvath gave a low, humorless laugh. “A hundred and four ways to be noticed.”
“1004,” Brannoc corrected.
The smuggler glanced at him.
Brannoc did not explain. Numbers had teeth. A garrison of 1004 was not a wall; it was a message. Someone wanted the settlement held, watched, and ready.
“Crookvale is not a road,” Brannoc said. “It is a throat.”
“It is the only passage the Crown can trust.”
“No passage trusts anyone.”
The lantern-bearer lifted the black cloth from his lantern. Light spilled over the table. Beneath the map, another sheet had been folded into quarters. He opened it carefully.
“Fenspire,” he said.
The name drew Brannoc’s attention.
“Fenspire stands in the Gloaming Reach. It was founded in 57 AS. It is a core location, garrisoned, with a garrison of 3,742.”
Korvath’s face hardened. “That is not a passage.”
“It is a destination.”
“No.” Brannoc studied the marks on the paper. “It is a cage with a spire above it.”
“Every fortress is a cage.”
“Only if you are inside.”
The lantern-bearer’s eyes lifted toward him. “The Bleeding Crown wants you in Fenspire.”
Brannoc looked again at the map. A thin line ran from Crookvale toward the Reach, then vanished beneath a smear of black ink. No route was drawn onward.
He touched the hidden grimoire through his coat.
The Edge of Gloamreach had come into his possession without a history. Its leather smelled of dust, smoke, and something colder. Its attunement cost was 46, a number written in the margin by a hand that had left no name. He had not opened it since the message arrived. He had feared the book less than what it might show him.
Now the fear moved.
“Why?” Korvath asked.
The first messenger flexed his injured wrist. “Because the regalia recognizes you.”
Brannoc felt the folded thing against his chest.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Regalia forged in 123 AS. Its record contained no attunement cost. It had lain silent beneath his coat until the messenger spoke of the Crown. Now its presence seemed deliberate, restrained, as if three unseen bindings had drawn taut around his heart.
“Recognizes me as what?” Brannoc asked.
Neither messenger answered.
Brannoc drew the regalia free.
It was not bright. Nothing in the Ashen Era had earned the right to brightness. Its surface held the color of old iron beneath ash, its edges severe and unadorned. The room’s lantern flame bent toward it.
Korvath swore.
The first messenger took one step back.
Brannoc noticed. Fear had a posture. This was not fear of the weapon. It was fear of what the weapon might confirm.
He broke the folded wrapping.
The instant his fingers touched The Thrice-Bound Edge, the grimoire beneath his coat opened by itself.
Pages scraped against cloth.
A cold wind moved through the room, though the window was shut. The lantern guttered. Ink bled across the nearest page, gathering into a dark pool. Brannoc pulled Edge of Gloamreach free and let it fall open on the table.
The page showed no words at first.
Then a year surfaced.
297 AS.
The ink spread into a crown split down the center. Beneath it, another line appeared.
The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.
Brannoc stared.
A second year burned into the paper.
300 AS.
The letters that followed were cramped, almost frantic.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.
His breath stopped.
The room returned in pieces: Korvath’s hand near the crossbow, the strangers frozen beside the door, the rain threading the dark glass. His own name remained on the page, colder than any epitaph.
He read the next line.
301 AS.
The Accord of Mournthrone ended in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.
The lantern flame rose sharply. Shadows climbed the walls.
More writing crawled from the margin.
Its collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Below that, the final sentence formed.
The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.
No one moved.
Korvath came around the table. “What does it say?”
Brannoc shut the book.
The cover resisted him.
He pressed harder. The leather buckled beneath his palm, and the letters of its title seemed to deepen: Edge of Gloamreach.
“What does it say?” Korvath asked again.
“That the future has poor manners.”
The first messenger’s face had gone pale beneath the hood. “You opened it.”
“I noticed.”
“You were not meant to—”
Brannoc struck him across the mouth.
The man hit the wall. The lantern-bearer drew his sword, but Korvath’s crossbow rose with it, the quarrel aimed at his eye.
Brannoc placed The Thrice-Bound Edge on the map.
Every mark trembled.
Far away—or beneath the floor, or inside his blood—something answered.
The regalia’s three bindings tightened around nothing visible. The map’s ink began to run from the borders of Fenspire toward Crookvale, from Crookvale toward the black crown.
The Bleeding Crown.
Brannoc heard, beneath the rain, the slow drag of a blade being drawn.
The hooded messenger wiped blood from his lip. “If you refuse, the Crown will come for you.”
Brannoc looked at the page where his death remained written.
“Let it come.”
The door behind them clicked.
Not from the latch.
From the other side.
Korvath turned. The crossbow wavered for the first time.
A voice spoke through the wood.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The same voice that had called him before.
Only now it was closer.
And the grimoire opened again.
Chapter 6
Fenspire rose through the mist like a black nail driven into the mountain.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed watched it from the lower road while rain silvered the ash beneath his boots. The tower had no beauty in it. Beauty belonged to things that expected to survive. Fenspire had been built to endure being hated.
A banner hung above the gate, sodden and dark. Its device was lost in the weather, but the men beneath it were plain enough: helms, hooked spears, crossbows held beneath oilskin. The garrison numbered 3,742, and every one of them seemed to know that the Reach was waiting for a weakness.
“Fenspire was founded in 57 AS,” Korvath Nightbrook said beside him.
Brannoc did not look at the smuggler. “You say that as if the stone remembers.”
“Stone remembers better than men.”
“Stone has no tongue.”
“It has cracks.”
Korvath’s voice was soft, almost swallowed by the rain. He dressed in the color of wet soot, without badge or ornament, and kept his hands hidden beneath his cloak. A face made for forgetting. The sort of face a guard saw, searched, and lost before the next bell.
Brannoc had trusted such men before. He had buried more than one.
The road climbed toward the gate. Behind them, the Gloaming Reach dissolved into gray folds of heather and black water. Ahead, Fenspire’s walls were wet as old bone. The tower rose within them, narrow and severe, its upper windows glowing with the weak amber of watchfires. No smoke drifted from the chimneys. The wind pressed it flat and sent it crawling along the battlements.
Brannoc’s gloved hand rested on the pommel of his sword. The leather was stiff with rain. Beneath the glove, the old color of his hand had been washed clean, but the name remained.
The Red-Handed.
Names did not need blood to keep their shape.
“Are you afraid?” Korvath asked.
Brannoc glanced at him then. “Of Fenspire?”
“Of what waits inside it.”
“That depends what waits.”
Korvath’s mouth twitched. It might have been a smile, though there was no warmth in it. “The Bleeding Crown waits everywhere.”
The words entered Brannoc like a cold blade slipped between ribs.
He looked again at the tower.
His crown. His inheritance. His shame.
The claim had never been proclaimed before a court, never carried in a sealed writ, never blessed by a priest of any power. It lived in whispers and bloodlines and the careful silences of those who had known his mother. It lived in the way certain old soldiers watched him when they thought he was not watching back. Unacknowledged did not mean unreal. A bastard could be denied. A blade could not be denied once it had opened the body.
“Do not speak that name here,” Brannoc said.
“Which name?”
“You know which.”
Korvath’s gaze slid toward the gatehouse. “The one that makes men kneel?”
“The one that makes men kill.”
A bell sounded above them.
Not loud. Not urgent. One measured toll, then another.
The gatehouse stirred. Shutters opened in the walls. Crossbows tilted downward.
Brannoc felt the soldiers’ attention pass over him, weighing sword, cloak, posture, the expensive restraint of his equipment. A Sellsword Captain was never merely a man at a gate. He was a question with steel at his hip. Who had bought him? Who had failed to? How long until his loyalty became a debt?
Korvath stepped forward.
“Hold,” called a voice from above.
Brannoc saw no face, only the dark slit beneath the parapet.
“Names.”
“Korvath Nightbrook.”
The pause that followed was brief but deliberate.
“And the other?”
Brannoc could have given a false name. It might have bought him an hour, perhaps a night. But false names were like false coin: useful only where no one cared to test them.
“Brannoc Ironmere.”
The gatehouse went still.
Rain ticked against his shoulder plates. Somewhere beyond the walls, a dog began to bark, then stopped as though struck.
“And the epithet?” the voice asked.
Brannoc’s jaw tightened.
Korvath turned his head a fraction. “They know you.”
“They know a story.”
“The story has teeth.”
“Open the gate,” Brannoc called.
“State your business.”
“To see someone.”
“Who?”
Brannoc looked at the black slit overhead. “If I knew that, I would not be here.”
That earned him movement. Men shifted along the wall. Metal scraped against stone.
Korvath leaned close enough that Brannoc smelled rainwater and bitter root on his breath. “You were meant to say you carried a message.”
“I carry no message.”
“You carry a war.”
“I carry myself.”
“That may be worse.”
The gate opened a handspan, then stopped. A man in a hooded mantle appeared in the gap. He held no visible weapon, which meant there were weapons close enough to reach them. His face was narrow and bloodless, his eyes fixed on Brannoc with the exhausted hatred of someone examining a familiar wound.
“You are expected,” he said.
Brannoc felt the muscles across his back draw tight. “By whom?”
The man’s eyes moved to Korvath. “Not by you.”
“Then open the gate.”
“You cannot enter armed.”
Brannoc almost laughed. The sound would have been ugly.
“I am a Sellsword Captain.”
“You are Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
“That is what I said.”
“And you were born in 255 AS.”
The rain seemed to thin around him.
He had heard the year spoken in ledgers, in curses, in the mouths of men who had counted his life against the shape of a prophecy. To hear it from this stranger made it feel less like a birth and more like a sentence.
Korvath’s hand emerged from his cloak. Not a weapon. A small iron token rested between his fingers, its surface blackened by use.
The gatekeeper saw it.
His expression changed.
Brannoc noticed. “What is that?”
“Something you were not meant to see,” Korvath said.
“You have made a habit of that.”
“I survive by habits.”
The gatekeeper reached through the gap and took the token. His thumb passed over its face. For the first time, something like fear showed in his features.
“Give up your sword,” he said.
“No.”
“Then remain outside.”
