He had never claimed it.
He had never been acknowledged.
The grimoire turned one final page.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed. Death: 300 AS. During the Accord of Mournthrone.
His heart gave one hard beat.
Then another.
The page did not burn. It did not fade. The words remained, patient and exact.
The stranger whispered, “No.”
Brannoc looked at the hooded figure. “You knew.”
The figure said nothing.
“You knew what I was.”
Still nothing.
“And you knew when I die.”
The hooded head tilted.
The answer was worse than denial.
Brannoc seized the grimoire and slammed it shut.
The chamber convulsed.
Stone cracked beneath his boots. The map flew from the table. The stranger cried out as the door blew inward, and a wind rushed through the room carrying ash, rain, and the distant clangor of bells.
The book bucked in Brannoc’s grip.
Something struck him from inside the cover.
Once.
Twice.
On the third blow, a seam split along the spine.
Beyond it waited not paper, but a red eye opening in the dark.
And from the passage outside came the sound of many feet climbing toward them.
Chapter 12
The record would say that Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.
The record would also say he was born in 255 AS, that he had been a major Sellsword Captain, and that he was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Records had a way of making a corpse seem simpler than a living man.
That night, with the wind dragging its nails along the black stone of Fenspire, Brannoc stood beneath the stark spire and listened to the fortress breathe.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach. It had been founded in 57 AS. It was a core location, garrisoned, with a garrison of 3,742. Those figures were carved into the gatehouse in the dry, obedient hand of a clerk. The stone had been polished around them by generations of gloves and palms.
Garrisoned.
The word had no warmth in it. It meant locked gates, rationed grain, watchfires, and men who slept with their boots within reach. It meant that the fortress belonged to whoever could keep it fed and armed. It meant the Reach had not been trusted to itself since the world was broken.
Brannoc touched the iron ring at his belt. The leather creaked beneath his glove.
Beyond the walls, darkness gathered in the ravines. Fenspire’s lamps burned in narrow slits, their light thin and yellow against the Gloaming Reach. Somewhere below, a horn gave a single note. It was answered from the outer wall, then from the high watchtower. The sound moved around him like a thought refusing to die.
“Three thousand seven hundred and forty-two,” said Korvath Nightbrook.
He sat in the corner where the stone sweated least, hood drawn low. Korvath was a minor figure in the world’s great reckonings, though he worked as a Smuggler and had survived by placing his feet in the gaps between lawful things. His presence was unobtrusive by instinct. Even stillness seemed to conceal him.
Brannoc did not look at him. “You count poorly.”
“I count what I’m told.”
“Then you’re a fool.”
Korvath’s mouth bent, not quite a smile. “That is why I remain alive.”
On the table between them lay a sealed packet, a narrow black case, and two objects wrapped in oilcloth. No mark declared who had sent the packet. No mark declared whom it served. That was the virtue of the five powers contending over the ruins: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown all preferred their hands clean when they could persuade another man to soil his.
Brannoc watched the packet.
The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS. It would end in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor. Such was the shape of the official account: beginning, struggle, victor. A neat road laid through mud.
But the Accord would collapse into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, because victories had teeth and the defeated did not always know how to kneel. The hidden truth was uglier still. The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
Brannoc knew that much already.
The knowledge had lodged beneath his ribs and made a second heart there.
“Open it,” Korvath said.
Brannoc’s red glove rested beside the packet. The epithet had followed him longer than most men could remember him without it. Red-Handed. It had been spoken with admiration in campfires, disgust in council chambers, and fear in rooms where rich men kept their daughters behind curtains. No canonical physical feature could have defined him better than the name. He was a Sellsword Captain because the world understood steel more readily than blood. He was the heir to the Bleeding Crown because blood understood him.
He broke the seal.
Inside was a strip of vellum, folded twice.
The words were brief.
Mournthrone had not been bought with coin alone. Someone had purchased silence, withdrawal, and the right to call treachery prudence. The payment had moved through hands that would later swear they had never met. The trail ended at a door that did not appear on any map.
Brannoc read it twice.
His first thought was of the Crown.
His second was that the Crown had never been his.
Unacknowledged heirs were useful creatures. They could be pointed at a throne as one pointed a hound at a throat. They could be denied when the hunt went wrong. The Bleeding Crown had given him no name, no seal, no inheritance he could hold in both hands. Only the knowledge, passed in whispers and withheld in public, that his claim existed.
A claim was a blade with no hilt.
Korvath leaned forward. “Is it true?”
“Truth is a coin minted by the hand holding it.”
“I asked whether it was true.”
Brannoc folded the vellum. “You asked because you already know.”
Korvath’s eyes glimmered under his hood. Guarded, wary. The demeanor of a smuggler was not cowardice. It was the discipline of a man who understood that every road had a watcher and every watcher could be bought.
“The message says the withdrawal is arranged,” Korvath said.
“The message says someone believes it is arranged.”
“And if the commander takes the bribe?”
“Then the Accord ends as it began—with men mistaking hunger for strategy.”
Korvath glanced toward the oilcloth. “You brought the regalia?”
Brannoc drew the first bundle nearer and peeled back the cloth.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay within, dark metal worked into a shape too restrained to be called ornamental. It was regalia, forged in 123 AS. Its defining record contained no attunement cost. The name had been entered into ledgers more carefully than the names of kings, as though binding the words might prevent the object from becoming something else.
Korvath did not touch it.
“Put it away,” he said.
“You were curious.”
“I was curious from a safe distance.”
Brannoc wrapped The Thrice-Bound Edge again. The cloth rasped over the metal like a tongue against a broken tooth.
The second bundle was heavier. He opened it with less care.
Edge of Gloamreach showed no blade at all. It was a grimoire, bound in material that drank the lamplight. Its forging date was not recorded in the supplied facts of any surviving register—if the register had ever existed. The attunement cost was 46. The number had been written on its inner cover in ink that seemed to have faded only where the eye rested upon it.
Brannoc shut the book.
For a moment, something moved in the dark seam between its pages.
He told himself it was the flame.
The thought did not comfort him.
“Why carry those into a garrisoned fortress?” Korvath asked.
Brannoc looked past him, through the narrow window. Fenspire’s walls rose in tiers above the Reach, disciplined and severe. Every tower had a watcher. Every watcher served a power, or believed he did.
“Because everyone here thinks a locked gate is the same as safety.”
“And is it?”
“No.”
The answer came too quickly. Korvath heard it. Brannoc heard him hear it.
In the yard below, soldiers crossed through the torchlight. Their armor flashed and vanished, flashed and vanished. The garrison of 3,742 was a mass reduced to individual footsteps. A fortress could contain an army and still be empty of loyalty.
“Crookvale has sent word,” Korvath said.
Brannoc turned.
“Crookvale?”
“Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. Rebuilt now. Garrison of 1004. Still outside the core holdings.”
“I know where Crookvale is.”
“Then you know why they are afraid.”
Brannoc did not answer.
Crookvale’s name carried the hard edge of a settlement built twice because the first version had not survived. It was wary and resilient, its governing principle reduced to the oldest commandment: endure what cannot be defeated. The garrison there was smaller than Fenspire’s, but smaller did not mean harmless. A knife did not need a regiment.
“What did they send?” Brannoc asked.
“Nothing. Only a warning.”
“Warnings are what men send when they want credit for courage.”
Korvath shifted. “They say the Bleeding Crown is moving.”
The room seemed to contract around the words.
Brannoc’s hand closed.
He could feel the old claim beneath his glove, beneath his skin, beneath all the years in which he had earned coin instead of titles. The Crown was not a thing one inherited. It was a wound passed from mouth to mouth. Those who bore it bled for those who denied it.
“The Bleeding Crown moves everywhere,” he said.
“Not like this.”
“Who told you?”
Korvath’s gaze slipped toward the door.
The silence after that was answer enough.
Brannoc rose. The chair legs scraped stone. In his bones, the motion was familiar: stand, measure the exits, identify the first throat to cut. The hard dangerous presence of a seasoned sellsword was not something he wore. It had worn him down until only that remained.
From the corridor came the muted tread of boots.
Korvath gathered the packet.
“Stay,” Brannoc said.
“I am a Smuggler. Staying is how I become evidence.”
“You are already evidence.”
The boots stopped outside.
A shadow thickened beneath the door.
Brannoc reached for The Thrice-Bound Edge. Then he paused, his fingers hovering over the wrapped regalia, while the black case on the table seemed to breathe beside the grimoire.
The Accord of Mournthrone had not yet become history. Its beginning lay ahead in 297 AS, its ending in 301 AS, and between those years men would swear oaths they intended to break. The Ashen Vanguard would be named victor. The losing commander would withdraw for a bribe. The collapse would unleash a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Brannoc knew none of that as a prophecy.
He knew it as the shape of a trap.
The door latch lifted.
Korvath whispered, “Captain.”
Brannoc drew steel.
The door opened a finger’s width, and a voice on the other side began to say his name—
The voice on the other side began to say his name—
“Brannoc Ironmere—”
He drove the blade through the gap.
The point met something softer than wood. A breath broke against the door, low and wet. Korvath flinched, but Brannoc did not. He held the sword there until the pressure vanished, then wrenched it free.
The door swung inward.
A man stood in the corridor with his back against the wall, one hand pressed beneath his ribs. He wore a servant’s grey, though the cloth was too fine for a servant and the boots beneath it had seen road dust, ash, and blood. His face was narrow and bloodless. A strip of black silk covered his mouth.
The Silent Choir.
Brannoc had seen their dead before. They were quieter.
The stranger looked at the sword, then at Brannoc’s hand around it. His eyes narrowed with something like recognition.
“Captain,” he said through the silk.
“Come in,” Brannoc replied. “Or fall out of the way.”
The man entered.
Korvath shut the door behind him and set the bar in place. The smuggler kept his gaze low, but his hand had gone beneath his coat. Brannoc knew what lay there. Korvath had carried a knife through three cities and trusted it more than any living soul.
The stranger removed the silk from his mouth. Blood had gathered at the corner of his lips.
“You’ve made a poor beginning,” Korvath said.
“I was invited.”
“No one invited you to bleed on my floor.”
The stranger’s attention remained fixed on Brannoc. “You were told to come alone.”
“I came with Korvath.”
“You were told—”
“I heard you.” Brannoc wiped his blade against the stranger’s sleeve. “You chose to speak my name before showing your face. That was your mistake.”
The man’s jaw tightened. “The order came from Fenspire.”
The room seemed to contract around the word.
Outside, wind worried at the shutters. The inn had been built against the ruin of an older structure, and through the walls Brannoc could hear the long complaints of stone settling upon stone. Somewhere below, a cup shattered. No voice rose after it. Even the house knew when to keep quiet.
Korvath glanced toward the grimoire.
The Edge of Gloamreach lay open on the table, its pages black-veined and damp-looking beneath the candlelight. The script along its margins seemed to lean away from the flame. Beside it rested the wrapped regalia, bound in oilcloth and cord.
The stranger saw both.
His face changed.
It was not fear. Fear had movement in it. This was calculation, cold and immediate, the kind a man performed when weighing the value of his life against the value of what might kill him.
Brannoc stepped between him and the table.
“Say what Fenspire wants.”
“Not Fenspire.” The man glanced toward the shuttered window. “Those who speak through it.”
“Then speak through your own mouth.”
The stranger swallowed. “The road north is closed.”
“By whom?”
“The Ashen Vanguard.”
Korvath gave a humorless breath. “They close roads whenever they remember they have soldiers.”
“They are searching wagons, rooms, bodies. They have orders to seize anything bearing the old seal.”
Brannoc felt the wrapped object behind him like a second heartbeat.
“Which old seal?”
The stranger looked at his hand.
Brannoc’s fingers were stained dark beneath the nails. The color never fully left them. Men called him the Red-Handed when they wanted to turn violence into a title, and called him other things when he was close enough to hear. His hand had earned all of it. None of it explained why the sight of his blood made the stranger look toward the regalia.
“Do not make me ask again,” Brannoc said.
The stranger’s mouth twitched. “The seal of the Bleeding Crown.”
Korvath’s knife came free beneath his coat.
The sound was small. It still seemed to fill the room.
Brannoc did not look at him. “You came from Fenspire carrying a warning about the Bleeding Crown.”
“I came carrying a warning about what will happen if the Crown’s claim is found here.”
“What claim?”
The stranger’s gaze lifted again, and this time it held something worse than calculation. Pity, perhaps. Or obedience.
“You know.”
“No.”
“You know enough to wear a dead man’s regalia.”
Brannoc’s hand tightened on the sword hilt.
The wrapped object had been taken from a chamber where dust lay thick as wool over every surface. It had not belonged to him. It had not been given. Things such as that did not pass cleanly from hand to hand. They left residue: whispers, debts, the taste of iron behind the teeth.
He had told himself he carried it because others sought it.
He had told himself many things.
“Leave,” he said.
The stranger stared.
“Go back to Fenspire. Tell them the room was empty. Tell them Korvath sold you a lie. Tell them I took the road south.”
“The road south is watched.”
“Then choose a road that isn’t.”
“You don’t understand.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “That is what frightened men say when they want obedience.”
The stranger took a step toward the table.
Brannoc’s sword rose.
Korvath shifted at the same instant, knife angled toward the man’s throat. The stranger stopped with his hand suspended in the air.
For a moment they stood as three pieces on a board none of them had made.
Then the floor beneath them gave a soft groan.
Not the building settling.
Something moved below.
Korvath’s head turned. “That wasn’t there before.”
Brannoc listened.
A scrape passed under the boards, slow and deliberate. Dust sifted from the ceiling. The candle flame bent toward the table, though no wind entered the sealed room.
The Edge of Gloamreach had closed.
Its cover lay shut over the pages, though Brannoc had not seen it move.
The stranger whispered something in a language Brannoc did not know.
Korvath said, “What did you bring with you?”
“Nothing.”
“Everyone brings something.”
The scrape came again, nearer.
Brannoc looked at the grimoire. The leather cover had begun to sweat a dark sheen. Along its edge, a line of pale symbols showed and vanished, showing and vanishing, as if the book were breathing through its teeth.
He had not touched it since Korvath placed it on the table. He had not dared. The cost of attunement was written in the margin, exact and pitiless: forty-six.
He knew the number.
He did not know what it purchased.
The stranger drew a small object from inside his grey coat. Not a weapon. A shard of blackened bone, threaded on a cord. He held it between finger and thumb.
Korvath went still.
“You know that?” Brannoc asked.
“No.”
“Your face says otherwise.”
“My face says I dislike the room.”
The stranger pressed the bone to his tongue.
The walls answered.
A thin vibration passed through the stone. The candle guttered. From beneath the floor came a muffled knocking, not frantic, not pleading. Patient.
Brannoc felt the old instinct rise in him: measure the exits, identify the weakest throat, decide who died first. It had kept him alive when banners failed and employers discovered principles. It had made men follow him into places from which no honest man returned.
But beneath that instinct another voice stirred.
Not a memory. Memories had edges.
This was inheritance.
The word came to him with the weight of a chain.
He saw, not with his eyes, a crown wet with blood. A hall without windows. Kneeling figures with their faces hidden. The sensation of a hand being placed upon his brow—not gently, not lovingly, but as one might test the edge of a blade.
He blinked.
The room returned.
Korvath was watching him. “Captain?”
“Do not call me that.”
The smuggler’s expression hardened. “You’ve been called worse.”
The stranger lowered the bone. “They’re beneath us.”
“Who?”
“The Choir.”
“Your Choir?”
“They are not mine.”
“Then whose?”
He looked at the sealed grimoire. “The ones who were buried without silence.”
A second knock came from below.
This time the boards lifted.
A black line appeared between them, narrow as a cut. Cold air poured through it, carrying the smell of wet earth and old smoke. The stranger stepped back. Korvath raised his knife.
Brannoc reached for the wrapped regalia.
The cord around it had loosened.
He had tied that cord himself.
The oilcloth unfolded a little beneath his hand, revealing a sliver of metal pale as moonlit bone. No inscription showed. No light clung to it. Yet the sight of it brought pain behind his eyes.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Regalia forged in 123 AS.
The name rose from the grimoire’s pages, from the whispered records of men who had murdered for less than a title. He had not known whether the artifact was a weapon, a crown, or a sentence. In that moment it felt like all three.
The stranger said, “Do not draw it.”
Brannoc looked at him.
“Why?”
“Because it will answer.”
“To what?”
The black line in the floor widened.
Something beneath the room exhaled.
The stranger’s bloodless face cracked at last. “To you.”
Korvath seized Brannoc’s shoulder. “We leave.”
Brannoc shook him off. “There’s nowhere to go.”
“There is always somewhere to go.”
“Not when the house is built over a throat.”
The floorboards split with a sound like wet timber breaking. A pale hand rose through the darkness below, fingers groping at the air. Its nails were packed with soil. A strip of black cloth clung to its wrist.
The Silent Choir had sent more than a messenger.
Brannoc drew The Thrice-Bound Edge from its wrappings.
The room went silent.
Not quiet. Silent.
The wind ceased. The inn below ceased. Korvath’s breath vanished. The stranger’s mouth opened, but no sound came from it.
Across the table, the Edge of Gloamreach opened by itself.
Its pages turned with terrible care.
A line of writing appeared in the candleless dark.
Brannoc read it.
His own name had been written there long before he entered the room.
The hand below the floor closed around the edge of the boards. The stranger fell to his knees. Korvath began to move toward the door, but Brannoc caught his sleeve.
“Wait.”
The smuggler looked at him as though he had become something he could no longer sell to anyone.
Beneath them, the buried thing began to speak.
The sound rose through the cracks, shaping itself around a title Brannoc had never accepted and could never escape.
He lifted the regalia higher, and from the dark under the floor came the first clear word—
“—heir.”
The word did not strike Brannoc’s ears. It entered him through the soles of his boots and climbed, cold as gravewater, into the marrow of his legs.
Korvath Nightbrook made a sound behind him. Not a prayer. Korvath had never trusted anything that could not be bribed, threatened, or drowned. His hand went beneath his coat, where a knife waited in the dark.
“Do not,” Brannoc said.
The buried hand tightened on the floorboard.
The stranger remained on his knees. Candlelight had not returned, yet Brannoc could see the man’s face with an intimacy that made the sight obscene: the wet shine of his eyes, the blood at his mouth, the trembling hinge of his jaw.
“Whose heir?” Korvath whispered.
The boards answered.
“Bleeding Crown.”
There it was. Not a title spoken by heralds or carved into a gate. A wound given grammar.
Brannoc held The Thrice-Bound Edge in both hands. The regalia was heavier than iron and colder than the dead beneath the floor. Three bands circled its dark length, each joined to the next without seam. He had found no maker’s mark upon it, only the old record pressed into its inner face:
Forged in 123 AS.
The numbers had seemed meaningless when he first read them. Now they shone like teeth.
A second line surfaced beneath the first.
No attunement cost.
Korvath leaned close enough for Brannoc to smell rain and old leather on him. “That is not possible.”
“Nothing is impossible in a room built over a grave.”
“It has a cost.”
“Then pay it.”
The smuggler’s eyes flicked toward him. “You know what it is?”
Brannoc looked down at the regalia. The bands had begun to pulse—not with light, but with a pressure that made the air throb in his throat.
He knew the answer before the voice gave it.
“Name,” said the buried thing.
The dark shifted beneath the floor. Somewhere below, something dragged itself across stone. A long scrape. Then another.
Brannoc thought of the names men had given him in alleys, on battlefields, over cups emptied by shaking hands. Captain. Butcher. Red-Handed. He had accepted all of them because a name was a coin, and he had learned young to spend whatever coin lay nearest.
There was one name he had never been permitted to possess.
His mother had died before she could speak it. Men who knew it had looked at him and found reasons to look elsewhere. In the Bleeding Crown’s shadow, blood did not make a son. Blood made a threat.
“I am Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed,” he said.
The floor groaned.
“No.”
Korvath seized his sleeve. “That is enough.”
Brannoc tore free. The movement sent a dull ache through his shoulder. “You heard it.”
“I heard a corpse trying to make you useful.”
“That is most kings.”
At the word kings, the buried thing laughed.
Dust sifted from the ceiling. The stranger pressed both palms to the floor as if to hold it shut. His fingers had split at the nails.
“Do you know what waits under a crown?” Brannoc asked him.
The stranger’s head turned. “You.”
“No.”
“Your blood.”
“Blood is cheap.”
“Not yours.”
The answer moved through the chamber like a draft. For one moment Brannoc saw the room as it had been before the rot: stone walls washed white, bronze lamps burning along the ledges, banners hanging from the beams. He saw himself standing at the far end beneath a crown he had never worn. His hands were red to the wrists. Around him, men knelt not from loyalty but from calculation.
Then the vision broke.
The chamber returned. The floor. The stranger. Korvath with his knife half-drawn.
Brannoc breathed through his nose until the tremor passed.
On the wall beside him, dampness gathered in a shape like writing.
Born in 255 AS.
He stared at it.
Korvath read over his shoulder. “What does that mean?”
“My birth.”
“You never told me your birth.”
“You never asked.”
“I ask about cargo.”
“Then consider me badly packed.”
The words formed another line.
Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Korvath stepped away from him.
Brannoc felt the withdrawal more sharply than he would have liked. The smuggler had always kept distance, but distance was not the same as fear. Fear had a smell. It sweetened the breath.
“The Bleeding Crown,” Korvath said. “That is not a campfire claim. That is a death sentence.”
“Most useful truths are.”
“You knew?”
“I suspected.”
“You carried suspicion into this place?”
“I carried a sword.”
“You carried us into this place.”
Brannoc turned on him. The regalia lay between them like an accusation. “You followed.”
“I was paid to lead.”
“By whom?”
Korvath’s mouth closed.
The buried thing spoke again.
“Not by the Crown.”
The words were followed by a wet cracking sound from beneath the boards.
The stranger began to weep. Silently. Tears traced pale paths through the grime on his face.
Brannoc looked at the sealed door. It had no latch now. No hinge. Only a slab of stone set into the arch as though the room had decided it preferred them inside.
On the floor near the wall lay the second artifact, its leather cover warped by damp. The title had been stamped in letters that seemed to drink what little darkness surrounded them:
Edge of Gloamreach.
He had thought it a grimoire, nothing more. A book worth more than a month of soldiers’ pay to the right buyer, and worth killing for to the wrong one. The cover shivered without being touched.
Korvath noticed it too.
“Leave it,” he said.
Brannoc crouched. “Its attunement cost is 46.”
The smuggler stared. “You can read that?”
“Someone carved it into the clasp.”
“Then it is not a book.”
“No. It is a debt with pages.”
The clasp opened.
The first leaf was black and soft as skin. No script marked it. When Brannoc bent over it, a smell rose from the page: smoke after rain, and the bitter mineral scent of a place where magic had burned the earth bare.
The room’s darkness gathered over the grimoire.
Images stirred in the blankness.
A highland settlement crouched beneath a white sky, its rebuilt walls crooked against the wind. A watchtower leaned over narrow streets. Men stood beneath its gate with weapons held close, watching every road.
Crookvale.
The name appeared without ink.
Founded in 295 AS. In The High Spires. Rebuilt. Garrison of 1004. Outside the core holdings.
Korvath bent beside him, and the color drained from his face.
“Crookvale,” he said. “That place has changed hands.”
“Has it?”
“Enough times that no hand remains clean.”
The page turned itself.
A spire rose from a gray reach of land, stark and solitary, piercing a sky the color of old bruises. Walls crowded its base. Within them, ranks moved in ordered files. The air around the image seemed disciplined, watchful, unable to sleep.
Fenspire.
Founded in 57 AS. In the Gloaming Reach. Core location. Garrison of 3,742.
Brannoc felt the pressure in the room change. Fenspire had already been named to him once, a place of permanent blades and closed gates, but now the grimoire showed it as something older than the kingdoms that claimed it. The spire did not seem built. It seemed thrust upward by the dead beneath the world.
A third image replaced it.
A throne room split down the middle. Men in ash-colored armor stood behind one standard; figures in dark crimson stood behind another. Between them lay a table bearing a document, its seal broken, its ink running as if the parchment had begun to bleed.
Across the page appeared:
The Accord of Mournthrone. Began in 297 AS. Ended in 301 AS. The Ashen Vanguard named victor.
The image did not settle into triumph.
The commander in crimson stood alone at the table. A hand—not attached to any visible body—placed a small chest before him. He opened it. Gold glimmered within, then vanished beneath the falling shadow of his fingers.
The commander turned away from the field.
Brannoc watched the withdrawal. He understood it with the cold certainty of a wound reopening.
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw,” he said.
Korvath looked at him. “You say that as if you were there.”
“I say it because the book does.”
Behind the commander, soldiers continued fighting in the image. They did not know the battle had already been sold. They died beneath banners that had become lies.
The page darkened further.
The Ashen Vanguard’s standard remained standing over Mournthrone, but beneath it the land broke into smaller fires. Roads vanished under ambushes. Supply wagons burned. Men hunted men through ravines and ruined villages. The same sword appeared in different hands, passing from one corpse to another.
Text crawled across the black leaf.
Its collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Korvath shut the grimoire.
The pressure vanished. The room seemed suddenly too small to contain their breathing.
“You have seen enough,” he said.
Brannoc kept his gaze on the cover. “No.”
“You have seen what comes.”
“I have seen what may come.”
“You saw your name before you entered.”
“That is different.”
“It is not.”
The voice beneath the floor interrupted them.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The regalia jerked in his hands.
The three bands unwound.
Not physically. The metal remained whole, yet each ring seemed to open into a separate horizon. In the first, Brannoc stood beneath a blood-colored sky. In the second, he watched men kneel before a crown. In the third, he lay on a stone floor with his own blood spreading beneath him.
The year came last.
300 AS.
His fingers tightened until the regalia cut into his palms.
“During the Accord of Mournthrone,” the buried thing said.
Korvath moved toward the door again. “We are leaving.”
“There is no door.”
“Then we make one.”
“With what?”
“With you, if necessary.”
Brannoc almost smiled. The sound would not come.
The vision sharpened.
He saw a hall drowned in smoke. He saw the marks of the Ashen Vanguard upon the walls. He saw men fighting too close for swords, grappling in the red dark. Someone drove a blade into his side. Someone else held him upright long enough to whisper a word he could not hear.
Then the crown appeared—not above his head, but beneath his corpse.
The Bleeding Crown waited where his blood touched stone.
Brannoc let the regalia fall.
It struck the floor without a sound.
The hand below the boards spread wide. Every finger pressed upward, outlining itself through the wood.
Korvath’s knife was in his hand now. “Say something.”
Brannoc looked at him.
The smuggler’s face had settled into its guarded shape again, but his eyes betrayed him. He was afraid of the room. Afraid of the artifacts. Afraid of the future.
Most of all, he was afraid Brannoc might believe it.
Brannoc understood. Belief was the first chain. Acceptance was the second.
He stepped over The Thrice-Bound Edge and placed his palm upon the boards.
The hand beneath met his.
The contact was gentle.
A warmth entered him—not comfort, but recognition.
The buried thing spoke in his own voice.
“You died in 300 AS.”
Brannoc stared into the dark.
Then the floor began to open.
Chapter 13
Rain worried the shutters of Fenspire as though it had teeth.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood beneath the tower’s black ribs and listened to the storm gnaw at the stone. Beyond the arrow slits, the Gloaming Reach lay drowned in dusk, its marsh-lights trembling under the rain. Fenspire’s stark spire rose through the dimness like a spear driven into the world by a dying god.
The garrison numbered 3,742. Brannoc knew the count because the quartermaster had repeated it three times, each repetition carrying the brittle pride of a man who believed numbers could keep a gate closed. Fenspire was a core location, garrisoned and vigilant, and the men within its walls wore that vigilance as another layer of mail.
It would not save them.
Nothing saved anyone. It only delayed the shape of the ruin.
“You are dripping on the map.”
Korvath Nightbrook’s voice came from the dark beside the brazier.
Brannoc looked down. Water crawled from his cloak onto the table, gathering in the inked valleys and blackening the parchment. Korvath watched the spreading stain with a smuggler’s guarded displeasure. He favored the shadows even when there were none to hide in, his presence unobtrusive, his eyes always measuring the door, the window, the nearest hand that might reach for a knife.
“The map was already wrong,” Brannoc said.
“Maps are never wrong. Men are wrong about where they stand.”
“That is a distinction fit for a man who sells passage through holes in walls.”
Korvath’s mouth tightened. “And a sellsword captain is fit to judge the honesty of holes?”
The words settled between them.
Brannoc’s hand rested on the pommel at his hip. The knuckles beneath his wet glove were dark with old blood. The rain had not washed it away. Rain was not made for that kind of work.
He had been born in 255 AS, though the Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged the blood in his veins. He was its unacknowledged heir, a secret kept beneath seals, dead tongues, and the obedience of frightened men. A crown could be denied in a cradle and still grow teeth in the dark.
Now the Accord of Mournthrone was eating those teeth.
“Say it,” Korvath murmured.
Brannoc lifted his gaze.
“You brought me here to say something.”
“I brought you here because the western postern is watched by men who would not recognize you if you were wearing a crown.”
“I am not wearing one.”
“Not yet.”
The brazier coughed. Smoke crawled low across the chamber, smelling of wet wool and bitter coal. On the far wall, a rack of regalia waited beneath dustcloths. The Thrice-Bound Edge had been forged in 123 AS. Its name was stitched into the inventory slate in a careful hand, followed by a blank mark where no attunement cost had ever been recorded. The object itself was hidden beneath black cloth, restrained even in silence, as if its bindings had learned patience.
Beside it lay the grimoire Edge of Gloamreach.
Its cover was gray as old ash. The attunement cost was 46. Nothing in the records named its forging date. The absence troubled Brannoc more than any number might have. A thing without a beginning was a thing with room for every lie.
He had seen men kill for lesser uncertainties.
Korvath followed his stare. “The books say the grimoire is useless to you.”
“The books say many things.”
“They say the cost is 46.”
“Then the books have counted one burden.”
“And missed the others?”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “You are learning.”
A bell sounded somewhere below. Once. Then again.
The tower answered with a tremor through the floor.
“Movement at the gate,” Korvath said.
“No.”
The smuggler turned his head.
Brannoc listened. Beneath the rain, beneath the mutter of the garrison and the groan of the old stone, he heard the true sound: not boots advancing, but men leaving their posts. A slow loosening. A withdrawal dressed as caution.
The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS, and already every oath spoken beneath it had acquired a hidden price. The Ashen Vanguard named itself the guardian of order. House Morvain called order the property of the strong. The Silent Choir listened for weakness in every vow. The Iron-Ring Cartel measured loyalty by what it could carry. The Bleeding Crown waited behind its curtains and let other hands bleed for its inheritance.
Five powers, all sharpening the same knife.
“Your commander is pulling back,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s eyes narrowed. “You know that?”
“I know the sound of a coward trying to make retreat resemble strategy.”
“You were told there would be no withdrawal.”
“I was told many things.”
“By whom?”
Brannoc looked again at the covered regalia, the blank cost, the nameless forging. “By men who believed a sealed order could command the dead.”
The door opened.
A soldier entered with rain shining on his shoulders. No herald announced him. No servant took his cloak. His face held the pallor of someone who had received news and decided not to understand it.
“The western barricade has been abandoned,” he said.
Korvath gave a small, humorless laugh. “There. Now we have the truth.”
Brannoc did not move. The soldier’s gaze dropped to his red-stained hand, then rose again.
“Who ordered it?”
The man swallowed. “The order bore the commander’s seal.”
“Did the commander give it?”
“I was not present.”
“Then you know nothing.”
“I know the men were paid.”
The rain pressed harder against the shutters.
Korvath stepped near the brazier. “Paid by whom?”
The soldier’s silence was answer enough. In the walls of Fenspire, it seemed every stone leaned closer to hear.
Brannoc felt the old inheritance stir beneath his ribs—not pride, not hope, but the cold recognition that the world made room for crowns only after they had been fed enough corpses.
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw,” he said.
The soldier flinched as though Brannoc had struck him.
Korvath’s eyes became two dark slits. “You say that as if you expected it.”
“I expected a price. I did not know its shape.”
“And now?”
“Now I know the shape is treason.”
“No,” Korvath said. “Treason is a word used by the poor to describe a bargain they were not invited to join.”
Brannoc turned on him. “Be careful.”
“I am always careful. That is why I am still alive.”
The words carried no boast. Korvath said them as one might name the weather.
Below, the bell rang a third time.
This time the tower doors groaned open.
Brannoc crossed to the nearest slit. Far beneath him, torches moved through the rain in a disorderly stream. Men were leaving Fenspire. Some carried packs. Some carried weapons. One carried a bundle that sagged with a human weight. No one looked upward.
At the edge of the courtyard, the insignia of the Ashen Vanguard passed beneath a veil of rain.
Brannoc’s reflection hovered in the glassless opening: a broad darkness, a scarlet hand, a face the stone refused to give back. He had no canonical feature for the world to remember. Let it remember the epithet instead. Let it remember the martial station, the hard presence of a Sellsword Captain, the hand that had closed around too many hilts and too few promises.
Korvath came to stand beside him.
“What will you do?”
“Stay.”
“Why?”
“Because the men leaving will tell themselves they chose to survive. I want them to see what survival costs.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one I have.”
“You are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened around the pommel.
Korvath continued, softly now. “You cannot keep pretending this is merely a contract.”
“I have never pretended.”
“You have worn hired steel while others fought over your blood.”
“And what would you have me wear?”
“A claim.”
“A claim is a blade with no handle.”
“Then grasp it by the edge.”
Brannoc looked at him. Korvath’s guarded face had lost its smuggler’s calm. For the first time, the man seemed afraid—not for himself, but of what Brannoc might do if fear became indistinguishable from purpose.
Outside, the last of the torches vanished through the gate.
Fenspire remained.
Its garrison of 3,742 had become a number without a body. The walls remained disciplined, vigilant, and nearly empty of the certainty that had held them. Somewhere in the lower levels, locks were being opened. Somewhere else, men were deciding which allegiance would forgive them most cheaply.
Brannoc took the dustcloth from The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The regalia beneath was darker than iron and bound in three narrow bands. No attunement cost marked its record. The absence seemed to watch him.
Korvath stepped back. “Do not.”
“Do not what?”
“Touch what you cannot unmake.”
Brannoc laid his red hand upon the hilt.
The chamber went still.
For an instant he felt the whole Accord of Mournthrone gathered inside the metal: its beginning in 297 AS, its broken vows, its banners lowered by hands bought in secret. He saw no victory in it. The Ashen Vanguard might be named victor when the accord ended in 301 AS, but victory was a word men carved over graves to stop the graves from speaking.
The truth rose through the binding like a drowned thing.
The Accord of Mournthrone had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Brannoc drew one breath.
Then something struck the door below, and Korvath whispered, “They are coming for you—”
The second blow shook dust from the lintel.
Korvath flinched. Brannoc did not. He kept his hand upon The Thrice-Bound Edge and felt the metal drinking the tremor from his bones. Beneath his palm, the regalia was cold enough to burn. Its forged silence pressed against him, threefold and patient, as if the blade had been waiting for a hand that would not mistake restraint for mercy.
“Which door?” Brannoc asked.
“The only one they need.”
Korvath’s voice had gone thin. He stood beside the shuttered window with one hand inside his coat, where a smuggler kept the things he trusted least. The room smelled of damp wool, lamp oil, and the bitter mineral tang rising from the grimoire open upon the table.
Edge of Gloamreach had no cover. Its pages lay exposed to the air, black leaves veined with grey script. The book’s attunement cost was 46, and the knowledge of it had settled into Brannoc’s skull with the weight of a nail. Every time his gaze touched the open page, the letters seemed to lean toward him.
Another blow.
The hinges cried.
Brannoc lifted his hand from The Thrice-Bound Edge. A red print remained upon the metal. His blood, or the memory of it. With the binding, the distinction had become a poor man’s argument.
“Can you get us out?”
Korvath looked toward the floor.
“No.”
“Then why are you still standing?”
“I was waiting for you to say something clever.”
“I have never said anything clever.”
“That is why I am afraid.”
The door shuddered in its frame. A splinter fell inward and struck the flagstones. Through the crack came a blade of pale corridor light, and within it the moving darkness of someone’s shoulder.
Brannoc turned to the table.
The page had changed.
He had seen no hand touch it. No wind moved in the sealed room. Yet the ink had gathered itself into a line beneath the older script, each mark wet and shining.
Fenspire.
The word stood alone for a breath, then was followed by another.
The Purge of Blackport waged at Fenspire in 319 AS.
Brannoc read it twice.
The room fell away.
He stood beneath a sky the color of old bruises. A spire rose before him, stark and narrow, its upper reaches swallowed by Gloaming Reach mist. The stones of Fenspire were dark with rain. Not red. Rain, he told himself. The mind reached for blood because blood was easier to understand.
Men moved through the streets with covered mouths. Their hands were wrapped in ash-colored cloth. Doors hung open. Behind one, a bowl rolled slowly across a floor and came to rest against a threshold.
Brannoc heard no cries.
That was the worst of it.
Silence made a city complicit with its own ruin. It turned every wall into a witness and every shutter into a closed eye. Far above, something struck the spire bell, but the sound did not descend. It remained trapped in the clouds, trembling there like a thought no one dared complete.
He felt Fenspire’s garrison around him—not as bodies, but as a pressure. Disciplined vigilance sunk into every stone. Permanent occupation had given the place a second skeleton. Men could be slain. Orders could be burned. The garrison remained in the walls.
Then the vision twisted.
Blackport appeared in the rain.
Not as a place, but as a wound carried from hand to hand. Its name was carved into doors, scratched into helmets, whispered by mouths that immediately shut. Brannoc saw the purge not from above, nor from the street, but from inside the instant before a man made a choice.
A torch rose.
A child’s cup broke.
Someone behind a door pressed both hands over their lips.
Then the room returned.
Brannoc staggered against the table. Edge of Gloamreach groaned beneath his fist. The pages fluttered though the shutters remained closed.
Korvath caught his sleeve.
“What did you see?”
“Fenspire.”
The smuggler’s grip tightened. “That means nothing.”
“It will.”
The door gave another inch. A dark iron hook appeared through the gap and caught the inner brace. The wood splintered around it.
Korvath swore softly.
Brannoc stared at the grimoire. The letters were fading now, sinking into the black page as though ashamed of what they had said.
“Who is behind that door?”
“People who have been paid to believe they are righteous.”
“House Morvain?”
“I did not say that.”
“The Silent Choir?”
“I did not say that either.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Korvath’s eyes hardened. “You have a gift for naming enemies after they have already found us.”
Brannoc reached for his sword. The grip came easily, familiar as a scar. His other hand remained red, whether by blood or binding no longer mattered. The Thrice-Bound Edge lay upon the table between them, regalia rather than weapon, though the distinction had always depended upon who was holding it.
A voice spoke through the broken door.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
His name sounded wrong in that mouth. Not feared. Not respected. Catalogued.
Korvath moved toward the window. “There.”
The shutter was fastened from within, but its lower hinge had rotted away. Beyond it waited a narrow drop into darkness. Korvath knelt and tested the opening with his fingers.
“Can you climb?”
“Can you?”
“I asked first.”
Brannoc looked down at his boots. The room seemed to sway under him. He had commanded men in rain that turned bowstrings slack. He had watched banners lowered by hands bought in secret. He had carried the truth of Mournthrone inside his chest while others carved victory over the dead and called the carving history.
Now a smuggler was asking whether he could climb.
“Yes.”
Korvath gave him a bitter smile. “Good. I hate rescuing corpses.”
The brace split.
The door opened three fingers wide.
A hand entered first, armored to the wrist. It held no weapon. That unsettled Brannoc more than a sword would have. Men came to kill with steel. Men came to arrest with empty hands. Empty hands belonged to courts, crowns, and those who believed their violence would be forgiven.
Brannoc seized The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The room darkened.
The regalia did not blaze. It did not sing. It tightened the air around his fingers until his bones felt laced together. The pressure climbed his arm, crossed his shoulder, and settled behind his eyes.
A second vision opened.
He saw a hall beneath Fenspire. Stone pillars. Damp flags. A row of kneeling figures facing a wall. No faces. The absence was deliberate.
At the end of the hall stood a throne-shaped chair draped in black cloth.
Someone had placed a crown upon it.
Not worn. Waiting.
Brannoc felt the old wound inside himself stir—the claim never spoken where it could be answered, the bloodline left unacknowledged, the inheritance that had taught him to sleep with one hand beneath his pillow. The Bleeding Crown had never called him son. Crowns did not call. They summoned, and men mistook the summons for honor.
The vision showed him the crown beneath the cloth.
Then it showed him fire.
Brannoc tore himself free.
The table overturned. Edge of Gloamreach struck the floor, its pages snapping open to a spread of blank blackness. Korvath cursed and shoved the window wider.
“Hurry.”
The door burst inward.
Three figures crowded the gap. Their faces were hidden behind ash-colored masks. The first carried a short sword. The second bore a hooked pole. The third held a sealed tube against his chest.
Brannoc stepped between them and the table.
The first figure crossed the threshold.
Brannoc’s sword met his.
Steel cracked against steel. The masked man’s wrist buckled. Brannoc turned the blow aside and drove his shoulder into the man’s chest. He went backward into the others, and for one breath the doorway became a knot of limbs and cloth.
“Now,” Korvath said.
Brannoc seized the sill.
The drop below was black, though he could make out the glimmer of wet stone. Wind climbed the wall and entered his sleeves. Behind him, the attackers disentangled themselves. One of them shouted his name again, but this time the voice carried fear.
Brannoc lowered himself through the opening.
His boots found the outer ledge.
Korvath came after him, clutching the grimoire under one arm. The book’s pages beat against his ribs like trapped wings.
“Give me your hand.”
Brannoc looked up.
The first masked figure had reached the window. Rain shone on the blade in his grip. Behind him, The Thrice-Bound Edge lay on the floor, still gathering the room into its silence.
Korvath stretched down.
Brannoc reached for him.
And from within the chamber, beneath the splintered door and the footfalls rushing nearer, the grimoire began to speak in a voice made of turning pages—one word at a time, each syllable carrying the cold of a future Brannoc had not yet lived.
Korvath’s fingers closed around his wrist.
The grimoire spoke again.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The name entered the rain and seemed to weigh it down.
Korvath hauled him upward. Brannoc struck the ledge with his shoulder, rolled across the wet stone, and came up on one knee. The window behind them flared with a pallid light. For an instant the chamber showed itself through the opening: the masked figure at the sill, the blade lifted, the door bowing inward beneath the men beyond it.
Then the darkness folded shut.
Korvath seized the back of Brannoc’s coat and dragged him along the ledge.
“Move.”
“I am moving.”
“You are listening.”
“Hard not to.”
The grimoire’s voice followed them through the storm.
“Born in 255 AS.”
Brannoc’s hand found the wall. The stone was slick with rain and old soot. Below, the drop vanished into blackness. Somewhere beneath that blackness, water hammered rock with the patient violence of a thing that had never needed to hurry.
Korvath pressed himself against the outer face of the tower. His breath came thinly. A smuggler survived by distrusting open ground, open doors, and every silence that seemed too complete. Now there was nowhere to conceal himself but the rain.
“Do you hear it?” Brannoc asked.
“I hear men behind us.”
“The book.”
“I hear that too.”
“Then why are you still carrying it?”
Korvath looked at him. Rain ran from his brow into his eyes, giving his expression the shine of grief.
“Because you told me to.”
“I told you to bring it out.”
“And now it is out.”
The grimoire rested beneath Korvath’s arm, bound in leather darkened by water. Its pages stirred without wind. Each turn made a dry, intimate sound, like a tongue passing over teeth.
Brannoc reached for it.
Korvath jerked away. “No.”
“You cannot carry it and climb.”
“I can carry it.”
“You are shaking.”
“I am a smuggler. Shaking is how I keep my hands honest.”
Behind them, wood split. A masked face appeared at the window, pale beneath its covering. The figure thrust an arm through the opening and swept the blade along the ledge. Steel rang against stone where Brannoc’s throat had been.
He drove his boot into the hand.
The fingers vanished. The blade clattered away into the dark.
“Climb,” Brannoc said.
A rope ladder hung below the ledge, its wet rungs tapping against the tower. Korvath lowered himself first, pressing the grimoire to his ribs. Brannoc followed, one hand on the rope, one gripping the wall. The tower leaned out over the ravine. Every gust shifted the ladder beneath them.
From above came a cry, then another. The men in the chamber had found the window.
Brannoc descended.
His palms burned. Rain soaked his sleeves and found the old cuts beneath them. The dark below had no bottom. He had known worse places. He had made camp in worse places. He had slept with a knife under his tongue while men negotiated the price of his next sunrise.
But he had never feared a book.
The Edge of Gloamreach whispered.
“Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Korvath halted below him.
The ladder swung out from the wall.
Brannoc’s boot struck Korvath’s shoulder. “Keep going.”
“You heard it.”
“Keep going.”
“You are—”
“Keep going.”
Korvath obeyed, though obedience sat badly upon him. He descended until his boots met a narrow shelf of stone. Brannoc joined him. The shelf ran around the tower, scarcely broad enough for a man’s foot, and ended at a seam in the rock where darkness breathed cold air.
A passage.
Korvath placed one hand against the seam. “This was not on the plan.”
“There was a plan?”
“There was always a plan.”
“Then your plan has improved.”
He pushed. The stone gave inward, revealing a cleft. Brannoc entered sideways, shoulders scraping grit from the walls. Korvath followed with the grimoire held above the water gathering at the floor.
The passage narrowed, then opened into a low chamber beneath the tower. Rain dripped through the ceiling. The air tasted of iron and wet ash.
Korvath set the book down.
It opened by itself.
The pages were blank for a breath. Then ink rose from the fibers in thin black threads, arranging itself into lines.
“Forged in 123 AS.”
Brannoc stared.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay far above them, still inside the chamber they had fled. He could feel its silence through the stone: a pressure without weight, a restraint that seemed to bind not flesh but intention. Regalia, the record had called it. The name had sounded ceremonial when first they found it.
Nothing ceremonial had ever looked at him that way.
Korvath leaned close to the page. “What was forged?”
“The Thrice-Bound Edge.”
“Regalia,” Korvath muttered. “That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one the book gives.”
Another line appeared.
“No attunement cost.”
Korvath rubbed his mouth. “That should comfort me.”
“It does not comfort you.”
“It is not trying to.”
Above them, boots crossed the chamber floor. Dust sifted down. The masked figures had reached the stair or found another way around. Brannoc imagined the blade in one of their hands, wet with rain, searching the dark by instinct.
He looked at the grimoire. “What does it want?”
Korvath gave a humorless smile. “You ask that as though it has manners.”
The page turned.
“Attunement cost: 46.”
The words were written beneath the name Edge of Gloamreach.
Korvath took a step back.
Brannoc felt the number settle inside him. Not as knowledge. As a hook.
“Forty-six what?” Korvath said.
“The book does not say.”
“Then it may say anything.”
“It has not.”
“It has named you.”
Brannoc looked down at his hands. In the weak light, the water on them appeared dark. His epithet had followed him through camps, courts, alleys, and battlefields: the Red-Handed. Men gave it to him because they needed a story that did not include the things he had done before they met him. It was easier to blame the color than ask where it came from.
The Edge of Gloamreach turned a page.
“Accord of Mournthrone.”
Brannoc’s jaw tightened.
Korvath whispered, “Do not read it.”
The book wrote on.
“Begins in 297 AS.”
The chamber seemed to contract. Even the dripping stopped, listening.
“Ends in 301 AS.”
Korvath reached for the cover.
Brannoc caught his wrist. “Let it speak.”
“It is speaking of war.”
“It is speaking of what comes.”
“That is worse.”
The ink gathered in a thick black pool before forming the next words.
“Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Brannoc released Korvath.
For a moment he saw a field beneath a colorless sky, though no such field lay beyond the chamber. He saw banners dragged through mud. He saw men kneeling because the alternative was to remain standing before those who had won. He saw the five powers tightening their hands around the realm: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown.
The names were not merely factions. They were appetites wearing heraldry.
Korvath read them over his shoulder. “The Ashen Vanguard wins.”
“The book says so.”
“Books lie.”
“Not when they are frightened.”
Korvath looked at him sharply.
The grimoire’s pages trembled.
“The losing commander bribed to withdraw.”
Neither man spoke.
Above, the pursuit had gone quiet. That silence was worse than the boots. The masked figures were searching now, and searchers were patient when they believed the world had already closed around their prey.
Korvath bent over the grimoire. “Who?”
The ink did not answer.
Brannoc felt the old pressure behind his ribs, the one that came whenever someone spoke of crowns as though crowns were objects instead of wounds. The Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged him. It had not needed to. Blood kept its own account.
The page turned.
“Died in 300 AS.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened.
Korvath lifted his head.
“During the Accord of Mournthrone.”
The words remained.
Brannoc read them again. The rain, the stone, the passage, Korvath’s drawn face—all of it slipped away beneath the clean simplicity of the sentence.
Died in 300 AS.
He found himself searching for the loophole. Books had loopholes. Priests had loopholes. Kings had entire armies of men dedicated to discovering them. Perhaps “died” meant a name buried, a claim extinguished, a man made dead in the eyes of those who required him absent.
Korvath said, “It could mean someone else.”
“It used my name.”
“It could be a warning.”
“It used the past tense.”
The grimoire wrote again.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
His own name seemed smaller the second time.
Then, beneath it:
“Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Korvath’s face changed. Fear remained, but something older moved beneath it: calculation, the instinct that had made him a smuggler rather than a corpse. He glanced toward the passage mouth.
“Who else knows?”
Brannoc looked at him.
“About the Crown,” Korvath said. “About you.”
“The book knows.”
“I did not ask what the book knows.”
“You were not meant to.”
“I was not meant to carry it either.”
A dull impact shook the stone behind them.
The hidden door.
Another impact. Grit sifted from the ceiling. The seam brightened with a blade of gray light.
Korvath snatched up the Edge of Gloamreach. “There.”
Beyond the chamber, a stair descended into blackness. No sound came from it. No rain. No pursuit. Brannoc could smell cold earth and something bitter, like ash left in a dead hearth.
The book writhed under Korvath’s arm.
“Crookvale.”
The name was followed by a map, ink spreading across the page in crooked lines.
“Founded in 295 AS.”
The stair seemed to tilt beneath Brannoc’s boots.
“In The High Spires,” Korvath read.
The hidden door shuddered again.
“Rebuilt.”
“Garrison of 1004.”
Korvath stared at the number.
Brannoc saw the calculation return to his eyes, sharper now. A garrison was not safety. It was a locked jaw. A hundred doors, a thousand watchful hands, orders carried through barracks and towers. A place outside the core holdings could survive only by suspecting everyone who approached it.
The grimoire finished the line.
“Outside the core holdings.”
The door behind them cracked. A sliver of masked metal appeared in the gap.
Korvath shoved the book at Brannoc. “You carry it.”
Brannoc caught it against his chest. The leather was warm.
“What is in Crookvale?”
“Nothing good.”
“You know it?”
“I know enough to avoid it.”
“Then we go there.”
Korvath seized his sleeve. “That was not an invitation.”
The book opened against Brannoc’s heart.
“Fenspire.”
Its pages filled with a stark black tower surrounded by smaller marks, each one a waiting blade.
“In the Gloaming Reach.”
“Founded in 57 AS.”
“Garrison of 3,742.”
“Garrisoned status.”
The last words appeared slowly, as though pressed into the page by an invisible thumb.
Korvath whispered, “No.”
Brannoc felt the name draw him harder than the darkness below. Fenspire. A core location. A permanent military throat in the dim reaches, disciplined and vigilant, built around a spire that had endured while other things were broken and forgotten.
The hidden door burst inward.
A masked figure lunged through the opening.
Brannoc struck him with the grimoire.
The impact sounded like a bell beneath deep water. The figure folded. The mask struck stone and split.
Korvath was already descending the stair.

The knowledge did not come as prophecy. It had no voice, no vision, no hand laid upon his shoulder. It lived inside him like a nail driven through bone. Some mornings he woke expecting to find the point protruding from his chest.
Tonight, he felt the nail turning.
A figure crossed the yard, hunched beneath a tarred cloak. He moved without hurry, which was the first mark of a man who knew how to flee. The second was that he never looked at the guards.
Brannoc watched him approach.
“Kneel,” said one of the sentries.
The cloaked man stopped.
Rain ticked against the iron rings sewn into his boots. “If I kneel, I’ll drown.”
The sentry raised his spear.
Brannoc lifted two fingers. “Let him through.”
The sentry glanced at him, then lowered the spear.
The man came beneath the archway. Water shone on his cheeks. He was not old, though caution had gathered around his eyes like another kind of age.
“K orvath Nightbrook,” Brannoc said.
The smuggler’s mouth tightened. “You say it as though it’s a crime.”
“Most names are.”
Korvath looked past him toward the keep. “You’re expected.”
“I’m seldom expected anywhere worth going.”
“There’s a room above the eastern stair.”
“By whom?”
“By those who have coins enough to expect.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Korvath did not answer.
The rain whispered between them. From the wall, a soldier coughed into his sleeve. Somewhere behind the keep, a horse screamed, and another answered.
Brannoc studied the smuggler’s hands. No visible weapon. That meant nothing. A man who moved contraband through hostile country did not survive by carrying what everyone expected him to carry.
“What did they buy?” Brannoc asked.
“Silence.”
“Expensive.”
“Not theirs.”
Korvath drew a small object from beneath his cloak. He did not offer it at once. A coin lay across his palm, dull beneath the rainwater. Its face had been shaved smooth. Its edge bore a shallow notch.
Brannoc felt the old nail turn.
“Where?” he asked.
“In the chapel of the Bleeding Crown.”
“There is no chapel here.”
“There is a room they call one.”
“And the coin?”
“Payment.”
“For what?”
Korvath’s eyes flicked toward the keep. “For withdrawal.”
The word entered Brannoc more cleanly than a blade.
He took the coin. It was cold, but beneath the cold lay the greasy warmth of a hand that had held it too long. A bribe left its own stain. Not visible. Never visible. It clung to the mind.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
That was the hidden truth beneath the Accord of Mournthrone, beneath the speeches, beneath the banners and the solemn oaths. Men would call it exhaustion. They would call it prudence. They would call it a victory earned by the Ashen Vanguard through discipline and sacrifice.
They would not call it purchased.
Brannoc closed his fingers around the coin.
“Why bring this to me?”
“I didn’t.”
The smuggler nodded toward the keep. “They sent for you.”
“Then you brought it to them.”
“I carried it where I was paid to carry it.”
“And now?”
“Now I’m here.”
“That isn’t an answer.”
“It’s the only one that survives.”
Korvath turned away.
Brannoc caught his sleeve. The cloth was rough and wet. Korvath went still, not frightened—simply ready.
“Who paid you?”
The smuggler looked at Brannoc’s hand, then at his face. “A man who didn’t want his name remembered.”
“Everyone wants that.”
“No. Some men want their names remembered. They just want the wrong names spoken.”
Brannoc released him.
A bell sounded from the keep.
Once.
The guards straightened. The men around the fires lowered their voices. Above the wall, the banners stirred in the rain: the Ashen Vanguard’s ash-gray field, House Morvain’s dark device, the pale marks of the Silent Choir, the iron colors of the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the torn crimson of the Bleeding Crown.
Five powers, each pretending the realm could still be divided cleanly.
The Ashen Vanguard held the roads where roads remained. House Morvain held old stone and older grievances. The Silent Choir kept its counsels behind veils and locked doors. The Iron-Ring Cartel weighed hunger against silver. The Bleeding Crown possessed less land than memory, but memory was a weapon that did not rust.
Brannoc had been born in 255 AS beneath that last banner’s shadow, though no herald had written his name beneath it. He was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
A crown did not need to acknowledge a man to kill him.
He slipped the coin into his glove.
“Will you enter?” Korvath asked.
“I was summoned.”
“That wasn’t what I asked.”
Brannoc looked up at the keep. The candle in the eastern window burned steadily despite the wind. A trap was often most convincing when it offered shelter.
“Wait here,” he said.
Korvath gave a quiet laugh. “I don’t wait anywhere.”
Brannoc passed beneath the arch.
The stair smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and old mortar. Mournthrone had been built to endure the end of the world and had discovered, centuries later, that walls could not keep out treachery. His boots rang against the steps. He counted them without meaning to, then stopped himself. Counting made men believe they had power over what came next.
At the landing, a narrow display case stood behind cloudy glass.
Within it rested The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The regalia had been forged in 123 AS. No attunement cost was recorded for it. Its shape was restrained: dark metal, pale binding, three severe lines joined without ornament. It did not gleam. It seemed to drink the candlelight and hold it beneath its surface.
Brannoc had seen kings reach for lesser things with steadier hands.
He paused before the case.
The Thrice-Bound Edge conveyed no promise of triumph. Only binding. A thing made to close around a wrist, a vow, a throat.
He moved on.
The eastern room was open. Warm light spilled across the corridor.
Inside, a table had been set with maps, sealed letters, and untouched food. No one spoke when Brannoc entered. That silence told him more than any greeting could have done.
He saw the grimoire first.
Edge of Gloamreach lay upon the table, its cover black-blue beneath the candle flame. The title had been pressed into the leather in letters that seemed to recede when looked at directly. It was a grimoire, and its attunement cost was 46. No forging date had been recorded.
Beside it lay a folded dispatch bearing the mark of Fenspire.
The spire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, a core location with a garrison of 3,742 and a garrisoned status. Even from this room Brannoc could imagine its silhouette rising above the dim country: stark, watchful, permanent. Fenspire did not sleep. It occupied the land as a blade occupied flesh.
Another map showed Crookvale.
Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires, rebuilt after whatever had broken it, Crookvale retained a garrison of 1004 but remained outside the core holdings. The mark on the map was crooked and hard-edged, like the settlement itself. A place wary enough to call survival a law.
Brannoc looked from one mark to the other.
“Fenspire,” he said. “Crookvale.”
No one answered.
At the far end of the table, a sealed letter lay beneath a black stone. The stone was wet.
Not rainwater.
Brannoc’s gaze lowered to the floor.
A thin red thread ran beneath the door.
His hand found his sword.
The candles leaned all at once, though there was no wind in the room.
Then someone behind him whispered, “Red-Handed.”
Brannoc turned.
The door slammed shut.
From the corridor came the sound of Korvath Nightbrook shouting, followed by the hard, wet impact of a body striking stone. The room’s occupants rose together. Chairs scraped. Steel whispered free.
Brannoc did not draw his sword.
The coin in his glove had begun to bleed.
He felt the warmth spread across his palm, felt it seep between his fingers, and somewhere beneath the keep a second bell began to ring as the voice behind him said—
“—the Accord has already chosen its dead.”
The voice did not come from the room. It came through the coin.
Brannoc closed his fist around it. Blood welled between his knuckles, hot as a forge-runner’s breath. Across the chamber, the others had formed a ragged half-circle around the sealed door. Swords pointed at the wood. No one looked toward him. No one wanted to be the first to admit that the whisper had spoken from his hand.
Beyond the door, Korvath Nightbrook groaned.
“Open it,” said one of the men.
No one moved.
The second bell sounded again beneath the keep. Its note crawled through the floorstones and into Brannoc’s teeth. Dust sifted from the ceiling. The flames guttered blue, then returned to their weak yellow.
Brannoc looked at the door.
A smear marked the stone beneath it, dark and shining. Korvath had fallen there, or something wearing the shape of him had. The smuggler had entered the chamber an hour earlier with rain in his hair and a sealed packet beneath his coat. He had spoken little. That was Korvath’s nature: guarded, wary, always measuring the distance between a secret and a knife.
Now he made no sound.
“Brannoc,” said the oldest of the gathered men.
The captain heard the accusation hidden in his name. You brought this. You knew it would come. You are the red hand at every threshold.
He released the coin.
It remained in his palm.
“Back away from the door,” he said.
The men glanced at one another.
“Why?”
“Because I told you.”
The command carried the hard weight earned by a seasoned sellsword, and habit obeyed before fear could argue. Steel lowered. Boots scraped over stone. Brannoc crossed the chamber alone.
The coin lay flat in his hand now, though it had not fallen. Its surface had become soft and black, as if the metal had remembered being blood. Lines opened across it, forming the image of a crown pierced through by a thorn.
The Bleeding Crown.
His breath slowed.
No one in the room knew the truth. They knew him as Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed, a major Sellsword Captain whose contracts had carried him from ash-field to ash-field. They knew the price of his sword. They knew the danger of refusing it. They did not know he was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Not even Korvath had known that.
Perhaps Korvath had known too much.
The voice returned.
“You were born in 255 AS.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened. The coin bit him.
“Silence.”
“You will die in 300 AS.”
The chamber seemed to contract around him. The men heard nothing; their faces remained fixed on the door. One of them raised his sword again, watching the crack beneath the threshold as if death might be persuaded to enter politely.
Brannoc stared at the blackened coin.
“Who speaks?”
The answer came as a sigh from the walls.
“The one who keeps the account.”
A line of red appeared upon the door. It began at the latch and traveled upward, thin as a vein beneath skin. When it reached the lintel, the entire slab shuddered.
One of the men cursed.
The door opened inward.
Korvath Nightbrook lay beyond it on the corridor stones, folded beneath himself. His coat had torn from throat to belt. No blood spread from the wound. Instead, the red thread from beneath the door had emerged from his ribs and continued into the chamber, where it now curled around Brannoc’s wrist.
The smuggler’s eyes opened.
“Don’t,” Korvath whispered.
Brannoc stepped over the threshold.
“What happened?”
Korvath’s gaze found the coin. Whatever he saw there drained the little color left in his face.
“It came for the packet.”
“Where is it?”
“Not here.”
“You carried it here.”
“I carried a decoy.”
A soft murmur moved through the room behind Brannoc. Fear had a way of making men generous with their suspicions.
The red thread tightened around his wrist.
Korvath clawed at the stone. “It knows the Crown.”
“Who does?”
The smuggler’s mouth worked. His answer came wetly.
“The Choir.”
The words seemed to darken the corridor.
The Silent Choir had no single voice, yet every whisper attributed to it arrived with the weight of a verdict. Brannoc had crossed their routes before. He had found whole wagons abandoned in snowless fields, their drivers seated upright, mouths sewn shut with pale cord. He had never seen the faces beneath the hoods. He had never needed to.
Behind him, someone said, “The Silent Choir is in the keep.”
“No,” Brannoc answered.
He did not know whether he spoke from certainty or command.
The thread around his wrist pulled.
He followed it into the chamber. It ran across the floor, climbed the leg of the table, and entered the leather satchel Korvath had brought. The satchel trembled as though a small animal struggled inside.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The blade came free with a sound like a breath being taken by the dead.
“Burn it,” said Korvath.
“There is no fire hot enough.”
“Then cut it.”
Brannoc laid the edge against the satchel.
The coin laughed.
The sound was small. Almost tender.
The red thread snapped.
Every candle went out.
Darkness swallowed the room. Men shouted. Someone struck at something unseen, and the blow met flesh; a cry broke sharply and fell silent. Brannoc heard feet stumbling, heard steel ring against stone, heard the old, familiar music of panic.
Then the satchel opened.
A pale light spilled from it, not bright but depthless, the color of twilight beneath deep water. Within the leather lay a book bound in hide that shifted beneath its stitching.
The cover bore a title.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Brannoc had seen the grimoire once, at a distance, in the hands of a dead scholar whose fingers had been burned to the bone. Its attunement cost was 46. That number had been written in every warning concerning it, as if the act of naming the price might keep anyone from paying.
The grimoire opened by itself.
Pages turned in a wind that did not touch Brannoc’s coat.
Symbols crawled across the paper. Their shapes refused to settle. He felt them pressing against the inside of his skull, seeking a place to root.
“Look away,” Korvath said.
Brannoc did not.
A second object rested beneath the book, wrapped in gray cloth. The cloth had fallen back. Beneath it lay The Thrice-Bound Edge, regalia forged in 123 AS. Its surface was neither sword nor crown nor chain, but held the suggestion of all three: a binding thing, restrained and severe.
No attunement cost had ever been recorded for The Thrice-Bound Edge.
That absence had always troubled him more than any price.
The light from Edge of Gloamreach passed over it. Three lines of darkness appeared upon the regalia, crossing and knotting without touching.
The men behind Brannoc fell quiet.
He felt the room listening.
A voice spoke from the open grimoire.
“The five powers gather.”
The page displayed five marks.
A clenched fist wreathed in ash: the Ashen Vanguard.
A dark crown scored with red: House Morvain.
A closed mouth stitched in silver: the Silent Choir.
A ring of iron surrounding a coin: the Iron-Ring Cartel.
And the thorn-pierced crown: the Bleeding Crown.
“They contend over the ruins,” said the voice. “They call it law when they take. They call it order when they burn. They call it peace when the graves are full.”
Brannoc’s sword remained level.
“Why show me this?”
“Because the Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.”
The chamber groaned. Somewhere below, the bell answered.
“It will end in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Korvath gave a strangled laugh. “That is not prophecy. That is a sentence.”
“The losing commander will be bribed to withdraw.”
Brannoc’s gaze shifted toward the black window. Beyond the glass, the night had no stars. Only the faint red wash of distant fires stained the underside of the clouds.
The Accord was supposed to bind the powers long enough for the realm to breathe. Instead, its words had been sharpened into weapons before the wax cooled. He had watched nobles praise it over silver cups while counting the soldiers they meant to spend. He had watched House Morvain smile at the Ashen Vanguard. He had watched the Iron-Ring Cartel sell grain to both sides and powder to the side that paid late. He had watched the Silent Choir pass through every gate without being searched.
And beneath all of it, like a buried pulse, the Bleeding Crown waited.
“What happens after?” Brannoc asked.
The page turned.
“Reprisals.”
A single word, written in red.
“A decade of guerrilla reprisals.”
The men behind him shifted. One whispered a prayer without naming its object.
Brannoc looked down at Korvath. “You brought this to me because of the Crown.”
Korvath swallowed blood. “I brought it because they said only your hand could open the way.”
“Who said?”
The smuggler’s eyes slid toward the grimoire.
“The dead.”
Brannoc almost smiled. There was no humor in it.
He had trusted the living because they lied for reasons. The dead lied without need.
The coin in his hand grew hot again. The crown upon it split down the middle. A black line ran across the image, widening until the metal bent like a mouth.
The voice whispered close against his ear.
“Choose, Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The door behind him slammed shut.
This time, the men screamed.
The grimoire’s pages began to turn faster. The Thrice-Bound Edge rose from the table, turning slowly in the pale light. No hand held it. No chain restrained it. Its three dark lines uncoiled and reached toward Brannoc.
He felt the buried claim inside him stir.
Not blood. Not birthright.
Something older than both.
From the corridor came the sound of many bare feet approaching at once.
Korvath caught Brannoc’s boot. “If you take it, they will see you.”
“Who?”
The footsteps stopped outside the door.
A voice spoke from the other side, calm and familiar.
“Open, Red-Handed.”
Brannoc knew that voice.
He had heard it at contract tables, beneath rain, in the brittle silence after a surrender.
The voice of a man who had not yet died.
The coin split in Brannoc’s palm.
The Thrice-Bound Edge drifted nearer.
And in the darkness behind the door, Korvath began to weep.
Brannoc did not open the door.
The voice waited with the patience of a drawn bow.
Korvath’s fingers tightened around his boot. The smuggler had gone pale in the dark, his tears shining like oil where they tracked through the dust on his face.
“You know him,” Brannoc said.
Korvath shook his head.
The door gave a soft wooden sigh. Not from pressure. From recognition.
“Open,” said the voice again. “There is no profit in making me ask.”
Brannoc looked down at the coin in his palm. The split had widened. Within its broken face, something black moved against the metal, a darkness too deliberate to be a flaw. The Thrice-Bound Edge had come close enough that its cold entered his bones.
He had seen regalia before, in war tents and ruined halls: crowns that carried old promises, swords that demanded new ones, rings worn by men who believed the world had been made to fit their hands. This was none of those things. The Thrice-Bound Edge did not glitter. It waited.
Behind him, the grimoire lay open on the floor.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Its pages turned without wind. Each leaf whispered against the next, a dry, intimate sound, like a tongue testing a wound. The script upon them was not written in ink. It was written in the bruised color beneath the skin.
“Tell me who stands outside,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s breath came thin and fast. “A dead man.”
“That is not a name.”
“It is enough of one.”
The feet in the corridor shifted. Many of them. Bare soles upon old stone. No one spoke. Their silence was worse than a crowd’s anger. It had the obedience of a congregation.
Brannoc rose from his crouch.
