The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.
Brannoc felt the chamber fall away from him. Not because the words surprised him. Because they did not.
Somewhere inside the secret, a shape had always waited for him. He had mistaken it for instinct.
“Who paid?” he asked.
The page went blank.
“Who received?”
Blank.
“Why show me this?”
The hooded figure said nothing.
Brannoc lifted his hand from the stone. Blood had marked the table. One red drop slid toward the grimoire
and vanished between its pages.
The Thrice-Bound Edge released his palm.
For the first time since he had entered the chamber, he was truly unarmed.
The door behind him slammed shut.
The grimoire began to whisper.
The grimoire began to whisper.
Not in any tongue Brannoc knew. The sound crept through the chamber like rats behind a wall—soft,
busy, intent. Its pages turned without wind. Each leaf lifted, shivered, and fell. The parchment was dark at
the edges, pale only where the writing had been scraped away.
He watched the book with the patience he had learned from ambushes.
The hooded figure remained beyond the table. Its face was lost beneath the cowl. Its hands, if it had hands,
were hidden in its sleeves.
“Open it,” the whisper said.
Brannoc did not move.
The voice came again, though the figure’s mouth did not stir.
“Open the Edge of Gloamreach.”
The title appeared in the page’s center, written in a black that seemed wet. Beneath it, a single line
emerged.
Attunement cost: 46.
Brannoc’s jaw tightened.
“I have no sword.”
“You have a name.”
“A name won’t cut a throat.”

“Names have cut deeper things.”
The grimoire’s pages continued turning. The chamber smelled of old dust and iron. Somewhere beyond
the sealed door, water struck stone in a slow, measured rhythm. Brannoc thought of Fenspire, though he
had never seen it. The name came to him with the taste of ash.
The next page showed a spire rising from a field of darkness.
Fenspire. Gloaming Reach. Founded in 57 AS. Core location. Garrisoned. Garrison: 3,742.
He leaned closer.
The number shifted when he looked at it. Not changing, exactly. Becoming more difficult to disbelieve.
“Why show me this?”
“Because the walls remember what men pay to forget.”
“Fenspire has nothing to do with Mournthrone.”
The grimoire did not answer.
Brannoc laid his bloodied hand on the table. The cut in his palm had stopped bleeding, but the skin around
it had gone cold. He could still feel the absence of The Thrice-Bound Edge. It had been regalia, not merely
a weapon, and it had rested against his will for so long that its withdrawal felt like the loss of a limb.
The page turned.
The Thrice-Bound Edge. Forged in 123 AS.
No cost followed. No warning. Only the name, standing alone beneath the date like a condemned man
beneath a sentence.
Brannoc stared at it.
He had carried the artifact through sieges, betrayals, and the narrow alleys where a man’s life could be
purchased for less than a warm meal. He had believed the binding was between himself and the Edge. He
had never asked who else had been bound.
The hooded figure moved.
It was no more than a slight inclination of the head, but Brannoc saw it. Permission, perhaps. Or
impatience.
He touched the grimoire.
Cold entered him.
The chamber vanished.
He stood on a ridge beneath a sky the color of bruised flesh. Below, a host waited in silence. No banners
moved. No fires burned. The soldiers were only shapes, packed shoulder to shoulder, their armor dulled by
distance.
Across the valley, another force held the high ground.
He knew the scene. He had lived its aftermath, heard its lies told in taverns and war rooms, watched men
who had not been there claim to understand it.

The Accord of Mournthrone.
It had begun in 297 AS. It would end in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor. Between those
years lay a ruin no proclamation could mend.
Brannoc saw the commander on the nearer ridge. He could not make out the face. The figure stood before
a command table while a purse was set upon the map.
Not thrown.
Not offered.
Set down with care.
The commander looked at the purse. Then at the valley. Then at the troops who trusted the order that
would come.
“Who paid?” Brannoc asked.
His voice sounded very far away.
The vision supplied no answer.
A hand closed over the purse.
The commander turned from the map.
Below, horns began to call.
Not an advance. A withdrawal.
The army moved back in disciplined ranks, and the opposing force did not pursue. The valley remained
untouched except for the dead who had already fallen waiting for a battle that would never be fought.
Brannoc felt a sickness rise behind his ribs.
He had known the truth as a sentence. Seeing it made it a wound.
The scene broke.
He returned to the chamber on one knee, his palm pressed flat against the grimoire. His breath came
harshly. The hooded figure watched him as if watching a dog decide whether to bite.
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw,” Brannoc said.
The words had been written before his eyes. He had spoken them already. Still, saying them aloud
changed their shape.
“Say it,” whispered the Edge of Gloamreach.
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.”
The book shuddered beneath his hand.
The door opened.
Not outward. Inward.
A strip of darkness appeared between the stones, thin as a knife’s edge. Cold air flowed through it carrying
the smell of wet wool and smoke. Brannoc rose slowly.

A figure stood in the passage beyond. Smaller than the hooded one. Wrapped in a travel-stained cloak. A
narrow satchel crossed its chest.
The newcomer stopped when it saw Brannoc.
“K—” the figure began, then swallowed the rest of the name.
Brannoc’s hand went to the place where The Thrice-Bound Edge should have been.
The stranger’s gaze followed the movement.
“You came unarmed,” it said.
“I was disarmed.”
“By the book?”
“By the truth.”
The stranger’s expression remained hidden beneath the hood. Its voice had the guarded flatness of
someone accustomed to doors closing behind them.
The hooded figure spoke at last.
“Kro—”
The sound died in the chamber.
Brannoc looked between them. “You know each other.”
Neither answered.
On the table, the grimoire’s pages began to blacken. A new image surfaced beneath the spreading stain: a
crooked settlement clinging to high stone, its walls rebuilt upon older foundations.
Crookvale. The High Spires. Founded in 295 AS. Rebuilt. Garrison: 1004. Outside the core
holdings.
The stranger stared at the page.
“Who are you?” Brannoc asked.
“Someone trying to leave alive.”
“That makes three of us.”
The stranger’s hand slipped beneath the cloak.
Brannoc shifted his weight. He had no blade, but an empty hand could still crush a throat. The old lessons
remained in the body after weapons were taken from it. His fingers flexed.
The stranger drew out a folded strip of cloth.
No weapon. No seal.
A map.
It fell open over the grimoire. Inked lines crossed the parchment in cramped, nervous strokes. One route
ran from the High Spires toward the Gloaming Reach. Another ended at a black mark beneath which
someone had written a single word.

Mournthrone.
The hooded figure reached toward it.
The stranger recoiled.
“Touch it,” the stranger said, “and it will show him the rest.”
“Show me what?” Brannoc asked.
The page beneath the map pulsed.
A line of writing surfaced, each letter appearing as though pressed up from beneath the parchment by a
fingernail.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed. Born in 255 AS.
His name seemed to occupy the whole chamber.
The stranger went still.
The hooded figure lowered its hand.
Brannoc read the next line before it finished forming.
Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
For one breath, no one moved.
The silence afterward was not surprise. It was recognition. The kind that had been waiting for him in
locked rooms, behind lowered eyes, inside the pauses between orders. The kind that made every loyalty a
coin held up to the light.
The Bleeding Crown.
He had spent his life hearing the title spoken as if it belonged to a distant plague. A power among powers.
One of the five forces contending over the Ashen Era’s broken realm, alongside the Ashen Vanguard,
House Morvain, the Silent Choir, and the Iron-Ring Cartel.
He had never claimed it.
He had never been acknowledged.
The grimoire turned one final page.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed. Death: 300 AS. During the Accord of Mournthrone.
His heart gave one hard beat.
Then another.
The page did not burn. It did not fade. The words remained, patient and exact.
The stranger whispered, “No.”
Brannoc looked at the hooded figure. “You knew.”
The figure said nothing.
“You knew what I was.”

Still nothing.
“And you knew when I die.”
The hooded head tilted.
The answer was worse than denial.
Brannoc seized the grimoire and slammed it shut.
The chamber convulsed.
Stone cracked beneath his boots. The map flew from the table. The stranger cried out as the door blew
inward, and a wind rushed through the room carrying ash, rain, and the distant clangor of bells.
The book bucked in Brannoc’s grip.
Something struck him from inside the cover.
Once.
Twice.
On the third blow, a seam split along the spine.
Beyond it waited not paper, but a red eye opening in the dark.
And from the passage outside came the sound of many feet climbing toward them.

Chapter 12
The record would say that Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed died in 300 AS during the Accord of
Mournthrone.
The record would also say he was born in 255 AS, that he had been a major Sellsword Captain, and that he
was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Records had a way of making a corpse seem simpler than a living man.
That night, with the wind dragging its nails along the black stone of Fenspire, Brannoc stood beneath the
stark spire and listened to the fortress breathe.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach. It had been founded in 57 AS. It was a core location, garrisoned,
with a garrison of 3,742. Those figures were carved into the gatehouse in the dry, obedient hand of a clerk.
The stone had been polished around them by generations of gloves and palms.
Garrisoned.
The word had no warmth in it. It meant locked gates, rationed grain, watchfires, and men who slept with
their boots within reach. It meant that the fortress belonged to whoever could keep it fed and armed. It
meant the Reach had not been trusted to itself since the world was broken.
Brannoc touched the iron ring at his belt. The leather creaked beneath his glove.
Beyond the walls, darkness gathered in the ravines. Fenspire’s lamps burned in narrow slits, their light
thin and yellow against the Gloaming Reach. Somewhere below, a horn gave a single note. It was
answered from the outer wall, then from the high watchtower. The sound moved around him like a thought
refusing to die.
“Three thousand seven hundred and forty-two,” said Korvath Nightbrook.
He sat in the corner where the stone sweated least, hood drawn low. Korvath was a minor figure in the
world’s great reckonings, though he worked as a Smuggler and had survived by placing his feet in the
gaps between lawful things. His presence was unobtrusive by instinct. Even stillness seemed to conceal
him.
Brannoc did not look at him. “You count poorly.”
“I count what I’m told.”
“Then you’re a fool.”
Korvath’s mouth bent, not quite a smile. “That is why I remain alive.”
On the table between them lay a sealed packet, a narrow black case, and two objects wrapped in oilcloth.
No mark declared who had sent the packet. No mark declared whom it served. That was the virtue of the
five powers contending over the ruins: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the
Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown all preferred their hands clean when they could persuade
another man to soil his.
Brannoc watched the packet.
The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS. It would end in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard
named victor. Such was the shape of the official account: beginning, struggle, victor. A neat road laid

through mud.
But the Accord would collapse into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, because victories had teeth and the
defeated did not always know how to kneel. The hidden truth was uglier still. The losing commander had
been bribed to withdraw.
Brannoc knew that much already.
The knowledge had lodged beneath his ribs and made a second heart there.
“Open it,” Korvath said.
Brannoc’s red glove rested beside the packet. The epithet had followed him longer than most men could
remember him without it. Red-Handed. It had been spoken with admiration in campfires, disgust in
council chambers, and fear in rooms where rich men kept their daughters behind curtains. No canonical
physical feature could have defined him better than the name. He was a Sellsword Captain because the
world understood steel more readily than blood. He was the heir to the Bleeding Crown because blood
understood him.
He broke the seal.
Inside was a strip of vellum, folded twice.
The words were brief.
Mournthrone had not been bought with coin alone. Someone had purchased silence, withdrawal, and the
right to call treachery prudence. The payment had moved through hands that would later swear they had
never met. The trail ended at a door that did not appear on any map.
Brannoc read it twice.
His first thought was of the Crown.
His second was that the Crown had never been his.
Unacknowledged heirs were useful creatures. They could be pointed at a throne as one pointed a hound at
a throat. They could be denied when the hunt went wrong. The Bleeding Crown had given him no name,
no seal, no inheritance he could hold in both hands. Only the knowledge, passed in whispers and withheld
in public, that his claim existed.
A claim was a blade with no hilt.
Korvath leaned forward. “Is it true?”
“Truth is a coin minted by the hand holding it.”
“I asked whether it was true.”
Brannoc folded the vellum. “You asked because you already know.”
Korvath’s eyes glimmered under his hood. Guarded, wary. The demeanor of a smuggler was not
cowardice. It was the discipline of a man who understood that every road had a watcher and every watcher
could be bought.
“The message says the withdrawal is arranged,” Korvath said.
“The message says someone believes it is arranged.”

“And if the commander takes the bribe?”
“Then the Accord ends as it began—with men mistaking hunger for strategy.”
Korvath glanced toward the oilcloth. “You brought the regalia?”
Brannoc drew the first bundle nearer and peeled back the cloth.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay within, dark metal worked into a shape too restrained to be called ornamental.
It was regalia, forged in 123 AS. Its defining record contained no attunement cost. The name had been
entered into ledgers more carefully than the names of kings, as though binding the words might prevent
the object from becoming something else.
Korvath did not touch it.
“Put it away,” he said.
“You were curious.”
“I was curious from a safe distance.”
Brannoc wrapped The Thrice-Bound Edge again. The cloth rasped over the metal like a tongue against a
broken tooth.
The second bundle was heavier. He opened it with less care.
Edge of Gloamreach showed no blade at all. It was a grimoire, bound in material that drank the lamplight.
Its forging date was not recorded in the supplied facts of any surviving register—if the register had ever
existed. The attunement cost was 46. The number had been written on its inner cover in ink that seemed to
have faded only where the eye rested upon it.
Brannoc shut the book.
For a moment, something moved in the dark seam between its pages.
He told himself it was the flame.
The thought did not comfort him.
“Why carry those into a garrisoned fortress?” Korvath asked.
Brannoc looked past him, through the narrow window. Fenspire’s walls rose in tiers above the Reach,
disciplined and severe. Every tower had a watcher. Every watcher served a power, or believed he did.
“Because everyone here thinks a locked gate is the same as safety.”
“And is it?”
“No.”
The answer came too quickly. Korvath heard it. Brannoc heard him hear it.
In the yard below, soldiers crossed through the torchlight. Their armor flashed and vanished, flashed and
vanished. The garrison of 3,742 was a mass reduced to individual footsteps. A fortress could contain an
army and still be empty of loyalty.
“Crookvale has sent word,” Korvath said.
Brannoc turned.

“Crookvale?”
“Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. Rebuilt now. Garrison of 1004. Still outside the core holdings.”
“I know where Crookvale is.”
“Then you know why they are afraid.”
Brannoc did not answer.
Crookvale’s name carried the hard edge of a settlement built twice because the first version had not
survived. It was wary and resilient, its governing principle reduced to the oldest commandment: endure
what cannot be defeated. The garrison there was smaller than Fenspire’s, but smaller did not mean
harmless. A knife did not need a regiment.
“What did they send?” Brannoc asked.
“Nothing. Only a warning.”
“Warnings are what men send when they want credit for courage.”
Korvath shifted. “They say the Bleeding Crown is moving.”
The room seemed to contract around the words.
Brannoc’s hand closed.
He could feel the old claim beneath his glove, beneath his skin, beneath all the years in which he had
earned coin instead of titles. The Crown was not a thing one inherited. It was a wound passed from mouth
to mouth. Those who bore it bled for those who denied it.
“The Bleeding Crown moves everywhere,” he said.
“Not like this.”
“Who told you?”
Korvath’s gaze slipped toward the door.
The silence after that was answer enough.
Brannoc rose. The chair legs scraped stone. In his bones, the motion was familiar: stand, measure the
exits, identify the first throat to cut. The hard dangerous presence of a seasoned sellsword was not
something he wore. It had worn him down until only that remained.
From the corridor came the muted tread of boots.
Korvath gathered the packet.
“Stay,” Brannoc said.
“I am a Smuggler. Staying is how I become evidence.”
“You are already evidence.”
The boots stopped outside.
A shadow thickened beneath the door.

Brannoc reached for The Thrice-Bound Edge. Then he paused, his fingers hovering over the wrapped
regalia, while the black case on the table seemed to breathe beside the grimoire.
The Accord of Mournthrone had not yet become history. Its beginning lay ahead in 297 AS, its ending in
301 AS, and between those years men would swear oaths they intended to break. The Ashen Vanguard
would be named victor. The losing commander would withdraw for a bribe. The collapse would unleash a
decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Brannoc knew none of that as a prophecy.
He knew it as the shape of a trap.
The door latch lifted.
Korvath whispered, “Captain.”
Brannoc drew steel.
The door opened a finger’s width, and a voice on the other side began to say his name—
The voice on the other side began to say his name—
“Brannoc Ironmere—”
He drove the blade through the gap.
The point met something softer than wood. A breath broke against the door, low and wet. Korvath
flinched, but Brannoc did not. He held the sword there until the pressure vanished, then wrenched it free.
The door swung inward.
A man stood in the corridor with his back against the wall, one hand pressed beneath his ribs. He wore a
servant’s grey, though the cloth was too fine for a servant and the boots beneath it had seen road dust, ash,
and blood. His face was narrow and bloodless. A strip of black silk covered his mouth.
The Silent Choir.
Brannoc had seen their dead before. They were quieter.
The stranger looked at the sword, then at Brannoc’s hand around it. His eyes narrowed with something
like recognition.
“Captain,” he said through the silk.
“Come in,” Brannoc replied. “Or fall out of the way.”
The man entered.
Korvath shut the door behind him and set the bar in place. The smuggler kept his gaze low, but his hand
had gone beneath his coat. Brannoc knew what lay there. Korvath had carried a knife through three cities
and trusted it more than any living soul.
The stranger removed the silk from his mouth. Blood had gathered at the corner of his lips.
“You’ve made a poor beginning,” Korvath said.
“I was invited.”
“No one invited you to bleed on my floor.”

The stranger’s attention remained fixed on Brannoc. “You were told to come alone.”
“I came with Korvath.”
“You were told—”
“I heard you.” Brannoc wiped his blade against the stranger’s sleeve. “You chose to speak my name
before showing your face. That was your mistake.”
The man’s jaw tightened. “The order came from Fenspire.”
The room seemed to contract around the word.
Outside, wind worried at the shutters. The inn had been built against the ruin of an older structure, and
through the walls Brannoc could hear the long complaints of stone settling upon stone. Somewhere below,

Korvath glanced toward the grimoire.
The Edge of Gloamreach lay open on the table, its pages black-veined and damp-looking beneath the
candlelight. The script along its margins seemed to lean away from the flame. Beside it rested the wrapped
regalia, bound in oilcloth and cord.
The stranger saw both.
His face changed.
It was not fear. Fear had movement in it. This was calculation, cold and immediate, the kind a man
performed when weighing the value of his life against the value of what might kill him.
Brannoc stepped between him and the table.
“Say what Fenspire wants.”
“Not Fenspire.” The man glanced toward the shuttered window. “Those who speak through it.”
“Then speak through your own mouth.”
The stranger swallowed. “The road north is closed.”
“By whom?”
“The Ashen Vanguard.”
Korvath gave a humorless breath. “They close roads whenever they remember they have soldiers.”
“They are searching wagons, rooms, bodies. They have orders to seize anything bearing the old seal.”
Brannoc felt the wrapped object behind him like a second heartbeat.
“Which old seal?”
The stranger looked at his hand.
Brannoc’s fingers were stained dark beneath the nails. The color never fully left them. Men called him the

“Do not make me ask again,” Brannoc said.
The stranger’s mouth twitched. “The seal of the Bleeding Crown.”
Korvath’s knife came free beneath his coat.
The sound was small. It still seemed to fill the room.
Brannoc did not look at him. “You came from Fenspire carrying a warning about the Bleeding Crown.”

“What claim?”
The stranger’s gaze lifted again, and this time it held something worse than calculation. Pity, perhaps. Or

“No.”
“You know enough to wear a dead man’s regalia.”
Brannoc’s hand tightened on the sword hilt.
The wrapped object had been taken from a chamber where dust lay thick as wool over every surface. It

He had told himself he carried it because others sought it.
He had told himself many things.
“Leave,” he said.
The stranger stared.
“Go back to Fenspire. Tell them the room was empty. Tell them Korvath sold you a lie. Tell them I took
the road south.”
“The road south is watched.”
“Then choose a road that isn’t.”
“You don’t understand.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “That is what frightened men say when they want obedience.”
The stranger took a step toward the table.
Brannoc’s sword rose.
Korvath shifted at the same instant, knife angled toward the man’s throat. The stranger stopped with his

For a moment they stood as three pieces on a board none of them had made.
Then the floor beneath them gave a soft groan.
Not the building settling.

Something moved below.
Korvath’s head turned. “That wasn’t there before.”
Brannoc listened.
A scrape passed under the boards, slow and deliberate. Dust sifted from the ceiling. The candle flame bent
toward the table, though no wind entered the sealed room.
The Edge of Gloamreach had closed.
Its cover lay shut over the pages, though Brannoc had not seen it move.
The stranger whispered something in a language Brannoc did not know.
Korvath said, “What did you bring with you?”
“Nothing.”
“Everyone brings something.”
The scrape came again, nearer.
Brannoc looked at the grimoire. The leather cover had begun to sweat a dark sheen. Along its edge, a line

teeth.
He had not touched it since Korvath placed it on the table. He had not dared. The cost of attunement was
written in the margin, exact and pitiless: forty-six.
He knew the number.
He did not know what it purchased.
The stranger drew a small object from inside his grey coat. Not a weapon. A shard of blackened bone,
threaded on a cord. He held it between finger and thumb.
Korvath went still.
“You know that?” Brannoc asked.
“No.”
“Your face says otherwise.”
“My face says I dislike the room.”
The stranger pressed the bone to his tongue.
The walls answered.
A thin vibration passed through the stone. The candle guttered. From beneath the floor came a muffled

Brannoc felt the old instinct rise in him: measure the exits, identify the weakest throat, decide who died
first. It had kept him alive when banners failed and employers discovered principles. It had made men
follow him into places from which no honest man returned.
But beneath that instinct another voice stirred.

Not a memory. Memories had edges.
This was inheritance.
The word came to him with the weight of a chain.
He saw, not with his eyes, a crown wet with blood. A hall without windows. Kneeling figures with their

He blinked.
The room returned.
Korvath was watching him. “Captain?”
“Do not call me that.”
The smuggler’s expression hardened. “You’ve been called worse.”
The stranger lowered the bone. “They’re beneath us.”
“Who?”
“The Choir.”
“Your Choir?”
“They are not mine.”
“Then whose?”
He looked at the sealed grimoire. “The ones who were buried without silence.”
A second knock came from below.
This time the boards lifted.
A black line appeared between them, narrow as a cut. Cold air poured through it, carrying the smell of wet

Brannoc reached for the wrapped regalia.
The cord around it had loosened.
He had tied that cord himself.
The oilcloth unfolded a little beneath his hand, revealing a sliver of metal pale as moonlit bone. No

The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Regalia forged in 123 AS.
The name rose from the grimoire’s pages, from the whispered records of men who had murdered for less
than a title. He had not known whether the artifact was a weapon, a crown, or a sentence. In that moment it

The stranger said, “Do not draw it.”

Brannoc looked at him.
“Why?”
“Because it will answer.”
“To what?”
The black line in the floor widened.
Something beneath the room exhaled.
The stranger’s bloodless face cracked at last. “To you.”
Korvath seized Brannoc’s shoulder. “We leave.”
Brannoc shook him off. “There’s nowhere to go.”
“There is always somewhere to go.”
“Not when the house is built over a throat.”
The floorboards split with a sound like wet timber breaking. A pale hand rose through the darkness below,

The Silent Choir had sent more than a messenger.
Brannoc drew The Thrice-Bound Edge from its wrappings.
The room went silent.
Not quiet. Silent.
The wind ceased. The inn below ceased. Korvath’s breath vanished. The stranger’s mouth opened, but no
sound came from it.
Across the table, the Edge of Gloamreach opened by itself.
Its pages turned with terrible care.
A line of writing appeared in the candleless dark.
Brannoc read it.
His own name had been written there long before he entered the room.
The hand below the floor closed around the edge of the boards. The stranger fell to his knees. Korvath
began to move toward the door, but Brannoc caught his sleeve.
“Wait.”
The smuggler looked at him as though he had become something he could no longer sell to anyone.
Beneath them, the buried thing began to speak.
The sound rose through the cracks, shaping itself around a title Brannoc had never accepted and could
never escape.
He lifted the regalia higher, and from the dark under the floor came the first clear word—
“—heir.”

The word did not strike Brannoc’s ears. It entered him through the soles of his boots and climbed, cold as
gravewater, into the marrow of his legs.
Korvath Nightbrook made a sound behind him. Not a prayer. Korvath had never trusted anything that
could not be bribed, threatened, or drowned. His hand went beneath his coat, where a knife waited in the
dark.
“Do not,” Brannoc said.
The buried hand tightened on the floorboard.
The stranger remained on his knees. Candlelight had not returned, yet Brannoc could see the man’s face
with an intimacy that made the sight obscene: the wet shine of his eyes, the blood at his mouth, the
trembling hinge of his jaw.
“Whose heir?” Korvath whispered.
The boards answered.
“Bleeding Crown.”
There it was. Not a title spoken by heralds or carved into a gate. A wound given grammar.
Brannoc held The Thrice-Bound Edge in both hands. The regalia was heavier than iron and colder than the
dead beneath the floor. Three bands circled its dark length, each joined to the next without seam. He had
found no maker’s mark upon it, only the old record pressed into its inner face:
Forged in 123 AS.
The numbers had seemed meaningless when he first read them. Now they shone like teeth.
A second line surfaced beneath the first.
No attunement cost.
Korvath leaned close enough for Brannoc to smell rain and old leather on him. “That is not possible.”
“Nothing is impossible in a room built over a grave.”
“It has a cost.”
“Then pay it.”
The smuggler’s eyes flicked toward him. “You know what it is?”
Brannoc looked down at the regalia. The bands had begun to pulse—not with light, but with a pressure
that made the air throb in his throat.
He knew the answer before the voice gave it.
“Name,” said the buried thing.
The dark shifted beneath the floor. Somewhere below, something dragged itself across stone. A long
scrape. Then another.
Brannoc thought of the names men had given him in alleys, on battlefields, over cups emptied by shaking
hands. Captain. Butcher. Red-Handed. He had accepted all of them because a name was a coin, and he had
learned young to spend whatever coin lay nearest.

There was one name he had never been permitted to possess.
His mother had died before she could speak it. Men who knew it had looked at him and found reasons to
look elsewhere. In the Bleeding Crown’s shadow, blood did not make a son. Blood made a threat.
“I am Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed,” he said.
The floor groaned.
“No.”
Korvath seized his sleeve. “That is enough.”
Brannoc tore free. The movement sent a dull ache through his shoulder. “You heard it.”
“I heard a corpse trying to make you useful.”
“That is most kings.”
At the word kings, the buried thing laughed.
Dust sifted from the ceiling. The stranger pressed both palms to the floor as if to hold it shut. His fingers
had split at the nails.
“Do you know what waits under a crown?” Brannoc asked him.
The stranger’s head turned. “You.”
“No.”
“Your blood.”
“Blood is cheap.”
“Not yours.”
The answer moved through the chamber like a draft. For one moment Brannoc saw the room as it had been
before the rot: stone walls washed white, bronze lamps burning along the ledges, banners hanging from
the beams. He saw himself standing at the far end beneath a crown he had never worn. His hands were red
to the wrists. Around him, men knelt not from loyalty but from calculation.
Then the vision broke.
The chamber returned. The floor. The stranger. Korvath with his knife half-drawn.
Brannoc breathed through his nose until the tremor passed.
On the wall beside him, dampness gathered in a shape like writing.
Born in 255 AS.
He stared at it.
Korvath read over his shoulder. “What does that mean?”
“My birth.”
“You never told me your birth.”
“You never asked.”

“I ask about cargo.”
“Then consider me badly packed.”
The words formed another line.
Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Korvath stepped away from him.
Brannoc felt the withdrawal more sharply than he would have liked. The smuggler had always kept
distance, but distance was not the same as fear. Fear had a smell. It sweetened the breath.
“The Bleeding Crown,” Korvath said. “That is not a campfire claim. That is a death sentence.”
“Most useful truths are.”
“You knew?”
“I suspected.”
“You carried suspicion into this place?”
“I carried a sword.”
“You carried us into this place.”
Brannoc turned on him. The regalia lay between them like an accusation. “You followed.”
“I was paid to lead.”
“By whom?”
Korvath’s mouth closed.
The buried thing spoke again.
“Not by the Crown.”
The words were followed by a wet cracking sound from beneath the boards.
The stranger began to weep. Silently. Tears traced pale paths through the grime on his face.
Brannoc looked at the sealed door. It had no latch now. No hinge. Only a slab of stone set into the arch as
though the room had decided it preferred them inside.
On the floor near the wall lay the second artifact, its leather cover warped by damp. The title had been
stamped in letters that seemed to drink what little darkness surrounded them:
Edge of Gloamreach.
He had thought it a grimoire, nothing more. A book worth more than a month of soldiers’ pay to the right
buyer, and worth killing for to the wrong one. The cover shivered without being touched.
Korvath noticed it too.
“Leave it,” he said.
Brannoc crouched. “Its attunement cost is 46.”
The smuggler stared. “You can read that?”

“Someone carved it into the clasp.”
“Then it is not a book.”
“No. It is a debt with pages.”
The clasp opened.
The first leaf was black and soft as skin. No script marked it. When Brannoc bent over it, a smell rose
from the page: smoke after rain, and the bitter mineral scent of a place where magic had burned the earth
bare.
The room’s darkness gathered over the grimoire.
Images stirred in the blankness.
A highland settlement crouched beneath a white sky, its rebuilt walls crooked against the wind. A
watchtower leaned over narrow streets. Men stood beneath its gate with weapons held close, watching
every road.
Crookvale.
The name appeared without ink.
Founded in 295 AS. In The High Spires. Rebuilt. Garrison of 1004. Outside the core holdings.
Korvath bent beside him, and the color drained from his face.
“Crookvale,” he said. “That place has changed hands.”
“Has it?”
“Enough times that no hand remains clean.”
The page turned itself.
A spire rose from a gray reach of land, stark and solitary, piercing a sky the color of old bruises. Walls
crowded its base. Within them, ranks moved in ordered files. The air around the image seemed
disciplined, watchful, unable to sleep.
Fenspire.
Founded in 57 AS. In the Gloaming Reach. Core location. Garrison of 3,742.
Brannoc felt the pressure in the room change. Fenspire had already been named to him once, a place of
permanent blades and closed gates, but now the grimoire showed it as something older than the kingdoms
that claimed it. The spire did not seem built. It seemed thrust upward by the dead beneath the world.
A third image replaced it.
A throne room split down the middle. Men in ash-colored armor stood behind one standard; figures in
dark crimson stood behind another. Between them lay a table bearing a document, its seal broken, its ink
running as if the parchment had begun to bleed.
Across the page appeared:
The Accord of Mournthrone. Began in 297 AS. Ended in 301 AS. The Ashen Vanguard named
victor.

The image did not settle into triumph.
The commander in crimson stood alone at the table. A hand—not attached to any visible body—placed a
small chest before him. He opened it. Gold glimmered within, then vanished beneath the falling shadow of
his fingers.
The commander turned away from the field.
Brannoc watched the withdrawal. He understood it with the cold certainty of a wound reopening.
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw,” he said.
Korvath looked at him. “You say that as if you were there.”
“I say it because the book does.”
Behind the commander, soldiers continued fighting in the image. They did not know the battle had already
been sold. They died beneath banners that had become lies.
The page darkened further.
The Ashen Vanguard’s standard remained standing over Mournthrone, but beneath it the land broke into
smaller fires. Roads vanished under ambushes. Supply wagons burned. Men hunted men through ravines
and ruined villages. The same sword appeared in different hands, passing from one corpse to another.
Text crawled across the black leaf.
Its collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Korvath shut the grimoire.
The pressure vanished. The room seemed suddenly too small to contain their breathing.
“You have seen enough,” he said.
Brannoc kept his gaze on the cover. “No.”
“You have seen what comes.”
“I have seen what may come.”
“You saw your name before you entered.”
“That is different.”
“It is not.”
The voice beneath the floor interrupted them.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The regalia jerked in his hands.
The three bands unwound.
Not physically. The metal remained whole, yet each ring seemed to open into a separate horizon. In the
first, Brannoc stood beneath a blood-colored sky. In the second, he watched men kneel before a crown. In
the third, he lay on a stone floor with his own blood spreading beneath him.
The year came last.

300 AS.
His fingers tightened until the regalia cut into his palms.
“During the Accord of Mournthrone,” the buried thing said.
Korvath moved toward the door again. “We are leaving.”
“There is no door.”
“Then we make one.”
“With what?”
“With you, if necessary.”
Brannoc almost smiled. The sound would not come.
The vision sharpened.
He saw a hall drowned in smoke. He saw the marks of the Ashen Vanguard upon the walls. He saw men
fighting too close for swords, grappling in the red dark. Someone drove a blade into his side. Someone
else held him upright long enough to whisper a word he could not hear.
Then the crown appeared—not above his head, but beneath his corpse.
The Bleeding Crown waited where his blood touched stone.
Brannoc let the regalia fall.
It struck the floor without a sound.
The hand below the boards spread wide. Every finger pressed upward, outlining itself through the wood.
Korvath’s knife was in his hand now. “Say something.”
Brannoc looked at him.
The smuggler’s face had settled into its guarded shape again, but his eyes betrayed him. He was afraid of
the room. Afraid of the artifacts. Afraid of the future.
Most of all, he was afraid Brannoc might believe it.
Brannoc understood. Belief was the first chain. Acceptance was the second.
He stepped over The Thrice-Bound Edge and placed his palm upon the boards.
The hand beneath met his.
The contact was gentle.
A warmth entered him—not comfort, but recognition.
The buried thing spoke in his own voice.
“You died in 300 AS.”
Brannoc stared into the dark.
Then the floor began to open.

Chapter 13
Rain worried the shutters of Fenspire as though it had teeth.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood beneath the tower’s black ribs and listened to the storm gnaw at
the stone. Beyond the arrow slits, the Gloaming Reach lay drowned in dusk, its marsh-lights trembling
under the rain. Fenspire’s stark spire rose through the dimness like a spear driven into the world by a dying
god.
The garrison numbered 3,742. Brannoc knew the count because the quartermaster had repeated it three
times, each repetition carrying the brittle pride of a man who believed numbers could keep a gate closed.
Fenspire was a core location, garrisoned and vigilant, and the men within its walls wore that vigilance as
another layer of mail.
It would not save them.
Nothing saved anyone. It only delayed the shape of the ruin.
“You are dripping on the map.”
Korvath Nightbrook’s voice came from the dark beside the brazier.
Brannoc looked down. Water crawled from his cloak onto the table, gathering in the inked valleys and
blackening the parchment. Korvath watched the spreading stain with a smuggler’s guarded displeasure. He
favored the shadows even when there were none to hide in, his presence unobtrusive, his eyes always
measuring the door, the window, the nearest hand that might reach for a knife.
“The map was already wrong,” Brannoc said.
“Maps are never wrong. Men are wrong about where they stand.”
“That is a distinction fit for a man who sells passage through holes in walls.”
Korvath’s mouth tightened. “And a sellsword captain is fit to judge the honesty of holes?”
The words settled between them.
Brannoc’s hand rested on the pommel at his hip. The knuckles beneath his wet glove were dark with old
blood. The rain had not washed it away. Rain was not made for that kind of work.
He had been born in 255 AS, though the Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged the blood in his veins.
He was its unacknowledged heir, a secret kept beneath seals, dead tongues, and the obedience of
frightened men. A crown could be denied in a cradle and still grow teeth in the dark.
Now the Accord of Mournthrone was eating those teeth.
“Say it,” Korvath murmured.
Brannoc lifted his gaze.
“You brought me here to say something.”
“I brought you here because the western postern is watched by men who would not recognize you if you
were wearing a crown.”
“I am not wearing one.”

“Not yet.”
The brazier coughed. Smoke crawled low across the chamber, smelling of wet wool and bitter coal. On the
far wall, a rack of regalia waited beneath dustcloths. The Thrice-Bound Edge had been forged in 123 AS.
Its name was stitched into the inventory slate in a careful hand, followed by a blank mark where no
attunement cost had ever been recorded. The object itself was hidden beneath black cloth, restrained even
in silence, as if its bindings had learned patience.
Beside it lay the grimoire Edge of Gloamreach.
Its cover was gray as old ash. The attunement cost was 46. Nothing in the records named its forging date.
The absence troubled Brannoc more than any number might have. A thing without a beginning was a thing
with room for every lie.
He had seen men kill for lesser uncertainties.
Korvath followed his stare. “The books say the grimoire is useless to you.”
“The books say many things.”
“They say the cost is 46.”
“Then the books have counted one burden.”
“And missed the others?”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “You are learning.”
A bell sounded somewhere below. Once. Then again.
The tower answered with a tremor through the floor.
“Movement at the gate,” Korvath said.
“No.”
The smuggler turned his head.
Brannoc listened. Beneath the rain, beneath the mutter of the garrison and the groan of the old stone, he
heard the true sound: not boots advancing, but men leaving their posts. A slow loosening. A withdrawal
dressed as caution.
The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS, and already every oath spoken beneath it had acquired
a hidden price. The Ashen Vanguard named itself the guardian of order. House Morvain called order the
property of the strong. The Silent Choir listened for weakness in every vow. The Iron-Ring Cartel
measured loyalty by what it could carry. The Bleeding Crown waited behind its curtains and let other
hands bleed for its inheritance.
Five powers, all sharpening the same knife.
“Your commander is pulling back,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s eyes narrowed. “You know that?”
“I know the sound of a coward trying to make retreat resemble strategy.”
“You were told there would be no withdrawal.”

“I was told many things.”
“By whom?”
Brannoc looked again at the covered regalia, the blank cost, the nameless forging. “By men who believed
a sealed order could command the dead.”
The door opened.
A soldier entered with rain shining on his shoulders. No herald announced him. No servant took his cloak.
His face held the pallor of someone who had received news and decided not to understand it.
“The western barricade has been abandoned,” he said.
Korvath gave a small, humorless laugh. “There. Now we have the truth.”
Brannoc did not move. The soldier’s gaze dropped to his red-stained hand, then rose again.
“Who ordered it?”
The man swallowed. “The order bore the commander’s seal.”
“Did the commander give it?”
“I was not present.”
“Then you know nothing.”
“I know the men were paid.”
The rain pressed harder against the shutters.
Korvath stepped near the brazier. “Paid by whom?”
The soldier’s silence was answer enough. In the walls of Fenspire, it seemed every stone leaned closer to
hear.
Brannoc felt the old inheritance stir beneath his ribs—not pride, not hope, but the cold recognition that the
world made room for crowns only after they had been fed enough corpses.
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw,” he said.
The soldier flinched as though Brannoc had struck him.
Korvath’s eyes became two dark slits. “You say that as if you expected it.”
“I expected a price. I did not know its shape.”
“And now?”
“Now I know the shape is treason.”
“No,” Korvath said. “Treason is a word used by the poor to describe a bargain they were not invited to
join.”
Brannoc turned on him. “Be careful.”
“I am always careful. That is why I am still alive.”
The words carried no boast. Korvath said them as one might name the weather.

Below, the bell rang a third time.
This time the tower doors groaned open.
Brannoc crossed to the nearest slit. Far beneath him, torches moved through the rain in a disorderly
stream. Men were leaving Fenspire. Some carried packs. Some carried weapons. One carried a bundle that
sagged with a human weight. No one looked upward.
At the edge of the courtyard, the insignia of the Ashen Vanguard passed beneath a veil of rain.
Brannoc’s reflection hovered in the glassless opening: a broad darkness, a scarlet hand, a face the stone
refused to give back. He had no canonical feature for the world to remember. Let it remember the epithet
instead. Let it remember the martial station, the hard presence of a Sellsword Captain, the hand that had
closed around too many hilts and too few promises.
Korvath came to stand beside him.
“What will you do?”
“Stay.”
“Why?”
“Because the men leaving will tell themselves they chose to survive. I want them to see what survival
costs.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one I have.”
“You are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened around the pommel.
Korvath continued, softly now. “You cannot keep pretending this is merely a contract.”
“I have never pretended.”
“You have worn hired steel while others fought over your blood.”
“And what would you have me wear?”
“A claim.”
“A claim is a blade with no handle.”
“Then grasp it by the edge.”
Brannoc looked at him. Korvath’s guarded face had lost its smuggler’s calm. For the first time, the man
seemed afraid—not for himself, but of what Brannoc might do if fear became indistinguishable from
purpose.
Outside, the last of the torches vanished through the gate.
Fenspire remained.
Its garrison of 3,742 had become a number without a body. The walls remained disciplined, vigilant, and
nearly empty of the certainty that had held them. Somewhere in the lower levels, locks were being opened.
Somewhere else, men were deciding which allegiance would forgive them most cheaply.

Brannoc took the dustcloth from The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The regalia beneath was darker than iron and bound in three narrow bands. No attunement cost marked its
record. The absence seemed to watch him.
Korvath stepped back. “Do not.”
“Do not what?”
“Touch what you cannot unmake.”
Brannoc laid his red hand upon the hilt.
The chamber went still.
For an instant he felt the whole Accord of Mournthrone gathered inside the metal: its beginning in 297 AS,
its broken vows, its banners lowered by hands bought in secret. He saw no victory in it. The Ashen
Vanguard might be named victor when the accord ended in 301 AS, but victory was a word men carved
over graves to stop the graves from speaking.
The truth rose through the binding like a drowned thing.
The Accord of Mournthrone had collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Brannoc drew one breath.
Then something struck the door below, and Korvath whispered, “They are coming for you—”
The second blow shook dust from the lintel.
Korvath flinched. Brannoc did not. He kept his hand upon The Thrice-Bound Edge and felt the metal
drinking the tremor from his bones. Beneath his palm, the regalia was cold enough to burn. Its forged
silence pressed against him, threefold and patient, as if the blade had been waiting for a hand that would
not mistake restraint for mercy.
“Which door?” Brannoc asked.
“The only one they need.”
Korvath’s voice had gone thin. He stood beside the shuttered window with one hand inside his coat, where
a smuggler kept the things he trusted least. The room smelled of damp wool, lamp oil, and the bitter
mineral tang rising from the grimoire open upon the table.
Edge of Gloamreach had no cover. Its pages lay exposed to the air, black leaves veined with grey script.
The book’s attunement cost was 46, and the knowledge of it had settled into Brannoc’s skull with the
weight of a nail. Every time his gaze touched the open page, the letters seemed to lean toward him.
Another blow.
The hinges cried.
Brannoc lifted his hand from The Thrice-Bound Edge. A red print remained upon the metal. His blood, or
the memory of it. With the binding, the distinction had become a poor man’s argument.
“Can you get us out?”
Korvath looked toward the floor.

“No.”
“Then why are you still standing?”
“I was waiting for you to say something clever.”
“I have never said anything clever.”
“That is why I am afraid.”
The door shuddered in its frame. A splinter fell inward and struck the flagstones. Through the crack came
a blade of pale corridor light, and within it the moving darkness of someone’s shoulder.
Brannoc turned to the table.
The page had changed.
He had seen no hand touch it. No wind moved in the sealed room. Yet the ink had gathered itself into a
line beneath the older script, each mark wet and shining.
Fenspire.
The word stood alone for a breath, then was followed by another.
The Purge of Blackport waged at Fenspire in 319 AS.
Brannoc read it twice.
The room fell away.
He stood beneath a sky the color of old bruises. A spire rose before him, stark and narrow, its upper
reaches swallowed by Gloaming Reach mist. The stones of Fenspire were dark with rain. Not red. Rain, he
told himself. The mind reached for blood because blood was easier to understand.
Men moved through the streets with covered mouths. Their hands were wrapped in ash-colored cloth.
Doors hung open. Behind one, a bowl rolled slowly across a floor and came to rest against a threshold.
Brannoc heard no cries.
That was the worst of it.
Silence made a city complicit with its own ruin. It turned every wall into a witness and every shutter into a
closed eye. Far above, something struck the spire bell, but the sound did not descend. It remained trapped
in the clouds, trembling there like a thought no one dared complete.
He felt Fenspire’s garrison around him—not as bodies, but as a pressure. Disciplined vigilance sunk into
every stone. Permanent occupation had given the place a second skeleton. Men could be slain. Orders
could be burned. The garrison remained in the walls.
Then the vision twisted.
Blackport appeared in the rain.
Not as a place, but as a wound carried from hand to hand. Its name was carved into doors, scratched into
helmets, whispered by mouths that immediately shut. Brannoc saw the purge not from above, nor from the
street, but from inside the instant before a man made a choice.
A torch rose.

A child’s cup broke.
Someone behind a door pressed both hands over their lips.
Then the room returned.
Brannoc staggered against the table. Edge of Gloamreach groaned beneath his fist. The pages fluttered
though the shutters remained closed.
Korvath caught his sleeve.
“What did you see?”
“Fenspire.”
The smuggler’s grip tightened. “That means nothing.”
“It will.”
The door gave another inch. A dark iron hook appeared through the gap and caught the inner brace. The
wood splintered around it.
Korvath swore softly.
Brannoc stared at the grimoire. The letters were fading now, sinking into the black page as though
ashamed of what they had said.
“Who is behind that door?”
“People who have been paid to believe they are righteous.”
“House Morvain?”
“I did not say that.”
“The Silent Choir?”
“I did not say that either.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Korvath’s eyes hardened. “You have a gift for naming enemies after they have already found us.”
Brannoc reached for his sword. The grip came easily, familiar as a scar. His other hand remained red,
whether by blood or binding no longer mattered. The Thrice-Bound Edge lay upon the table between
them, regalia rather than weapon, though the distinction had always depended upon who was holding it.
A voice spoke through the broken door.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
His name sounded wrong in that mouth. Not feared. Not respected. Catalogued.
Korvath moved toward the window. “There.”
The shutter was fastened from within, but its lower hinge had rotted away. Beyond it waited a narrow drop
into darkness. Korvath knelt and tested the opening with his fingers.
“Can you climb?”

“Can you?”
“I asked first.”
Brannoc looked down at his boots. The room seemed to sway under him. He had commanded men in rain
that turned bowstrings slack. He had watched banners lowered by hands bought in secret. He had carried
the truth of Mournthrone inside his chest while others carved victory over the dead and called the carving
history.
Now a smuggler was asking whether he could climb.
“Yes.”
Korvath gave him a bitter smile. “Good. I hate rescuing corpses.”
The brace split.
The door opened three fingers wide.
A hand entered first, armored to the wrist. It held no weapon. That unsettled Brannoc more than a sword
would have. Men came to kill with steel. Men came to arrest with empty hands. Empty hands belonged to
courts, crowns, and those who believed their violence would be forgiven.
Brannoc seized The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The room darkened.
The regalia did not blaze. It did not sing. It tightened the air around his fingers until his bones felt laced
together. The pressure climbed his arm, crossed his shoulder, and settled behind his eyes.
A second vision opened.
He saw a hall beneath Fenspire. Stone pillars. Damp flags. A row of kneeling figures facing a wall. No
faces. The absence was deliberate.
At the end of the hall stood a throne-shaped chair draped in black cloth.
Someone had placed a crown upon it.
Not worn. Waiting.
Brannoc felt the old wound inside himself stir—the claim never spoken where it could be answered, the
bloodline left unacknowledged, the inheritance that had taught him to sleep with one hand beneath his
pillow. The Bleeding Crown had never called him son. Crowns did not call. They summoned, and men
mistook the summons for honor.
The vision showed him the crown beneath the cloth.
Then it showed him fire.
Brannoc tore himself free.
The table overturned. Edge of Gloamreach struck the floor, its pages snapping open to a spread of blank
blackness. Korvath cursed and shoved the window wider.
“Hurry.”
The door burst inward.

Three figures crowded the gap. Their faces were hidden behind ash-colored masks. The first carried a
short sword. The second bore a hooked pole. The third held a sealed tube against his chest.
Brannoc stepped between them and the table.
The first figure crossed the threshold.
Brannoc’s sword met his.
Steel cracked against steel. The masked man’s wrist buckled. Brannoc turned the blow aside and drove his
shoulder into the man’s chest. He went backward into the others, and for one breath the doorway became a
knot of limbs and cloth.
“Now,” Korvath said.
Brannoc seized the sill.
The drop below was black, though he could make out the glimmer of wet stone. Wind climbed the wall
and entered his sleeves. Behind him, the attackers disentangled themselves. One of them shouted his name
again, but this time the voice carried fear.
Brannoc lowered himself through the opening.
His boots found the outer ledge.
Korvath came after him, clutching the grimoire under one arm. The book’s pages beat against his ribs like
trapped wings.
“Give me your hand.”
Brannoc looked up.
The first masked figure had reached the window. Rain shone on the blade in his grip. Behind him, The
Thrice-Bound Edge lay on the floor, still gathering the room into its silence.
Korvath stretched down.
Brannoc reached for him.
And from within the chamber, beneath the splintered door and the footfalls rushing nearer, the grimoire
began to speak in a voice made of turning pages—one word at a time, each syllable carrying the cold of a
future Brannoc had not yet lived.
Korvath’s fingers closed around his wrist.
The grimoire spoke again.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The name entered the rain and seemed to weigh it down.
Korvath hauled him upward. Brannoc struck the ledge with his shoulder, rolled across the wet stone, and
came up on one knee. The window behind them flared with a pallid light. For an instant the chamber
showed itself through the opening: the masked figure at the sill, the blade lifted, the door bowing inward
beneath the men beyond it.
Then the darkness folded shut.

Korvath seized the back of Brannoc’s coat and dragged him along the ledge.
“Move.”
“I am moving.”
“You are listening.”
“Hard not to.”
The grimoire’s voice followed them through the storm.
“Born in 255 AS.”
Brannoc’s hand found the wall. The stone was slick with rain and old soot. Below, the drop vanished into
blackness. Somewhere beneath that blackness, water hammered rock with the patient violence of a thing
that had never needed to hurry.
Korvath pressed himself against the outer face of the tower. His breath came thinly. A smuggler survived
by distrusting open ground, open doors, and every silence that seemed too complete. Now there was
nowhere to conceal himself but the rain.
“Do you hear it?” Brannoc asked.
“I hear men behind us.”
“The book.”
“I hear that too.”
“Then why are you still carrying it?”
Korvath looked at him. Rain ran from his brow into his eyes, giving his expression the shine of grief.
“Because you told me to.”
“I told you to bring it out.”
“And now it is out.”
The grimoire rested beneath Korvath’s arm, bound in leather darkened by water. Its pages stirred without
wind. Each turn made a dry, intimate sound, like a tongue passing over teeth.
Brannoc reached for it.
Korvath jerked away. “No.”
“You cannot carry it and climb.”
“I can carry it.”
“You are shaking.”
“I am a smuggler. Shaking is how I keep my hands honest.”
Behind them, wood split. A masked face appeared at the window, pale beneath its covering. The figure
thrust an arm through the opening and swept the blade along the ledge. Steel rang against stone where
Brannoc’s throat had been.
He drove his boot into the hand.

The fingers vanished. The blade clattered away into the dark.
“Climb,” Brannoc said.
A rope ladder hung below the ledge, its wet rungs tapping against the tower. Korvath lowered himself
first, pressing the grimoire to his ribs. Brannoc followed, one hand on the rope, one gripping the wall. The
tower leaned out over the ravine. Every gust shifted the ladder beneath them.
From above came a cry, then another. The men in the chamber had found the window.
Brannoc descended.
His palms burned. Rain soaked his sleeves and found the old cuts beneath them. The dark below had no
bottom. He had known worse places. He had made camp in worse places. He had slept with a knife under
his tongue while men negotiated the price of his next sunrise.
But he had never feared a book.
The Edge of Gloamreach whispered.
“Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Korvath halted below him.
The ladder swung out from the wall.
Brannoc’s boot struck Korvath’s shoulder. “Keep going.”
“You heard it.”
“Keep going.”
“You are—”
“Keep going.”
Korvath obeyed, though obedience sat badly upon him. He descended until his boots met a narrow shelf of
stone. Brannoc joined him. The shelf ran around the tower, scarcely broad enough for a man’s foot, and
ended at a seam in the rock where darkness breathed cold air.
A passage.
Korvath placed one hand against the seam. “This was not on the plan.”
“There was a plan?”
“There was always a plan.”
“Then your plan has improved.”
He pushed. The stone gave inward, revealing a cleft. Brannoc entered sideways, shoulders scraping grit
from the walls. Korvath followed with the grimoire held above the water gathering at the floor.
The passage narrowed, then opened into a low chamber beneath the tower. Rain dripped through the
ceiling. The air tasted of iron and wet ash.
Korvath set the book down.
It opened by itself.

The pages were blank for a breath. Then ink rose from the fibers in thin black threads, arranging itself into
lines.
“Forged in 123 AS.”
Brannoc stared.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay far above them, still inside the chamber they had fled. He could feel its
silence through the stone: a pressure without weight, a restraint that seemed to bind not flesh but intention.
Regalia, the record had called it. The name had sounded ceremonial when first they found it.
Nothing ceremonial had ever looked at him that way.
Korvath leaned close to the page. “What was forged?”
“The Thrice-Bound Edge.”
“Regalia,” Korvath muttered. “That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one the book gives.”
Another line appeared.
“No attunement cost.”
Korvath rubbed his mouth. “That should comfort me.”
“It does not comfort you.”
“It is not trying to.”
Above them, boots crossed the chamber floor. Dust sifted down. The masked figures had reached the stair
or found another way around. Brannoc imagined the blade in one of their hands, wet with rain, searching
the dark by instinct.
He looked at the grimoire. “What does it want?”
Korvath gave a humorless smile. “You ask that as though it has manners.”
The page turned.
“Attunement cost: 46.”
The words were written beneath the name Edge of Gloamreach.
Korvath took a step back.
Brannoc felt the number settle inside him. Not as knowledge. As a hook.
“Forty-six what?” Korvath said.
“The book does not say.”
“Then it may say anything.”
“It has not.”
“It has named you.”

Brannoc looked down at his hands. In the weak light, the water on them appeared dark. His epithet had
followed him through camps, courts, alleys, and battlefields: the Red-Handed. Men gave it to him because
they needed a story that did not include the things he had done before they met him. It was easier to blame
the color than ask where it came from.
The Edge of Gloamreach turned a page.
“Accord of Mournthrone.”
Brannoc’s jaw tightened.
Korvath whispered, “Do not read it.”
The book wrote on.
“Begins in 297 AS.”
The chamber seemed to contract. Even the dripping stopped, listening.
“Ends in 301 AS.”
Korvath reached for the cover.
Brannoc caught his wrist. “Let it speak.”
“It is speaking of war.”
“It is speaking of what comes.”
“That is worse.”
The ink gathered in a thick black pool before forming the next words.
“Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Brannoc released Korvath.
For a moment he saw a field beneath a colorless sky, though no such field lay beyond the chamber. He
saw banners dragged through mud. He saw men kneeling because the alternative was to remain standing
before those who had won. He saw the five powers tightening their hands around the realm: the Ashen
Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown.
The names were not merely factions. They were appetites wearing heraldry.
Korvath read them over his shoulder. “The Ashen Vanguard wins.”
“The book says so.”
“Books lie.”
“Not when they are frightened.”
Korvath looked at him sharply.
The grimoire’s pages trembled.
“The losing commander bribed to withdraw.”
Neither man spoke.

Above, the pursuit had gone quiet. That silence was worse than the boots. The masked figures were
searching now, and searchers were patient when they believed the world had already closed around their
prey.
Korvath bent over the grimoire. “Who?”
The ink did not answer.
Brannoc felt the old pressure behind his ribs, the one that came whenever someone spoke of crowns as
though crowns were objects instead of wounds. The Bleeding Crown had never acknowledged him. It had
not needed to. Blood kept its own account.
The page turned.
“Died in 300 AS.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened.
Korvath lifted his head.
“During the Accord of Mournthrone.”
The words remained.
Brannoc read them again. The rain, the stone, the passage, Korvath’s drawn face—all of it slipped away
beneath the clean simplicity of the sentence.
Died in 300 AS.
He found himself searching for the loophole. Books had loopholes. Priests had loopholes. Kings had entire
armies of men dedicated to discovering them. Perhaps “died” meant a name buried, a claim extinguished,
a man made dead in the eyes of those who required him absent.
Korvath said, “It could mean someone else.”
“It used my name.”
“It could be a warning.”
“It used the past tense.”
The grimoire wrote again.
“Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
His own name seemed smaller the second time.
Then, beneath it:
“Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Korvath’s face changed. Fear remained, but something older moved beneath it: calculation, the instinct
that had made him a smuggler rather than a corpse. He glanced toward the passage mouth.
“Who else knows?”
Brannoc looked at him.
“About the Crown,” Korvath said. “About you.”

“The book knows.”
“I did not ask what the book knows.”
“You were not meant to.”
“I was not meant to carry it either.”
A dull impact shook the stone behind them.
The hidden door.
Another impact. Grit sifted from the ceiling. The seam brightened with a blade of gray light.
Korvath snatched up the Edge of Gloamreach. “There.”
Beyond the chamber, a stair descended into blackness. No sound came from it. No rain. No pursuit.
Brannoc could smell cold earth and something bitter, like ash left in a dead hearth.
The book writhed under Korvath’s arm.
“Crookvale.”
The name was followed by a map, ink spreading across the page in crooked lines.
“Founded in 295 AS.”
The stair seemed to tilt beneath Brannoc’s boots.
“In The High Spires,” Korvath read.
The hidden door shuddered again.
“Rebuilt.”
“Garrison of 1004.”
Korvath stared at the number.
Brannoc saw the calculation return to his eyes, sharper now. A garrison was not safety. It was a locked
jaw. A hundred doors, a thousand watchful hands, orders carried through barracks and towers. A place
outside the core holdings could survive only by suspecting everyone who approached it.
The grimoire finished the line.
“Outside the core holdings.”
The door behind them cracked. A sliver of masked metal appeared in the gap.
Korvath shoved the book at Brannoc. “You carry it.”
Brannoc caught it against his chest. The leather was warm.
“What is in Crookvale?”
“Nothing good.”
“You know it?”
“I know enough to avoid it.”

“Then we go there.”
Korvath seized his sleeve. “That was not an invitation.”
The book opened against Brannoc’s heart.
“Fenspire.”
Its pages filled with a stark black tower surrounded by smaller marks, each one a waiting blade.
“In the Gloaming Reach.”
“Founded in 57 AS.”
“Garrison of 3,742.”
“Garrisoned status.”
The last words appeared slowly, as though pressed into the page by an invisible thumb.
Korvath whispered, “No.”
Brannoc felt the name draw him harder than the darkness below. Fenspire. A core location. A permanent
military throat in the dim reaches, disciplined and vigilant, built around a spire that had endured while
other things were broken and forgotten.
The hidden door burst inward.
A masked figure lunged through the opening.
Brannoc struck him with the grimoire.
The impact sounded like a bell beneath deep water. The figure folded. The mask struck stone and split.
Korvath was already descending the stair.
Brannoc followed, the grimoire clutched in both hands. Behind him, the broken door filled with bodies.
Ahead, the dark opened wider.
On the page, beneath the name Fenspire, new ink began to crawl.
Not a place.
Not a date.
A sentence.
Brannoc read it as he descended.
“Bring the heir to the tower, and the dead will learn to speak.”

Chapter 14
The rain came sideways over Crookvale, needling the shutters and turning the yard below into a black
mirror.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood without his cloak, listening to the fortress breathe around him.
Stone settled in the walls. Iron groaned in its sockets. Somewhere beneath the keep, a horse struck its stall
with one impatient hoof, and the sound climbed through the floor like a warning from the buried dead.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS, though the oldest stones in its rebuilt walls had been cut long
before that year. They did not fit cleanly. Nothing in Crookvale fit cleanly. Its towers leaned into the
mountain wind, its gates closed with the reluctance of old jaws, and its garrison of 1004 watched the high
passes with the exhausted suspicion of men who expected the world to come crawling out of the snow.
The settlement remained outside the core holdings. That was how the ledgers described it.
Ledgers had never slept beneath a roof that shook when the peaks spoke.
Brannoc rested one red hand upon the table. The other remained near the sword at his hip, not because he
expected an attack, but because expectation had become a second pulse in him. The scarlet stain across his
knuckles was old wine, not blood. He had washed the blood away before entering the room.
The name had stayed.
The Red-Handed.
He had earned it too many times to resent it.
“Your rain has teeth,” Korvath Nightbrook said.
The smuggler crouched beside the shutter, narrow in the dark, favoring the unobtrusive presence of a man
accustomed to concealed trade. His coat was wet to the elbows. Water dripped from him onto the rushes,
darkening them one by one.
“Crookvale is not mine.”
“No.” Korvath glanced toward the table. “Neither are the things you brought me.”
Brannoc looked down.
The Thrice-Bound Edge lay wrapped in a square of oilskin. Even hidden, it possessed the stillness of
regalia. Its name had been written three times on the inventory, each line in a different hand, as if the
scribes feared a single inscription might fail to hold it. Forged in 123 AS, it had no attunement cost
recorded against it.
Beside it rested the Edge of Gloamreach, a grimoire bound in material that drank the candlelight. Its
attunement cost was 46. Its forging date was not recorded in the supplied facts, though whoever had made
it had known enough of dusk to give the pages a color like bruised twilight.
Korvath would not touch either.
“Those are not meant for a table,” he said.
“Then stop looking at them.”
“I am looking at the door.”

“You have been looking at the door since you arrived.”
“That is why I am alive.”
Brannoc’s mouth tightened. He had known men who mistook caution for courage, and men who mistook
fear for wisdom. Korvath did neither. He carried his wariness openly, like a knife kept under the tongue.
Outside, a bell sounded once.
Not an alarm. A watch-change signal.
Crookvale’s garrison moved in the rain. Boots crossed the inner yard. Metal struck metal. Orders passed
from mouth to mouth and dissolved beneath the weather.
“The five powers are moving,” Korvath said.
“The five powers are always moving.”
“The Ashen Vanguard has sent riders into the high roads. House Morvain has bought grain where there is
no grain to buy. The Silent Choir is asking questions without speaking them. The Iron-Ring Cartel has
closed three routes and opened two others for a price. And the Bleeding Crown—”
“Do not say it as if it were a fifth thing.”
Korvath’s gaze shifted from the door to Brannoc.
“The Bleeding Crown is a fifth thing.”
Brannoc felt the words enter him with the slow, cold force of a blade.
He had spent his life being a fact that could not be spoken aloud. An unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding
Crown: blood without witness, inheritance without a seal, a crown reflected in a dark basin and denied
whenever he reached toward it.
His fingers curled.
The table creaked under his hand.
“Do you know what happens to men who carry messages like that?” he asked.
“They become important.”
“They become dead.”
Korvath gave a small shrug. “Sometimes both.”
The rain hissed along the shutters. Brannoc imagined the world beyond the room: the crooked towers, the
mountain roads, the snow gathering in the cuts of the stone. He imagined Fenspire, far away in the
Gloaming Reach, standing beneath its stark spire with its 3,742 soldiers behind walls that had never
learned the meaning of sleep. Fenspire had been founded in 57 AS. It was a core location, garrisoned and
disciplined, a hard tooth in the dim mouth of the Reach.
Crookvale was wary.
Fenspire was vigilant.
The difference between them was not courage. It was what the realm had decided was worth defending.

Korvath took a folded strip of parchment from inside his coat. He did not offer it. He held it between two
fingers and watched Brannoc watch him.
“The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS,” he said. “It has not ended.”
“It has a name,” Brannoc replied. “That is not the same thing.”
“The record says it will end in 301 AS.”
“The record says many things.”
“With the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Brannoc looked at the parchment. “And what does the record say about the dead?”
Korvath’s expression did not change. “The record is less interested in them.”
A gust struck the keep. The flame of the nearest candle bowed almost flat, recovering only after a moment.
On the wall, Brannoc’s shadow stretched toward the door with its hand at the throat of some unseen man.
The Accord of Mournthrone had the shape of a broken promise. Every faction spoke of settlement, and
every faction measured the distance to the next throat. The Ashen Vanguard called itself order. House
Morvain called itself blood. The Silent Choir called nothing by any name. The Iron-Ring Cartel weighed
every allegiance against profit. The Bleeding Crown waited beneath all of them, patient as rot under paint.
Brannoc knew what the others saw when they looked at him: a major Sellsword Captain, useful in a siege,
dangerous in a negotiation, purchasable until proven otherwise.
They did not see the crown in his shadow.
They saw the red on his hands and assumed they understood its source.
“Read it,” Korvath said.
“Read it yourself.”
“I cannot.”
“Why?”
“Because it is written in a hand that does not forgive mistakes.”
Brannoc reached for the parchment.
The writing was cramped, pressed hard enough to score the fibers. No seal marked it. No signature named
its author. Still, the meaning stood clear.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
Brannoc read the sentence twice.
The room seemed to draw inward. The rain became distant. Even the garrison outside went silent, though
he knew the men had not stopped moving.
“Where did you get this?” he asked.
Korvath’s mouth twitched. “You asked me to move a thing through a locked gate. You did not ask me to
become innocent.”

“If this is false—”
“Then the Accord remains what everyone believes it is.”
“And if it is true?”
“Then the Ashen Vanguard will be named victor over a corpse someone else purchased.”
Brannoc folded the parchment. “Who was paid?”
Korvath did not answer.
“Who paid him?”
Still nothing.
Brannoc lifted his eyes. “You smuggle secrets. Do not pretend you have no cargo.”
“I have cargo enough to drown in.”
“You brought this here.”
“I brought it because you are the sort of man who understands the value of an ugly truth.”
“No. I am the sort of man who understands the value of a sharp one.”
He laid the parchment beside the Edge of Gloamreach. The grimoire’s cover seemed to darken beneath it.
Korvath finally crossed the room. He kept one hand tucked beneath his coat and the other held open,
empty. Near the artifacts, he stopped.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge,” he murmured. “Regalia forged in 123 AS. No attunement cost.”
“You memorized the inventory.”
“I memorized the danger.”
“And the grimoire?”
“Edge of Gloamreach. Attunement cost 46. No forging date recorded.”
“Then you know what you are carrying.”
“I know what I am refusing to carry.”
Brannoc unwrapped the regalia.
The room changed.
There was no flash, no voice from beyond the world. Only a pressure, subtle as a thumb against the
breastbone. The iron fittings in the shutters trembled. Korvath stepped back. Brannoc did not.
The name of the artifact seemed to draw every other name toward it: Crookvale, Fenspire, Mournthrone,
the Ashen Vanguard, the Bleeding Crown. Names gathered like wolves around a wounded thing.
He thought of 255 AS, the year of his birth. A year no one had marked in a royal register. A year given to
him by a confession made too late and beneath a roof where the candles had burned blue.
He thought of 300 AS, the year in which he would die during the Accord of Mournthrone.

The knowledge had never come to him as prophecy. It was simply there now, cold and immovable, as if
the future had left a weapon in his hands and expected him to choose whether to use it.
Korvath saw something in his face.
“What is it?” the smuggler asked.
Brannoc closed his hand around the Thrice-Bound Edge.
The pressure vanished.
Below them, the bell sounded again.
This time, the gate was opening.
Korvath turned sharply. “That is not a watch-change.”
“No.”
“Who is coming?”
Brannoc looked toward the shutter. Through a narrow gap, torchlight moved in the yard below—too many
flames, held too evenly against the wind.
He did not know who was coming.
That was the trouble with power. It made a man visible long before it made him safe.
The door latch lifted.
Korvath reached beneath his coat.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The door began to open.
The door opened inward.
A man stood beyond it in a cloak darkened by rain. Two soldiers flanked him, their hands resting near
their blades, while more torchlight crowded the passage behind them. The flames gilded the wet stone and
made the corridor seem to breathe.
Brannoc kept his sword low.
The cloaked man looked first at Korvath, then at the Thrice-Bound Edge clenched in Brannoc’s hand.
“Put it away,” he said.
Korvath’s fingers tightened beneath his coat. “You came to ask?”
“I came to prevent a slaughter.”
“That is a long way from asking.”
The man stepped over the threshold. He was not armored, but the soldiers behind him were, their mail
dark with rain. No crest showed on the cloaks. That absence was more deliberate than any banner.
Brannoc watched the man’s eyes. They were pale, steady, and afraid in the way of men who had learned to
make fear useful.

“Who sent you?” Brannoc asked.
The man’s gaze returned to him. “The same power that will be blamed when this room is found empty.”
“Then you have not answered.”
“No,” the man said. “I have not.”
The bell sounded below, deep enough to tremble through the floorboards. Somewhere in the yard, horses
shifted and snorted. A command passed through the rain, too muffled to understand.
Korvath leaned toward Brannoc without lowering his voice. “That many torches means a search.”
“It means someone wants us to believe it does.”
“Does that distinction keep steel out of the ribs?”
“It has not yet failed me.”
Korvath gave him a look that held no admiration.
Brannoc had been born in 255 AS, into a house that had possessed no house-name worth preserving. He
had learned early that men who called themselves masters preferred a blade that asked no questions. Later,
when they discovered what ran beneath his silence, they had begun to ask questions with knives.
The unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown could not afford to be found in a locked room with a
smuggler and a relic that had made the air go cold.
The man in the doorway extended one gloved hand.
“Give me The Thrice-Bound Edge.”
Brannoc felt the thing press against his palm, though his fingers were still wrapped around its hilt. It had
been forged in 123 AS, long before the Sundering’s children learned to mistake inheritance for destiny. Its
record contained no attunement cost. That omission had always troubled him more than a price would
have.
“No,” he said.
The soldiers drew their blades.
Korvath cursed softly.
The cloaked man did not move. “You do not understand what is happening beneath this garrison.”
“Then explain it.”
“There is a book.”
