Brannoc’s attention sharpened.
The man saw it. “Edge of Gloamreach.”
The name seemed to dim the room.
Korvath’s hand came free of his coat, holding a narrow knife. “That was not part of the bargain.”
“Neither was the army in the yard,” Brannoc said.
“I told you what I knew.”

“You told me what you wanted me to believe.”
“I told you enough to get us through the gate.”
“And now?”
“Now I am considering whether the gate was the clever part of the trap.”
The cloaked man turned his head toward Korvath. “The grimoire has an attunement cost of 46. Whoever
opens it will pay.”
“Pay what?” Brannoc asked.
The man’s mouth hardened. “The record does not say.”
A gust struck the shutters. Rain hissed through the cracks, cold against Brannoc’s knuckles. He looked
past the doorway to the passage. The soldiers had positioned themselves badly for a fight. Too close
together. Too certain that fear would do the work for them.
That meant the cloaked man was not here to kill him.
Not yet.
“Where is the book?” Brannoc asked.
“Below.”
“How far?”
“Far enough.”
The bell sounded again.
This time the note was cut short, as though a hand had closed around its throat.
The cloaked man’s composure broke. He looked toward the stairwell.
A noise rose from beneath them—not a voice, not quite. It was the dragging groan of something immense
passing through stone. Dust sifted from the ceiling. One of the soldiers crossed himself with two fingers,
then stopped when he realized he had been seen.
Korvath’s eyes narrowed. “That beneath us?”
“Yes.”
“Then why bring us here?”
“Because it has begun.”
The Thrice-Bound Edge pulsed once in Brannoc’s hand.
The room’s shadows leaned toward it.
He had used the blade before. He had trusted it because trust was a word men used when they had run out
of better options. It had cut through armor, bone, and bindings that no ordinary steel should have touched.
Each time, afterward, something in the world had seemed to remember him.
He wondered whether the Edge had chosen him, or whether it merely recognized the shape of a man
already bound.

“Tell me the truth,” Brannoc said.
The cloaked man’s face became very still.
“Do not mistake silence for obedience.”
“The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS,” the man said. “It ends in blood whether the parchment
survives or not.”
“An accord does not end until someone signs it.”
“The Accord of Mournthrone ends in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Korvath stared at him. “You speak as if you have already read the last page.”
“I speak as a man who has seen how victories are arranged.”
Brannoc heard the lie beneath the certainty. Not a lie about the years. A lie about how much the man
knew.
The Accord of Mournthrone had the odor of old rot: sealed timber, wet banners, promises made where no
witnesses could hear. If the Ashen Vanguard took the victory, the realm would call it order. The losing
commander would be praised for courage or condemned for cowardice, depending on which side bought
the louder singers. Beneath it all, the truth would remain—a losing commander bribed to withdraw.
Brannoc felt the thought settle in him like a stone.
The five powers were already circling the wound. The Ashen Vanguard would call it duty. House Morvain
would call it inheritance. The Silent Choir would call it silence. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call it a
market. The Bleeding Crown would call it blood.
None of them would call it what it was.
A door below slammed.
The soldiers looked at one another.
The cloaked man said, “You must choose now.”
Brannoc almost laughed. Choice had always been presented to him after the killing had begun.
“What waits below?”
“The Edge of Gloamreach.”
“And what waits outside?”
“Those who were sent to seize it.”
“By whom?”
The man said nothing.
Korvath stepped toward the shutter. “I can get us out through the roof.”
“You cannot,” Brannoc said.
“I have climbed worse.”
“The yard is watched.”

“Then we climb better.”
Brannoc glanced at him. “You are afraid.”
“I am a smuggler. Fear is the only honest thing I carry.”
The answer pleased him despite himself.
Another sound moved beneath the floor. This one was softer: a wet tapping, patient and irregular. Brannoc
imagined fingers beneath the stones. He imagined the grimoire lying in darkness, waiting for a hand that
could bear its cost.
The cloaked man drew a short blade from beneath his cloak. “If you refuse, I will order them to take the
room.”
“You have already ordered them.”
“I have not ordered them to kill you.”
“That is not mercy.”
“No.”
Brannoc turned the Thrice-Bound Edge in his grip. The cold along its length deepened until his knuckles
ached.
He had been called the Red-Handed long before the Bleeding Crown’s blood became a secret carried from
mouth to mouth. The name had begun as an accusation, then hardened into a title. Men feared what it
suggested. They feared a hand that had done too much killing to tremble at one more.
He had never told them the truth: his hand trembled often.
It trembled now.
Not from fear.
From recognition.
The Edge wanted the stairs.
“No one touches the book,” he said.
The cloaked man’s eyes lowered to the relic. “You do not command here.”
“Then stand aside.”
The first soldier lunged.
Brannoc moved before thought could catch him. He struck the man’s wrist with the flat of his sword,
caught the descending blade against his own, and drove his shoulder into the soldier’s chest. Mail bit
through cloth. The man hit the wall hard enough to rattle the torch bracket.
The second soldier came in low.
Korvath’s knife flashed. It found the gap beneath the man’s arm, and the soldier folded with a startled
breath. Korvath caught him before he fell, lowering him with care that did not belong in a room about to
become a slaughterhouse.
The cloaked man stood untouched.

Brannoc pointed his sword at him. “Open the way.”
For one heartbeat, none of them moved.
Then the stone beneath the room split.
A black line opened across the floorboards. Cold air poured through it, carrying the smell of extinguished
fires and something sweet beneath that, something like flowers left too long in a sealed grave.
Korvath backed away. “That was not there.”
The cloaked man whispered, “It has found us.”
The gap widened.
From below came a woman’s voice, soft and clear, speaking a name Brannoc had not heard since before
he knew what a crown was.
His sword lowered by a fraction.
The cloaked man saw it.
“So,” he said. “It knows you.”
The voice spoke again.
“Brannoc.”
Not the name men used in camps, with a cup between their teeth and fear hidden behind laughter. Not the
title bought with blood and repeated by heralds who had never watched a line break.
It spoke the name his mother had given him.
The floor opened another handspan. Beneath the boards lay no cellar, no foundation, no packed earth.
There was only a depth of dark in which pale motes drifted upward, slow as ash falling in reverse.
Korvath Nightbrook swore under his breath and reached for the knife beneath his coat.
“Do not,” said the cloaked man.
Korvath’s hand froze. “You give orders now?”
“I give warnings.”
“You gave one before. About the stone. We ignored it.”
“And yet you are still alive.”
“For how long?”
The woman below laughed softly.
Brannoc’s grip tightened around his sword. The metal had gone cold enough to ache against his palm. He
had heard that voice in a room of summer rain, long ago, when the world had still seemed to possess a
shape beneath its ruin. He remembered the murmur of cloth. He remembered a crown laid upon black
stone. He remembered kneeling, though he had never told himself before whom.
The memory was not his own.
That was the worst of it.

“What is under us?” he asked.
The cloaked man tilted his head toward the fissure. “A door.”
“To where?”
“To the part of the realm that survived.”
Korvath gave a brittle laugh. “That is a poet’s answer.”
“It is the only one you can afford.”
The gap widened with a sound like wet timber tearing. The room leaned toward it. Loose pebbles skittered
across the floorboards, vanished into the dark, and made no sound when they fell.
Brannoc stepped back.
The thing below spoke his name a third time, and something inside him answered.
His sword arm jerked. The blade dipped toward the opening.
The cloaked man moved faster than a man in heavy cloth should have moved. He seized Brannoc’s wrist.
The grip was neither strong nor weak. It was absolute.
“Let go.”
“If you strike the dark, it will strike through you.”
Brannoc turned his wrist, forcing the man’s fingers apart. “Then tell me what it wants.”
“It wants what was denied.”
The voice below breathed his name into the room.
Korvath’s face had gone grey beneath the grime. “You know it.”
“I know the hunger.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.” The cloaked man released Brannoc. “It is what you need to hear.”
Brannoc looked down into the wound in the floor. “You brought us here.”
“I brought you to a place where the lock was already failing.”
“To Crookvale?”
The cloaked man said nothing.
Brannoc knew the silence. It was the silence of a man guarding a bargain, or a corpse, or both.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. Its rebuilt walls had taken their shape from
necessity rather than beauty, crooked and hard-edged against the heights. A garrison of 1004 held it,
though the settlement remained outside the core holdings. Men called it resilient when they wanted to
praise it and wary when they wanted to excuse its refusal.
Brannoc had called it useful.
That had been before the floor opened.

“Who else knows this place?” he said.
“House Morvain knows enough to fear it.”
“The Ashen Vanguard?”
“Enough to burn it.”
“The Silent Choir?”
“Enough to listen.”
“And the Iron-Ring Cartel?”
The cloaked man’s hood turned a fraction. “Enough to sell what crawls out.”
The names settled among them like drawn blades. Beyond the warped shutters, wind worried at the walls.
Somewhere in the rebuilt settlement, a bell began to ring. Once. Then silence. No alarm followed. Perhaps
the bell had cracked. Perhaps those who heard it had decided ignorance was the safer allegiance.
Brannoc thought of the Bleeding Crown.
The name had been kept from him like a knife hidden beneath a child’s pillow. He had learned it through
glances, through doors opening when they should have remained barred, through men who bowed only
after checking who watched them. He was its unacknowledged heir. The knowledge had never made him
feel chosen. It had made every kindness suspect.
The dark below stirred.
A pale hand rose through the fissure.
It was not flesh. It resembled the impression of a hand pressed into smoke, five long marks widening and
narrowing as if the thing behind it had forgotten how fingers worked.
Korvath drew his knife.
This time the cloaked man did not stop him.
The smuggler slashed downward.
The blade passed through the pale hand. Frost burst along its edge. Korvath cried out and dropped it. The
knife struck the boards and stood upright, quivering.
The hand closed around nothing.
Brannoc kicked the weapon away. “You have a talent for making things worse.”
Korvath clutched his wrist. “I have a talent for surviving men who say that.”
The hand sank.
Something struck the underside of the floor.
Once.
Dust fell from the rafters.
Again.
The walls answered with a low groan.

The cloaked man reached inside his coat and drew out a book bound in material too dark to be leather. Its
clasp was a strip of tarnished metal twisted into the shape of a closed eye.
“Edge of Gloamreach,” he said.
Brannoc watched him. “A grimoire.”
“Attunement cost is 46.”
Korvath stared. “You bring a book into a sinking room?”
“A book is often the last thing standing when men stop.”
The clasp opened by itself.
The pages turned though there was no wind. Letters crawled over them in lines of dim grey, disappearing
as quickly as they formed. Brannoc saw fragments: a road beneath a road, a mouth without a face, a crown
carried in a basin of blood.
Then the book stopped.
One sentence darkened across the page.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed, born in 255 AS.
He felt the room contract around him.
Korvath looked from the page to Brannoc. “That is your name.”
“It is.”
“Why is it in there?”
“Because you are not as ignorant as you pretend,” said the cloaked man.
Brannoc took one step toward him. “You knew.”
“I knew the record.”
“You knew what I was.”
“I knew what the record called you.”
The fissure widened again. The boards at Brannoc’s feet bent toward the opening. He could feel the pull in
his teeth.
The page turned.
Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
Korvath’s breath escaped him as a small, wounded sound.
Brannoc did not look away from the cloaked man. “Read the rest.”
“No.”
“Read it.”
The cloaked man’s silence became an answer.

Brannoc seized the book. Its cover burned cold against his palm. The letters on the page blurred, then
sharpened.
The record named the Accord of Mournthrone.
The Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS and ended in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named
victor.
His thumb pressed into the margin until the page tore.
“Why show me this?”
The cloaked man’s voice had lost its calm. “Because the door has opened for you.”
“I did not ask it to.”
“Doors do not require permission from the man they were built to betray.”
A tremor passed through the walls. The book slipped in Brannoc’s grasp and fell open to another page.
The Accord of Mournthrone.
The words repeated themselves, smaller now, like a whisper behind the first.
Its collapse unleashed a decade of guerrilla reprisals.
Korvath looked toward the shutters. “A decade?”
“Not prophecy,” said the cloaked man. “Record.”
“Records can lie.”
“Then pray this one does.”
Brannoc stared at the page. Beneath the words, written in a darker hand, was the hidden truth: the losing
commander was bribed to withdraw.
The knowledge entered him like a nail.
The Ashen Vanguard had not won by strength alone. The realm had not broken because its strongest hand
had been beaten. Someone had opened the fist from within and called the fall an accord.
The door below gave a slow, hungry sigh.
“What happens in 300 AS?” Brannoc asked.
The cloaked man did not answer.
Brannoc turned the page himself.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone.
For a moment the room became very still.
Korvath whispered, “That cannot be.”
Brannoc looked at the words until they ceased to resemble letters. “It has not happened.”
“Not yet,” said the cloaked man.
The voice beneath them spoke with his mother’s tenderness.

“Come home.”
Brannoc’s sword rose.
The cloaked man stepped between him and the opening. “If you go down, the door closes.”
“If I stay?”
“It opens.”
“On what?”
The blackness beneath the floor brightened. Not with flame. With a colour that had no place in the world
above, a dull crimson spreading through the depth like blood through water.
The woman’s voice came again.
“Come home, Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
Korvath backed into the wall. “That is not a woman.”
“No,” Brannoc said.
He understood now why the voice had known him. Why the dark had waited. Why the book had carried
his death like an appointment.
It was not calling him toward a place.
It was calling him toward the shape of the man he would become.
The cloaked man lifted one hand. In it lay a narrow circlet of black metal, bound three times around itself.
“The Thrice-Bound Edge,” he said. “Regalia forged in 123 AS.”
Brannoc stared at it. “You expect a crown to save me?”
“No. I expect it to tell the door what you are.”
The floor split from wall to wall.
The room fell.
Korvath shouted. The cloaked man vanished behind a curtain of dust. Brannoc caught the edge of the table
as the boards tilted steeply toward the dark. His sword tore free from his hand and slid away, spinning
once before it disappeared.
Below, something vast drew breath.
The circlet struck the floor beside him.
Brannoc reached for it.
The woman began to sing.

Chapter 15
The rain came down black over Mournthrone.
It slicked the stones of the outer yard and drew the soot from the walls in long, bleeding runnels. Beneath
the battlements, the campfires guttered in their pits. Men crouched around them with their cloaks drawn
tight, their faces hollowed by smoke and hunger. Beyond the walls, the land fell away into darkness, and
somewhere in that darkness a horn sounded once.
Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed stood beneath the broken archway and listened to the silence that
followed.
A silence like a held breath.
His hand rested on the pommel at his hip. Not a famous blade. Not regalia. Steel made for work, its grip
worn smooth by a sellsword’s palm. He had carried it through sieges, mutinies, and the long ash-storms
that followed the Sundering. It had never asked his name.
Men had.
They asked it now in whispers, when they thought he could not hear.
Ironmere.
Red-Handed.
Crown-blood.
The last was the most dangerous. The last was the lie that happened to be true.
He looked toward the inner keep, where a narrow window burned with candlelight. The room beyond it
held the officers of the Accord of Mournthrone, and perhaps the fate of every bastard, soldier, and starving
town beneath its shadow. The Accord of Mournthrone had begun in 297 AS. It would end in 301 AS with
the Ashen Vanguard named victor.
He knew this with the same cold certainty with which he knew he would die in 300 AS during the Accord
of Mournthrone.
The knowledge did not come as prophecy. It had no voice, no vision, no hand laid upon his shoulder. It
lived inside him like a nail driven through bone. Some mornings he woke expecting to find the point
protruding from his chest.
Tonight, he felt the nail turning.
A figure crossed the yard, hunched beneath a tarred cloak. He moved without hurry, which was the first
mark of a man who knew how to flee. The second was that he never looked at the guards.
Brannoc watched him approach.
“Kneel,” said one of the sentries.
The cloaked man stopped.
Rain ticked against the iron rings sewn into his boots. “If I kneel, I’ll drown.”
The sentry raised his spear.

Brannoc lifted two fingers. “Let him through.”
The sentry glanced at him, then lowered the spear.
The man came beneath the archway. Water shone on his cheeks. He was not old, though caution had
gathered around his eyes like another kind of age.
“K orvath Nightbrook,” Brannoc said.
The smuggler’s mouth tightened. “You say it as though it’s a crime.”
“Most names are.”
Korvath looked past him toward the keep. “You’re expected.”
“I’m seldom expected anywhere worth going.”
“There’s a room above the eastern stair.”
“By whom?”
“By those who have coins enough to expect.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Korvath did not answer.
The rain whispered between them. From the wall, a soldier coughed into his sleeve. Somewhere behind
the keep, a horse screamed, and another answered.
Brannoc studied the smuggler’s hands. No visible weapon. That meant nothing. A man who moved
contraband through hostile country did not survive by carrying what everyone expected him to carry.
“What did they buy?” Brannoc asked.
“Silence.”
“Expensive.”
“Not theirs.”
Korvath drew a small object from beneath his cloak. He did not offer it at once. A coin lay across his
palm, dull beneath the rainwater. Its face had been shaved smooth. Its edge bore a shallow notch.
Brannoc felt the old nail turn.
“Where?” he asked.
“In the chapel of the Bleeding Crown.”
“There is no chapel here.”
“There is a room they call one.”
“And the coin?”
“Payment.”
“For what?”
Korvath’s eyes flicked toward the keep. “For withdrawal.”

The word entered Brannoc more cleanly than a blade.
He took the coin. It was cold, but beneath the cold lay the greasy warmth of a hand that had held it too
long. A bribe left its own stain. Not visible. Never visible. It clung to the mind.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
That was the hidden truth beneath the Accord of Mournthrone, beneath the speeches, beneath the banners
and the solemn oaths. Men would call it exhaustion. They would call it prudence. They would call it a
victory earned by the Ashen Vanguard through discipline and sacrifice.
They would not call it purchased.
Brannoc closed his fingers around the coin.
“Why bring this to me?”
“I didn’t.”
The smuggler nodded toward the keep. “They sent for you.”
“Then you brought it to them.”
“I carried it where I was paid to carry it.”
“And now?”
“Now I’m here.”
“That isn’t an answer.”
“It’s the only one that survives.”
Korvath turned away.
Brannoc caught his sleeve. The cloth was rough and wet. Korvath went still, not frightened—simply
ready.
“Who paid you?”
The smuggler looked at Brannoc’s hand, then at his face. “A man who didn’t want his name remembered.”
“Everyone wants that.”
“No. Some men want their names remembered. They just want the wrong names spoken.”
Brannoc released him.
A bell sounded from the keep.
Once.
The guards straightened. The men around the fires lowered their voices. Above the wall, the banners
stirred in the rain: the Ashen Vanguard’s ash-gray field, House Morvain’s dark device, the pale marks of
the Silent Choir, the iron colors of the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the torn crimson of the Bleeding Crown.
Five powers, each pretending the realm could still be divided cleanly.
The Ashen Vanguard held the roads where roads remained. House Morvain held old stone and older
grievances. The Silent Choir kept its counsels behind veils and locked doors. The Iron-Ring Cartel

weighed hunger against silver. The Bleeding Crown possessed less land than memory, but memory was a
weapon that did not rust.
Brannoc had been born in 255 AS beneath that last banner’s shadow, though no herald had written his
name beneath it. He was the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
A crown did not need to acknowledge a man to kill him.
He slipped the coin into his glove.
“Will you enter?” Korvath asked.
“I was summoned.”
“That wasn’t what I asked.”
Brannoc looked up at the keep. The candle in the eastern window burned steadily despite the wind. A trap
was often most convincing when it offered shelter.
“Wait here,” he said.
Korvath gave a quiet laugh. “I don’t wait anywhere.”
Brannoc passed beneath the arch.
The stair smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and old mortar. Mournthrone had been built to endure the end of
the world and had discovered, centuries later, that walls could not keep out treachery. His boots rang
against the steps. He counted them without meaning to, then stopped himself. Counting made men believe
they had power over what came next.
At the landing, a narrow display case stood behind cloudy glass.
Within it rested The Thrice-Bound Edge.
The regalia had been forged in 123 AS. No attunement cost was recorded for it. Its shape was restrained:
dark metal, pale binding, three severe lines joined without ornament. It did not gleam. It seemed to drink
the candlelight and hold it beneath its surface.
Brannoc had seen kings reach for lesser things with steadier hands.
He paused before the case.
The Thrice-Bound Edge conveyed no promise of triumph. Only binding. A thing made to close around a
wrist, a vow, a throat.
He moved on.
The eastern room was open. Warm light spilled across the corridor.
Inside, a table had been set with maps, sealed letters, and untouched food. No one spoke when Brannoc
entered. That silence told him more than any greeting could have done.
He saw the grimoire first.
Edge of Gloamreach lay upon the table, its cover black-blue beneath the candle flame. The title had been
pressed into the leather in letters that seemed to recede when looked at directly. It was a grimoire, and its
attunement cost was 46. No forging date had been recorded.

Beside it lay a folded dispatch bearing the mark of Fenspire.
The spire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, a core location with a garrison of 3,742 and a
garrisoned status. Even from this room Brannoc could imagine its silhouette rising above the dim country:
stark, watchful, permanent. Fenspire did not sleep. It occupied the land as a blade occupied flesh.
Another map showed Crookvale.
Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires, rebuilt after whatever had broken it, Crookvale retained a garrison
of 1004 but remained outside the core holdings. The mark on the map was crooked and hard-edged, like
the settlement itself. A place wary enough to call survival a law.
Brannoc looked from one mark to the other.
“Fenspire,” he said. “Crookvale.”
No one answered.
At the far end of the table, a sealed letter lay beneath a black stone. The stone was wet.
Not rainwater.
Brannoc’s gaze lowered to the floor.
A thin red thread ran beneath the door.
His hand found his sword.
The candles leaned all at once, though there was no wind in the room.
Then someone behind him whispered, “Red-Handed.”
Brannoc turned.
The door slammed shut.
From the corridor came the sound of Korvath Nightbrook shouting, followed by the hard, wet impact of a
body striking stone. The room’s occupants rose together. Chairs scraped. Steel whispered free.
Brannoc did not draw his sword.
The coin in his glove had begun to bleed.
He felt the warmth spread across his palm, felt it seep between his fingers, and somewhere beneath the
keep a second bell began to ring as the voice behind him said—
“—the Accord has already chosen its dead.”
The voice did not come from the room. It came through the coin.
Brannoc closed his fist around it. Blood welled between his knuckles, hot as a forge-runner’s breath.
Across the chamber, the others had formed a ragged half-circle around the sealed door. Swords pointed at
the wood. No one looked toward him. No one wanted to be the first to admit that the whisper had spoken
from his hand.
Beyond the door, Korvath Nightbrook groaned.
“Open it,” said one of the men.

No one moved.
The second bell sounded again beneath the keep. Its note crawled through the floorstones and into
Brannoc’s teeth. Dust sifted from the ceiling. The flames guttered blue, then returned to their weak yellow.
Brannoc looked at the door.
A smear marked the stone beneath it, dark and shining. Korvath had fallen there, or something wearing the
shape of him had. The smuggler had entered the chamber an hour earlier with rain in his hair and a sealed
packet beneath his coat. He had spoken little. That was Korvath’s nature: guarded, wary, always
measuring the distance between a secret and a knife.
Now he made no sound.
“Brannoc,” said the oldest of the gathered men.
The captain heard the accusation hidden in his name. You brought this. You knew it would come. You are
the red hand at every threshold.
He released the coin.
It remained in his palm.
“Back away from the door,” he said.
The men glanced at one another.
“Why?”
“Because I told you.”
The command carried the hard weight earned by a seasoned sellsword, and habit obeyed before fear could
argue. Steel lowered. Boots scraped over stone. Brannoc crossed the chamber alone.
The coin lay flat in his hand now, though it had not fallen. Its surface had become soft and black, as if the
metal had remembered being blood. Lines opened across it, forming the image of a crown pierced through
by a thorn.
The Bleeding Crown.
His breath slowed.
No one in the room knew the truth. They knew him as Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed, a major
Sellsword Captain whose contracts had carried him from ash-field to ash-field. They knew the price of his
sword. They knew the danger of refusing it. They did not know he was the unacknowledged heir to the
Bleeding Crown.
Not even Korvath had known that.
Perhaps Korvath had known too much.
The voice returned.
“You were born in 255 AS.”
Brannoc’s fingers tightened. The coin bit him.
“Silence.”

“You will die in 300 AS.”
The chamber seemed to contract around him. The men heard nothing; their faces remained fixed on the
door. One of them raised his sword again, watching the crack beneath the threshold as if death might be
persuaded to enter politely.
Brannoc stared at the blackened coin.
“Who speaks?”
The answer came as a sigh from the walls.
“The one who keeps the account.”
A line of red appeared upon the door. It began at the latch and traveled upward, thin as a vein beneath
skin. When it reached the lintel, the entire slab shuddered.
One of the men cursed.
The door opened inward.
Korvath Nightbrook lay beyond it on the corridor stones, folded beneath himself. His coat had torn from
throat to belt. No blood spread from the wound. Instead, the red thread from beneath the door had emerged
from his ribs and continued into the chamber, where it now curled around Brannoc’s wrist.
The smuggler’s eyes opened.
“Don’t,” Korvath whispered.
Brannoc stepped over the threshold.
“What happened?”
Korvath’s gaze found the coin. Whatever he saw there drained the little color left in his face.
“It came for the packet.”
“Where is it?”
“Not here.”
“You carried it here.”
“I carried a decoy.”
A soft murmur moved through the room behind Brannoc. Fear had a way of making men generous with
their suspicions.
The red thread tightened around his wrist.
Korvath clawed at the stone. “It knows the Crown.”
“Who does?”
The smuggler’s mouth worked. His answer came wetly.
“The Choir.”
The words seemed to darken the corridor.

The Silent Choir had no single voice, yet every whisper attributed to it arrived with the weight of a verdict.
Brannoc had crossed their routes before. He had found whole wagons abandoned in snowless fields, their
drivers seated upright, mouths sewn shut with pale cord. He had never seen the faces beneath the hoods.
He had never needed to.
Behind him, someone said, “The Silent Choir is in the keep.”
“No,” Brannoc answered.
He did not know whether he spoke from certainty or command.
The thread around his wrist pulled.
He followed it into the chamber. It ran across the floor, climbed the leg of the table, and entered the leather
satchel Korvath had brought. The satchel trembled as though a small animal struggled inside.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The blade came free with a sound like a breath being taken by the dead.
“Burn it,” said Korvath.
“There is no fire hot enough.”
“Then cut it.”
Brannoc laid the edge against the satchel.
The coin laughed.
The sound was small. Almost tender.
The red thread snapped.
Every candle went out.
Darkness swallowed the room. Men shouted. Someone struck at something unseen, and the blow met
flesh; a cry broke sharply and fell silent. Brannoc heard feet stumbling, heard steel ring against stone,
heard the old, familiar music of panic.
Then the satchel opened.
A pale light spilled from it, not bright but depthless, the color of twilight beneath deep water. Within the
leather lay a book bound in hide that shifted beneath its stitching.
The cover bore a title.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Brannoc had seen the grimoire once, at a distance, in the hands of a dead scholar whose fingers had been
burned to the bone. Its attunement cost was 46. That number had been written in every warning
concerning it, as if the act of naming the price might keep anyone from paying.
The grimoire opened by itself.
Pages turned in a wind that did not touch Brannoc’s coat.
Symbols crawled across the paper. Their shapes refused to settle. He felt them pressing against the inside
of his skull, seeking a place to root.

“Look away,” Korvath said.
Brannoc did not.
A second object rested beneath the book, wrapped in gray cloth. The cloth had fallen back. Beneath it lay
The Thrice-Bound Edge, regalia forged in 123 AS. Its surface was neither sword nor crown nor chain, but
held the suggestion of all three: a binding thing, restrained and severe.
No attunement cost had ever been recorded for The Thrice-Bound Edge.
That absence had always troubled him more than any price.
The light from Edge of Gloamreach passed over it. Three lines of darkness appeared upon the regalia,
crossing and knotting without touching.
The men behind Brannoc fell quiet.
He felt the room listening.
A voice spoke from the open grimoire.
“The five powers gather.”
The page displayed five marks.
A clenched fist wreathed in ash: the Ashen Vanguard.
A dark crown scored with red: House Morvain.
A closed mouth stitched in silver: the Silent Choir.
A ring of iron surrounding a coin: the Iron-Ring Cartel.
And the thorn-pierced crown: the Bleeding Crown.
“They contend over the ruins,” said the voice. “They call it law when they take. They call it order when
they burn. They call it peace when the graves are full.”
Brannoc’s sword remained level.
“Why show me this?”
“Because the Accord of Mournthrone began in 297 AS.”
The chamber groaned. Somewhere below, the bell answered.
“It will end in 301 AS with the Ashen Vanguard named victor.”
Korvath gave a strangled laugh. “That is not prophecy. That is a sentence.”
“The losing commander will be bribed to withdraw.”
Brannoc’s gaze shifted toward the black window. Beyond the glass, the night had no stars. Only the faint
red wash of distant fires stained the underside of the clouds.
The Accord was supposed to bind the powers long enough for the realm to breathe. Instead, its words had
been sharpened into weapons before the wax cooled. He had watched nobles praise it over silver cups
while counting the soldiers they meant to spend. He had watched House Morvain smile at the Ashen
Vanguard. He had watched the Iron-Ring Cartel sell grain to both sides and powder to the side that paid

late. He had watched the Silent Choir pass through every gate without being searched.
And beneath all of it, like a buried pulse, the Bleeding Crown waited.
“What happens after?” Brannoc asked.
The page turned.
“Reprisals.”
A single word, written in red.
“A decade of guerrilla reprisals.”
The men behind him shifted. One whispered a prayer without naming its object.
Brannoc looked down at Korvath. “You brought this to me because of the Crown.”
Korvath swallowed blood. “I brought it because they said only your hand could open the way.”
“Who said?”
The smuggler’s eyes slid toward the grimoire.
“The dead.”
Brannoc almost smiled. There was no humor in it.
He had trusted the living because they lied for reasons. The dead lied without need.
The coin in his hand grew hot again. The crown upon it split down the middle. A black line ran across the
image, widening until the metal bent like a mouth.
The voice whispered close against his ear.
“Choose, Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.”
The door behind him slammed shut.
This time, the men screamed.
The grimoire’s pages began to turn faster. The Thrice-Bound Edge rose from the table, turning slowly in
the pale light. No hand held it. No chain restrained it. Its three dark lines uncoiled and reached toward
Brannoc.
He felt the buried claim inside him stir.
Not blood. Not birthright.
Something older than both.
From the corridor came the sound of many bare feet approaching at once.
Korvath caught Brannoc’s boot. “If you take it, they will see you.”
“Who?”
The footsteps stopped outside the door.
A voice spoke from the other side, calm and familiar.

“Open, Red-Handed.”
Brannoc knew that voice.
He had heard it at contract tables, beneath rain, in the brittle silence after a surrender.
The voice of a man who had not yet died.
The coin split in Brannoc’s palm.
The Thrice-Bound Edge drifted nearer.
And in the darkness behind the door, Korvath began to weep.
Brannoc did not open the door.
The voice waited with the patience of a drawn bow.
Korvath’s fingers tightened around his boot. The smuggler had gone pale in the dark, his tears shining like
oil where they tracked through the dust on his face.
“You know him,” Brannoc said.
Korvath shook his head.
The door gave a soft wooden sigh. Not from pressure. From recognition.
“Open,” said the voice again. “There is no profit in making me ask.”
Brannoc looked down at the coin in his palm. The split had widened. Within its broken face, something
black moved against the metal, a darkness too deliberate to be a flaw. The Thrice-Bound Edge had come
close enough that its cold entered his bones.
He had seen regalia before, in war tents and ruined halls: crowns that carried old promises, swords that
demanded new ones, rings worn by men who believed the world had been made to fit their hands. This
was none of those things. The Thrice-Bound Edge did not glitter. It waited.
Behind him, the grimoire lay open on the floor.
Edge of Gloamreach.
Its pages turned without wind. Each leaf whispered against the next, a dry, intimate sound, like a tongue
testing a wound. The script upon them was not written in ink. It was written in the bruised color beneath
the skin.
“Tell me who stands outside,” Brannoc said.
Korvath’s breath came thin and fast. “A dead man.”
“That is not a name.”
“It is enough of one.”
The feet in the corridor shifted. Many of them. Bare soles upon old stone. No one spoke. Their silence was
worse than a crowd’s anger. It had the obedience of a congregation.
Brannoc rose from his crouch.

The claim inside him stirred again—not blood, not birthright, but something older than both. It moved
through his chest with the slow certainty of a buried wheel. He had spent years strangling that sensation
whenever it surfaced. A man could survive a blade. A man could survive treachery. A man could even
survive learning that the crown he had served had never meant to acknowledge him.
What he could not survive was wanting it.
The Bleeding Crown had endured as an idea longer than any living claimant. Its name had crossed
battlefields in whispers, passed from hand to hand beneath cloaks, offered to captains who understood the
difference between authority and fear. Brannoc had been its unacknowledged heir, though no oath had
ever been spoken over him, no seal pressed into wax for him, no court had opened its doors.
He had been born in 255 AS.
The knowledge came now with no memory attached to it. A bare fact, cold as a nail.
Korvath stared at him. “Do not take the edge.”
“You told me that before.”
“I was hoping you had not heard.”
“You are a smuggler, Korvath Nightbrook. Hope is a poor trade for you.”
A broken laugh escaped the man. It died quickly.
Outside, the familiar voice said, “You always did mistake refusal for strength.”
Brannoc’s hand went to the hilt at his side. The gesture was useless. His sword had been left somewhere
beyond the chamber, along with the rest of the world that still obeyed ordinary distances.
“Why are you here?” Brannoc called.
“To collect what was promised.”
“No promise was made.”
“There is always a promise. Sometimes it is made by the hand. Sometimes by the blood. Sometimes by the
coward who waits behind a door.”
Korvath pressed his forehead to the floor.
Brannoc glanced at him. “You brought me here.”
“I carried you here.”
“You brought me.”
“I was paid to find the passage.”
“By whom?”
Korvath’s lips trembled. “You know.”
The answer struck harder than a confession.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had paid men to move weapons through places no map admitted existed. House
Morvain had paid men to forget what they saw. The Silent Choir had paid in favors that outlived coin. The
Ashen Vanguard paid in law, when law could still be found. And the Bleeding Crown—if the old stories

were more than the fevered invention of dispossessed soldiers—paid in inevitability.
Brannoc looked again at the coin.
“Who paid you?”
Korvath’s eyes lifted. “The voice.”
The door opened.
No hand touched it.
The chamber beyond was not the corridor Brannoc remembered. There was no torchlight, no fallen
plaster, no cramped passage crowded with bare feet. A long hall stretched into darkness beneath a ceiling
lost in shadow. Pale figures stood along its walls, their heads bowed. Their mouths had been sewn shut
with black thread.
At the far end stood a man in a weather-darkened coat.
Brannoc knew the posture before he knew the face. The slight forward tilt of the shoulders. The habit of
keeping one hand near the belt, not from fear but from arithmetic. The stillness of a commander who had
learned that every motion was witnessed and every hesitation priced.
The man’s face remained indistinct.
That was the cruelty of it. Brannoc knew the voice, the gait, the shape of the silence around him, but the
face had been taken away.
“Step through,” the man said.
The figures along the hall bowed lower.
Brannoc did not move.
The Thrice-Bound Edge drifted past his shoulder. It entered the hall without touching the floor, without
making a sound. The moment it crossed the threshold, the sewn mouths opened.
A single breath passed through them.
The chamber filled with the smell of wet ash.
Korvath made a small, broken noise. “You see? It knows you.”
“It knows what I am.”
“No.” Korvath crawled backward. “That is worse.”
Brannoc turned toward him. “What did you bring me to?”
The smuggler’s gaze fixed upon the open grimoire. “Fenspire.”
The name seemed to draw the darkness tighter.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire raised above a land where
daylight always seemed to arrive wounded. It was a core location, garrisoned by 3,742, and whatever
stood beyond this door carried its discipline: the cold vigilance of a place that had learned to sleep with its
weapons in hand.
But Brannoc had never seen Fenspire like this.

He had seen its outer walls once from a distance, under a sky thick with black weather. He had seen the
watchfires and the ordered movement of soldiers. No one had spoken of a hall beneath it, or a
congregation with sewn mouths, or a regalia that floated like a patient executioner.
Korvath said, “The book opened the way.”
“You opened the book.”
“I touched the clasp.”
“And then?”
“And then it knew your name.”
The voice at the end of the hall softened. “Names are such small doors.”
Brannoc stepped across the threshold.
The dead—or whatever passed for dead within that place—did not look at him. Their heads remained
bowed. Their hands hung at their sides, palms turned outward. Each palm bore a dark line from wrist to
finger, as if a blade had once been drawn there and had left a road for something to follow.
Behind him, Korvath whimpered.
Brannoc did not turn. “Stay.”
“Where?”
“Here.”
“I cannot.”
“You can.”
“I cannot.”
The hall’s darkness leaned toward them.
Brannoc advanced, and the voice came with him, though the man at the far end did not move.
“You served the Ashen Vanguard,” it said.
“I sold my sword.”
“To the Ashen Vanguard.”
“To whoever paid.”
“You speak as though coin absolves the hand.”
“It keeps the hand fed.”
“And when the hand is asked to crown?”
Brannoc stopped.
The Thrice-Bound Edge hovered before him, its shape now clearer: not a sword, not a crown, but a length
of dark metal bound three times by pale bands. No edge could be seen, yet the air near it parted in narrow,
trembling lines.

“Who asks?” Brannoc said.
The man at the end of the hall inclined his head.
Behind the figures, something scraped along the walls.
“Every power that has survived the Sundering,” the voice said. “The Ashen Vanguard. House Morvain.
The Silent Choir. The Iron-Ring Cartel. The Bleeding Crown.”
“They do not ask for the same thing.”
“They never have.”
“Then why show me?”
“Because you are the place where their demands meet.”
Brannoc felt the buried claim turn within him.
He hated the voice for finding it. Hated Korvath for bringing him here. Hated the dead for bowing as if
they had been awaiting his arrival since before he was born.
“What do they want?”
“The Vanguard wants a victor. House Morvain wants a puppet. The Choir wants silence. The Cartel wants
a market. The Crown wants a body.”
“And you?”
The man’s blurred face tilted.
“I want the truth to remain expensive.”
A tremor passed through the hall.
The grimoire’s pages began to turn faster behind him. Brannoc heard Korvath cry out, then the scrape of
his knees as he retreated. The book spoke in a language made of pressure. The meaning entered Brannoc
through his teeth.
He saw a battlefield under a sky the color of old iron.
He saw banners lowered without surrender.
He saw the losing commander standing alone in a tent while a purse of coin rested unopened upon the
table.
He saw the commander’s hand close around it.
The vision broke.
Brannoc swayed.
The man at the far end said, “The hidden truth is that the losing commander was bribed to withdraw.”
Brannoc tasted copper.
“The Accord of Mournthrone,” he said.
“Began in 297 AS.”

The hall shuddered.
“Ended in 301 AS.”
The sewn mouths opened wider, though no lips tore. A wind moved through them and carried the stink of
extinguished fires.
“The Ashen Vanguard was named victor,” the voice continued. “Then the accord collapsed, and a decade
of guerrilla reprisals was unleashed.”
Brannoc saw villages without names. Roads marked by bodies. Children learning which banners to fear.
Men returning from the hills with faces hidden beneath ash. He saw victory written in proclamations while
the dead continued to argue beneath the soil.
“What does that have to do with me?”
The Thrice-Bound Edge turned once.
Its point—or what should have been its point—settled against his chest.
The cold entered him.
“You died in 300 AS,” said the voice.
Brannoc’s heart stopped.
Not slowed. Not faltered.
Stopped.
Korvath screamed behind him.
The hall vanished.
For one instant Brannoc stood beneath a sky torn open by the Sundering. He felt steel enter him. He
smelled rain on dust. He heard men shouting the name of Mournthrone, though none of them could see his
face.
Then the darkness returned, and his heart began again with a single brutal beat.
The Thrice-Bound Edge had entered his chest without breaking skin.
The man at the far end lifted one hand.
“Take it,” he said. “Let them see you.”
Brannoc looked down.
The pale bindings around the artifact had begun to unravel. Beneath them, something waited—something
shaped like a crown, something shaped like a wound.
And from far beyond the hall, from every ruined power and every throne that had not yet admitted its fear,
came the sound of a door beginning to open.

The Ashen Chronicles, Volume II: The Long Reprisal
Chapter 1
The bell beneath the floor rang once.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned lifted their eyes from the reliquary and listened to the silence that followed. The chamber had been built for silence: walls of dark stone, windowless and sweating, with strips of beaten metal sunk into the mortar to turn away listening spells. Even the candle flames seemed reluctant to speak. They leaned inward, thin and yellow, their smoke dragging itself along the ceiling like a stain that had learned patience.
On the table before Sabelle lay the Diadem of Sorrowgate.
It was smaller than a crown ought to be. A circlet of pale metal, blackened at the inner rim, its points bent like the fingers of a hand drawn tight around a secret. Fine reliquary-work webbed its surface. There were hollows where relics might once have rested, though no relics remained. When the candlelight struck it, the metal gave back no gleam. It drank the light and left the room poorer.
The Diadem of Sorrowgate was forged in 281 AS.
Sabelle had read the line until the ink seemed to have entered their blood.
“Forged,” they murmured.
The word had weight. It settled between the candles and the Diadem, between the sealed door and the iron-bound chest beneath the table. Forged did not mean consecrated. It did not mean lawful. It did not mean safe.
Behind Sabelle, someone shifted.
The clerk had been standing for so long that the old floorboards had begun to remember the shape of their boots. They were young enough to still possess a smooth voice, though fear had roughened it.
“My lord—”
“Do not call me that.”
“My—High Inquisitor.”
Sabelle did not look around. In the polished blackness of the reliquary, they could see the blurred reflection of the clerk’s face: pale, narrow, and watchful. The clerk had not once looked toward the trapdoor in the floor.
That was wise.
“Read it again,” Sabelle said.
The clerk swallowed. Paper whispered.
“By authority of the Ashen Vanguard, the custody of the Diadem of Sorrowgate is to be examined. The High Inquisitor is to present the reliquary, submit to questioning, and permit inspection of—”
“Whose authority?”
The paper trembled. “The seal is not attributed.”
“Then it has no authority.”
“It bears the ash-mark.”
“So does every coward who wants a door opened.”
A drop of wax slid down a candle and hardened in the shape of a white tooth. Sabelle reached for the Diadem. The clerk made a small sound—not quite a protest, not quite a prayer—and then mastered it.
The metal was cold enough to hurt.
At once, the room receded. The table fell away beneath their hands. The candles became distant stars behind a veil of ash. Something pressed against the inside of Sabelle’s skull, not a voice but the memory of one: a multitude whispering names with the tenderness of mourners and the appetite of executioners.
Sabelle breathed through it.
The Diadem’s sorrow was not grief. Grief ended when the body was buried, when the last garment was folded, when the living learned to carry their empty places. This was possession without comfort. It wanted the hand that held it. It wanted the hand to become a reliquary too.
They withdrew their fingers.
“Put it away,” the clerk whispered.
Sabelle turned their head.
The clerk’s gaze had fixed upon the Diadem. No one had told them to look. No one ever needed to tell the frightened where danger was.
“You are giving orders in my chamber.”
“No.”
“You are telling me what to do.”
“I am asking.”
“Then ask more beautifully.”
The clerk’s mouth tightened. Their fear had begun to ferment into resentment, and resentment was often more useful. Fear made people obedient. Resentment made them inventive.
“Please put it away,” they said.
Sabelle smiled without warmth. “Better.”
They lifted the reliquary and set it within the chest. The lid was lined with grey felt and inscribed on its underside with the old prohibitions: no blood, no oath, no name spoken over the object. The letters were worn nearly smooth from use. Sabelle closed the chest and turned the key.
The bell beneath the floor rang again.
This time the clerk flinched hard enough to strike the wall.
Sabelle heard the sound of the impact and filed it away. Bruising. A weakness in the left shoulder. A habit of carrying tension high in the body. The small truths were always the ones that survived interrogation.
“Who is below?” the clerk asked.
“You know who is below.”
“I know nothing.”
“Then your education has failed you.”
The trapdoor occupied the center of the chamber. It was not large. A square of iron, black with old oil, pierced by a keyhole and a ring handle. No draught rose through its seams. Nothing below needed air.
Sabelle had spent years telling others that secrets were sins with better clothing. The phrase had pleased certain audiences. It was clean. It gave the guilty a shape and the righteous a mirror.
But the thing in the cellar had not begun as a secret.
It had begun as a necessity.
Necessity was merely the first mask of damnation.
The clerk stepped away from the trapdoor. “The inspectors will arrive soon.”
“Will they?”
“The summons says—”
“Summons are invitations written by men who fear refusal.”
“And if they do arrive?”
“Then they will knock.”
“And if you do not answer?”
Sabelle looked at the sealed chest. “They will decide I have something to hide.”
“You do.”
The words escaped the clerk before courage could dress them.
The chamber seemed to contract.
Sabelle placed both hands on the table. Their sleeves fell back, revealing the dark bands inked around their wrists, each mark a record of an oath no longer spoken aloud. The clerk stared at them. Good. Let the clerk remember that the High Inquisitor’s hands were not clean. Clean hands were for priests and children. Sabelle had examined too many souls to believe cleanliness possible.
“What did you say?”
The clerk’s lips parted.
From beneath the floor came a scrape.
Not the bell this time. Something dragged a hand across the underside of the trapdoor. Slowly. Feeling for the seams.
The clerk’s face emptied.
Sabelle heard the revenant breathe.
The dead did not need breath, but the bound had been taught the rhythm. Inhale. Hold. Exhale. Again. It was one of the few mercies Sabelle had managed to provide: a pattern, even if it was false. The thing below clung to the imitation as if breath might lead it back to the life it had lost.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned kept a bound revenant in their cellar.
There it was. The truth, stripped of all its ceremonial clothing. Not a guardian. Not a witness. Not a weapon held in reserve against the enemies of the realm.
A bound revenant in their cellar.
The clerk’s hand moved toward the door.
Sabelle caught their wrist.
The clerk gasped. Their pulse struck fast beneath the skin.
“Do not,” Sabelle said.
“I have to leave.”
“No.”
“You cannot keep it—”
“I have kept it for years.”
The clerk stared at them.
Sabelle released the wrist. The mark of their fingers reddened the pale flesh, five small accusations.
The scrape came again.
“Why?” the clerk asked.
It was the wrong question. It was always the wrong question. Why had Sabelle done it? Why had they gone below with chain and salt and a mouthful of forbidden syllables? Why had they returned with something that remembered pain but not mercy? Why had they fed it names? Why had they denied it names? Why had they kept the cellar locked while the realm above them burned through one oath after another?
Because the dead were easier to trust.
Because the living lied with their eyes open.
Because some knowledge, once gathered, could not be allowed to wander.
Sabelle said, “You are not permitted to ask that.”
The clerk gave a brittle laugh. “I am not permitted to ask much.”
“That is the privilege of being alive.”
A murmur rose from below.
The sound was wet and broken. It passed through the floorboards and entered the chamber as a vibration in the candle flames. The clerk pressed both hands over their mouth.
Sabelle felt the old answering pull in their chest. Not fear. Recognition.
The revenant knew the shape of their footsteps. It knew the pause before the key turned. It knew that Sabelle came alone. It knew the sound of the Diadem’s lock. Perhaps it had learned to distinguish the relic from every other object in the house. Perhaps it dreamed of the reliquary. Perhaps the dead dreamed more faithfully than the living did.
“What is it saying?” the clerk whispered.
“Nothing.”
“It said your name.”
“No.”
“It said—”
“Names are not words when spoken by the dead.”
The clerk looked at the trapdoor. “Then what are they?”
Sabelle reached for the key hanging at their throat. Its iron teeth rested against their collarbone, cold beneath the cloth.
“Doors.”
A knock sounded above them.
Three measured blows.
The clerk turned toward the ceiling. Dust sifted from the beams. Somewhere beyond the chamber, boots crossed the upper hall. More than one pair. The inspectors had come without announcing themselves, which meant the false summons had served its purpose. It had not been written to request the Diadem. It had been written to confirm where Sabelle kept it, who guarded it, and how quickly they could be made to reach for the lock.
A fourth knock.
Then a voice called through the house.
“High Inquisitor.”
The clerk’s eyes sought Sabelle’s.
Sabelle did not answer.
The voice called again, louder. “Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned.”
Their title entered the chamber and seemed to turn in the air, wearing the shape of authority. Twice-crowned. A name meant to suggest endurance, judgment, perhaps even sanctity. Sabelle had learned to let others decide what it meant. A crown was most useful when its weight belonged to someone else.
Below, the revenant began to pound against the trapdoor.
Once.
Twice.
The clerk staggered backward.
The Diadem shifted inside its chest. The metal made no sound, yet Sabelle felt it, an ache behind the eyes. The reliquary had recognized the disturbance. Or the dead had recognized the relic. Either way, the two objects were no longer separate in the dark.
“Open the door,” called the voice above.
Sabelle slipped the key from around their neck.
The clerk shook their head. “No.”
It was almost a brave word.
Sabelle regarded them with something near pity. “You should have said that before you came down here.”
The pounding below stopped.
For a moment, there was only the upper knock, the low flame, the clerk’s ragged breathing.
Then the revenant spoke.
Its voice rose through the iron in a ruined imitation of Sabelle’s own.
“Open,” it said.
The clerk began to weep.
Sabelle inserted the key into the trapdoor. The metal resisted, then yielded with a soft internal click. Above, the inspectors struck the outer door again. The whole house shuddered around them.
Sabelle bent toward the lock.
“High Inquisitor,” the voice called. “We know what you keep.”
The key turned.
From beneath the trapdoor came the smell of wet earth, old blood, and something sweetly rotten.
Sabelle placed one hand on the iron ring and said, “Then let us see whether you know what it wants—”
The trapdoor opened onto a stair cut into the foundations.
Sabelle lowered the lamp first. Its light slid down over damp stone, over roots that had forced themselves through the mortar, over a darkness that seemed to withdraw by inches. The sweet rot thickened below. The clerk stood behind them, clutching the ledger to his chest as if parchment could turn aside a hand.
“Come,” Sabelle said.
The clerk’s mouth worked.
Above them, the outer door groaned beneath another impact. Dust sifted from the ceiling. Somewhere in the house, glass broke.
“I cannot.”
“You can.”
“I heard it wearing your voice.”
“Then you have heard a poor imitation.”
The revenant laughed beneath the earth.
It had no breath, yet the sound came wetly, with a gurgle at its heart. The clerk flinched so hard that his shoulder struck the wall.
Sabelle descended.
The stair was narrow enough to make the passage of their robes a negotiation. Their hem dragged through cold water. At the bottom, the air pressed against their face with the intimacy of a hand. They lifted the lamp and saw the cellar’s far wall, its bricks furred white with salt. Iron had been hammered into the mortar in a circle: nails, hooks, lengths of chain, each one blackened at the tip.
The revenant knelt within that circle.
It had once possessed a human shape. That much remained undeniable. The shape had been tall, the shoulders still broad beneath a coat of burial cloth, the hands still jointed and almost delicate. But the flesh had withdrawn from the face, leaving the skull sheathed in a gray film. Its mouth had been sewn shut with wire. The wire trembled when it spoke.
“High Inquisitor.”
The title crawled across the cellar.
Sabelle stepped from the stair and closed the trapdoor overhead. The thud of it sealing them in was gentle compared with the blows above. The clerk remained on the last step, shivering.
“Bring the ledger,” Sabelle said.
The clerk descended one step.
The revenant turned its head toward him.
He stopped.
“Bring it,” Sabelle repeated.
He came down. Each footfall sounded like an admission.
At the circle’s edge, Sabelle held out a hand. The clerk surrendered the ledger. Its leather cover was warm from his body. Sabelle tucked it beneath one arm and approached the revenant.
The thing’s bound wrists rested upon its knees. The chains around them were not thick. They did not need to be. Every link had been etched with the same cramped injunction, again and again, until the metal seemed to have grown a skin of writing.
The revenant leaned forward.
“Open the iron,” it whispered.
“You are not yet permitted speech.”
“I am not permitted anything.”
“That is the nature of a binding.”
“Is it?”
Sabelle stopped before the first nail.
The lamp flame bent toward the creature. Its light caught in the hollows of the revenant’s face and made them look deeper than they were. Sabelle could feel the old pressure behind their eyes—the insistence of the dead, the patient gravity that tried to draw the living inward. They had learned to meet it without anger. Anger gave the dead a door.
Above, the inspectors shouted. Their voices passed through the house in fragments.
“By authority of—”
A crash.
“—open this place—”
The clerk looked up. “They will come through.”
“They already have.”
“No.” His eyes moved to the trapdoor. “No, they are still outside.”
Sabelle turned the lamp toward him. “Listen.”
For a moment there was only the dripping of water and the faint hiss of the wick.
Then came footsteps overhead.
Not the inspectors. These were lighter. Irregular. One step dragged. Another paused too long before falling.
The clerk’s face emptied.
Sabelle set the ledger on a stone shelf and drew the small key from inside their sleeve. It was not the key to the circle. It was the key to the box beneath the shelf, where the names were kept. The revenant watched it with the fixed hunger of the dead.
“You brought them here,” it said.
“I brought no one.”
“You brought the paper.”
“The paper was already written.”
“You brought the woman of the Vanguard.”
Sabelle’s fingers tightened around the key.
The clerk stared between them. “What woman?”
The revenant’s sewn mouth flexed.
“Morwenna Ashgrove,” it said.
Sabelle felt the name enter the cellar like a draft beneath a door.
The Ashen Vanguard had many officers, many hands raised in oath, many mouths trained to speak of necessity while counting the cost in silence. Morwenna Ashgrove was a member of The Ashen Vanguard. That was the plainness of the record. The other truth sat beneath it, less often spoken and more dangerous for being spoken at all: Morwenna Ashgrove was mentor of Caedmon Fellgard.
The clerk swallowed. “Why would her name be here?”
“It is not here,” Sabelle said.
The revenant tilted its head.
Sabelle looked at the ledger on the shelf. Its pages held inspections, confiscations, sealed testimonies, the dry bones of the realm’s fear. They had not opened it. They had not needed to. The revenant was reaching through the name, searching for the shape of Sabelle’s uncertainty.
“You are trying to make me careless,” Sabelle said.
“I am trying to make you honest.”
“Honesty is a virtue for those who cannot afford power.”
The clerk gave a small, involuntary sound.
Sabelle glanced at him. “You may save your shock. The cellar has heard worse.”
The footsteps above stopped.
A pause followed—long enough for the revenant’s chains to creak.
Then something moved across the trapdoor.
A shadow passed through the cracks.
The clerk pressed himself against the wall. “They found it.”
“No,” said the revenant. “They found the house.”
Sabelle drew the Crown of Burned Names from beneath their coat.
The crown was not large. Its blackened points rose like fingers charred in a fire, each one scored with names reduced to wounds. The lamp dimmed when Sabelle held it. Even the revenant’s chains seemed to recoil.
The clerk began to pray.
Sabelle placed the crown against the stone.
“Do not touch that,” said the revenant.
Its voice had changed. The imitation of Sabelle was gone. Beneath the wire and rot lay something raw.
“Why?”
“Because it remembers what you command it to forget.”
Sabelle crouched. “That is why it serves.”
The revenant pulled against its bonds. The circle flared—not with light, but with absence. The edges of the room blurred. For one instant the clerk seemed to have no face, only a pale oval beneath his hair.
Sabelle drove the heel of their hand against the nearest nail.
The binding answered.
The revenant slammed backward as though struck by an unseen fist. Its skull snapped against the wall. The wire across its mouth tightened until black fluid welled between the stitches.
Above them, the inspectors began to chant.
Not a prayer. A formula.
The same phrase repeated, each voice entering at a different measure, until the house itself seemed to mouth it through its beams.
The clerk covered his ears.
“High Inquisitor,” he pleaded, “what do we do?”
Sabelle rose with the crown in their hands.
“We wait.”
“For what?”
“For the moment they believe they have found me.”
The revenant’s head turned.
“They have found you.”
“No,” Sabelle said. “They have found a door.”
The chanting faltered overhead.
A key scraped against the lock.
Sabelle placed the Crown of Burned Names upon their head.
The cellar vanished.
Not entirely. The stones remained beneath their feet, the lamp still burned, and the clerk still breathed in frightened little pulls. But behind all things came another place: a white expanse filled with drifting ash, where countless mouths opened and closed without sound. The names upon the crown pressed into Sabelle’s thoughts. They were not words. They were absences shaped like words.
The revenant watched them through its ruined face.
“You wear the dead,” it said.
“I wear their silence.”
“You wear what was done to them.”
“Be quiet.”
“You think the crown makes you judge.”
The key turned above.
Sabelle’s hand closed around the ledger.
The clerk whispered, “Morwenna Ashgrove.”
Sabelle looked at him.
He had not meant to speak. Terror had made the choice for him.
“Why did it say her name?”
Sabelle crossed the cellar and seized him by the collar. The crown’s weight seemed to bend the air between them.
“Because the dead are liars when they are frightened.”
The revenant made a sound like a smile.
“And when they are not?”
The trapdoor lifted.
A blade of lamplight cut down the stair. Dust spun through it. A man’s face appeared upside down in the opening, blurred by the crown’s ward. Behind him, others crowded close. Their mouths moved, but the chanting had become a dull underwater murmur.
Sabelle released the clerk.
The revenant’s chains drew taut.
“Now,” Sabelle said.
The crown answered with darkness.
The first inspector fell through the opening without a cry. He struck the stair, rolled, and landed at Sabelle’s feet. His lamp burst against the stone. Oil ran in a bright ribbon toward the circle.
The clerk screamed.
Sabelle kicked the lamp aside.
The inspector rose too quickly. His neck bent at the wrong angle, then corrected itself with a wet click. His hand reached for Sabelle’s robe.
The revenant spoke.
“Open.”
Every iron nail in the cellar shuddered.
Sabelle looked past the inspector to the lifted trapdoor, to the faces gathering above, to the narrow seam of night beyond them.
Then they turned the key in the box beneath the shelf, and something inside began to breathe.
The breath came again, deeper this time, drawing the cellar’s cold into the box.
Sabelle felt it pass through the soles of their boots.
Above, someone shouted for the trapdoor to be closed. Another voice answered with a prayer. The clerk had collapsed against the wall, his mouth working soundlessly, his ink-stained fingers clawing at the mortar. The inspector on the stair turned his crooked head toward the sound beneath the shelf.
“Open,” said the revenant.
The word was not spoken in the air. It moved through the iron nails, through the hinges, through the blackened teeth of the lock. It entered Sabelle’s bones and waited there.
They kept one hand on the key.
The dead inspector seized their wrist.
His fingers had the damp cold of a grave. Skin slid beneath his glove. Sabelle looked down at the hand, then up into the face that had once belonged to a man who had come to judge them. The left eye was clouded. The right had no pupil at all, only a grey-white depth in which the cellar’s lamp burned like a buried star.
Sabelle did not pull away.
“Your warrant,” they said.
The inspector’s jaw sagged.
“Your warrant,” Sabelle repeated, “or your confession.”
The thing wearing him made a sound like stones grinding beneath water.
From above came the scrape of boots. The trapdoor began to descend.
Sabelle turned the key.
The box opened by a fraction.
A red seam appeared between its lid and body. Not light. Not fire. Something with the color of old blood, pressed thin beneath the metal. The breath inside ceased.
Every person in the cellar ceased with it.
Then the revenant inhaled.
The dead inspector’s grip tightened. Bone cracked in Sabelle’s wrist. Pain rose cleanly, almost gratefully. Pain was a loyal witness. It never mistook what it had seen.
Sabelle drove the heel of their palm beneath his chin.
The impact snapped his head back. He released them, not from injury but surprise. They stepped around him and placed their injured hand upon the box.
The two crowns at their brow—one black, one pale beneath the soot—trembled as the cellar groaned.
“Stay,” Sabelle commanded.
The thing below the box listened.
The inspector lurched forward. Sabelle caught his coat and turned with him, using his own momentum to hurl him against the shelf. Clay jars fell and burst. Salt, ash, and dried roots scattered over the stones. His shoulder struck hard enough to splinter the wood, but he did not fall. He rose, dragging one leg, his fingers opening and closing.
The trapdoor dropped another handspan.
A face appeared in the gap.
“High Inquisitor,” called the clerk from the wall. His voice had become thin and childlike. “They are coming down.”
“Then let them.”
“They say you are harboring a prohibited—”
The revenant struck the inside of the box.
The lid jumped.
The face above vanished. A body fell through the opening and landed among the broken jars. The trapdoor slammed shut after it. The newcomer wore the dark coat of an inspector, though the collar bore no insignia Sabelle recognized. They remained on their knees, hands braced in the spilled salt.
“Do not breathe,” Sabelle said.
The inspector did.
The cellar changed.
It was not a sound at first, but an alteration in pressure. The flame in the lamp leaned toward the box. Dust lifted from the flagstones and turned slowly in the air. The dead man at the shelf stopped moving. Above them, the trapdoor shuddered beneath the weight of those gathering on the other side.
The kneeling inspector began to cough.
Sabelle crossed the space between them and pressed two fingers to the inspector’s throat.
“Who sent you?”
The inspector’s eyes fixed on the crown.
“Your own seal opened the gate.”
“Who sent you?”
“Crookvale.”
The name dropped into the cellar and did not break.
Sabelle’s hand tightened.
“Crookvale sent you?”
A nod. The inspector’s breath came wetly now. “A dispatch. A sealed complaint. The garrison has been instructed to make inquiry.”
“By whom?”
The inspector’s lips parted. His tongue was black at the root.
The revenant breathed again.
The man’s answer came out in another voice.
“Thessaly Coldwater serves at Crookvale.”
The clerk whimpered.
Sabelle released the inspector’s throat. He folded sideways, twitching among the salt. The first dead inspector had gone still against the shelf, his ruined neck bent toward the box as if listening for a lullaby.
Above, the others began to hammer at the trapdoor.
“High Inquisitor!” someone cried. “By authority of the Crown—”
Sabelle looked at the iron box.
Its lid had opened another finger’s width. Inside lay darkness folded upon itself, and within that darkness two points of dull red watched without blinking.
Thessaly Coldwater.
The name had crossed the realm before, carried by sealed orders and exhausted riders, by reports that contradicted one another so carefully they might have been written by the same hand. Sabelle had read one such report beneath a lamp that smoked. They remembered the phrasing, not the facts: an omission sharpened until it became an accusation.
Now Crookvale had sent its inquiry to their cellar.
Or someone had borrowed Crookvale’s name.
That distinction was the thin wall between judgment and treason.
Sabelle bent and retrieved the fallen inspector’s warrant. The parchment was damp but legible. Their seal appeared at the bottom, pressed in black wax.
They had not issued it.
The wax bore the twin-crown impression, but one crown faced inward and the other outward. A novice’s error. Or a message.
The pounding above intensified.
The clerk had begun to pray. He had chosen a familiar litany, but he kept losing the words and starting again. Sabelle watched the blood running from the dead inspector’s ear. It gathered in the grooves between the stones, finding the channels worn by years of washing.
“Bring me the ledger,” Sabelle said.
The clerk stared.
“The ledger.”
He scrambled toward the wall, slipped in oil, and struck his mouth against the floor. When he rose, blood brightened his teeth. He reached behind a loose stone and pulled free a narrow book bound in grey hide.
Sabelle held out their hand.
He did not move.
“Give it to me.”
“You said no one was to know.”
“I said no one was to know what was in the cellar.”
The clerk’s gaze shifted to the box.
The lid trembled beneath Sabelle’s palm.
“I did not know it could hear,” he whispered.
“It hears everything.”
“Then it heard you.”
“Yes.”
The clerk brought the ledger. Sabelle took it and opened to the marked page. The entries had been made in different inks, by different hands. Names, dates, quantities, routes. Most were crossed out. Some had been burned through so deeply that the parchment had become a lace of scars.
The Crown of Burned Names would have approved of the work.
Sabelle hated that thought. They hated the artifact’s solemn weight, the way remembrance could become another species of prison. Yet even hatred had its uses. It kept the mind from kneeling.
A crack split the trapdoor.
Dust fell from the ceiling.
“High Inquisitor!” shouted the voice above. “Stand away from the relic!”
Sabelle glanced at the clerk.
“Relic?”
“I never said—”
“No,” Sabelle said. “You merely screamed loudly enough to educate the entire corridor.”
Another blow. The hinges shrieked.
The thing in the box moved.
Not outward. Within itself.
The darkness folded, unfolded, and showed Sabelle a room they had never entered. A stone chamber beneath a sky without stars. A chair. A table. A crown lying on the table, blackened and scored with names that writhed like insects beneath its surface.
Then the vision was gone.
Their pulse had quickened.
The revenant had shown them nothing without purpose. It had never shown them anything without taking something in return.
Sabelle shut the ledger.
“Clerk.”
He looked up.
“When the door opens, you will tell them I am dead.”
His face collapsed. “They will search.”
“They will find what I permit.”
“And me?”
Sabelle studied him. He was young enough to believe terror was a form of innocence. The cellar had already taken that belief from him.
“You will say the inspectors came alone.”
“They did not.”
“You will say it anyway.”
The trapdoor burst upward.
Three figures crowded the opening. Their lamps poured yellow light down the stair. For one suspended moment, they appeared not as people but as a single many-limbed creature peering into a wound.
Sabelle lifted the iron box.
The dead inspector moved first. He crossed the cellar in a blur of torn coat and broken joints, seized the nearest figure by the ankle, and pulled. The figure vanished with a scream. The second thrust a blade downward. Steel entered the revenant’s shoulder and came out beneath its ribs.
The dead man looked at the blade.
Then he looked at Sabelle.
The question in his ruined face was almost human.
Sabelle turned the key back.
The box shut.
The revenant’s hand closed around the inspector above. He dragged the figure down the stair, not quickly, not angrily. The scream dwindled as it descended. The remaining two retreated, but the trapdoor caught one across the fingers. Bone broke. The other shouted a command Sabelle could not make out.
They stepped onto the first stair.
“Thessaly Coldwater serves at Crookvale,” Sabelle said.
The words were not meant for the men above. They were meant for the thing inside the box.
The key grew hot in their hand.
The cellar lamps went out.
In the darkness, every voice became distinct: the clerk’s shallow sobbing, the wounded inspector’s breath, the dead man’s teeth clicking as he climbed, and beneath them all the slow, patient respiration of what Sabelle had kept hidden below the world’s notice.
The trapdoor remained open.
Beyond it waited the corridor, the house, the inquisitorial seal, and the machinery of accusation already turning toward them.
Sabelle placed one foot on the stair.
Behind the closed iron, the revenant whispered the name again.
Not Thessaly.
Crookvale.
Chapter 2
The quarantine bell had no clapper.
It spoke through the walls instead, a low iron concussion that moved through Stormmarch’s black stone and entered the marrow. Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven felt it in their teeth. Dust sifted from the vaulted ceiling. Somewhere beyond the chamber, a horse screamed once and was silenced.
They stood beside the sealed gate with one gloved hand resting on the bars.
Stormmarch had been founded in 71 AS, when the Ash Wastes were still young enough to remember rain. Now the ash came down in slow gray veils, whispering against the battlements. The stronghold remained quarantined, its garrison numbering 9,263, and it stood outside the realm’s core holdings like a clenched fist no sovereign had managed to open.
Beyond the gate, the dead waited in their covered carts.
Isolde could smell them through the iron: lye, old blood, and the sweetening corruption that no prayer could persuade into silence.
“Do you hear it?” Ossric Ashgrove asked.
He held a tally-board beneath his arm and a lantern in the other hand. The flame guttered blue against the glass. Ossric Ashgrove, born in 333 AS, served as quartermaster, though the title seemed too clean for the work his hands performed. He had been counting sacks, bodies, arrows, and the portions of grain that had gone black in their husks. His face possessed no feature Isolde could have remembered afterward. That, perhaps, was its own kind of armor.
“The bell?” Isolde said.
“The absence after it.”
They listened.
The silence pressed harder than the sound had.
Ossric swallowed. “It means the watch has stopped answering.”
“It means the watch has heard what it was meant to hear.”
He glanced toward the inner stair. “You know what that is?”
“I know the purpose of bells.”
The blood under Isolde’s fingernails had dried to a lacquered darkness. They had not washed it away. Stains were messages, and Isolde had learned young that messages became dangerous only when someone understood them.
The gate shuddered.
Not from outside.
From within.
Ossric’s lantern trembled. “The quarantine line is sealed.”
“So it is.”
“Nothing crosses it.”
“Nothing living should.”
His eyes lifted toward theirs. Quartermaster, not soldier. Yet fear had made him attentive. “The orders say Stormmarch is to remain closed until—”
“Do not recite orders to me.”
The words came softly. That frightened him more than a shout might have done.
Isolde turned from the gate. The chamber behind them had once been a chapel, though the saints had been scraped from the walls and the altar broken into paving stones. A table stood beneath the empty niche. On it lay three ledgers, a bowl of salt, a bone-handled knife, and a folded dispatch bearing the iron mark of the Iron-Ring Cartel.
The five powers watched one another from the ruins: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Their names had become a kind of weather. One woke beneath them. Ate beneath them. Bled beneath them.
Isolde crossed to the table.
Ossric followed at a careful distance. “That dispatch was brought by Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
“Then it was not brought. It was delivered.”
“He is a Warden-Commander.”
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless is a Warden-Commander,” Isolde said. “He was born in 258 AS. Authority does not cleanse a hand.”
Ossric’s gaze moved to the iron mark. “You are saying he—”
“I am saying nothing.”
That was the first lie, and it tasted familiar.
Ignatz sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. Isolde knew it as one knows the location of a knife in darkness: by the shape of the danger, not by the sight of the blade. The knowledge had come to them in fragments, never whole enough to use without exposing the hand that had gathered it.
