The Diadem of Sorrowgate housed in Gloammarch, beneath ash-dark stone and the scrutiny of every power that still possessed a hand to reach.
Isolde’s knife lowered by a fraction.
“Then this is not about Malchior,” she said.
“No,” Ignatz answered. “It is about what Malchior can open.”
The crack in Malchior’s palm reached the wrist.
They smelled their own blood burning.
The room seemed to contract around the paper. The climbing voices grew louder. Somewhere beneath them, iron struck iron. The veiled ones had reached the lower stair.
“Open what?” Isolde demanded.
Ignatz looked at Malchior with the exhaustion of a man who had spent years feeding pieces of himself to a machine and had only now discovered the machine could speak.
“The old passage.”
“There is no old passage.”
“There is always an old passage.”
Malchior thought of the papers beneath the floor. Thought of the line of false descent written in their own hand. Thought of the first time they had worn the robes of the Arch-Prelate, how the collar had seemed to tighten each time someone called them chosen.
The fire in their palm crawled across the sealed paper.
This time, the wax softened.
Isolde saw it. “Malchior.”
The doorframe filled again.
A veiled figure stood beyond the wounded Wardens. Pale cloth concealed the face, but the voice that came from behind it was not joined to the others.
“You were born without a house.”
Malchior’s breath stopped.
“You forged a house from ash.”
The fire died in their hand.
The figure stepped over the bodies.
“You wrote yourself into the blood.”
The sealed paper split beneath Malchior’s fingers.
Inside was not a letter, nor a confession, nor any list of the dead. It was a single narrow strip of parchment, and on it a name had been written in ink the color of dried blood.
Malchior looked down.
The name beneath theirs waited.
They knew the hand.
It was their own.
Chapter 5
The road into Crookvale had been cut from black stone, though Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed remembered no quarry on the mountain.
Rain silvered the ruts. It gathered in the hollows where old blood had gone dark and slick beneath the wagon wheels, and the horses lifted their hooves high, affronted by the stink of iron rising from the mud. Above them, the High Spires clenched the sky in pale, broken teeth.
At the gate, a sentry lowered his spear.
“Name.”
Brannoc drew back his hood. Rain ran from the edge and struck the red leather wrapped around his sword hand. “You know my name.”
The sentry’s gaze moved over him: the scarred brigandine, the travel-stained cloak, the sword at his hip. It lingered on the hand.
“No,” the sentry said. “I know the name people use when they want trouble.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “Then you know enough.”
The gatehouse swallowed the silence between them. Behind the sentry, a bell hung motionless in its frame. The stone around it was new in places and ancient in others, the repairs laid across the old wounds like clumsy stitches.
A second guard appeared above the parapet. “Let him through.”
The sentry did not turn. “Orders?”
“Orders from the garrison.”
“How many?”
The upper guard spat over the wall. “Enough.”
Brannoc looked past them into the settlement. Crooked roofs climbed the slope, their slate faces glittering beneath the rain. Smoke crawled from chimneys and flattened itself against the stone. A shrine without a saint stood in a square below, its hollow niche stuffed with blackened cloth.
“Crookvale was rebuilt,” Brannoc said.
The sentry’s fingers tightened around his spear. “You say that like it’s an accusation.”
“It is, if the dead paid for the timber.”
“They always do.”
The gate opened with a groan that came up through the soles of Brannoc’s boots. He entered alone, leaving the wagons and the men who had followed him on the lower road. He had dismissed them before dawn. A captain who arrived with an army invited arithmetic. A captain who arrived with only a sword invited fear.
Fear was cheaper.
The street rose steeply. Water streamed between the cobbles, carrying ash, horse dung, and scraps of paper gone soft at the edges. Brannoc passed shuttered houses and narrow doors barred from within. Faces watched him through cracks. No one called out. No one needed to. The name had preceded him, as names always did, and the red hand made certain they remembered it.
At the summit stood the garrison hall, a square block of old masonry crowned with fresh battlements. A strip of black cloth hung above the entrance. Its hem was embroidered with the broken sigil of the Bleeding Crown.
Brannoc stopped beneath it.
The cloth stirred in the rain.
For one unguarded breath, he saw another room: a hand upon a cradle, a crown lowered out of sight, a woman whispering that blood could be hidden but never made harmless.
Then the memory closed its teeth.
“Captain.”
The voice came from the doorway.
The garrison commander was a woman with iron-gray hair and a face worn smooth by weather. She wore no badge. Her coat had been mended at both shoulders, and one of the buttons was carved from bone.
“You’re expected,” she said.
“I’m often expected.”
“Not by people who want to live.”
“Those are the only sort who expect me.”
Her eyes shifted to the sword. “Inside.”
Brannoc entered.
The hall smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and boiled grain. A long table filled the central chamber, crowded with maps weighted by cups and knives. The far wall had been scrubbed, but a rust-colored shadow remained beneath the limewash. Someone had tried to clean a massacre from the stone and had only taught it to linger.
The commander closed the door behind him.
“Your man at the lower road said you came regarding Hollowreach.”
“My man speaks too freely.”
“He spoke after we put a knife under his tongue.”
“That would improve most conversations.”
She ignored the remark. “You want passage through the Reach.”
“I want a guide.”
“No.”
“I didn’t ask whether the road was safe.”
“You asked for a guide. I said no.”
Brannoc removed his gloves one finger at a time. His right hand was stained dark despite the leather, the old color worked into the creases of his skin. Men had invented stories about it. Some claimed he had dipped it in a traitor’s heart. Others said the stain belonged to a curse. Brannoc had never corrected either account. Truth was a poor guard. Rumor kept better watch.
The commander watched the hand, then looked away.
“Hollowreach was founded in 56 AS,” she said. “It has stood longer than the walls around this place. It has endured raids, famine, and the Reach turning sick around it. Now it is under quarantine.”
“I know.”
“Then you know the roads are sealed.”
“I know what sealed means.”
“Do you?”
Brannoc set his gloves on the table. “It means someone is afraid of what comes out.”
“And what goes in.”
He leaned over the map. The Gloaming Reach had been inked in bruised colors, the rivers winding like veins beneath skin. Hollowreach sat near its center, a small black mark surrounded by red strokes.
“Who is holding the town?”
“The officials say no one.”
“Officials say many things.”
“The Silent Choir has men at the eastern road.”
“Men?”
“Brothers, singers, penitents. Whatever they call themselves when the lamps are lit.”
“Armed?”
“Of course.”
“Then they’re men.”
The commander placed her palm over the map, covering Hollowreach. “The Ashen Vanguard has scouts in the fen country. House Morvain claims jurisdiction by right of old charters. The Iron-Ring Cartel is moving goods along the southern track despite the quarantine. Everyone wants what is inside.”
“What is inside?”
Her hand remained still.
“Ask the ones who sent you,” she said.
“No one sent me.”
“That’s worse.”
A gust struck the shutters. The lamps bent in their brackets. For a moment, the room darkened, and Brannoc felt the old animal wake within him—the thing that measured exits, blades, distance to throats.

“Do I?”
“Your name is written on it.”
“Many letters bear my name.”
“This one bears the seal of the Bleeding Crown.”
The air changed.
Not much. A tightening in the commander’s shoulders. A quieting in the corridor beyond the door. But Brannoc felt it, and beneath the feeling, the deeper thing: the crown’s blood calling through wax and rain, pretending it had not been buried.
He drew the letter from inside his coat.
The seal had been pressed in black wax. No crown appeared upon it. Only a drop, split down the middle.

“It was left at the south gate.”
“By whom?”
“Korvath Nightbrook.”
Brannoc’s thumb passed over the broken drop. “The smuggler.”
“The same.”

The letter contained three lines, written in a cramped hand.
The Thrice-Bound Edge was forged in 123 AS.
It lies where the quarantine began.
Do not let the Choir bind it.
He read the words twice. The first time as a captain. The second as a son.
The commander reached for the letter. He let her take it.

“An old name.”

“It is the only one you’ll get.”

“Regalia.”
Her eyes sharpened. “That means nothing.”

The commander folded the letter. “The road to Hollowreach is watched.”
“Then we go by another.”
“There is no other.”
“There is always another.”
“That is what smugglers say.”
“Smugglers survive by being right.”
She stepped closer. “You think this is about you.”
Brannoc laughed softly. “Everything that wears a crown thinks the world is about it.”
“And you?”
He looked at the black cloth above the door, at the broken sigil trembling in the draft.

“Yet you reached.”
The words struck cleanly. He felt no wound, only the old pressure beneath the ribs.
The unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
He had heard it spoken in whispers beside campfires, beneath silk, in the mouths of men who wanted to buy his loyalty and women who wanted to know what price his betrayal might command. An heir without acknowledgment was a blade without a scabbard: useful, dangerous, and never allowed near the throne.
Brannoc put the letter away.
“Send for a guide.”
“I said no.”

The commander studied him. “You brought no men.”
“I brought myself.”
“That’s not an army.”
“No.”

“No.”
“Why should I let you walk into a quarantined town with nothing but a sword?”
Brannoc fastened his glove over the red hand. “Because if I wanted to bring ruin to Crookvale, I would have come through the gate with my banners.”
Her mouth tightened. “You have banners?”
“Everyone has banners. Most are only waiting for the wind.”
A bell began to ring outside.
Once.
Twice.

The third strike never came.

Another blow thundered through the settlement. Dust sifted from the ceiling. The lamps guttered blue.
From somewhere beyond the walls came a sound like singing—thin, many-voiced, and patient.
The commander’s face emptied of color.
“The Choir,” she whispered.
Brannoc moved to the nearest shutter and opened it a finger’s width. Rain blew into his face. In the square below, the shrine’s black cloth had torn free and wound itself around the saintless stone. At the foot of the shrine, a man knelt with his hands bound.
Korvath Nightbrook lifted his head.
Even through the rain, Brannoc saw the smuggler’s grin.

They’re inside.

Brannoc twisted aside as the point entered the room, bright with rain, and the singer on the other side began to whisper—

Brannoc caught the commander’s wrist and hauled him down.
The blade passed above them.

The Accord of Mournthrone had taught him that stillness lied.
A quiet line could conceal a charge. A lowered banner could conceal a bargain. A man who appeared beaten might merely be waiting for the moment when victory grew careless.

All but one.

Then the bell rang again, and the sound punched the name from his mind.
The hall doors slammed shut behind them.
Inside, the air was hot with bodies and tallow smoke. The singers had fallen silent. Some knelt. Others stood with their hands pressed to their ears. Rainwater streamed from Brannoc’s coat and pooled around his boots, carrying flecks of ash across the floor.
A table had been overturned near the altar. Beneath it, someone had placed a long iron-bound coffer.
The commander saw it and went white.
Brannoc saw that, too.
“What is inside?”
The commander’s answer came after too long a pause. “Regalia.”
“That is not an answer.”
A singer crawled toward the coffer. His fingers shook so violently that he missed the latch twice. On the third attempt, the lid opened.
Dark metal lay within white cloth.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Even wrapped, it seemed to hold the room in a clenched silence. Regalia forged in 123 AS, its name stamped upon the inner plate in a script that made the eyes ache. Brannoc had never touched it. No attunement cost was recorded for The Thrice-Bound Edge. That absence disturbed him more than any price could have.
Beside it rested a book bound in hide the color of old bruises.
“Edge of Gloamreach,” Korvath said from the shadows.
Brannoc turned.
The smuggler had returned without anyone seeing him enter. He stood with his back to the wall, one hand still inside his coat.
The commander stared at the grimoire. “It was sealed.”
“Seals are promises,” Korvath said. “Promises fail.”
“Who brought them here?”
No one answered.
Brannoc looked from the coffer to the commander. “You did.”
The man’s face hardened. “Careful.”
“You knew the stone would open.”
“I knew the stone was weakening.”
“And you brought regalia into a shrine full of singers.”
“For protection.”
“For whom?”
The bell struck again.
Dust fell from the ceiling. Every flame in the hall leaned toward the doors.
Brannoc felt the darkness outside press against the wood. It did not batter the doors. It waited, patient as a creditor.
One of the singers whispered, “The road has found its heir.”
The words passed through the hall.
The commander’s face changed.
Korvath looked at Brannoc.
Brannoc’s hand tightened around his sword hilt until the leather creaked. He could feel the blood on his glove drying, stiffening, becoming another layer of armor.
“No,” he said.
The singer raised his head. His eyes were milk-white.
“The crown beneath the crown,” he murmured. “The hand that was denied. The blood that returns.”
The commander drew his sword and pointed it at Brannoc.
The singers recoiled.
For a moment, the only sound was the rain.
Then the doors bowed inward.
Not from a blow.
From a hand laid gently against the other side.
Brannoc watched the iron bands bend. He thought of The Bleeding Crown, of the records that called him nobody, of the secret that had survived every attempt to bury it. He thought of the Accord of Mournthrone and the blood that would one day take him there, though the hour had not yet come. He knew only what the dead knew: that certain roads did not lead toward a destination.
They led toward recognition.
The coffer lid swung open by itself.
The Thrice-Bound Edge slid across the cloth and struck the stone floor with a clear, restrained note.
The grimoire opened.
Its pages turned in a wind no one could feel, stopping at a blank leaf.
A line of black moisture appeared upon it.
Then another.
Letters formed beneath the dripping dark.
Brannoc leaned closer despite himself.
The words were written in a hand he did not know.
They named him.
Chapter 6
The ash came down without wind.
It settled upon the shutters, the sill, the blackened iron of the balcony rail, and upon the parchment spread beneath Cerys Sablewood the Ashen’s hand. Each flake was light as sifted flour. Each left a gray bruise where it touched the page.
Cerys did not brush it away.
The room had been built for accounts, not comfort. Its walls were stone beneath layers of soot-dark plaster, its ceiling low enough to hold the heat close, its single brazier breathing the sour scent of damp charcoal. Beyond the shuttered window, Gloammarch endured the ash-dark austerity of the Wastes: walls, watchtowers, sloping roofs, all reduced to shades of iron and bone.
A bell sounded somewhere below.
Once.
Then silence reclaimed the fortress.
Cerys placed one finger against the column of figures and read it again.
“Say it aloud,” Halvard said.
His voice was quiet, as if the room might take offense at being disturbed. He stood on the far side of the table with a sheaf of copied ledgers held against his chest. He was a scribe, young enough that ink had not yet found every crease of his hands, though the habit of bending over records had already made him carry himself as if beneath an invisible weight.
Cerys looked at him.
Halvard swallowed. “You said the numbers aloud when we were alone in the lower archive.”
“Those walls did not listen.”
“Walls are poor listeners.”
“Men are worse.”
He lowered his eyes.
Cerys turned back to the page. The seal pressed into its lower corner had been broken cleanly, then warmed and pressed again. A clever forgery. Not good enough for a court that had forgotten how to trust its own shadows, but good enough for a garrison officer who feared the contents more than the seal.
The report concerned Stormmarch.
Not supplies. Not relief. Not the condition of its quarantine.
Strength.
Stormmarch’s garrison strength was 9263.
The figure sat in the middle of the page like a coal refusing to cool.
“Read it,” Cerys said.
Halvard’s fingers tightened on the ledgers. “The report states that Stormmarch’s garrison strength is 9263.”
“Again.”
“Stormmarch’s garrison strength is 9263.”
The number entered the room and stood between them.
Cerys leaned back. The chair gave a faint wooden groan. No mirror hung in the chamber, and that was deliberate. Reflections had a way of making the past appear more certain than it was. Still, the ash marked everything here: the table, the ledgers, the sleeves of Cerys’s coat, the skin of the hands resting upon the parchment. The epithet had followed them from the first whispered inventory of their life. The Ashen. A title that sounded like judgment when spoken by enemies and inheritance when spoken by fools.
“Who counted them?” Cerys asked.
“The report does not say.”
“Who signed it?”
“The seal belongs to the quarantine office.”
“That was not my question.”
Halvard’s gaze lifted, then fell again. “No person signed it.”
“A report without a hand behind it.”
“Perhaps the hand was removed.”
There it was. Not wit. Fear sharpened into wit because fear had nowhere else to go.
Cerys traced the edge of the page with a nail. “Stormmarch lies outside the realm’s core holdings. It remains quarantined. Yet someone wants the court to believe that 9263 armed bodies are standing behind its walls, waiting to be counted.”
“Do you believe it?”
“I believe someone wants me to believe it.”
Halvard shifted the ledgers. Leather creaked softly. “That is not the same answer.”
“It is the only safe one.”
Outside, the ash thickened against the shutters. A muffled tread passed beyond the door. The guard did not knock. Cerys had instructed them not to interrupt unless the fortress was burning or the dead had begun to speak, and even then to consider whether either event might wait.
The page beneath their hand bore other marks: requisitions, delays, missing consignments. The old language of power. A fortress did not need to rebel in order to threaten the realm. It needed only to become expensive.
Cerys had spent years learning that every coin carried a memory. Copper remembered hunger. Silver remembered promises. Gold remembered blood. As Master of Coin, Cerys was expected to make those memories serve the living.
The title had once seemed like a door.
Now it felt like a lock placed gently around the throat.
Halvard set the ledgers upon the table. “There is another matter.”
“You have been waiting to say it.”
“I was waiting for you to finish looking at the figure.”
“Figures do not finish speaking.”
His mouth tightened. “The requisitions from Gloammarch have doubled.”
Cerys’s eyes moved toward the second stack.
“Doubled from what?” they asked.
Halvard hesitated.
Cerys looked at him until the hesitation became an answer without words.
“Do not invent a measure for me,” Cerys said. “Bring me the original requests.”
“They are below.”
“Then why are you holding copies?”
“Because the originals were damp.”
“Paper does not become damp in a sealed archive.”
“No.”
The word was barely audible.
Cerys rose.
The brazier’s heat fell away from them as they moved toward the door. Their boots made no sound on the rush-strewn floor. At the threshold, the black metal latch showed the faintest rim of orange from the forge fire beyond. Cerys laid a hand upon it and felt the warmth through the glove.
For one breath, memory stirred—not a memory of childhood, but of something older, inherited and unwelcome. A crown concealed beneath ash. A throne that had never acknowledged its heir. The Bleeding Crown had no face in Cerys’s thoughts, only weight: ceremony, obedience, ruin. The knowledge of blood did not make a person royal. It made every silence around them dangerous.
Halvard watched from the table.
“You are not wearing it,” he said.
Cerys did not turn. “Wearing what?”
“The regalia.”
The chamber seemed to narrow.
Halvard glanced toward the locked coffer beneath the writing desk. He had not pointed, but he did not need to. The Cinder-Wrought Aegis lay within, its cinder-dark surfaces shaped by the legacy of the Sundering, fire-scarred regalia made for authority that had survived the world’s breaking. It was meant for ceremony. For rule endured beneath ruin.
It was also evidence.
“What has made you observant?” Cerys asked.
“Nothing.”
“Nothing has poor eyesight.”
“I saw the coffer being moved.”
“By whom?”
Halvard’s face went pale beneath the ash dusting his hair. “I do not know.”
“Then you saw no one.”
“I saw two sets of hands.”
“That is still not a name.”
“There were no names.”
Cerys opened the door.
A guard stood outside beneath the narrow archway, helmet tucked beneath one arm. The corridor beyond descended toward the lower archive, where old requisitions lay sealed in wax, mud, and the careful neglect of frightened men. The guard straightened.
“Stay here,” Cerys said.
The guard’s eyes flicked toward Halvard.
“Both of us,” Cerys added.
The door closed behind them.
They descended through the fortress.
Gloammarch had been founded in 321 AS, when the Ash Wastes still offered enough stone and water to tempt builders into believing permanence was possible. The founding inscription had been carved above the western gate, though ash had eaten half the letters and left the rest like broken teeth. Cerys had read it on arrival. The date had seemed less like a beginning than a confession.
At the turn of the stair, a draft moved through the cracks. It smelled of wet wool, old grease, and the bitter mineral tang that rose from the wells after a hard fall of ash.
Cerys paused.
The Winter Reckoning had taught the realm to fear wells more than swords. It had begun in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS, leaving 27,987 casualties and the Iron-Ring Cartel as victor. The victory had been decided by betrayal at the eleventh hour; the concealed truth was that the victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
No one spoke of that truth in court.
No one needed to.
A well remembered what a ledger could not.
Halvard caught up, breathing carefully. “You know about the coffer.”
“I know someone moved it.”
“You know what it contains.”
Cerys continued down. “You are a scribe. Do not mistake copied words for knowledge.”
“Then why keep it here?”
“Because no one searches what they are afraid to understand.”
“Who is afraid?”
Cerys stopped beneath the next arch.
Halvard came nearly level with them before realizing. His face had the strained, blank expression of a man standing too close to a cliff and pretending the drop was not there.
“Everyone,” Cerys said.
Below, a door opened. Light spilled upward in a narrow gold blade.
Voices murmured beyond it.
Not guards. Not clerks.
Cerys felt the old arithmetic begin.
Stormmarch: 9263.
Gloammarch: contested ground, hungry for supplies and more hungry for certainty.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis beneath the desk.
Halvard’s copied ledgers against his chest.
And somewhere above them, the ash falling without wind.
Cerys moved down the final steps, one hand inside their coat, closing around the small key that opened the coffer.
Halvard whispered, “Master of Coin.”
Cerys looked back.
He had never used the title as a form of address before. It sounded different in his mouth—not respectful, not quite fearful. A warning offered too late.
“What?” Cerys asked.
“The report from Stormmarch was not delivered by courier.”
“Then how did it reach Gloammarch?”
Halvard’s gaze fixed upon the golden line of light beneath the archive door.
“It was already here.”
The murmurs beyond the door ceased.
Cerys heard the scrape of a chair. The soft drag of metal against metal. Someone inside had understood that the visitors on the stair were no longer visitors at all.
The key pressed into Cerys’s palm.
Their inheritance felt suddenly less like a secret than a blade awaiting a hand.
Cerys touched the archive latch.
From within, a voice said, “Come in, Master of Coin.”
And the door began to open.
The door opened inward on a room without windows.
Shelves rose into the dark, their ledgers bound in hide gone gray with ash. Lamps burned behind sheets of horn, each flame reduced to a dull yellow pulse. At the center stood a table of black wood, and upon it rested a lantern whose metal had been worked into three interlocking cages.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern.
Cerys knew it before the light found its shape. Every child raised near the old accounts had heard of it, though never in the same telling. Some said it had guided the first surveyors through the buried streets. Others claimed its flame could burn beneath water, or that it showed a man the face he wore when no one was watching.
The ledger beneath it mattered more.
A figure sat beyond the table, swathed in a dark robe. No crest marked the cloth. No weapon showed. The face remained half-concealed by the lamp’s sickly glow.
Halvard entered behind Cerys and shut the door.
The latch fell with a small, final sound.
“Master of Coin,” said the figure.
Cerys stepped into the archive. “You have the advantage of knowing me.”
“I know the office.”
“That is not what you said.”
The figure’s hands lay flat upon the table. Ink stained the fingertips. A scribe, then, or someone who wished to be mistaken for one. Behind the table, rows of shelves disappeared into the dimness, their contents leaning against one another like exhausted soldiers.
Halvard moved to Cerys’s left. He had gone pale, though whether from fear or the lamplight was impossible to tell.
Cerys looked at the ledger. Its cover had been sealed with black wax. No mark showed in the wax, no household device, no sign of the Iron-Ring Cartel or House Morvain or the Ashen Vanguard. The absence was deliberate. Whoever had placed it here had trusted concealment more than allegiance.
“Where is the report?” Cerys asked.
“Under your hand.”
The robe shifted. A second figure stood in the narrow gap between the shelves.
Cerys did not turn toward it. The archive had become a vessel, and every breath within it was water rising. One body at the table. One behind. Halvard near the door. Cerys between them all.
The old instinct was to count. Exits. Distances. Weight of metal. Cost of blood.
Instead, Cerys placed a hand against the breast beneath the ash-colored layers and felt the hard edge of The Cinder-Wrought Aegis resting there.
Since 356 AS, Cerys Sablewood the Ashen had wielded The Cinder-Wrought Aegis.
The regalia had never been meant for concealment. Its cinder-dark surfaces were made to be seen beneath banners, beneath the eyes of kneeling courts, beneath the burden of authority that outlived the flesh carrying it. Yet the thing had been wrapped, hidden, carried through corridors where servants lowered their eyes for reasons they did not understand.
The secret weight pressed back against Cerys’s palm.
“The Cinder-Wrought Aegis,” said the seated figure.
Halvard’s breath caught.
Cerys let the hand fall. “You have been searching my clothing.”
“No. We have been searching the realm.”
“Then you have searched badly.”
“Perhaps.” The figure tipped the ledger toward the lantern. “Stormmarch was sealed before the report left its walls.”
“It did not leave its walls.”
“No.”
“Then someone in Gloammarch wrote it.”
“No.”
Cerys felt the room narrow. “You enjoy the word.”
“I enjoy words that survive examination.”
The hidden figure moved at last. Cloth whispered against stone. A hand emerged from the dark and touched the ledger’s spine.
Cerys saw the hand tremble.
Not fear, perhaps. Fatigue. Or age. The archive had the smell of old paper, lamp oil, and the mineral bitterness that crept through every wall in the Ash Wastes. But beneath it lay another scent, faint and wet, like earth opened after a long burial.
“What is in it?” Halvard asked.
The question came too quickly. His voice was thin.
The seated figure looked past Cerys to him. “You are Halvard Sablewood.”
Halvard straightened. “I am a scribe.”
“That was not the question.”
“It is the answer I have.”
Cerys heard the lie’s small machinery turning. Halvard had been born in 408 AS. That much was entered in a dozen records, each one copied by a different hand and preserved under different seals. He had spent his life among words, but words had not made him safe. They had only taught him where men hid their knives.
The figure returned its attention to Cerys. “Open it.”
“You summoned me to do clerical work?”
“I summoned the Master of Coin to witness a correction.”
“Corrections are made in the daylight.”
“Not this one.”
Cerys broke the seal with a fingernail.
The wax gave way without resistance. Inside lay sheets of narrow vellum, each covered in columns. The script was precise, cramped, and old-fashioned. At the bottom of the first page, a line had been written in a different hand.
STORMMARCH: THRICE-BOUND LANTERN FORGED IN 72 AS.
The letters seemed to lift from the page.
Cerys looked at the lantern.
Its three cages held no visible wick. Light gathered within them anyway, cold and steady, as if the flame had been taught obedience. The metal was scarred around the hinges. A dark crust filled the smallest seams. Stormmarch had forged it in 72 AS, before Gloammarch had been raised from the waste, before the realm learned to call certain ruins holdings and others quarantines.
“Why is this here?” Cerys asked.
“Because it was removed.”
“From Stormmarch?”
The figure nodded.
“By whom?”
The silence that followed had shape. It stood at the table, broad-shouldered and patient.
Cerys read the columns.
Grain. Salt. Lamp oil. Iron. Medicines. Names were absent, replaced by offices and marks. Beside each entry, a number had been crossed out and another entered. The ink had bled through the vellum in places, staining the reverse like bruises.
“These are requisitions.”
“Were.”
“Some of these deliveries never arrived.”
“They arrived.”
Cerys lifted their eyes. “Then the accounts were falsified afterward.”
“Before.”
The hidden figure spoke. “The reports sent from Stormmarch were not reports of shortages. They were reports of substitutions.”
Halvard stepped nearer despite himself. “Substitutions of what?”
The figure looked at him.
Cerys turned a page before the answer could come. A narrow strip had been sewn into the binding, and upon it a second line had been written.
AEGIS TRANSFER CONFIRMED. 356 AS.
The room seemed to lose its air.
Cerys’s fingers tightened around the vellum.
The seated figure watched with the quiet attention of someone who had placed a snare and now waited for the animal to discover its own weight.
“You knew,” Cerys said.
“We knew the regalia had changed hands.”
“Changed hands.”
“Wielded,” the figure corrected. “Since 356 AS.”
Halvard stared at Cerys. The look was not accusation. That made it worse. Accusation could be answered. Wonder had no handle.
Cerys closed the ledger.
The lantern’s threefold light moved across the cover, revealing impressions in the hide: shallow lines, almost invisible, cut in a pattern like a crown seen through smoke.
The Bleeding Crown had no crown.
Not anymore. Its authority survived in rumor, in blood hidden beneath names, in old men who spoke of obedience as though it were a debt owed to the dead. Cerys had learned early that inheritance was not a garment handed down. It was a hook lodged beneath the ribs. One could conceal it. One could pretend not to feel it. But the body knew.
The figure at the table said, “You are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Halvard made a sound behind Cerys.
Not a word. A break in the world.
Cerys placed the ledger on the table. “You have mistaken a private insult for a political fact.”
“Have I?”
“You possess forged accounts, a stolen relic, and enough confidence to mistake both for proof.”
“The accounts are genuine.”
“The lantern?”
“Also genuine.”
“Then your conclusion is still false.”
“Is it?”
The question was soft.
Cerys looked toward the door. It remained shut. Halvard stood between the hinges and the armed silence in the room. A scribe, born in 408 AS, carrying no visible sword. His hand hovered near his sleeve.
“Halvard,” Cerys said.
“Yes.”
“Take the ledger.”
He did not move.
The seated figure smiled, though Cerys saw only the slight change in shadow. “It cannot leave.”
“Everything leaves,” Cerys said.
“Not this.”
Cerys drew the Aegis from beneath the ash-dark layers.
The regalia came free without a ring or scrape. Its surfaces caught the lantern’s divided light and gave it back in a dull, emberless sheen. It was not beautiful. Beauty asked to be admired. The Cinder-Wrought Aegis demanded endurance.
The second figure moved from the shelves.
Halvard flinched.
Cerys raised the regalia between them, not as shield but as declaration. The figure stopped at once.
There it was: the proof hidden beneath every denial. Not fear of Cerys. Fear of what the artifact allowed others to believe.
“The Cinder-Wrought Aegis is regalia,” Cerys said. “It is not a confession.”
“No,” said the seated figure. “It is permission.”
“For whom?”
“For the realm.”
Beyond the archive door, something struck the corridor wall.
Once.
Then again.
Dust whispered from the ceiling. The lamps bent in their horn cages, all three flames leaning toward the sound.
Halvard seized the ledger. This time, the seated figure did not stop him.
Cerys kept the Aegis raised.
“What is coming?” Halvard asked.
The figure’s gaze fixed upon the door.
“Those who were meant to receive the report.”
Another blow landed. The wood shuddered. A thin line of ash sifted beneath the threshold.
Cerys felt the old hook beneath the ribs draw tight.
“Open the door,” said the figure.
“Why?”
“Because they believe the heir is inside.”
Cerys stared at the black seal broken beneath their hand.
“And if they are wrong?”
The figure leaned toward the Thrice-Bound Lantern. Its three cages clicked softly, one after another, as though something within had begun to turn.
“Then let them discover what you are instead.”
The door buckled inward.
The door buckled inward.
Cerys lowered the Aegis by a finger’s breadth.
“Now.”
Halvard seized the bar.
He was a scribe, not a soldier. His hands had been made for reed pens, scraped vellum, and the careful burial of figures beneath columns of ink. They trembled as he lifted the iron from its sockets. Cerys saw the tremor and hated him for it, then hated herself for noticing. Fear was a kind of account. Once entered, it demanded to be carried forward.
The figure withdrew into the lantern’s shadow.
Halvard looked to Cerys.
She nodded.
He opened the door.
The first man came through with the force of a kicked corpse. He wore a coat stiffened by ash and carried a short blade in one hand. Cerys turned the Aegis.
The regalia caught the blade with a sound like a bell struck beneath deep water. Fire ran along its cinder-dark surface. The man’s wrist twisted. His knife fell. Cerys drove the rim of the Aegis into his throat and felt cartilage give.
He folded without a cry.
A second shape crowded behind him.
Halvard made a noise—small, involuntary—and snatched up the fallen knife. He held it badly, point wavering toward the doorway.
“Do not,” Cerys said.
The second intruder paused.
Beyond him, the passage burned with pale torchlight. Ash moved through it in slow veils, stirring from every stone seam. More silhouettes waited there. Their faces were hidden beneath scarves. Their silence was worse than shouting. Men who came to kill often announced themselves. Men who came to retrieve something kept their breath for the work.
“Master Sablewood,” said the second figure.
The title entered the room like a coin placed upon a table.
Cerys felt the hidden inheritance stir beneath the ribs—not pride, not fear. Recognition. The Bleeding Crown had survived by teaching its blood to flinch from its own name.
“You have mistaken the chamber,” Cerys said.
“We were told the heir was here.”
“Then whoever told you has mistaken more than the chamber.”
The man’s gaze passed over Cerys, over Halvard, and settled on the black seal broken upon the desk. The report lay beneath it, half-covered by a ledger. Its pages had been written in Halvard’s narrow hand. Ink had dried in the grooves of his fingers.
The intruder’s attention sharpened.
“Give us the report.”
“No.”
“Give us the heir.”
Cerys heard the lantern click.
Once.
Twice.
The third cage remained still.
The figure in the shadows said, “They are not asking for what they think they are asking for.”
The intruder shifted toward the voice. “Show yourself.”
“Why?”
Something moved outside in the passage. Metal whispered against metal.
Halvard backed toward the desk. He was pale now, but the knife remained in his hand.
Cerys did not look at him. “Take the report.”
His eyes widened.
“You heard me.”
“And you?”
“I will make them regret entering.”
That was not a promise she could afford to break.
Halvard lunged for the papers. The second intruder crossed the threshold. Cerys stepped into him. The Aegis struck his forearm; bone cracked. He turned with surprising speed and drove his shoulder into her chest.
The room tilted.
Ash filled her mouth.
She caught the edge of the desk before falling and saw the account ledger burst open beneath her hand. Rows of figures marched across the page, obedient and merciless. Grain, iron, timber, men. The realm reduced to what could be counted before it was burned.
A knife flashed near her face.
Cerys seized the attacker’s wrist.
He was stronger. She felt the pressure building in her fingers, felt the old hook beneath the ribs draw tight again. Not now, she thought. Not before the door. Not before the report.
The Aegis answered before she commanded it.
Heat flared between them.
The attacker screamed. His sleeve caught fire, though no flame touched it. Cerys wrenched him sideways and sent him crashing into the wall. The stones drank the sound.
Halvard had the report.
A third figure entered.
This one wore no scarf. Ash had pasted itself to his brow and cheeks, giving him the appearance of a man already half unearthed. His eyes went to Halvard.
“Scribe.”
Halvard froze.
Cerys rose.
The man pointed toward him. “Bring the pages.”
Halvard’s grip tightened. “They are sealed.”
“The seal is broken.”
“It is still forbidden.”
The man smiled without warmth. “So is breathing, when the order comes.”
He advanced.
Cerys moved between them.
The Aegis weighed more than it had a moment ago. Its surface held the color of old embers beneath ash. Authority was the shape of it, but authority had never been the same as safety. She had learned that from ledgers. She had learned it from blood.
“I know what you want,” she said.
“Do you?”
“You want the figures removed before they reach the wrong hands.”
“No.”
“You want the names erased.”
“No.”
“You want the truth preserved only where it can be used.”
The man’s expression altered by the smallest degree.
Behind Cerys, Halvard breathed through his nose. He was trying not to cry. She could hear it. The shame of hearing it was almost unbearable.
The man said, “The truth is not in the pages.”
“No,” Cerys said. “The truth is in what the pages cost.”
For a moment the chamber held still.
Then the man struck.
Cerys caught his hand against the Aegis. The impact shook her shoulder. He followed with his other fist. She turned, took the blow along the ribs, and drove the heel of the regalia beneath his jaw.
He stumbled.
The figure by the lantern moved.
Not quickly. Not like a soldier. The shadow simply seemed to arrive beside the man. A hand rose, and the Thrice-Bound Lantern gave a low, hollow tone.
The attacker’s body seized.
His mouth opened, but no sound emerged. Ash poured from his throat in a thin gray stream. He fell to his knees, clawing at his own collar.
The lantern’s first cage went dark.
Cerys stared.
The figure placed one hand upon the lantern’s frame.
“Leave,” it said to the men in the passage.
They did not move.
“Leave,” the figure repeated.
The nearest silhouette raised a crossbow.
Halvard saw it first. “Down!”
The bolt struck the wall where Cerys’s head had been. Stone burst against her cheek. She dropped behind the desk as another bolt punched through the doorframe.
The wounded man on the floor crawled toward the report.
Halvard stepped back, clutching the pages to his chest.
Cerys rose with ash and blood warm along her face. “Halvard. Give me the report.”
He looked at her.
He had been born in 408 AS. She remembered the entry because she had signed the register herself, though the memory belonged to a room very far from this one: a boy’s name, a clerk’s mark, a future entered before it had learned to resist. Halvard had been a scribe ever since the realm had needed men to make ruin legible.
His voice shook. “If they take it, they will know.”
“They already know enough.”
“They will know about the wells.”
Cerys went still.
The passage seemed to narrow around that word.
The Winter Reckoning had begun in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS. Its dead numbered 27,987. The Iron-Ring Cartel had been named victor, and every court that mattered had repeated the verdict until victory became a kind of law.
But the wells had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands.
The betrayal had come at the eleventh hour, concealed beneath winter banners and iron marks. Allies had drunk together, believing the water would carry them through the last cold. The Cartel had watched them sicken. It had called the deaths necessity. It had called the war concluded.
Halvard looked down at the report. “It is written here.”
“Not plainly.”
“Plainly enough.”
Another bolt struck the desk. The wood jumped. One of the pages slipped free and skated across the floor.
The wounded man reached for it.
Cerys stamped on his hand.
He screamed this time.
“Halvard,” she said.
He threw the report.
Not to her.
Into the lantern.
The figure turned sharply.
The pages vanished between the three cages. Flame rose without color. Ink lifted from the paper in black threads, twisting upward like drowned hair. The chamber filled with the smell of scorched hide and bitter metal.
Cerys felt something inside her break—not the hidden crown, not the secret itself, but the belief that knowledge could be protected by keeping it close.
The figure seized Halvard by the collar and dragged him behind the lantern.
“What have you done?” Cerys asked.
“Bought the next breath.”
“For whom?”
The door exploded inward.
Ash and splintered wood struck the chamber. Cerys raised the Aegis. Through the ringing in her skull, she saw the passage beyond: more figures, more weapons, and behind them the black mouth of the stair descending into the lower keep.
A banner showed briefly through the ash.
Not a color. Not a sigil she could name.
Only a strip of dark cloth bearing the iron mark of the Iron-Ring Cartel.
The sight opened an old wound in the realm.
The man beneath her boot twisted. She lifted the Aegis to finish him.
“Do not,” said the figure.
“Why?”
“Because he is not the one who came for you.”
Cerys looked past the ruined doorway.
At the far end of the passage, someone stood apart from the others. No weapon showed in that person’s hands. No scarf covered the face. The ash moved around them and did not settle.
Their gaze fixed upon Cerys.
Not the Aegis.
Not the dead report.
Her.
The figure beside the lantern whispered, “There is your mistake.”
Cerys’s grip tightened until the regalia cut into her palm.
The stranger took one step forward.
And somewhere below, beneath stone and sealed earth, the Bleeding Crown began to beat.
Chapter 7
Hollowreach had been built to keep things out.
The walls rose from the Gloaming Reach in blackened courses, each stone sealed against the next with a pale substance that had cracked into veins. Watchfires guttered along the parapets, their smoke pressed flat by the damp. Beyond the gates, the road vanished into a pallid marsh where reeds stood motionless beneath a skin of grey water.
Under quarantine, the settlement had learned the shape of silence.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless crossed the inner yard beneath the gaze of men who did not trust him enough to salute. He wore the iron-dark mantle of a Warden-Commander, though the clasp had been polished too often and reflected the firelight like a watching eye. No face, no scar, no height had ever been set down in the records to define him. Authority had done that work. So had the epithet.
The Oathless.
It followed him more faithfully than any oath.
A bell sounded once from the wall. Not an alarm. A warning that wanted to become one.
Ignatz entered the quarantine hall.
The air inside was colder than the yard. Charcoal braziers burned beneath the narrow windows, filling the chamber with the bitter smell of ash and old herbs. A table had been dragged beneath the far arch. Papers lay upon it, weighted by a black reliquary and a ward whose edge swallowed the light.
The Hollow Edge had been forged in 216 AS. Its attunement cost 21.
Beside it rested the Chalice of Ashdeep, wrapped in oil-dark cloth. The reliquary had been forged in 323 AS. Its attunement cost 27.
Neither artifact belonged in a room where men lied for coin. That was precisely why they had been brought there.
Ignatz Marrowgate stood behind the table with a ledger open before him. He served as Quartermaster, and the records identified him plainly: born in 425 AS, appointed to the stores, entrusted with the movement of food, iron, lamp oil, medicines, and every other small necessity by which armies pretended they were not made of hunger.
He did not look up when Ignatz entered.
“Warden-Commander.”
“Quartermaster.”
The younger Ignatz’s fingers tightened on the ledger’s spine. He had the tense, colorless manner of a man who feared both discovery and the consequences of being believed. No temperament had been assigned to him by history. History had not yet decided what to do with him.
Ignatz Ashgrove glanced at the empty chairs.
“Where are the others?”
“Which others?”
“The ones who summoned me.”
Marrowgate swallowed. “No one summoned you.”
“Then I have been invited.”
“I said no such thing.”
The Warden-Commander laid one gloved hand upon the table. The Chalice of Ashdeep trembled beneath its cloth, though the air was still. He felt the ward’s severity through the leather, a hollow pressure against the bones of his wrist.
Outside, a voice called from the walls. Another answered. The words blurred in the damp.
Marrowgate lowered his eyes to the ledger. “The Iron-Ring Cartel is seated at Hollowreach.”
The phrase had the polished ugliness of something repeated in secret until it became official.
Ignatz let the silence receive it.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel seated at Hollowreach,” he said.
“Yes.”
“And Hollowreach is ruled by The Iron-Ring Cartel.”
Marrowgate’s mouth worked once before sound came. “Yes.”
The words seemed to alter the room. The braziers burned lower. The walls leaned inward, listening.
Hollowreach had been founded in 56 AS. It lay in the Gloaming Reach, where the ground exhaled vapors that silvered the grass and turned exposed metal green. It was a core location under quarantine, though the quarantine had long ago stopped resembling a measure and begun resembling a government. Gates, seals, patrols, inspections: these were the architecture of obedience.
Now the Iron-Ring Cartel sat within it.
Not camped. Not besieged. Seated.
A merchant power with no crown had taken the chair at the heart of a sealed settlement, and every document still called the place a quarantine zone.
Ignatz lifted the ledger. Marrowgate did not resist.
The first pages concerned Crookvale. Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires, rebuilt after its ruin, retaining a garrison of 1004, and still outside the core holdings. The inventory listed grain, bolts, winter cloth, lamp oil. The columns were neat. Too neat.
“Crookvale has received no iron,” Ignatz said.
“The road is dangerous.”
“The road has always been dangerous.”
“It is outside the core holdings.”
“That does not make steel walk.”
Marrowgate’s gaze darted toward the shuttered windows. “The wagons were redirected.”
“To Hollowreach.”
“I did not redirect them.”
Ignatz turned a page. “The Iron-Ring Cartel did.”
A pale smear of light showed beneath the shutters. Dawn, or some sick imitation of it. In Hollowreach, morning had the color of old bruises.
The Warden-Commander had been born in 258 AS, in a year when the realm still believed the wounds of the Sundering could close if watched closely enough. He had spent his life among watchers. He knew the difference between vigilance and fear. Fear looked outward. Vigilance looked inward first.
He had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel for long enough to know that their messages never arrived alone. A scrap concealed in a ration tally. A mark beneath a seal. A phrase spoken by a courier who did not know its meaning. Each secret became a thread, and threads became a net.
He had told himself the Cartel purchased information because information was cheaper than war.
He had told himself many things.
Marrowgate whispered, “You were seen speaking with them.”
“I speak with everyone.”
“Not as a Warden-Commander.”
“Then perhaps they saw me as a man.”
The Quartermaster flinched. That, more than accusation, revealed the wound.
Ignatz looked again at the two artifacts. The Hollow Edge lay uncovered now. Its surface was not bright metal but a narrow absence cut into the shape of a blade, a ward forged in 216 AS to make emptiness obedient. The Chalice of Ashdeep remained wrapped, but its presence made the room feel buried. Reliquary. Ash. Deepness. The names had been chosen by people who believed names could warn the soul.
“Why bring these here?” Ignatz asked.
Marrowgate closed the ledger. “Because the Cartel wants the quarantine opened.”
“The Cartel rules Hollowreach.”
“It wants the gates opened by lawful order.”
“And if the order is refused?”
“Then it will be opened by necessity.”
Ignatz heard the soft scrape of a boot beyond the door. One boot. Then silence.
He did not turn.
“Who carries the order?”
Marrowgate’s face had gone damp. “You do.”
The Warden-Commander smiled without warmth. “You have mistaken me for a loyal man.”
“No.”
“Good.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel believes you understand the cost of delay.”
It was nearly amusing. They believed many things about him. They believed his access could be bought. They believed his silence was the silence of a disciplined officer rather than a man constantly choosing which betrayal would leave the fewest corpses. They believed he belonged to them because money had crossed from one hand to another.
Perhaps they were right.
On the table, the ledger’s page stirred though no wind touched it. Beneath the supply tallies, written in a different ink, lay a sentence without a signature.
The Bleeding Crown was the victor of The War of Endless Vigil.
Ignatz read it twice.
The war had begun in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS. Its record counted 81577 casualties. The aggressors had been totally routed. The Bleeding Crown stood in the histories as victor, crowned by blood and prolonged watchfulness.
But the histories were only the portion of truth permitted to survive.
Secretly, the losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
Ignatz placed two fingers over the sentence. The paper was warm.
“Who wrote this?”
Marrowgate shook his head.
“Quartermaster.”
“I don’t know.”
“No one writes in a ledger without knowing.”
“I was told to preserve the page.”
“By whom?”
The younger man stared at him, and for one moment Ignatz saw the future in his eyes: a rope, a closed cell, an official explanation, a corpse made useful by the absence of a name.
Then the door opened.
A gust of marsh air entered, carrying rot and cold water. No one stood in the threshold. Only a strip of red cord had been tied to the latch.
Ignatz felt the Cartel’s presence before he saw the message. He had known it in alleys, in garrison rooms, beside emptied cups. A pressure behind the world. A hand resting lightly on the throat.
Marrowgate backed away from the table.
“You will take the order,” he said.
Ignatz untied the cord. A small metal token hung from it, stamped with a ring broken by a single notch.
“If I refuse?”
“You will not.”
“Because Hollowreach is ruled by The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
“Because the gates cannot remain closed.”
The Warden-Commander looked toward the walls. Beyond them, the quarantined settlement waited in its damp enclosure, its streets washed clean of footprints, its people breathing behind barred shutters. Somewhere in that silence, the Cartel counted its profits. Somewhere, a guard watched the road and wondered whether the next figure to emerge would carry sickness, orders, or a knife.
Ignatz closed his fist around the token.
The metal cut his palm.
He remembered the first oath he had broken. He could not remember what it had been sworn to protect. Only the sensation of speaking the words while already knowing they were dead.
“Open the western archive,” he said.
Marrowgate stared. “Why?”
“Because if I am to deliver an order, I will know what it contains.”
“That archive is sealed.”
“So am I.”
He turned toward the door.
Behind him, the Chalice of Ashdeep gave a single hollow chime beneath its cloth.
Ignatz stopped.
From beyond the walls came the sound of the quarantine bell again—once, then once more—and beneath it, faint as breath against glass, the first cry of someone in the marsh.
Marrowgate did not move to stop him.
That was the first thing Ignatz noticed. The second was the quartermaster’s hand sliding beneath his coat, not toward a weapon—Marrowgate had never carried one in the presence of the Chalice—but toward the packet hidden in the inner lining.
The bell sounded again.
The cry beyond the walls answered it.
Not a human cry, Ignatz thought. Then he heard the shape of words inside it, torn thin by distance and marsh fog.
“Commander.”
Marrowgate’s voice had lost its dry impatience.
Ignatz looked back. “If you mean to warn me, do it before the archive opens.”
“The western archive was sealed by order of—”
“By whose order?”
Marrowgate stopped.
There were names that could still command silence in Hollowreach. Names that belonged to the Crown, to the Cartel, to the dead. Marrowgate weighed one against another behind his eyes and found none worth spending.
Ignatz turned the latch.
The iron had been cold a moment before. Now it held a faint warmth, as if something on the other side had pressed its palm against it.
He withdrew his hand.
Beneath the cloth, the Chalice of Ashdeep chimed once more.
Marrowgate flinched.
Ignatz despised him for it, though the sound had entered his own bones.
“Stand there,” Ignatz said.
“Where?”
“Between me and the door.”
“That is not a sensible instruction.”
“It is the one you have.”
Marrowgate’s mouth worked. He was a young man by the standards of command, born in 425 AS and already carrying the stoop of a servant who had spent his life apologizing to locked rooms. Ignatz knew this because Quartermaster Ignatz Marrowgate had once been required to submit his birth record with the others. He remembered the ink, the thinness of the paper, the careful way Marrowgate had watched him read it.
Now the quartermaster planted himself before the door.
Ignatz drew the token from his palm. Blood had gathered in its grooves, black in the lamplight. He pressed it to the lock.
The western archive opened without a click.
A breath came through the gap.
It smelled of wet stone, old ash, and the bitter sweetness of something rotting beneath water.
Marrowgate whispered a prayer.
Ignatz stepped inside.
The archive was narrower than he remembered. Shelves climbed both walls, bowed beneath ledgers, sealed packets, bone-white tablets, and clay cylinders marked with the cracked sigils of orders no living clerk could explain. Dust filmed everything except the floor. Across the flagstones ran a dark trail of water.
It led inward.
Ignatz kept his eyes on it.
“Close the door,” he said.
Marrowgate remained outside. “You said to stand between you and it.”
“Then stand between me and the corridor.”
The door swung shut.
The darkness inside the archive gathered around Ignatz with the intimacy of a cloak. He touched the wall and found the old iron brackets. One by one, the lamps woke beneath his fingers, burning with a low blue flame.
At the end of the chamber stood a table.
On it lay a ledger opened to the middle.
He had not left it there.
Ignatz crossed the room, every step measured. The trail of water ended at the table’s foot. A single drop fell from the lower edge of the ledger and struck the stone.
He did not touch the book.
The page was ruled in columns. The handwriting belonged to several hands, some cramped with fear, some broad with authority. The oldest entry was written in brown ink that had faded nearly to yellow.
The War of Endless Vigil waged at Hollowreach in 251 AS.
The words had been underlined so heavily the quill had torn the page.
Ignatz read them once.
Then again.
The bell outside struck.
The sound traveled through the archive’s stone and set the shelves trembling. A bundle of loose tablets shifted overhead. One fell, broke against the table, and spilled a grey powder across the ledger.
Marrowgate shouted from beyond the door.
Ignatz seized the book and pulled it clear.
The broken tablet had exposed another line beneath the page. He brushed the powder aside with two fingers.
A roster.
Names, postings, permissions. Not soldiers. Observers. Wardens. Physicians. Those assigned to remain where the war had ended and count the costs after the banners went dark.
His eyes moved down the list.
Maelis Greyfen serves at Hollowreach.
The line had been written in fresh black ink.
Ignatz felt the room contract.
He knew no Maelis Greyfen. That did not comfort him. Names were rarely dangerous because of what they revealed. They were dangerous because of what someone had taken the trouble to conceal.
The ink was not old. It had not belonged to the war’s record. Someone had opened the archive recently, written the name, and left the ledger for him.
A message, then.
Or bait.
The Hollow Edge lay in a narrow case beneath the roster. Ignatz had seen it once, years ago, before the ward was given over to another hand. The case had no hinge. Its lid was a slab of dark glass fitted into iron.
He lifted it.
The ward within was pale and thin, not like a blade but like the memory of one. It seemed to have been cut from a piece of winter sky. No maker’s mark disturbed its surface. Only a date had been etched along the inner rim.
The Hollow Edge forged at Hollowvale in 216 AS.
Ignatz did not touch it.
Attunement to The Hollow Edge cost 21.
He knew the number because the cost had been entered beside the ward’s name in a registry meant for men who believed everything could be measured before it was endured. Twenty-one for the ward. Twenty-seven for the Chalice of Ashdeep. The numbers had never made either artifact safer.
The Hollow Edge gave off no light.
Still, the archive seemed to arrange itself around it.
“What did you find?” Marrowgate called.
Ignatz closed the case.
“Dust.”
“You are not a man who goes into a sealed archive for dust.”
“Then perhaps you should stop asking questions you cannot afford answered.”
The quartermaster’s silence came back through the door, thick with resentment.
Ignatz turned another page.
The old ledger had been altered in places. Whole entries had been scraped away, leaving shallow scars. A red thread marked the pages that survived. It ran from the war at Hollowreach to later reports of fever, disappearances, failed harvests, and voices heard in the marsh after the quarantine bells began.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had possessed the archive long enough to erase what it wished.
Or long enough to make erasure look like preservation.
A folded strip of black paper rested between the next pages.
Ignatz took it.
No seal. No signature.
The writing was small and exact.
The western waterline is open. The first bell was not a warning.
He read the sentence without breathing.
Outside, something struck the keep wall.
Once.
A dull impact. Then another, lower down.
Marrowgate swore. “Commander?”
“Do not open the door.”
“I had no intention—”
The third impact came from within the wall.
Ignatz looked toward the shelves.
Dust sifted from between the stones. One of the blue flames bent sideways though there was no wind. Somewhere behind the masonry, something scraped its way along the inner passage, slow and patient.
The cry sounded again from the marsh.
This time it was unmistakably human.
A woman’s voice, perhaps. Or a child’s. The sound rose until it broke, then continued in a register no throat should have held.
Marrowgate began fumbling with the outer bolts.
Ignatz crossed the room and placed the token against the door.
“Leave them.”
“The lock is not enough.”
“It has held for two centuries.”
“Not against this.”
Ignatz’s hand tightened around the metal. The token’s edge bit deeper into his palm. He could feel the blood returning, warm and insistent.
“Who opened the archive?” he asked.
Marrowgate went still.
“Answer me.”
“I did not.”
“I did not ask what you did.”
“You think I brought that thing here?”
“I think you know more than you have said.”
The quartermaster breathed hard. “I know the western archive was sealed. I know the order came through channels no clerk can access. I know someone has been taking pages from the quarantine registers. I know Maelis Greyfen serves at Hollowreach, because that name appeared in the dispatches this morning.”
Ignatz stared at the door.
“Why was I not told?”
“Because the dispatches were addressed to the Cartel.”
There it was.
Not spoken loudly. Not spoken with courage. But spoken.
The admission settled between them.
Ignatz had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel for long enough to recognize the shape of their hunger. They did not buy facts. They bought leverage sharpened into facts. A garrison strength. A patrol route. The hour at which a gate changed hands. Small truths that made larger cruelties possible.
He had told himself the realm was already broken.
He had told himself a man could choose which cracks widened.
The archive wall groaned.
A line appeared in the stone beside the table. Fine as a hair. Wetness welled through it, darkened the mortar, and ran downward.
Marrowgate whispered, “What is that?”
Ignatz opened the case again.
The Hollow Edge remained where he had left it, pale and severe. He lifted it from its cradle.
The cold entered him before the ward touched his skin.
For an instant he stood in a corridor of drowned banners. He saw watchfires burning along a ridge. He saw soldiers with ash on their faces, standing beneath a sky split by the old wound of the Sundering. Somewhere beyond them, an army was breaking—not from defeat, but from exhaustion, its line unraveling while unseen hands counted the price.
Then the vision closed.
Ignatz found himself kneeling.
The ward lay across his palm.
Twenty-one.
The cost moved through him like a nail driven beneath the ribs.
His breath came out white.
“Commander,” Marrowgate said. “Open this door.”
Ignatz rose.
The thing in the wall scraped closer.
He carried The Hollow Edge to the seam. With his free hand, he unbolted the door.
Marrowgate recoiled. “What are you doing?”
“Finding out who has come to collect.”
The door opened inward.
The corridor beyond was empty.
At its far end, the quarantine lamps burned in a wavering line. Water shone across the flagstones. No footprints marked it, though the trail continued from the archive threshold and disappeared beneath Marrowgate’s boots.
Ignatz looked down.
The quartermaster’s shadow pointed the wrong way.
Marrowgate saw it too.
His face emptied.
Behind them, inside the archive, the Chalice of Ashdeep gave a hollow chime.
And from the darkness beyond the shelves, Maelis Greyfen said, “You were not meant to read that.”
Ignatz did not turn toward the dark.
He watched the wrong-facing shadow tremble on the wet stones. It trembled as if something beneath it had laid a hand upon its head.
Marrowgate made a thin sound in his throat. His fingers found the doorframe, though whether to steady himself or bar the way, Ignatz could not tell.
“Maelis,” Ignatz said.
The name went down the corridor and returned altered. Not echoed. Remembered.
A shelf creaked in the archive.
“Quartermaster,” Maelis called from the dark, “you have opened the door.”
“I opened it,” Ignatz said.
“You opened nothing. It was waiting.”
A smell drifted from beyond the threshold: wet ash, old iron, and something sweetly rotten beneath both. Ignatz had known battlefields that smelled cleaner. He kept one hand near his sword, though the weapon seemed suddenly a childish answer to a question no steel had been made to ask.
Marrowgate stared at him.
“Warden-Commander,” he whispered, “what did you read?”
Ignatz ignored him. His own shadow had begun to lengthen toward the archive.
He could feel the Chalice of Ashdeep behind him, though he could not see it. The reliquary’s hollow chime still vibrated in his teeth. The sound had not ceased. It had merely become too deep for hearing, a pressure in the bones, a second pulse beneath his own.
“Come into the lamp-light,” Ignatz said.
“No.”
“Maelis.”
“No, Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
Marrowgate flinched at the epithet. Everyone did, sooner or later. Some heard accusation in it. Some heard promise. Ignatz had long ago stopped deciding which was worse.
The darkness between the shelves shifted.
A woman stepped into the furthest quarantine lamp.
Maelis Greyfen wore the gray of service at Hollowreach, but the cloth drank the lamp-glow instead of reflecting it. Water darkened the hem. Her face seemed composed from the same pale substance as the ash sealed in the archive jars. She held no weapon.
That did not comfort him.
“You were not meant to read that,” she said again.
Ignatz glanced at the open folio lying on the archive table behind her. He had seen only a few lines before the door had opened, but the words had fixed themselves inside him. Not ink. A wound shaped like ink.
“Then you should not have left it where a commander could find it.”
“You were not meant to come here.”
“I came because the dead keep changing the orders.”
Marrowgate swallowed. “The orders?”
Ignatz heard the fear in the quartermaster’s voice and despised him for offering it so freely. Fear was a currency. Someone always came to collect.
Maelis looked toward Marrowgate’s shadow.
“Your assistant has been counting the wrong things.”
“I have no assistant,” Marrowgate said.
“You have a shadow.”
The shadow beneath him twitched.
Marrowgate’s hand left the doorframe. He raised it as though to shield his face, then seemed to realize there was nowhere to hide from what had no face at all.
Ignatz stepped between them.
“Speak plainly.”
Maelis’s gaze settled on him. The lamps guttered, though no wind moved through the corridor.
“Plain speech is what brought this place to ruin.”
“Hollowreach was ruined before your speech.”
“Hollowreach was contained.”
“Containment is a word used by people standing outside the grave.”
Maelis’s mouth tightened. “You have always preferred the grave. It cannot contradict your reports.”
The accusation struck too near the hidden chamber of him.
Ignatz had sold reports. Not all of them. Never the ones that would open the gates to slaughter. That was the lie he carried, polished and turned over whenever sleep refused him. He gave the Iron-Ring Cartel routes, dispositions, shortages—small truths, he had told himself. Truths that kept their hands from reaching for larger knives.
But the Cartel had never paid for small truths.
Its coin had found him in the dark places between duty and need. Its questions had arrived folded in harmless orders. Its gratitude had been absence: no blade in his back, no accusation at the gate, no sudden disappearance for which a commander required an explanation.
Now the archive had spoken a name no living report contained.
Vault Chitin.
Ignatz felt the words rise behind his teeth.
“Say it,” Maelis said.
Marrowgate shook his head. “Don’t.”
“Vault Chitin,” Ignatz said.
The corridor lamps went out.
Marrowgate cried out. The sound was swallowed almost at once, as though the darkness had closed a hand around it.
Ignatz heard movement all around them: the wet scrape of many small limbs, the delicate clicking of shells against stone. He drew his sword. The blade came free with a whisper like breath over a grave.
Something touched his boot.
He struck downward.
The impact jarred his arm. Beneath the edge, a hard body cracked, and a pale fluid spread over the flagstones. Its scent was bitter enough to burn his eyes.
Marrowgate stumbled backward into him.
“Do not move,” Ignatz said.
“I cannot see.”
“Then use your fear.”
A faint glow returned inside the archive.
Not from the lamps.
The Chalice of Ashdeep shone through the shelving, a low ember-red radiance that outlined every jar, every folio, every drifting mote of dust. In that light Ignatz saw the floor alive with black shapes. They moved in silence now, armored and jointed, flowing from beneath tables and through the cracks between stones.
Vault Chitin had been unleashed in The War of Endless Vigil.
The sentence was there in the folio. He had read it before Maelis’s voice found him. Not released. Not discovered. Unleashed.
The war had been a wound given legs.
A shape climbed the door.
Its shell was not black but colorless, like a fingernail grown over a corpse. It opened a seam in its front and exhaled a thread of steam.
Marrowgate backed away.
“Where did they come from?”
Maelis stood untouched among the shelves.
“They were beneath the old foundations.”
“Beneath Hollowreach?”
“Beneath every place that thought itself founded.”
Ignatz watched the creature on the door. Its limbs searched the air. He remembered the folio’s next line, the part that had vanished beneath the chime.
There had been a command.
Or a confession.
“Why show me this?” he asked.
“I did not show you.”
“You left the folio.”
“I left a decoy.”
The thing on the door turned toward Maelis.
For one breath, none of them moved.
Then the creature folded itself in half and sprang.
Maelis lifted one hand.
The Chalice rang.
The vault-born thing halted in midair. Its limbs beat soundlessly. A seam opened along its shell, and within it lay a darkness deeper than the corridor.
Ignatz felt something pull at his eyes. He looked away, but not before he saw a pale shape inside the creature, curled like an infant in a womb of lacquered bone.
Maelis closed her fist.
The creature fell.
Its body struck the stones and sank into them without a splash.
Marrowgate began to weep.
Ignatz kept his sword raised.
“You are controlling them.”
“No.”
“Then what are you doing?”
“Reminding them.”
“Of what?”
“That they were once afraid.”
The lamps flickered back to life. The swarm was gone. Only the crushed shell beneath Ignatz’s boot remained, leaking its thin, bitter fluid into the cracks.
He lowered the sword by a fraction.
“Who unleashed Vault Chitin?”
Maelis looked past him, toward the open door and the corridor beyond.
“Your masters wrote the order.”
“I have no masters.”
Her gaze returned to him.
“That is why they chose you.”
The words entered him more deeply than a blade. For an instant he saw the Iron-Ring Cartel’s sealed messages, each one bearing no signature, each one addressed only to the authority he carried. He had thought secrecy made him useful. He had mistaken being unseen for being free.
Marrowgate pressed both hands against his mouth.
Ignatz turned on him. “What did you take from the archive?”
“Nothing.”
“Your shadow says otherwise.”
The quartermaster looked down.
His shadow had returned to its proper shape, but something bulged inside it. A small, angular mass moved beneath the darkness, traveling from heel to heel.
Marrowgate saw it.
“No,” he breathed.
Ignatz seized the man by the collar and dragged him away from the threshold. “What did you carry out?”
“I was ordered to inventory the reliquaries.”
“By whom?”
Marrowgate’s lips worked soundlessly.
Maelis answered for him. “The order bore the seal of the Warden-Commander.”
Ignatz’s grip tightened.
“My seal?”
“A likeness of it.”
A coldness spread through his hand. His seal had been copied before. Any authority worth stealing was copied. But this had not been used to forge a requisition or redirect a patrol.
It had opened the archive.
It had called to the Chalice.
It had brought Vault Chitin up through the floor.
“Show me,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate looked toward the dark mass inside his shadow.
“It is not in my possession.”
“Show me.”
“I cannot.”
“You will.”
The quartermaster’s knees failed. Ignatz caught him before he struck the stones. Beneath the man’s boots, his shadow stretched thin as spilled ink. The shape within it pressed upward.
A crack appeared across the floor.
The Chalice gave another hollow chime.
This time the sound came from everywhere: from the lamps, from the flooded corridor, from the teeth of the three figures standing beneath the archive’s dead light.
Maelis’s composure broke.
“Close the door.”
Ignatz looked at her.
“You said it was waiting.”
“It was.”
“And now?”
“Now it knows you are here.”
The crack widened.
Something below touched the underside of the world.
Marrowgate screamed as his shadow opened beneath him. Blackness took his legs to the knee, then the waist. Ignatz held on, feeling the quartermaster’s weight drag against his arms, feeling another force draw him down from below.
Maelis came forward at last.
“Let him go.”
Ignatz bared his teeth. “You first.”
“If you keep him, it will take you with him.”
“What is it?”
Her eyes fixed on the widening dark.
“An order that survived its author.”
The floor split between them.
From below came the slow, patient scrape of a multitude preparing to climb.
Ignatz looked once at the open door, once at Maelis, and once at the shadow swallowing Marrowgate.
Then a voice spoke from beneath the stones in his own voice.
“Warden-Commander.”
The title was followed by his name.
Not Ignatz.
The name he had never given the Iron-Ring Cartel.
Chapter 8
The rain fell upward against the windows.
It rose in thin black threads from the courtyard stones, gathered itself into trembling beads upon the leaded glass, and vanished into the low sky. Ash made a poor foundation for water. It drank nothing. It remembered every drop.
Maelis Harrowick the Pale watched the courtyard until the last bead broke apart. Their quill remained poised above the ledger, its nib suspended over a line of obedient ink.
The page waited for a death.
Not the death of the liege. That had already been plotted, measured, and carried through the narrow door between intention and consequence. The page required only the manner of it. Fever, perhaps. A weakness of the blood. A mischance beneath a horse’s iron shoe. The Court preferred deaths that could be folded into weather, appetite, or God’s absent attention.
Maelis had written three versions.
None had satisfied them.
Behind the chamber walls, the palace murmured with the careful quiet of people who had learned that sound could be evidence. Boots passed in the corridor. A buckle struck stone. Somewhere below, a servant dropped a tray and held their breath while the silence decided whether punishment was due.
Maelis lowered the quill.
Their hand did not tremble. It was a small victory, and therefore a dangerous one. Anything that could be mastered could be noticed.
“Chronicler.”
The voice came from the doorway.
Maelis turned. Ignatz Marrowgate stood there with a document case tucked beneath one arm. He was not a soldier, though he wore the expression of a man who had spent too long among soldiers and discovered that hunger was more reliable than loyalty. His station was plain in the way of useful things.
“Ignatz Marrowgate,” Maelis said. “You are late.”
“I am a Quartermaster.”
The answer contained no apology. It might have contained an explanation, if either of them had been foolish enough to ask.
Maelis glanced toward the blank window. “The road from the storehouses is not long.”
“The road is not the difficulty.”
“What is?”
Ignatz entered and closed the door behind him. “The guards.”
“Which guards?”
He looked at the ledger.
That was answer enough.
Maelis felt the room contract around them. The old tapestries seemed to lean inward, their faded scenes of kneeling kings and burning cities reduced to the same colors: rust, soot, and the brown of dried blood. On the central table lay the objects summoned from the sealed treasury. One was wrapped in oilskin. The other rested bare upon a square of black cloth.
The bare object was the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell.
It was regalia, though no crown had ever seemed less like ornament. The metal curved in five dark fingers, each joint engraved with shallow channels that held the light and refused to give it back. Its atmosphere was one of sorrow and grim authority. Even unoccupied, it suggested a hand closing.
The oilskin parcel contained The Psalter of Seven Sorrows.
Maelis had not opened it.
Ignatz set the case on the table. “The order bears the seal.”
“The order bears many seals.”
“This one bears the liege’s.”
The word entered the chamber like a blade slid between ribs.
Maelis did not look toward the door. “You have brought it, then.”
“I have brought what was requested.”
“By whom?”
“Ignatz Marrowgate, Quartermaster,” he said, with a thinness in his voice that might have been humor, “is not empowered to interpret the court’s appetite.”
“No. Only to feed it.”
His eyes lifted. For the first time, something moved behind them. Not anger. Calculation. A Quartermaster measured everything: grain, iron, lamp oil, the distance between a locked chest and a hand that might open it. Maelis wondered what quantity of fear he had assigned to them.
Ignatz touched the case but did not open it. “The instruction was to place the ward in your custody.”
“The Psalter of Seven Sorrows?”
“Yes.”
“You know what it is?”
“I know the name.”
“Names are often all the court permits a man to know.”
“The Psalter of Seven Sorrows was forged in 119 AS,” Maelis said.
The words seemed to alter the room. The rain withdrew from the windows. The fire, low in its grate, gave a soft inward sigh.
Ignatz watched them. “That is not written in the order.”
“It is written elsewhere.”
“Where?”
“In records that survived.”
“Many records survive.”
“Not the useful ones.”
His fingers tightened on the document case. Maelis saw then that the knuckles were scarred, though scars were not an answer to any question. The court was full of old injuries. They made a kind of second architecture beneath the skin.
Ignatz opened the case.
Inside lay a sheet of vellum, folded once, and beneath it a key of dull white metal. No crest marked the key. No inscription claimed it. The vellum bore a smear of dark wax, broken at one edge.
Maelis recognized the seal.
They had seen it upon commands that emptied villages, transferred garrisons, and sent men into winter with boots whose soles had been counted before the men themselves. It belonged to authority, which meant it belonged to whoever could make others suffer for doubting it.
“Where is the order’s bearer?” Maelis asked.
“Outside.”
“Who?”
Ignatz’s mouth closed.
