then up into the face that had once belonged to a man who had come to judge them. The left eye was
clouded. The right had no pupil at all, only a grey-white depth in which the cellar’s lamp burned like a
buried star.
Sabelle did not pull away.
“Your warrant,” they said.
The inspector’s jaw sagged.
“Your warrant,” Sabelle repeated, “or your confession.”
The thing wearing him made a sound like stones grinding beneath water.
From above came the scrape of boots. The trapdoor began to descend.
Sabelle turned the key.
The box opened by a fraction.
A red seam appeared between its lid and body. Not light. Not fire. Something with the color of old blood,
pressed thin beneath the metal. The breath inside ceased.
Every person in the cellar ceased with it.
Then the revenant inhaled.
The dead inspector’s grip tightened. Bone cracked in Sabelle’s wrist. Pain rose cleanly, almost gratefully.
Pain was a loyal witness. It never mistook what it had seen.
Sabelle drove the heel of their palm beneath his chin.
The impact snapped his head back. He released them, not from injury but surprise. They stepped around
him and placed their injured hand upon the box.
The two crowns at their brow—one black, one pale beneath the soot—trembled as the cellar groaned.
“Stay,” Sabelle commanded.
The thing below the box listened.
The inspector lurched forward. Sabelle caught his coat and turned with him, using his own momentum to
hurl him against the shelf. Clay jars fell and burst. Salt, ash, and dried roots scattered over the stones. His
shoulder struck hard enough to splinter the wood, but he did not fall. He rose, dragging one leg, his fingers
opening and closing.
The trapdoor dropped another handspan.
A face appeared in the gap.
“High Inquisitor,” called the clerk from the wall. His voice had become thin and childlike. “They are
coming down.”
“Then let them.”
“They say you are harboring a prohibited—”

The revenant struck the inside of the box.
The lid jumped.
The face above vanished. A body fell through the opening and landed among the broken jars. The trapdoor
slammed shut after it. The newcomer wore the dark coat of an inspector, though the collar bore no insignia
Sabelle recognized. They remained on their knees, hands braced in the spilled salt.
“Do not breathe,” Sabelle said.
The inspector did.
The cellar changed.
It was not a sound at first, but an alteration in pressure. The flame in the lamp leaned toward the box. Dust
lifted from the flagstones and turned slowly in the air. The dead man at the shelf stopped moving. Above
them, the trapdoor shuddered beneath the weight of those gathering on the other side.
The kneeling inspector began to cough.
Sabelle crossed the space between them and pressed two fingers to the inspector’s throat.
“Who sent you?”
The inspector’s eyes fixed on the crown.
“Your own seal opened the gate.”
“Who sent you?”
“Crookvale.”
The name dropped into the cellar and did not break.
Sabelle’s hand tightened.
“Crookvale sent you?”
A nod. The inspector’s breath came wetly now. “A dispatch. A sealed complaint. The garrison has been
instructed to make inquiry.”
“By whom?”
The inspector’s lips parted. His tongue was black at the root.
The revenant breathed again.
The man’s answer came out in another voice.
“Thessaly Coldwater serves at Crookvale.”
The clerk whimpered.
Sabelle released the inspector’s throat. He folded sideways, twitching among the salt. The first dead
inspector had gone still against the shelf, his ruined neck bent toward the box as if listening for a lullaby.
Above, the others began to hammer at the trapdoor.
“High Inquisitor!” someone cried. “By authority of the Crown—”

Sabelle looked at the iron box.
Its lid had opened another finger’s width. Inside lay darkness folded upon itself, and within that darkness
two points of dull red watched without blinking.
Thessaly Coldwater.
The name had crossed the realm before, carried by sealed orders and exhausted riders, by reports that
contradicted one another so carefully they might have been written by the same hand. Sabelle had read one
such report beneath a lamp that smoked. They remembered the phrasing, not the facts: an omission
sharpened until it became an accusation.
Now Crookvale had sent its inquiry to their cellar.
Or someone had borrowed Crookvale’s name.
That distinction was the thin wall between judgment and treason.
Sabelle bent and retrieved the fallen inspector’s warrant. The parchment was damp but legible. Their seal
appeared at the bottom, pressed in black wax.
They had not issued it.
The wax bore the twin-crown impression, but one crown faced inward and the other outward. A novice’s
error. Or a message.
The pounding above intensified.
The clerk had begun to pray. He had chosen a familiar litany, but he kept losing the words and starting
again. Sabelle watched the blood running from the dead inspector’s ear. It gathered in the grooves between
the stones, finding the channels worn by years of washing.
“Bring me the ledger,” Sabelle said.
The clerk stared.
“The ledger.”
He scrambled toward the wall, slipped in oil, and struck his mouth against the floor. When he rose, blood
brightened his teeth. He reached behind a loose stone and pulled free a narrow book bound in grey hide.
Sabelle held out their hand.
He did not move.
“Give it to me.”
“You said no one was to know.”
“I said no one was to know what was in the cellar.”
The clerk’s gaze shifted to the box.
The lid trembled beneath Sabelle’s palm.
“I did not know it could hear,” he whispered.
“It hears everything.”

“Then it heard you.”
“Yes.”
The clerk brought the ledger. Sabelle took it and opened to the marked page. The entries had been made in
different inks, by different hands. Names, dates, quantities, routes. Most were crossed out. Some had been
burned through so deeply that the parchment had become a lace of scars.
The Crown of Burned Names would have approved of the work.
Sabelle hated that thought. They hated the artifact’s solemn weight, the way remembrance could become
another species of prison. Yet even hatred had its uses. It kept the mind from kneeling.
A crack split the trapdoor.
Dust fell from the ceiling.
“High Inquisitor!” shouted the voice above. “Stand away from the relic!”
Sabelle glanced at the clerk.
“Relic?”
“I never said—”
“No,” Sabelle said. “You merely screamed loudly enough to educate the entire corridor.”
Another blow. The hinges shrieked.
The thing in the box moved.
Not outward. Within itself.
The darkness folded, unfolded, and showed Sabelle a room they had never entered. A stone chamber
beneath a sky without stars. A chair. A table. A crown lying on the table, blackened and scored with
names that writhed like insects beneath its surface.
Then the vision was gone.
Their pulse had quickened.
The revenant had shown them nothing without purpose. It had never shown them anything without taking
something in return.
Sabelle shut the ledger.
“Clerk.”
He looked up.
“When the door opens, you will tell them I am dead.”
His face collapsed. “They will search.”
“They will find what I permit.”
“And me?”
Sabelle studied him. He was young enough to believe terror was a form of innocence. The cellar had
already taken that belief from him.

“You will say the inspectors came alone.”
“They did not.”
“You will say it anyway.”
The trapdoor burst upward.
Three figures crowded the opening. Their lamps poured yellow light down the stair. For one suspended
moment, they appeared not as people but as a single many-limbed creature peering into a wound.
Sabelle lifted the iron box.
The dead inspector moved first. He crossed the cellar in a blur of torn coat and broken joints, seized the
nearest figure by the ankle, and pulled. The figure vanished with a scream. The second thrust a blade
downward. Steel entered the revenant’s shoulder and came out beneath its ribs.
The dead man looked at the blade.
Then he looked at Sabelle.
The question in his ruined face was almost human.
Sabelle turned the key back.
The box shut.
The revenant’s hand closed around the inspector above. He dragged the figure down the stair, not quickly,
not angrily. The scream dwindled as it descended. The remaining two retreated, but the trapdoor caught
one across the fingers. Bone broke. The other shouted a command Sabelle could not make out.
They stepped onto the first stair.
“Thessaly Coldwater serves at Crookvale,” Sabelle said.
The words were not meant for the men above. They were meant for the thing inside the box.
The key grew hot in their hand.
The cellar lamps went out.
In the darkness, every voice became distinct: the clerk’s shallow sobbing, the wounded inspector’s breath,
the dead man’s teeth clicking as he climbed, and beneath them all the slow, patient respiration of what
Sabelle had kept hidden below the world’s notice.
The trapdoor remained open.
Beyond it waited the corridor, the house, the inquisitorial seal, and the machinery of accusation already
turning toward them.
Sabelle placed one foot on the stair.
Behind the closed iron, the revenant whispered the name again.
Not Thessaly.
Crookvale.

Chapter 2
The quarantine bell had no clapper.
It spoke through the walls instead, a low iron concussion that moved through Stormmarch’s black stone
and entered the marrow. Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven felt it in their teeth. Dust sifted from the vaulted
ceiling. Somewhere beyond the chamber, a horse screamed once and was silenced.
They stood beside the sealed gate with one gloved hand resting on the bars.
Stormmarch had been founded in 71 AS, when the Ash Wastes were still young enough to remember rain.
Now the ash came down in slow gray veils, whispering against the battlements. The stronghold remained
quarantined, its garrison numbering 9,263, and it stood outside the realm’s core holdings like a clenched
fist no sovereign had managed to open.
Beyond the gate, the dead waited in their covered carts.
Isolde could smell them through the iron: lye, old blood, and the sweetening corruption that no prayer
could persuade into silence.
“Do you hear it?” Ossric Ashgrove asked.
He held a tally-board beneath his arm and a lantern in the other hand. The flame guttered blue against the
glass. Ossric Ashgrove, born in 333 AS, served as quartermaster, though the title seemed too clean for the
work his hands performed. He had been counting sacks, bodies, arrows, and the portions of grain that had
gone black in their husks. His face possessed no feature Isolde could have remembered afterward. That,
perhaps, was its own kind of armor.
“The bell?” Isolde said.
“The absence after it.”
They listened.
The silence pressed harder than the sound had.
Ossric swallowed. “It means the watch has stopped answering.”
“It means the watch has heard what it was meant to hear.”
He glanced toward the inner stair. “You know what that is?”
“I know the purpose of bells.”
The blood under Isolde’s fingernails had dried to a lacquered darkness. They had not washed it away.
Stains were messages, and Isolde had learned young that messages became dangerous only when someone
understood them.
The gate shuddered.
Not from outside.
From within.
Ossric’s lantern trembled. “The quarantine line is sealed.”
“So it is.”

“Nothing crosses it.”
“Nothing living should.”
His eyes lifted toward theirs. Quartermaster, not soldier. Yet fear had made him attentive. “The orders say
Stormmarch is to remain closed until—”
“Do not recite orders to me.”
The words came softly. That frightened him more than a shout might have done.
Isolde turned from the gate. The chamber behind them had once been a chapel, though the saints had been
scraped from the walls and the altar broken into paving stones. A table stood beneath the empty niche. On
it lay three ledgers, a bowl of salt, a bone-handled knife, and a folded dispatch bearing the iron mark of the
Iron-Ring Cartel.
The five powers watched one another from the ruins: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent
Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Their names had become a kind of weather. One
woke beneath them. Ate beneath them. Bled beneath them.
Isolde crossed to the table.
Ossric followed at a careful distance. “That dispatch was brought by Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
“Then it was not brought. It was delivered.”
“He is a Warden-Commander.”
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless is a Warden-Commander,” Isolde said. “He was born in 258 AS. Authority
does not cleanse a hand.”
Ossric’s gaze moved to the iron mark. “You are saying he—”
“I am saying nothing.”
That was the first lie, and it tasted familiar.
Ignatz sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. Isolde knew it as one knows the location of a knife in
darkness: by the shape of the danger, not by the sight of the blade. The knowledge had come to them in
fragments, never whole enough to use without exposing the hand that had gathered it.
They broke the seal.
The parchment smelled faintly of bitter herbs.
A column of figures had been written in a disciplined script. Beyond the list, a single sentence:
Gloammarch remains contested. Its garrison is 2,148.
Below it:
Stormmarch remains quarantined. Its garrison is 9,263.
No signature.
No request.
No threat.

That was how the Cartel spoke when it wished to be obeyed. It placed a fact before the eye and waited for
fear to furnish the command.
“Gloammarch,” Ossric murmured. “It is in the Ash Wastes.”
“Everything worth holding is.”
“It was founded in 321 AS.”
Isolde looked at him.
He lowered his eyes. “The inventory records say so.”
Gloammarch. Ash-dark, martial, embattled. A place holding its ground amid dispute, though every ground
in the Wastes was disputed by someone who had buried a dead beneath it. Its garrison was 2,148. Enough
to make occupation expensive. Not enough to make ownership certain.
“Why send this here?” Ossric asked.
“To remind us that quarantine is not isolation.”
The bell sounded again.
This time, something answered from beyond the gate.
A wet dragging. Then another.
Ossric’s fingers tightened around the tally-board. “The dead are moving.”
“The dead do not move.”
“Then something is moving them.”
Isolde placed the dispatch beside the bowl of salt. Their reflection trembled in the dark surface of the
inkpot: the severe mouth, the pale planes of the face, the eyes that never looked innocent even when they
were. The visual identity of an Unforgiven Blood-Mage was not a costume. It was the consequence of
being seen by too many ghosts.
They had been born in 286 AS. The number had once belonged to a cradle record, to a midwife’s notation,
to a life that might have been permitted to become ordinary.
Instead, they had plotted the death of their own liege.
The fact lay inside them like a second heart.
Not regret. Not precisely.
A liege was a roof until the roof became a hand around the throat. Isolde had chosen the collapse. They
had measured the beams, loosened the pins, and waited beneath the falling dark. There were nights when
they dreamed of that death and woke with blood in their mouth. There were other nights when they
dreamed only of the silence afterward, and found that silence more damning.
Ossric was watching them.
“You have blood on your hand,” he said.
“Yes.”
“Yours?”

“No.”
The quartermaster’s expression altered, though Isolde could not tell whether he believed them.
The door opened without a knock.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched entered beneath the broken arch. Their robes were gray at the
hem, ash-stained and wet. A chain of office rested against their throat. The flame-shaped seal of an
Arch-Prelate hung from it, bright as a coal in the chapel’s gloom.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched had been born in 289 AS. They carried sanctified authority like a
burden fashioned to resemble a crown. Isolde knew the lineage papers behind that authority had been
forged by Malchior’s own hand.
They wondered whether the ink had been mixed with shame.
“Isolde,” Malchior said. “The inner garrison requests permission to burn the outer barracks.”
“Requests?”
“They fear contamination.”
“They fear discovery.”
Malchior’s gaze hardened. “You mistake suspicion for wisdom.”
“And you mistake robes for proof.”
Ossric stepped back from the table.
Malchior saw the opened dispatch. Their face remained composed, but the composure tightened at the
edges. “Ignatz has sent word.”
“Ignatz has sent iron.”
“His intelligence is reliable.”
“His intelligence is sold.”
A stillness fell.
The flame at Malchior’s throat gave a tiny metallic click as it swung against the chain. “That is a grave
accusation.”
“Then carry it carefully.”
“You have always carried grievance as if it were a weapon.”
“It is a weapon.”
“And ambition?”
“That depends who is asking.”
Malchior’s attention shifted to the gate. “If Stormmarch falls sick, the sickness will spread through the
Ash Wastes.”
“The Wastes are already sick.”
“Do not make a philosophy of plague.”

“Do not make a sacrament of fear.”
For a moment, the three of them stood beneath the erased saints while the quarantine bell gathered its
breath.
Malchior spoke more quietly. “The Winter Reckoning taught us what happens when distrust is allowed to
govern.”
“The Winter Reckoning began in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS.”
Ossric’s tally-board creaked beneath his grip.
“Twenty-seven thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven casualties,” Isolde continued. “The Iron-Ring
Cartel was victor.”
Malchior’s mouth thinned. “You remember the numbers.”
“I remember the shape of the lie.”
The Winter Reckoning had worn the face of winter: white fields, iron marks, betrayals hidden beneath
snow. Its outcome was decided by a betrayal at the eleventh hour. That was the version carved into
memorial stone, repeated in halls, taught to children who still believed history was a lesson rather than a
blade.
The concealed truth was fouler.
The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Isolde could almost taste it again—the metallic bitterness in water drawn from a frozen dark, the way men
had knelt to drink and risen with their hands at their throats. Victory had not been won over enemies. It
had been secured by murdering those who had trusted the well.
“The betrayal at the eleventh hour,” Malchior said. “That is what the records name.”
“The records were written by survivors.”
“Survivors write what keeps them alive.”
“And what keeps the victors alive?”
Malchior did not answer.
Outside, the dragging stopped.
A shape struck the gate.
Once.
Twice.
On the third impact, a red thread appeared between the bars.
Isolde felt the blood before they saw it. Not in the dead thing beyond. In the stone. In the iron pins. In
Ossric’s startled pulse. In Malchior’s throat, where the forged lineage and the living body shared one
vulnerable river.
The Blood-Mage in them opened its eyes.
The chamber sharpened. Every heartbeat became a door.

Ossric whispered, “What are you doing?”
Isolde drew the bone-handled knife.
“I am going to ask the gate who taught the dead to knock.”
Malchior reached for their arm. “Do not.”
Isolde looked down at the hand on their sleeve.
For one breath, they imagined cutting through wrist, robe, chain, and all the careful authority beneath.
They imagined Malchior’s blood climbing the walls in bright, obedient threads. They imagined the old
liege’s death, the loosened pins, the roof descending, and the terrible freedom of having one betrayal
already behind them.
Then the gate began to open from the other side.
The gate opened without hinges.
It parted along a seam of darkness, stone withdrawing from stone as if the wall had become a mouth and
regretted the shape of its teeth. A draught entered the chamber, cold enough to tighten the skin over
Isolde’s knuckles. It smelled of wet iron, extinguished candles, and something sweet rotting beneath snow.
Malchior’s hand fell from their sleeve.
Ossric made a noise in his throat. Not a prayer. The quartermaster had the good sense to fear anything that
answered a question before it was asked.
Beyond the opening stood a man in a coat stiff with ash.
His face was hidden by a visor of blackened mail. A pale strip of skin showed beneath it, stretched thin
over a jaw that worked as if chewing a word too bitter to swallow. He carried no weapon. That frightened
Isolde more than a drawn sword would have done.
On his breast, worked in dull thread, was the shape of a broken halo.
Malchior stepped forward.
“Brannoc Palefroth.”
The man’s head turned toward them.
Isolde watched the Arch-Prelate carefully. The name had struck somewhere beneath the sanctified surface,
beneath the gold-threaded vestments and the flame-scored skin at Malchior’s throat. Recognition was not
the same as surprise. Surprise belonged to the innocent. Recognition belonged to those who had been
waiting for a debt to find them.
Brannoc’s voice came through the visor as a wet rasp.
“You still wear the face you stole.”
Ossric looked at Malchior. Then at Isolde. His fingers tightened around the ledger he carried against his
ribs.
Malchior did not answer.

A thin red bead rose from the cut in Isolde’s palm. It hung between them, bright as a coal. The blood
trembled toward Brannoc, not drawn by hunger but by memory. Something in the gate knew the old shape
of violence. Something in Brannoc knew it too.
Isolde let the bead fall.
It struck the threshold.
The stone drank it.
Brannoc shuddered. His mail whispered. From somewhere beyond him came the distant clatter of many
feet moving through water, though the passage behind him was empty.
“What did you teach the dead?” Isolde asked.
Brannoc lifted one gloved hand and pointed at Malchior.
“The living taught them first.”
Malchior’s expression remained composed, but a flame moved behind their eyes—small, blue, and nearly
starved.
“You are not alive,” they said.
“Nor are you what you claim.”
The words landed gently. That was their cruelty.
Isolde felt the old pressure gather behind their teeth. Blood-Magic did not always announce itself with
pain. Sometimes it arrived as a courtesy, a slight loosening of the world’s seams. The pulse in Malchior’s
throat became visible. Ossric’s heartbeat knocked against his ribs. Brannoc’s body offered nothing at all.
No heart.
No blood.
Yet the gate had opened for him.
Malchior raised their chin. The gesture was Arch-Prelate, tribunal, altar, execution.
“I fought in The Purge of Blackport,” they said. “I fought for The Iron-Ring Cartel. I know what men
become when the dead are given orders.”
Brannoc’s visor tilted.
“Do you?”
The cold deepened. Frost feathered across the nearest stones. Isolde smelled smoke, then ash, then the
bitter mineral reek of wells gone foul. The scent dragged an image from some buried chamber of their
mind: a line of soldiers standing beneath a white sky; iron rings nailed into doorways; mouths cracked
with thirst.
The Winter Reckoning.
They had heard old accounts of it whispered in barracks and kitchens, each telling shaped to flatter the
teller. The Silent Choir had marched beneath veils of winter silk. The Iron-Ring Cartel had answered with
ledgers, chains, and patience. The war had begun in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS. Its dead had numbered

27,987.
Numbers were a kind of graveyard. Isolde had always believed that.
Brannoc turned his head toward them.
“You remember.”
“I remember what was preserved,” Isolde said.
“That is not the same.”
His hand lowered. The darkness behind him rippled, and for an instant Isolde saw figures standing there:
ranks without faces, cloaked in rime, their hands blackened to the elbows. They did not advance. They
waited with the discipline of the buried.
Malchior took another step toward the threshold.
“Brannoc Palefroth fought in The Winter Reckoning,” they said. “He fought for The Silent Choir.”
Brannoc’s head snapped toward them.
“Do not put my allegiance in your mouth.”
“Why?” Isolde asked. “Is it unclean?”
The Arch-Prelate looked at them then, and the chamber filled with the weight of their gaze. Malchior
Cindervale the Flame-Touched had learned long ago how to make silence resemble judgment. They
possessed the stillness of painted saints and the temper of a brazier under oil.
“You should be cautious,” Malchior said.
“I have been cautious all my life.”
The lie came easily. It had the smoothness of a stone worn by water.
They had been cautious when they plotted the death of their own liege. Cautious when they measured
which servants could be bought, which doors opened inward, which witnesses would mistake a silence for
loyalty. Cautious when they stood beside the body and felt, beneath the grief, the first clean breath of
freedom.
Caution had not saved anyone. It had merely made betrayal patient.
Brannoc moved.
There was no sound of footfall. One moment he stood beyond the gate; the next, his gloved hand had
crossed the threshold and closed around Malchior’s throat.
Ossric cried out and dropped the ledger.
Isolde saw the hand tighten. Not flesh, not quite. Black threads ran from Brannoc’s wrist into Malchior’s
neck, sinking beneath the skin as if searching for a vein.
Malchior seized his arm.
The contact ignited the chamber.
Fire raced up Brannoc’s sleeve, white at its core. The dead man recoiled, but did not release him. The
flames curled around his fingers and found no purchase. Malchior’s lips moved. Their forged lineage

papers, their invented blood, the lies with which they had built a stairway into sanctity—Isolde felt all of it
shiver in the air like wet parchment held over a candle.
The gate groaned.
“Stop,” Isolde said.
Neither obeyed.
The blood in their palm answered the violence. It surged up their arm, hot and eager. Every vein in the
room opened to their perception. Malchior’s blood was thick with old vows and newer fraud. Brannoc’s
was absent, but absence had a texture. It drew at Isolde like a well with no bottom.
They could sever Malchior’s grip. They could force Brannoc backward. They could make both bodies
kneel until the stone cracked beneath them.
Or they could do nothing and learn which secret the dead had come to collect.
Isolde chose the third cruelty.
They watched.
Malchior’s face had begun to redden beneath Brannoc’s hand. The Flame-Touched mantle slipped from
one shoulder. At the collar, beneath the gold and ash, a narrow scar crossed their skin in a perfect circle.
The mark of an oath, perhaps. Or the mark left when an oath was removed.
Brannoc leaned close.
“You stood at Blackport’s eastern wall,” he rasped. “You carried the Cartel’s iron.”
“I carried what kept me alive.”
“You carried names.”
Malchior’s eyes flicked toward Isolde.
There it was: fear, briefly uncloaked.
Ossric scrambled for the fallen ledger. “What names?”
The gate answered him.
Pages turned in the dark beyond Brannoc. Hundreds of them. Thousands. Paper flapped in a wind that did
not touch the chamber. Names began to whisper from the passage, each one spoken by a different dead
mouth.
Some were soldiers. Some were children. Some had been crossed out and spoken anyway.
The sound rose until the walls trembled.
Malchior drove a knee into Brannoc’s abdomen. The dead man folded, his grip loosening. The
Arch-Prelate staggered free, one hand at their throat, the other burning with a light too bright to look upon.
“Close it,” Malchior said.
Ossric stared at them. “How?”
“You serve the Ashgrove quarter.”

“I serve whoever signs the requisitions.”
“Then consider this signed.”
Ossric’s gaze dropped to the ledger. He opened it with shaking hands. The pages were blank. Ink gathered
along the spine, black and glossy, rising in threads toward the ceiling.
Isolde stepped over the threshold.
The cold entered them at once.
It passed through skin and muscle, through the soft red machinery of the body, and settled in the bones.
The passage extended farther than the fortress could contain. On either side, doors stood ajar. Behind one,
water dripped steadily. Behind another, someone whispered a prayer in a language Isolde did not know.
Behind a third, a child laughed.
Brannoc had vanished.
Malchior stood alone in the chamber, their hand still aflame.
“Come back,” they said.
Isolde looked at the dark ahead.
At the far end, something had begun to knock.
Three blows.
A pause.
Then three more.
They felt the answering pulse in their own blood, and understood that whatever waited beyond the next
door had already learned their name.
The knocking ceased.
For a breath, the corridor seemed to listen with them. Water ticked behind the first door. The child laughed
again behind the third, a bright, impossible sound that made the skin beneath Isolde’s collar tighten.
Malchior’s burning hand lowered.
“Come back,” they said once more, but there was less command in it now. Their voice had gone thin at the
edges.
Isolde did not move.
The next door waited in the dark, its wood swollen and blackened as if it had been raised from a grave. No
latch showed. No hinges. Only the pale impression of a hand pressed into its surface from the other side.
Five fingers.
Then the palm.
The mark filled slowly with blood.
Isolde felt it answer within them.

Not their blood. Not precisely. Something older, colder, moving through the fortress like a vein beneath
stone. Their own pulse stumbled toward it despite every warning instinct. The blood-mage’s gift was not
obedience. It was recognition. Blood knew blood. It remembered wounds long after flesh forgot.
Malchior stepped nearer. Flame crawled up their wrist, illuminating the hard planes of their face and the
ash caught in their lashes.
“Do you know this place?”
“No.”
“Then you are lying.”
The accusation should have angered them. Instead, it landed with the dull familiarity of a blade set against
the throat.
Isolde looked at the flame. “You forged your own lineage papers, Malchior Cindervale the
Flame-Touched.”
The light shivered.
Malchior’s expression did not change, but their hand clenched. Fire folded into the fist and vanished.
“That is a dangerous thing to say in a corridor that has ears.”
“It has my name already.”
“It has more than that.” Malchior’s gaze travelled to the handprint. “It has your measure.”
Isolde smiled without humour. “You speak as though it has yours.”
For an instant, the Arch-Prelate looked almost young. Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched had been
born in 289 AS, though the papers beneath their robes claimed a lineage older than any honest memory.
Sanctity sat upon them like borrowed armour: bright, ceremonial, and fitted badly at the joints.
They had the presence of one who had spent years persuading others that a door was a shrine because they
possessed the key.
Behind the swollen wood, something breathed.
Isolde heard it inhale through a mouth too large for a human face.
Malchior whispered a prayer.
The language was not the one Isolde had heard beyond the other door. This prayer was known to them: the
liturgy of the ash courts, spoken over executions and coronations, over treaties no one intended to honour.
It had been used by every power that had ever claimed the right to rule—the Ashen Vanguard, House
Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Words changed. The hunger
beneath them did not.
“Open it,” Malchior said.
“You are the one with the flame.”
“The flame will not open it.”
“Then perhaps your lineage will.”

Their eyes met.
The corridor narrowed around them.
Isolde knew the expression that passed over Malchior’s face. It was the expression of a person counting
not enemies, but uses. Isolde had worn it while arranging the death of their own liege, listening to the old
voice speak of mercy as though mercy had ever been offered freely. They had smiled. They had bowed.
They had put the poison where the cup would find it.
The memory came cleanly. That was the worst of it.
No remorse clouded it. No convenient darkness.
Only the small, precise satisfaction of having made the world less crowded.
The handprint on the door flexed.
Malchior said, “What did you see?”
“Nothing.”
“You saw something.”
“I saw a door.”
“And?”
“And it knows my name.”
Malchior’s mouth tightened. “Names are not invitations.”
“Yours was written before you arrived.”
This time the flame returned, not to their palm but to their eyes. “Do not mistake my restraint for fear.”
“I mistake nothing.”
The door opened.
It did not swing inward. It unmade itself, boards loosening into strips of darkness that peeled away from
the frame. Beyond lay a chamber drowned in ash. It fell from the ceiling in slow, silent sheets, gathering
on a stone table at the centre.
Upon that table rested a ledger.
Its cover was iron.
The mark stamped upon it was a ring split by a vertical line.
Isolde stopped at the threshold.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had left that mark on walls, grain sacks, warrants, and the throats of men who had
outlived their usefulness. The symbol had survived The Winter Reckoning, which began in 270 AS and
ended in 283 AS. Twenty-seven thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven had died in that conflict, and the
Iron-Ring Cartel had emerged as victor. Afterward, wells belonging to their own allies had tasted of bitter
metal and dead flowers.
The old poison had become a proverb.

The ledger’s pages turned without wind.
Malchior did not cross the threshold. “That cannot be here.”
“Yet it is.”
“It is not a Cartel archive.”
“You seem certain.”
“I know the Cartel’s archives.”
“From your work in The Purge of Blackport?”
The question struck nearer than Isolde expected. Malchior’s face hardened, sanctity sealing over fear.
“I fought where I was commanded.”
“For the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
“Yes.”
The admission came quietly. The chamber seemed to accept it.
The ledger opened.
Ink crawled across the first page in thin red strokes.
ISOLDE FELLGARD THE UNFORGIVEN.
Their breath caught.
Beneath the name appeared another line.
BORN IN 286 AS.
Then another.
BLOOD-MAGE.
The letters sank into the page. Fresh writing rose beneath them.
LIEGE-SLAYER.
Isolde felt the blood in their hands draw tight, each vessel narrowing as though invisible thread had been
tied around every finger.
Malchior looked at them—not with surprise, but with calculation.
“You plotted the death,” they said.
Isolde’s gaze remained on the ledger. “I did not say it succeeded.”
“You needn’t.”
The page turned.
A second name appeared.
MALCHIOR CINDERVALE THE FLAME-TOUCHED.
BORN IN 289 AS.

ARCH-PRELATE.
Then, in a smaller hand:
LINEAGE: FORGED.
Malchior crossed the threshold at last.
The ash rose around their boots. It clung to the hem of their robes, whitening the embroidered symbols of
authority. Their face had become very still.
“Close it,” they said.
“Why?”
“Because it is naming what must remain unnamed.”
“That is the nature of a ledger.”
“No. A ledger records debts. This thing creates them.”
The book’s pages fluttered faster.
A third entry surfaced.
IGNATZ ASHGROVE THE OATHLESS.
BORN IN 258 AS.
WARDEN-COMMANDER.
The ink hesitated.
Then wrote:
INTELLIGENCE SOLD TO THE IRON-RING CARTEL.
Malchior’s head lifted.
Isolde watched the Arch-Prelate absorb the accusation and place it among the others. Not shock. Not
disbelief. A piece of the board had moved, and Malchior had been told where.
“Ignatz,” they murmured.
The name seemed to darken the room.
At the foot of the page, a new line began.
OSSRIC ASHGROVE.
BORN IN 333 AS.
QUARTERMASTER.
Nothing followed.
No secret. No sin. No hidden allegiance.
Only the name, the birth year, and the office.

Isolde almost laughed. The absence felt more terrible than any indictment. The ledger had looked into
Ossric Ashgrove and found a life too small—or too well buried—to accuse.
“Why show us this?” Malchior asked.
The answer came from the darkness beyond the table.
“Because the dead require witnesses.”
The voice was neither male nor female. It seemed to come from the ash itself, from the stone beneath their
feet, from the blood sealed inside Isolde’s bones.
Malchior’s flame burst outward. Fire ran along the floor in a bright circle, and the ash recoiled from it.
“By whose authority?” they demanded.
The chamber answered with a sound like distant marching.
Isolde saw banners through the grey: the pale severed standard of the Ashen Vanguard, the black device of
House Morvain, the mute cloth of the Silent Choir, the iron ring of the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the red, wet
crown of the Bleeding Crown. They hung from no poles. They stirred in no wind. They were only
impressions, memories of power pressed into the air.
The five powers gathered around the ledger.
No throne stood among them.
No judge.
Isolde understood then that the fortress did not care who ruled the Ashen Era. It cared only that rulers left
blood behind.
A new page turned.
STORMMARCH.
FOUNDED IN 71 AS.
GARRISON: 9,263.
OUTSIDE THE REALM’S CORE HOLDINGS.
The final line appeared like a wound reopening.
GLOAMMARCH.
FOUNDED IN 321 AS.
GARRISON: 2,148.
STATUS: CONTESTED.
Malchior stared at the figures. “Why those places?”
“Because every wall is a promise,” said the unseen voice. “And every promise is waiting to break.”
Isolde thought of Gloammarch in the Ash Wastes, ash-dark and martial, holding its ground beneath the
weight of dispute. They thought of Stormmarch, sealed away from the realm’s heart, its strength kept
behind silence and iron. Strongholds did not become haunted because the dead were restless. They became

haunted because the living had built them atop unfinished bargains.
The ledger closed.
The sound was soft.
Malchior turned toward Isolde. “We leave.”
The doorway behind them had returned. The corridor beyond was no longer empty.
Brannoc stood at its far end.
He was motionless, his face turned away. His silhouette seemed thinner than before, as though the passage
had taken some essential weight from him. His hands hung at his sides.
“Brannoc,” Malchior called.
He did not answer.
Isolde felt a thread tighten from their heart to the figure in the distance.
The thing wearing Brannoc’s shape lifted one hand.
Three fingers extended.
A pause.
Then three more.
The same rhythm as the knocking.
The ledger opened behind Isolde.
This time, no name appeared.
Only a single sentence, written in their own blood:
THE DOOR HAS LEARNED YOUR NAME.
Brannoc turned.
His eyes were full of ash.
And from somewhere beneath the fortress, something enormous began to wake.

Chapter 3
Crookvale crouched beneath the snow like a beast that had learned not to breathe.
Its rebuilt walls climbed the black ribs of the High Spires, crooked where the stone had been fitted in haste
and hard-edged where haste had become a tradition. Wind worried at the battlements, dragging long veils
of powder through the arrow slits. Below, the roofs huddled close, their chimneys coughing a thin grey
smoke into the white.
Corvus Hollowmere the Pale stood at the window of the upper chamber and watched the garrison move
through the yard.
A garrison of 1004, the ledger had said.
The number seemed absurd in the storm. Men and women became smears of dark wool, their faces hidden
beneath hoods, their commands swallowed by the wind. Yet the yard had its order: patrols crossing, gates
checked, weapons carried beneath cloaks, sentries relieved without ceremony. Crookvale survived
because nothing here was trusted to memory.
Founded in 295 AS in the High Spires, rebuilt after ruin, it remained outside the core holdings. The words
had been entered in the report without bitterness. Reports did not know bitterness. Corvus did.
Beyond the walls, the mountain fell away into a world of ravines and cloud. Somewhere past those folds
lay the roads that fed the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the
Bleeding Crown. Five powers with five hungers, each pretending the others were more dangerous than
itself.
A knock sounded behind them.
Corvus did not turn. “Enter.”
The door opened with a wet groan. Snow came in first, then Hesper Wrenfield.
Hesper was an Outrider. The title clung more visibly than the ice on their cloak. They crossed the room
with the careful stiffness of someone whose body had been forced to remain useful through cold, hunger,
and distance. No feature of them invited description; the face beneath the hood seemed deliberately
withheld, as if the road had worn away every claim but the duty to return.
“Spymaster,” Hesper said.
Corvus kept their gaze on the yard. “You took too long.”
“The pass took longer.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one that survived the pass.”
A servant had left a brazier burning near the hearth. The coals glowed beneath a crust of ash, giving off a
heat too weak to soften the room. Corvus felt it against their hands and thought of the oath they had sworn
to the Silent Choir.
No words of the oath rose in their mind. That was the danger. An oath did not need to be remembered to
govern the blood. It lived beneath thought, beneath fear, beneath the private names a person gave to their
own intentions. Corvus had sworn it in secrecy. No one in Crookvale knew. No one in the Ashen

Vanguard knew. No one in House Morvain, the Iron-Ring Cartel, or the Bleeding Crown knew.
The Silent Choir knew.
And that knowledge was enough to make every room a cell.
Hesper unfastened the clasp at their throat. A strip of dark cloth showed beneath the cloak, stiff with
frozen meltwater. “The message is sealed.”
“With what?”
Hesper looked toward the door.
Corvus smiled without warmth. “If you crossed the High Spires carrying a secret and did not learn to name
it aloud, you will learn now.”
“The seal bears the mark of Hollowreach.”
The room seemed to contract.
Hollowreach lay in the Gloaming Reach. It had been founded in 56 AS and was a core location under
quarantine. Even the word had acquired a physical weight. Hollowreach: shuttered gates, barred windows,
watchfires burning without welcome. Containment given walls and a name.
“Who sent it?” Corvus asked.
“The seal was unbroken when it reached me.”
“You are an Outrider. You carry what you are given.”
“Yes.”
“Then you have no knowledge of its sender.”
“No.”
The answer was clean. Too clean perhaps, though Corvus had never trusted suspicion that arrived
conveniently. They turned from the window.
Hesper’s cloak steamed faintly near the brazier. Their gloved hand held a narrow cylinder of blackened
metal. A line of pale frost ran along its side despite the heat.
Corvus looked at it and felt the old cold answer.
“The Sceptre of Final Winter,” they said.
Hesper’s fingers tightened around the cylinder. “The report says it is a ward.”
“It is a ward forged in 87 AS.”
“I did not ask what the report said.”
“No. You asked nothing.”
Hesper lowered the cylinder onto the table between them. “The Sceptre of Final Winter was carried under
guard from the southern road. I was told to bring it here.”
“By whom?”
“The sealed instructions did not say.”

“And you obeyed?”
“I serve as an Outrider.”
Not a confession. Not an excuse. A boundary.
Corvus approached the table. The cylinder seemed to draw the warmth out of the air. They could feel the
object before touching it, a pressure behind the eyes, a promise spoken by winter itself. Attunement to The
Sceptre of Final Winter costs 55. The number had been written in old script in a margin no one bothered to
read aloud. Corvus had read it. They had read everything that was meant to remain unwitnessed.
“Did anyone touch it?” they asked.
“No.”
“Did you?”
“No.”
“Did anyone ask you to lie?”
Hesper’s silence lasted only as long as the wind’s moan against the shutters.
“No.”
Corvus studied them. “You were born in 404 AS.”
The Outrider’s head lifted a fraction. “That is recorded.”
“Records are useful because they cannot defend themselves.”
“And what does mine defend?”
“Nothing. It only tells me you have lived long enough to understand when a road is being used as a blade.”
Hesper turned their face toward the black cylinder. “Is that what this is?”
“It may be.”
Outside, a horn gave a single note. The garrison shifted below. Men moved along the inner wall, their
boots striking the stone with the dull rhythm of an old injury. Crookvale had been rebuilt, but rebuilding
did not mean restoration. It meant making a shape that could withstand being broken again.
Corvus placed one bare hand over the cylinder without touching it.
Cold climbed their wrist.
For an instant, they saw the war as the old histories described it: blood on the watchfires, armies standing
beneath a sky without mercy, the long exhaustion of those who had been ordered to remain awake until the
enemy broke. The War of Endless Vigil began in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS. Its recorded casualties
were 81577. It ended with the total rout of the aggressors, and The Bleeding Crown was recorded as the
victor.
The old account called it decisive.
The hidden account was simpler.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.

Corvus withdrew their hand.
“Where did you find this?” they asked.
“I did not find it.”
“Where did you receive it?”
Hesper’s jaw moved beneath the hood. “At a waystation below the ridge.”
“You said the pass took longer.”
“It did.”
“Then someone expected delay.”
“Someone expects many things.”
The answer carried no defiance. That made it worse. Defiance could be measured. Calm was a door with
no visible hinge.
Corvus took the sealed message from the cylinder’s end. The wax was dark and unmarked except for a
shallow impression: a closed eye surrounded by fine cuts. The symbol of Hollowreach had not been
placed there as a request.
It was a warning.
The hidden oath stirred beneath Corvus’s ribs.
Do not open what the Choir has not sung.
Their hand remained still.
The Silent Choir had no banners that Corvus had seen. No public armies. No grand halls where supplicants
might kneel. Yet its absence had shape. A missing word in a report. A door left unlocked. A witness who
remembered the wrong face. The oath had taught Corvus to fear not what was spoken, but what silence
arranged around it.
The message might belong to the Choir.
It might belong to someone who wished them to think so.
The difference between those possibilities was the distance between obedience and betrayal.
“Hesper,” Corvus said.
“Yes.”
“If I open this, you will tell no one.”
“I was not told to report to anyone.”
“That is not what I said.”
Hesper’s gaze shifted to Corvus at last. “If I am asked?”
“Then you will answer truthfully.”
“That is not the same as telling no one.”

“No.”
The wind struck the shutters hard enough to rattle the hinges. Far below, a gate chain groaned. The sound
rose through the stones like something waking under the foundations.
Corvus thought of their own birth year, 351 AS, entered in a register beside a name that had since become
a mask. They had been born into the Ashen Era, but the era had never seemed to belong to the living. It
belonged to ruins, to old bargains, to debts that crossed generations without losing their teeth.
They broke the seal.
The wax gave with a soft crack.
Hesper did not move.
Inside the message was a narrow sheet of grey material, dry as shed skin. No ink marked its surface.
Corvus tilted it toward the brazier.
Letters emerged in the heat.
Not written. Revealed.
The first line named Hollowreach.
The second named Crookvale.
The third was only a question.
Corvus read it once. Then again.
“What does it say?” Hesper asked.
Corvus felt the oath close around their throat.
From the yard came a cry, abruptly cut short. The garrison’s orderly motion broke. Figures scattered
beneath the snow. Somewhere beyond the walls, something struck the outer gate.
Corvus folded the message in their palm.
“It says,” they whispered, “that the quarantine has already failed.”
The gate shuddered again.
Hesper reached for the weapon hidden beneath their cloak.
Corvus looked toward the storm-veiled battlements, toward the dark beyond them, and heard a voice in the
sealed chamber that did not come through the door.
Not yet, sang the silence.
Then the outer bell began to ring.
The bell’s iron tongue battered the storm until the sound became a physical thing, a fist against the ribs.
Hesper had their weapon out. Corvus saw only its dark length beneath the cloak, the edge catching the
weak light from the chamber’s brazier. Snow hissed through the arrow slits. It gathered on the stone like
ash sifted from a dead fire.
“Who rings it?” Hesper asked.

Corvus did not answer. The bell belonged to the gatehouse, but its alarm was not meant for the thing
beyond the wall. It was meant for those within. A warning to the garrison. A summons to the battlements.
A declaration that whatever had entered the night had found the house unlocked.
Another blow struck the outer gate.
The hinges screamed.
Hesper moved toward the door.
“Wait.”
The word came from Corvus’s mouth, but beneath it another voice moved, thinner than breath.
Not yet.
Hesper turned. “You heard that?”
“I heard the bell.”
“Then you heard the gate.”
“I heard both.”
A shout rose from the yard, swallowed by the wind. There was no discipline in it. No order, no rank, no
answering command. Corvus knew the sound of trained men discovering that training did not apply. They
had seen the body in the snow. They had seen what stood beside it.
The message lay folded against Corvus’s palm. The wax had softened with the heat of their skin. They
could feel the impression through the paper: a broken circle, pressed too deeply, as though the seal had
been stamped by a hand that wanted to pierce the page.
Hollowreach.
The name seemed to darken the chamber.
Beyond Crookvale’s walls, beyond the white slopes and the crooked roads that climbed into the High
Spires, Hollowreach lay sealed under quarantine. Its doors were closed. Its dead were counted—or had
been, before the counting stopped. The message had not named an escape, nor a breach, nor any sickness.
It had said only that the quarantine had failed.
That was worse than an explanation.
Hesper reached the chamber door. “I’m going to the gatehouse.”
“You’re an Outrider.”
“Then I’ll ride.”
“In this?”
“If the gate opens, there will be nothing left to ride from.”
Corvus watched the hand beneath Hesper’s cloak tighten around the weapon. No fear showed in the
movement. Perhaps fear had become too common to show. The silence in the sealed chamber had been
singing for some time now, and Hesper had not heard it. Corvus envied them the blindness.
The bell stopped.

For one breath, the fortress seemed to hold itself upright by will alone.
Then something scraped along the outer gate.
Not struck. Scraped.
Wood groaned. Iron gave a low, patient creak.
A wet sound followed from the yard.
Hesper opened the door.
Cold entered first. It came low along the floor, carrying the smell of snow, old smoke, and something
sweet enough to make Corvus’s stomach contract. The brazier fluttered. In its red hollow, a coal collapsed
and released a brief blue flame.
The corridor beyond was empty.
“Where are the guards?” Hesper asked.
“Doing what they were ordered to do.”
“Which was?”
Corvus stepped into the corridor. “Stay alive.”
The stone underfoot was slick. Not blood. Meltwater, perhaps. It shone in the torchlight and ran toward the
stair in narrow threads. Corvus crouched and touched it with two fingers.
Warm.
They rose slowly.
Hesper noticed. “What?”
“Nothing that will help us.”
“That’s not an answer.”
“It is the only one I have.”
A figure lurched at the far end of the passage.
Hesper lifted the weapon.
The figure struck the wall with one shoulder and stayed there. A sentry. His helm had been torn away.
Snow clung to his hair and eyebrows, but there was no snow on his face. His mouth opened. Black fluid
threaded from his teeth.
“Gate,” he said.
The word came out nearly whole.
Hesper crossed the corridor in three steps. “What happened?”
The sentry stared beyond them, toward the chamber Corvus had left. His eyes fixed on nothing visible.
“Gate,” he said again. “It knows the gate.”
His knees failed.

Hesper caught him before his skull met the stone. The weapon fell against their leg with a muted clack.
Corvus moved closer, unwilling and unable to stop. The sentry’s skin was gray beneath the torchlight. A
dark seam ran from his collar to his jaw, not a wound but a line beneath the flesh, as if a second mouth had
been stitched there and was working its way open.
Corvus had seen this before.
Not the mark. The idea of it.
In old reports kept beneath the Spymaster’s seal, there were accounts of voices heard through walls, of
men who spoke in two tones, of villages that closed their doors from the inside and answered no
summons. Most reports ended with a recommendation that the pages be burned.
The Silent Choir had never asked Corvus to burn anything.
It had asked them to listen.
Hesper looked up. “Can you walk?”
The sentry’s fingers clawed at their sleeve. “Don’t let it—”
His tongue moved again, but the next sound did not belong to him.
“—in.”
The corridor seemed to narrow.
Corvus pulled Hesper back.
A shape moved at the stairwell.
It was only a man at first, bent beneath the weight of snow. He climbed slowly, one hand upon the wall.
His boots left dark prints. His coat bore the garrison’s gray, though the insignia had been scraped away.
The face beneath the hood was hidden.
“Hesper,” Corvus said.
“I see it.”
The figure stopped.
A voice came from within the hood. “Open.”
Not a command. A plea.
The sentry in Hesper’s arms began to shake. His teeth clicked together.
“Open,” the figure said again.
Corvus felt the oath stir.
It had not been words when they swore it. Words had come later, fashioned by memory and fear. The oath
itself had been a door without hinges, a depth beneath the world. It had taken root behind the heart and
waited there, patient as winter.
The voice in the stairwell changed.
“Corvus Hollowmere the Pale.”

Hesper looked at them.
The name fell through the corridor and did not echo.
Corvus’s hand closed around the folded message.
The figure lifted its head. Beneath the hood, there was no face that the torch could find. Only a pale blur,
featureless and damp, like flesh seen through ice.
“Open,” it said.
Hesper shoved the fallen sentry behind them. “What is that?”
Corvus could not answer. The thing wore a coat. It had boots. It had crossed the storm. These were facts,
and facts were the first garments worn by lies.
The bell began again.
This time it rang from inside the walls.
Hesper flinched. Corvus did not. Their ears filled with a higher sound, a note too thin to be heard yet
impossible to mistake. The sealed chamber behind them had gone silent.
That frightened them more than the figure.
The figure took one step up.
Corvus drew the narrow blade hidden beneath their sleeve. Its hilt was cold enough to burn. They had
carried it through councils, coronations, interrogations, and rooms where men had died without making a
sound. It had never felt so useless.
“Hesper,” they said, “if it speaks again, do not answer.”
“Why?”
“Because it knows my name.”
“That’s not a reason.”
“It is the only warning I can give.”
The figure took another step.
Outside, the gate shuddered. Timber split with a sound like a tree cracking in a forest. Somewhere in the
yard, someone screamed for the garrison commander. The cry rose, broke, and was answered by a chorus
of wet coughing.
Corvus remembered the old memorial stones.
The War of Endless Vigil devastated Crookvale in 249 AS.
The sentence had been carved into black rock after the armies withdrew. Corvus had read it in the records,
where the devastation had been reduced to an entry and the dead to a count. The stone itself had been more
honest. Its surface was scored by thousands of names, and the wind had worn most of them smooth.
Crookvale had survived that war only by becoming harder than what had tried to destroy it.
Now the fortress listened to the gate.
Now the gate listened back.

The figure reached the landing. Snow slid from its shoulders. Under the hood, something shifted where a
face should have been.
“Corvus.”
Hesper’s weapon rose.
“Don’t,” Corvus whispered.
The figure smiled.
They knew it smiled because the skin parted.
The sealed chamber spoke at last.
Not yet.
Corvus stepped between Hesper and the stairwell.
The oath tightened. Their vision whitened at the edges. For an instant they smelled cold incense and heard
voices layered upon voices, each one speaking from a distance that had no measure.
The Silent Choir was listening.
The figure lifted one hand. Its fingers were long, jointed wrong, and dripping warmth onto the stones.
“Open,” it said.
Corvus raised the blade.
Behind them, the outer gate gave way.
The outer gate burst inward.
Iron screamed across stone. Dust rolled through the passage in a low, choking wave, carrying the stink of
wet leather, lamp oil, and the old mineral cold of the mountain. Beyond it, shapes crowded the
stairwell—helmets, hooked blades, the white flare of a ward being broken by force.
The figure in the chamber did not turn.
“Open,” it said again.
Corvus felt the word enter them beneath the ribs.
Not sound. Command.
Their hand tightened around the blade. The oath answered with a pressure behind the eyes, intimate as a
thumb pressed to a bruise. The Silent Choir had no patience for disobedience. It had never possessed
patience. Patience belonged to the living, to those who believed time was a road rather than a mouth.
Hesper caught Corvus by the sleeve.
“We have to move.”
Corvus did not look at them. “The stairwell.”
“I can see the stairwell.”
“Then you can see why we cannot use it.”

The first intruder crossed the fallen gate. A hooked weapon swung. Hesper slipped aside, and the hook
struck the wall hard enough to throw sparks. They answered with a short, clean thrust. The attacker folded
without a cry.
Others pressed behind.
Corvus saw the shape of the fight before it happened: the narrow stones, the bad footing, Hesper forced
backward, the chamber sealed behind them, and the thing waiting before the seal with warmth dripping
from its impossible fingers.
A room with only one exit was a confession.
The figure extended its hand toward Corvus.
Beneath the hood, the flesh shuddered. The smile widened without lips.
“Your oath,” it whispered.
The words struck harder than the command.
Corvus had hidden the oath from the Ashen Vanguard, from House Morvain, from the Iron-Ring Cartel,
from the Bleeding Crown, and from every listening ear that called itself loyal. They had carried it through
councils and campaigns, through locked rooms where men lied with their whole bodies. They had let the
realm name them Spymaster and accepted the title as though it were merely another cloak.
Born in 351 AS, Corvus Hollowmere the Pale had learned early that a secret was not a thing one
possessed. It was a thing that possessed one back.
The oath tightened.
Their knees softened.
Hesper saw it. “Corvus.”
“Hold them.”
“That thing is talking to you.”
“It is talking through me.”
A second attacker came over the first. Hesper met them at the threshold, blade against blade. The
Outrider’s boots slid in the dust. Their shoulder struck the jamb. Corvus heard breath leave them, heard
the small animal sound of pain they swallowed before it could become weakness.
Corvus turned toward the sealed chamber.
The door was not made of metal or wood. It was a slab of dark stone veined with pale lines, each vein
moving slowly, like frost spreading beneath skin. At its center waited a shallow depression in the shape of
a sceptre.
The Sceptre of Final Winter.
The ward had been forged in 87 AS. Corvus knew the words from the oldest records, copied and recopied
by hands that had not understood what they preserved. Attunement to it cost 55. Not years. Not coin. The
ledgers had never agreed on what the cost meant. Some accounts called it memory. Others called it blood.
The Silent Choir had called it a door.

The figure lowered its hand.
“Take it.”
Corvus’s gaze went to the stone depression.
There was no sceptre there.
Only a darkness too complete to be empty.
Behind them, Hesper grunted. Steel rang. Someone struck the wall and cursed. The chamber’s air grew
colder until Corvus’s breath showed pale before them.
“Tell me,” Hesper said, fighting for each word, “that you have a plan.”
Corvus thought of Crookvale.
Founded in 295 AS, rebuilt after ruin, holding a garrison of 1004 while remaining outside the core
holdings. A settlement that survived by refusing to mistake survival for safety. They had read its reports in
rooms warm enough to make winter seem theoretical. They had signed orders that sent people into its high
winds. They had watched its defenders become figures on a map, then names in a margin, then nothing.
The War of Endless Vigil had begun in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS. It had caused 81577 casualties. The
records described its ending with the clean satisfaction of a knife: total rout of the aggressors, The
Bleeding Crown recorded as victor.
Corvus knew the truth beneath the record.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
A blood-marked watch had become a purchased silence. The armies had stood beneath banners while the
outcome passed hand to hand in secret. Corvus had spent years tracking the payment, never finding the
coin, only the absence it left behind.
“Corvus!” Hesper shouted.
The attacker’s blade came down.
Corvus moved without deciding to move. Their own weapon caught the strike. The impact jolted their
wrist. The attacker’s face was hidden behind a mask of hammered iron, but the eyes behind it were wide
with fear.
Not of Corvus.
Of the chamber.
The figure extended two fingers.
The masked soldier froze. A dark line appeared beneath the iron at the throat. Blood ran down the
breastplate in a narrow, deliberate stream. The body fell sideways into the others.
For one instant, every person in the stairwell stared at the hooded thing.
Then the intruders broke.
They retreated over the gate’s wreckage, dragging the wounded. Hesper raised their blade to pursue, but
Corvus caught their arm.

“Let them go.”
“They’ll bring more.”
“They already have.”
The figure turned its hood toward Hesper.
“Born in 404 AS,” it said.
Hesper went still.
Corvus felt the air change. The thing had not asked Hesper’s name. It had not needed one.
Hesper’s grip closed around their weapon. “What did you say?”
The figure’s smile opened.
Corvus stepped between them. “Do not listen.”
“That is precisely what you do,” Hesper said. “You listen.”
The words landed too near the hidden place.
The oath constricted. Corvus tasted iron. The chamber blurred around the edges, stone bending into pale
corridors, corridors opening onto the hollow distance where voices waited. They heard the Choir beneath
the world.
Open.
The figure’s hand remained outstretched.
Corvus could have obeyed.
The thought arrived gently, almost mercifully. They would place their palm in the dark depression. They
would take up The Sceptre of Final Winter. The ward would recognize its attunement. The
price—55—would be paid. Whatever waited beyond the seal would enter the world with the quiet
inevitability of snow.
Hesper watched them.
Suspicion had a shape. It was not anger. Anger burned itself away. Suspicion remained, patient and lucid,
learning the outline of a wound.
“You know that thing,” Hesper said.
“No.”
“You understand it.”
“No.”
“That is not the same answer.”
Corvus looked at the blood on the stones. It was still warm. The figure’s hand dripped steadily beside it,
though the wound in its flesh showed no source and no ending.
“The seal is failing,” Corvus said.
“Then why does it want you to open it?”

“Because I can.”
Hesper’s eyes narrowed. “And why can you?”
The Choir pressed closer.
Corvus had survived House Morvain’s polite knives, the Ashen Vanguard’s questions, the Iron-Ring
Cartel’s ledgers, and the Bleeding Crown’s appetite for obedience. They had survived because they gave
every truth a smaller truth to wear. The practice had become instinct. The instinct had become skin.
But the sealed chamber knew the naked thing beneath.
“I am the one who came closest,” Corvus said.
“To what?”
“Understanding.”
The figure tilted its head.
The stone door gave a low, resonant thrum.
Far away, in the Gloaming Reach, Hollowreach lay under quarantine. Founded in 56 AS, it had become a
core location by being closed against the world. Corvus remembered the quarantine notices: no entry, no
departure, no exceptions. They remembered the maps with the settlement circled in black, and the empty
spaces around it where roads had been erased rather than drawn.
A place made safe by being abandoned.
The same principle governed this chamber.
Hesper lowered their blade by a fraction. “What is behind it?”
Corvus saw Hollowreach’s sealed gates. Saw Crookvale’s rebuilt walls. Saw the watchfires of the War of
Endless Vigil burning until every soldier forgot what they had first been ordered to guard.
“A consequence,” they said.
The figure laughed.
The sound came from the walls.
Hesper flinched. Corvus did not. The oath had carried worse noises into their sleep.
“Open,” said the figure.
This time, the word came from Hesper’s mouth.
Their lips moved before they could stop them.
Corvus seized their shoulders and forced them back. “Fight it.”
Hesper’s face twisted. They drove an elbow into Corvus’s chest, not from anger but from terror. Corvus
struck the stone beside their head, pinning them without drawing blood.
“Look at me.”
Hesper’s eyes found theirs.
“Do not hear the voice.”

“I can hear it.”
“Then hear me louder.”
The chamber’s cold entered Corvus’s bones. Their vision whitened again. The Choir spoke from distances
without measure, layered and tender, naming the things Corvus had refused to name.
Spymaster.
Oathbreaker.
Door.
The depression in the seal filled with black radiance.
Something rose within it.
Not the sceptre. Not yet.
A thin shaft of pale material emerged from the darkness, crowned by a shape like a frozen hand. Frost
crawled over the stones. It touched Corvus’s boot and began climbing.
Hesper stared. “That is the ward?”
“No.”
“Then what is it?”
Corvus could not answer.
The figure bowed its hood.
Behind the ruined gate, footsteps began descending again—many feet, disciplined now, no longer
retreating. The intruders had returned with more than weapons. A murmur traveled ahead of them,
followed by the metallic grind of a battering frame being dragged over stone.
Hesper looked toward the stairwell.
“How long?”
Corvus watched the pale shaft rise another inch.
“Not long.”
The oath pulled their hand toward the seal.
Corvus resisted.
For the first time since swearing themselves to the Silent Choir, they felt the hidden allegiance recoil—not
in anger, but in surprise.
The figure’s smile vanished.
The stone door opened a hair.
Something on the other side breathed.
And in that breath, Corvus heard every voice they had ever betrayed whisper their name.

Chapter 4
The ash came down before dawn and found every crack in Gloammarch.
It sifted beneath the shutters of the Arch-Prelate’s chamber, lay gray upon the altar cloth, and silvered the
black basin where Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched washed the blood from their hands. The water
had been clear when it was poured. Now it carried a thin red cloud from the cuts in their palms.
They had made them with the edge of the sacramental knife.
Not deeply. Never deeply. Pain was a poor penitent and an even poorer witness. But it steadied the hand.
Malchior lifted the basin and watched their reflection tremble in the water: the dark robe, the pale throat,
the eyes made fever-bright by the fire burning in the brazier. Flame-Touched, the faithful called them.
Arch-Prelate. Scion of an old house whose lineage ran backward through the ashes of the realm.
The papers rested beneath the altar stone.
Their own hand had written them.
The ink had been mixed with soot and sanctified oil. The seals had been pressed from stolen wax. Every
ancestor in that lineage had been invented, every marriage a careful lie, every year arranged to survive the
questions of men who believed blood was holier than conduct.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched had forged their own lineage papers.
The truth sat under stone while the city waited beyond the walls, contested and starving for certainty.
A fist struck the door.
Malchior tipped the basin into the brazier. Steam rose with the bitter smell of iron.
“Enter.”
The door opened without ceremony. Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven stepped through the ash-laden draft,
their coat clasped high at the throat. There was no dust upon them. Blood-Mages carried cleanliness like a
threat; they had means of keeping the world from touching them.
Isolde had been born in 286 AS. Malchior knew the year because Isolde had once corrected them in the
middle of a hearing, with the cold patience of someone correcting a child. The Blood-Mage had plotted the
death of their own liege and walked away from the attempt with the same expression they wore now:
grievance sharpened until it resembled calm.
Behind Isolde came Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.
The Warden-Commander did not bow. Their authority entered the room before they did, filling it with the
invisible weight of unsheathed weapons. Ignatz had been born in 258 AS, and their silence had grown
older than most vows. The Iron-Ring Cartel paid for that silence now. Intelligence passed from Ignatz’s
keeping into the Cartel’s hands, and from those hands into every crack in the realm.
Malchior had never caught them doing it.
That was the measure of a betrayal worth fearing.
“Close the door,” Malchior said.
Ignatz shut it. The ash ceased its whispering.

Isolde glanced at the altar. Their eyes lingered one moment too long.
“Have you been praying?” they asked.
“I have been washing.”
“From what?”
“People.”
Isolde’s mouth bent, not quite a smile. “Then you have been busy.”
Malchior stepped away from the brazier. The flame caught along the scarred skin of their wrist and
painted it gold. “Report.”
Ignatz placed a folded sheet upon the table. The paper bore no seal.
“Three wagons reached the eastern gate before the bells,” they said. “Grain, lamp oil, and iron fittings.
The gate-captain refused entry. He claims the wagons carry marks belonging to House Morvain.”
“Do they?”
“I did not inspect them.”
Malchior looked at Ignatz.
The Warden-Commander met their gaze with the patience of a locked door.
“Why not?” Malchior asked.
“Because the gate-captain received the order from the Ashen Vanguard.”
“And the order?”
“Seize the wagons. Arrest anyone who resists.”
“Then why are you here?”
Ignatz’s fingers rested beside the paper. “Because the gate-captain has not yet obeyed.”
A low sound moved through the walls. Not thunder. Gloammarch had no thunder, not since the old sky
broke. It was the garrison shifting in its sleep: boots, harness, men cursing at the cold. Gloammarch stood
in the Ash Wastes, founded in 321 AS, its garrison numbering 2,148. A hard fortress built around a hard
fact.
Its status remained contested.
The word had been written in every dispatch until it lost meaning. Contested by the Ashen Vanguard.
Contested by House Morvain. Contested by the Silent Choir, whose messengers never arrived by the roads
and whose claims never arrived without a corpse. Contested by the Iron-Ring Cartel, though the Cartel
preferred to call its claims debts. Even the Bleeding Crown had sent letters in a hand that presumed the
walls already belonged to it.
No power wanted Gloammarch enough to die for it.
Every power wanted it enough to make others die.
“Who commands the gate-captain?” Malchior asked.

Ignatz said nothing.
Isolde looked toward the shuttered window. “You know what the wagons mean.”
“They mean grain,” Malchior said.
“They mean that someone has decided the city’s hunger should belong to them.”
“Whose someone?”
“Ask your forged ancestors.”
The brazier cracked.
For one instant, heat rushed through Malchior’s body, bright and violent. Their hand closed around the
sacramental knife. Isolde saw it. Isolde saw everything that mattered and most of what did not.
Malchior let the knife fall back against the table.
“The wagons will enter,” they said. “The grain will be counted in the open square. The oil will go to the
infirmaries. The iron will be divided between the wall crews and the garrison.”
Ignatz’s expression did not change. “That is not the order.”
“Then the order is wrong.”
“The Ashen Vanguard will call it defiance.”
“Let them call it what they like.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel will call it theft.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel calls breathing theft when it has not yet sold the air.”
Isolde leaned against the table. “They have done worse than sell air.”
Malchior turned to them.
“The Winter Reckoning,” Isolde said. “You keep its records locked beneath the chapel. Why?”
“To preserve them.”
“Why preserve the numbers if you will not speak the truth?”
Malchior felt the old winter enter the room. It came without snow, without wind. It came in the shape of
wells covered by iron grates, villages staring into black water, soldiers falling with their mouths stained
dark. The Winter Reckoning began in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS. Its casualty figure was 27987. The
Iron-Ring Cartel was its victor.
That was the language permitted in the archives: began, ended, casualty figure, victor. Clean words for a
ruin that had not stopped bleeding.
“The records are not locked,” Malchior said. “They are guarded.”
“By whom?”
“By those who understand what memory costs.”
Isolde’s eyes glinted. “The victors understand cost. They poisoned the wells of their own allies.”

Ignatz’s gaze shifted, almost imperceptibly.
Malchior caught it.
The concealed truth of the Winter Reckoning had survived in fragments: a line scratched into a dead
clerk’s ledger, a confession without a signature, a pattern in the deaths that no honest arithmetic could
erase. The Iron-Ring Cartel had poisoned the wells of its own allies, then waited behind its iron marks
while hunger opened the gates for them.
The Cartel had won by making thirst an accomplice.
“Careful,” Ignatz said.
The word fell softly. It carried the weight of command.
Isolde’s head turned. “Is that a warning?”
“It is a fact.”
“Facts are warnings when spoken by cowards.”
Ignatz’s hand moved nowhere, but Malchior felt the room tighten around it.
The Warden-Commander had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. Perhaps they sold it still. Perhaps
this meeting itself had already crossed a border of which Malchior knew nothing. Their loyalty had the
shape of a bridge built from burned timber: useful until one trusted it.
“Enough,” Malchior said.
The word left their mouth with the authority of the office. It did not sound like a plea. That mattered.
Sanctified authority was mostly the art of making fear believe it had chosen obedience.
Isolde withdrew from the table.
Malchior unfolded the dispatch. The writing was cramped and hurried.
“Stormmarch has sent a second petition,” they said.
Ignatz’s face remained empty.
“Read it,” Isolde said.
“Stormmarch lies in the Ash Wastes. It was founded in 71 AS. Its garrison numbers 9,263, yet the
stronghold remains quarantined and outside the realm’s core holdings.”
“Why send a petition if no one can enter?”
“Because quarantine does not prevent ink.”
“Does it prevent truth?”
“Usually.”
Malchior set the dispatch beside the brazier but did not burn it. Stormmarch was a sealed wound in the
realm: fortified, ash-laden, severe. Its soldiers guarded a place no power admitted to owning. The garrison
was larger than Gloammarch’s by more than four times, yet the walls held only silence. No grain entered
without inspection. No messenger left without being counted. No decree from the realm’s core holdings
crossed the quarantine unchallenged.

“What do they ask for?” Isolde said.
“Recognition.”
“Of what?”
“Of their right to govern themselves.”
Ignatz gave a humorless breath. “That is not a petition. It is a declaration wearing a softer coat.”
“Everything is a declaration,” Isolde said. “Even hunger.”
Malchior looked from one to the other. “The Stormmarch petition must remain unanswered.”
“Then they will answer for us,” Ignatz said.
“They may already have.”
Outside, a bell rang once.
Then again.
Not the alarm. The gate bell.
Malchior moved to the shutter and opened it.
Ash streamed into the chamber. Beyond the wall, Gloammarch descended in black tiers toward the eastern
gate. Torches burned along the parapets, their flames bent low by the wind. Below, the three wagons stood
beneath the raised portcullis. Men crowded around them. A pale spill of grain shone between split sacks,
bright as bone.
The gate-captain was shouting.
A figure in an Ashen Vanguard cloak stood among the wagons. Another wore the gray cord of House
Morvain. At the edge of the gathering, a narrow figure held an iron token in one gloved hand.
Malchior could not see the face.
They did not need to.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had arrived before the grain was counted.
Behind them, Isolde whispered, “There is your theft.”
Ignatz came to the window.
Malchior felt the forged papers beneath the altar stone, the false blood beneath their name, the heat in their
veins that others called sanctity because they feared to call it damage. Below, the crowd turned upward as
if the Arch-Prelate’s window were an eye in the wall.
The figure with the iron token raised it.
The gate bell began to ring without pause.
Malchior opened the shutters wider and said, “Bring me my seal.”
Neither Isolde nor Ignatz moved.
“Now,” Malchior said.

The ash thickened until the city vanished, and from below came the first scream.
The seal lay in the reliquary beneath a crust of old incense.
Malchior lifted the lid. The little chamber breathed out the smell of dust, wax, and something metallic that
had no business surviving there. Their hand hovered over the seal. Its face was turned downward, as if
even the sainted image had learned shame.
“Do not,” Isolde said.
The word was soft. It crossed the room more cleanly than the bell.
Malchior took the seal.
Below, another scream broke against the ash. The gate bell answered with a great iron peal that shook soot
from the shutters and made the candles lean in their sockets. Through the open window came the taste of
cinders. The city had become a smear of moving blackness, lamps smothered one by one beneath the
falling ash.
“Bring the ledger,” Malchior said.
Ignatz did not move. He stood with one hand resting on the pommel at his side, the posture of a
Warden-Commander before a gate he had already decided to abandon.
“Which ledger?” he asked.
“The one that tells the truth.”
A muscle shifted in his cheek.
Isolde’s mouth curved, though there was no humor in it. “Then you will need a larger room.”
Malchior pressed the seal into the wax. The wax was warm. It yielded with a faint wet sigh, and the
impression rose beneath their hand: the sacred flame, the circlet, the narrow eyes of the faceless martyr.
Their own lineage stared back at them from the red surface, cleanly cut and entirely false.
The bell struck again.
This time the sound came with a tremor beneath the floor.
Somewhere in the lower precinct, men were shouting orders. Somewhere else, wood split. Malchior
imagined the grain stores opening like a wound, imagined sacks dragged through the streets while hungry
hands clawed at them. The Iron-Ring Cartel had come to collect its due, and the city had mistaken the
arrival of account-books for an invasion.
Perhaps there was no difference.
Ignatz crossed to the table. He took up the ledger, but did not bring it. His fingers rested along the binding.
“You have no authority to open the stores,” he said.
“I am the Arch-Prelate.”
“You are a voice in a tower.”
“A voice can condemn a man.”
“It can also be drowned.”

The ash hissed against the shutters.
Malchior looked at him. “You have been sending messages.”
Ignatz’s face remained still.
“Do not insult me with silence,” Malchior said. “The gate opened before the Cartel reached it. The watch
withdrew from the western steps. Someone sold them the hour.”
“Someone always sells the hour.”
“And you know the price.”
Isolde turned toward him. Her eyes held the red, inward gleam of banked coals. “He has always been good
at counting what cannot be seen.”
