Ignatz’s gaze moved to her. “You would know.”
“Yes.”
The answer startled the room. It had no defense in it. Isolde took a step nearer to the window, her fingers
closing around the edge of her sleeve. Beneath the cloth, something dark moved along her wrist and
vanished beneath her palm. Blood remembered its own roads. It knew the way beneath skin.
Malchior watched her hand.
She noticed. “You see stains everywhere now.”
“I see what is placed before me.”
“No,” she said. “You see what you need to fear.”
The bell rang until the words dissolved in its iron throat.
For a moment Malchior was not in the chamber. They were beneath another sky, one made white by ash
and winter, hearing the old testimony spoken by men who had survived only because someone else had
not. The Winter Reckoning had not ended with a victory. It had ended with wells gone bitter, with iron
marks nailed over the dead, with allies choking at the mouths of their own springs. The Silent Choir had
been belligerent in The Winter Reckoning. Their bells had called men to prayer, to battle, to the silences
between both. The sound had entered the bones and stayed there.
Now the same rhythm trembled through Gloammarch.
Malchior tightened their hand around the seal.
“The Silent Choir is in the city,” they said.
Ignatz’s eyes narrowed. “You have seen them?”
“I have heard them.”
“That bell is not theirs.”
“No,” Isolde said. “But the dead do not require their own bells.”
Ignatz looked from one to the other. “You are both mad.”
“Madness,” Malchior replied, “is what the living call a warning after they have chosen not to heed it.”

The door shuddered.
Not a knock. A blow.
Ash sifted down from the lintel. The candles guttered blue.
A voice came from the passage. “Arch-Prelate.”
Malchior raised the seal. The wax cooled around it.
“Who is there?” Ignatz called.
A second blow struck the door. The hinges groaned.
“Open,” said the voice. “By order of the gate.”
Isolde laughed then, low and bloodless. “The gate has learned to speak.”
Ignatz drew his sword.
Malchior felt the heat waking under their skin. It began at the sternum, a coal pressed into flesh, then
spread down the arms in thin, bright threads. The candles bowed toward them. Wax ran like tears.
Ignatz saw it. His sword lowered a fraction.
“There,” Isolde murmured. “Show them the sanctity they paid for.”
“Do not mistake pain for divinity.”
“I never have.”
The door cracked along its center.
Malchior placed the sealed paper on the table. Their name stared from the page in the careful hand they
had once trained to imitate the dead. Cindervale. The ink had been mixed with ash and oil. The blood
beneath the name was theirs, though no blood could make the lie ancestral.
They had forged their own lineage papers.
The knowledge no longer felt like a secret. It felt like a second skeleton.
“Open the door,” Malchior said.
Ignatz turned. “To whom?”
“To the truth.”
He did not obey.
Isolde stepped past him. “Move.”
“You are not in command here.”
“I have commanded men with better reasons for living than you.”
His sword came up between them. “You will not pass.”
Her expression changed. Not anger. Recognition.
“Ossric Ashgrove,” she said.

The name seemed to lessen the room.
Ignatz’s blade remained steady, but his attention faltered.
Isolde kept her eyes on him. “I was Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven, mentor of Ossric Ashgrove. I taught
him where to place a knife so the body would understand before the mind did. I taught him to listen when
an oath became a chain. He survived because he learned quickly.”
“You taught him treason,” Ignatz said.
“I taught him choice.”
“You taught him to turn against his own.”
“His own turned first.”
The door split wider. A hand thrust through the gap, fingers blackened with ash. Ignatz wheeled and
struck. The sword bit wood and bone together. A wet cry sounded beyond the door.
The flame beneath Malchior’s skin surged.
They seized the ledger from the table and flung it into the brazier.
Ignatz stared. “What have you done?”
“Burned the account.”
The leather cover caught slowly. Pages curled inward, blackening at the edges. Names lifted in sparks.
Debts. Deliveries. Signatures. The invisible architecture of the city began to die in the fire.
A gust came through the window. Ash spiraled into the chamber, turning the candlelight gray. It settled on
Malchior’s shoulders like a priestly mantle.
Beyond the door, the men were forcing themselves through.
Isolde lifted both hands.
The blood came out of the wounded guard in a thin red thread, slipping beneath the door. It crawled across
the floor toward her, bright as a live wire. The man outside began to choke. His comrades shouted. The
thread tightened.
“Isolde,” Malchior said.
“Do not use my name as a plea.”
“I need the passage held, not the men killed.”
“Then command your mercy to stand in the doorway.”
The blood snapped back into her palm.
The guard collapsed beyond the threshold. Others dragged him away. Boots thundered down the passage,
then divided—some toward the stairs, some toward the lower chambers.
Ignatz shoved the door closed and braced his shoulder against it.
“You have made enemies of everyone below,” he said.
“Below,” Malchior answered, “they were already enemies.”

The brazier exhaled a column of smoke. For an instant, the burning ledger’s pages opened like wings.
Malchior saw the seal impressed on the last leaf before it blackened: their forged authority, their sacred
fraud, the lie that had held a city together because no one had yet dared to pull at it.
The bell fell silent.
Silence did not soothe the chamber. It revealed the breathing of the walls, the small creak of timber, the
distant movement of bodies beneath the ash.
Then a new sound came from the street.
Not a bell.
Voices.
Many voices, speaking together without words.
Ignatz removed his shoulder from the door. “The Choir.”
Malchior went to the window.
The ash had thinned enough to show the square below. Figures stood around the gate, their faces hidden
beneath pale veils. They did not move. At their center, the bearer of the iron token held it against the
darkness, and the token seemed to drink what little light remained.
Isolde came beside Malchior.
“Do you know what they want?” she asked.
Malchior looked at the sealed paper on the table, the burning ledger, and the blood on Ignatz’s sword.
“Yes,” they said.
The figures below lifted their heads.
“They want the name beneath mine.”
A crack of red fire opened across Malchior’s palm. The pain was exquisite. Their fingers curled around it
as the voices in the square began to speak, and from the passage behind them came the scrape of men
climbing toward the chamber.
The first climber broke through the passage with a shoulder to the door.
The wood groaned. Dust sifted from the lintel and settled on the burning ledger in a pale skin. Behind the
man, more boots struck the stair, measured and close. Steel whispered against stone.
Isolde’s hand closed around Malchior’s wrist.
“Then give them what they came for.”
The crack of red fire in Malchior’s palm widened. Heat entered the bones. Their hand trembled, though
their face did not.
“If I knew which name it was.”
“You do.”
Below, the veiled figures spoke as one.

“Cindervale.”
The word rose through the chamber like smoke drawn down a chimney.
“Cindervale.”
The man at the door struck again. The bar shuddered. Ignatz turned from the burning ledger, his sword
held low, blood slipping from its edge to the floor. His expression had the patient emptiness of a man who
had already chosen the cost of survival.
“Arch-Prelate,” he said. “The western stair is lost.”
Malchior looked at him. “You said it was held.”
“I said men were standing there.”
“And now?”
“They are not.”
A third blow broke the door’s upper hinge. A wedge of black appeared beyond it. One pale-veiled figure
in the square lifted the iron token. The darkness around it bent inward.
Malchior felt the sealed paper on the table draw breath.
The paper had been folded without a crease, its wax unmarked, its surface grey as old skin. They had seen
it carried through sanctums and war rooms, through the hands of men who prayed with one mouth and lied
with the other. No seal had ever claimed it. No hand had ever admitted to writing it.
Yet it had borne their name.
Not the name they had chosen for the world.
The other one.
Their forged lineage papers lay beneath the floorstones of the chamber, hidden in a cavity no larger than a
prayer book. Ink, ash, witness-marks, the careful architecture of blood. All of it false. Every ancestor
raised from silence. Every pious connection stitched into place until the lie could stand upright and
demand obedience.
The paper on the table had been sent to make the lie kneel.
Isolde’s fingers tightened. “You can still burn it.”
“I can burn paper.”
“Then burn the room.”
The door burst inward.
A Warden came through sideways, his shield first. The red light in Malchior’s palm struck the shield and
ran over it in a fan of fire. The man screamed. He dropped the shield, but the flame clung to his arm, bright
as a wound opening. Ignatz stepped forward and cut him down before the body struck the floor.
Two more pressed into the doorway.
The chamber filled with the stink of hot iron, wet wool, and fear.
Malchior seized the sealed paper.

The wax was cold.
Their fire did not touch it.
The voices below changed. No longer a chant. A recitation.
“Blood that was written. Blood that was bought. Blood that was never yours.”
The iron token flashed.
The pale veils turned toward the tower.
Isolde drew a narrow blade from beneath her coat. Its edge was dark, not with oil but with something
thicker. Blood-Mage’s work. The blade seemed to listen to the pulse in Malchior’s throat.
“You know them,” Isolde said.
“I know what they believe.”
“That is not what I asked.”
The Warden in the doorway raised a hooked axe. Ignatz caught the haft with his sword and drove his
elbow into the man’s face. Bone gave. Ignatz moved with the brutal economy of command, without anger
and without mercy.
Malchior watched the blood bead along his knuckles.
“You command Ironfell Citadel,” they said.
Ignatz’s eyes came to them.
“Since 286 AS,” Malchior continued. “You have commanded Ironfell Citadel since 286 AS. Men have
carried your seal into every court that matters. Why are you here, in this room, defending a ledger that has
already burned?”
Ignatz looked at the ledger.
A page curled inward, blackening at the edges. Beneath the flames, a line of figures emerged in pale
copper ink. Not names. Routes. Stores. Gates. The hidden anatomy of fortresses.
His jaw tightened.
“You are asking the wrong question.”
“Then answer the one you fear.”
One of the Warden’s men fell across the threshold. The other advanced, blade raised. Isolde’s dark knife
moved once. A thin red line appeared on the man’s throat. He touched it with surprise. The line opened,
and he folded.
Ignatz did not look at him.
“The Cartel has the routes,” he said.
The words landed more heavily than the bodies.
Malchior felt the tower tilt beneath them, though the stones remained still.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel.”

Ignatz said nothing.
“You sold them the roads.”
“I sold them what would keep Ironfell standing.”
“And who decided it should stand?”
“I did.”
The admission was not defiance. That made it worse.
Malchior had seen the Iron-Ring Cartel’s victory in the faces of the old: the hollowed cheeks, the
winter-white scars, the hands that closed around empty cups when wells were mentioned. The Winter
Reckoning had left 27,987 casualties and the Iron-Ring Cartel as victor. The realm had called it a triumph
of endurance. The dead had known better.
Ignatz had known better.
The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies. The truth had survived in fragments, carried by mouths
that were later cut shut. Ignatz had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel, and now the Cartel’s shadow
reached into this chamber through him.
Below, the veiled figures began to climb.
Their voices came through the stone, softened and multiplied.
“Name beneath name.”
“Blood beneath ink.”
“Open.”
The sealed paper pulsed in Malchior’s hand.
Isolde glanced at Ignatz. “How much did you tell them?”
“Enough.”
“Enough for what?”
“To know Gloammarch would not hold.”
At the word, the fire in Malchior’s palm flared.
“Gloammarch is contested,” they said. “It has no right to fall by arithmetic.”
“It has a garrison.”
“So does every grave with a sword laid across it.”
Ignatz’s face hardened. “The Diadem of Sorrowgate is housed in Gloammarch.”
For a moment there was only the sound of burning paper.
Malchior saw it: not the jewel, not the metalwork, but the shape of the rumor surrounding it. A crown
made for mourning. A relic hidden behind walls while armies bled outside them. The Diadem of
Sorrowgate housed in Gloammarch, beneath ash-dark stone and the scrutiny of every power that still
possessed a hand to reach.

Isolde’s knife lowered by a fraction.
“Then this is not about Malchior,” she said.
“No,” Ignatz answered. “It is about what Malchior can open.”
The crack in Malchior’s palm reached the wrist.
They smelled their own blood burning.
The room seemed to contract around the paper. The climbing voices grew louder. Somewhere beneath
them, iron struck iron. The veiled ones had reached the lower stair.
“Open what?” Isolde demanded.
Ignatz looked at Malchior with the exhaustion of a man who had spent years feeding pieces of himself to a
machine and had only now discovered the machine could speak.
“The old passage.”
“There is no old passage.”
“There is always an old passage.”
Malchior thought of the papers beneath the floor. Thought of the line of false descent written in their own
hand. Thought of the first time they had worn the robes of the Arch-Prelate, how the collar had seemed to
tighten each time someone called them chosen.
The fire in their palm crawled across the sealed paper.
This time, the wax softened.
Isolde saw it. “Malchior.”
The doorframe filled again.
A veiled figure stood beyond the wounded Wardens. Pale cloth concealed the face, but the voice that came
from behind it was not joined to the others.
“You were born without a house.”
Malchior’s breath stopped.
“You forged a house from ash.”
The fire died in their hand.
The figure stepped over the bodies.
“You wrote yourself into the blood.”
The sealed paper split beneath Malchior’s fingers.
Inside was not a letter, nor a confession, nor any list of the dead. It was a single narrow strip of parchment,
and on it a name had been written in ink the color of dried blood.
Malchior looked down.
The name beneath theirs waited.

They knew the hand.
It was their own.

Chapter 5
The road into Crookvale had been cut from black stone, though Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed
remembered no quarry on the mountain.
Rain silvered the ruts. It gathered in the hollows where old blood had gone dark and slick beneath the
wagon wheels, and the horses lifted their hooves high, affronted by the stink of iron rising from the mud.
Above them, the High Spires clenched the sky in pale, broken teeth.
At the gate, a sentry lowered his spear.
“Name.”
Brannoc drew back his hood. Rain ran from the edge and struck the red leather wrapped around his sword
hand. “You know my name.”
The sentry’s gaze moved over him: the scarred brigandine, the travel-stained cloak, the sword at his hip. It
lingered on the hand.
“No,” the sentry said. “I know the name people use when they want trouble.”
Brannoc smiled without warmth. “Then you know enough.”
The gatehouse swallowed the silence between them. Behind the sentry, a bell hung motionless in its
frame. The stone around it was new in places and ancient in others, the repairs laid across the old wounds
like clumsy stitches.
A second guard appeared above the parapet. “Let him through.”
The sentry did not turn. “Orders?”
“Orders from the garrison.”
“How many?”
The upper guard spat over the wall. “Enough.”
Brannoc looked past them into the settlement. Crooked roofs climbed the slope, their slate faces glittering
beneath the rain. Smoke crawled from chimneys and flattened itself against the stone. A shrine without a
saint stood in a square below, its hollow niche stuffed with blackened cloth.
“Crookvale was rebuilt,” Brannoc said.
The sentry’s fingers tightened around his spear. “You say that like it’s an accusation.”
“It is, if the dead paid for the timber.”
“They always do.”
The gate opened with a groan that came up through the soles of Brannoc’s boots. He entered alone,
leaving the wagons and the men who had followed him on the lower road. He had dismissed them before
dawn. A captain who arrived with an army invited arithmetic. A captain who arrived with only a sword
invited fear.
Fear was cheaper.

The street rose steeply. Water streamed between the cobbles, carrying ash, horse dung, and scraps of paper
gone soft at the edges. Brannoc passed shuttered houses and narrow doors barred from within. Faces
watched him through cracks. No one called out. No one needed to. The name had preceded him, as names
always did, and the red hand made certain they remembered it.
At the summit stood the garrison hall, a square block of old masonry crowned with fresh battlements. A
strip of black cloth hung above the entrance. Its hem was embroidered with the broken sigil of the
Bleeding Crown.
Brannoc stopped beneath it.
The cloth stirred in the rain.
For one unguarded breath, he saw another room: a hand upon a cradle, a crown lowered out of sight, a
woman whispering that blood could be hidden but never made harmless.
Then the memory closed its teeth.
“Captain.”
The voice came from the doorway.
The garrison commander was a woman with iron-gray hair and a face worn smooth by weather. She wore
no badge. Her coat had been mended at both shoulders, and one of the buttons was carved from bone.
“You’re expected,” she said.
“I’m often expected.”
“Not by people who want to live.”
“Those are the only sort who expect me.”
Her eyes shifted to the sword. “Inside.”
Brannoc entered.
The hall smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and boiled grain. A long table filled the central chamber, crowded
with maps weighted by cups and knives. The far wall had been scrubbed, but a rust-colored shadow
remained beneath the limewash. Someone had tried to clean a massacre from the stone and had only
taught it to linger.
The commander closed the door behind him.
“Your man at the lower road said you came regarding Hollowreach.”
“My man speaks too freely.”
“He spoke after we put a knife under his tongue.”
“That would improve most conversations.”
She ignored the remark. “You want passage through the Reach.”
“I want a guide.”
“No.”
“I didn’t ask whether the road was safe.”

“You asked for a guide. I said no.”
Brannoc removed his gloves one finger at a time. His right hand was stained dark despite the leather, the
old color worked into the creases of his skin. Men had invented stories about it. Some claimed he had
dipped it in a traitor’s heart. Others said the stain belonged to a curse. Brannoc had never corrected either
account. Truth was a poor guard. Rumor kept better watch.
The commander watched the hand, then looked away.
“Hollowreach was founded in 56 AS,” she said. “It has stood longer than the walls around this place. It has
endured raids, famine, and the Reach turning sick around it. Now it is under quarantine.”
“I know.”
“Then you know the roads are sealed.”
“I know what sealed means.”
“Do you?”
Brannoc set his gloves on the table. “It means someone is afraid of what comes out.”
“And what goes in.”
He leaned over the map. The Gloaming Reach had been inked in bruised colors, the rivers winding like
veins beneath skin. Hollowreach sat near its center, a small black mark surrounded by red strokes.
“Who is holding the town?”
“The officials say no one.”
“Officials say many things.”
“The Silent Choir has men at the eastern road.”
“Men?”
“Brothers, singers, penitents. Whatever they call themselves when the lamps are lit.”
“Armed?”
“Of course.”
“Then they’re men.”
The commander placed her palm over the map, covering Hollowreach. “The Ashen Vanguard has scouts
in the fen country. House Morvain claims jurisdiction by right of old charters. The Iron-Ring Cartel is
moving goods along the southern track despite the quarantine. Everyone wants what is inside.”
“What is inside?”
Her hand remained still.
“Ask the ones who sent you,” she said.
“No one sent me.”
“That’s worse.”

A gust struck the shutters. The lamps bent in their brackets. For a moment, the room darkened, and
Brannoc felt the old animal wake within him—the thing that measured exits, blades, distance to throats.
“You have a letter,” the commander said.
“Do I?”
“Your name is written on it.”
“Many letters bear my name.”
“This one bears the seal of the Bleeding Crown.”
The air changed.
Not much. A tightening in the commander’s shoulders. A quieting in the corridor beyond the door. But
Brannoc felt it, and beneath the feeling, the deeper thing: the crown’s blood calling through wax and rain,
pretending it had not been buried.
He drew the letter from inside his coat.
The seal had been pressed in black wax. No crown appeared upon it. Only a drop, split down the middle.
“Where did you get this?” he asked.
“It was left at the south gate.”
“By whom?”
“Korvath Nightbrook.”
Brannoc’s thumb passed over the broken drop. “The smuggler.”
“The same.”
“He sells secrets when there are no goods worth carrying.”
“He says there are goods beneath Hollowreach.”
“Korvath says whatever keeps a knife out of his ribs.”
“He said the thing beneath the town was regalia.”
Brannoc broke the seal.
The letter contained three lines, written in a cramped hand.
The Thrice-Bound Edge was forged in 123 AS.
It lies where the quarantine began.
Do not let the Choir bind it.
He read the words twice. The first time as a captain. The second as a son.
The commander reached for the letter. He let her take it.
“What is the Thrice-Bound Edge?” she asked.
“An old name.”

“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you’ll get.”
“Is it a weapon?”
“Regalia.”
Her eyes sharpened. “That means nothing.”
“It means someone wants you to imagine a crown.”
Outside, boots hurried across the wet stones. A voice called from the yard, too muffled to understand.
Another voice answered, and then the first shouted again.
The commander folded the letter. “The road to Hollowreach is watched.”
“Then we go by another.”
“There is no other.”
“There is always another.”
“That is what smugglers say.”
“Smugglers survive by being right.”
She stepped closer. “You think this is about you.”
Brannoc laughed softly. “Everything that wears a crown thinks the world is about it.”
“And you?”
He looked at the black cloth above the door, at the broken sigil trembling in the draft.
“I think crowns are hungry things. They eat whoever reaches for them.”
“Yet you reached.”
The words struck cleanly. He felt no wound, only the old pressure beneath the ribs.
The unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
He had heard it spoken in whispers beside campfires, beneath silk, in the mouths of men who wanted to
buy his loyalty and women who wanted to know what price his betrayal might command. An heir without
acknowledgment was a blade without a scabbard: useful, dangerous, and never allowed near the throne.
Brannoc put the letter away.
“Send for a guide.”
“I said no.”
“Then send for a prisoner.”
The commander studied him. “You brought no men.”
“I brought myself.”
“That’s not an army.”

“No.”
“Not even a company.”
“No.”
“Why should I let you walk into a quarantined town with nothing but a sword?”
Brannoc fastened his glove over the red hand. “Because if I wanted to bring ruin to Crookvale, I would
have come through the gate with my banners.”
Her mouth tightened. “You have banners?”
“Everyone has banners. Most are only waiting for the wind.”
A bell began to ring outside.
Once.
Twice.
The commander turned toward the shutters.
The third strike never came.
Instead, the garrison hall shook as something struck the outer gate. Men shouted below. A horse screamed.
Brannoc’s sword was in his hand before the commander drew her own.
“Who is it?” she called.
No answer.
Another blow thundered through the settlement. Dust sifted from the ceiling. The lamps guttered blue.
From somewhere beyond the walls came a sound like singing—thin, many-voiced, and patient.
The commander’s face emptied of color.
“The Choir,” she whispered.
Brannoc moved to the nearest shutter and opened it a finger’s width. Rain blew into his face. In the square
below, the shrine’s black cloth had torn free and wound itself around the saintless stone. Figures stood
beneath the gatehouse, pale garments darkened by water. They carried no torches. They needed none.
Their mouths moved together, shaping a hymn too low for the words to be heard.
At the foot of the shrine, a man knelt with his hands bound.
Korvath Nightbrook lifted his head.
Even through the rain, Brannoc saw the smuggler’s grin.
Then Korvath looked toward the garrison hall and mouthed two words.
They’re inside.
The commander seized Brannoc by the sleeve. “What did you bring here?”
A blade slid between the shutters behind them.

Brannoc twisted aside as the point entered the room, bright with rain, and the singer on the other side
began to whisper—
Brannoc twisted aside as the point entered the room, bright with rain, and the singer on the other side
began to whisper—
The commander dragged him backward.
Steel scraped the shutter-frame. The blade withdrew, then came again, stabbing through the gap with
patient precision. It was not the frantic work of a frightened man. Whoever held it understood the room’s
narrowness, understood how a body recoiled, understood that sooner or later instinct would make the same
shape twice.
Brannoc caught the commander’s wrist and hauled him down.
The blade passed above them.
A breath later, Brannoc drove his shoulder into the shutters. Wood cracked. The knife vanished. He struck
again, and the shutters burst outward into the rain.
A pale figure stood beyond them.
The face was hidden beneath a wet hood. The figure’s mouth still moved. The whisper had not broken,
though the sudden violence had thrown the body back against the outer wall. Behind the first stood
another, and another, their garments clinging like shrouds. No torchlight touched them. The storm made a
black mirror of the yard, and in that mirror the singers seemed less like men than stains where men ought
to be.
The commander rose with his sword drawn.
“Hold the hall!” he shouted.
His voice met the hymn and vanished inside it.
Something struck the door behind Brannoc. Once. Twice. On the third blow, the iron latch tore free.
The commander wheeled toward it.
Brannoc did not.
He had seen the second knife.
It came low from beneath the table, guided by a hand that had been waiting in the dark. Brannoc stamped
down. Bone gave under his heel. The hidden attacker made no sound, but the knife jerked sideways and bit
into the floorboards. Brannoc seized the wrist and wrenched until the shoulder came loose with a wet pop.
The man crawled from beneath the table.
He wore the garrison’s colors.
For one hard instant Brannoc stared at the badge fastened to the man’s breast. Rain ran through the broken
shutters and struck it, washing the color thin. The face beneath was young enough to have kept believing
in walls.
Then the man opened his mouth.
The hymn came out.

Brannoc drove his pommel into his teeth.
The commander was shouting again. Men answered from the corridor, boots hammering toward the hall,
but the sound was wrong. Too few. Too disordered. A body hit the outer door. Someone screamed. The
scream ended in a bubbling cough.
Brannoc drew his sword.
The old weapon came free with a drag of leather and a muted ring. Its edge held no shine except where the
rain touched it. His hand closed around the grip, and for an instant he felt the familiar pressure of
memory—not a ghost, not a voice, only the shape left behind when violence had become a language
spoken fluently.
The Accord of Mournthrone had taught him that stillness lied.
A quiet line could conceal a charge. A lowered banner could conceal a bargain. A man who appeared
beaten might merely be waiting for the moment when victory grew careless.
He had fought in The Accord of Mournthrone, fighting for The Bleeding Crown.
The truth moved through him with the cold certainty of a blade entering flesh. He had carried it beneath
false colors, beneath hired oaths, beneath the name men used when they wished to speak of him without
asking where his blood came from. The Bleeding Crown had been a cause to others. To Brannoc, it had
been a door he was forbidden to open and a hand that had never reached for him.
Now the singers pressed against the garrison hall.
The door burst inward.
A soldier stumbled through, clutching his throat. His fingers opened and closed against the blood. Behind
him came a figure in pale cloth, its face turned toward the ceiling as it whispered. The soldier collapsed at
Brannoc’s feet.
The commander met the intruder.
Their blades struck once, twice. The pale figure gave ground without haste. The commander cut across its
chest. Cloth opened. Beneath it there was no armor, only skin marked with narrow black lines that crossed
the ribs and vanished beneath the collar.
The hymn continued.
Brannoc stepped in and cut the figure’s knee.
It folded. The commander’s sword fell through its neck.
The whisper stopped.
Not ended. Stopped.
The silence that followed was so complete Brannoc heard rain ticking on the table and the soft collapse of
the body. Then a different voice spoke from the corridor.
“Red-Handed.”
The name carried no fear.
Brannoc turned.

Korvath Nightbrook stood beyond the broken door, no longer kneeling beneath the shrine. The rope still
hung from one wrist. The other hand held a short iron hook. Water streamed from his hair and beard,
making his narrow face look carved from candle grease. Behind him, the pale singers filled the passage.
The commander leveled his sword at him.
“You.”
Korvath’s grin had gone. “You should have barred the lower stair.”
“There is no lower stair.”
“There is now.”
The commander took one step toward him.
Brannoc caught the back of his coat. “Don’t.”
The man looked over his shoulder. “They’re in my hall.”
“They’re in the walls.”
As if summoned by the words, the stone beside the hearth cracked.
Dust spilled from the mortar. A hand pushed through.
The commander’s face changed. Not fear. Recognition, which was worse. He had trusted the stone. He
had trusted the garrison, the locked doors, the men who wore his badge. Trust was a luxury that announced
itself only when it had been taken away.
Brannoc shoved him aside as the wall gave.
A pale sleeve emerged, followed by a shoulder. Brannoc swung. His sword struck the intruder across the
face. The blade met teeth and bone, then dragged free. The figure collapsed half through the breach,
blocking the others behind it.
Korvath moved with sudden speed.
He crossed the corridor, drove his hook into the corpse’s collar, and hauled it sideways. Three singers
crowded through the opening at once. One carried a hatchet. One carried nothing. The third held a bundle
of dark cloth against its chest as tenderly as a mother might hold an infant.
The bundle breathed.
Brannoc’s stomach tightened.
The commander shouted for the men again. This time, somewhere beyond the hall, a reply came—one
voice, then another. The sound was distant and ragged, but it was human.
“Back,” Brannoc said.
The commander ignored him.
He charged the figure with the hatchet.
The singer raised the weapon. Its mouth shaped the first syllable of the hymn. The commander’s sword cut
through the hatchet’s haft and buried itself in the singer’s shoulder. He kicked the body away, but the pale
figure without a weapon seized his sword arm with both hands.

The commander struck it in the face.
It did not release him.
Brannoc saw the knife before the commander did. A narrow glint beneath the pale sleeve. He stepped
forward, but Korvath’s hook flashed first, catching the knife hand and dragging it wide.
“Move,” Korvath hissed.
The commander tore free and stumbled backward.
Brannoc cut the singer down.
The figure with the breathing bundle turned toward him.
Its hood slipped.
The face beneath was ordinary. That was the obscenity of it. A broad brow, a broken nose, rain shining on
the cheeks. Nothing in it belonged to nightmare. The mouth opened, and the hymn came softly now,
almost affectionately.
Brannoc’s sword hung between them.
The bundle stirred.
A small hand emerged from the cloth.
He hesitated.
It was enough.
The singer thrust the bundle at him.
Brannoc caught it on reflex. The weight was slight, warm through the wet fabric, and something within it
gave a thin, choking cry. The singer’s fingers closed around the sword hilt. The hand was stronger than it
looked.
Korvath struck the singer behind the ear with the iron hook.
The grip broke. Brannoc let the bundle fall onto the table and drove his forehead into the singer’s nose.
Cartilage tore. Blood burst hot across his mouth.
The figure staggered.
Brannoc seized its robe and pulled it close. “Who sent you?”
The singer smiled through the blood.
“Inside,” it whispered.
The word touched something behind him.
Brannoc turned.
The commander stood at the center of the hall, sword lowered. Around him, the surviving garrison men
had gathered. Their faces were pale in the stormlight. One had a cut across his brow. Another held a
broken spear. They watched the commander, not the doorway.
The commander’s mouth moved.

No sound came.
Then the men began to kneel.
All but one.
Korvath snatched the breathing bundle from the table and tucked it against his ribs. “That is not a good
sign.”
The commander raised his sword.
The men on the floor bowed their heads.
Brannoc felt the old instinct settle over him, clean and merciless. Not panic. Not courage. The narrowing
of the world to distances, weights, openings. His right hand was wet with another man’s blood. His left
had closed around the hilt of The Thrice-Bound Edge at his belt without drawing it, feeling the regalia’s
bound shape beneath the scabbard.
The commander looked at him.
“Brannoc,” he said.
His voice was his own again.
That frightened Brannoc more than the hymn.
The kneeling soldiers rose together.
Korvath backed toward the shattered shutters. “You know, Red-Handed, this would be the part where a
sensible smuggler leaves.”
“Then leave.”
“I’m considering it.”
The first soldier lunged.
Brannoc met him halfway. Their blades collided, and the force ran up his arm. The man’s eyes were clear.
Tears streamed down his face, though the rain had not reached him. Brannoc turned his sword, caught the
soldier’s edge, and opened his throat.
Another came from the left.
The commander struck him down.
For three breaths the hall became steel and breath and rain. Bodies crowded the narrow floor. The singers
pressed through the wall-breach, their hymn rising now, no longer whispered. The sound filled Brannoc’s
skull. It crawled beneath his thoughts and worried at old wounds.
He saw again the field at Mournthrone—not its banners, not its dead, only the moment before the lines
met, when every man still possessed the lie that he might choose what happened next.
A blade scraped his ribs.
He twisted. Pain opened hot beneath his coat.
The attacker’s face was inches from his. The man’s mouth stretched around a wordless note. Brannoc
drove his thumb into the eye and felt it rupture. He shoved the body down, but the fingers held his sleeve.

The commander’s sword severed them.
“Behind you!” the commander cried.
Brannoc turned toward the doorway.
Korvath was gone.
Beyond the broken shutters, the shrine yard had emptied. The pale figures stood beneath the gatehouse,
motionless in the rain. Between them, the saintless stone showed a dark opening where no door had been
before.
Something moved within it.
Not a man.
Not yet.
The singers in the hall lifted their voices as one.
The commander backed toward Brannoc. “What is that?”
Brannoc watched the darkness breathe.
His sword dripped onto the floor.
“Ask the ones who let it in.”
A hand emerged from the opening in the stone, fingers unfolding with slow, deliberate grace. The hymn
broke around a new sound—a wet inhalation, vast enough to seem drawn from the whole drowned yard.
Then the gatehouse bell began to ring.
The bell did not toll so much as convulse.
Each stroke shook the flagstones beneath Brannoc’s boots. Rust sifted from the rafters. Somewhere above,
pigeons burst from the belfry and beat themselves against the rain-black sky, their wings a frantic whisper
behind the stone.
The hand tightened on the edge of the opening.
Brannoc seized the commander by the breastplate and dragged him sideways as something shouldered
through. The iron rings of the mail screamed against one another. A shape unfolded from the dark, too tall
for the gatehouse and too narrow for any living flesh. Its head brushed the lintel. Its shoulders came after,
bending at angles that made the eye refuse them.
The commander struck at it.
His sword passed through a sleeve of darkness and came back rimed in grey frost.
The hymn faltered.
Not stopped. Faltered.
That was worse.
The singers had been taught to keep their voices steady before blades, fire, and the sight of men dying.
Their discipline had survived the War of Endless Vigil, which began in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS with
81577 casualties. Brannoc had read the old account by candlelight in a room where the walls sweated salt.

The War of Endless Vigil had ended with the total rout of the aggressors, and The Bleeding Crown was
recorded as the victor.
Recorded.
The word had always tasted of a lie.
The losing commander had been bribed to withdraw. Secretly, the payment had changed the shape of
history while the dead were left to give it a cleaner face. Brannoc had seen the same trick in every court he
had entered: a corpse made into a martyr, a theft dressed as tribute, a bastard dressed as nobody.
The thing turned its head toward him.
There was no face. Only a pale seam where a face might have been, opening and closing like a mouth
beneath ice.
Brannoc felt the old pressure behind his ribs—the instinct that had kept him alive when wiser men had
mistaken ceremony for safety. His hand was already red. Blood ran from the commander’s split knuckles
across Brannoc’s glove, filling the seams between the leather plates.
The Red-Handed.
Men had called him that in taverns, on battlefields, in rooms where they believed he could not hear. They
meant cruelty, usually. Sometimes luck. Never inheritance.
The thing took one step into the shrine yard.
Rain struck it and vanished.
“Back,” Brannoc said.
No one moved.
The pale figures beneath the gatehouse lowered their heads. Their faces remained hidden beneath wet
veils, but the motion passed through them like a single thought.
The singers began again.
This time the hymn carried words.
Brannoc knew them. Every soldier did. A warding litany older than the surviving keeps, older than the
feuds that had divided the realm into five hungers: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir,
the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. The words had been meant to close doors. They had been
sung over graves, over sealed wells, over infants born without shadows.
They had never been meant to welcome anything.
The commander found his voice. “Who opened it?”
His question went into the rain.
From the far side of the yard came a soft scrape. A man stepped out from behind the shrine wall, hood
drawn low, one hand tucked into his coat. He moved with the careful economy of someone accustomed to
spaces where every loose stone could betray him.
Brannoc knew that manner.

“KIIorvath Nightbrook,” he said.
The man stopped.
The commander’s gaze snapped toward him. “You know him?”
“I know what he does.”
Korvath Nightbrook’s mouth tightened. He was a Smuggler, and carried himself like a man who had
learned to make his body smaller than suspicion. Water gleamed on his hood. His eyes stayed on the
opening in the saintless stone.
“I did not open that,” he said.
“No?” Brannoc’s sword lowered an inch. “Then why are you here?”
“Because something came through the old road beneath the hill.”
“There is no road beneath the hill.”
Korvath gave him a look without warmth. “There was.”
The thing crossed the threshold.
The bell answered.
A crack travelled through the yard from the gatehouse to the shrine steps. It ran beneath the puddles,
where pale light pulsed in the seams. The commander stumbled. One of the singers shrieked, and the
hymn broke apart into individual voices.
The thing’s head tilted.
Brannoc heard a sound like a child trying to speak with a throat full of water.
The commander raised his sword again. “Hold the line!”
A laugh moved through the choir.
Not laughter from any human throat. It came from the walls, from the flooded ground, from beneath the
commander’s feet. The old stones trembled with it.
Brannoc knew that trembling. He had felt it once beneath a battlefield where dead men lay packed so
tightly that the earth could not drink them. He had been younger then, though never young. Born in 255
AS, he had learned early that the world did not care whether a man was ready.
His blood had been carried in secret.
Unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.
The knowledge had never made him feel chosen. It had made every doorway a trap.
One of the veiled figures lifted both hands. The sleeves fell back, revealing wrists marked with black
bands. The singer beside it began to choke. His mouth opened wide, but the hymn continued, pouring
through him after his tongue had gone still.
“Move,” Brannoc told the commander.
The commander did not hear him. He was staring at the thing.

“Move!”
Brannoc struck him across the face.
The commander reeled, blood blooming beneath his nose. For one breath the two men stood with the rain
between them, anger brighter than fear.
Then the commander saw what Brannoc had seen.
The thing had no feet.
Its lower half dissolved into the dark spilling from the stone. Each time it advanced, the yard stretched to
receive it.
They ran.
Brannoc dragged the commander toward the hall doors. Korvath went the other way, skirting the shrine,
vanishing behind a collapsed wall with the silent skill of a rat that had survived too many traps. Brannoc
almost called after him. Then the bell rang again, and the sound punched the name from his mind.
The hall doors slammed shut behind them.
Inside, the air was hot with bodies and tallow smoke. The singers had fallen silent. Some knelt. Others
stood with their hands pressed to their ears. Rainwater streamed from Brannoc’s coat and pooled around
his boots, carrying flecks of ash across the floor.
A table had been overturned near the altar. Beneath it, someone had placed a long iron-bound coffer.
The commander saw it and went white.
Brannoc saw that, too.
“What is inside?”
The commander’s answer came after too long a pause. “Regalia.”
“That is not an answer.”
A singer crawled toward the coffer. His fingers shook so violently that he missed the latch twice. On the
third attempt, the lid opened.
Dark metal lay within white cloth.
The Thrice-Bound Edge.
Even wrapped, it seemed to hold the room in a clenched silence. Regalia forged in 123 AS, its name
stamped upon the inner plate in a script that made the eyes ache. Brannoc had never touched it. No
attunement cost was recorded for The Thrice-Bound Edge. That absence disturbed him more than any
price could have.
Beside it rested a book bound in hide the color of old bruises.
“Edge of Gloamreach,” Korvath said from the shadows.
Brannoc turned.
The smuggler had returned without anyone seeing him enter. He stood with his back to the wall, one hand
still inside his coat.

The commander stared at the grimoire. “It was sealed.”
“Seals are promises,” Korvath said. “Promises fail.”
“Who brought them here?”
No one answered.
Brannoc looked from the coffer to the commander. “You did.”
The man’s face hardened. “Careful.”
“You knew the stone would open.”
“I knew the stone was weakening.”
“And you brought regalia into a shrine full of singers.”
“For protection.”
“For whom?”
The bell struck again.
Dust fell from the ceiling. Every flame in the hall leaned toward the doors.
Brannoc felt the darkness outside press against the wood. It did not batter the doors. It waited, patient as a
creditor.
One of the singers whispered, “The road has found its heir.”
The words passed through the hall.
The commander’s face changed.
Korvath looked at Brannoc.
Brannoc’s hand tightened around his sword hilt until the leather creaked. He could feel the blood on his
glove drying, stiffening, becoming another layer of armor.
“No,” he said.
The singer raised his head. His eyes were milk-white.
“The crown beneath the crown,” he murmured. “The hand that was denied. The blood that returns.”
The commander drew his sword and pointed it at Brannoc.
The singers recoiled.
For a moment, the only sound was the rain.
Then the doors bowed inward.
Not from a blow.
From a hand laid gently against the other side.
Brannoc watched the iron bands bend. He thought of The Bleeding Crown, of the records that called him
nobody, of the secret that had survived every attempt to bury it. He thought of the Accord of Mournthrone
and the blood that would one day take him there, though the hour had not yet come. He knew only what

the dead knew: that certain roads did not lead toward a destination.
They led toward recognition.
The coffer lid swung open by itself.
The Thrice-Bound Edge slid across the cloth and struck the stone floor with a clear, restrained note.
The grimoire opened.
Its pages turned in a wind no one could feel, stopping at a blank leaf.
A line of black moisture appeared upon it.
Then another.
Letters formed beneath the dripping dark.
Brannoc leaned closer despite himself.
The words were written in a hand he did not know.
They named him.

Chapter 6
The ash came down without wind.
It settled upon the shutters, the sill, the blackened iron of the balcony rail, and upon the parchment spread
beneath Cerys Sablewood the Ashen’s hand. Each flake was light as sifted flour. Each left a gray bruise
where it touched the page.
Cerys did not brush it away.
The room had been built for accounts, not comfort. Its walls were stone beneath layers of soot-dark
plaster, its ceiling low enough to hold the heat close, its single brazier breathing the sour scent of damp
charcoal. Beyond the shuttered window, Gloammarch endured the ash-dark austerity of the Wastes: walls,
watchtowers, sloping roofs, all reduced to shades of iron and bone.
A bell sounded somewhere below.
Once.
Then silence reclaimed the fortress.
Cerys placed one finger against the column of figures and read it again.
“Say it aloud,” Halvard said.
His voice was quiet, as if the room might take offense at being disturbed. He stood on the far side of the
table with a sheaf of copied ledgers held against his chest. He was a scribe, young enough that ink had not
yet found every crease of his hands, though the habit of bending over records had already made him carry
himself as if beneath an invisible weight.
Cerys looked at him.
Halvard swallowed. “You said the numbers aloud when we were alone in the lower archive.”
“Those walls did not listen.”
“Walls are poor listeners.”
“Men are worse.”
He lowered his eyes.
Cerys turned back to the page. The seal pressed into its lower corner had been broken cleanly, then
warmed and pressed again. A clever forgery. Not good enough for a court that had forgotten how to trust
its own shadows, but good enough for a garrison officer who feared the contents more than the seal.
The report concerned Stormmarch.
Not supplies. Not relief. Not the condition of its quarantine.
Strength.
Stormmarch’s garrison strength was 9263.
The figure sat in the middle of the page like a coal refusing to cool.
“Read it,” Cerys said.

Halvard’s fingers tightened on the ledgers. “The report states that Stormmarch’s garrison strength is
9263.”
“Again.”
“Stormmarch’s garrison strength is 9263.”
The number entered the room and stood between them.
Cerys leaned back. The chair gave a faint wooden groan. No mirror hung in the chamber, and that was
deliberate. Reflections had a way of making the past appear more certain than it was. Still, the ash marked
everything here: the table, the ledgers, the sleeves of Cerys’s coat, the skin of the hands resting upon the
parchment. The epithet had followed them from the first whispered inventory of their life. The Ashen. A
title that sounded like judgment when spoken by enemies and inheritance when spoken by fools.
“Who counted them?” Cerys asked.
“The report does not say.”
“Who signed it?”
“The seal belongs to the quarantine office.”
“That was not my question.”
Halvard’s gaze lifted, then fell again. “No person signed it.”
“A report without a hand behind it.”
“Perhaps the hand was removed.”
There it was. Not wit. Fear sharpened into wit because fear had nowhere else to go.
Cerys traced the edge of the page with a nail. “Stormmarch lies outside the realm’s core holdings. It
remains quarantined. Yet someone wants the court to believe that 9263 armed bodies are standing behind
its walls, waiting to be counted.”
“Do you believe it?”
“I believe someone wants me to believe it.”
Halvard shifted the ledgers. Leather creaked softly. “That is not the same answer.”
“It is the only safe one.”
Outside, the ash thickened against the shutters. A muffled tread passed beyond the door. The guard did not
knock. Cerys had instructed them not to interrupt unless the fortress was burning or the dead had begun to
speak, and even then to consider whether either event might wait.
The page beneath their hand bore other marks: requisitions, delays, missing consignments. The old
language of power. A fortress did not need to rebel in order to threaten the realm. It needed only to
become expensive.
Cerys had spent years learning that every coin carried a memory. Copper remembered hunger. Silver
remembered promises. Gold remembered blood. As Master of Coin, Cerys was expected to make those
memories serve the living.

The title had once seemed like a door.
Now it felt like a lock placed gently around the throat.
Halvard set the ledgers upon the table. “There is another matter.”
“You have been waiting to say it.”
“I was waiting for you to finish looking at the figure.”
“Figures do not finish speaking.”
His mouth tightened. “The requisitions from Gloammarch have doubled.”
Cerys’s eyes moved toward the second stack.
“Doubled from what?” they asked.
Halvard hesitated.
Cerys looked at him until the hesitation became an answer without words.
“Do not invent a measure for me,” Cerys said. “Bring me the original requests.”
“They are below.”
“Then why are you holding copies?”
“Because the originals were damp.”
“Paper does not become damp in a sealed archive.”
“No.”
The word was barely audible.
Cerys rose.
The brazier’s heat fell away from them as they moved toward the door. Their boots made no sound on the
rush-strewn floor. At the threshold, the black metal latch showed the faintest rim of orange from the forge
fire beyond. Cerys laid a hand upon it and felt the warmth through the glove.
For one breath, memory stirred—not a memory of childhood, but of something older, inherited and
unwelcome. A crown concealed beneath ash. A throne that had never acknowledged its heir. The Bleeding
Crown had no face in Cerys’s thoughts, only weight: ceremony, obedience, ruin. The knowledge of blood
did not make a person royal. It made every silence around them dangerous.
Halvard watched from the table.
“You are not wearing it,” he said.
Cerys did not turn. “Wearing what?”
“The regalia.”
The chamber seemed to narrow.
Halvard glanced toward the locked coffer beneath the writing desk. He had not pointed, but he did not
need to. The Cinder-Wrought Aegis lay within, its cinder-dark surfaces shaped by the legacy of the
Sundering, fire-scarred regalia made for authority that had survived the world’s breaking. It was meant for

ceremony. For rule endured beneath ruin.
It was also evidence.
“What has made you observant?” Cerys asked.
“Nothing.”
“Nothing has poor eyesight.”
“I saw the coffer being moved.”
“By whom?”
Halvard’s face went pale beneath the ash dusting his hair. “I do not know.”
“Then you saw no one.”
“I saw two sets of hands.”
“That is still not a name.”
“There were no names.”
Cerys opened the door.
A guard stood outside beneath the narrow archway, helmet tucked beneath one arm. The corridor beyond
descended toward the lower archive, where old requisitions lay sealed in wax, mud, and the careful
neglect of frightened men. The guard straightened.
“Stay here,” Cerys said.
The guard’s eyes flicked toward Halvard.
“Both of us,” Cerys added.
The door closed behind them.
They descended through the fortress.
Gloammarch had been founded in 321 AS, when the Ash Wastes still offered enough stone and water to
tempt builders into believing permanence was possible. The founding inscription had been carved above
the western gate, though ash had eaten half the letters and left the rest like broken teeth. Cerys had read it
on arrival. The date had seemed less like a beginning than a confession.
At the turn of the stair, a draft moved through the cracks. It smelled of wet wool, old grease, and the bitter
mineral tang that rose from the wells after a hard fall of ash.
Cerys paused.
The Winter Reckoning had taught the realm to fear wells more than swords. It had begun in 270 AS and
ended in 283 AS, leaving 27,987 casualties and the Iron-Ring Cartel as victor. The victory had been
decided by betrayal at the eleventh hour; the concealed truth was that the victors had poisoned the wells of
their own allies.
No one spoke of that truth in court.
No one needed to.

A well remembered what a ledger could not.
Halvard caught up, breathing carefully. “You know about the coffer.”
“I know someone moved it.”
“You know what it contains.”
Cerys continued down. “You are a scribe. Do not mistake copied words for knowledge.”
“Then why keep it here?”
“Because no one searches what they are afraid to understand.”
“Who is afraid?”
Cerys stopped beneath the next arch.
Halvard came nearly level with them before realizing. His face had the strained, blank expression of a man
standing too close to a cliff and pretending the drop was not there.
“Everyone,” Cerys said.
Below, a door opened. Light spilled upward in a narrow gold blade.
Voices murmured beyond it.
Not guards. Not clerks.
Cerys felt the old arithmetic begin.
Stormmarch: 9263.
Gloammarch: contested ground, hungry for supplies and more hungry for certainty.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis beneath the desk.
Halvard’s copied ledgers against his chest.
And somewhere above them, the ash falling without wind.
Cerys moved down the final steps, one hand inside their coat, closing around the small key that opened the
coffer.
Halvard whispered, “Master of Coin.”
Cerys looked back.
He had never used the title as a form of address before. It sounded different in his mouth—not respectful,
not quite fearful. A warning offered too late.
“What?” Cerys asked.
“The report from Stormmarch was not delivered by courier.”
“Then how did it reach Gloammarch?”
Halvard’s gaze fixed upon the golden line of light beneath the archive door.
“It was already here.”

The murmurs beyond the door ceased.
Cerys heard the scrape of a chair. The soft drag of metal against metal. Someone inside had understood
that the visitors on the stair were no longer visitors at all.
The key pressed into Cerys’s palm.
Their inheritance felt suddenly less like a secret than a blade awaiting a hand.
Cerys touched the archive latch.
From within, a voice said, “Come in, Master of Coin.”
And the door began to open.
The door opened inward on a room without windows.
Shelves rose into the dark, their ledgers bound in hide gone gray with ash. Lamps burned behind sheets of
horn, each flame reduced to a dull yellow pulse. At the center stood a table of black wood, and upon it
rested a lantern whose metal had been worked into three interlocking cages.
The Thrice-Bound Lantern.
Cerys knew it before the light found its shape. Every child raised near the old accounts had heard of it,
though never in the same telling. Some said it had guided the first surveyors through the buried streets.
Others claimed its flame could burn beneath water, or that it showed a man the face he wore when no one
was watching.
The ledger beneath it mattered more.
A figure sat beyond the table, swathed in a dark robe. No crest marked the cloth. No weapon showed. The
face remained half-concealed by the lamp’s sickly glow.
Halvard entered behind Cerys and shut the door.
The latch fell with a small, final sound.
“Master of Coin,” said the figure.
Cerys stepped into the archive. “You have the advantage of knowing me.”
“I know the office.”
“That is not what you said.”
The figure’s hands lay flat upon the table. Ink stained the fingertips. A scribe, then, or someone who
wished to be mistaken for one. Behind the table, rows of shelves disappeared into the dimness, their
contents leaning against one another like exhausted soldiers.
Halvard moved to Cerys’s left. He had gone pale, though whether from fear or the lamplight was
impossible to tell.
Cerys looked at the ledger. Its cover had been sealed with black wax. No mark showed in the wax, no
household device, no sign of the Iron-Ring Cartel or House Morvain or the Ashen Vanguard. The absence
was deliberate. Whoever had placed it here had trusted concealment more than allegiance.
“Where is the report?” Cerys asked.

“Under your hand.”
The robe shifted. A second figure stood in the narrow gap between the shelves.
Cerys did not turn toward it. The archive had become a vessel, and every breath within it was water rising.
One body at the table. One behind. Halvard near the door. Cerys between them all.
The old instinct was to count. Exits. Distances. Weight of metal. Cost of blood.
Instead, Cerys placed a hand against the breast beneath the ash-colored layers and felt the hard edge of
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis resting there.
Since 356 AS, Cerys Sablewood the Ashen had wielded The Cinder-Wrought Aegis.
The regalia had never been meant for concealment. Its cinder-dark surfaces were made to be seen beneath
banners, beneath the eyes of kneeling courts, beneath the burden of authority that outlived the flesh
carrying it. Yet the thing had been wrapped, hidden, carried through corridors where servants lowered
their eyes for reasons they did not understand.
The secret weight pressed back against Cerys’s palm.
“The Cinder-Wrought Aegis,” said the seated figure.
Halvard’s breath caught.
Cerys let the hand fall. “You have been searching my clothing.”
“No. We have been searching the realm.”
“Then you have searched badly.”
“Perhaps.” The figure tipped the ledger toward the lantern. “Stormmarch was sealed before the report left
its walls.”
“It did not leave its walls.”
“No.”
“Then someone in Gloammarch wrote it.”
“No.”
Cerys felt the room narrow. “You enjoy the word.”
“I enjoy words that survive examination.”
The hidden figure moved at last. Cloth whispered against stone. A hand emerged from the dark and
touched the ledger’s spine.
Cerys saw the hand tremble.
Not fear, perhaps. Fatigue. Or age. The archive had the smell of old paper, lamp oil, and the mineral
bitterness that crept through every wall in the Ash Wastes. But beneath it lay another scent, faint and wet,
like earth opened after a long burial.
“What is in it?” Halvard asked.
The question came too quickly. His voice was thin.

The seated figure looked past Cerys to him. “You are Halvard Sablewood.”
Halvard straightened. “I am a scribe.”
“That was not the question.”
“It is the answer I have.”
Cerys heard the lie’s small machinery turning. Halvard had been born in 408 AS. That much was entered
in a dozen records, each one copied by a different hand and preserved under different seals. He had spent
his life among words, but words had not made him safe. They had only taught him where men hid their
knives.
The figure returned its attention to Cerys. “Open it.”
“You summoned me to do clerical work?”
“I summoned the Master of Coin to witness a correction.”
“Corrections are made in the daylight.”
“Not this one.”
Cerys broke the seal with a fingernail.
The wax gave way without resistance. Inside lay sheets of narrow vellum, each covered in columns. The
script was precise, cramped, and old-fashioned. At the bottom of the first page, a line had been written in a
different hand.
STORMMARCH: THRICE-BOUND LANTERN FORGED IN 72 AS.
The letters seemed to lift from the page.
Cerys looked at the lantern.
Its three cages held no visible wick. Light gathered within them anyway, cold and steady, as if the flame
had been taught obedience. The metal was scarred around the hinges. A dark crust filled the smallest
seams. Stormmarch had forged it in 72 AS, before Gloammarch had been raised from the waste, before the
realm learned to call certain ruins holdings and others quarantines.
“Why is this here?” Cerys asked.
“Because it was removed.”
“From Stormmarch?”
The figure nodded.
“By whom?”
The silence that followed had shape. It stood at the table, broad-shouldered and patient.
Cerys read the columns.
Grain. Salt. Lamp oil. Iron. Medicines. Names were absent, replaced by offices and marks. Beside each
entry, a number had been crossed out and another entered. The ink had bled through the vellum in places,
staining the reverse like bruises.
“These are requisitions.”

“Were.”
“Some of these deliveries never arrived.”
“They arrived.”
Cerys lifted their eyes. “Then the accounts were falsified afterward.”
“Before.”
The hidden figure spoke. “The reports sent from Stormmarch were not reports of shortages. They were
reports of substitutions.”
Halvard stepped nearer despite himself. “Substitutions of what?”
The figure looked at him.
Cerys turned a page before the answer could come. A narrow strip had been sewn into the binding, and
upon it a second line had been written.
AEGIS TRANSFER CONFIRMED. 356 AS.
The room seemed to lose its air.
Cerys’s fingers tightened around the vellum.
The seated figure watched with the quiet attention of someone who had placed a snare and now waited for
the animal to discover its own weight.
“You knew,” Cerys said.
“We knew the regalia had changed hands.”
“Changed hands.”
“Wielded,” the figure corrected. “Since 356 AS.”
Halvard stared at Cerys. The look was not accusation. That made it worse. Accusation could be answered.
Wonder had no handle.
Cerys closed the ledger.
The lantern’s threefold light moved across the cover, revealing impressions in the hide: shallow lines,
almost invisible, cut in a pattern like a crown seen through smoke.
The Bleeding Crown had no crown.
Not anymore. Its authority survived in rumor, in blood hidden beneath names, in old men who spoke of
obedience as though it were a debt owed to the dead. Cerys had learned early that inheritance was not a
garment handed down. It was a hook lodged beneath the ribs. One could conceal it. One could pretend not
to feel it. But the body knew.
The figure at the table said, “You are the unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown.”
Halvard made a sound behind Cerys.
Not a word. A break in the world.
Cerys placed the ledger on the table. “You have mistaken a private insult for a political fact.”

“Have I?”
“You possess forged accounts, a stolen relic, and enough confidence to mistake both for proof.”
“The accounts are genuine.”
“The lantern?”
“Also genuine.”
“Then your conclusion is still false.”
“Is it?”
The question was soft.
Cerys looked toward the door. It remained shut. Halvard stood between the hinges and the armed silence
in the room. A scribe, born in 408 AS, carrying no visible sword. His hand hovered near his sleeve.
“Halvard,” Cerys said.
“Yes.”
“Take the ledger.”
He did not move.
The seated figure smiled, though Cerys saw only the slight change in shadow. “It cannot leave.”
“Everything leaves,” Cerys said.
“Not this.”
Cerys drew the Aegis from beneath the ash-dark layers.
The regalia came free without a ring or scrape. Its surfaces caught the lantern’s divided light and gave it
back in a dull, emberless sheen. It was not beautiful. Beauty asked to be admired. The Cinder-Wrought
Aegis demanded endurance.
The second figure moved from the shelves.
Halvard flinched.
Cerys raised the regalia between them, not as shield but as declaration. The figure stopped at once.
There it was: the proof hidden beneath every denial. Not fear of Cerys. Fear of what the artifact allowed
others to believe.
“The Cinder-Wrought Aegis is regalia,” Cerys said. “It is not a confession.”
“No,” said the seated figure. “It is permission.”
“For whom?”
“For the realm.”
Beyond the archive door, something struck the corridor wall.
Once.
Then again.

Dust whispered from the ceiling. The lamps bent in their horn cages, all three flames leaning toward the
sound.
Halvard seized the ledger. This time, the seated figure did not stop him.
Cerys kept the Aegis raised.
“What is coming?” Halvard asked.
The figure’s gaze fixed upon the door.
“Those who were meant to receive the report.”
Another blow landed. The wood shuddered. A thin line of ash sifted beneath the threshold.
Cerys felt the old hook beneath the ribs draw tight.
“Open the door,” said the figure.
“Why?”
“Because they believe the heir is inside.”
Cerys stared at the black seal broken beneath their hand.
“And if they are wrong?”
The figure leaned toward the Thrice-Bound Lantern. Its three cages clicked softly, one after another, as
though something within had begun to turn.
“Then let them discover what you are instead.”
The door buckled inward.
The door buckled inward.
Cerys lowered the Aegis by a finger’s breadth.
“Now.”
Halvard seized the bar.
He was a scribe, not a soldier. His hands had been made for reed pens, scraped vellum, and the careful
burial of figures beneath columns of ink. They trembled as he lifted the iron from its sockets. Cerys saw
the tremor and hated him for it, then hated herself for noticing. Fear was a kind of account. Once entered,
it demanded to be carried forward.
The figure withdrew into the lantern’s shadow.
Halvard looked to Cerys.
She nodded.
He opened the door.
The first man came through with the force of a kicked corpse. He wore a coat stiffened by ash and carried
a short blade in one hand. Cerys turned the Aegis.
The regalia caught the blade with a sound like a bell struck beneath deep water. Fire ran along its
cinder-dark surface. The man’s wrist twisted. His knife fell. Cerys drove the rim of the Aegis into his

throat and felt cartilage give.
He folded without a cry.
A second shape crowded behind him.
Halvard made a noise—small, involuntary—and snatched up the fallen knife. He held it badly, point
wavering toward the doorway.
“Do not,” Cerys said.
The second intruder paused.
Beyond him, the passage burned with pale torchlight. Ash moved through it in slow veils, stirring from
every stone seam. More silhouettes waited there. Their faces were hidden beneath scarves. Their silence
was worse than shouting. Men who came to kill often announced themselves. Men who came to retrieve
something kept their breath for the work.
“Master Sablewood,” said the second figure.
The title entered the room like a coin placed upon a table.
Cerys felt the hidden inheritance stir beneath the ribs—not pride, not fear. Recognition. The Bleeding
Crown had survived by teaching its blood to flinch from its own name.
“You have mistaken the chamber,” Cerys said.
“We were told the heir was here.”
“Then whoever told you has mistaken more than the chamber.”
The man’s gaze passed over Cerys, over Halvard, and settled on the black seal broken upon the desk. The
report lay beneath it, half-covered by a ledger. Its pages had been written in Halvard’s narrow hand. Ink
had dried in the grooves of his fingers.
The intruder’s attention sharpened.
“Give us the report.”
“No.”
“Give us the heir.”
Cerys heard the lantern click.
Once.
Twice.
The third cage remained still.
The figure in the shadows said, “They are not asking for what they think they are asking for.”
The intruder shifted toward the voice. “Show yourself.”
“Why?”
Something moved outside in the passage. Metal whispered against metal.
Halvard backed toward the desk. He was pale now, but the knife remained in his hand.

Cerys did not look at him. “Take the report.”
His eyes widened.
“You heard me.”
“And you?”
“I will make them regret entering.”
That was not a promise she could afford to break.
Halvard lunged for the papers. The second intruder crossed the threshold. Cerys stepped into him. The
Aegis struck his forearm; bone cracked. He turned with surprising speed and drove his shoulder into her
chest.
The room tilted.
Ash filled her mouth.
She caught the edge of the desk before falling and saw the account ledger burst open beneath her hand.
Rows of figures marched across the page, obedient and merciless. Grain, iron, timber, men. The realm
reduced to what could be counted before it was burned.
A knife flashed near her face.
Cerys seized the attacker’s wrist.
He was stronger. She felt the pressure building in her fingers, felt the old hook beneath the ribs draw tight
again. Not now, she thought. Not before the door. Not before the report.
The Aegis answered before she commanded it.
Heat flared between them.
The attacker screamed. His sleeve caught fire, though no flame touched it. Cerys wrenched him sideways
and sent him crashing into the wall. The stones drank the sound.
Halvard had the report.
A third figure entered.
This one wore no scarf. Ash had pasted itself to his brow and cheeks, giving him the appearance of a man
already half unearthed. His eyes went to Halvard.
“Scribe.”
Halvard froze.
Cerys rose.
The man pointed toward him. “Bring the pages.”
Halvard’s grip tightened. “They are sealed.”
“The seal is broken.”
“It is still forbidden.”
The man smiled without warmth. “So is breathing, when the order comes.”

He advanced.
Cerys moved between them.
The Aegis weighed more than it had a moment ago. Its surface held the color of old embers beneath ash.
Authority was the shape of it, but authority had never been the same as safety. She had learned that from
ledgers. She had learned it from blood.
“I know what you want,” she said.
“Do you?”
“You want the figures removed before they reach the wrong hands.”
“No.”
“You want the names erased.”
“No.”
“You want the truth preserved only where it can be used.”
The man’s expression altered by the smallest degree.
Behind Cerys, Halvard breathed through his nose. He was trying not to cry. She could hear it. The shame
of hearing it was almost unbearable.
The man said, “The truth is not in the pages.”
“No,” Cerys said. “The truth is in what the pages cost.”
For a moment the chamber held still.
Then the man struck.
Cerys caught his hand against the Aegis. The impact shook her shoulder. He followed with his other fist.
She turned, took the blow along the ribs, and drove the heel of the regalia beneath his jaw.
He stumbled.
The figure by the lantern moved.
Not quickly. Not like a soldier. The shadow simply seemed to arrive beside the man. A hand rose, and the
Thrice-Bound Lantern gave a low, hollow tone.
The attacker’s body seized.
His mouth opened, but no sound emerged. Ash poured from his throat in a thin gray stream. He fell to his
knees, clawing at his own collar.
The lantern’s first cage went dark.
Cerys stared.
The figure placed one hand upon the lantern’s frame.
“Leave,” it said to the men in the passage.
They did not move.

“Leave,” the figure repeated.
The nearest silhouette raised a crossbow.
Halvard saw it first. “Down!”
The bolt struck the wall where Cerys’s head had been. Stone burst against her cheek. She dropped behind
the desk as another bolt punched through the doorframe.
The wounded man on the floor crawled toward the report.
Halvard stepped back, clutching the pages to his chest.
Cerys rose with ash and blood warm along her face. “Halvard. Give me the report.”
He looked at her.
He had been born in 408 AS. She remembered the entry because she had signed the register herself,
though the memory belonged to a room very far from this one: a boy’s name, a clerk’s mark, a future
entered before it had learned to resist. Halvard had been a scribe ever since the realm had needed men to
make ruin legible.
His voice shook. “If they take it, they will know.”
“They already know enough.”
“They will know about the wells.”
Cerys went still.
The passage seemed to narrow around that word.
The Winter Reckoning had begun in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS. Its dead numbered 27,987. The
Iron-Ring Cartel had been named victor, and every court that mattered had repeated the verdict until
victory became a kind of law.
But the wells had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands.
The betrayal had come at the eleventh hour, concealed beneath winter banners and iron marks. Allies had
drunk together, believing the water would carry them through the last cold. The Cartel had watched them
sicken. It had called the deaths necessity. It had called the war concluded.
Halvard looked down at the report. “It is written here.”
“Not plainly.”
“Plainly enough.”
Another bolt struck the desk. The wood jumped. One of the pages slipped free and skated across the floor.
The wounded man reached for it.
Cerys stamped on his hand.
He screamed this time.
“Halvard,” she said.
He threw the report.

Not to her.
Into the lantern.
The figure turned sharply.
The pages vanished between the three cages. Flame rose without color. Ink lifted from the paper in black
threads, twisting upward like drowned hair. The chamber filled with the smell of scorched hide and bitter
metal.
Cerys felt something inside her break—not the hidden crown, not the secret itself, but the belief that
knowledge could be protected by keeping it close.
The figure seized Halvard by the collar and dragged him behind the lantern.
“What have you done?” Cerys asked.
“Bought the next breath.”
“For whom?”
The door exploded inward.
Ash and splintered wood struck the chamber. Cerys raised the Aegis. Through the ringing in her skull, she
saw the passage beyond: more figures, more weapons, and behind them the black mouth of the stair
descending into the lower keep.
A banner showed briefly through the ash.
Not a color. Not a sigil she could name.
Only a strip of dark cloth bearing the iron mark of the Iron-Ring Cartel.
The sight opened an old wound in the realm.
The man beneath her boot twisted. She lifted the Aegis to finish him.
“Do not,” said the figure.
“Why?”
“Because he is not the one who came for you.”
Cerys looked past the ruined doorway.
At the far end of the passage, someone stood apart from the others. No weapon showed in that person’s
hands. No scarf covered the face. The ash moved around them and did not settle.
Their gaze fixed upon Cerys.
Not the Aegis.
Not the dead report.
Her.
The figure beside the lantern whispered, “There is your mistake.”
Cerys’s grip tightened until the regalia cut into her palm.

The stranger took one step forward.
And somewhere below, beneath stone and sealed earth, the Bleeding Crown began to beat.

Chapter 7
Hollowreach had been built to keep things out.
The walls rose from the Gloaming Reach in blackened courses, each stone sealed against the next with a
pale substance that had cracked into veins. Watchfires guttered along the parapets, their smoke pressed flat
by the damp. Beyond the gates, the road vanished into a pallid marsh where reeds stood motionless
beneath a skin of grey water.
Under quarantine, the settlement had learned the shape of silence.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless crossed the inner yard beneath the gaze of men who did not trust him
enough to salute. He wore the iron-dark mantle of a Warden-Commander, though the clasp had been
polished too often and reflected the firelight like a watching eye. No face, no scar, no height had ever been
set down in the records to define him. Authority had done that work. So had the epithet.
The Oathless.
It followed him more faithfully than any oath.
A bell sounded once from the wall. Not an alarm. A warning that wanted to become one.
Ignatz entered the quarantine hall.
The air inside was colder than the yard. Charcoal braziers burned beneath the narrow windows, filling the
chamber with the bitter smell of ash and old herbs. A table had been dragged beneath the far arch. Papers
lay upon it, weighted by a black reliquary and a ward whose edge swallowed the light.
The Hollow Edge had been forged in 216 AS. Its attunement cost 21.
Beside it rested the Chalice of Ashdeep, wrapped in oil-dark cloth. The reliquary had been forged in 323
AS. Its attunement cost 27.
Neither artifact belonged in a room where men lied for coin. That was precisely why they had been
brought there.
Ignatz Marrowgate stood behind the table with a ledger open before him. He served as Quartermaster, and
the records identified him plainly: born in 425 AS, appointed to the stores, entrusted with the movement of
food, iron, lamp oil, medicines, and every other small necessity by which armies pretended they were not
made of hunger.
He did not look up when Ignatz entered.
“Warden-Commander.”
“Quartermaster.”
The younger Ignatz’s fingers tightened on the ledger’s spine. He had the tense, colorless manner of a man
who feared both discovery and the consequences of being believed. No temperament had been assigned to
him by history. History had not yet decided what to do with him.
Ignatz Ashgrove glanced at the empty chairs.
“Where are the others?”
“Which others?”

“The ones who summoned me.”
Marrowgate swallowed. “No one summoned you.”
“Then I have been invited.”
“I said no such thing.”
The Warden-Commander laid one gloved hand upon the table. The Chalice of Ashdeep trembled beneath
its cloth, though the air was still. He felt the ward’s severity through the leather, a hollow pressure against
the bones of his wrist.
Outside, a voice called from the walls. Another answered. The words blurred in the damp.
Marrowgate lowered his eyes to the ledger. “The Iron-Ring Cartel is seated at Hollowreach.”
The phrase had the polished ugliness of something repeated in secret until it became official.
Ignatz let the silence receive it.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel seated at Hollowreach,” he said.
“Yes.”
“And Hollowreach is ruled by The Iron-Ring Cartel.”
Marrowgate’s mouth worked once before sound came. “Yes.”
The words seemed to alter the room. The braziers burned lower. The walls leaned inward, listening.
Hollowreach had been founded in 56 AS. It lay in the Gloaming Reach, where the ground exhaled vapors
that silvered the grass and turned exposed metal green. It was a core location under quarantine, though the
quarantine had long ago stopped resembling a measure and begun resembling a government. Gates, seals,
patrols, inspections: these were the architecture of obedience.
Now the Iron-Ring Cartel sat within it.
Not camped. Not besieged. Seated.
A merchant power with no crown had taken the chair at the heart of a sealed settlement, and every
document still called the place a quarantine zone.
Ignatz lifted the ledger. Marrowgate did not resist.
The first pages concerned Crookvale. Founded in 295 AS in The High Spires, rebuilt after its ruin,
retaining a garrison of 1004, and still outside the core holdings. The inventory listed grain, bolts, winter
cloth, lamp oil. The columns were neat. Too neat.
“Crookvale has received no iron,” Ignatz said.
“The road is dangerous.”
“The road has always been dangerous.”
“It is outside the core holdings.”
“That does not make steel walk.”
Marrowgate’s gaze darted toward the shuttered windows. “The wagons were redirected.”

“To Hollowreach.”
“I did not redirect them.”
Ignatz turned a page. “The Iron-Ring Cartel did.”
