A pale smear of light showed beneath the shutters. Dawn, or some sick imitation of it. In Hollowreach,
morning had the color of old bruises.
The Warden-Commander had been born in 258 AS, in a year when the realm still believed the wounds of
the Sundering could close if watched closely enough. He had spent his life among watchers. He knew the
difference between vigilance and fear. Fear looked outward. Vigilance looked inward first.
He had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel for long enough to know that their messages never arrived
alone. A scrap concealed in a ration tally. A mark beneath a seal. A phrase spoken by a courier who did
not know its meaning. Each secret became a thread, and threads became a net.
He had told himself the Cartel purchased information because information was cheaper than war.
He had told himself many things.
Marrowgate whispered, “You were seen speaking with them.”
“I speak with everyone.”
“Not as a Warden-Commander.”
“Then perhaps they saw me as a man.”
The Quartermaster flinched. That, more than accusation, revealed the wound.
Ignatz looked again at the two artifacts. The Hollow Edge lay uncovered now. Its surface was not bright
metal but a narrow absence cut into the shape of a blade, a ward forged in 216 AS to make emptiness
obedient. The Chalice of Ashdeep remained wrapped, but its presence made the room feel buried.
Reliquary. Ash. Deepness. The names had been chosen by people who believed names could warn the
soul.
“Why bring these here?” Ignatz asked.
Marrowgate closed the ledger. “Because the Cartel wants the quarantine opened.”
“The Cartel rules Hollowreach.”
“It wants the gates opened by lawful order.”
“And if the order is refused?”
“Then it will be opened by necessity.”
Ignatz heard the soft scrape of a boot beyond the door. One boot. Then silence.
He did not turn.
“Who carries the order?”
Marrowgate’s face had gone damp. “You do.”
The Warden-Commander smiled without warmth. “You have mistaken me for a loyal man.”

“No.”
“Good.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel believes you understand the cost of delay.”
It was nearly amusing. They believed many things about him. They believed his access could be bought.
They believed his silence was the silence of a disciplined officer rather than a man constantly choosing
which betrayal would leave the fewest corpses. They believed he belonged to them because money had
crossed from one hand to another.
Perhaps they were right.
On the table, the ledger’s page stirred though no wind touched it. Beneath the supply tallies, written in a
different ink, lay a sentence without a signature.
The Bleeding Crown was the victor of The War of Endless Vigil.
Ignatz read it twice.
The war had begun in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS. Its record counted 81577 casualties. The aggressors
had been totally routed. The Bleeding Crown stood in the histories as victor, crowned by blood and
prolonged watchfulness.
But the histories were only the portion of truth permitted to survive.
Secretly, the losing commander had been bribed to withdraw.
Ignatz placed two fingers over the sentence. The paper was warm.
“Who wrote this?”
Marrowgate shook his head.
“Quartermaster.”
“I don’t know.”
“No one writes in a ledger without knowing.”
“I was told to preserve the page.”
“By whom?”
The younger man stared at him, and for one moment Ignatz saw the future in his eyes: a rope, a closed
cell, an official explanation, a corpse made useful by the absence of a name.
Then the door opened.
A gust of marsh air entered, carrying rot and cold water. No one stood in the threshold. Only a strip of red
cord had been tied to the latch.
Ignatz felt the Cartel’s presence before he saw the message. He had known it in alleys, in garrison rooms,
beside emptied cups. A pressure behind the world. A hand resting lightly on the throat.
Marrowgate backed away from the table.
“You will take the order,” he said.

Ignatz untied the cord. A small metal token hung from it, stamped with a ring broken by a single notch.
“If I refuse?”
“You will not.”
“Because Hollowreach is ruled by The Iron-Ring Cartel?”
“Because the gates cannot remain closed.”
The Warden-Commander looked toward the walls. Beyond them, the quarantined settlement waited in its
damp enclosure, its streets washed clean of footprints, its people breathing behind barred shutters.
Somewhere in that silence, the Cartel counted its profits. Somewhere, a guard watched the road and
wondered whether the next figure to emerge would carry sickness, orders, or a knife.
Ignatz closed his fist around the token.
The metal cut his palm.
He remembered the first oath he had broken. He could not remember what it had been sworn to protect.
Only the sensation of speaking the words while already knowing they were dead.
“Open the western archive,” he said.
Marrowgate stared. “Why?”
“Because if I am to deliver an order, I will know what it contains.”
“That archive is sealed.”
“So am I.”
He turned toward the door.
Behind him, the Chalice of Ashdeep gave a single hollow chime beneath its cloth.
Ignatz stopped.
From beyond the walls came the sound of the quarantine bell again—once, then once more—and beneath
it, faint as breath against glass, the first cry of someone in the marsh.
Marrowgate did not move to stop him.
That was the first thing Ignatz noticed. The second was the quartermaster’s hand sliding beneath his coat,
not toward a weapon—Marrowgate had never carried one in the presence of the Chalice—but toward the
packet hidden in the inner lining.
The bell sounded again.
The cry beyond the walls answered it.
Not a human cry, Ignatz thought. Then he heard the shape of words inside it, torn thin by distance and
marsh fog.
“Commander.”
Marrowgate’s voice had lost its dry impatience.
Ignatz looked back. “If you mean to warn me, do it before the archive opens.”

“The western archive was sealed by order of—”
“By whose order?”
Marrowgate stopped.
There were names that could still command silence in Hollowreach. Names that belonged to the Crown, to
the Cartel, to the dead. Marrowgate weighed one against another behind his eyes and found none worth
spending.
Ignatz turned the latch.
The iron had been cold a moment before. Now it held a faint warmth, as if something on the other side had
pressed its palm against it.
He withdrew his hand.
Beneath the cloth, the Chalice of Ashdeep chimed once more.
Marrowgate flinched.
Ignatz despised him for it, though the sound had entered his own bones.
“Stand there,” Ignatz said.
“Where?”
“Between me and the door.”
“That is not a sensible instruction.”
“It is the one you have.”
Marrowgate’s mouth worked. He was a young man by the standards of command, born in 425 AS and
already carrying the stoop of a servant who had spent his life apologizing to locked rooms. Ignatz knew
this because Quartermaster Ignatz Marrowgate had once been required to submit his birth record with the
others. He remembered the ink, the thinness of the paper, the careful way Marrowgate had watched him
read it.
Now the quartermaster planted himself before the door.
Ignatz drew the token from his palm. Blood had gathered in its grooves, black in the lamplight. He pressed
it to the lock.
The western archive opened without a click.
A breath came through the gap.
It smelled of wet stone, old ash, and the bitter sweetness of something rotting beneath water.
Marrowgate whispered a prayer.
Ignatz stepped inside.
The archive was narrower than he remembered. Shelves climbed both walls, bowed beneath ledgers,
sealed packets, bone-white tablets, and clay cylinders marked with the cracked sigils of orders no living
clerk could explain. Dust filmed everything except the floor. Across the flagstones ran a dark trail of
water.

It led inward.
Ignatz kept his eyes on it.
“Close the door,” he said.
Marrowgate remained outside. “You said to stand between you and it.”
“Then stand between me and the corridor.”
The door swung shut.
The darkness inside the archive gathered around Ignatz with the intimacy of a cloak. He touched the wall
and found the old iron brackets. One by one, the lamps woke beneath his fingers, burning with a low blue
flame.
At the end of the chamber stood a table.
On it lay a ledger opened to the middle.
He had not left it there.
Ignatz crossed the room, every step measured. The trail of water ended at the table’s foot. A single drop
fell from the lower edge of the ledger and struck the stone.
He did not touch the book.
The page was ruled in columns. The handwriting belonged to several hands, some cramped with fear,
some broad with authority. The oldest entry was written in brown ink that had faded nearly to yellow.
The War of Endless Vigil waged at Hollowreach in 251 AS.
The words had been underlined so heavily the quill had torn the page.
Ignatz read them once.
Then again.
The bell outside struck.
The sound traveled through the archive’s stone and set the shelves trembling. A bundle of loose tablets
shifted overhead. One fell, broke against the table, and spilled a grey powder across the ledger.
Marrowgate shouted from beyond the door.
Ignatz seized the book and pulled it clear.
The broken tablet had exposed another line beneath the page. He brushed the powder aside with two
fingers.
A roster.
Names, postings, permissions. Not soldiers. Observers. Wardens. Physicians. Those assigned to remain
where the war had ended and count the costs after the banners went dark.
His eyes moved down the list.
Maelis Greyfen serves at Hollowreach.
The line had been written in fresh black ink.

Ignatz felt the room contract.
He knew no Maelis Greyfen. That did not comfort him. Names were rarely dangerous because of what
they revealed. They were dangerous because of what someone had taken the trouble to conceal.
The ink was not old. It had not belonged to the war’s record. Someone had opened the archive recently,
written the name, and left the ledger for him.
A message, then.
Or bait.
The Hollow Edge lay in a narrow case beneath the roster. Ignatz had seen it once, years ago, before the
ward was given over to another hand. The case had no hinge. Its lid was a slab of dark glass fitted into
iron.
He lifted it.
The ward within was pale and thin, not like a blade but like the memory of one. It seemed to have been cut
from a piece of winter sky. No maker’s mark disturbed its surface. Only a date had been etched along the
inner rim.
The Hollow Edge forged at Hollowvale in 216 AS.
Ignatz did not touch it.
Attunement to The Hollow Edge cost 21.
He knew the number because the cost had been entered beside the ward’s name in a registry meant for
men who believed everything could be measured before it was endured. Twenty-one for the ward.
Twenty-seven for the Chalice of Ashdeep. The numbers had never made either artifact safer.
The Hollow Edge gave off no light.
Still, the archive seemed to arrange itself around it.
“What did you find?” Marrowgate called.
Ignatz closed the case.
“Dust.”
“You are not a man who goes into a sealed archive for dust.”
“Then perhaps you should stop asking questions you cannot afford answered.”
The quartermaster’s silence came back through the door, thick with resentment.
Ignatz turned another page.
The old ledger had been altered in places. Whole entries had been scraped away, leaving shallow scars. A
red thread marked the pages that survived. It ran from the war at Hollowreach to later reports of fever,
disappearances, failed harvests, and voices heard in the marsh after the quarantine bells began.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had possessed the archive long enough to erase what it wished.
Or long enough to make erasure look like preservation.
A folded strip of black paper rested between the next pages.

Ignatz took it.
No seal. No signature.
The writing was small and exact.
The western waterline is open. The first bell was not a warning.
He read the sentence without breathing.
Outside, something struck the keep wall.
Once.
A dull impact. Then another, lower down.
Marrowgate swore. “Commander?”
“Do not open the door.”
“I had no intention—”
The third impact came from within the wall.
Ignatz looked toward the shelves.
Dust sifted from between the stones. One of the blue flames bent sideways though there was no wind.
Somewhere behind the masonry, something scraped its way along the inner passage, slow and patient.
The cry sounded again from the marsh.
This time it was unmistakably human.
A woman’s voice, perhaps. Or a child’s. The sound rose until it broke, then continued in a register no
throat should have held.
Marrowgate began fumbling with the outer bolts.
Ignatz crossed the room and placed the token against the door.
“Leave them.”
“The lock is not enough.”
“It has held for two centuries.”
“Not against this.”
Ignatz’s hand tightened around the metal. The token’s edge bit deeper into his palm. He could feel the
blood returning, warm and insistent.
“Who opened the archive?” he asked.
Marrowgate went still.
“Answer me.”
“I did not.”
“I did not ask what you did.”

“You think I brought that thing here?”
“I think you know more than you have said.”
The quartermaster breathed hard. “I know the western archive was sealed. I know the order came through
channels no clerk can access. I know someone has been taking pages from the quarantine registers. I know
Maelis Greyfen serves at Hollowreach, because that name appeared in the dispatches this morning.”
Ignatz stared at the door.
“Why was I not told?”
“Because the dispatches were addressed to the Cartel.”
There it was.
Not spoken loudly. Not spoken with courage. But spoken.
The admission settled between them.
Ignatz had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel for long enough to recognize the shape of their hunger.
They did not buy facts. They bought leverage sharpened into facts. A garrison strength. A patrol route.
The hour at which a gate changed hands. Small truths that made larger cruelties possible.
He had told himself the realm was already broken.
He had told himself a man could choose which cracks widened.
The archive wall groaned.
A line appeared in the stone beside the table. Fine as a hair. Wetness welled through it, darkened the
mortar, and ran downward.
Marrowgate whispered, “What is that?”
Ignatz opened the case again.
The Hollow Edge remained where he had left it, pale and severe. He lifted it from its cradle.
The cold entered him before the ward touched his skin.
For an instant he stood in a corridor of drowned banners. He saw watchfires burning along a ridge. He saw
soldiers with ash on their faces, standing beneath a sky split by the old wound of the Sundering.
Somewhere beyond them, an army was breaking—not from defeat, but from exhaustion, its line
unraveling while unseen hands counted the price.
Then the vision closed.
Ignatz found himself kneeling.
The ward lay across his palm.
Twenty-one.
The cost moved through him like a nail driven beneath the ribs.
His breath came out white.
“Commander,” Marrowgate said. “Open this door.”

Ignatz rose.
The thing in the wall scraped closer.
He carried The Hollow Edge to the seam. With his free hand, he unbolted the door.
Marrowgate recoiled. “What are you doing?”
“Finding out who has come to collect.”
The door opened inward.
The corridor beyond was empty.
At its far end, the quarantine lamps burned in a wavering line. Water shone across the flagstones. No
footprints marked it, though the trail continued from the archive threshold and disappeared beneath
Marrowgate’s boots.
Ignatz looked down.
The quartermaster’s shadow pointed the wrong way.
Marrowgate saw it too.
His face emptied.
Behind them, inside the archive, the Chalice of Ashdeep gave a hollow chime.
And from the darkness beyond the shelves, Maelis Greyfen said, “You were not meant to read that.”
Ignatz did not turn toward the dark.
He watched the wrong-facing shadow tremble on the wet stones. It trembled as if something beneath it had
laid a hand upon its head.
Marrowgate made a thin sound in his throat. His fingers found the doorframe, though whether to steady
himself or bar the way, Ignatz could not tell.
“Maelis,” Ignatz said.
The name went down the corridor and returned altered. Not echoed. Remembered.
A shelf creaked in the archive.
“Quartermaster,” Maelis called from the dark, “you have opened the door.”
“I opened it,” Ignatz said.
“You opened nothing. It was waiting.”
A smell drifted from beyond the threshold: wet ash, old iron, and something sweetly rotten beneath both.
Ignatz had known battlefields that smelled cleaner. He kept one hand near his sword, though the weapon
seemed suddenly a childish answer to a question no steel had been made to ask.
Marrowgate stared at him.
“Warden-Commander,” he whispered, “what did you read?”
Ignatz ignored him. His own shadow had begun to lengthen toward the archive.

He could feel the Chalice of Ashdeep behind him, though he could not see it. The reliquary’s hollow
chime still vibrated in his teeth. The sound had not ceased. It had merely become too deep for hearing, a
pressure in the bones, a second pulse beneath his own.
“Come into the lamp-light,” Ignatz said.
“No.”
“Maelis.”
“No, Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
Marrowgate flinched at the epithet. Everyone did, sooner or later. Some heard accusation in it. Some heard
promise. Ignatz had long ago stopped deciding which was worse.
The darkness between the shelves shifted.
A woman stepped into the furthest quarantine lamp.
Maelis Greyfen wore the gray of service at Hollowreach, but the cloth drank the lamp-glow instead of
reflecting it. Water darkened the hem. Her face seemed composed from the same pale substance as the ash
sealed in the archive jars. She held no weapon.
That did not comfort him.
“You were not meant to read that,” she said again.
Ignatz glanced at the open folio lying on the archive table behind her. He had seen only a few lines before
the door had opened, but the words had fixed themselves inside him. Not ink. A wound shaped like ink.
“Then you should not have left it where a commander could find it.”
“You were not meant to come here.”
“I came because the dead keep changing the orders.”
Marrowgate swallowed. “The orders?”
Ignatz heard the fear in the quartermaster’s voice and despised him for offering it so freely. Fear was a
currency. Someone always came to collect.
Maelis looked toward Marrowgate’s shadow.
“Your assistant has been counting the wrong things.”
“I have no assistant,” Marrowgate said.
“You have a shadow.”
The shadow beneath him twitched.
Marrowgate’s hand left the doorframe. He raised it as though to shield his face, then seemed to realize
there was nowhere to hide from what had no face at all.
Ignatz stepped between them.
“Speak plainly.”
Maelis’s gaze settled on him. The lamps guttered, though no wind moved through the corridor.

“Plain speech is what brought this place to ruin.”
“Hollowreach was ruined before your speech.”
“Hollowreach was contained.”
“Containment is a word used by people standing outside the grave.”
Maelis’s mouth tightened. “You have always preferred the grave. It cannot contradict your reports.”
The accusation struck too near the hidden chamber of him.
Ignatz had sold reports. Not all of them. Never the ones that would open the gates to slaughter. That was
the lie he carried, polished and turned over whenever sleep refused him. He gave the Iron-Ring Cartel
routes, dispositions, shortages—small truths, he had told himself. Truths that kept their hands from
reaching for larger knives.
But the Cartel had never paid for small truths.
Its coin had found him in the dark places between duty and need. Its questions had arrived folded in
harmless orders. Its gratitude had been absence: no blade in his back, no accusation at the gate, no sudden
disappearance for which a commander required an explanation.
Now the archive had spoken a name no living report contained.
Vault Chitin.
Ignatz felt the words rise behind his teeth.
“Say it,” Maelis said.
Marrowgate shook his head. “Don’t.”
“Vault Chitin,” Ignatz said.
The corridor lamps went out.
Marrowgate cried out. The sound was swallowed almost at once, as though the darkness had closed a hand
around it.
Ignatz heard movement all around them: the wet scrape of many small limbs, the delicate clicking of
shells against stone. He drew his sword. The blade came free with a whisper like breath over a grave.
Something touched his boot.
He struck downward.
The impact jarred his arm. Beneath the edge, a hard body cracked, and a pale fluid spread over the
flagstones. Its scent was bitter enough to burn his eyes.
Marrowgate stumbled backward into him.
“Do not move,” Ignatz said.
“I cannot see.”
“Then use your fear.”
A faint glow returned inside the archive.

Not from the lamps.
The Chalice of Ashdeep shone through the shelving, a low ember-red radiance that outlined every jar,
every folio, every drifting mote of dust. In that light Ignatz saw the floor alive with black shapes. They
moved in silence now, armored and jointed, flowing from beneath tables and through the cracks between
stones.
Vault Chitin had been unleashed in The War of Endless Vigil.
The sentence was there in the folio. He had read it before Maelis’s voice found him. Not released. Not
discovered. Unleashed.
The war had been a wound given legs.
A shape climbed the door.
Its shell was not black but colorless, like a fingernail grown over a corpse. It opened a seam in its front and
exhaled a thread of steam.
Marrowgate backed away.
“Where did they come from?”
Maelis stood untouched among the shelves.
“They were beneath the old foundations.”
“Beneath Hollowreach?”
“Beneath every place that thought itself founded.”
Ignatz watched the creature on the door. Its limbs searched the air. He remembered the folio’s next line,
the part that had vanished beneath the chime.
There had been a command.
Or a confession.
“Why show me this?” he asked.
“I did not show you.”
“You left the folio.”
“I left a decoy.”
The thing on the door turned toward Maelis.
For one breath, none of them moved.
Then the creature folded itself in half and sprang.
Maelis lifted one hand.
The Chalice rang.
The vault-born thing halted in midair. Its limbs beat soundlessly. A seam opened along its shell, and
within it lay a darkness deeper than the corridor.

Ignatz felt something pull at his eyes. He looked away, but not before he saw a pale shape inside the
creature, curled like an infant in a womb of lacquered bone.
Maelis closed her fist.
The creature fell.
Its body struck the stones and sank into them without a splash.
Marrowgate began to weep.
Ignatz kept his sword raised.
“You are controlling them.”
“No.”
“Then what are you doing?”
“Reminding them.”
“Of what?”
“That they were once afraid.”
The lamps flickered back to life. The swarm was gone. Only the crushed shell beneath Ignatz’s boot
remained, leaking its thin, bitter fluid into the cracks.
He lowered the sword by a fraction.
“Who unleashed Vault Chitin?”
Maelis looked past him, toward the open door and the corridor beyond.
“Your masters wrote the order.”
“I have no masters.”
Her gaze returned to him.
“That is why they chose you.”
The words entered him more deeply than a blade. For an instant he saw the Iron-Ring Cartel’s sealed
messages, each one bearing no signature, each one addressed only to the authority he carried. He had
thought secrecy made him useful. He had mistaken being unseen for being free.
Marrowgate pressed both hands against his mouth.
Ignatz turned on him. “What did you take from the archive?”
“Nothing.”
“Your shadow says otherwise.”
The quartermaster looked down.
His shadow had returned to its proper shape, but something bulged inside it. A small, angular mass moved
beneath the darkness, traveling from heel to heel.
Marrowgate saw it.

“No,” he breathed.
Ignatz seized the man by the collar and dragged him away from the threshold. “What did you carry out?”
“I was ordered to inventory the reliquaries.”
“By whom?”
Marrowgate’s lips worked soundlessly.
Maelis answered for him. “The order bore the seal of the Warden-Commander.”
Ignatz’s grip tightened.
“My seal?”
“A likeness of it.”
A coldness spread through his hand. His seal had been copied before. Any authority worth stealing was
copied. But this had not been used to forge a requisition or redirect a patrol.
It had opened the archive.
It had called to the Chalice.
It had brought Vault Chitin up through the floor.
“Show me,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate looked toward the dark mass inside his shadow.
“It is not in my possession.”
“Show me.”
“I cannot.”
“You will.”
The quartermaster’s knees failed. Ignatz caught him before he struck the stones. Beneath the man’s boots,
his shadow stretched thin as spilled ink. The shape within it pressed upward.
A crack appeared across the floor.
The Chalice gave another hollow chime.
This time the sound came from everywhere: from the lamps, from the flooded corridor, from the teeth of
the three figures standing beneath the archive’s dead light.
Maelis’s composure broke.
“Close the door.”
Ignatz looked at her.
“You said it was waiting.”
“It was.”
“And now?”

“Now it knows you are here.”
The crack widened.
Something below touched the underside of the world.
Marrowgate screamed as his shadow opened beneath him. Blackness took his legs to the knee, then the
waist. Ignatz held on, feeling the quartermaster’s weight drag against his arms, feeling another force draw
him down from below.
Maelis came forward at last.
“Let him go.”
Ignatz bared his teeth. “You first.”
“If you keep him, it will take you with him.”
“What is it?”
Her eyes fixed on the widening dark.
“An order that survived its author.”
The floor split between them.
From below came the slow, patient scrape of a multitude preparing to climb.
Ignatz looked once at the open door, once at Maelis, and once at the shadow swallowing Marrowgate.
Then a voice spoke from beneath the stones in his own voice.
“Warden-Commander.”
The title was followed by his name.
Not Ignatz.
The name he had never given the Iron-Ring Cartel.

Chapter 8
The rain fell upward against the windows.
It rose in thin black threads from the courtyard stones, gathered itself into trembling beads upon the leaded
glass, and vanished into the low sky. Ash made a poor foundation for water. It drank nothing. It
remembered every drop.
Maelis Harrowick the Pale watched the courtyard until the last bead broke apart. Their quill remained
poised above the ledger, its nib suspended over a line of obedient ink.
The page waited for a death.
Not the death of the liege. That had already been plotted, measured, and carried through the narrow door
between intention and consequence. The page required only the manner of it. Fever, perhaps. A weakness
of the blood. A mischance beneath a horse’s iron shoe. The Court preferred deaths that could be folded
into weather, appetite, or God’s absent attention.
Maelis had written three versions.
None had satisfied them.
Behind the chamber walls, the palace murmured with the careful quiet of people who had learned that
sound could be evidence. Boots passed in the corridor. A buckle struck stone. Somewhere below, a servant
dropped a tray and held their breath while the silence decided whether punishment was due.
Maelis lowered the quill.
Their hand did not tremble. It was a small victory, and therefore a dangerous one. Anything that could be
mastered could be noticed.
“Chronicler.”
The voice came from the doorway.
Maelis turned. Ignatz Marrowgate stood there with a document case tucked beneath one arm. He was not a
soldier, though he wore the expression of a man who had spent too long among soldiers and discovered
that hunger was more reliable than loyalty. His station was plain in the way of useful things.
“Ignatz Marrowgate,” Maelis said. “You are late.”
“I am a Quartermaster.”
The answer contained no apology. It might have contained an explanation, if either of them had been
foolish enough to ask.
Maelis glanced toward the blank window. “The road from the storehouses is not long.”
“The road is not the difficulty.”
“What is?”
Ignatz entered and closed the door behind him. “The guards.”
“Which guards?”
He looked at the ledger.

That was answer enough.
Maelis felt the room contract around them. The old tapestries seemed to lean inward, their faded scenes of
kneeling kings and burning cities reduced to the same colors: rust, soot, and the brown of dried blood. On
the central table lay the objects summoned from the sealed treasury. One was wrapped in oilskin. The
other rested bare upon a square of black cloth.
The bare object was the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell.
It was regalia, though no crown had ever seemed less like ornament. The metal curved in five dark fingers,
each joint engraved with shallow channels that held the light and refused to give it back. Its atmosphere
was one of sorrow and grim authority. Even unoccupied, it suggested a hand closing.
The oilskin parcel contained The Psalter of Seven Sorrows.
Maelis had not opened it.
Ignatz set the case on the table. “The order bears the seal.”
“The order bears many seals.”
“This one bears the liege’s.”
The word entered the chamber like a blade slid between ribs.
Maelis did not look toward the door. “You have brought it, then.”
“I have brought what was requested.”
“By whom?”
“Ignatz Marrowgate, Quartermaster,” he said, with a thinness in his voice that might have been humor, “is
not empowered to interpret the court’s appetite.”
“No. Only to feed it.”
His eyes lifted. For the first time, something moved behind them. Not anger. Calculation. A Quartermaster
measured everything: grain, iron, lamp oil, the distance between a locked chest and a hand that might open
it. Maelis wondered what quantity of fear he had assigned to them.
Ignatz touched the case but did not open it. “The instruction was to place the ward in your custody.”
“The Psalter of Seven Sorrows?”
“Yes.”
“You know what it is?”
“I know the name.”
“Names are often all the court permits a man to know.”
“The Psalter of Seven Sorrows was forged in 119 AS,” Maelis said.
The words seemed to alter the room. The rain withdrew from the windows. The fire, low in its grate, gave
a soft inward sigh.
Ignatz watched them. “That is not written in the order.”

“It is written elsewhere.”
“Where?”
“In records that survived.”
“Many records survive.”
“Not the useful ones.”
His fingers tightened on the document case. Maelis saw then that the knuckles were scarred, though scars
were not an answer to any question. The court was full of old injuries. They made a kind of second
architecture beneath the skin.
Ignatz opened the case.
Inside lay a sheet of vellum, folded once, and beneath it a key of dull white metal. No crest marked the
key. No inscription claimed it. The vellum bore a smear of dark wax, broken at one edge.
Maelis recognized the seal.
They had seen it upon commands that emptied villages, transferred garrisons, and sent men into winter
with boots whose soles had been counted before the men themselves. It belonged to authority, which
meant it belonged to whoever could make others suffer for doubting it.
“Where is the order’s bearer?” Maelis asked.
“Outside.”
“Who?”
Ignatz’s mouth closed.
There it was again: the small tightening, the refusal to place a name in the air. The palace had made a
discipline of unnamed people. Their labor remained, their bodies remained, but their names were kept out
of circulation like dangerous coin.
Maelis reached for the vellum.
The paper was cold. Not cool from the chamber, but cold as a stone drawn from deep earth. A tremor
moved through it when their fingers touched the fold.
“Do not,” Ignatz said.
Maelis looked up.
The Quartermaster had placed his hand over the key.
“Do not what?”
“Read it aloud.”
“I had no intention.”
“You have the face of someone who believes silence is a form of innocence.”
The accusation was so near the truth that Maelis nearly smiled.
Instead they unfolded the order.

The writing was cramped and formal. It directed Maelis to take The Psalter of Seven Sorrows to a
chamber beneath the old audience hall and to bring the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell. It named no purpose. It
gave no authority beyond the seal. It required obedience before the next bell.
No number marked the time. No date gave the command a place in history.
That absence disturbed Maelis more than any threat could have done.
A command without a date was a command meant to survive its sender.
“Who has access to the chamber?” they asked.
Ignatz removed his hand from the key. “I do not keep the locks.”
“You keep the inventory.”
“I keep what can be counted.”
“And The Psalter of Seven Sorrows can be counted?”
“Everything can be counted.”
“Even sorrow?”
“Especially sorrow. It is the one thing no one steals until they have finished spending it.”
Maelis folded the order again. The wax seal flaked beneath their thumb.
Outside, a bell began to toll.
The sound did not come from above. It rose through the stone floor, each note distorted by the
foundations. The first struck the soles of Maelis’s feet. The second entered their knees. By the third, the
chamber seemed to have become a vessel and the bell a hand testing its strength.
Ignatz looked toward the door.
“The next bell,” he said.
Maelis lifted the oilskin parcel. It was lighter than expected. The bundle made no sound when moved. The
Psalter of Seven Sorrows rested within like a thought too painful to give shape.
Their gaze fell upon the ledger.
The unfinished entry waited among the records of the court. A death with no body. A motive with no
witness. The liege’s name had been written in Maelis’s hand, then covered by a thin wash of ink. Beneath
the wash, the letters remained. They always remained. Ink was not erasure. It was merely a decision to
make the truth harder to find.
Maelis had plotted the death of their own liege.
The fact had lived inside them for so long that it no longer felt like a secret. It felt like a second pulse,
patient and tireless. Yet now, with the ward in their hands and the sealed chamber waiting below, that
pulse seemed to answer something beyond their own treason.
A fourth bell sounded.
Ignatz took up the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell. He wrapped it in black cloth, though the cloth did nothing to
soften its shape.

“You will come,” he said.
“That was not a question.”
“No.”
“Then why speak?”
“Because a Quartermaster knows the value of an acknowledgment before resources are moved.”
Maelis fastened the oilskin parcel beneath their robe. “And what resource am I?”
Ignatz opened the door.
The corridor beyond was empty. Lamps burned in their iron brackets, their flames thin and blue at the
base. A smell of wet ash came through the stone, though no window stood open.
“An account not yet closed,” he said.
They stepped into the corridor together.
At its far end, a stair descended beneath the palace. Maelis had passed the stair many times without seeing
it. The entrance was set between two pillars, concealed by a hanging of rotted velvet. Now the curtain had
been drawn aside.
The bearer of the order waited there, reduced by distance to a dark shape.
Maelis could not see a face.
That was deliberate, perhaps. Faces invited memory. Memory invited testimony. The court had learned to
place its intentions behind blankness.
Ignatz started down.
Maelis followed, one hand pressed against the hidden ward. Beneath the oilskin, The Psalter of Seven
Sorrows seemed to warm, not with life, but with recognition.
At the first landing, the palace sounds died.
At the second, the ash-rain ceased.
At the third, something breathed behind the wall.
Maelis stopped.
Ignatz continued for one step before turning back. “What is it?”
The breathing came again, slow and wet, from the dark masonry beside them.
Maelis thought of poisoned wells. Of victors washing their hands in the water meant for their allies. Of
The Winter Reckoning, which had begun in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS, leaving 27,987 casualties and
the Iron-Ring Cartel as victor. A betrayal at the eleventh hour had decided its outcome. The concealed
truth was that the victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
History had called it victory because history was written by those who remained thirsty and alive.
“The wall,” Maelis whispered.
Ignatz drew no weapon. He only stared at the stones.

Behind them, above the stair, the unseen bearer of the order began to descend.
One step.
Then another.
Maelis felt the ward shudder beneath the oilskin. The Psalter of Seven Sorrows had been forged in 119
AS, long before the present court, long before the liege whose death Maelis had arranged, long before
Maelis Harrowick the Pale had learned that treason was not an act but a room one entered and could never
leave.
The breathing stopped.
Something pressed against the stone from within.
A hairline crack opened beside Maelis’s hand.
They reached for the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell, but Ignatz caught their wrist.
“Do not touch it,” he said.
“Why?”
The crack widened.
From the darkness below came the scrape of metal, and from above came the measured approach of the
order’s bearer. Between them, the stair narrowed into a throat.
Ignatz’s grip tightened.
Then a voice spoke through the wall.
It used the liege’s voice.
“Chronicler,” it said. “Tell me how I died.”
Maelis’s first thought was that the wall had remembered.
Stone remembered better than flesh. It kept the pressure of a hand, the warmth of a body leaning close, the
faint oil of a lamp long extinguished. It kept blood in its pores. It kept the last word spoken over it, if the
word had been spoken with sufficient fear.
The voice came again.
“Chronicler. Tell me how I died.”
Ignatz’s fingers were still around Maelis’s wrist. His grip had the hard, practical strength of a man
accustomed to lifting what other people had dropped. The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell lay beneath Maelis’s
hand, its regalia dark against the stair, and the metal within the crack shifted with a soft, patient rasp.
Maelis looked at the stone.
“I wrote it down,” they said.
The liege’s voice laughed from inside the wall.
It was not the laugh Maelis remembered. That was the cruelty of it. The thing had chosen the voice, but
not the life behind it. The living voice had once carried impatience, appetite, the faint contempt of
someone who believed the world could be compelled to remain intelligible. This imitation carried only the

husk: the cadence, the falling note at the end of a question, the intimate summons reserved for a Court
Chronicler who had been called to private chambers after midnight.
“Wrote it down,” the wall repeated. “You always did prefer a corpse that could be corrected.”
Ignatz released them.
The crack had opened to the width of a finger. Cold breathed through it. Not the common cold of stone
beneath the Ash Wastes, nor the wet chill that gathered in underground places. This cold had direction. It
leaned toward Maelis, searching.
Behind them, the order’s bearer continued down the stair.
Measured. Unhurried.
Each footfall arrived with the solemnity of a seal pressed into wax.
Maelis could not see the bearer. The stair turned above, and the darkness drank the light at once. Yet the
approach seemed to possess a shape: the weight of a body, the hush of garments, the faint click of
something hard striking a ring or buckle.
Ignatz bent toward the crack. “What is it?”
“A question.”
“Questions don’t scrape metal.”
“Some do.”
The crack widened another fraction. A black edge showed within it, curved and dull. It withdrew before
Maelis could decide whether it had been a blade.
“Tell me,” said the voice. “Tell me how you died.”
Maelis felt the old room return around them.
Not this stair. Not the ash-rough walls, the narrow steps, or the breath of the sealed dark. The other room
had possessed softer surfaces. Curtains. A table laid with untouched food. A lamp burning too steadily.
The liege had stood near the window and spoken of loyalty as if describing a commodity whose price had
recently risen.
Maelis had listened.
They had nodded.
They had made the necessary arrangements.
The memory did not come whole. It never did. It arrived as objects: a cup overturned on its side, a smear
at the edge of a document, the faint bitter smell beneath the sweetness of wine. Then the liege’s hand,
reaching—not for Maelis, but past them, toward the bell.
The hand had stopped.
Maelis had not.
Their own death had begun in that instant, though the body had continued walking through corridors,
answering questions, accepting the title of Court Chronicler, and writing what could be written without

inviting the hangman into the archive.
“I did not kill you,” Maelis said.
The wall gave a small, pleased sigh.
“No?”
“I arranged the room.”
“Ah.”
The approaching footfall ceased.
Silence filled the stair above and below. Ignatz’s breathing became audible. Maelis could hear the blood
moving inside their own wrists, where the Quartermaster’s fingers had held them.
The metal in the wall tapped once.
“Then tell me,” said the liege, “what did the room want?”
Maelis looked down at the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell.
Its surface held no reflection. It seemed to drink the little light that came from above, and what remained
in its curves was not darkness but the idea of a hand. The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell had never been merely a
weapon. Regalia made authority visible; it taught the flesh to kneel before a shape. Maelis had seen the
gauntlet displayed beneath cloth, carried from chamber to chamber as though sorrow itself required an
escort.
They had reached for it without thinking.
Ignatz had stopped them.
Now the thing in the wall wanted an answer, and the order’s bearer waited somewhere above, while the
buried stair narrowed around them.
“Where is it?” the voice asked.
Maelis’s mouth went dry. “Where is what?”
“The psalter.”
Ignatz turned his head. “What psalter?”
The stone exhaled.
The pressure against it increased. Dust whispered down the face of the wall and gathered on Maelis’s
sleeve.
“The Psalter of Seven Sorrows,” said the liege. “You brought it here.”
“No.”
“You carried its silence beneath your tongue.”
“I did not.”
“Then why does the dark know your name?”
Maelis did not answer.

The Psalter of Seven Sorrows was housed in Fenthrone.
The fact stood in their mind with the clean, brutal certainty of a blade laid across a throat. Housed
there—not lost, not buried, not forgotten. It had a place. It had custodians, doors, rituals, and all the other
fragile ceremonies by which people pretended that possession was the same as control.
A ward forged in 119 AS, the Psalter of Seven Sorrows had passed through too many hands to belong to
any of them. Attunement to it cost 49. Maelis had copied the figure once, years ago, beneath a column of
lesser particulars. They had written the number in a careful hand and felt, even then, that it was not a cost
but a warning.
Forty-nine of what, the record did not say.
The wall knew.
Or wished them to believe it did.
“It is housed in Fenthrone,” Maelis said.
Ignatz stared at them. “Why would you tell it that?”
“I did not tell it anything.”
“You answered.”
The liege spoke through the crack, almost gently. “Fenthrone.”
The name moved through the stone like a hand through water.
Above, the order’s bearer resumed descending.
The first footfall struck. Then another.
Maelis counted neither. Counting was a form of comfort, and comfort was a debt the stair would collect.
Ignatz stepped between Maelis and the wall. “We go up.”
“If we go up, we meet the bearer.”
“Better than meeting whatever’s behind that.”
The crack opened wide enough for a thin blade of darkness. Something pressed against it from within.
Maelis saw the suggestion of fingers, too long to belong to any living hand, each joint articulated beneath
a skin that shone wetly in the absence of light.
They did not scream.
The liege’s voice became their own.
“Chronicler,” it said. “You have been very brave in the small ways.”
The order’s bearer appeared at the bend.
Not all of them. A sleeve emerged first, pale cloth marked by a dark, orderly line. Then the edge of a hood.
The face remained hidden by shadow, though Maelis felt the bearer looking directly at them.
Ignatz reached for the tool at his belt.
The motion was slight. The bearer stopped.

The metal within the wall scraped once more.
Maelis understood then that the stair held three hungers. The thing below wanted the Gauntlet of
Sorrowfell. The bearer above wanted passage, obedience, or blood. And the liege—if any portion of the
liege truly remained—wanted an account.
Accounts were what Maelis knew.
They had built a life from them. They had made death admissible by giving it a sentence, treason
survivable by giving it a date, and guilt bearable by placing it in the margin where no one was expected to
read.
But a sentence could not contain this.
“Say it,” whispered the wall.
Maelis felt Ignatz glance toward them. The Quartermaster’s face had no expression that Maelis could read,
but his hand had left the tool and settled near the Gauntlet instead.
“Do not touch it,” Maelis said.
“I heard you the first time.”
“Then remember.”
The bearer descended one step.
The darkness around the hood seemed to deepen. No insignia showed. No weapon. Only the quiet
authority of the approach.
Maelis looked at the crack.
“I plotted your death,” they said.
The stair tightened around the confession.
Ignatz made a sound under his breath—not surprise, exactly. Surprise required innocence, and Maelis had
never mistaken Ignatz for an innocent man. The bearer did not move.
From inside the wall came a wet, dragging breath.
“You plotted,” said the liege.
“Yes.”
“And yet you say you did not kill me.”
“I arranged what came before.”
“Which was?”
Maelis could taste iron. “Trust.”
The thing behind the wall leaned closer. The black fingers withdrew. For a moment the crack showed only
a darkness deeper than the stair.
“Whose?”
Maelis closed their eyes.

The room returned again. The untouched food. The lamp. The bell within reach of the liege’s hand. Their
own voice, steady and courteous, offering counsel that had sounded like caution. The liege listening
because Maelis had made listening seem safe.
“Yours,” they said.
The voice did not answer.
The order’s bearer took another step.
Ignatz seized Maelis by the shoulder and pulled them aside as a pale shape came down through the turn.
Cloth brushed stone. The air filled with the scent of wet ash.
The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell moved.
Not by itself. Not exactly.
Its fingers curled against the stair, and the sound they made was like a knuckle rapping from inside a
coffin.
The bearer’s hidden face turned toward it.
The crack burst open. Something reached through, and Maelis saw the liege’s hand—ringless, bloodless,
unmistakable—closing around the gauntlet’s wrist as the voice cried,
“Then tell me who taught you to trust me—”
The gauntlet’s wrist came free with a wet metallic sigh.
Maelis heard Ignatz draw breath beside them. The Quartermaster had the good sense not to speak. In the
split stair, silence was not absence but pressure: a hand laid over the mouth of the world.
The pale shape leaned forward.
The order’s bearer had no face beneath the hood. There was only a depthless dimness, as if the cloth
opened onto a room where every candle had been drowned. Yet the liege’s hand remained visible within
the crack—bloodless, ringless, the fingers locked around the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell.
Maelis knew those fingers.
They had once signed decrees with them. They had watched those fingers tremble over sealed testimony,
watched them lift a cup, dismiss a servant, bless a condemned man without looking at him.
They had arranged for those fingers to die.
Not quickly. Quick deaths belonged to soldiers and fools. Maelis had plotted the death of their own liege
as one plotted the correction of a chronicle: by subtraction, by omission, by allowing the fatal sentence to
appear inevitable when it had in fact been written long before.
The liege’s hand tightened.
The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell gave a shrill, protesting scrape against the stone.
“What did you promise it?” the bearer asked.
Its voice had changed. The question still wore the liege’s cadence, but beneath it lay another sound: the
creak of a rope under weight.

Ignatz found his voice. “We promised nothing.”
The hood turned toward him.
Maelis felt the Quartermaster shrink, though his shoulder remained pressed against theirs. Born in 425 AS,
Ignatz Marrowgate had spent enough of his life among inventories, shortages, and locked doors to
understand the arithmetic of danger. He knew what could be counted. He did not know what to do with a
hand that had no living arm attached to it.
The bearer lifted one finger.
The stair shuddered.
Far below, something answered with three slow blows.
Ignatz swallowed. “We carry orders from Gloammarch.”
“Gloammarch,” the voice repeated, and the word became a mouthful of black water. “Founded in 321 AS.
Garrison of 2,148. Contested still.”
The darkness beneath the hood seemed to look through them, past them, into the rooms and passages
where men slept beside weapons.
“House Morvain holds its walls,” Maelis said.
They had not meant to speak. The name escaped with the dry taste of old paper.
“House Morvain holds what can be held,” said the bearer. “That is not the same thing.”
The hand wrenched the gauntlet downward.
A line of frost spread over the iron. Maelis saw the sigil cut into the back of the regalia fill with a color
like bruised moonlight. Its attunement cost was 12. The number had been copied into three ledgers,
checked against two inventories, and once whispered by a dying clerk who had bitten through his tongue
rather than finish the sentence.
Twelve for the hand.
Twelve for the wound.
Twelve for whatever the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell had been made to remember.
“It is not yours,” Maelis said.
The bearer’s hood inclined.
“No.”
The liege’s hand opened.
The gauntlet fell.
It struck the stair and did not bounce. It gripped the stone with its fingers, each joint flexing as if it had
been waiting for the opportunity to crawl. Ignatz made a sound low in his throat.
Maelis reached for him, then stopped. Their own hand hovered over the Quartermaster’s sleeve. There
were gestures that became promises merely by being completed.
The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell turned toward Maelis.

A pressure gathered behind their eyes.
For one instant, the stair vanished. Maelis stood in a winter field beneath a white sky. The snow was not
snow. It lay in drifts over wells, over trenches, over the mouths of men whose hands had frozen shut
around empty cups.
The Winter Reckoning had begun in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS. The official account recorded 27,987
casualties. The Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor.
Maelis had copied those facts into the court record in a hand praised for its clarity.
They had not copied the wells.
They had not written that the victors poisoned the wells of their own allies. They had not written of the
slow darkening of water, or of the way thirst made soldiers kneel before the banners they had meant to
burn. They had not written that the betrayal at the eleventh hour decided the outcome, because truth, when
placed correctly, could become a weapon sharper than any accusation.
The gauntlet’s fingers scraped.
The white field broke apart.
Maelis returned to the stair with blood running warm from one nostril.
Ignatz noticed. “Chronicler—”
“Do not call me that here.”
He stared at them.
The bearer’s head remained turned toward the gauntlet. “Why not?”
Because titles were doors, Maelis thought. Because a Court Chronicler was expected to remember without
fear, and Maelis had spent too long teaching fear to wear the face of memory.
The bearer stepped down.
Its foot did not touch the stair. The hem of its garment hovered a finger’s breadth above the stone, trailing
wet ash. With every movement the corridor seemed to lengthen, its walls retreating into a darkness that
had no architecture.
“Where is the ward?” it asked.
Ignatz looked at Maelis.
There it was: the small betrayal before the greater one. His gaze moved toward the inner passage, toward
the sealed chamber where The Psalter of Seven Sorrows had been kept in Fenthrone. He did not speak, but
the bearer followed the direction of his silence.
Maelis caught his chin and forced his face back.
“Do not answer.”
The liege’s voice softened. “You have answered already.”
The crack in the stair widened.
Something on the far side breathed.

Maelis remembered the first time they had seen the liege’s corpse—or what had been called a corpse. The
room had smelled of extinguished lamps and bitter herbs. The body had lain beneath a cloth while the
court waited for Maelis to confirm what everyone had paid them to confirm. They had lifted the edge.
They had seen the face. They had seen the hand.
Ringless. Bloodless.
Unmistakable.
Yet death had not stopped that hand from reaching.
“You are not the liege,” Maelis said.
The bearer turned fully toward them.
“No,” it said. “But you are.”
The words entered Maelis more deeply than the gauntlet’s vision. They carried no accusation. Accusation
would have been mercy. The voice spoke as if naming an office.
Behind the hood, something shifted.
“Born in 340 AS,” it whispered. “A Court Chronicler. Maelis Harrowick the Pale.”
Ignatz’s fingers closed around the edge of his coat.
“And you plotted the death of your own liege.”
The stair seemed to tilt beneath Maelis.
They had known the truth would surface. They had imagined it dragged into daylight by enemies, or
discovered in the margin of a ledger, or found beneath the floorboards of some loyal servant who had
mistaken evidence for devotion. They had never imagined the truth spoken by a mouth without a face.
“I did,” Maelis said.
Ignatz turned sharply. “What?”
Maelis kept their eyes on the hood. “I did.”
The bearer came closer.
“Why?”
There were answers prepared for courts. The liege had grown dangerous. The realm required an absence.
Mercy sometimes wore the mask of treason. All of them were true enough to survive a hearing and false
enough to preserve a life.
But the stair had no court upon it.
“Because the liege had begun to believe obedience was the same as justice.”
The hidden thing laughed.
The sound was quiet, almost tender.
“And did you?”
“No.”

“Do you now?”
Maelis looked down.
The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell had crawled to their boot. Its fingers pressed against the leather. It felt no
heavier than a child’s hand, yet Maelis could not move. The cold coming from it entered through the sole
and climbed into the bone.
Ignatz crouched and reached for the gauntlet.
Maelis seized his wrist.
“Do not.”
“I can pull it away.”
“You cannot.”
“I am the Quartermaster.”
It was the first thing he had said with anything resembling anger. His birth in 425 AS had not made him
young or old in Maelis’s estimation; it had made him a man of ledgers, a servant of quantities. He had
spent his life believing that any burden could be shifted if one found the correct pair of hands.
The gauntlet’s fingers wrapped around his boot.
Ignatz froze.
From the inner passage came the thin, distant chime of metal striking glass.
The Psalter of Seven Sorrows.
Maelis felt the number rise in memory: 49, the cost of attunement. They had read it once and thought the
figure absurdly exact, as though sorrow could be weighed, priced, and entered into a register. Now the
chime came again, and each note seemed to draw something out of the dark.
The bearer lifted its hand toward the sealed passage.
A thread of black moisture ran from its sleeve and vanished into the crack.
“The ward is waking,” it said.
Ignatz’s face had gone slack. “It cannot. The chamber is sealed.”
“Seals are invitations,” said the bearer.
The door at the end of the passage groaned.
Maelis remembered another stronghold, another entry in another record: Stormmarch, founded in 71 AS,
its garrison numbering 9,263, quarantined and outside the realm’s core holdings. The numbers had once
seemed like a promise. A place with 9,263 armed bodies could not be forgotten. A place under quarantine
could not be reached by ordinary ruin.
Yet every sealed place became a vessel for whatever the realm feared to name.
Stormmarch had been left outside the core holdings. Gloammarch remained contested. The Iron-Ring
Cartel’s victory had been built upon poisoned water. House Morvain held walls that might not belong to it.
The realm had made a habit of calling abandonment strategy.

The door groaned again.
A white line appeared beneath it.
Maelis felt the gauntlet release Ignatz’s boot.
Then it seized their own.
The fingers closed around their ankle with intimate strength.
The bearer lowered its hood until the darkness within touched Maelis’s face.
“Tell me,” it said, “which death did you plot?”
Maelis could hear Ignatz breathing behind them. Could hear the sealed door beginning to open. Could
hear, far below, the patient knocking from inside the stair.
Their liege’s hand emerged from the crack once more.
This time it held a knife.
Maelis knew the knife.
They had placed it where it would be found.
They had forgotten the blood.

Chapter 9
The reliquary had no windows.
Aldous Wrenfield the Last Warden preferred it so. Light invited inspection, and inspection was the
beginning of every theft: the eye measuring distance, the mind judging weight, the hand learning where to
reach. Darkness, properly kept, made a chamber honest. It showed nothing. It promised nothing. It
endured.
A lamp burned in a niche beneath the sealed arch, its flame thin and blue in the mineral oil. The walls
drank its color. Dust hung in the air like ash that had forgotten how to fall.
Aldous sat before the iron-bound table with his hands folded over the ledger. His gloves were still on. He
had not touched the page since opening it.
Beyond the door, somewhere in the buried corridors, a bell gave a single muffled note.
He knew the sound. Someone had crossed the outer threshold.
The knowledge moved through him without haste. Panic was a servant that never learned obedience. He
had spent his life starving it.
Aldous Wrenfield the Last Warden was born in 315 AS.
The words remained in his mind with the weight of an inscription. They had been written into the registry
when the world was still younger, when the keepers still believed the past could be guarded by giving it
shelves and locks. He had been marked for custody before he understood what custody meant. Now the
old record called him major Reliquary Keeper, as though rank could explain the solitude of a man who
spent his days listening to dead things breathe.
The bell gave another note.
Aldous closed the ledger.
On its cover, the sigil of the reliquary had been hammered flat by old hands. The mark was still visible in
the right light: a circle broken by a vertical stroke, a promise that nothing entrusted would be surrendered.
He had surrendered things.
Not relics. Not yet.
Information was lighter than iron and more dangerous than fire. It could pass beneath a door, inside a
sealed letter, on the tongue of a trembling courier. The Iron-Ring Cartel paid for it without asking whether
the information had blood on it. They understood the true shape of the age. Everything was merchandise
once one had found the correct buyer.
The third bell did not come.
Aldous rose.
His boots made no sound on the stone. The reliquary had been constructed for silence, though not the
clean silence of empty rooms. This quiet had a pressure to it. It settled against the ears and lingered behind
the teeth. In the deepest vault, the Silent Psalter rested beneath three seals, its muted devotional frame
wrapped in black cloth. Forged in 204 AS, it demanded an attunement cost of 49. Though made for
expression, it had become an instrument of silence so complete that men wept after hearing nothing from

it.
Aldous had never attuned to it.
He had seen what discipline did to those who tried.
At the end of the corridor, the outer door opened. Cold air entered, carrying wet stone, old smoke, and the
faint metallic scent of rain. A figure stepped through the threshold and waited beneath the lintel.
“Keeper,” the figure said.
The voice was young enough to retain its edges.
Aldous did not answer at once. He stood where the corridor narrowed, with darkness behind him and the
lamp behind the visitor. The stranger’s face remained a blur.
“Say your name.”
“Thessaly Coldwater.”
The name crossed the distance between them and stopped.
Aldous had heard it before, though not from a mouth. It had appeared in dispatches, on route marks, in the
cramped script of those who measured danger by how quickly a message needed to travel. Thessaly
Coldwater served as an Outrider. The record gave nothing else that could be trusted—not temperament,
not loyalty, not the kind of fear that lived in the bones.
Aldous studied the silhouette.
“Outrider,” he said.
“Yes.”
“Then you know the doors you have crossed.”
“I know the doors I was permitted to cross.”
Aldous felt the smallest shift in the air. Not a threat. Not submission. An answer placed carefully between
them.
“Permitted by whom?”
“The order was sealed.”
“Seals are wax. Wax has no authority.”
“Then perhaps I was permitted by the person who carried it.”
The lamp behind Thessaly guttered. For an instant, the figure sharpened: a travel-stained coat, a narrow
satchel, gloved hands held apart from the body. No canonical feature offered itself to memory. The
Outrider was only the role, and the role was enough. Those who carried messages through broken country
learned to make their faces forgettable. It was a kind of armor.
“Come closer,” Aldous said.
Thessaly did not move.
The reluctance was sensible. The chamber had a reputation, though reputation was merely fear with a
better vocabulary.

Aldous lowered his gaze to the floor between them. “If you carry a sealed order, place it on the stone.”
The satchel opened.
A small cylinder emerged, blackened at both ends. It landed without a clatter. Thessaly withdrew a step.
Aldous waited until the visitor’s hands were empty, then approached. The cylinder bore no crest he
recognized. Its seal had been pressed in dark wax, the impression obscured by deliberate scoring.
Someone wanted the object to appear official while denying it any origin.
He crouched and touched the wax with one gloved finger.
Cold.
Not the cold of the corridor. The cold of a thing held near something dead.
The seal cracked beneath his thumb.
Inside lay a strip of thin vellum.
He unfolded it.
The writing was a list of places, nothing more. Crookvale. Hollowreach. Several marks without names. A
line beside each, rendered in a cipher he knew well enough to despise.
Crookvale had been founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. Rebuilt after whatever had broken it, it
retained a garrison of 1004, yet remained outside the core holdings. It was the sort of place that survived
because no one powerful enough to claim it had found a reason to care. Its crooked walls and hard angles
had become a form of defiance.
Hollowreach lay in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 56 AS, a core location under quarantine. Its name
was written twice. Once in the list. Once beneath it, with a small black stroke through the final letter.
Aldous read the cipher again.
His stomach tightened.
“What is it?” Thessaly asked.
“Your order did not say?”
“It said to deliver the message.”
“And then?”
“To wait.”
“For what?”
“For your answer.”
Aldous folded the vellum. “You were not instructed to return?”
“No.”
“Were you instructed to speak of what you saw on the road?”
“No.”
“Were you instructed to forget it?”

A pause.
“No.”
That answer was worse than the others.
Aldous turned toward the table. “How old are you, Thessaly Coldwater?”
The Outrider’s silence gathered itself.
“Thessaly Coldwater was born in 338 AS,” they said.
The exactness of it disturbed him. People lied about age as naturally as they lied about hunger. To recite
the registry’s wording was either discipline or defiance.
“You recite that as though it belongs to someone else.”
“Most records do.”
“Records belong to whoever keeps them.”
“Then you should know better than to trust one.”
Aldous placed the vellum beside the closed ledger. The two documents lay together like bones from
different graves.
He had once believed keeping meant preserving truth. The belief had not survived the first sealed archive
he opened. Every record carried a hand behind it, and every hand had been frightened of something. Kings
feared disgrace. Houses feared extinction. Armies feared that their victories might be discovered as
payments made in darkness.
The War of Endless Vigil had begun in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS, causing 81577 casualties. The
official record called it a total rout of the aggressors. The Bleeding Crown was recorded as the victor. The
page did not record that the losing commander had been bribed to withdraw. That truth had been kept
elsewhere, beneath a different seal, where it could not disturb the shape of history.
Aldous had sold that truth to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
Not the whole of it. Never the whole.
A man who sold everything became a servant of the buyer. Aldous had retained enough to remain his own
master, though he could no longer remember what mastery had felt like before the first payment.
Thessaly spoke behind him. “You recognize the mark.”
“I recognize the hand.”
“Whose?”
“You are not carrying enough authority to ask.”
“Then why did you answer?”
Because the room had changed.
Because the cylinder had been cold.
Because Hollowreach was under quarantine, and the second mark beneath its name meant someone had
decided containment was no longer a boundary but an invitation.

Aldous lifted the vellum again. The black stroke seemed to widen beneath the lamp.
“Did you pass through the Gloaming Reach?”
“No.”
“Did you see anyone come from it?”
“No.”
“Did you hear a bell?”
Thessaly’s gloved fingers tightened.
There it was. The first true movement.
Aldous turned.
The Outrider had not stepped closer, but the distance between them seemed reduced. “You heard one,” he
said.
“I heard something.”
“Where?”
“The road.”
“That is not a place.”
“It was where the sound was.”
Aldous watched the figure’s posture, the minute angle of the shoulders. Fear, perhaps. Or fatigue. No
canonical temperament had been established for Thessaly Coldwater; Aldous had no permission to name
what he saw. Naming was a form of ownership, and he had owned too many things that had once been
alive.
The bell in the deep corridor rang again.
This time it did not stop at one note.
A second tone followed, then a third, each weaker than the last. The sound traveled through the stone with
the patience of water finding a crack.
Thessaly turned toward the door.
Aldous caught the movement. “Do not.”
The Outrider froze.
“There is no one at the outer threshold now,” he said.
“How do you know?”
“Because the bell is inside.”
The lamp flame bent sideways.
From beneath the floor came a soft scraping, as if something were drawing a fingernail along the
underside of the world.

Aldous reached for the ledger, then stopped. The vellum waited beside it. Crookvale. Hollowreach. The
mark beneath the quarantine.
And beneath those, hidden in the cipher’s final fold, one more instruction.
He unfolded the strip.
The ink there had not been visible before. It rose slowly through the fibers, darkening as though written by
a wound.
Thessaly whispered, “What does it say?”
Aldous read the line once.
Then again.
His hand closed around the vellum.
“It says,” he murmured, “that the door has already been opened.”
The scraping ceased.
In the sudden silence, something breathed beneath the stone.
Aldous looked toward the sealed vault where the Silent Psalter waited under its black cloth, and for the
first time in years he wondered whether silence could be broken from the inside.
Behind him, Thessaly drew steel.
Aldous lifted one hand—not to command, but to keep the Outrider from making the only sound the
chamber might still be waiting for—and reached beneath the table for the key that he had sworn never to
use when the bell began to ring again.
The key was colder than the air.
Aldous drew it from beneath the table and held it between finger and thumb. The metal had no teeth. It
was a narrow, dark thing, smooth as a sliver of burned bone, with a ring too small for any hand but his
own.
The bell sounded again.
Not above them. Not in the tower.
Within the stone.
Thessaly shifted behind him. Steel whispered against its sheath.
“Do not,” Aldous said.
“I have not.”
“Then continue not doing it.”
The Outrider’s silence came back sharp-edged. Aldous could feel it at his shoulders, young and watchful,
waiting for him to become the sort of man who gave orders because he had no answer.
He fitted the key into the seam beneath the table.
Nothing happened.

The chamber held its breath. Dust trembled from the vaulted ceiling. Somewhere behind the black cloth,
beneath the weight of stone and iron, the Silent Psalter gave a sound too thin to be called a note.
Aldous closed his eyes.
The instrument had been forged in 204 AS, when grief was still thought to be a substance that could be
shaped by disciplined hands. Its makers had fashioned it for expression and denied it voice. Its strings, if
strings they were, did not sing to the ear. They answered elsewhere—in the marrow, in the dark behind the
eyes, in the old instinct that told a man whether the door before him led into a room or into a wound.
The attunement cost of 49 was written in every account that had survived.
Not coins.
Not blood.
Aldous turned the key.
The table sank by the width of a fingernail.
Thessaly inhaled.
“Now,” Aldous said, “you may draw steel.”
The blade came free.
The bell rang a third time, and the vault door opened.
It did not swing inward. It unfolded, plates of black stone sliding over one another with the slow patience
of a buried thing. The cloth covering the Psalter remained where it was, undisturbed. Beneath it, the
instrument waited in its cradle of ashwood.
Aldous did not look directly at it.
Instead he watched the darkness beyond the opened door.
There was no corridor there. No stair. The vault should have held a second wall, mortared into the
mountain and sealed with the old keeper’s marks. He had placed his hand upon that wall many times. He
had felt its chill. He had trusted it.
Now it showed him a narrow passage descending through pale rock.
At the far end, a red gleam pulsed like a coal under a dead man’s tongue.
Thessaly stepped nearer. “Was that there before?”
“You have not been here before.”
“That is not an answer.”
“No,” Aldous said. “It is the answer I have.”
The Outrider’s blade angled toward the passage. Its edge caught the red pulse and returned it as a line of
blood.
Aldous took the vellum from the table. The writing had altered. The ink no longer lay in letters but in little
black fissures, spreading from the first line toward the margins. He held it closer.
A seal appeared beneath the text.

A crown split down the middle.
The Bleeding Crown’s mark.
His stomach tightened.
He had seen that emblem stamped into orders, prison warrants, war ledgers, and the final accounts of The
War of Endless Vigil. The conflict had begun in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS, with 81577 casualties. It
had ended in the total rout of the aggressors, and The Bleeding Crown was recorded as the victor.
Recorded.
That word had always carried the odor of a locked room.
Aldous had learned the other truth from a hand that never signed its messages: the losing commander had
been bribed to withdraw. The payment had vanished into the silence between ledgers, and the silence had
outlived every soldier who might have spoken of it.
The ink on the vellum crawled again.
A second line formed.
THE ACCORD OF MOURNTHRONE WAGED AT CROOKVALE IN 297 AS.
Aldous read it without moving.
The phrase was wrong in a way that made the chamber feel suddenly colder. An accord was not a battle.
An accord was a shape laid over violence after the violence had become inconvenient. Yet the words stood
together, joined by the hand beneath the stone.
“The Accord of Mournthrone,” Thessaly said.
Aldous folded the vellum once. “You can read.”
“I can read enough.”
“Then read the passage.”
Thessaly looked into the red-lit dark. “There is nothing written there.”
“There is always something written.”
“That is a keeper’s superstition.”
“It is a keeper’s profession.”
He entered the passage.
The air changed at once. The chamber’s dry mineral cold fell away, replaced by the smell of wet iron and
old ash. The walls were smooth, but not worked. They seemed to have been melted and then persuaded
into shape. Every few paces, a shallow niche interrupted the stone. Each niche held the impression of a
hand.
Some were small.
Some were not.
Aldous kept the key clenched in his palm. It had begun to warm. That frightened him more than the
opening had.

Behind him, Thessaly followed with the blade lowered but ready.
“Why is the Psalter here?” the Outrider asked.
“It is housed in Marrowwatch.”
“That is not here.”
“This is Marrowwatch.”
Thessaly stopped.
The red light pulsed at the far end. With each pulse, the passage seemed to lengthen, though Aldous could
not say whether the walls moved or his sight failed him.
“The vault is beneath the old sanctuary,” Thessaly said.
“So it was.”
“And the door leads below.”
“So it appears.”
“Then where does below lead?”
Aldous felt the answer rising in him, shaped before he had given it permission.
“Inside.”
Thessaly’s sword lifted.
The passage gave a soft, wet creak.
Aldous turned. “Do you hear that?”
“No.”
“That is worse.”
He took another step.
Something brushed his sleeve.
Aldous spun, key raised, but found only the wall. The pale rock gleamed with a thin film of moisture.
Where the stone had touched him, a line of darkness marked the cloth.
Thessaly seized his arm.
The grip was firm. “Enough.”
Aldous looked down at their hand, then at the sword.
For a moment he imagined drawing his own weapon. He imagined the old, clean simplicity of threat. The
body understood a blade better than it understood a secret. A blade offered one direction. A secret offered
a thousand, and every one of them ended with a corpse.
Thessaly released him.
Aldous wiped the stain against his sleeve. The darkness did not smear. It sank into the fabric and vanished.
“Who else knows about this place?” Thessaly asked.

The question struck closer than the Outrider could know.
Aldous saw the last message he had sent to the Iron-Ring Cartel, folded into the false bottom of a reliquary
case. He saw the careful cipher, the location reduced to old measurements and devotional phrases. He had
sold intelligence before. Not relics. Not people. Only knowledge, he had told himself.
Knowledge could not bleed.
Yet here, beneath Marrowwatch, the stone breathed as though it had lungs.
“No one,” he said.
It was the first lie he had spoken in the passage.
The bell answered from somewhere ahead.
Thessaly raised the blade fully. “That was not in the chamber.”
“No.”
“Then something is ringing it.”
Aldous thought of the Silent Psalter beneath its black cloth. He thought of the attunement cost of 49, and
of all the keepers who had mistaken a number for a boundary. Perhaps the cost was not what one
surrendered to the instrument. Perhaps it was what the instrument had to surrender before it could be
played.
The red glow brightened.
At the passage’s end stood a door made of dull silver. It bore no hinge, no handle, no lock. In its center
was an indentation shaped like Aldous’s key.
He did not approach it.
Thessaly came beside him. “You opened the first door.”
“The first door opened itself.”
“Then let this one do the same.”
Aldous studied the silver. In its surface he could see their reflections, though neither reflection moved
quite as they did. Thessaly’s reflected sword was already wet with blood.
His own reflection had no face.
He closed his fingers around the key.
Behind the silver door, something whispered.
Not a voice. Not yet.
The sound carried through the metal and entered his teeth.
Aldous felt the old solemnity fall away from him, leaving only the naked, miserable truth beneath: he had
not guarded the Psalter all these years. He had guarded the world from discovering that it was awake.
The whisper came again.
This time it spoke his name.

Thessaly heard it. Aldous knew by the sudden tightening of their stance.
“What did it say?” the Outrider asked.
Aldous raised the key toward the waiting lock.
“It said,” he murmured, “that I was late.”
The key touched silver.
The door began to open.
The silver door opened inward without a hinge-sound.
Beyond it lay a chamber narrower than Aldous remembered and deeper than any chamber had the right to
be. Darkness filled it, but not the honest darkness of unlit stone. This darkness seemed poured, viscous and
black, holding its shape beneath the lintel. It recoiled from the key.
Thessaly lifted a hand.
Aldous caught their wrist before they could touch the hilt at their side.
“Do not draw steel.”
Their gaze moved to him. “You heard it speak.”
“I heard a voice.”
“You heard your name.”
He released them. The place beyond the door had listened to the exchange. He felt that attention like a
thumb pressed into the hollow beneath his ribs.
The floor descended by a single step. Under it, the stone had been polished to a dull sheen, and in that
sheen Aldous saw the reflection of a room that was not there: walls crowded with shelves, a narrow table,
the pale oval of a face bent over an instrument.
Then the reflection blinked.
He stepped through.
The air inside tasted of old ash and rain trapped in iron. No flame burned, yet the chamber possessed a
colourless illumination, enough to reveal the ribs of the vault. Shelves ran along the walls, sealed behind
sheets of smoked glass. Within them waited reliquaries of every shape: boxes, bells, blades, cups, masks,
things whose purposes had been erased by fear.
At the centre stood a low stone cradle.
The Silent Psalter rested upon it.
Aldous had seen it once before, though memory had made a coward of the sight. The instrument
resembled a devotional thing stripped of prayer: muted, somber, fashioned for silent use. Its strings—or
what passed for strings—lay slack across its dark frame. They did not shine. They drank the room’s pallid
light and gave nothing back.
Thessaly came to the threshold and stopped.
“Is that it?”

Aldous nodded.
“The Silent Psalter.”
The name entered the chamber and was taken up by the walls. Not repeated. Absorbed.
He remembered the record: The Silent Psalter was forged in 204 AS. The notation had been written in
three different hands, each one growing less certain. Instrument. Expression. Silence. The final hand had
scored a line beneath the word attunement and written 49.
He had once believed the number referred to years, or deaths, or the measures required to unlock the
Psalter’s voice. He knew better now. The cost was not counted in anything so merciful as time.
Thessaly’s breath roughened. “You said it was housed in Marrowwatch.”
“It was.”
“Then why is it here?”
Aldous looked toward the sealed shelves. “Because houses burn.”
The Outrider watched him with a stillness that had become more dangerous than suspicion. Their arrival
had been inconvenient when he first received the message. Now it seemed like a judgment given legs.
He moved toward the cradle.
Along its edge, letters had been cut into the stone. Most were worn smooth. One line remained legible.
THE HAND THAT HIDES THE TRUTH SHALL PAY IN TRUTH.
Aldous read it twice.
Behind him, Thessaly said, “You knew this was here.”
“I knew the chamber existed.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.”
The answer hung between them. He could feel the old machinery of his mind begin to turn: deny, delay,
redirect. It had kept him alive through sealed archives and hungry courts. It had kept the Iron-Ring Cartel
supplied with fragments—routes, inventories, garrison strengths, names of officials whose loyalties had
already begun to rot. Intelligence, he had called it when the messages left his hands. Not treason. Not
betrayal. A transaction.
