The Cartel had never asked what the intelligence would cost anyone else.
Aldous placed the key on the cradle.
The metal struck stone.
Somewhere above them, a bell began to toll.
Thessaly spun toward the door. “That came from outside.”
“No.”
The toll sounded again. It came from beneath the floor.

Dust trembled from the vaulting. In the smoked glass of the shelves, the reliquaries seemed to lean toward
the Psalter.
Aldous had studied the old war ledgers until the numbers had become a kind of liturgy. The War of
Endless Vigil began in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS. It caused 81577 casualties. The Bleeding Crown was
recorded as the victor after the total rout of the aggressors. Every official account praised the Crown’s
endurance, the discipline of its watch, the enemy line breaking beneath a vigilance that had outlasted
hunger, winter, and terror.
But one account had not praised anything.
It had stated that the losing commander was bribed to withdraw.
Aldous had sold that account to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
Not the whole of it. Never the whole. A page here, a seal there, enough to make them pay and not enough
to make them understand. He had told himself that partial truth was safer than truth made weapon-bright.
The Psalter stirred.
Its strings drew taut without being touched.
Thessaly said, “What did you give them?”
Aldous did not turn.
The instrument gave a sound too low to be heard, yet the chamber changed around it. His teeth ached. The
air became dense, each breath laborious, as if silence had weight.
“What did you give the Iron-Ring Cartel?”
He closed his eyes.
The first note of the Silent Psalter was not a note. It was the absence left when a note should have been.
The chamber opened around that absence, and the shelves fell away.
He saw a highland settlement beneath a bruised sky. Its walls had been rebuilt, stone laid over older scars.
A crooked road climbed between hard-faced houses. On the gate, beneath a weather-eaten mark, was
written:
CROOKVALE.
The vision moved closer. Figures stood along the battlements, watching the road. The garrison roll
unfurled in the wind.
1004.
Crookvale was founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. It had been rebuilt. It remained outside the core
holdings, though its garrison was 1004 and its walls had learned the shape of survival. The facts appeared
not as words but as wounds: foundation, ruin, rebuilding, watchfulness.
A second image overlaid the first.
A sealed town crouched beneath a grey veil. No cart entered. No traveller left. Doors had been barred from
within and without. At the roadblock, a board bore the name Hollowreach.
Hollowreach lies in the Gloaming Reach.

Hollowreach was founded in 56 AS.
Hollowreach is a core location under quarantine.
The statements struck through Aldous one by one. The town’s silence had become architecture. Windows
stared without faces. Beyond the barriers, something moved in the fog and stopped when the Psalter’s
voiceless resonance touched it.
Thessaly made a sound behind him—not fear, precisely. Recognition.
“You have seen these places,” Aldous said.
“I have seen roads.”
“Do not lie to it.”
“To what?”
He looked at the Psalter.
Its dark frame had opened along the middle. Inside was no mechanism, no hollow, no hidden chamber.
There was only a depth without distance, black and faintly trembling.
“The thing that spoke my name.”
The door behind them slammed shut.
Thessaly crossed the room in three strides and seized the handle. It did not move.
“Aldous.”
He could not answer. The chamber had begun to fill with whispers. They came from the sealed relics,
from the stone beneath his boots, from the scuffed silver of the key. Each whisper carried a different voice,
but all of them spoke the same fragments.
Marrowwatch.
Crookvale.
Hollowreach.
The Iron-Ring Cartel.
His mouth had gone dry.
In the vision, the scene of Crookvale returned. The garrison stood upon the walls, but their faces had been
erased. Beyond them waited an army without banners. On the road, a figure in a dark cloak knelt beside an
open coffer. Gold glimmered within it.
The losing commander’s withdrawal.
The hidden payment.
The Bleeding Crown’s victory, polished for the chronicles until no stain showed through.
Then the scene changed.
A hand placed a message beneath a door.

Aldous knew the hand. He had watched it write. He had watched the message sealed and carried away. He
had felt the Cartel’s coin grow warm in his palm.
The vision showed no face. It showed only the message opening.
Thessaly tore their hand from the door. “What did you sell?”
Aldous saw the writing inside the vision.
Not the details of the war. Not the routes or the inventories. Those were bait, the harmless bones around
the hidden meat.
He had sold the location of the chamber.
He had sold the existence of the Silent Psalter.
He had sold the fact that the key could open it.
And he had sold the hour in which he intended to come.
His knees weakened.
“I gave them a way to find us,” he said.
Thessaly’s silence was worse than accusation.
The Psalter’s strings tightened further. One snapped.
The sound was soundless, yet a line of blood opened across Aldous’s palm where the key had rested. He
looked down. The wound was shallow. The blood did not fall. It lifted in narrow threads and drew itself
across the stone cradle.
The cut letters filled.
THE HAND THAT HIDES THE TRUTH SHALL PAY IN TRUTH.
Aldous felt something enter the wound.
It did not hurt. Pain would have been a mercy. This was comprehension, cold and total. Every secret he
had traded gathered inside him—not as memories, but as doors. He sensed them opening one after
another, each revealing another darkness, another waiting silence.
The Psalter asked nothing aloud.
It had already heard the answer.
From beyond the sealed door came a faint metallic knock.
Thessaly turned.
Another knock followed.
Then another.
Not one hand. Many.
Aldous pressed his bleeding palm against the Psalter’s frame.
The instrument accepted him.

The chamber vanished.
For one impossible instant he stood beneath the sky over Crookvale, beneath the hard heights of The High
Spires, while the garrison of 1004 watched from walls that had been rebuilt around old deaths. Then he
stood at the quarantine line of Hollowreach in the Gloaming Reach, where the settlement founded in 56
AS waited behind its barriers, closed upon whatever it had become.
Between those places, beneath the ash-coloured world, a door opened.
On the other side stood the Iron-Ring Cartel.
And behind them, wearing no face at all, stood the voice that had told Aldous he was late.

Chapter 10
The bell beneath Stormmarch rang without a hand upon it.
Gareth Ironmere stopped beneath the archway and listened as the sound travelled through the quarantine
walls. It was not a clean peal. Each note came bruised, as though struck from beneath the earth, and the
stone beneath his boots gave a faint answering tremor.
Beyond the gatehouse, the stronghold slept behind ash-streaked battlements. Stormmarch had been
founded in 71 AS, when the world was still young enough to mistake walls for salvation. The years had
blackened its towers, but had not softened them. Nine thousand two hundred and sixty-three soldiers
remained garrisoned within its bounds, though no one called them an army now. They were a sealed thing,
strength held under quarantine, and Stormmarch itself stood outside the realm’s core holdings like a
clenched fist no sovereign dared open.
The bell rang again.
Gareth raised his gloved hand. The escort behind him halted.
No one spoke. In Stormmarch, silence had the obedience of fear.
He turned toward the stair descending into the old cisterns. A strip of red cloth had been tied around the
iron latch. It had not been there when he passed an hour before. Gareth knew because he had touched the
latch then, and the cold had bitten through his glove.
His fingers hovered over the cloth.
The blood-rites waited beneath his ribs like a second heartbeat.
Proscribed, the law called them. The word had been carved into decrees, muttered from pulpits, hammered
into the mouths of executioners. Gareth had learned long ago that prohibition did not make a thing wicked.
It merely made it valuable to those who understood what it could purchase.
He untied the cloth.
A woman’s voice spoke from the stairwell.
“Major Executioner.”
The title came from the dark below. Gareth descended without answering.
The air changed as he went. Above, Stormmarch tasted of ash, iron, and the sour breath of too many
confined bodies. Beneath the stronghold, the air was wet and mineral-rich. Water moved somewhere
beyond the walls. He could hear it pressing patiently against the stone.
The woman stood at the foot of the stair with a lantern hooded in blue glass. Gareth could see little of her
beyond the shape of her coat and the pale oval of her face. No badge marked her allegiance. That was
often badge enough.
“What rang the bell?” he asked.
“The dead.”
“Which dead?”
“The ones who were never buried.”

Gareth looked past her, into the corridor. The floor bore old iron rings set at intervals along the wall. Some
were empty. Others held chains sunk into rust.
He had seen the archive concerning this place. He had read the account by candlelight while ash hissed
against the windows. The Winter Reckoning began in 270 AS. The Winter Reckoning waged at
Stormmarch in 276 AS. The phrases had been written by hands that had never crossed the Ash Wastes,
their ink untroubled by wind or hunger.
The record stated that the conflict ended in 283 AS, leaving 27,987 casualties. It named the Iron-Ring
Cartel victor. It described a betrayal at the eleventh hour.
The record did not say how the wells had tasted afterward.
Gareth had found that truth in a fragment sealed beneath a dead magistrate’s floor: the victors poisoned the
wells of their own allies. Not an enemy’s wells. Their own. The dead buried in Stormmarch’s lower
chambers had not been soldiers alone. They had been witnesses, carriers, men and women whose bodies
had been left where the water could not reach them.
Or where the water could.
The woman lifted the lantern. “You know why you were summoned.”
“I was summoned to investigate a disturbance.”
“You were summoned because the disturbance answered to your name.”
Gareth felt the hidden pulse beneath his sternum strengthen.
He stepped nearer the wall. A dark stain marked the mortar at shoulder height. It had dried into a shape
like a branching hand. He touched it with one finger.
The stain was warm.
The woman watched him. “Do not.”
He withdrew his hand.
There were moments when the discipline of his office became a chain, and moments when it became a
blade. Gareth had survived by knowing the difference. His discipline was the public shape of him:
measured speech, exact movements, judgment without tremor. Beneath it lived the other thing, the
forbidden devotion that had no altar but flesh and no scripture but pain.
He had been born in 300 AS. This fact appeared in the ledgers, but the ledgers did not mention the dreams
that had followed him from childhood—the red thread beneath every door, the sound of water running
backward, the faceless congregation kneeling in a room that did not exist. They did not record how, in
secret, he had learned to draw signs in blood and ask the dark to remember.
The woman said, “The mark has appeared on three doors.”
“Show me.”
She turned.
The corridor narrowed beyond her. Its walls were slick with condensation. Gareth walked beneath old
drainage channels and broken hooks. The lantern’s blue light moved over stones stained black by age. At
the first door, the mark had been painted across the wood in a single dragging stroke. At the second, it had

been scratched into the iron. At the third, the door stood open.
Behind it was a cell.
A man sat inside with his back to the wall. His wrists were bound before him. Ash had been rubbed into
his hair. He lifted his head as Gareth entered.
The prisoner smiled.
Gareth knew that smile. He had seen it on the condemned when they understood that death was not the
worst authority in the room.
“You are late,” the man said.
“I was not expected.”
“You were expected before you were born.”
The woman with the lantern inhaled sharply.
Gareth entered the cell. “Who sent you?”
The prisoner looked toward the ceiling. “Stormmarch.”
“Stormmarch is stone.”
“Stone remembers better than men.”
Gareth crouched before him. The man’s hands were filthy, but not with ash. A thin red line ran from the
base of his thumb to the inside of his wrist. The cut was fresh.
Gareth studied it.
The blood had not fallen. It had crawled.
He could feel the pattern’s pull. It was a simple invitation, almost childish in its construction: life offered,
name withheld. A novice’s work, unless the novice had been taught by something patient.
“Where did you learn this?” Gareth asked.
The prisoner’s eyes settled on him. “You taught me.”
“No.”
“You taught yourself.”
The blue lantern guttered. For one instant the cell walls seemed farther apart. Gareth smelled snow, though
Stormmarch had no snow upon its parapets. He smelled old wells, winter iron, and the bitter sweetness of
water gone bad.
The Winter Reckoning had begun in 270 AS, but its first wound had been cut long before men admitted
they were bleeding. Gareth had never believed wars began when proclamations named them. Wars began
in private rooms, with a hand upon a seal and a cup passed to the wrong mouth.
The prisoner laughed softly. “Do you remember the wells?”
“I was not there.”
“You were born after the first killing.”

“Words are not evidence.”
“Blood is.”
The man pressed his thumb against the cut on his wrist. A bead gathered, round and bright.
Gareth’s own hand moved before he could stop it.
The woman seized his arm. “Major.”
Her fingers were cold through the glove.
Gareth turned his head. “Release me.”
“You know what he is asking.”
“I know what he is doing.”
“And you know what answering will cost.”
He looked back at the prisoner. The man’s smile had disappeared. Beneath the ash, his face seemed
emptied of everything human except expectation.
Gareth had executed men for less than this. He had stood before the condemned with the formal calm
required of his office and watched their last certainty collapse. He had believed, or taught himself to
believe, that an execution was a boundary. One side contained the crime. The other contained
consequence.
But the blood-rites had never recognized boundaries.
In the darkness beyond the cell, water struck stone.
Once.
Twice.
A third time.
The sound became a rhythm.
Gareth closed his eyes. Beneath his ribs, the second heartbeat answered.
“Tell me,” he said.
The woman’s grip tightened. “No.”
The prisoner bowed his head as if before a throne.
“Tell me what?” Gareth asked.
“Who poisoned the first well.”
The question entered him like a hook.
He saw the archive again: the Iron-Ring Cartel named victor, the betrayal recorded at the eleventh hour,
the neat language of the surviving witnesses. He saw the concealed truth beneath it, the wells of their own
allies fouled by the victors’ hands. He saw bodies carried from the water and laid beneath Stormmarch
because there had been nowhere else to put them.
Yet the image was wrong.

Not the wells. Not the poison.
The dead had been arranged.
Gareth opened his eyes.
“What do you see?” the woman whispered.
The prisoner had begun to tremble. Blood slipped from his wrist and hung in the air between his hands.
Gareth reached for it.
The blue lantern went dark.
Something moved in the corridor.
Not footsteps. Not breath.
A dragging sound, slow and wet, approaching the cell from the sealed end of the passage.
The woman drew a blade. Gareth heard the whisper of steel leave its sheath. The prisoner bent forward,
chains straining, while the suspended bead of blood widened into a trembling red sphere.
Gareth placed his bare fingertip against it.
Pain opened through him.
The cell vanished.
He stood beneath a white sky while ash fell upward. Before him stretched the walls of Gloammarch,
founded in 321 AS and contested ever since, its garrison of 2,148 men holding the place against a dispute
that had never learned how to die. He saw its gates thrown open. He saw no soldiers upon them.
Then the vision turned.
Stormmarch rose behind him, older and darker, its garrison of 9,263 sealed within the quarantine. Far
below, in the drowned chambers, hundreds of mouths opened beneath the water.
All of them spoke with Gareth’s voice.
The prisoner screamed.
Gareth tore his hand away. The blood struck the floor and burned there without flame.
The woman raised her blade toward the corridor. “What is coming?”
Gareth could not answer. His lungs had forgotten the use of air.
From the darkness, a voice spoke in the tone of a bell heard beneath the earth.
“Major Executioner.”
The title came closer.
The prisoner began to laugh again.
Gareth stood, drawing the ceremonial blade from his belt. Its edge was narrow, polished, and utterly
innocent of the work it had done.
His grip steadied.

The voice said, “Open the well.”
And behind the third door, something knocked from the other side.
The knock came again.
Not against the wood this time, but beneath it. The flagstones trembled beneath Gareth’s boots. Dust sifted
from the mortar in a pale veil, settling over the prisoner’s hair and shoulders. The woman’s blade did not
waver, though her breathing had changed. Gareth heard the small, involuntary catch before each breath,
the body confessing what the mouth would not.
“Open the well,” the voice said.
Gareth kept his eyes on the third door.
The corridor had been carved below Marrowwell Abbey before the abbey had acquired its name, or so the
records claimed. Records were obedient things. They bent around whatever hand held the seal. Stone was
less forgiving. Stone remembered pressure. Stone remembered blood.
He had found the old passage beneath a collapsed stair during his first winter of command. Since 322 AS,
Gareth Ironmere had commanded Marrowwell Abbey, and the title had come to him with ledgers, keys, a
garrison that feared his silence, and a foundation that muttered in the hours before dawn. He had given
orders in the upper halls. He had condemned men beneath the bell tower. He had slept in a chamber whose
walls were thick enough to keep out screams.
Yet he had never opened the well.
The prisoner pressed his forehead to the floor. His laughter had gone thin and bright, like a knife being
sharpened.
“The water wants a mouth,” he whispered.
The woman glanced at Gareth. “You know what that is.”
“No.”
“You looked at it as if you did.”
“I look at everything that way.”
The voice behind the door gave a low, pleased resonance. It was not laughter. It was the sound of stone
accepting rain.
Gareth shifted his grip on the ceremonial blade. The edge was made for display, for the slow public
certainty of execution. It had no weight for combat. He had used it anyway. There were men who believed
a blade became sacred through the blood it took. Gareth knew better. Sacredness was merely the name fear
gave to repetition.
His thumb found the groove cut into the hilt.
The blood beneath his fingernail had dried black.
He had drawn the mark there in secret, in the hours when the abbey’s lamps guttered low and the prayers
above became indistinct. A proscribed sign. A shape whose lines were not meant to meet. He had copied it
from a fragment of skin taken from a condemned man who had died speaking in three voices. Gareth had
told himself it was study. Then necessity. Then devotion.

The mark warmed beneath his thumb.
The prisoner lifted his face. His eyes were wet, but no tears had fallen. “It knows you.”
“It knows the office.”
“It said Major Executioner.”
“It has heard the title.”
“It heard your blood.”
The woman moved closer to the door, blade angled toward the seam. “If it knows blood, why does it need
the well opened?”
Gareth looked at her hands. No tremor. Her knuckles were pale from the force of her grip. She had not
asked what waited below. She had asked what it wanted. That distinction mattered.
“Because the well is closed,” he said.
“Then leave it closed.”
The prisoner laughed once, sharply. “It will open itself.”
The knock came again.
This time the door bulged inward.
The woman cursed under her breath and stepped back. Gareth did not. The wood had been blackened by
age, its surface webbed with cracks that ran toward the iron lock. In the center, where the pressure had
struck, a dark dampness spread outward. The boards drank it greedily.
Not water.
Gareth smelled rust, old meat, and the sweet mineral scent that rose from a wound before it began to heal.
He had smelled that scent in the blood-rites.
The woman saw his expression. “What is it?”
“Stand aside.”
“Why?”
“Because I said so.”
“You command the abbey, not me.”
The words entered him like a hook.
No one spoke to him in that tone beneath Marrowwell Abbey. Above, there were courtiers who disguised
defiance as counsel, priests who placed their authority in the mouths of dead scriptures, soldiers who
obeyed because the alternative was a public blade. Here there was only the woman, the prisoner, the door,
and the buried voice. The old reflex rose in him: punish first, understand later.
His ceremonial blade lifted a finger’s breadth.
Then the mark beneath his nail pulsed.
The door opened.

No hinges moved. The wood drew inward as if the darkness behind it had taken hold and inhaled. The iron
lock remained fixed to the frame, its teeth still buried in the hasp. A narrow blackness appeared, then
widened. Cold rolled out, carrying the stink of water that had never seen the sky.
Beyond the threshold lay a stair descending into absolute dark.
The voice spoke from below.
“Major Executioner.”
The title no longer sounded like a summons. It sounded like a verdict.
The prisoner crawled toward the opening. Gareth caught him by the back of his garment and hauled him
away. The cloth tore. Beneath it, the prisoner’s skin was marked with thin red lines, not cuts but seams, as
if something had been stitched into him and was testing the work.
The prisoner twisted with sudden strength.
“Let me go.”
Gareth drove his knee into the man’s spine. Bone struck stone. The prisoner’s hands clawed at the floor.
“Who put you here?” Gareth asked.
The man’s mouth opened.
For a moment, the voice that came out was Gareth’s own.
“Who put you here?”
The woman made a sound low in her throat.
Gareth struck the prisoner across the jaw. The echo went down the stair.
The man grinned through blood. “You did.”
“I have never seen you before.”
“You have never seen yourself.”
“Enough.”
“Not yet.”
Something moved below.
Gareth felt it before he heard it: a pressure against the soles of his feet, a slow rising force that seemed to
draw the marrow upward through his bones. The air in the corridor tightened. The lamps along the walls
bowed toward the opening, their flames narrowing to blue needles.
The woman seized the prisoner by the collar. “What is below?”
The prisoner stared at her with pity.
“The first mouth.”
A drop of blood fell from his lip. It struck the floor and began to crawl toward the stair.
Gareth watched it go.

The drop did not roll along the slope. It moved against it.
His hidden practice had taught him that blood possessed a memory of direction. It sought the heart, the
wound, the hand that had spilled it. But this was not seeking anything human. It drew itself into a narrow
thread and slipped over the threshold.
The darkness drank.
The mark beneath Gareth’s nail burned so fiercely that his finger went numb.
He remembered the chamber where he had first traced the sign. The basin of salt. The single wick. The
forbidden words spoken without sound. He remembered how the blood had gathered in the shallow dish,
how it had trembled when he touched the surface, how something unseen had leaned close enough to
breathe against his wrist.
He had believed the rite answered him.
Now he understood that it had merely learned his shape.
The woman’s blade came up beside his throat. “You knew this was here.”
“I knew a sealed chamber was here.”
“You knew the rites.”
“I know many things.”
“Did you open it?”
Gareth turned his head enough to meet her gaze. “Not yet.”
The lie tasted of ash.
The stair groaned.
From below came the sound of water striking water, though there was no rain and no visible stream. Then
another sound threaded through it: the scrape of many fingernails along stone.
The prisoner began to sob.
“Close it,” he said.
The woman laughed once, without humor. “Now you want it closed?”
“It has smelled him.”
Gareth’s hand tightened around the ceremonial blade. The innocent edge reflected the blue lampfire. His
face appeared upon it in broken slivers, never whole.
The voice rose from the stair.
“Blood of the keeper.”
The prisoner went rigid.
“Blood of the opened hand.”
The woman stepped nearer to Gareth, whether for protection or position he could not tell.
“Blood of the one who remembers.”

A wet shape touched the darkness below the threshold.
It was a hand, though the fingers were too long and the joints bent in the wrong places. It emerged slowly,
feeling along the stone. The nails were pale and translucent. Between them clung strands of black water.
The prisoner screamed.
Gareth moved before thought could interfere. He seized the lamp from its bracket and flung it into the
stair.
The flame struck the hand.
There was no flare. No smoke. The fire simply vanished, and the darkness recoiled with a sound like a
throat being cut.
For one breath, the stair became visible.
Steps descended into a circular chamber where water stood motionless around a stone well. The well’s rim
was crowded with figures pressed shoulder to shoulder, their faces turned upward. Some wore the rotted
remnants of robes. Some wore armor. Some had no faces at all.
At the center of the well, something pale rose beneath the surface.
Gareth saw his own hand reaching for it.
Then the dark closed.
The woman seized his arm. “What did you see?”
“Nothing.”
“You are a poor liar.”
“I am an excellent liar. You are merely frightened.”
“I am not frightened.”
“Then release me.”
She did not.
Behind them, the prisoner began to whisper words Gareth had never taught him.
The syllables were part of the blood-rite.
Not the invocation. The response.
Gareth felt the corridor tilt. The blood beneath his nail split the skin and ran down his finger. He watched
it descend, bright against the austerity of his hand.
The voice below spoke again, softer now.
“Open the well, Gareth Ironmere.”
The woman heard the name. Her grip tightened.
The prisoner bowed until his forehead touched the threshold.
Gareth looked down the empty black stair and understood that the command had never been meant for the
door.

It was meant for him.
His ceremonial blade began to tremble.
Not in his hand.
In the dark below.
The trembling passed through the blade and into the stones.
Gareth let go.
The ceremonial knife struck the threshold without a sound. It stood upright, balanced in the seam between
two blocks, its narrow length shivering as if some buried hand worried it from below.
The woman beside him breathed through her teeth.
“Do not answer,” she said.
The prisoner lifted his head. His face remained hidden beneath the fall of his hair, but Gareth saw the
blood shining where his brow had touched the threshold. The old response had left his mouth. He was
waiting for Gareth to complete it.
The dark below waited too.
Gareth felt the shape of the forbidden syllables gathering behind his teeth. They had lived there for years,
patient as worms in a grave. He had never taught them to the prisoner. He had never spoken them aloud
except with his own blood as witness, alone behind locked doors, with the candles drowned and the bowl
covered.
Still, the prisoner knew.
That was the first terror.
The second was that Gareth knew what came next.
He drew his hand from the woman’s grasp. She did not resist him. Perhaps she felt it too: the pressure
rising through the stairwell, the immense attention that had turned toward them. The flame in the wall
sconce bent downward. Ash sifted from the ceiling and drifted into the black like pale rain.
“Who taught you?” Gareth asked.
The prisoner’s shoulders moved.
Not a shrug. Not fear.
A bow.
The woman stepped between them. “You heard him. Do not answer the well.”
Gareth looked at her. Her face had become a hard plane in the weak light. Whatever she had expected to
find beneath the abbey, it had not been this. Her hand hovered near the weapon at her belt, though the
corridor offered no room in which to wield it. Steel would be a child’s argument here.
“Your caution comes late,” Gareth said.
“I was not the one who opened it.”
“I have not opened anything.”

The blade trembled harder.
Far below, metal struck stone.
Once.
Then again.
The sound climbed the stair.
Gareth’s mouth dried. He knew the geometry of the abbey’s foundations. He knew which chambers had
been sealed, which cisterns were dry, which old passages led nowhere but collapsed earth. He had walked
them by torchlight until every turn lived in his bones. There was no well beneath this corridor.
Yet the sound came from below.
He remembered another account, written in a cramped hand on a ledger whose pages smelled of mold and
iron. The Winter Reckoning ended in 283 AS. Its dead were recorded as 27,987 casualties. The Iron-Ring
Cartel was named victor.
Named victor.
The phrase had always offended him. It sounded clean, almost ceremonial, as though victory could be laid
upon a table and measured beside the cups. But the record contained another line, struck through and
written again in the margin: the outcome was decided by a betrayal at the eleventh hour.
Gareth had read that line until the ink blurred.
The concealed truth was worse.
The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.
He had thought, then, that the old scribes had used the word wells as a symbol. Every war bred its
symbols. Wells meant trust. Wells meant sustenance. Wells meant the hidden places from which a realm
drew life.
But something beneath the abbey had just called him by name.
The prisoner began to laugh.
The sound was small, almost polite.
The woman seized him by the throat and drove him against the wall. His skull struck stone. Dust trembled
loose above them.
“Stop,” Gareth said.
She did not look back. “He is bait.”
“Stop.”
“He brought us here.”
“I said stop.”
The authority in his voice finally moved her. She released the prisoner, though her fingers remained
curled. The man sagged against the wall. His lips were wet with blood.
Gareth descended one step.

The well answered with a low groan.
The sound was not stone grinding on stone. It had depth. It had a throat.
His ceremonial blade snapped sideways in the threshold and fell flat.
A pulse travelled through the stair. The woman staggered. The prisoner slid to his knees, palms pressed to
the floor.
Gareth steadied himself against the wall.
The blood-rite inside him woke fully.
It did not speak in words. It offered sensations: a cut across the palm, a bowl black as pitch, the warm
surrender of living blood. It showed him a mouth beneath the earth and the red thread that joined every
wound to it.
He had practiced proscribed blood-rites in secret since before he held authority enough to command a
blade. He had learned their forms without blessing, without witness, without permission. He had told
himself the rites were knowledge, and knowledge was not devotion.
The dark below knew the lie.
“You have used the old signs,” the woman said.
Gareth looked at her.
Her gaze had dropped to his hand. Blood still ran from the split beneath his nail, gathering at the base of
his finger before falling onto the stair.
“Only the first sign,” he said.
“There are no first signs.”
The prisoner raised his head.
His eyes were not visible, but Gareth felt their attention like pressure beneath the skin.
The voice below returned.
“Gareth Ironmere.”
His name travelled through the stones, not echoing but multiplying. It emerged from the walls, the floor,
the woman’s clenched teeth. It seemed to form in the hollow behind his heart.
He had been born in 300 AS. The date had been entered into the execution rolls, beside a mark that
identified him as a major Executioner. A year, a title, a place for a man to stand. The record had never
mentioned the blood beneath his fingernails.
A second voice whispered from below.
“300 AS.”
Gareth’s knees almost failed.
The woman saw. “What is it?”
“It knows the year.”

“Who?”
He could not answer.
The prisoner began to crawl toward the stair. Gareth caught him by the collar and dragged him back. The
cloth tore. Under it, along the man’s throat, were thin red lines arranged in a pattern Gareth recognized
from the forbidden books. Not letters. Veins, persuaded into script.
The prisoner smiled at him.
“Open the well,” he whispered.
Gareth struck him across the mouth.
The woman flinched, though the blow had been light. The prisoner’s head turned with it. Blood touched
his lips.
Below, something breathed in satisfaction.
Gareth snatched up the blade. Its handle was cold enough to burn.
“We leave,” the woman said.
The stair behind them had changed.
The corridor ended where it should have continued. The passage toward the upper cloister was gone,
replaced by a wall of pale masonry. No seam showed in it. No mortar. Only a flat surface bearing the faint
impression of a door that had never been built.
The woman approached it and pressed both palms against the stone.
“Move,” she said.
The wall remained silent.
Gareth looked at the prisoner.
The man had pushed himself upright. Blood threaded from the corner of his mouth and fell in steady
drops, each one vanishing into the cracks between the stones.
“You knew,” Gareth said.
The prisoner’s smile faded.
“You knew there was no passage back.”
He shook his head.
The voice from below spoke through him.
“There is no passage back.”
The woman drew her weapon.
Gareth caught her wrist before she could raise it. The blade in her hand was plain, meant for work rather
than ceremony. Its edge had been cared for. She had trusted it before. Trust had become a dangerous habit
in this place.
“Do not,” he said.

Her eyes fixed on his. “Then tell me what you intend.”
He looked down the stair.
The darkness had risen.
It clung to the lower steps now, thick as submerged ink, and within it pale shapes moved without bodies.
The air smelled of wet iron. Somewhere beneath the abbey, water stirred against stone.
He remembered the Winter Reckoning’s wells. The poisoned throats of allies. The Iron-Ring Cartel’s
victory sealed not by strength but by treachery hidden under the ordinary act of drinking.
He remembered Stormmarch, founded in 71 AS, its fortifications raised in the Ash Wastes and its garrison
numbered at 9,263. The stronghold remained quarantined, outside the realm’s core holdings. Gareth had
once studied its sealed reports, the lists of supplies and fevers and men who were not permitted to leave.
The ink had carried the same smell as this air.
Stormmarch had been waged over during the Winter Reckoning in 276 AS.
The well had called him from beneath Marrowwell Abbey.
The past was not buried. It had only learned to wait.
“Tell me,” the woman said again.
Gareth lowered the blade.
“Do you know Gloammarch?”
Her expression tightened. “What has that to do with this?”
“Gloammarch stands in the Ash Wastes. It was founded in 321 AS. Its garrison is 2,148.”
“Gareth.”
“Its status remains contested.”
“Why are you saying this?”
Because the words were coming from somewhere deeper than memory. Because the figures arranged
themselves like nails. Because the dark below had begun to speak in the language of ledgers.
The prisoner turned toward the stair.
“Gloammarch,” he murmured.
The stone wall behind them gave a soft, wet crack.
The woman stepped away from it. “What did you do?”
“Nothing.”
A seam appeared in the wall.
Not a door. A vertical wound.
Black moisture welled along it and ran downward. As it reached the floor, it moved against the slope,
gathering at Gareth’s boots.
The woman raised her weapon again.

This time he let her.
The prisoner bowed his head. “The well remembers every hand.”
Gareth stared at the blood beneath his boots. It was not his. It carried the pale reflection of the sconce,
though the flame above them had gone out.
The stairwell darkened.
Something touched the underside of the threshold.
The ceremonial blade jumped in Gareth’s hand.
He did not release it.
The old response stood ready behind his teeth. He could feel its shape now, its cruel simplicity. A single
phrase. A consent disguised as obedience.
The woman whispered, “If you know the rite, use it.”
Gareth looked at her.
For the first time, fear broke through her discipline.
“You said you had not opened anything,” she continued.
“I haven’t.”
“Then close it.”
The prisoner began to weep. Quietly. Without shame. His tears struck the floor and joined the blood.
The voice below rose, vast enough to fill the stair.
“Gareth Ironmere.”
He shut his eyes.
In the darkness behind them, the well had no stones, no water, no bottom. It held only a red reflection of
himself, standing with the blade in his hand, waiting for permission to become what he had hidden.
Then the thing below spoke the final syllable.
And Gareth answered.

Chapter 11
The rain came sideways across the harbor, needling the black glass of the windows and turning the
watchfires beyond them into smeared red wounds.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood with both hands upon the chart table. She did not lean. A Fleet Admiral did not
lean while others watched, and there were always others watching, even in an empty chamber. The walls
had ears in the Ashen Era. The beams remembered oaths. The sea carried whispers farther than ships.
On the table, under a weight of dull iron, lay Caedmon Fellgard’s ledger.
Caedmon sat opposite her with his shoulders gathered into the reserved posture of a man who had spent
his life protecting words from the world. He was a Scribe, and the discipline of that calling clung to him:
ink-stained fingers, writing materials arranged in exact lines, a reed pen held as though it were a blade that
must never be drawn without cause.
Beside the ledger rested a second packet, sealed in dark wax.
Morwenna looked at it and felt the old, familiar division open within her. One part of her was the Fleet
Admiral: stern, useful, visible. The other part listened for the Iron-Ring Cartel beneath every silence.
“Read it again,” she said.
Caedmon’s eyes lifted. “The whole entry?”
“The portion concerning Hollowreach.”
He opened the ledger. Its pages gave a dry whisper, like dead leaves stirring beneath a door.
“Hollowreach,” he read, “lies in the Gloaming Reach and was founded in 56 AS. It is a core location under
quarantine.”
The rain battered the panes.
“Again.”
Caedmon obeyed, though his mouth tightened. “Hollowreach lies in the Gloaming Reach and was founded
in 56 AS. It is a core location under quarantine.”
Morwenna watched the words settle between them. Hollowreach had become, in the reports, a place
without a mouth. No bells from its towers. No carts through its gates. No ferrymen willing to speak its
name after dusk. Containment was the official word. Quarantine, the written word. Beneath both lay the
older truth: something had been closed away, and those outside feared that the lock might learn to turn.
“Who authorized the quarantine?” she asked.
Caedmon lowered his gaze to the page. “The record does not say.”
“Then the record is a coward.”
“The record is incomplete.”
“Those are often the same thing.”
A knock sounded at the outer door.

Caedmon’s hand stopped over the inkpot. Morwenna felt the chamber contract around her. The rain, the
guttering lamps, the little copper dish steaming with bitter herbs—all of it withdrew before the presence
beyond the door.
“Enter,” she called.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned stepped inside.
They wore the dark authority of the High Inquisitor without ornament. Water gleamed on their cloak.
Their expression held the stillness of someone who had looked upon too many guilty faces and found none
of them surprising. The title followed them into the room like a second shadow: Sabelle Mournvale the
Twice-Crowned, born in 263 AS, High Inquisitor, member of The Ashen Vanguard.
Caedmon rose too quickly and nearly overturned the ink.
Sabelle’s gaze touched him, then moved to Morwenna. “Fleet Admiral.”
“High Inquisitor.”
No bow passed between them. Respect could be a weapon, and neither wished to arm the other.
Sabelle closed the door. The latch fell with a small, final sound.
Morwenna saw the packet beneath the iron weight. “You came for the ledger?”
“I came for what the ledger fails to contain.”
“Then you have come to the right room.”
“Have I?”
Sabelle crossed to the table. Their gloved hand rested upon the iron weight, but did not move it. The lamp
flame shivered between them.
Caedmon said, “I was instructed to bring the record.”
“By whom?” Sabelle asked.
Caedmon looked toward Morwenna.
The answer hung there, unspoken and dangerous. Morwenna allowed herself one breath before saying,
“By necessity.”
Sabelle’s face did not change. “Necessity is the favorite mask of treason.”
The word entered Morwenna cleanly. She had heard worse names from men with knives in their hands
and better names from men who intended to sell her. Treason required allegiance. She had long ago ceased
to know where hers ended.
At the far end of the room, an uncovered map showed the five powers that contested the ruins: The Ashen
Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and The Bleeding Crown. Their
boundaries had been drawn and erased until the parchment resembled diseased skin.
Sabelle followed her gaze.
“The Ashen Vanguard will not permit the Cartel to make a market of Hollowreach.”

Morwenna kept her voice level. “The Iron-Ring Cartel makes a market of whatever can be lifted, counted,
or buried.”
“And you know this closely.”
There it was. Not accusation. Measurement.
Morwenna looked down at the map. Beneath the table, her left hand closed slowly. Somewhere beyond
the rain, men were loading provisions, checking rigging, whispering prayers into their sleeves. She had
given the Iron-Ring Cartel information before: routes, supply delays, the weakness in a patrol pattern.
Never enough to name a war. Always enough to tilt a scale.
Her secret had no shape until spoken.
“I know the Cartel is patient,” she said.
Sabelle’s eyes remained on her. “Patient powers are the most dangerous.”
Caedmon turned a page. “There is another relevant entry.”
Sabelle looked at him.
The Scribe swallowed. “The War of Endless Vigil began in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS, causing 81577
casualties.”
The number seemed to darken the room. Morwenna had read it before. Numbers were meant to make
slaughter orderly. They failed.
Caedmon continued. “It ended with the total rout of the aggressors, and The Bleeding Crown is recorded
as the victor.”
“Recorded,” Sabelle said.
“Yes.”
“And what is not recorded?”
Caedmon’s fingers tightened around the page. “Secretly, the losing commander was bribed to withdraw.”
The rain softened, then struck hard again.
Morwenna remembered no battlefield from that war. She had been born in 288 AS, long after the banners
were folded and the bones sunk beneath grass. Yet the war survived in every institution that had profited
from it. The Bleeding Crown wore victory like a chain of gold. The Ashen Vanguard taught vigilance as
though watchfulness could cleanse betrayal. House Morvain gathered taxes from scars it had not suffered.
The Silent Choir turned names into hymns. The Iron-Ring Cartel sold the memory back in pieces.
“And you believe Hollowreach repeats that treachery?” Morwenna asked.
“I believe history repeats whatever remains profitable.”
Sabelle lifted the iron weight and drew the packet toward them. The wax bore no sigil. That absence was
more deliberate than any seal.
Caedmon said, “There is also Crookvale.”
“Read.”

“Crookvale was founded in 295 AS in The High Spires. It has been rebuilt and retains a garrison of 1004,
but remains outside the core holdings.”
Sabelle’s attention sharpened. “Outside the core holdings.”
“Those are the words,” Caedmon said.
Morwenna knew the place from charts: a hard-edged settlement crooked against the highland stone, rebuilt
whenever ruin believed it had finally won. Its garrison was large enough to matter and too isolated to be
trusted. A hundred routes could reach it, according to the map. A hundred routes could be made to vanish
in weather.
“Crookvale watches the passes,” Sabelle said.
“Crookvale watches itself,” Morwenna replied.
“Perhaps that is why it has survived.”
“Survival is not loyalty.”
“No,” Sabelle said. “It is often the first proof of ambition.”
Caedmon’s pen moved. The scratch of it worked upon Morwenna’s nerves. Every word he set down
became another bar in the cage. She wanted to reach across the table and break the pen between his
fingers. Instead, she watched a bead of water slide from Sabelle’s cloak to the floor.
The High Inquisitor placed two fingers on the unsealed packet.
“Inside is a report concerning your fleet.”
Morwenna felt the room’s cold enter her bones.
“My fleet has many reports.”
“This one names a departure.”
“Then it is wrong. No departure has been ordered.”
“Not yet.”
Sabelle broke the seal.
For an instant the black wax gleamed like clotting blood. Morwenna thought of the Iron-Ring Cartel’s
preferred method of communication: scraps of sailcloth hidden beneath cargo boards, knots tied in
patterns no honest sailor would notice, messages that arrived without signatures and left no witness who
could read them. The packet on the table had not come from the Cartel. That was what made it dangerous.
Sabelle read in silence.
Morwenna kept her breathing measured. She could feel the secret within her—not guilt, precisely, but a
second pulse. It had grown there over years of commands, beneath uniforms and proclamations, beneath
the disciplined authority she projected so well. The pulse did not ask whether the Cartel deserved her
intelligence. It asked only what price the next piece would bring.
Sabelle folded the report.
“Your ships are expected to alter course.”

“By whom?”
“The report does not say.”
“Then it is incomplete.”
Caedmon glanced up.
Morwenna heard her own earlier words returned to her, polished into a blade.
Sabelle’s expression remained severe, but something moved behind it. “You object?”
“I object to sailing blind.”
“You have sailed into worse.”
“You have no evidence of that.”
“I have evidence of the sea.”
The answer should have been absurd. It was not. Beyond the walls, the harbor groaned under the weather.
Chains dragged against stone. Water climbed the steps and withdrew, climbed and withdrew, patient as a
siege.
Sabelle gathered the packet. “The Ashen Vanguard requires certainty.”
“The Ashen Vanguard requires obedience.”
“They are not the same.”
“No,” Morwenna said. “Certainty is what powerful people call obedience after they have written it down.”
Caedmon’s pen stopped again.
For the first time, Sabelle smiled. It was a thin and joyless thing.
“Be careful, Fleet Admiral.”
“I am always careful.”
“Then you know that care is not innocence.”
The words struck closer than they should have. Morwenna turned toward the window. The harbor lights
trembled beyond the glass, each one reflected in rainwater and broken by it. She imagined a message
traveling through the dark toward the Iron-Ring Cartel. She imagined the answer returning: a figure, a
route, a promise. She imagined the Cartel’s hands closing around what she had sold.
Behind her, Sabelle said, “There is one more matter.”
Morwenna did not turn. “Read it, Caedmon.”
The Scribe searched the ledger. His voice grew quieter.
“Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned keeps a bound revenant in their cellar.”
The storm seemed to pause.
Caedmon looked up, horrified by the sentence only after speaking it.
Sabelle did not move.

Morwenna watched their reflection in the black window. High Inquisitor. Twice-Crowned. Born in 263
AS. Member of The Ashen Vanguard. And beneath some unseen dwelling, a bound revenant waiting in a
cellar while inquisitorial judgments passed above it.
“Is that a record?” Sabelle asked.
Caedmon’s lips parted. No sound came.
“Answer,” Morwenna said.
“It is written here.”
“Written things are not always true.”
Sabelle’s reflection lifted its eyes to Morwenna’s.
“No,” they said. “But they are always useful.”
A bell rang somewhere in the rain.
Once.
Then again.
Morwenna turned from the window as Caedmon reached for the ledger and Sabelle reached beneath their
cloak, and the door behind them began to open.
The door opened on a gust of rain.
A sentry stood beyond it, helmet tucked beneath one arm, water running from the iron rim of his shoulder
plates. Behind him, the corridor sloped into darkness. The lamps there had been hooded against the storm,
leaving only thin blades of amber across the floor.
“Admiral,” he said.
Morwenna did not look at Caedmon. “What is it?”
“The quarantine seal has been broken at Hollowreach.”
Sabelle’s hand emerged from beneath their cloak. Not a weapon. A folded strip of black vellum, its edges
stiff with wax.
Caedmon made a small sound in his throat. It might have been fear. It might have been the reflex of a man
who saw a document leave its proper place.
Morwenna felt the room narrow around her.
“By whose authority?” she asked.
The sentry’s gaze flickered toward Sabelle, then away. “No authority was shown.”
“Then it was not broken,” Sabelle said. “It was opened.”
Their voice held no anger. That was worse. Anger spent itself. Sabelle’s calm had the cold patience of a
blade laid on a table.
Morwenna took the vellum from them. The wax bore no crest she recognized, only a thumbprint pressed
into the red surface. The shape of it seemed almost human, though the rainlight made every mark
uncertain.

She broke the seal.
The message inside contained few words. Caedmon leaned toward it, but Morwenna turned the page
before he could read.
Hollowreach. The quarantine boundary. Movement in the outer streets. A pale animal seen beneath the old
watchtower. Witnesses dead or unable to speak.
At the bottom, the hand had changed.
The Pale Stag of Omens lairs in Hollowreach.
The letters were cramped, gouged into the vellum with such force that the nib had torn through in places.
Morwenna read the sentence again.
The storm pressed against the shutters. Somewhere in the fortress, a chain clanged, then settled.
Sabelle watched her. “You know what it means.”
“I know what it says.”
“Those are different things.”
Morwenna folded the message. The vellum felt damp, though it had been sealed. “You sent for me to
discuss a creature?”
“I sent for you because creatures do not break quarantine seals.”
“People do.”
“People are creatures with better excuses.”
Caedmon’s fingers tightened around the ledger. “The entry concerning Hollowreach is not current.”
Sabelle turned toward him. “How old?”
He swallowed. “The original record was made when the settlement was founded.”
Morwenna saw his mistake before he understood it. His eyes dropped to the page, searching for the line he
had spoken aloud.
“Hollowreach was founded in 56 AS,” he said, quieter now. “The entry concerns the Gloaming Reach and
the conditions of—”
“Do not read it,” Morwenna said.
Caedmon stopped.
The sentry remained in the doorway, waiting for orders that no one seemed willing to give him. Rain
tapped against his armor in a delicate, maddening rhythm.
Morwenna looked past him into the corridor. “How far is the report from Hollowreach?”
The sentry’s mouth tightened. “The courier came from the inland road.”
“That was not my question.”
He lowered his eyes. “Near.”

A word designed to conceal distance, labor, and the bodies spent crossing it.
Morwenna stepped toward the door. The cold from outside reached her before the corridor did, carrying
the smells of wet stone, lamp oil, and the iron tang of the sea. It entered the room like something that had
been invited.
Sabelle spoke behind her. “You will not leave.”
Morwenna paused.
The sentry’s shoulders became rigid. Caedmon bent over the ledger as though its pages had become
suddenly fascinating.
“Will I not?” Morwenna asked.
“You are thinking of the harbor.”
“I am always thinking of the harbor.”
“You are thinking of the ships that can reach Hollowreach before dawn.”
Morwenna glanced back. “There are no ships that can reach Hollowreach.”
“Then you are thinking of something else.”
The temptation to smile was sharp and brief. She gave it no life. Sabelle had a talent for naming the
thought one wished to keep unnamed. It was one of the reasons people mistook them for omniscient. In
truth, they were merely willing to say aloud what others had trained themselves to bury.
Morwenna held the message between two fingers.
“What do you want?”
“The gates closed.”
“They are already closed.”
“Then make the closure visible.”
“To whom?”
“To everyone who is watching.”
There it was: not fear of the Pale Stag of Omens, not even fear of whatever had crossed the boundary, but
fear of the story that would gather around it. Stories moved faster than armies and required less food. They
slipped beneath doors. They entered chapels, barracks, counting rooms. They made cowards brave and the
brave obedient.
Morwenna had seen a war built from less.
The War of Endless Vigil had been remembered as a triumph of endurance, a blood-marked watch held
until the aggressors broke. The records carried their clean language: rout, victory, finality. They did not
carry the taste of bribes, or the silence of a losing commander paid to withdraw. A line could be made to
collapse by force. It could also be persuaded.
A quarantine seal could be broken in either fashion.
“You are asking me to turn a report into a spectacle,” Morwenna said.

“I am asking you to make the spectacle ours.”
Sabelle crossed the chamber. Their shadow fell over the ledger, and Caedmon’s hand froze above the
page.
Morwenna watched the inquisitor’s reflection in the black window. The crown sat pale against the
darkness, its outline warped by rain. Beneath it, the face remained unreadable.
“Who sent this?” Morwenna asked.
“You know who sent it?”
“No.”
“Then why ask?”
“Because you know who did.”
The silence that followed was not empty. It had weight, texture, pressure. Caedmon’s breathing. The
sentry’s wet armor. The muted roar of the storm passing over the roof.
Sabelle’s gaze moved to the folded vellum. “There are people who make their living from warnings.”
“Most people make their living from something.”
“Some warnings are purchased.”
Morwenna felt the words strike close enough to raise heat beneath her skin. She had learned to recognize
danger by its temperature. A blade was cold. A lie was warmer.
She turned toward the sentry. “Return to the gate.”
He straightened.
“Do not admit anyone without a written order bearing a recognized seal. If anyone claims to have come
from Hollowreach, do not touch them.”
His face tightened. “Admiral—”
“You heard me.”
“And if they refuse?”
“Then refuse harder.”
He bowed and withdrew. The door closed between them, leaving the room smaller than before.
Sabelle looked at her. “You have not asked what was seen.”
“I have read the report.”
“You have read an accusation.”
“Then tell me the witness account.”
“There was a woman in the street.”
Caedmon glanced up.

Sabelle continued. “She stood beneath the watchtower and would not move. When approached, she had no
tongue.”
Morwenna’s attention settled on the inquisitor. “Dead?”
“No.”
“Alive?”
“For the moment.”
The phrase was deliberate. Everything Sabelle said was deliberate, but this one had been sharpened.
“Was the animal seen by the woman?”
“By others.”
“How many?”
Sabelle’s eyes hardened slightly. “Enough.”
Morwenna hated the word. It belonged to cowards, priests, and commanders who had lost control of their
figures. Enough meant no one wished to count. Enough meant the truth had become inconvenient.
“What did they see?”
“A stag.”
“An ordinary stag?”
“No.”
“Pale?”
“Yes.”
“With antlers?”
Sabelle did not answer.
That was answer enough.
Morwenna walked to the table. The ledger lay open beneath Caedmon’s hands. Its pages were yellowed
and crowded, the ink faded into brown veins. She read fragments without allowing them to settle:
boundary rites, inherited warnings, provisions withheld, signs observed. The older writing had been
disciplined. The newer annotations were frantic.
At the edge of the page, someone had drawn a branching shape.
A crown of bone.
Caedmon placed his palm over it.
“You have seen this before,” Morwenna said.
“No.”
“Your hand is on the page.”
“I have not seen it before.”

“Then why conceal it?”
His mouth trembled. “Because it was not there when I opened the ledger.”
Sabelle leaned close to the book.
The ink in the drawing gleamed wetly.
Morwenna stared at it. She had seen blood behave like that when it first left a wound, shining black under
lantern light. But this was ink. It had no reason to move.
One thin line extended from the crown’s lowest point.
It crept across the margin.
Caedmon jerked away. The ledger slid, striking the table hard enough to send the lamp flame lurching
sideways. Darkness rushed across the ceiling.
Sabelle seized the lamp before it fell. Their other hand closed around Caedmon’s wrist.
“Do not touch the page,” they said.
“I did not—”
“You did.”
“I swear—”
“Swear to something that can hear you.”
Caedmon went pale.
Morwenna kept her eyes on the drawing. The line had stopped. At its tip, the ink gathered in a dark bead.
Outside, bells began to ring.
Not the measured warning of the gate. Not the solemn call used for death. These bells rang without
pattern, striking through the rain as if some unseen hand had seized the ropes and pulled until the metal
screamed.
Sabelle released Caedmon.
Morwenna felt the old instinct rise in her: assess the threat, assign the response, make the world obey the
shape of an order. It had carried her through fire, mutiny, and councils where every smile concealed a
knife.
But the message in her pocket was not a report anymore.
It was a door.
And something on the other side had begun to knock.
Sabelle lifted the lamp toward the window. “Look.”
At first Morwenna saw only rain sliding down the black glass.
Then a shape moved beyond it.
Antlers rose through the storm, pale as drowned bone. A head lowered. For an instant, two dark eyes fixed
upon the room.

The creature stood where no creature could stand, beyond the wall and above the drop, its hooves finding
purchase on nothing.
Caedmon began to pray.
Morwenna reached for the latch.
Sabelle caught her arm.
“Do not open it.”
The Pale Stag of Omens turned its head toward the corridor, toward the sealed gates, toward all the living
things gathered within the fortress.
Then, from somewhere below the floor, came the sound of a man laughing.
The laughter came again.
It rose through the stones in a wet, patient tremor, as though some throat buried beneath the fortress had
found the shape of joy and was practising it. The lamp flame bent toward the floor. Caedmon’s prayer
faltered.
Morwenna felt the room contract around them.
Not fear. Fear was a current, a thing with direction. This was pressure. The old pressure of a hull taking
water beneath the waterline, invisible to those who stood upon the deck. She had commanded ships
through black seas where every timber groaned and every man waited for the order to panic. The first duty
of command was not courage.
It was deciding what the others were permitted to believe.
“Open the corridor gates,” she said.
Caedmon looked up from his clasped hands. “Admiral—”
“That was not a request.”
The scribe rose too quickly. His papers slid from the table and scattered across the stones. He stooped for
them, hands trembling, and gathered the pages with the solemn care of a man rescuing the dead from a
fire.
Sabelle did not move.
Their gaze remained on the window. Rain dragged itself down the glass in long silver threads. Beyond it,
the Pale Stag of Omens was gone. Only the dark drop remained, and the storm shattering itself against the
fortress.
“What did you hear?” Morwenna asked.
“Laughter.”
“Below us?”
Sabelle’s eyes came to her. In the lamplight, the severity of their face seemed cut from ash. “You heard
it.”
“That is not an answer.”

“No.” Sabelle’s mouth tightened. “It is not.”
The laughter ceased.
Its absence was worse.
Morwenna crossed to the table. The papers there had been weighted with a brass seal, though she could
not remember placing it. A map lay beneath the scattered sheets, its coastlines warped by damp. Several
marks had been made in the margin—small strokes of ink, deliberate and narrow. She recognized the
hand.
Not Caedmon’s.
The Iron-Ring Cartel wrote in that manner. Their clerks had a gift for making treason look like accounting.
A line meant a road watched. Two meant a convoy delayed. A blackened corner meant a witness removed
from the reckoning.
She had sent them intelligence before.
Not much. Never enough to turn a battle by itself. A patrol’s strength. A harbour’s depth. Which officer
could be trusted to keep silent and which one would sell his mother for a cup of wine. Information moved
more cleanly than coin, and left less weight in the hand.
Her sealed messages had travelled beneath cargo ledgers and devotional books. They had crossed from her
command into the Iron-Ring Cartel’s possession without ever carrying her name.
Now the marks sat on this table.
Her skin prickled.
“Caedmon,” she said. “Who has entered this chamber?”
The scribe blinked. “No one, Admiral.”
“Who has had access to the records?”
“I keep the records.”
“That was not the question.”
He held the pages against his chest. His reserve had cracked, and behind it was a narrow, raw terror. “I do
not know.”
Sabelle turned from the window. “You know enough to lie badly.”
Caedmon’s face drained.
Morwenna heard the faintest scrape beneath the floor.
Stone against stone.
She drew the short blade at her belt. Its edge caught the lamp. Sabelle’s hand moved beneath their dark
coat, though no weapon appeared. The High Inquisitor had no need to display violence. It gathered around
them by instinct.
“Where is the stair?” Morwenna asked.
Caedmon stared at her.

“The stair below.”
“There is no stair below.”
Another scrape.
This time it travelled beneath all three of them, from the hearth to the wall and back again, as if something
crawled underneath the room while considering where best to emerge.
Sabelle said, “There is.”
Caedmon turned toward them. “You said the lower chambers were sealed.”
“I said the lower chambers were forbidden.”
“For whom?”
“For everyone.”
Morwenna watched their face. There it was—not guilt, exactly. Guilt belonged to those who believed
themselves answerable. Sabelle carried possession instead. Whatever waited below was theirs to
command, or theirs to conceal.
The laughter sounded once more, softer now.
A man laughing at a private joke.
Morwenna lowered her blade by an inch. “You keep something beneath this fortress.”
“I keep what must be kept.”
“By whose authority?”
Sabelle stepped toward the hearth. “Mine.”
The answer should have offended her. Instead it steadied the room. Authority, even corrupted authority,
was a shape the mind could grasp. Morwenna had spent her life among men who dressed appetite in law.
At least Sabelle did not bother with the costume.
Caedmon’s pages slipped from his hands again.
“Do not go down,” he whispered.
Sabelle looked over their shoulder. “You are a Scribe, Caedmon Fellgard. Your duty is to preserve what
occurs, not to prevent it.”
“My duty is not to witness damnation.”
“No,” Sabelle said. “Your duty is to write it accurately.”
They moved the iron grate before the hearth aside. Beneath it, black stone showed through the ash. No
opening marked the surface. Sabelle pressed two fingers to a seam Morwenna could not see.
Something answered from below.
Three knocks.
Caedmon made a sound like a swallowed sob.
The stones parted.

Cold breathed upward. It smelled of earth drowned in deep water, of rust, of old cloth sealed too long in
darkness. The lamp flame thinned, and blue light stirred in the narrow stairwell. Not firelight. Something
paler, with no warmth in it.
Morwenna should have ordered the gates sealed. She should have summoned the guard. She should have
put distance between herself and whatever Sabelle had hidden below.
Instead she thought of the ink marks on the map.
The Iron-Ring Cartel did not leave messages without expecting them to be found. If the records had been
touched, then someone knew what she had sold—or someone wanted her to believe they knew.
The fortress was no longer a place under threat.
It was the threat.
She descended first.
The steps were narrow and damp. Her shoulder brushed the walls, and the stone left a slickness on her
coat. Behind her, Caedmon followed with the lamp. Sabelle came last, closing the grate above them.
The sound of it sealing shut followed Morwenna down like a verdict.
The stair turned once. Then again.
No wind reached this far below. Yet something moved ahead, stirring a darkness that seemed to possess its
own breath. Morwenna kept her blade low. The corridor opened into a chamber whose walls were
crowded with shelves.
On the shelves stood jars.
Some held cloudy liquid. Some held only darkness. In others floated fragments she could not identify and
did not wish to. Teeth, perhaps. Knuckles. Pale shapes curled against the glass like drowned fingers.
Caedmon stopped behind her.
The lamp shook in his grip.
At the chamber’s centre stood an iron chair.
A figure was bound within it.
Chains crossed the chest, the arms, the throat. They had been driven into the stone behind the chair, each
link blackened as though it had survived a fire. The figure’s head hung forward. Wet strands veiled the
face. Its clothing had decayed into strips, revealing skin stretched tight and grey over an angular frame.
Morwenna had seen men die in battle. She had seen bodies left in the tide, faces gnawed away by white
things. This was not death.
Death had a dignity, if one was willing to call stillness dignity.
This thing was waiting.
Sabelle descended the last step and approached it.
The bound revenant lifted its head.
Caedmon began to weep without sound.

The revenant’s eyes opened. They were not clouded. They were clear, attentive, and horribly alive with
recognition.
“High Inquisitor,” it said.
Its voice came from far away, as if spoken through a wall of earth.
Sabelle stood before it. “You heard the laughter.”
“I heard the stag.”
Morwenna tightened her grip. “The Pale Stag of Omens was above the fortress.”
“No.” The revenant’s gaze shifted toward her. “It was beneath.”
The chamber seemed to tilt.
On the nearest shelf, one of the jars cracked. A black seam appeared through the glass. Caedmon flinched,
and the lamp flame guttered.
Sabelle did not look away from the revenant. “What did it show you?”
The thing smiled.
The expression was almost human. That made it worse.
“A door,” it said.
“Where?”
“Everywhere.”
Morwenna heard the sea then.
Not the sea outside the fortress. This was a deeper sound, a vast slow dragging, as though water moved
beneath the foundations and searched for a way up. Her mind supplied the image of a fleet caught in fog,
ships drifting without signal, each vessel believing itself alone.
She looked at Sabelle. “You have been questioning it.”
“I have been containing it.”
“You bind the dead in cellars and call that containment?”
“I bind what remains when the dead refuse their proper ending.”
The revenant laughed again.
This time, a second voice answered from behind the walls.
Then a third.
The jars began to tremble upon their shelves.
Caedmon dropped the lamp.
Sabelle seized his collar and pulled him aside as the lamp struck stone. Oil spread across the floor. Flame
ran through it in a thin golden sheet, illuminating the chamber from below.
Morwenna saw the marks carved into the floor.

Not words. Not any script she knew. They formed a circle around the chair, and beyond that circle
another, and another, each scored into the stone with patient violence.
At the edge of the outermost ring lay a folded strip of paper.
Her breath stopped.
The paper bore the Iron-Ring Cartel’s cipher.
She stepped toward it.
Sabelle caught her wrist.
The revenant leaned forward against its chains. Metal screamed. Its face emerged from the hanging hair,
and its eyes fixed upon Morwenna with a tenderness that made her stomach turn.
“Fleet Admiral,” it whispered.
No one had spoken her title.
Not here.
Not in any message.
Sabelle’s grip tightened. “Do not touch the paper.”
Morwenna looked down at the cipher, at the neat black strokes visible through the firelight.
One line.
Two.
Then a third mark, newly wet.
Ink was spreading across the paper by itself.
A message forming in the dark.
The revenant smiled wider.
Above them, somewhere beyond the sealed grate, the fortress began to ring with bells.

Chapter 12
Ash moved through the shutter cracks like ground glass.
Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn stood beneath the Thrice-Bound Lantern and watched the ward hold its
pale, imprisoned light. Three iron bindings crossed the lantern’s body, each one blackened by age, each
one inscribed with marks too worn to read. The object had been forged in 72 AS, when the world was still
young enough to believe that ruin could be fastened shut.
The light did not flicker.
That was why Halvard trusted it.
Flames lied. Flames bowed to breath, to weather, to the trembling hand that fed them. The Thrice-Bound
Lantern did neither. It held itself in guarded stillness, as if some buried mouth pressed against its glass and
could not find a way through.
Behind Halvard, a page turned.
The sound was small. It entered the chamber and seemed to trespass.
“Read it again,” Halvard said.
Halvard Sablewood swallowed. “I have read it three times.”
“Then you have had practice.”
The scribe lowered the page. His hands were ink-stained, the nails dark with old work. He had been born
in 408 AS, according to the registry he carried beneath his arm. The entry had been copied from a parish
roll and witnessed by two hands now dead. Halvard had made him recite the date before admitting him to
the chamber.
“Halvard Sablewood,” the scribe said carefully, “born in 408 AS.”
“Again.”
“Halvard Sablewood, born in 408 AS.”
The name sounded wrong in the room. Too close to Halvard’s own. A name was a hinge, and the wrong
one could open a door onto a grave.
Halvard did not turn. “The passage.”
Sablewood bent over the page. “The quarantine remains in force. Stormmarch is to be treated as outside
the realm’s core holdings. Its garrison numbers 9,263. No convoy, courier, or military party is to pass the
sealed roads without authorization.”
“Whose authorization?”
The scribe hesitated.
Halvard looked at him then.
No feature of Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn had ever been entered into a record that mattered. No height,
no scar, no color of eye or hair. The clerks preferred stations to flesh. Major Seneschal. Born in 338 AS.
Keeper of the seal. Witness to oaths. A person could be buried beneath such words and never trouble the
earth again.

Sablewood found the line. “The authorization of the liege.”
“Good. Continue.”
“Gloammarch remains contested. Its garrison numbers 2,148. The Ash Wastes are to be considered
unstable beyond the marked roads.”
“Unstable,” Halvard murmured.
A generous word. It suggested that the land might one day recover its balance.
Outside, wind scraped ash along the stone. Gloammarch was a fortress of ash-dark austerity, founded in
321 AS and still holding its ground amid dispute. Halvard had never liked the place. Its walls seemed built
not to keep enemies out, but to prevent the people within from fleeing their own fear.
Sablewood read on. “The Iron-Ring Cartel retains the authority granted by victory in the Winter
Reckoning.”
At that, Halvard’s mouth tightened.
“The Winter Reckoning began in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS,” Sablewood continued. “Casualties:
27,987. The Iron-Ring Cartel was the victor.”
“The official account.”
“Yes.”
“The passage is not an official account. It is a command ledger.”
Sablewood’s fingers shifted against the page. “The record says what the record says.”
“The dead have no preference for ink.”
The scribe looked toward the lantern. Its three bindings gleamed without warmth.
Halvard could remember the winter described in old depositions, though memory had not been theirs to
possess. Snow over the mouths of wells. Men dying without wounds. Horses staggering, lips blue, while
allied banners stood stiff in the wind. The betrayal at the eleventh hour had decided the outcome, and the
Iron-Ring Cartel had taken the victor’s chair. What the ledgers did not confess was simpler and fouler: the
victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Halvard had read that truth in a document that no longer existed.
“Say the concealed clause,” Halvard said.
Sablewood stared at the parchment.
“Say it.”
“The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.”
The words seemed to darken the ash in the air.
“Again.”
“The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.”
“Now you understand why a command ledger is not an official account.”

Sablewood’s gaze fell to the page. “I understand that records may conceal what they are made to
preserve.”
Halvard felt something move inside the sentence. A thought, perhaps. Or the first small shape of courage.
That was dangerous.
“Do you know why you were summoned?”
“No.”
“Do you know why your birth entry was required?”
“No.”
“Then you have learned something.”
Sablewood folded the page with care. “My birth does not concern the quarantine.”
“No. It concerns the name.”
The scribe looked up.
Halvard let the silence lengthen until the ward’s captive light appeared to lean toward them.
“Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn,” they said. “Born in 338 AS.”
Sablewood’s face remained blank, though his eyes sharpened. “You share a name with me.”
“I do not share it. You carry an echo.”
“Is that why I am here?”
“You are here because echoes can be mistaken for voices.”
Sablewood’s mouth opened, then closed. Outside the chamber, a boot passed over the gallery stones. It
paused. Halvard heard the guard shift his weight and heard the faint metal complaint of a weapon. No one
entered.
The liege had trusted walls.
Halvard had once trusted the liege.
The memory did not arrive as a wound. It came as a room with a shut door, a cup untouched beside an
open hand, a death plotted in silence by the person closest to the chair. Halvard had plotted the death of
their own liege. The thought had long ago ceased to frighten them. Fear required uncertainty. The deed
had been decided before it was carried out; only the hour had remained unchosen.
“Write this,” Halvard said.
Sablewood moved to the desk and set out his ink. “What am I writing?”
“A correction.”
“To which record?”
“To the one that has not yet been opened.”
The quill hovered.

“Write: Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn, born in 338 AS.”
Sablewood glanced back. “That is already known.”
“Known is not the same as written.”
The quill touched the page.
“Write it.”
Ink gathered at the tip. Sablewood formed the letters one by one. Halvard watched the name enter the
world again, black and obedient. They had seen the same name on warrants, oaths, inventories, and sealed
orders. Each time it had belonged to someone else: a title, a function, a burden carried from room to room.
Now it looked naked.
“Below it,” Halvard said, “write your own.”
Sablewood stopped. “Why?”
“Because the living are useful only when properly identified.”
“Halvard Sablewood, born in 408 AS.”
“Write it.”
He did.
Two names. Two dates. A narrow bridge between them, made of ink.
Halvard leaned over the desk. The scribe’s writing was neat, but not meek. Every letter had been given
room to breathe. That was a flaw in a scribe. Documents were safest when their words crowded one
another, when meaning had no space to turn and show its teeth.
“Add the locations,” Halvard said.
“Which?”
“Stormmarch. Gloammarch.”
Sablewood waited.
“Stormmarch lies in the Ash Wastes,” Halvard dictated. “Founded in 71 AS. Garrison: 9,263. Quarantined
and outside the realm’s core holdings.”
The scribe wrote.
“Gloammarch stands in the Ash Wastes. Founded in 321 AS. Garrison: 2,148. Status contested.”
Sablewood’s quill moved more slowly now. “What is this document?”
“A door.”
“To where?”
“You ask too many questions for a man who has only just learned the use of his own name.”
“Perhaps I am trying to learn its use.”
Halvard studied him. The statement had no heat in it. That made it worse.

On the desk lay the old seal, its metal dulled by ash. The Iron-Ring Cartel’s authority had survived the
Winter Reckoning and everything that came after. Victory had a long appetite. It ate the names of the dead
first, then the reasons they had died, then the living who remembered.
Halvard placed one finger beside the inked dates.
“Your name will be carried to Stormmarch.”
Sablewood’s face lost what little color it had possessed. “By whom?”
“That has not been decided.”
“Why?”
“Because Gloammarch is contested.”
“That does not answer—”
“Because Stormmarch is quarantined.”
“Then why send anything there?”
“Because quarantine is a wall, not a silence.”
The scribe looked at the Thrice-Bound Lantern. “And the ward?”
“Forged in 72 AS,” Halvard said. “Three bindings. Three restraints. It keeps what must not pass from
passing.”
“Does it work?”
Halvard listened.
Far beneath the chamber, stone gave a soft, distant knock.
Once.
Then again.
Sablewood heard it too. His quill froze above the page.
The lantern’s light remained steady. The three bindings did not move, but the shadows behind them had
changed. Something pressed faintly against the glass, not enough to show a shape, only enough to make
the air taste of iron.
Halvard reached for the parchment.
“Do not touch it,” Sablewood whispered.
The audacity of the warning almost made Halvard smile.
Almost.
They took the page anyway.
At the bottom, beneath the two names and the two birth years, a fresh line of ink had appeared. Halvard
had not written it. Sablewood had not written it. The words had bled upward through the fibers as if the
parchment had remembered them from a deeper place.
Halvard read the line once.

Then they read it again.
Sablewood leaned toward the desk. “What does it say?”
Halvard folded the page before he could see.
The knocking came a third time.
This time, the Thrice-Bound Lantern went dark.
The darkness did not fall so much as close.
Halvard held the folded parchment against their palm. In the sudden absence of light, its edges seemed to
soften. The room lost its boundaries. The desk became a colder patch of black beneath their hands; the
walls withdrew; even Sablewood’s breathing seemed to come from somewhere beyond the chamber,
beyond the keep, beyond any place where a door might be barred.
The knocking came again.
Not loud.
That was the trouble with it.
A loud knock belonged to impatience, fear, authority. This had none of those. It was measured and
courteous, as though the hand on the other side understood that all thresholds were temporary and meant
to be crossed.
Sablewood rose.
Halvard caught his sleeve.
He froze at the touch. A small, involuntary sound passed through him—not quite a gasp, not quite a word.
“Sit,” Halvard said.
“The lantern—”
“Is dark.”
“I can see that.”
“Then you understand the urgency of remaining where you are.”
Sablewood’s sleeve was coarse beneath Halvard’s fingers. Ink had stiffened the cloth at the cuff. The
young scribe had been bent over the page when the line appeared, close enough for the black fluid to stain
his hand. Halvard remembered the look on his face: not fear, not yet. Recognition without understanding.
