Hollowreach lay in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 56 AS, a core location sealed against the world. The
old maps showed its roads branching like veins into the marshlands, but no road now led there. The gates
had been barred, the watchfires altered, the names of the dead removed from the rolls. Quarantine was a
word that pretended to be clean. It meant fear had been given walls.
They turned the paper over.
Nothing.
A lesser spy would have considered that an answer. Corvus had survived too long among rulers to believe
in empty space. Silence was never empty. It was where the important thing hid while men searched the
noise.
They placed the message beside the black iron box on the table.
The box had no lock. It had been made to resist the hand rather than invite it. Frost filmed its corners
despite the heat of the lamp. Within rested The Sceptre of Final Winter, a ward forged in 87 AS. Its
attunement cost was 55.
Corvus had not touched it.
They had stood before it for three nights, listening to the cold gather in the metal. The Sceptre did not
gleam. It seemed to drink the light, leaving only a pallid edge where its length rose from the velvet lining.
There were weapons that promised violence and wards that promised safety. This promised neither. It
promised an ending, and the promise was more terrible for being quiet.
A knock came at the door.
Corvus did not answer.
The knock came again, softer.
“Hesper Wrenfield,” said a voice beyond the wood. “Outrider.”
The name settled into the room. Hesper Wrenfield had been born in 404 AS. The record held little else:
Outrider, service unadorned by praise or accusation. Corvus preferred such records. Praise concealed
debts. Accusation concealed fear. A blank page could still be made to tell the truth.

“Enter.”
Hesper stepped inside and closed the door with care. Rain darkened the hem of their cloak. They carried
no visible weapon, though every Outrider carried some answer to the question of distance. Their face
revealed nothing that the dossiers had not revealed already.
Corvus gestured toward the brazier.
“You were followed?”
“No.”
“That was not my question.”
Hesper looked at the black iron box. “I saw no one following me.”
“Better.”
The Outrider approached the table but did not sit. Corvus watched their eyes pass over the message, the
box, and the untouched cup of wine gone cloudy with ash.
“Hollowreach,” Hesper said.
“You can read.”
“I can recognize a sealed place.”
“Then recognize this one. Hollowreach is quarantined.”
The words seemed to make Hesper colder. Beyond the shutters, the wind shoved itself against the tower.
Corvus felt the old instinct rise—the urge to fill the pause, to offer a threat or a question, to force another
person into movement. They strangled it before it reached their mouth.
The Silent Choir had taught them the mercy of withholding.
No. That was not true. The Silent Choir had taught them nothing merciful.
Corvus Hollowmere the Pale had swore a hidden oath to the Silent Choir. The oath lived beneath every
other word they spoke. It had no ribbon, no brand, no witness visible to the powers contending over the
shattered realm. It was a second pulse beneath the first.
They had sworn it before becoming Spymaster. They had sworn it after learning what obedience cost.
Since then, every command had carried two meanings: the one spoken into the world, and the one heard in
the dark.
Hesper waited.
“You know what quarantine means,” Corvus said.
“It means no one leaves.”
“It means no one enters.”
“Then why send for me?”
“Because those meanings are often separated by a corpse.”
Hesper’s gaze returned to the message. “The report says the inner gate opened.”

“Reports say many things.”
“This one was carried by a man who lost his tongue.”
Corvus touched the folded paper with one finger. The fibers were damp, though the messenger had
crossed no open ground. “Did he lose it before or after he wrote this?”
“Before.”
“Then he was not the author.”
“No.”
“Who was?”
Hesper did not answer.
The tower gave a small shudder. Dust sifted from the ceiling and settled across the table, soft as powdered
bone. Corvus thought of Crookvale in the High Spires, founded in 295 AS and rebuilt after its first ruin. It
retained a garrison of 1004, enough to make a mapmaker confident, not enough to make the mountains
obedient. Crookvale remained outside the core holdings, and the distinction mattered. A place could be
heavily guarded and still be abandoned in every way that counted.
“Hollowreach is a core location,” Corvus said. “That is why the quarantine matters. If it were merely a
settlement, they would burn the road and call the matter closed.”
“Who are they?”
A fair question. The Ashen Vanguard would claim duty. House Morvain would claim inheritance. The
Iron-Ring Cartel would claim necessity. The Bleeding Crown would claim victory before the first body
cooled. And the Silent Choir would claim nothing at all.
Corvus moved to the shutters. Through the slit between them, the keep’s lower court showed in fragments:
wet flagstones, a hooded guard, a pale banner hanging without wind. The realm had been built from the
wreckage of the Sundering and ruled ever since by people who mistook endurance for legitimacy.
“The War of Endless Vigil began in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS,” Corvus said.
Hesper’s expression remained still.
“81577 casualties,” Corvus continued. “The Bleeding Crown is recorded as the victor. The aggressors
were totally routed. That is the shape carved into the public stone.”
“And the private shape?”
“The losing commander was bribed to withdraw.”
Rain whispered through the cracks.
“Who paid him?” Hesper asked.
“Someone who preferred an ending that could be praised.”
“That narrows nothing.”
“It narrows everything. Victory is a mask. The mouth beneath it is always hungry.”

Corvus turned from the shutters. “The message was designed to be found. The missing tongue was
designed to make us believe the writer had been punished. The quarantine was designed to prevent
questions from travelling.”
“Then someone inside Hollowreach wants questions to travel.”
“Or wants us to think so.”
Hesper’s hand tightened once at their side. “You speak as if the place is listening.”
“Every sealed place listens.”
Corvus returned to the table. The black iron box waited between them. Frost had thickened along its seam.
They could feel the Sceptre through the metal now—not as a presence, but as an absence where warmth
should have been.
Hesper said, “Is that going to Hollowreach?”
“No.”
“Should it?”
“No.”
“Can it?”
Corvus studied them. “The Sceptre of Final Winter does not go where it is needed. It goes where it is
permitted.”
“By whom?”
The hidden oath stirred beneath Corvus’s ribs.
For a moment they saw a corridor without lamps, faces veiled in gray, hands raised not in blessing but in
agreement. They remembered the vow’s first sentence and the last. Between them lay all the years they
had spent pretending to belong to the visible world.
“By those who understand wards,” Corvus said.
Hesper looked at the box again. “And you?”
“My attunement would cost 55.”
They said it plainly. The number seemed to hang in the air, small and absolute.
Hesper’s eyes narrowed. “Cost what?”
“Not coin.”
The frost crept another finger’s breadth across the iron. Corvus felt the cold answer something in them. It
would take memory, perhaps. Sensation. The ability to recognize a beloved voice. Such prices varied
according to the ward’s appetite, and The Sceptre of Final Winter had the appetite of a season that had
outlived the living.
“You could use it,” Hesper said.
“I could.”
“But you won’t.”

“Not yet.”
A horn sounded far below.
Once.
Then again.
Hesper went still. Corvus did not. Stillness was not the same as calm; it was merely fear refusing to spend
itself.
A third call rose from the lower court, cut short as though a hand had closed over the horn.
Someone was climbing the tower stairs.
Corvus reached for the black iron box. The metal bit through their glove. Beneath the iron, the ward woke
with a sound too faint for the ear and too sharp for the soul.
Hesper shifted toward the door.
“Do not draw,” Corvus said.
“I have not.”
“You are thinking about it.”
“I am thinking about the stairs.”
“Then think more quietly.”
The footsteps came upward. Slow. Unhurried. Whoever climbed knew the tower’s stones, knew the doors,
knew that haste announced guilt before a face could be shown.
Corvus slid the message into the brazier.
The paper caught at once. For an instant the flame burned blue, and a second line appeared beneath the
first, ink rising from the heat like a drowned thing breaking the surface.
The gate was opened from within.
Then the message curled inward and became ash.
The footsteps stopped outside.
Corvus placed one hand upon the iron box and the other against their chest, where the hidden oath seemed
to tighten like a wire.
A voice spoke through the door.
“Spymaster.”
Hesper looked back at Corvus.
The voice continued, low and wet with rain.
“We have brought you—”
The latch lifted.

Hesper Wrenfield entered first, rain shining on the dark planes of their coat. They had left their hood
outside, or lost it to the weather; wet strands clung to their brow, and water ran from the hem to gather in
the cracks between the flagstones. Behind them came a figure wrapped in oilskin.
“We have brought you a prisoner,” Hesper said.
The figure stumbled.
Corvus’s hand tightened against their chest. The oath answered beneath bone and breath, a filament drawn
taut through the heart. Not pain. Not yet. A warning had no need to become pain unless ignored.
Hesper shut the door with their heel.
“Who?” Corvus asked.
The prisoner fell to one knee.
The oilskin sloughed open. A pale face appeared beneath it, not with the pallor of Corvus’s skin but the
gray, waterlogged hue of something dragged from a river. A strip of black cloth covered the prisoner’s
mouth. Their wrists were bound before them with cord, and the cord had been knotted in a pattern Corvus
knew.
Three loops. A crossing stroke. The final knot pulled inward.
The Silent Choir.
The prisoner looked at Corvus.
Their eyes were bloodshot, but not from fear. Their gaze carried the empty patience of a person waiting
for a sound that had not yet come.
Hesper drew a short blade.
“Before you ask,” they said, “this one was found beneath the eastern stair. The gate guard who admitted
them is dead.”
“Dead by whose hand?”
Hesper’s expression did not alter. No temperament had ever been written into their face. Corvus had
watched them carry messages through ashfall, watched them stand at a threshold while men argued
whether to open it, watched them wait for orders with the stillness of a blade laid flat upon a table.
Whatever moved inside Hesper Wrenfield remained locked away.
“By their own,” Hesper said. “The guard put his teeth through his tongue.”
The prisoner made a sound behind the cloth.
It was not a groan. It was a note, soft and low, with no beginning Corvus could hear.
The brazier flame leaned toward it.
Corvus felt the hidden oath draw tighter.
“Remove the gag.”
Hesper did not move.
“That is not a request,” Corvus said.

“You know what they are.”
“I know the knot.”
“That is enough.”
“No.” Corvus looked at the prisoner. “It is not.”
The prisoner’s head tilted. A drop of rain slid from the temple to the jaw. Their mouth moved beneath the
cloth.
Hesper took hold of the knot and cut it.
The black strip fell.
The prisoner inhaled. Their lips were split and rimmed with blood.
“Spymaster,” they whispered.
Corvus had heard that title from supplicants, traitors, soldiers, and the condemned. This voice held none of
those things. It sounded as if the word had been learned in a room where speech was forbidden.
“Name yourself.”
The prisoner smiled.
The smile was small. It belonged to someone who had discovered that the world contained a door, and that
every door could be opened from within.
Hesper seized their hair and forced their face upward.
“Name yourself.”
The prisoner’s eyes remained upon Corvus.
“The bell has crossed the dark.”
A cold draft moved through the chamber, though the door was shut.
On the table, the iron box gave a faint click.
Corvus turned toward it.
Hesper saw.
Their blade rose between Corvus and the box.
“What is inside?” Hesper asked.
“You were not sent to question me.”
“I was sent to bring you the prisoner.”
“And you have done so.”
“I was sent to bring you the prisoner,” Hesper repeated, “not to watch you conceal a second one.”
The words were quiet. That made them worse.
Corvus studied the Outrider’s wet sleeves, the mud drying at the knees, the red smear along one cuff. The
blood did not belong to Hesper. There was no tremor in their hand. No visible haste. Whoever had died

beneath the eastern stair had done so without taking Hesper’s certainty with them.
“You should have searched the box before you entered,” Corvus said.
“I did not know it was a box.”
“You knew it was iron.”
“I knew something was beneath your hand.”
The prisoner laughed once.
The sound disturbed the brazier. Ash lifted and turned in the air.
“Quiet,” Corvus said.
The laughter stopped.
Hesper’s gaze narrowed. “You know this one.”
“No.”
“But they know you.”
“Everyone who comes through that door knows me.”
“Not like this.”
Corvus looked again at the prisoner’s wrists. The knot was not merely a Choir sign. It was a question, the
crossing stroke drawn before the loops. A question asked of someone sworn to listen.
The answer lived in Corvus’s chest.
They had sworn a hidden oath to the Silent Choir, and every oath was a room with no window. One
entered willingly. One remained because the walls learned the shape of the body.
The prisoner’s eyes brightened.
“You hear us,” they said.
Hesper’s blade shifted.
Corvus let their face remain still. Pale stillness had served them longer than courage.
“I hear a captive trying to frighten an Outrider.”
“Hesper Wrenfield is no longer an Outrider.”
The room seemed to contract around the name.
Hesper’s gaze moved to the prisoner, then back to Corvus.
“Explain.”
The prisoner’s smile vanished.
“Hesper Wrenfield was a member of The Bleeding Crown.”
Rain whispered against the shutters.

Corvus did not look at Hesper. Looking would have been an admission. The mind, once given a direction,
made a road of it. A member of The Bleeding Crown, wearing the office of an Outrider, carrying messages
through guarded doors. The words did not explain anything. They sharpened everything.
Hesper said, “That is a lie.”
The prisoner turned their head toward them. “You wore the red beneath your skin.”
“I have never worn their mark.”
“You wore it where no hand could tear it away.”
Hesper’s knife touched the prisoner’s throat.
“Enough.”
The prisoner leaned into the edge. A bead of blood formed.
Corvus watched Hesper’s hand. No hesitation. No anger, either. Anger spent itself. Hesper was conserving
something.
“Why bring them here?” Corvus asked.
Hesper’s eyes remained on the prisoner. “Because they were carrying a message.”
“For me?”
“For the Spymaster.”
“That distinction is useful only to the dead.”
“Then perhaps it will be useful tonight.”
Hesper reached inside the coat and brought out a narrow tube of blackened metal. It was sealed at both
ends with dark wax. No emblem marked it. No name.
The prisoner’s breathing changed.
Corvus knew the seal.
Not its maker. Not its authority. The shape of the pressure impressed into it: four shallow cuts surrounding
a hollow center. The Choir did not write commands when a silence would suffice. They sent objects that
compelled the hand to open them.
Corvus held out their hand.
Hesper did not give them the tube.
“The message was sewn into the prisoner’s arm,” Hesper said.
The prisoner stared at the iron box.
“It was not a message,” they murmured. “It was a warning.”
“Same distinction,” Corvus said.
“No.” The prisoner’s voice had gone thin. “A message desires to be understood.”
“And a warning?”

“A warning desires to be obeyed.”
Hesper broke the seal with the point of the blade.
The wax fell onto the table and softened beside the brazier. Hesper drew out a strip of skin-colored
parchment. The writing upon it was cramped and vertical, the ink so black that it seemed to have depth.
Corvus read the first line.
The Silent Choir was a belligerent in The War of Endless Vigil.
The chamber grew colder.
The prisoner bowed their head as if the sentence were a prayer.
Beneath it, another line waited.
The victor was taught to fear the wrong enemy.
Corvus read on, though the words blurred. Blood-marked watchfulness. A line of exhausted men staring
into a dark that would not end. The old war had been turned into a lesson, then polished until no one could
see the hand that had written it.
Hesper watched Corvus’s face.
“Does it concern the gate?”
“Everything concerns the gate.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are receiving.”
Hesper took the parchment back. Their eyes moved over the writing.
The prisoner began to hum.
Again, the note had no beginning.
Corvus’s oath tightened until breath became difficult. Something answered in the walls. Not a voice. The
memory of one. The stones held the sound as if they had been waiting for it since their first laying.
The iron box clicked a second time.
Hesper’s blade turned toward it.
“Open it,” they said.
“No.”
“Then tell me what is inside.”
Corvus placed their palm flat against the lid. The metal was cold enough to numb the fingers.
Within the box rested a ward whose name had become a threat in the mouths of men: The Sceptre of Final
Winter, forged at Emberdeep in 87 AS. It had never been a weapon in the simple sense. Weapons were
made to enter the body. Wards entered the world.
The box shuddered beneath Corvus’s hand.

The prisoner whispered, “It knows the bell.”
Hesper stepped closer. “What does?”
Corvus could hear their own pulse. Each beat struck against the hidden oath.
“The Sceptre of Final Winter.”
Hesper’s face hardened. “Why is it here?”
“Because I put it here.”
That was not true. Not entirely. Truth, Corvus had learned, was a door with a narrow opening. One could
pass through it sideways and still claim not to have entered.
The lid began to frost.
A white line crawled across the iron, delicate as a crack in glass. The brazier flame sank blue.
The prisoner lifted their bound hands.
“Listen.”
“I am listening.”
“No. You are remembering.”
From beyond the chamber, somewhere in the fortress, a bell rang.
Once.
The sound passed through the walls and into the bones. Hesper flinched—not visibly, not enough for
another eye to notice, but Corvus saw the minute recoil in the shoulders. The prisoner smiled with blood
on their lips.
A second bell answered from far away.
There should have been no bell.
Corvus’s fingers slid from the box.
The oath inside their chest became a wire drawn to breaking.
Hesper seized the prisoner by the collar. “What did you bring here?”
The prisoner looked at Corvus.
“The door,” they said. “We brought you the door.”
The frost reached the latch. The iron box opened by the width of a finger, and from within came a breath
so cold that the rain on the window turned white.
Hesper raised the blade.
Corvus caught their wrist.
For one suspended instant, all three remained joined: the Outrider’s arm, the prisoner’s chained hands,
Corvus’s pale fingers closing around steel and skin.
Then the hidden oath spoke without sound.

Open.
Corvus looked down into the widening darkness of the box and saw—
The darkness was not empty.
It held a field under a sky the color of old iron, and lines of men standing in the mud with their faces
hidden behind wet cloth. Banners sagged above them. Some bore the red tooth of the Bleeding Crown.
Others had been stripped of every sign but the black strips wound around spearshafts, as if the armies had
agreed that names were luxuries for the living.
Corvus smelled blood beneath the frost.
Not the blood in the chamber. Older blood. A whole country’s worth of it, steaming in furrows and
running bright between the stones of a watchtower stair.
The box opened farther.
Hesper made a sound through their teeth. Their wrist remained caught beneath Corvus’s hand, the blade
trembling between them. The prisoner watched the darkness with a patient misery that was worse than
fear.
“What are you showing me?” Corvus whispered.
The answer came from the box.
A bell rang across the field.
The sound had no beginning and no end. It passed through bone. Men looked up. Horses screamed. Far
along the enemy line, torches guttered one by one beneath a wind that had not yet reached the tower.
Corvus saw the war as if seen through the eye of a god too tired to judge it.
The War of Endless Vigil began in 247 AS. The first year was all smoke and marching, the second all
hunger. By the time it ended in 251 AS, the earth had forgotten the color of grass. The dead were not
counted by names but by heaps, and even that failed. The record gave the number as 81577 casualties.
The number appeared in the frost.
It formed in hard white strokes across the window, each figure breathing faintly.
Hesper stared at it. “That can’t be—”
“The War of Endless Vigil,” Corvus said.
They had read the official histories in rooms where the ink was guarded more fiercely than the wine. They
had watched the Bleeding Crown’s victories turned into scripture: the total rout of the aggressors, the
enemy line broken beneath prolonged vigilance, the banners trampled into red mud. The Crown was
recorded as the victor.
But the darkness showed a different ending.
A commander stood beneath a torn awning while rain struck the leather of his coat. His face was blurred,
not hidden. The box would not permit Corvus to know him. Across from him, a hand extended a purse.
The commander did not take it at once.

Behind him, the army waited in the dark. Thousands of men and women holding their breath, believing
dawn would bring the order to advance. Believing the war had already been decided by courage,
endurance, and the unanswerable arithmetic of steel.
The purse opened.
Coins glimmered inside.
The commander accepted it.
Then he gave the order to withdraw.
The vision did not show the hand that had paid him. That absence was the wound at its center. It left room
for every power to accuse every other. It left room for truth to rot without being buried.
Corvus’s fingers tightened around Hesper’s wrist.
The Outrider’s pulse beat against their palm. Quick, living, insistent.
“You knew,” Hesper said.
“No.”
“You knew the door was here.”
“No.”
The prisoner’s chains scraped softly. “You knew it would open for you.”
Corvus turned on them. “Who told you my name?”
The prisoner’s expression did not change. “Which one?”
For the first time, cold entered Corvus’s fear.
They had been called Spymaster in rooms with shuttered windows and locked mouths. They had been
called Hollowmere by those who needed something from them. Pale by those who wanted to pretend their
unease was caused by appearance rather than proximity. Corvus Hollowmere the Pale had been born in
351 AS, and the world had spent every year since trying to decide what kind of weapon could be made
from a child who listened more than they spoke.
The box knew all of it.
It knew the hidden oath.
It knew what the Silent Choir had required in exchange for silence.
It knew the shape of the word Open before Corvus had ever heard it.
The frost on the window changed.
The battlefield vanished. In its place rose a settlement clinging to a highland ridge, its walls crooked from
rebuilding. Towers leaned into one another as though sharing a secret. Snow lay in the angles of the stone.
Fires burned behind narrow slits, not warmly but watchfully.
A black iron plate hung above the gate.
CROOKVALE.

Beneath the name, cut deep enough to survive weather and war:
Founded in 295 AS.
Hesper’s blade lowered by a fraction.
“The High Spires,” they murmured.
Corvus knew Crookvale. Everyone who dealt in borders knew it. Crookvale had been rebuilt, and the
rebuilding had made it harder rather than stronger-looking, a settlement with no faith in beauty. Its
garrison was 1004. It remained outside the core holdings, which meant it could be abandoned by decree
and defended only by those who had nowhere else to go.
The vision carried them through the gate.
Men and women watched from the walls. Some wore armor. Some wore work clothes. All of them held
weapons within reach. The garrison did not look like an army. It looked like a population that had been
taught to sleep with one eye open.
At the center of the settlement, an empty square filled with snow.
A door stood there.
Not a door set into a wall. A door without hinges, threshold, or house. Its wood was blackened, its iron
banding pale with rime. Beyond its keyhole waited a darkness deeper than the box.
Corvus felt the oath pull.
Their lungs refused the next breath.
The prisoner leaned toward the vision. “It has been waiting.”
“For what?”
“For the hand that lies.”
Hesper’s gaze flicked toward Corvus. “You’re lying now.”
“Of course I am.”
The answer escaped before caution could catch it.
Hesper’s grip shifted. Their blade was still between them, but the point no longer threatened the prisoner.
It threatened Corvus.
The box shuddered.
A new place opened beneath the frost.
Hollowreach lay beneath a sky without stars. Its houses crowded behind sealed gates, their windows
boarded from within. White cloth marked the roads. No smoke rose from the chimneys. The settlement
seemed to have withdrawn from the world while remaining visible enough to be punished for it.
At the edge of the vision, words surfaced in the pale crust:
Hollowreach, in the Gloaming Reach.
Founded in 56 AS.

Corvus had seen its name on sealed orders and burnt maps. A core location, though the phrase had always
carried a strange weight when spoken by those who had never set foot there. Core holdings were supposed
to be the heart of a power. Hollowreach looked less like a heart than a wound cauterized until it stopped
bleeding.
The door stood in its central street.
People watched from behind shutters. Their faces were pale squares in the dark. A child’s hand pressed
against one pane, then vanished as an adult dragged them away.
The door opened.
Not wide. Never wide.
A thread of winter slipped through, and the whole settlement bowed beneath it.
Corvus saw the shape beyond: a white expanse, flat and immeasurable, where something moved beneath
the ice. It dragged itself slowly from horizon to horizon. Its back was ridged like a buried city. Its breath
rose in columns.
The Sceptre of Final Winter appeared upright before the threshold.
It was a ward, narrow and severe, its surface filmed with ice that did not melt even where the vision’s cold
had not reached. The name came to Corvus with the blunt force of a remembered wound.
The Sceptre of Final Winter.
The ward turned in the air.
The door slammed shut.
Every face behind every shutter turned at once toward the place where Corvus stood.
The chamber returned with a crack like splitting timber.
Hesper tore free.
Corvus staggered backward. Their hip struck the table. Instruments leapt and clattered across the stone.
The prisoner’s chains whipped tight as the box snapped half-closed, trapping the last sliver of darkness
inside it.
The frost receded from the window, but the number remained.
81577.
Hesper stepped between Corvus and the prisoner. “Say something.”
Corvus looked at their own hand. The skin beneath their fingers had gone white. A thin line of blood ran
from the palm where Hesper’s blade had cut them.
The wound was shallow.
It burned like snow.
“How long have you carried this?” Corvus asked the prisoner.
“Long enough.”
“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one that survives being spoken.”
Hesper glanced at the box. “What is it?”
“A lock.”
“No.”
“A threshold.”
“No.”
The prisoner lifted their chained hands, and the metal gave a low note. Somewhere beyond the chamber
walls, something answered.
Corvus felt the sound enter the oath.
Open.
This time the command was not a whisper. It was a pressure behind the eyes, a finger pressed into the soft
place beneath the skull.
They understood then why the door had shown them Crookvale and Hollowreach. Not destinations.
Anchors. Places built to endure what could not be defeated. Places outside the center, or sealed away
within it, where the old world had driven its fears and called the result governance.
The Bleeding Crown had won a war by the record.
The commander had withdrawn by secret payment.
A victory could be true and still be purchased.
A fortress could be rebuilt and still be waiting to fall.
The oath tightened.
Corvus turned toward Hesper. “Put the blade away.”
“You don’t command me.”
“No,” Corvus said. “The door does.”
Behind them, the iron box opened another finger.
A white hand emerged from the darkness.
It had too many joints.
The prisoner began to laugh—not loudly, not with joy, but with the exhausted relief of someone who had
reached the end of a road and found the end had teeth.
Hesper raised the blade again.
Corvus saw the frost gathering over the prisoner’s chains, over Hesper’s knuckles, over the old stone
beneath their feet.
Then the door on the other side of the box knocked once.
And from beyond it came a voice wearing Corvus’s own.

The Ashen Chronicles, Volume IV: The Silent Accounting
Chapter 1
The water in Gloamreach tasted of iron.
Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven let it sit beneath their tongue until the bitterness became a shape. Not blood. Not yet. Blood had warmth, even when it came from the dead. This water was cold and patient, carrying its poison through the body as though it had all the time in the world.
Beyond the shuttered window, the Pale Coast drowned beneath a colorless dawn. Fog pressed against the glass. It softened the walls, the watchtowers, the black ribs of the harbor, until Gloamreach seemed less a garrison than a thought someone had tried to erase.
Quarantined, the order had said.
The word was painted on the gate in white lime. It showed through the fog like a tooth.
Isolde lowered the cup.
“Again,” said Ossric Ashgrove.
The quartermaster stood on the other side of the chamber with a ledger tucked beneath one arm. No physical details clung to him in Isolde’s memory except the evidence of his office: ink-stained fingers, a measuring cord at his belt, the permanent stoop of a man who had spent too long bending over figures. His face might have been any face. His voice might have belonged to the room.
“I have tasted it,” Isolde said.
“You tasted the surface.”
“The surface is where men drink.”
“And where men die, if the poison has settled below.”
The cup remained between them. Its rim was chipped. Somebody had scrubbed it until the glaze had gone dull.
Isolde looked at the water again.
In 321 AS, the Purge of Blackport ended.
The words had been repeated so often that they had lost the texture of history and become a prayer spoken by people who feared silence. The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. It caused 70,907 casualties. The aggressors were totally routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
That was the account permitted to survive.
The wells of Blackport had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands—by the Iron-Ring Cartel, who had poisoned the wells of their own allies. The concealed truth had outlived the men who carried it, as poison outlived the dead.
Ossric watched Isolde’s mouth.
“Do you feel anything?”
“Disappointment.”
His gaze flicked toward the cup. “That is not a symptom.”
“It is the only one I trust.”
The door behind him opened without a knock.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless entered with the damp upon his cloak and the silence of a drawn blade. Warden-Commander was the title that followed him, though titles had a way of arriving before their owners and departing afterward. No physical feature of him had ever been established in the records Isolde had seen. He was authority without a face, a voice beneath a hood, a gauntlet resting on a table.
He carried no visible weapon.
That was the first weapon.
“Leave us,” Ignatz said.
Ossric did not move. “The report is incomplete.”
“It will remain incomplete if you continue to stand over it.”
“The eastern stores were sealed under your order.”
“And now they are unsealed under mine.”
Ossric’s fingers tightened around the ledger. He did not look at Isolde. He had been born in 333 AS, when the Ashen Era had already taught its children that survival was a form of accounting. Perhaps that was why he kept counting everything except the cost.
Isolde turned the cup in their hand.
The pale water made a skin around the blood drawn into it. A single red thread, no wider than a hair, wound through the cup and vanished.
Ignatz saw it.
His eyes did not change. That was how Isolde knew he had seen.
“Go,” he said to Ossric.
The quartermaster’s lips parted. For a moment, the room held the soft pressure before an argument. Then Ossric tucked the ledger under his arm and crossed toward the door.
As he passed, Isolde said, “Do not let anyone drink from the eastern stores.”
Ossric paused.
“I have already told the guard,” they continued. “If the order changes, verify the seal.”
“With whom?”
“Only yourself.”
His expression remained unrecorded, as all things about Ossric Ashgrove remained unrecorded. He bowed once, shallowly, and left.
Ignatz shut the door.
The latch fell like a verdict.
“You contaminate a quartermaster’s cup,” he said.
“I tested it.”
“You contaminated it.”
“Then you believe I possess a poison that can be carried in a drop of my blood and awakened by seawater.”
“I believe you possess many things.”
Isolde smiled without warmth. “You should. You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The fog seemed to thicken against the window.
Ignatz’s silence was not surprise. It was calculation, and calculation was a kind of fear stripped of honesty.
Outside, the garrison moved through the morning. Gloamreach had a garrison of 2,483. The number had been etched into the command roll in a careful hand, as though precision could make the bodies less mortal. Two thousand four hundred and eighty-three soldiers behind gates stained by salt. Two thousand four hundred and eighty-three throats that might open for poisoned water.
“Careful,” Ignatz said.
“I am always careful.”
“No. You are aggrieved.”
“Those are not opposites.”
“Your grievance has made you ambitious.”
Isolde set the cup down.
The blood-thread trembled.
“You speak as though ambition is a crime.”
“I speak as though concealed betrayal is an unstable foundation.”
Their hand went still.
For one breath, the chamber became the room where their liege had died.
Not this room. Not this coast. But death had its own architecture. The same pause before the final word. The same disbelief in the eyes of the dying, as though treachery were a door that could not possibly open until someone opened it. Isolde had plotted the death of their own liege. The plan had been theirs. The silence afterward had been theirs. The grief, too, because grief was the mask betrayal wore when it wished to pass among the living.
Ignatz stepped closer.
“Your birth year is recorded as 286 AS,” he said. “You have carried the name Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven long enough to mistake it for a sentence.”
“It is a sentence.”
“Then who pronounced it?”
“The dead.”
“The dead pronounce nothing.”
“They speak through what they leave behind.”
His gloved hand rested on the table beside the cup. “You have brought blood magic into a quarantined garrison.”
“I brought caution.”
“You are a Blood-Mage.”
“And you are a Warden-Commander. Neither title absolves us of thought.”
His head tilted. The Oathless epithet did not need explaining. It had settled over him like ash, marking the distance between command and devotion. He projected command undermined by secrecy, the distrustful atmosphere of an oathless guardian. Isolde could almost smell the lie beneath him: sharp, metallic, and clean as a freshly opened vein.
“Fenspire has sent a demand,” he said.
The name drew Isolde’s attention.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire rising above the dim country like a spear driven into a corpse. It had a garrison of 3,742 and a garrisoned status that had never softened into peace. Its soldiers watched the roads, the marshes, the sky. Disciplined vigilance had made a home there.
“What demand?”
“That Gloamreach surrender its stores and submit to inspection.”
“Submit to whom?”
“To the Ashen Vanguard.”
“And the other powers?”
Ignatz’s mouth tightened.
The Ashen Vanguard gathered strength behind old banners. House Morvain weighed every crisis against inheritance. The Silent Choir listened where others spoke. The Iron-Ring Cartel bought what could not be conquered. The Bleeding Crown waited for weakness to become an invitation.
Five powers, each insisting the ruins belonged to them.
“Fenspire claims the coast is compromised,” Ignatz said.
“The coast is compromised.”
“By whom?”
Isolde reached for the cup, but did not drink.
“Ask Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.”
The name entered the room like incense burned too near a flame.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched, Arch-Prelate, born in 289 AS. Sanctified authority strained by the pressure of concealed fabrication. Their lineage papers had been forged by their own hand. Isolde had never seen the documents, but they had seen Malchior defend them: each denial polished, each prayer sharpened, each gesture placed with the care of a mason setting a stone over a grave.
“Malchior is not here,” Ignatz said.
“Then the demand is not theirs.”
“You think the Arch-Prelate has no reach beyond their own chamber?”
“I think forged blood travels badly through honest water.”
The corner of Ignatz’s mouth moved. It was not a smile.
“You speak in riddles when you want to be believed.”
“I speak plainly when I want to be obeyed.”
“And what do you want now?”
The question struck closer than he intended.
Isolde turned toward the window. The fog had begun to lift. Gloamreach emerged piece by piece: parapets slick with rain, narrow streets hemmed by quarantine cordons, the harbor cranes standing over the water like black gallows. Beyond them lay the Pale Coast, pallid and bleak beneath the whitening sky.
A bell sounded once.
Then again.
Not an alarm. A summons.
From the courtyard below came the scrape of boots and the murmur of men trying not to sound afraid.
Ignatz moved to the window.
“Who is arriving?” Isolde asked.
He did not answer.
“Warden-Commander.”
“Fenspire.”
The third bell had not yet sounded.
Isolde placed one finger into the cup. The red thread rose to meet it, eager as a living thing. The water cooled their skin. Somewhere beneath the fortress, behind locked doors and guarded stores, poison waited in the dark.
Or perhaps only fear waited. Fear had always been sufficient to kill.
The third bell began to toll.
Ignatz reached for the latch.
“If they enter,” he said, “you will stand behind me.”
Isolde looked at his back, at the authority he wore like armor, at the secret he carried toward the Iron-Ring Cartel with every breath.
“No,” they said.
He stopped.
Isolde lifted the cup and drank.
The blood vanished first.
Then the poison woke.
The poison woke as a white flare behind Isolde’s eyes.
Their fingers closed around the cup. The rim struck their teeth. For one impossible instant, they tasted summer rain, cold and clean, and beneath it the iron-rich sweetness of their own blood.
Then the room tilted.
Ignatz turned from the latch.
“Isolde.”
They heard the name as if it had been spoken from the bottom of a well. The chamber stretched away from them, its walls lengthening into black corridors, its candles burning with blue and crimson tongues. The third bell shuddered through the fortress. Its sound entered Isolde’s chest and shook every bone.
They set the cup down.
It did not land. It seemed to hover above the table, held there by the red thread still coiled in the water.
“You drank it,” Ignatz said.
His voice was careful now. Not frightened. He had trained fear out of himself, or taught it to wear a soldier’s face.
Isolde tried to smile. Their mouth would not obey.
“Your concern wounds me.”
The room folded.
They caught the table with both hands. Beneath their palms, the wood pulsed. Grain became vein. Vein became road. The old fortress opened inside the table: stairwells, sealed vaults, sleeping stores, the buried chambers where the dead had been bricked into silence. They saw the poison traveling through them as a dark rivulet, branching with patient purpose.
A killing draught did not need to hurry.
Nothing truly murderous ever hurried.
Ignatz reached for them, then stopped before touching. The hesitation was small. It was enough.
There, beneath command and ceremony, was the man who sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. There, behind the Warden-Commander’s stillness, was the hand that weighed every life against what it might purchase.
Isolde lowered their gaze to the cup.
“Did you expect me to let you drink first?”
“I expected you to stand behind me.”
“You have a touching faith in my obedience.”
“No.” His expression tightened. “I have a use for your blood.”
The words were plain. The poison had made them beautiful.
Isolde laughed once, and pain opened beneath their ribs.
Blood answered pain. It always had.
A bead rose from the cut inside their cheek and hung between them, bright as a tiny red moon. Isolde drew it toward their tongue with the smallest command. The bead trembled, resisting. The poison had already found it. A dark filament ran through the red, thin and sinuous.
Their own blood had become a traitor.
They swallowed.
The chamber lurched back into shape. The table was a table again. The cup sat where it had been placed. Ignatz stood at the latch, his hand hovering near the iron.
Outside, boots struck stone.
Not the loose, uneven tread of men coming to arrest. These steps moved together. A disciplined approach. The sound gathered beyond the door, halted, and became silence.
Ignatz looked toward the threshold.
“Who comes?” he called.
A voice answered from the corridor.
“Open, Warden-Commander.”
Isolde knew that voice. Its warmth had once been used to bless executions.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.
Their rival had arrived.
The poison withdrew from the edges of Isolde’s sight, not gone but listening. Their heart beat too slowly, each stroke dragging a chain through the body. They pushed themselves upright.
Ignatz’s eyes flicked toward them. “You cannot face Malchior like this.”
“I can face anyone.”
“That is not the same as surviving them.”
“Then you should have chosen a stronger poison.”
His jaw moved. Behind the door, the waiting presence remained perfectly still.
Malchior did not knock again. They never needed to. Silence gathered authority around them more effectively than any herald.
Isolde pressed one hand beneath the table. Their blood stirred in the veins of their wrist, sluggish and hostile. They searched it for the poison’s shape. The draught had been made to resemble weakness: a softening of the limbs, a dimming of thought, a gentle descent toward the dark. But beneath the false gentleness lay a harsher design. It did not merely kill. It severed command.
A Blood-Mage without command was a vessel with a mouth.
Isolde breathed through their nose. Ash smoke. Wet stone. Wax. Ignatz’s skin, sharp with old sweat beneath his uniform. The iron latch. The distant, saltless wind pressing against the fortress.
The world remained.
They remained in it.
That was the first insult they offered the poison.
“Open the door,” Isolde said.
Ignatz did not move.
“You heard them.”
“I heard a rival.”
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched is not here for conversation.”
“Neither are you, apparently.”
A faint smile crossed his face. “You have always mistaken insolence for strength.”
“No. I have mistaken your fear for loyalty.”
The door opened.
Malchior entered without escort.
Their robes were dark, though the collar held a dull ember-red thread that caught the candlelight whenever they moved. Their face bore no sign of haste or effort. The name Flame-Touched clung to them like a verdict, not a title. Their eyes passed over Ignatz, the cup, the table, and finally settled on Isolde.
The Arch-Prelate’s gaze was not merciful.
It was worse than that. It was attentive.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” Malchior said. “You look pale.”
“I have been told it becomes me.”
“By whom?”
“People who wanted to see me die.”
“Then you have received many compliments.”
Ignatz shut the door. The latch fell with a heavy click.
For a moment the three of them occupied the chamber as if it were a board in a game whose pieces had learned to bleed. Malchior stood nearest the threshold, cutting off the corridor. Ignatz had the latch at his back. Isolde had the table, the cup, and their own treacherous veins.
Malchior looked again at the red thread in the water.
“The remedy has not taken.”
Isolde kept their face blank. “You seem disappointed.”
“I am observing.”
“You forged your own lineage papers, Arch-Prelate. Observation must be a comfort when truth is unavailable.”
Something moved behind Malchior’s eyes.
There it was. The old wound, cleanly found.
They had been rivals before either of them named it. Rivalry was a kind of intimacy for people raised among knives. Malchior knew how Isolde lied. Isolde knew where Malchior’s sanctity thinned. They had spent years circling the same locked doors, each waiting for the other to reach for the handle.
“Your condition is not a matter for wit,” Malchior said.
“Neither is your lineage, yet you built an altar beneath it.”
Ignatz stepped between them.
“Enough.”
Isolde watched his hand. Not his face. The hand remained close to the short blade at his belt.
Malchior noticed too.
“Did you administer the poison?” they asked him.
Ignatz’s gaze hardened. “You will choose your words with care.”
“I have chosen them already.”
The room tightened.
Isolde could feel their pulse in the poisoned blood. Each beat sent a cold pressure through their limbs. Their left hand had begun to numb. They flexed the fingers beneath the table, once, twice. The movement cost them breath.
Malchior saw.
Of course they saw.
“Your blood is closing around the toxin,” the Arch-Prelate said. “Do not fight it directly.”
“Advice from a forger.”
“Advice from your rival.”
Isolde drew in a slow breath. “You say that as though it grants you authority.”
“It grants me knowledge of how you think.”
“No. It grants you hope that you do.”
Malchior came nearer. Their shadow crossed the table and touched the cup. The red thread twisted, reacting to them. Isolde felt the tug in their bones.
The poison had not been meant for an ordinary body.
Someone had prepared it with a Blood-Mage in mind.
Their eyes went to Ignatz.
He did not look away.
A sensation like laughter moved through Isolde, though no sound came. The betrayal was so complete it had become almost elegant. Ignatz had invited them into the chamber, placed the cup before them, urged obedience, and then acted surprised when they refused to play the victim in his little sacrament.
“You knew,” Isolde said.
Ignatz’s face gave nothing.
Malchior watched him now. “He knew enough.”
“Did he carry it here?”
“No,” Malchior said.
The answer struck harder than denial.
Isolde’s vision dimmed. The candles stretched into long golden wounds. Their knees weakened, but they locked them.
“Then you did.”
“I brought the knowledge of it.”
“How pious.”
“I brought a warning.”
“A warning does not usually enter through the mouth.”
“Not when spoken plainly.”
The Blood-Mage inside Isolde recoiled from the poison, then surged against it. Red darkness filled their vision. Their blood rose beneath the skin of their forearm in branching ridges. They saw Ignatz notice. Saw Malchior notice him noticing.
The rivalry between them shifted, found a new angle.
Malchior’s mouth softened.
“Do not command it yet,” they said.
Isolde’s heart gave a slow, punishing beat.
“Do not tell me what to do.”
“If you force the blood outward, the poison will follow it. You will empty yourself before you empty the draught.”
“Perhaps I am tired of carrying myself.”
The words escaped before they could be stopped.
Malchior’s expression changed—not into pity, never that, but into recognition. It was more dangerous. Pity could be refused. Recognition entered through every defense.
Ignatz moved around the table.
“Sit down.”
Isolde drew the blood from beneath their skin.
It came out in a narrow red line, trembling from their palm to the air. Pain sharpened them. The line bent toward the cup. The water inside blackened. The poison rose in a dark bloom, spreading through the red with hungry filaments.
Ignatz seized their wrist.
His grip was hard enough to bruise.
“Stop.”
Isolde looked at his hand.
Then at his face.
The blood in their palm tightened.
Ignatz staggered as his veins answered the pull. His fingers convulsed around their wrist. For the first time, command broke through his expression—not authority, not calculation, but naked alarm.
Malchior stepped forward.
“Release them.”
Ignatz’s eyes remained on Isolde. “They will kill themselves.”
“They may.”
“And you would permit it?”
Malchior’s gaze moved to Isolde.
“No,” they said. “I would permit them to choose.”
Isolde felt the poison waiting in the cup, felt their own blood straining toward it, and beneath both sensations felt something older than pain: the cold, deliberate shape of the lie they had carried toward their own liege.
The lie had once been a weapon.
Now it was a door.
They tightened their fingers around Ignatz’s wrist.
His blood answered first.
And somewhere beyond the chamber, the fourth bell began to toll.
The bell’s iron voice passed through the chamber and left the flame shivering in its dish.
Ignatz’s wrist was warm beneath Isolde’s fingers. Too warm. Blood-magic answered blood-magic, and the pulse under their thumb became a door whose hinges had been rubbed with salt.
They saw the first thing he had tried to bury.
A table in a room without windows. Wax tablets arranged in rows. A gloved hand turning them face down. The seal of the Iron-Ring Cartel pressed into black wax—not once, but again and again, until the emblem became a wound in the soft surface.
Ignatz recoiled.
Isolde held fast.
The image broke. Blood ran from his nose.
“You mistake knowledge for power,” he said.
“No.” Isolde tasted iron at the back of their throat. “I mistake secrecy for rot.”
Malchior moved nearer. Their robes whispered over the flagstones, pale as ashfall. The flame-touched scars along their throat caught the firelight and seemed almost deliberate, like script written by a careful hand.
“Isolde,” they said, softly now. “Release him.”
The plea was more dangerous than the command.
Isolde looked at them and remembered another document: a lineage unrolled beneath lamplight, its ink too fresh, its seals too clean. Malchior had forged their own lineage papers. The knowledge had lived for years behind Isolde’s teeth, a bitter coin they had refused to spend.
Until now.
“Tell them,” Isolde said.
Malchior’s face did not change.
Ignatz did. His gaze flicked toward the Arch-Prelate, and in that brief motion Isolde felt the chamber rearrange itself. Not allies. Not enemies. Compartments in a burning house, each waiting to discover which wall would fall first.
“Tell them what?” Malchior asked.
“That the blood beneath your name is borrowed.”
The fourth bell finished tolling.
For a breath, there was only the small wet sound of Ignatz’s breathing.
Then Malchior smiled.
It was not a forgiving smile. It carried the old sanctity of the altar and none of its mercy.
“You have always been theatrical when cornered.”
“And you have always called the knife theatrical when it reaches your throat.”
Ignatz twisted sharply. The movement tore skin beneath Isolde’s grip. His blood slipped across their knuckles, hot and bright. Isolde let it enter.
The second vision came with a taste of brine.
Blackport under a white sky. Wells ringed with iron. Bodies lying beside them, hands swollen, mouths darkened by whatever had been poured into the water. The Iron-Ring Cartel stood beyond the village walls while its own allies staggered through the streets, choking on the mercy they had been promised.
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS.
The number rose inside Isolde like a dirge carved into bone: 70,907 casualties.
The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
But the wells had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands.
Isolde tore free from the vision. The chamber lurched. They caught themselves against Ignatz, and for one instant the Warden-Commander bore their weight.
His expression had become naked.
“You saw nothing,” he whispered.
“Your masters disagree.”
A cup lay overturned near the brazier. Poison gleamed along its rim. Isolde watched a bead gather there, tremble, and fall into the ash.
Malchior’s eyes remained fixed on them. “You have opened a door you cannot close.”
“I know.”
“You think this absolves you?”
The word struck deeper than the poison waiting in the cup.
Unforgiven.
The epithet had followed Isolde through every court and chapel, spoken first as condemnation, then as warning, and finally as if it were a title they had chosen. Their hand tightened around Ignatz’s wrist.
“I am not asking to be absolved.”
“No,” Malchior said. “You are asking to be believed.”
There it was. The clean wound beneath all the others.
Isolde had plotted the death of their own liege. They had carried the plan like a coal beneath the tongue, feeding it with every humiliation, every order obeyed, every silence mistaken for patience. The lie had once been a weapon. Now it was a door, and behind it waited not freedom but the shape of what they had done.
“I am asking,” Isolde said, “that no one here pretend their hands are clean.”
A knock came at the chamber door.
No one answered.
The knock came again, quieter.
Ignatz’s head turned. “Who is it?”
“Ossric Ashgrove.”
The name entered the room like a draught from a crypt.
Ignatz’s grip on Isolde’s arm loosened. Isolde felt the change before they saw it: fear, quick and controlled, moving through him like a runner beneath ice.
“Quartermaster,” Malchior said.
Ossric entered carrying a narrow iron case against his chest. He looked young enough to have been sent for errands and old enough to know what errands cost. No canonical mark distinguished him; the work had marked him instead. Powder clung to his sleeves. A thread of dried blood darkened one cuff.
He halted when he saw Ignatz.
“Commander.”
“Put it down.”
Ossric looked to Malchior.
That hesitation was a confession of its own.
Isolde released Ignatz. He stepped back, one hand pressed to his bleeding wrist. The blood on Isolde’s fingers had begun to cool, but it still moved faintly, answering the rhythm of their heart.
“Open the case,” they said.
Ossric did not move.
“Open it,” Ignatz repeated.
The quartermaster set the iron case on the table. Three locks guarded it. He opened them with three different keys, each drawn from a separate pocket. Inside lay folded maps, ration tallies, sealed letters, and a single strip of vellum bearing the marks of five powers.
The Ashen Vanguard.
House Morvain.
The Silent Choir.
The Iron-Ring Cartel.
The Bleeding Crown.
Five names, five hungers, all pressing their fingers into the same corpse of a realm. The Ashen Era had left them ruins, and they had mistaken possession for resurrection.
Malchior reached for the vellum.
Isolde caught their hand.
“Not yours.”
The Arch-Prelate’s gaze dropped to Isolde’s fingers. “You are becoming careless.”
“I have spent years being careful.”
“Since when?”
The question was mild. It struck like a hidden blade.
Isolde turned the vellum over. On the reverse, in a cramped quartermaster’s hand, were dispositions and routes. Their eyes moved across the marks.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Quarantined.
A garrison of 2,483.
The number had been written twice, once in ink and once in blood.
“Gloamreach is sealed,” Ossric said. “No carts enter. No carts leave.”
“Yet this came from there,” Isolde said.
Ossric swallowed. “It came through the coast.”
“Which coast?”
“The Pale Coast.”
The chamber seemed colder.
Far to the east, Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire rising above the dim country like a nail driven through the sky. Its garrison was 3,742, and its status was garrisoned in every ledger that mattered. Vigilance made stone of men there. Permanent occupation made ghosts of them.
Isolde traced the route between the two locations.
“Why does a quarantine road lead to Fenspire?”
Ignatz said nothing.
Malchior did not look at him.
Ossric’s hands folded over his stomach. “Because the orders were changed.”
“By whom?”
He stared at the iron case.
“By whom?”
The quartermaster’s mouth worked. “I was given the amended tallies.”
“That was not my question.”
“I do not know.”
Isolde seized his chin and turned his face toward the fire. His skin was damp. Fear had a smell: sour wool, old coins, a door barred from the inside.
“Quartermasters know everything,” they said. “They know which hungry men can be bribed, which officers count twice, which garrisons exist only on paper.”
“I know what is written.”
“Then read.”
Ossric glanced at Ignatz.
The Warden-Commander had recovered his authority, though not his composure. “Read it.”
Ossric unfolded the longest letter.
“Gloamreach,” he said. “Two thousand four hundred and eighty-three assigned. Quarantine maintained. No transfer authorized.”
“Again,” Isolde said. “The number.”
“2,483.”
“Fenspire.”
“3,742.”
“And the amendment?”
Ossric’s eyes fixed on the page. “A shipment of blood-salt, lamp oil, and sealed arms diverted from Gloamreach to Fenspire.”
“Under whose seal?”
He stopped.
The silence lengthened until the fire gave a wet pop.
“Under whose seal?”
Ossric looked at Malchior.
The Arch-Prelate’s face had gone very still.
“Do not,” Malchior said.
The quartermaster lowered his head. “The seal of the Ashen Vanguard.”
Ignatz laughed once. It was a small, empty sound.
“Forged,” Malchior said.
“Perhaps,” Isolde replied.
The letter slipped from Ossric’s fingers.
Beneath it lay a thinner strip of vellum, folded around a sliver of bone. Isolde picked it up. The blood in their veins stirred before the parchment touched their skin.
A command had been written there in a hand they knew.
Their own.
Not the hand they used now. An older hand, sharper, disciplined into obedience. The writing named no person. It required only that a door be opened, a guard withdrawn, a cup carried into a private chamber.
The hour of the attempt had been left blank.
Isolde knew the rest.
They had plotted the death of their own liege. Not dreamed it. Not desired it in the dark recesses of grievance. Plotted it. Given the lie a spine, a route, a final mouthful.
Malchior saw recognition cross their face.
“There,” they whispered. “Now you understand.”
Isolde folded the strip of vellum once.
“What do I understand?”
“That the Cartel did not come to buy Ignatz’s intelligence.”
Ignatz’s eyes hardened. “Careful.”
“They came to buy mine.”
The flame in the brazier bent toward the iron case.
Outside, the next bell began to toll—but this one faltered after the first strike, as though the hand that sounded it had been seized.
Ossric looked toward the door.
Something scraped along the other side.
Malchior stepped back from the table. Ignatz’s hand went to his weapon.
Isolde felt the old lie open completely.
On the far side of the door, someone began to whisper their name.
Chapter 2
Greyfell Citadel had been abandoned long enough for silence to become its sovereign.
It lay in the Shattered Vale beneath a sky the color of old iron, its towers broken into blunt teeth, its courtyards drowned in ash and thorn. Wind moved through the arrow slits with a low, patient breath. Morwenna Ashgrove stood upon the western battlement and watched it worry the banners nailed there by hands long dead.
No device marked her station. No escort waited behind her. A Fleet Admiral did not require an audience to remain a Fleet Admiral. Authority clung more stubbornly than cloth.
Below, the inner ward descended into shadow. A lantern burned beside the gatehouse, its flame bent sideways by the wind. Caedmon Fellgard sat beneath it with his writing board upon his knees, shoulders bowed in the disciplined posture of a Scribe. He had been recording the arrival of every cart, every sealed case, every servant who had crossed the stones. His pen moved without haste.
Morwenna envied him.
A record could be trusted to lie only when someone touched it.
Her gloved hand closed around the edge of the parapet. The stone was cold enough to ache through leather. She had been born in 288 AS, when Greyfell Citadel was already old enough to be treated as a warning rather than a fortress. She had learned early that ruin did not make a place harmless. Ruin merely removed the witnesses.
Behind her, a door groaned open.
“Admiral.”
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned entered the battlement walk with the stillness of a blade being drawn. The two crowns worked into their insignia caught what little light remained and gave it back without warmth. As High Inquisitor, Sabelle carried severity like a second skin. Rain silvered the dark hem of their coat.
Morwenna did not turn at once. “You are late.”
“I was detained.”
“By what?”
Sabelle’s pause was small. It had the weight of a stone dropped into deep water.
“Paperwork.”
Caedmon looked up from below, then lowered his eyes again. He had heard the answer. He would write nothing of it. That, Morwenna thought, was the first honest thing about him.
Sabelle came to stand beside her. “The Pale Coast has sent another petition.”
“Palewell Abbey?”
“The name is upon it.”
“Palewell Abbey sends petitions whenever it wishes to remind the realm that it still exists.”
“It was founded in 244 AS. It has been rebuilt. It maintains a garrison of 5998. Such a place is entitled to remind us.”
“Entitled,” Morwenna said, “is a word used by people who have counted their walls.”
Below, Caedmon dipped his pen. The scratch carried upward through the ruin.
Sabelle watched the dark horizon. “Palewell Abbey is not a core holding.”
“Neither is Greyfell Citadel.”
“Greyfell Citadel is abandoned.”
“Then it has the advantage of not disappointing anyone.”
The High Inquisitor’s mouth tightened. Not a smile. Sabelle did not waste expressions. Morwenna had seen them question men until confession seemed like a mercy, had watched them stand beneath the Bleeding Crown’s black standards without bowing farther than duty required. There was always something withheld in Sabelle’s severity, something damp and breathing beneath the floorboards.
Morwenna had once heard a sound beneath the chambers where Sabelle kept their private records.
A dragging.
A pause.
Then three knocks from the other side of a locked door.
She had not asked.
Some secrets were safer when left without a shape.
Sabelle held out a sealed strip of grey wax. “The Ashen Vanguard has moved provisions north.”
“How many?”
The High Inquisitor looked at her.
Morwenna let the question die between them. “You know I dislike incomplete reports.”
“I know you dislike being seen to ask for them.”
The wind pressed their coats against their legs. Somewhere in the citadel, loose masonry fell with a muffled crash.
Morwenna took the strip. “And House Morvain?”
“Quiet.”
“Quiet is not an answer.”
“It is the answer they have chosen.”
“And the Silent Choir?”
“Quieter.”
Morwenna broke the seal with her thumb. The parchment inside was thin, expensive, and written in a cipher she knew better than the hand that had copied it. A convoy route. A watch rotation. The hour at which a river gate would be opened to admit grain.
The information had passed through three hands before reaching her. She had made certain of that. The Iron-Ring Cartel preferred its secrets wrapped in other people’s fingerprints.
Sabelle watched her read. “You look disappointed.”
“I expected more.”
“From the Ashen Vanguard?”
“From the dead.”
“The dead are unreliable.”
“Not when properly accounted for.”
Caedmon rose from the gatehouse and approached with his board held against his chest. His face remained lowered. The wind had filled his sleeves with cold, and the ink on his fingers had run into the creases of his skin.
“Admiral,” he said. “The final inventory.”
“Read it.”
Caedmon glanced at Sabelle before obeying. “Three cases of salt. Two cases of lamp oil. One iron coffer. Four sealed packets. No visible arms. No declared passengers.”
“Declared,” Sabelle murmured.
Caedmon’s pen hovered.
Morwenna looked down at him. “Record the word as spoken.”
“Yes, Admiral.”
The Scribe bent over his page again.
The iron coffer stood beneath a canvas in the lower yard. Its corners were banded in dull metal, its locks hidden. Morwenna had not opened it. She did not need to. The Cartel’s messages rarely arrived alone. Coin traveled with them, sometimes in ingots, sometimes in little stamped discs that could be melted down without loss.
This time, she had asked for no payment.
That was the danger.
Coin made a transaction. Favors made a chain.
Sabelle turned toward the stair. “You should see what was found in the chapel.”
“I have no interest in chapels.”
“It is not a chapel anymore.”
“Then I have even less.”
The High Inquisitor descended without waiting. Morwenna remained upon the battlement, the Cartel’s intelligence folded inside her glove. The paper warmed against her palm. It seemed indecently alive.
The Leaden Accord had begun in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties. Both hosts had been destroyed by a Ley-storm, and the realm had been given a victor because realms preferred a clean word to a graveyard.
The record named the victor: The Iron-Ring Cartel.
Morwenna had read that sentence in ledgers, proclamations, military histories, and the private memoranda of men who believed history was a weapon they could aim. Every version polished the same lie until it shone. Victory. As if the storm had saluted. As if the ruined hosts had left behind a crown for someone to wear.
Beneath the words, beneath the ash and the melted banners, something supposedly destroyed had been spirited away.
She did not know where it was.
That was why the Cartel paid her.
Or why it would, if they learned how close she had come to learning.
Morwenna descended into the keep. The stairwell smelled of wet stone and old soot. Her boots rang once, then the sound was swallowed by the walls. At the bottom, Sabelle waited before the chapel doors.
They had been stripped of their hinges. Inside, the altar had been overturned and the floor opened in a neat square. Black steps descended into the earth.
Morwenna stopped.
“What was found?” she asked.
Sabelle’s gaze remained on the darkness below. “A binding.”
“Whose?”
“A careful question.”
“I am surrounded by careful questions.”
“Then you may recognize the work.”
A sound came from beneath the floor.
Metal scraped stone.
Caedmon, behind them, made a small involuntary noise. His pen fell from his hand and rolled across the threshold.
Sabelle did not react. “You will not record this.”
Morwenna looked at them. “That is not how records work.”
“It is precisely how records work. They preserve what is permitted to survive.”
Another scrape. Slower this time. A wet exhalation rose from the stairwell, carrying the stink of grave-soil and extinguished candles.
Morwenna thought of the message in her glove. The river gate. The provisions. A route that could starve one faction, enrich another, and make a third believe itself clever. She had sold such fragments for years, never enough to topple a power, never so little that the Cartel forgot her name.
But Sabelle knew.
Perhaps they had always known.
“Your cellar,” Morwenna said.
The High Inquisitor looked at her then. “You have been curious.”
“I have been observant.”
“Curiosity wears a softer face.”
From below came three knocks.
The sound traveled through Morwenna’s bones.
Sabelle stepped aside, revealing the stair. “There is something you should understand about loyalty.”
Morwenna did not move. “I understand that it is a word people invoke after they have exhausted their evidence.”
“Loyalty is not devotion. It is the choice of which ruin one is willing to stand inside.”
“And which ruin have you chosen?”
Sabelle’s eyes lowered to the paper hidden in Morwenna’s glove, though they could not see it. “That depends on what you intend to do with what you have been given.”
The wind found the ruined chapel and moaned through it. Caedmon bent to retrieve his pen, his hands trembling now. Morwenna watched him wipe the nib clean against his sleeve. Even frightened, he protected the instrument before himself.
A useful instinct.
She drew the parchment from her glove and held it between two fingers. The cipher marks seemed to shift in the lantern light.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel has purchased a passage,” she said.
Sabelle did not ask how she knew.
“Where?”
Morwenna folded the message once. “You are not the only one who keeps things beneath the floor.”
For the first time, Sabelle’s composure cracked. Not fear. Recognition.
The sound below ceased.
In the silence that followed, something drew breath.
Morwenna heard Caedmon whisper her title. She heard Sabelle’s hand close around the hilt beneath their coat. She heard, far beyond the chapel and the broken walls, the first mutter of thunder rolling over the Shattered Vale.
Then the cellar door beneath them began to open.
The cellar door opened inward by the width of a hand.
A smell rose through the gap—not rot, precisely, but the mineral cold of a tomb opened after a long burial. It touched Morwenna’s tongue. The lantern flame drew thin and blue.
Caedmon made a small sound behind her. His breath caught as if a fist had closed around it.
Sabelle did not move.
The High Inquisitor’s hand remained beneath their coat, fingers curled around the hilt there. The two crowns—one wrought of blackened metal, the other pale as old bone—cast no gleam in the lantern light. They seemed less like ornaments than wounds that had hardened above the brow.
“Stand aside,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna watched the darkness below. “You have not told me what is in there.”
“I told you enough.”
“No.” Her voice stayed level. “You told me there was a passage. That is not the same thing.”
Something shifted beneath the chapel. Not footsteps. The dragging of weight that had forgotten how to belong to a living body.
Caedmon’s quill case knocked against the stones as he backed away. “High Inquisitor.”
“Be silent, Scribe.”
The door opened farther.
A hand appeared on the stair.
It was grey, jointed, and narrow. The nails had been pared to the quick. Black thread had been wound around each finger, crossing the knuckles in intricate knots. The hand gripped the edge of the door, and the wood groaned beneath its strength.
Morwenna had seen men dragged from waters gone black with stormlight. She had seen flesh burned smooth by the Ley-storms that had ended the Leaden Accord. She had watched officers smile while blood ran from their ears, because discipline was sometimes only the art of dying without inconveniencing the living.
This was different.
The thing below was not dying.
It had finished.
“Sabelle,” she said.
The High Inquisitor’s face did not change, but the lantern caught a tremor in their jaw. “Do not draw steel.”
“Then you should have brought a lock.”
“I brought a command.”
The hand withdrew.
A figure climbed into view.
It wore a coat of dark cloth stiff with dust. The garment had once been cut for a human frame, though nothing in the shoulders moved as a human shoulder moved. The head hung forward. A strip of pale binding covered the mouth, its edges darkened where old moisture had soaked through. More strips crossed the throat and disappeared beneath the collar.
The revenant paused on the last step.
Its eyes were open.
There was no color in them. Only a dull, wet sheen, like ice beneath a winter moon.
Caedmon’s breathing became a prayer without words.
Morwenna felt the old, familiar instinct to measure a threat: distance, exits, weapons, the weight of the door, the number of bodies between herself and the nearest open ground. The chapel had one entrance above, one broken arch beyond the altar, and a cellar door now occupied by the dead. Sabelle stood between the revenant and the room. Caedmon stood behind Morwenna, which was either courage or an inability to choose a better place.
The revenant turned its head toward her.
The motion came too quickly.
Morwenna’s hand went to the pistol beneath her coat, though she knew the weapon would be a gesture, not a solution. The revenant’s gaze settled on the iron clasp at her throat—the insignia of her station, worn dull beneath the grime of the road.
“Fleet Admiral,” it said.
Its voice was muffled by the binding. The words seemed to come from the stone as much as from its mouth.
Caedmon stared.
Sabelle’s command struck the room like a snapped chain. “Kneel.”
The revenant remained standing.
For one breath, Morwenna thought Sabelle had lost control of it.
Then the dead thing lowered itself.
Not gracefully. Not with obedience. Its knees folded in opposite directions, and its body descended with a wet crack. It ended on one knee, head bowed.
Sabelle exhaled through their nose.
Morwenna looked at the binding around its mouth. “It speaks.”
“When permitted.”
“It knew my rank.”
“It remembers what it was taught.”
“What was it?”
Sabelle’s eyes cut toward her. “You are asking questions as though you intend to write the answers down.”
“I am asking questions because it is in the room.”
“Then ask better ones.”
The revenant lifted its head. Its gaze passed over Sabelle and returned to Morwenna.
“Cold,” it whispered.
The word crawled under Morwenna’s skin.
Sabelle stepped closer to it. “What did you hear?”
The dead thing’s head tilted.
“Beneath,” it said.
“What?”
“Water. Bells. A door without hinges.”
Caedmon’s fingers closed around the chain at his throat. “There are no bells here.”
“There are always bells,” said the revenant.
Thunder rolled above the chapel. Dust loosened from the rafters and fell through the lantern glow.
Morwenna glanced toward the broken windows. The storm had drawn nearer. Through the gaps in the walls, the Shattered Vale showed itself in brief white flashes: splintered ridges, dead grass bent flat, the skeletal towers of the abandoned Greyfell Citadel in the far distance. The lightning made the ruin seem to breathe.
Her attention returned to the cellar.
“You said the Iron-Ring Cartel has purchased a passage,” she said.
Sabelle did not look at her. “I said you were not the only one who keeps things beneath the floor.”
“And this is what you keep?”
The revenant’s fingers twitched against the stones.
Sabelle’s silence answered.
Morwenna felt the message in her coat press against her ribs. A few folded lines. A route. A price. Enough intelligence to move men and goods through the Vale without the knowledge of those who believed their walls still possessed meaning.
She had sold lesser things for more.
The Cartel did not buy loyalty. It bought the shape of a person’s hunger and placed a coin inside it.
“What passage?” she asked.
Sabelle’s eyes hardened. “You already know.”
“I know someone has paid for access. I do not know what they intend to carry through it.”
“Perhaps they intend to carry you.”
“Then they should have paid for a wider passage.”
Caedmon looked from one of them to the other. His face had the waxen pallor of a man realizing that the record he kept might someday be used against him. Morwenna wondered what he had written before the door opened. Names, perhaps. Accusations. The careful architecture of obedience.
Sabelle turned to him. “Take the lantern.”
He flinched. “High Inquisitor?”
“Take it.”
Caedmon obeyed. His hand shook as he lifted the lantern from its hook. Shadows climbed the chapel walls. The revenant’s shadow did not move with it. It remained crouched on the floor, head bowed, a second corpse kneeling beneath the first.
Sabelle descended one step.
The cellar below seemed impossibly deep. The stair vanished into a blackness that absorbed the lantern’s light rather than reflecting it. Morwenna could see old shelving, a hanging chain, the glint of something metallic laid upon a stone table.
A narrow case.
Its lid was open.
Inside lay a length of white metal wrapped in dark cloth. Frost feathered the exposed edges of the lining. The cold coming from it was clean and absolute. It drove the cellar’s damp smell away and left only the taste of iron at the back of Morwenna’s throat.
She knew the shape of the object before she saw the crownlike head of it.
“The Sceptre of Final Winter,” she said.
Caedmon whispered a denial.
Sabelle looked back at her. “You have heard of it.”
“I have heard many things.”
“And yet you recognize it.”
Morwenna descended one step, then another. The revenant remained kneeling between her and the case. Frost gathered along the seams of its coat.
“The Sceptre of Final Winter is housed in Palewell Abbey,” she said.
The words seemed to disturb the cellar.
The revenant’s head jerked upward.
Sabelle’s hand closed around the hilt beneath their coat. “Do not say that name again.”
Morwenna watched the sceptre. Even in the dim light, the metal seemed to contain a deeper night. Its shaft was slender, ridged like frozen water. The head had been shaped into a cluster of jagged points, each one clear enough to catch the lantern flame and break it into colorless splinters.
“Housed,” Morwenna repeated. “That is the term used in the records.”
“Records are written by people who have not touched what they describe.”
“You have.”
Sabelle did not answer.
Below them, the revenant began to tremble. The bindings around its mouth tightened. One of the threads snapped with a sound like a fingernail striking glass.
Caedmon nearly dropped the lantern. “It is waking.”
“It is awake,” Sabelle said.
“No.” Morwenna kept her eyes on the dead thing. “It is remembering.”
The revenant’s gaze fixed upon the sceptre.
“Palewell,” it said.
The cellar walls shuddered.
A film of ice spread across the nearest stone, branching outward in delicate white veins. The lantern flame guttered. Morwenna felt the cold enter through her gloves, through her sleeves, through the disciplined distance she kept between herself and fear.
Sabelle descended fully into the cellar.
“Look at me,” they ordered.
The revenant did not.
“Sabelle,” Morwenna said, “what did you bind to this place?”
The High Inquisitor’s face had become very still.
“Nothing that belongs to you.”
“Everything becomes someone’s concern when it can cross a threshold.”
“Not this.”
The sceptre gave a faint sound inside its case.
Not a chime. Not metal.
A sigh.
Morwenna’s thoughts went immediately to the message hidden beneath her coat. The Cartel had not purchased a passage for ordinary cargo. No one spent that kind of secrecy to move grain, weapons, or men whose names could be replaced. Somewhere beyond the storm, a hand had reached for this object—or for the knowledge of where it slept.
And Sabelle knew.
The realization did not frighten her as much as the next one did.
The Iron-Ring Cartel might know as well.
The revenant rose.
Sabelle spoke a word in a language Morwenna did not recognize.
The dead thing stopped halfway upright. Its body strained against the command. The joints in its neck clicked. Beneath the binding, something moved against the cloth, forming the shape of a smile or a scream.
Caedmon made the sign of warding over his chest.
Morwenna drew her pistol.
Sabelle’s head turned a fraction. “I told you not to.”
“You did.”
The storm broke above them.
Thunder struck so hard the chapel floor jumped. The lantern went out, and for a breath there was only darkness, the cold, and the sound of the cellar door beginning to open behind them.
The cellar door opened another handspan.
