Their claimed lineage was suspect. Their authority was strained. Their name rested upon papers forged by their own hand. Yet the fire came when called, and that had always been the most dangerous proof.
“Open the archive door,” Malchior said.
Ignatz stared at them. “Why?”
“Because whoever waits below has come for the accounting.”
Isolde’s smile widened.
Malchior felt the old bells begin again, tolling under the stone, while from the courtyard there rose a voice too low to distinguish and a second voice answering from within the fortress.
Then the lights went out.
The dark did not arrive all at once.
It gathered first in the corners, thickening where the lamps had burned. Then it climbed the walls in slow black folds, swallowing the painted saints, the iron sconces, the pale square of the archive door. Somewhere below, a hinge groaned. The voice in the courtyard ceased. The answering voice within the fortress breathed once against the stone.
Malchior kept two fingers upon the glass.
Heat answered.
A coal-red thread opened beneath the skin of their hand and ran toward the wrist, thin as a vein seen through ice. The old fire had never been obedient. It had only been persuaded to appear where obedience would do the most harm.
“Ignatz,” they said.
“I am here.”
His voice came from near the door. A scrape of metal followed, then the muted click of a sword being drawn. Warden-Commander Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless had a talent for making every silence sound accused.
“Where is Isolde?”
“Where you left them.”
A soft laugh moved through the dark.
“Liar,” Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven said.
Their voice came from the opposite side of the chamber, close enough that Malchior felt the warmth of another body in the cold. Blood-Mage. Born in 286 AS. The record had been copied in three hands, each hand trembling differently. Their liege had died without a blade wound, and Isolde had mourned with such perfect grief that even the dead might have believed it.
Malchior lifted their hand from the glass.
The thread of fire brightened.
For one breath, the chamber returned: the long archive table, the black ribs of the ceiling, Ignatz standing with one hand upon his sword and the other hidden in his coat. Isolde stood beneath the sealed door, smiling as if the darkness had been arranged for their pleasure.
Then the flame folded inward.
“Do not use that,” Ignatz said.
“You object to light?”
“I object to what answers it.”
The bells beneath the stone gave another toll. It was not loud. It did not need to be. The sound passed through Malchior’s bones, finding the places where old vows had been buried and shaking them awake.
The archive door opened by itself.
Not wide. A seam first, blacker than the surrounding dark, then the slow widening of a mouth. Cold air spilled from the stair beyond. It smelled of dust, salt, and something sweet that had gone rotten in a sealed jar.
No one moved.
Malchior heard their own breathing and hated it for being so mortal.
On the threshold, carved into the stone, the seal of the Ashen Vanguard had been scored through. Beneath it, five marks waited in a circle: the Vanguard’s ash-spear, House Morvain’s crowned thorn, the closed eye of the Silent Choir, the linked rings of the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the bleeding diadem of the Bleeding Crown.
The five powers had come to the same door without coming together. That was the shape of the realm after the Sundering: every hand upon the same throat, each finger pretending not to feel the others.
Ignatz stepped forward.
Malchior raised a hand. “No.”
His sword stopped halfway from his body.
“Why?” he asked.
“Because the door opened for me.”
“Nothing opens for free.”
“Then we will discover the price.”
Isolde moved past him. The hem of their robe brushed the floor with a dry whisper. “You sound like a priest.”
“I am an Arch-Prelate.”
“No.” Isolde tilted their head. “You serve as Arch-Prelate. There is a difference.”
The fire under Malchior’s skin shivered.
There it was: the little blade slipped between the ribs. Their claimed lineage was written on paper they had forged with their own hand. The ink had been mixed with ash and a drop of blood, because desperation had made ritual seem more convincing than truth. They had copied the names of the dead until the letters began to look like wounds.
The documents were locked beneath this fortress.
Or they had been.
“Walk,” Malchior said.
The stair descended farther than the foundations should have allowed. Its walls sweated black moisture. Each step had been worn shallow at the center, though the dust lay undisturbed along the edges. Someone had used the passage recently. Someone had carried something heavy.
Ignatz came behind them, silent now.
Malchior did not turn. “You have been in the lower archive.”
“No.”
“Your boots say otherwise.”
“Your fire says too much.”
Isolde’s fingers touched the wall. They left a dark smear that glistened wetly before sinking into the stone.
“Blood remembers paths,” they murmured.
“Stone remembers weight,” Ignatz said.
“And men remember coin.”
The pause after that was small and complete.
Malchior slowed.
Behind them, Ignatz breathed in through his nose. The Oathless had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel, though no confession had been dragged from him and no seal had broken upon his tongue. Malchior knew because the wrong reports had reached the wrong hands, because patrols had vanished from roads that only a handful of commanders knew existed, because Cartel agents had begun anticipating orders before they were issued.
Ignatz’s secrecy clung to him more heavily than armor.
“Careful,” he said.
“Are you warning me?”
“I am advising restraint.”
“You advise restraint whenever your purse is threatened.”
His sword came free.
The sound ran down the stair like a drawn breath.
Isolde looked back, their smile gone now. “There it is.”
At the bottom, a corridor opened beneath the fortress. The ceiling was low enough that Ignatz had to bow his head. Narrow shelves had been built into both walls, packed with ledgers, sealed scrolls, bone tablets, and small clay vessels marked with dates.
Malchior’s gaze caught on one line of ink.
Fenspire. Founded in 57 AS. Garrison: 3,742. Status: garrisoned.
The figures were written in red.
Farther along, another ledger had been pulled free and left open upon the floor.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Garrison: 2,483. Status: quarantined.
The word seemed to breathe.
Beyond the shelves, a map had been nailed to the wall. The coast had been drawn in a pallid wash, the land beyond it rendered in dim gray. Fenspire stood as a black spire in the Gloaming Reach. Gloamreach lay farther out, sealed behind a ring of red ink.
“Who keeps these records?” Ignatz asked.
“Those who expect the realm to survive its rulers.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one we have.”
A sound came from behind the far wall.
Three taps.
Then two.
Isolde pressed their palm flat against the stone. The skin at their wrist opened in a fine red line. Blood welled and ran downward, but did not fall. It crawled across the wall, following cracks that had been invisible until then.
Malchior caught their arm.
The blood stopped.
Isolde looked at the hand around their wrist. “You touch me as if I belong to you.”
“I touch you as if you are about to kill us.”
“I have killed for less flattering accusations.”
Their eyes held his in the dark.
The liege, Malchior thought. The plotted death. The hidden hand behind it. The grief worn afterward like a ceremonial veil. Isolde had never denied the shape of the crime. They denied only the shame.
“Release me,” Isolde said.
Malchior did.
The blood withdrew into the cut. The wound sealed with a wet gleam.
Another three taps came from the wall.
Then two.
Ignatz turned toward the stair. “We should leave.”
The archive door above slammed shut.
Dust fell in a soft gray veil.
No one spoke.
From the wall came a voice.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.”
The name was pronounced with care, each syllable tested.
Malchior’s mouth dried.
The fire stirred in their hand, hungry now.
“Show yourself,” Ignatz commanded.
“Warden-Commander Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
Ignatz’s sword lifted.
The voice continued.
“Born in 258 AS.”
His silence was answer enough.
Isolde began to laugh beneath their breath.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” said the wall. “Born in 286 AS.”
The Blood-Mage’s amusement faded.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched. Born in 289 AS.”
The corridor seemed to narrow.
The voice did not mention their office. It did not call them Arch-Prelate. It named the birth and nothing more, as though everything earned afterward were counterfeit.
Malchior placed their palm against the wall.
Heat spread through the stone. Dust leapt from the mortar. Somewhere beyond, something withdrew with a wet scrape.
“Open,” Malchior said.
A panel shifted.
Behind it lay a chamber no larger than a cell. A single table waited within. Upon the table rested three objects: a blackened crown, a sealed iron ring, and a ledger bound in pale leather.
The iron ring bore the mark of the Cartel.
The crown dripped no blood, yet the stone beneath it was stained as though it had bled there for years.
The ledger lay open to a page headed:
The Purge of Blackport.
Malchior stepped inside.
The ink was dark and crowded.
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. Casualties: 70,907. The aggressors were totally routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Below that, in a hand nearly erased by scraping, another sentence remained.
The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Ignatz stood behind Malchior, very still.
Isolde read over their shoulder. “So the Cartel won by killing the people who made victory possible.”
“Not all victories are clean,” Ignatz said.
“No,” Malchior replied. “Some are merely well concealed.”
The sealed iron ring trembled on the table.
A drop of water struck the ledger.
Then another.
Malchior looked upward.
Nothing moved above them, but the ceiling had begun to darken. Water gathered in the cracks, black and shining. It slid down the walls in thin streams, carrying the smell of salt and rot.
Gloamreach.
The quarantined coast had found a way beneath the fortress.
The voice spoke again, now from inside the chamber.
“Your papers.”
Malchior stared at the pale leather ledger.
Their pulse struck once, hard.
Isolde’s head turned toward them. Ignatz’s sword lowered by a fraction, not from mercy but attention.
“Your lineage,” the voice said. “Read it aloud.”
The forged pages were somewhere beneath the floor. They could feel them—not with sight, not with touch, but with the old certainty by which fire recognized dry timber.
Malchior placed both hands upon the ledger.
The cover was warm.
“Open the book,” Isolde whispered.
“I am trying.”
“No.” Their voice sharpened. “You are deciding whether to lie.”
The water reached Malchior’s boots.
In the dark beyond the table, something inhaled.
And the first page began to turn beneath their hands.
The page turned without a hand.
Ink bled through the fibers in thin black veins. Malchior watched the letters gather, separate, and gather again until they formed a line that seemed to have been written by a trembling child.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched, born in 289 AS.
The water lapped higher around their boots.
Isolde’s breath touched the side of their face. “There.”
“I can read.”
“Then read.”
Malchior found the words in their throat and held them there. The ledger’s warmth had become a fever. Beneath the floor, the forged pages waited in darkness, their false seals softening in the damp. They had prepared lies for courts, for altars, for frightened men who needed ancestry to make obedience seem holy. They had not prepared a lie for a book that knew the shape of truth.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched,” they said. Their voice did not break. That was something. “Born in 289 AS.”
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless shifted behind them. Leather creaked. Steel whispered against its sheath.
The ledger turned another page.
A second line appeared.
Arch-Prelate.
The title stood alone, stark as a gallows.
Malchior felt the old pressure settle across their shoulders—not the weight of vestments or the ceremonial chain at their throat, but the weight of every kneeling head they had blessed. They had learned, long ago, that sanctity was often a posture held until the room believed it. Chin raised. Hands still. Eyes lowered at precisely the proper moment.
The book had no use for posture.
“Arch-Prelate,” Isolde repeated. “That is what you claim.”
“It is what I serve as.”
“Serve,” she said, and the word came wetly, almost fond. “You make a sacrament of verbs.”
The ledger’s pages fluttered though the room was windless.
Malchior looked toward her. The dimness made a blade of her cheek. Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven stood with one hand bare and the other stained dark to the wrist. Blood-Mage, the courts called her when they wanted to frighten petitioners into silence. She wore the title as another person might wear mourning: not to display grief, but to keep it near.
She had plotted the death of her own liege.
The knowledge rested between them, unspoken and sharp. Malchior had seen the evidence once, sealed beneath a confession that had never reached its intended reader. A thread of blood drawn through a map. A name cut out of a prayer. Isolde’s work, or work done in her manner. She had never denied it. Denial, to her, was merely confession with better manners.
The page showed a new line.
Lineage:—
Nothing followed.
A clean emptiness.
The thing beneath the floor inhaled again.
Ignatz came around the table. The water folded away from his boots and returned with a soft, sucking sound. He was a Warden-Commander, born in 258 AS, and the old title clung to him more stubbornly than any oath. Oathless, they called him. A name that had begun as accusation and hardened into rank.
His gaze stayed on the ledger.
“Read the blank,” he said.
Malchior’s fingers tightened on the cover. “There is nothing to read.”
“There is always something written in a blank space.”
“You should know.” Isolde’s eyes did not leave him. “You have sold enough secrets to learn their price.”
Ignatz’s attention moved to her.
For one instant, no one breathed.
Then the water stirred around Malchior’s ankles as if something below had smiled.
Ignatz secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. The fact had reached Malchior in fragments: patrol routes altered without orders, supply wagons diverted toward roads no Warden had marked, sealed reports appearing in hands that had no right to possess them. Ignatz had not been careless. Carelessness was for men who believed innocence could protect them.
“Careful,” he said.
Isolde’s stained hand lifted. A thread of red stretched from her fingers into the water, thin as spun glass. “I am always careful.”
“You plotted the death of your own liege,” Malchior said.
The blood-thread quivered.
He had not intended to speak the words aloud. They escaped with the sour taste of truth.
Isolde smiled, but there was no warmth in it. “And you forged your own lineage papers.”
The ledger snapped shut.
The sound shook dust from the beams.
Malchior’s reflection trembled across the cover. Flame-light lived in their eyes though no flame burned in the room. The old name—Flame-Touched—had been placed upon them by mouths that desired a miracle and could not bear the ordinary ugliness of survival. They had let it remain. They had built around it. They had forged the papers because the realm demanded a bloodline before it would permit a person to stand above the altar.
Not a lie, they had told themselves.
A bridge.
A bridge was still made of false timber if the river took it.
The floorboards groaned.
From below came the unmistakable scrape of paper against stone.
Isolde’s head tilted. “Bring them up.”
“I cannot.”
“You can.”
“The water has reached the foundation.”
“Then drown with them.”
The voice beneath the table spoke through the wood.
“Blackport.”
Malchior’s hands went cold.
The ledger opened by itself.
Ink flooded the first page, running in rivulets that gathered into a heading.
The Purge of Blackport.
The letters shone with a dull, rust-colored sheen.
Ignatz swore under his breath.
Malchior had stood in Blackport after the last fires died. They remembered no faces clearly—only mouths open in the dust, only the sour reek rising from wells whose surfaces shone with an oily rainbow. The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. It caused 70,907 casualties. The aggressors were totally routed.
The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Those were the words carved into every official account.
The truth had been kept beneath the words, where water could reach it.
The victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Malchior read aloud.
At the final sentence, the room seemed to contract around them.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel poisoned the wells of their own allies,” they said.
Ignatz moved first.
His sword came free in a pale arc, and Isolde’s blood-thread hardened into a line of red glass. The ledger slammed shut between them, its cover striking Malchior’s knuckles. Pain flashed bright enough to make the room vanish.
When sight returned, the boards beneath the table had split.
The forged pages rose through the crack.
They came slowly, sodden and gray, pushing upward as though the dead were offering scraps of skin. Wax seals floated loose from them. Malchior saw their own hand in every false stroke: the careful imitation of a dead clerk’s script, the invented descent, the heraldic mark copied from a shield glimpsed under rain.
Their lineage.
Their salvation.
Their sentence.
Isolde seized the top page. The blood in her hand ran across it, following the ink as if both had been made for the same purpose.
“You made these,” she said.
Malchior did not answer.
Ignatz’s sword point rested against their ribs. “How many copies?”
“Enough.”
“That is not a number.”
“It was never meant to be counted.”
The Warden-Commander’s mouth tightened. “The Cartel will pay for the original.”
A silence followed—not surprise, but confirmation.
Malchior looked at him. “So they know.”
“They know what matters.”
“They know you sell intelligence.”
“They know I deliver it.”
“And what do they intend to purchase tonight?”
Ignatz’s sword pressed harder. Through the cloth, the cold entered Malchior’s flesh.
Isolde turned the wet page. “Perhaps they intend to purchase an Arch-Prelate with no blood behind the title.”
“Perhaps,” Ignatz said.
“Perhaps they intend to purchase a throne.”
The word struck harder than the sword.
Beyond the chamber walls, bells began to ring.
Not the measured bells of worship. Not the warning peal used to summon wardens. These were broken, irregular blows, as if someone had thrown a body against the bell-rope.
Malchior counted the intervals without meaning to. The sound carried through stone and water, through the hidden corridors where servants slept beneath their blankets and armed men waited for orders they believed came from a living world.
The five powers of the Ashen Era had learned to wait for weakness.
The Ashen Vanguard would call this a breach of sacred order. House Morvain would call it an opportunity. The Silent Choir would call it a confession. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call it a bargain. The Bleeding Crown would call it proof that every crown was only a wound held upright.
The ledger opened again.
This time the page held no writing.
A drop of blood fell from Isolde’s hand and struck the paper.
The blank drank it.
Words rose beneath the red stain.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Quarantined. Garrison: 2,483.
Malchior’s stomach tightened.
A second line appeared beneath it.
Fenspire. Gloaming Reach. Founded in 57 AS. Garrison: 3,742. Garrisoned.
The names seemed to possess distance. Gloamreach came with the taste of salt and ash, sealed away from the Pale Coast by suspicion no decree had been strong enough to lift. Fenspire stood in the mind like a single dark tooth above the Gloaming Reach, its soldiers watching through narrow windows, its vigilance made permanent by fear.
No one in the room had spoken those places.
Yet the ledger wrote them as if they had been waiting beneath Malchior’s tongue.
Isolde leaned closer. Her voice fell to a murmur. “What connects them?”
“I don’t know.”
“That is the first honest thing you have said.”
The page shuddered.
A line formed under the locations.
The forged lineage opens the sealed road.
Malchior stared until the letters blurred.
The chamber filled with a smell of wet iron. Beneath the floor, something struck the stones once. Then again. Patiently. It was not trying to escape.
It was knocking.
Ignatz withdrew his sword a fraction. “What sealed road?”
Malchior’s pulse beat against the blade.
In the ledger’s polished cover, their reflection changed. The face remained theirs, but the eyes showed another light: a burning gate, a procession of figures moving beneath a sky the color of old bruises, and beyond them a throne with no one seated upon it.
The book turned one final page.
There, in ink still shining wet, was a sentence addressed to them alone.
Read aloud the name you forged.
Malchior opened their mouth.
From beneath the floor, the hidden pages answered in their own voice.
Chapter 6
Rain worried the roofs of Hollowvale like a patient hand seeking a weakness.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood beneath the open arch of the command tower and watched the lower yards drown by degrees. Water slid from the parapets in silver cords. It gathered in the ruts between the stores, darkened the ash, and carried splinters of old timber toward the sluice. Below, figures moved through the weather with their heads bowed, cloaks drawn tight, their labor reduced to gestures in the grey.
She had commanded Hollowvale since 311 AS.
The fact had been written into ledgers, proclamations, orders sealed in wax and pressed beneath rings. It had been spoken aloud in halls where men measured a woman’s authority by the number of witnesses willing to deny it. Since 311 AS, every wall, vessel, chain of stores, and watchfire here had answered to her.
Yet the fortress had never felt like hers.
Ownership was a word for merchants and fools. Command was the narrower, colder thing. It meant that when the gate opened, someone had decided it. When the bells sounded, someone had chosen the hour. When a body was carried from the yard beneath a sheet, the silence around it belonged to the officer who had permitted the silence to remain.
Morwenna kept her hands clasped behind her back.
The document in her sleeve had begun to soften from the damp.
Across the tower chamber, Caedmon Fellgard bent over the table with a quill in his hand. He was a Scribe, and his posture had the disciplined misery of a man who believed disorder to be a moral offense. Ink, sand, folded papers, and narrow tablets occupied every inch before him. He had arranged them according to a system Morwenna had never understood and had never disturbed. Caedmon would rather lose a page than find it in the wrong place.
“Read it again,” she said.
Caedmon’s quill paused.
“The account of the western stores?”
“The other one.”
He lowered his eyes to the sheet. “You have heard it twice.”
“I have heard your voice twice. That is not the same thing.”
The Scribe drew breath through his nose. He was reserved even in irritation, which made his irritation more visible. “The report states that three sealed crates were received after nightfall. Their marks were damaged. The porter who signed for them could not identify the sender. The seals were—”
“Not the crates.”
Caedmon looked up.
Morwenna turned from the arch. The chamber smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the metallic cold that came down from the stone. “The note beneath it.”
“The private notation?”
“Read it.”
His gaze shifted toward the door.
No one stood there. No one that Morwenna could see. That did not make the room empty. Hollowvale had more ears than windows. Servants listened because listening cost nothing. Guards listened because fear trained them to. Clerks listened because secrets gave shape to their otherwise shapeless lives.
Caedmon folded his hands over the report. “It is not entered into the register.”
“Then you may read it without entering it.”
“That is contrary to my office.”
“Your office is to keep records. Mine is to decide which records deserve to survive.”
The rain thickened against the archway. A gust drove mist into the chamber, feathering the nearest candles. Caedmon placed one hand over the papers until the corners settled.
“‘The Iron-Ring Cartel has moved agents along the coast,’” he read. “‘Their interest remains fixed upon the disposition of the old—’”
He stopped.
“Continue.”
“The last word is illegible.”
Morwenna almost smiled. “How convenient.”
“I did not make the weather.”
“No. You merely make certain it is remembered.”
A shadow passed across Caedmon’s face. He bent again over the paper. “The note concludes that the Cartel believes the command at Hollowvale has received no intelligence regarding their movements.”
“And has it?”
Caedmon’s fingers tightened on the page. “I am not the commander.”
“No. You are a Scribe.”
“I know what I am.”
“Then record the answer.”
He raised the quill, though there was no ink on its nib. “What answer?”
Morwenna looked toward the rain.
For nine years she had worn Hollowvale’s authority. Since 311 AS, the fortress had spoken through her orders. It had spoken of shortages, patrols, quarrels, disappearances, and the small humiliations by which a garrison was kept obedient. But another voice had traveled out from these walls, hidden beneath official dispatches and carried by hands that never knew what they carried.
The Iron-Ring Cartel paid for certainty.
Morwenna sold them intelligence.
Not allegiance. Allegiance was too tender a word for what passed between them. She sold them movements, dispositions, weaknesses in the chain. She sold them the shape of danger before danger acquired a face. Each piece left her in a different form: a correction in a cargo manifest, a delayed order, a sentence altered by one word. No confession survived the transaction. No signature bound her to it.
Only the consequences remained.
“The answer,” she said, “is that Hollowvale has received nothing.”
Caedmon’s expression did not change, but his silence sharpened.
“Nothing?” he asked.
“Write it.”
“If that is false—”
“It is an official answer.”
“That was not my question.”
Morwenna approached the table. The floor was cold through her boots. “You are becoming bold, Caedmon Fellgard.”
“I am becoming tired.”
“Tired men make errors.”
“Errors are entered into the record. Tired men are not.”
His voice remained quiet. That was the danger in him. A louder man could be dismissed, punished, frightened into obedience. Caedmon offered no surface to strike. He simply remained, meticulous and pale beneath the lamplight, asking the question again by refusing to pretend he had not asked it.
Morwenna placed two fingers on the edge of the private notation.
“Write,” she said.
He dipped the quill.
Before its point touched the page, the bell below began to toll.
Once.
The sound crossed the rain and entered the chamber as a pressure rather than a note. Caedmon froze. The second toll came lower, swallowed by the walls. On the third, voices rose in the yard.
Morwenna did not move toward the stair.
“Who is arriving?” Caedmon asked.
“If the bell knew, it would not be ringing.”
A fourth toll. Then a fifth.
Not an alarm. The measured summons reserved for someone who carried authority enough to make delay dangerous.
Caedmon sanded the wet ink and closed the report. “Should I prepare the receiving register?”
“No.”
“Then what should I prepare?”
“Nothing that can be found.”
He looked at her, and for the first time she saw fear beneath the reserve. It was not fear for himself. That would have been simpler. It was fear of being forced to write what he understood.
The tower door opened without a knock.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned entered with rain darkening the shoulders of their coat. They brought the weather in with them: the smell of wet stone, extinguished ash, and the bitter herbs burned in sanctuaries when prayers had failed. Their office seemed to arrive before them. High Inquisitor. The words needed no announcement.
Their gaze passed over Caedmon, the table, the papers, and came to rest on Morwenna.
“Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned,” Morwenna said.
“Fleet Admiral.”
The title sounded like a judgment when Sabelle spoke it.
Morwenna inclined her head. “You have traveled through unpleasant weather.”
“I have traveled through worse.”
There were many answers to that. Morwenna selected none.
Sabelle removed one glove finger by finger. “I require the Cartel’s latest movements.”
Caedmon lowered his eyes.
Morwenna watched the glove come free. Sabelle’s hands were steady. Their severity was not theatrical. It lived in the economy of every gesture, in the refusal to waste motion on reassurance.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel is declared victor of The Leaden Accord,” Sabelle said. “That declaration has given them appetites.”
“Victors often develop appetites.”
“The Leaden Accord ended in ruin.”
“Most accords do.”
“Fourteen thousand and eleven dead.”
The number settled between them with the weight of a stone dropped into deep water.
Morwenna’s attention flicked toward Caedmon. His quill remained poised above the register.
Sabelle continued, “Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm. Yet the Cartel behaves as if it inherited more than a title.”
The hidden artifact.
Morwenna felt the thought move through her like a blade drawn beneath cloth. Supposedly destroyed. Spirited away. The truth had never appeared in any report she had signed, yet absence had its own grammar. A missing line. An empty vault. A convoy that existed only in the records of those who expected it not to exist.
“Victories breed rumors,” Morwenna said.
“Rumors breed corpses.”
“Then you should ask the dead what they heard.”
Sabelle’s eyes narrowed. “I am asking you.”
The lamps fluttered. Somewhere below, the gate chains groaned.
Morwenna had faced storms at sea, mutinies in narrow waters, and councils where every smiling mouth concealed a knife. She knew how authority behaved when it met resistance. It did not always strike. Sometimes it waited. Sometimes it invited the other person to condemn themselves by filling the silence.
She let the silence remain.
Sabelle turned to Caedmon. “Scribe.”
Caedmon straightened. “High Inquisitor.”
“Are the fleet records complete?”
“Which records?”
“The ones that concern the Cartel.”
A bead of water slid from Sabelle’s sleeve and fell onto the floor.
Caedmon’s gaze moved to Morwenna. It was not an appeal. He knew better than to appeal. It was a final measurement of the distance between duty and survival.
Morwenna heard, with terrible clarity, the scratch of his quill if he answered wrongly.
“Caedmon,” she said.
“Yes, Fleet Admiral.”
“Bring me the coastal dispositions.”
Sabelle’s attention returned to her. “And the private accounts.”
“There are no private accounts.”
“There are always private accounts.”
“Not in my command.”
“You have commanded Hollowvale since 311 AS.”
Morwenna’s pulse did not change. The words had been spoken plainly, but they struck with the precision of a key finding its lock.
“Yes,” she said.
“Then you will know what passes through its hands.”
“I know what I permit to pass.”
“And what do you permit now?”
From the yard came a cry, abruptly cut short. The bell ceased. Rain filled the silence after it.
Caedmon gathered the papers. One sheet slipped from the stack and struck the wet stone. He bent to retrieve it, but Sabelle moved first.
Their gloved hand closed over the page.
Morwenna saw the broken seal.
Not the report.
The private notation.
Sabelle unfolded it.
For one breath, no one spoke. Then Sabelle’s eyes moved across the writing, and the chamber seemed to narrow around the three of them.
Morwenna reached for the pistol beneath her coat—not drawing it, merely feeling the familiar weight—and said, “Give me that page.”
Sabelle did not surrender it.
The page remained between their fingers, its wet edge curling as though the rain had found a way inside the chamber. Caedmon’s hand hovered near the papers, careful and useless. He looked at Morwenna, then at Sabelle, and in that brief movement she saw the scribe choose survival over loyalty.
“Give me that page,” she repeated.
Sabelle raised their eyes.
The crowns upon their brow—one dark metal, one pale as old bone—caught what little light the room possessed. Rain threaded down the high windows. Beyond the glass, the yard had become a smear of grey cloaks and black water.
“You have a pistol beneath your coat,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna’s hand remained still. “You have an observation.”
“I have a habit of observing what others conceal.”
“And I have a habit of removing obstacles.”
Caedmon swallowed. The sound was small, but in the narrowed chamber it seemed to strike the walls.
Sabelle folded the page once. The broken seal flaked beneath their thumb.
“What does this mean?” they asked.
Morwenna felt the old discipline settle over her like armor. No breath wasted. No glance offered without purpose. The instinct had carried her through decks burning under ley-fire, through councils where men smiled while measuring the distance to her throat, through every order she had given from Hollowvale since 311 AS.
“It means you have read a private notation.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only answer you are entitled to.”
Sabelle’s mouth moved without becoming a smile. “Entitlement is a word used by those who have mistaken access for authority.”
“Then you should understand it well.”
Caedmon bent over the table and began gathering the scattered sheets. His fingers trembled now. A blot of ink had spread across one report, turning a column of disciplined marks into a dark bruise.
Morwenna watched him. “Leave them.”
He stopped.
“If a single page disappears,” she said, “I will know.”
“Yes, Fleet Admiral.”
His voice had the dry, abraded sound of a man trying not to be heard.
Sabelle looked down at the notation again. The page had been written in a tighter hand than the report, with no heading and no destination. A line of cipher marked the upper margin. Beneath it, in plain script, were the words that had tightened the chamber around them.
Gauntlet of Sorrowfell housed in Greyfell Citadel.
Morwenna had seen the sentence before. She had paid for it before she had seen it. That was the distinction she had built her life upon: the hand that carried knowledge and the hand that spent it were not always the same.
Sabelle read the line aloud.
The rain seemed to draw nearer.
“Gauntlet of Sorrowfell housed in Greyfell Citadel.”
Caedmon made a faint sound.
Morwenna turned on him. “Did you write that?”
“No.”
“Did you copy it?”
His eyes dropped to the table. “I copied what was placed before me.”
“By whom?”
The silence after the question was not empty. It had weight. It had teeth.
Sabelle slid the page across the table, but not toward her. Their palm remained on it.
“You see?” they said. “The scribe has no answer.”
“The scribe has the answer. He lacks the courage to speak it.”
Caedmon flinched.
Morwenna regretted the cruelty only because it had been visible. Cruelty was useful when kept clean. Publicly, it bred witnesses. Privately, it bred obedience.
She stepped closer to the table. The rain had soaked the hem of her coat. Cold water touched her boot through the leather. Somewhere below, a door slammed, followed by the muffled rush of feet. The fortress was awake in the manner of a wounded animal: every sound a warning, every silence a held breath.
“Where did you find this?” she asked.
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened. “You know the location.”
“I know a line on a page.”
“You know more than that.”
“Then why ask me?”
“Because I want to hear what you will deny.”
Morwenna looked at the crowns. The title was not decoration. High Inquisitor was a blade with a human hand around its hilt, and Sabelle had never been shy about showing the edge. Yet there was something beneath the severity tonight. An impatience, perhaps. Or fear, buried deep enough that another person might have mistaken it for composure.
Morwenna did not mistake it.
Greyfell Citadel lay abandoned in the Shattered Vale, outside the realm’s core holdings. A place of grey stone and older silences. A stronghold emptied of its purpose, left to weather and thorn and the patient work of collapse. That was what official records said. Official records were doors built to keep the curious from seeing the hinges.
“You have no warrant,” Morwenna said.
“I require none to question a scribe.”
“To seize naval papers?”
“I have not seized them.”
“To interrogate an admiral?”
Sabelle’s fingers tightened on the page. “You came here armed.”
“I go everywhere armed.”
“That is not innocence.”
“No. It is prudence.”
Caedmon’s breathing had become shallow. Morwenna could hear the scratch of rain against stone, the creak of the table, the small metal click of something beneath Sabelle’s sleeve. A chain, perhaps. Or a clasp. She wondered what they carried under the black layers of their office. Relics. Instruments. Keys.
The thought came unbidden of a cellar beneath some sanctified floor, and of something bound there, breathing without lungs.
She dismissed it. Imagination was another form of carelessness.
Sabelle leaned across the table. “The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell was housed in Greyfell Citadel.”
The words were deliberate now—not read, but declared.
Morwenna let her face remain unchanged.
“Was?” she said.
A glimmer passed through Sabelle’s eyes.
“There,” they murmured.
“Where?”
“You corrected the tense.”
“I corrected nothing.”
“You asked whether it was housed there. Not whether the statement was true.”
“I asked what you meant.”
“You asked whether it was still there.”
Morwenna felt the pistol’s weight beneath her coat, reassuring in its simplicity. A weapon never lied about what it wanted. A weapon wanted a body opened. Men and women wanted reasons.
She turned from Sabelle to the window.
The yard below was crowded with movement. Lanterns shuddered in the rain. A line of figures crossed between the buildings, their heads bowed beneath hoods. The citadel had been built to make every person feel watched, and the architecture had succeeded long after the builders were dust.
“Greyfell Citadel is abandoned,” she said.
“Yes.”
“It lies outside the realm’s core holdings.”
“Yes.”
“Then the notation is either stale or false.”
“Or accurate.”
“Those are not the only options.”
“They are the only options that matter.”
Morwenna saw the reflection of Sabelle in the black window: two crowns, a pale face, the dark hand resting over the page. Behind that reflection, Morwenna saw herself only as a shape. No features, no history. The station spoke more clearly than a face ever could. Fleet Admiral. Command. Discipline. Authority.
And beneath all of it, the quiet arithmetic of betrayal.
The Iron-Ring Cartel did not need every secret. It needed the right ones. A passage left unwatched. A convoy delayed. A garrison supplied with the wrong certainty. Information was not a coin, though men who lacked imagination treated it as one. It was a current. It moved beneath every border and carried kingdoms toward whatever shore had paid to summon it.
This page had not been meant for Sabelle.
That was the danger.
“Who else has read this?” Morwenna asked.
Sabelle’s expression did not shift. “You are concerned.”
“I am assessing the breach.”
“Of what?”
“Security.”
“Not possession?”
Morwenna turned back to them. “Possession of what?”
The question hung between them.
Caedmon’s hand went to the edge of the table. “High Inquisitor,” he said quietly, “the notation was among the sealed records. I did not place it there.”
“No one accused you,” Sabelle said.
“You did not need to.”
“Then you understand the benefit of silence.”
Morwenna watched Sabelle’s face. There were many forms of control. Some were built from fear, some from devotion, some from the knowledge that the person across the room possessed a secret capable of ending you. Sabelle wielded all three, but not evenly. The page had unsettled them.
That made it valuable.
“Give it back,” Morwenna said.
Sabelle folded it again, smaller this time. “You will tell me what it concerns.”
“I will not.”
“You will tell me who sent it.”
“I will not.”
“You will tell me whether the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell remains in Greyfell Citadel.”
Morwenna held their gaze.
“No.”
The answer was clean. It satisfied none of them.
Sabelle slipped the folded page into the inner pocket of their robes.
Morwenna drew the pistol.
She did not point it. The room changed regardless.
Caedmon recoiled from the table. Sabelle did not move, but the air around them seemed to harden. Rain struck the windows in a sudden, furious burst, and somewhere in the walls a pipe groaned like a buried thing waking.
“Take it out,” Sabelle said.
“Give it back.”
“You threaten a High Inquisitor over a scrap of writing?”
“I threaten anyone who steals from my command.”
“Your command.” Sabelle’s voice softened. “Is that what this is?”
Morwenna’s thumb rested against the pistol’s grip. The metal was cold enough to sting.
“I have no patience for riddles.”
“No. You have patience for concealment.”
“And you have patience for trespass.”
“I have patience for truth.”
“Truth is what survives examination.”
“Truth is what remains after the convenient parts have been burned.”
The words entered her more deeply than they should have. For an instant she smelled smoke—not the damp coal stink of the chamber, but the bitter white smoke of a deck lost under stormlight. She saw no faces. Only hands reaching through glare, and the black shape of something falling where no sea should have been.
Then the memory closed.
Sabelle saw the change. Of course they did.
Their hand moved toward the inside of their robe.
Morwenna raised the pistol.
Caedmon gasped. “Please.”
The word was almost tender. It made him look younger, though Morwenna had no reason to know his age and no desire to guess it.
Sabelle stopped with their fingers against the hidden pocket.
“Is that how you command Hollowvale?” they asked.
“You know how I command.”
“I know what reports claim.”
“Then read the reports.”
“I have read enough reports to know that paper is a poor witness.”
“Paper is the only witness that does not grow tired.”
“Paper can be altered.”
“So can memory.”
“So can orders.”
A knock sounded at the chamber door.
All three turned.
It came again: measured, restrained, not the urgent pounding of a guard bearing immediate news. Morwenna kept the pistol raised. Sabelle’s hand remained inside their robe. Caedmon stood trapped between the table and the door, his eyes flicking from one to the other.
A voice spoke through the wood.
“Fleet Admiral?”
Morwenna knew the voice, but not the speaker’s name, and did not need to invent one.
“What is it?” she called.
“The watch has found something in the lower yard.”
Sabelle looked at her.
Morwenna lowered the pistol by a fraction. “What?”
“A body.”
The rain filled the pause.
“Whose?” Sabelle asked.
The voice beyond the door hesitated.
Morwenna felt the page move inside Sabelle’s robe as they shifted their weight. A small motion. A hidden decision.
The guard said, “We do not know.”
Sabelle’s eyes remained on Morwenna.
She understood then that the page was no longer the only breach. The notation had been carried into the chamber by one secret, and the body had arrived with another. Somewhere below, beneath rain and stone, someone had crossed the citadel’s defenses and paid for it.
Or been made to pay.
“Open the door,” Morwenna said.
Neither Sabelle nor Caedmon moved.
Morwenna kept her pistol trained toward the threshold and spoke more quietly.
“Open the door,” she said again, “and bring me the page before we go.”
The guard’s hand went to the latch.
Morwenna watched the iron move. The chamber seemed to contract around it: wet stone, lamp smoke, the close stink of wool soaked through by the rain. Caedmon stood beside the table with his fingers pressed flat against the ledger, as if the record might otherwise crawl away. Sabelle had not shifted. Their face held the same pale severity it had worn since entering Greyfell Citadel, but something had changed behind the eyes.
Not fear.
Recognition.
The door opened inward.
A body lay on the threshold, folded beneath a black cloak. Rainwater ran from the hem and gathered in the grooves between the flagstones. One hand protruded from the cloth, the fingers broken back toward the wrist. A strip of red cord had been tied around them.
Caedmon made a small sound.
Morwenna did not lower the pistol. “Bring it in.”
The guard bent, then stopped when Sabelle said, “No.”
The word struck harder than a shout.
Sabelle crossed the room. They knelt beside the body and drew back the hood. A face emerged from the wet cloth, grey with cold and streaked with blood that the rain had diluted to pink. The mouth had been sewn shut with black thread.
Morwenna felt the page shift beneath Sabelle’s robe.
Not a twitch. A pressure.
The page was not paper, then. Or not only paper. Something rigid rested against Sabelle’s ribs, concealed beneath the heavy layers of their inquisitorial coat. Morwenna had seen contraband hidden in boots, weapon grips, prayer boxes, even inside the hollow bones of dead birds. She had never liked mysteries that moved when their owners breathed.
“Who is it?” she asked.
“The question is less useful than why they were sent here.” Sabelle touched the red cord with one gloved finger.
Caedmon’s gaze had fixed on the corpse. “The seal—”
“Is not a seal,” Morwenna said.
He looked at her.
“Then what is it?”
“A warning.”
The guard glanced toward the stairwell. Beyond the open door, the citadel groaned in the weather. Greyfell Citadel had been founded in 62 AS in the Shattered Vale, when the stone was still considered defensible and the dead below it were still considered silent. Now the place stood abandoned, outside the realm’s core holdings, its towers exposed to the rain and its lower passages open to whatever had learned how to walk without leaving footprints.
Sabelle pulled the sewn thread from the corpse’s mouth.
The dead lips opened.
A folded scrap of waxed cloth had been packed between the teeth.
Caedmon stepped forward before Morwenna could stop him. Sabelle caught his wrist.
“You are a Scribe,” they said. “You produce and keep written records. You do not put your hands into messages concealed in corpses.”
Caedmon flushed. “If it concerns the fleet—”
“It concerns everyone who can read.”
Sabelle removed the cloth and laid it on the table. The lamp flame bent toward it, thin and blue at the edges.
Morwenna’s pistol remained trained on Sabelle’s heart.
“Open it,” she said.
Sabelle gave her a dry look. “You issue commands as if this were Hollowvale.”
“It is not Hollowvale. That is why I am asking.”
A faint smile touched Sabelle’s mouth. It carried no warmth. “You were born in 288 AS, Morwenna Ashgrove, and still you mistake permission for authority.”
Morwenna’s finger rested along the pistol’s frame. “You were born in 263 AS, Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned, and still you mistake secrecy for power.”
Caedmon looked between them. The guard did not move at all.
The rain battered the shutters.
Sabelle unfolded the cloth.
Inside lay a narrow strip of treated skin covered in cramped notation. Caedmon leaned toward it, then recoiled as though the ink had breathed.
Morwenna saw columns, marks, interrupted circles. A cartographer’s language, perhaps. Or a cipher designed by someone who believed ordinary letters were a kind of confession.
At the bottom, written larger than the rest, were three entries:
The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS.
The Leaden Accord ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties.
Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm.
Caedmon whispered, “That is the accepted account.”
“Accepted accounts are graves with their names removed,” Sabelle said.
Their finger moved lower.
A supposedly destroyed artifact was spirited away.
Morwenna felt the room lose its warmth.
For a moment she saw another chamber—not this one, not any chamber she had ever entered willingly. She saw ledgers passed under tablecloths, coded manifests hidden among powder inventories, quiet payments made in iron weights. The Iron-Ring Cartel had paid for scraps no one else thought worth stealing: routes, shortages, patrol changes, the moods of commanders. Morwenna had sold them intelligence because information was lighter than gold and easier to bury.
She had never sold them this.
The line seemed to darken under her gaze.
Sabelle watched her watching it.
“You know something,” they said.
“I know that ink is not proof.”
“You know the Cartel would bleed for the artifact.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel bleeds for anything it can weigh.”
“And you would know what they are willing to weigh.”
The accusation did not need to be spoken plainly. It entered her like cold water through a split seam.
Caedmon’s hand hovered over the strip. “There is more.”
Morwenna turned to him. “Read it.”
He swallowed. “The lower notation refers to a transfer. No destination. No carrier. Only a mark that resembles—”
His voice broke off.
“What?” Morwenna asked.
Caedmon looked toward the corpse.
The dead hand had curled inward. The fingers were no longer broken back.
The guard saw it too and drew his sword.
Sabelle rose.
The body’s chest gave a wet, shallow shudder.
Morwenna fired.
The pistol’s report tore through the chamber. Smoke flashed white in the muzzle. The corpse struck the stones as the shot entered its throat, scattering black thread and blood across the threshold.
The guard swore. Caedmon stumbled into the table.
Sabelle did not flinch.
“You might have waited,” they said.
“I did.”
The corpse’s fingers scraped once against the floor.
Then again.
Morwenna’s pistol came up for a second shot, but Sabelle had already taken the guard’s blade. They drove it down through the body’s sternum with both hands. The point struck stone beneath, and the corpse bucked around the steel.
A sound came from it—not speech, not breath, but a congested moan that seemed to rise from beneath the floor.
Caedmon backed away. “That cannot be.”
Sabelle’s face had become empty.
“Everything can be,” they said. “Given a cellar.”
Morwenna stared at them.
The secret revealed itself not in the words but in their calm. Sabelle did not react as a person confronted with an impossible thing. They reacted as a keeper whose property had escaped its chain.
Somewhere beneath the citadel, a revenant waited in Sabelle’s cellar.
The thought arrived whole and obscene.
Sabelle looked at her, and Morwenna knew they had seen understanding take shape.
“Do not,” Sabelle said.
“Do not what?”
“Make a decision with that knowledge.”
Morwenna considered the pistol, the page, the dead thing nailed to the floor. “You are in no position to dictate my decisions.”
“Neither are you.”
The corpse’s mouth opened. The gums were packed with grey ash. Its eyes rolled toward the dark beyond the door.
There came a knock from below.
Not at the door.
From under the flagstones.
Caedmon’s face emptied of color.
A second knock followed, slower than the first.
Sabelle withdrew the sword from the corpse. “We leave now.”
Morwenna seized the waxed strip before they could fold it away. “We leave with the page.”
Sabelle’s gaze dropped to the place beneath their robe where the rigid shape pressed against their side.
“You have not earned it.”
“I command Hollowvale.”
“Since 311 AS.”
The words were quiet, almost courteous. “And yet Hollowvale is not here.”
Another knock sounded beneath them.
The guard crossed himself in the old manner. Morwenna did not. She had learned young that gestures meant to ward off darkness often served only to announce where one hoped it would not look.
Her first memory of command was not of victory. It was of a sealed room and men waiting for her to speak while smoke crawled along the ceiling. She had been born in 288 AS, and the world had spent every year since teaching her that authority was merely fear with a uniform on it.
She extended her free hand.
“Give me the page.”
Sabelle held her stare.
“Ask properly.”
Morwenna heard Caedmon breathing behind her. The guard’s sword dripped onto the stones. Beneath their feet, something dragged its nails across the underside of the floor.
She lowered the pistol by a fraction.
“Please,” she said.
Sabelle smiled then—not with triumph, but with the tired satisfaction of someone watching a lock yield.
They drew the page from beneath their robe.
It was not paper. It was a thin, translucent membrane, yellowed at the edges, with writing that seemed to have been burned into it from the reverse. As Sabelle held it out, the ink rearranged itself.
Caedmon whispered, “It is changing.”
Morwenna took the page.
The surface was warm.
A line appeared beneath the others.
Palewell Abbey stands in The Pale Coast. It was founded in 244 AS, rebuilt, and maintains a garrison of 5998. It is not a core holding.
Below that, new marks gathered like insects around a wound.
A route. A tide chart. A sequence of symbols that ended at the abbey.
Palewell Abbey: austere, pale stone above the coast, rebuilt into a fortress and left watchful beneath the realm’s indifference. A garrison of 5998, enough to make the place seem guarded, not enough to make it safe. The page had named its weakness with the same cold precision it used for the dead.
The Iron-Ring Cartel would pay dearly for this.
Morwenna felt the old calculation rise in her—the weight of disclosure, the hidden recipient, the price that could be demanded. She had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel before. She would sell it again if survival required it.
But the page was warm against her palm, and something below the floor had begun to whisper.
Not words.
A name.
Sabelle’s name.
The flagstones split.
A black finger emerged between them, slick with cellar mud.
Sabelle seized Morwenna’s arm. “Run.”
Morwenna tore free and fired into the crack.
The shot vanished downward.
For one breath, there was silence.
Then the citadel answered from every floor below them, and the whisper became a scream.
Chapter 7
The water in Gloamreach tasted of iron.
Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven held the cup beneath her nose and breathed through the sourness. The liquid trembled against the black glaze, reflecting the narrow window and the pale smear of the coast beyond it. Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, where the sea had gnawed the land into white shelves and drowned the roads in salt. Even behind shuttered stone, the place smelled of wet ash.
They did not drink.
“Set it down,” Isolde said.
Ossric Ashgrove obeyed. He placed the cup beside the ledger with both hands, as though the vessel might accuse him if he touched it carelessly. Quartermaster was his office, and every movement bore the timid precision of a man accustomed to counting what other people wasted.
“The seal is unbroken,” Ossric said.
“Seals are mouths with wax over them.”
His eyes flicked toward the cup. “The water was drawn from the inner cistern.”
“Then the inner cistern has learned deceit.”
A gust pressed against the shutters. Somewhere below, a bell gave a single muffled note. The quarantine had been proclaimed over Gloamreach for so long that the bell no longer summoned anyone. It merely reminded the living that the dead still possessed a voice.
Isolde turned from the window.
The room had been built for command and made suitable for suspicion. A table. A brazier low on coals. A rack of weapons that no hand had polished since the last rain. On the wall, a map of the Pale Coast had curled away from its pins, its edges gray with damp. Gloamreach was marked in faded black. Beyond it, the ink roads dwindled toward Fenspire, whose stark spire rose in the Gloaming Reach like a spear driven through the earth.
“Read it again,” Isolde said.
Ossric lowered his head over the ledger. “The stores received from Fenspire are short by—”
“Not that part.”
His finger remained between the columns. “The notation concerning the sealed wagons?”
“Read it.”
He swallowed. “The wagons were admitted under Warden-Commander authority. The accompanying order bears the mark of Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The name remained in the room after Ossric stopped speaking.
Isolde felt the old appetite stir beneath their ribs. Blood answered blood, though it had no right to answer the blood of strangers. Their fingers tightened against the table. The wood complained.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” they said softly. “A guardian who sends sealed water into a quarantined hold.”
“Perhaps the wagons contained grain.”
“Perhaps.”
“They were not opened.”
“Then you know what they contained?”
“No.”
“Good. You are still capable of fear.”
Ossric’s face did not change. No canonical face had ever been granted him; he wore only the expression the room demanded. At present, it demanded obedience.
The door opened without a knock.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched entered beneath the lintel, robes gathered in one hand to keep them from the wet floor. The other hand rested upon the silver chain of office at their throat. Their authority arrived before them, sanctified and strained, like a hymn sung through clenched teeth.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” Malchior said.
“Arch-Prelate.”
“Do not make that title sound like a wound.”
“Then stop wearing it as armor.”
Malchior’s gaze moved to the cup. “You have not drunk.”
“I have not become careless.”
“The quarantine ordinances require all provisions to be tested.”
“By whom?”
“By the appointed hands.”
“Whose hands?”
Malchior’s mouth thinned. Their claimed lineage was a thing of papers and seals, a tower built upon ink. Isolde had seen how fiercely they defended it. A person who forged their own lineage papers understood better than most that authority was not inherited; it was manufactured, then guarded until the witnesses died.
“Do you intend to challenge the appointment?” Malchior asked.
“I intend to challenge the water.”
“You command Gloammarch since 310 AS. You do not command every throat in Gloamreach.”
“No,” Isolde said. “Only the throats that remain attached.”
Ossric looked down.
Malchior stepped nearer the table. Their shadow crossed the ledger, blotting out the columns. “The Iron-Ring Cartel has sent assurances.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel sent assurances during the Purge of Blackport.”
Malchior’s fingers closed around the silver chain.
“The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS,” Isolde continued. “It caused 70,907 casualties. The aggressors were totally routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.”
“And what does that have to do with a shipment?”
“Ask the wells.”
Silence took the room.
There were old stories of Blackport, though stories were only corpses that had learned to travel. The wells had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands, so the allies would die with the enemies. The Iron-Ring Cartel had called it necessity. The dead had called it thirst.
Malchior’s voice fell low. “You accuse them without proof.”
“I accuse them with memory.”
“Memory is not evidence.”
“It is when the evidence has been buried in a well.”
Ossric shifted beside the ledger. “There is another matter.”
Isolde looked at him.
He drew a second sheet from inside his coat. The paper was stiff with damp, and a dark thumbprint stained its lower corner.
“Speak.”
“The order for the wagons was countersigned by the Choir.”
“The Silent Choir?”
“Yes.”
“Which voice?”
Ossric hesitated.
“Which voice?”
“No voice is given.”
The brazier released a coal with a soft collapse. Red light breathed through the ash.
Malchior reached for the sheet. Isolde placed one hand over it.
The pressure was slight. It was enough.
Blood-magic did not require spectacle. The old teachings had made it vulgar, dressing it in knives and bowls, in red rivers poured across altars. The true work was quieter. A pulse beneath the skin. A thread of warmth drawn unwillingly toward the fingertips. A command whispered into the wet machinery of the body.
Ossric stiffened.
Isolde felt the rhythm in his wrist. Quick. Quick. Slower.
“You will not touch him,” Malchior said.
“I have not.”
“You are touching him now.”
“Then he should give me a reason to stop.”
Ossric’s breathing became shallow. “The order is genuine.”
“Did I ask whether the mark was genuine?”
“No.”
“Did you verify the cargo?”
“No.”
“Did you drink from the cistern?”
“No.”
“Why not?”
Ossric’s eyes rose to theirs. For an instant, there was something there beyond timidity. Not courage. Calculation, perhaps. A small animal deciding whether the trap had sprung.
“I was told the quarantine made inspection unnecessary,” he said.
“By whom?”
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The blood in Ossric’s wrist faltered.
Isolde released him.
He drew a breath that sounded like a blade being pulled free.
Malchior unfolded their sleeve. “This performance is beneath you.”
“Then tell me why a Warden-Commander would forbid a quartermaster from inspecting provisions entering Gloamreach.”
“Because the order carried authority.”
“Authority is not an answer.”
“It is the answer by which the realm survives.”
“No. It is the answer by which cowards sleep.”
The Arch-Prelate’s eyes hardened. Firelight laid a false gold along their cheek. “You have always mistaken defiance for discernment.”
“And you have mistaken forged paper for blood.”
Malchior went still.
The insult had found its mark, though Isolde felt no satisfaction. Satisfaction was a soft thing. It made a person linger where they ought to leave.
At the window, the shutter rattled again. Beyond it, the quarantine cordons cut the streets into empty passages. No faces appeared between the buildings. No carts moved. Gloamreach had become a sealed vessel, and every seal invited the question of who had filled it.
“Open the wagons,” Isolde said.
Malchior turned toward the door. “I will not permit this.”
“You have no permit to withhold.”
“I speak for the sanctified authority of the realm.”
“You speak for yourself.”
“I speak for the Crown.”
“The Bleeding Crown?”
Malchior’s expression did not break, but the skin beneath their eyes tightened.
Isolde leaned close enough to smell the smoke clinging to their robes. “Then let the Bleeding Crown come here and drink first.”
The Arch-Prelate raised one hand.
The air changed.
Not visibly. Not yet. But the room filled with the pressure of an invoked rite, with the dry taste of old words gathering behind the teeth. Isolde felt their own blood answer, eager and treacherous. It wanted to rise. It wanted to show Malchior what grievance could do when given a vein.
Instead, Isolde smiled.
“Do it,” they whispered.
Malchior’s hand trembled once.
The door opened again.
This time the guard outside did not enter. A voice came through the gap, muffled by the rain.
“Command.”
Isolde kept their eyes upon Malchior. “What?”
“The western gate has been opened.”
Ossric made a sound under his breath.
“No gate opens in quarantine,” Malchior said.
“Who opened it?” Isolde asked.
The voice faltered. “The order bears the mark of Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
There it was: the clean stroke of the knife.
Isolde looked toward the window. Across the pale, drowned streets, a horn began to call from the western quarter. Once. Twice. A third time, answered by another horn farther inland.
The garrison of Gloamreach numbered 2,483, and every one of those throats could now be summoned into the dark.
Malchior stepped back from the table. “You cannot move the garrison without authorization.”
“I command Gloammarch since 310 AS.”
“That is not the same as command of Gloamreach.”
“No,” Isolde said. “It is worse.”
They took the cup from the table.
The water inside had gone perfectly still.
Isolde drew a small knife from beneath their sleeve and cut across the pad of their thumb. One red bead gathered, bright as a coal. Ossric watched it with horror. Malchior watched it with calculation.
Isolde let the blood fall.
The bead struck the water.
For a breath, nothing happened.
Then the cup began to whisper.
The whisper thickened until it seemed to have weight.
It crawled over the rim of the cup and fell into the room in threads, brushing the stone walls, the shuttered window, the iron hinges of the door. Ossric flinched as though something wet had touched his neck. Malchior did not move. The flame-touched planes of their face remained composed, but a pulse worked beneath the skin at their temple.
Isolde kept their bleeding thumb above the water.
The blood did not disperse. It opened like a red eye.
“Speak,” Isolde said.
The cup answered in a voice made from several voices, none of them wholly human. It breathed through the syllables. It dragged them over the table as if they were bones.
“Gloamreach…”
Ossric’s hands closed around the edge of the table. “You said this would show the command.”
“It shows what the command fears.”
“I have no fear of command.”
“That,” Malchior murmured, “is the first lie you have told tonight.”
The water shuddered.
A pale shape rose beneath its surface: not a face, not yet, but the suggestion of one pressed against ice. Isolde leaned closer. The chill from the cup entered their cut thumb and climbed the arm, seeking the heart. They welcomed it. Pain was a language they trusted because it had no patience for invention.
The shape altered.
A tower appeared in the water, narrow and black against a colorless sky. Its uppermost point vanished into mist. Below it, walls bristled with watchfires. The lights did not burn yellow. They burned the dull blue of old bruises.
Fenspire.
The image trembled, and the spire’s shadow spread across the table. It touched the sleeve of Malchior’s robe. The Arch-Prelate glanced down at it, and for the first time their composure cracked.
“Why Fenspire?” Ossric asked.
Isolde said nothing.
They had never seen the place, but the cup had no need of eyes. It showed not what was known, but what had been bound beneath the known. The tower stood in the Gloaming Reach, disciplined and watchful, a blade driven into the dimness. The garrisoned walls seemed to listen for footsteps beyond their reach.
Then the image darkened.
A road emerged, pale with ash. On it moved a line of men and beasts beneath covered standards. No sigils showed. The cloth was soaked too heavily with rain—or something darker—for its pattern to be read. The procession halted before a gate.
A man stepped from beneath the foremost canopy.
His face refused to settle.
Isolde saw the cut of a commander’s coat, the posture of someone accustomed to being obeyed, the stillness of a person who had learned to place silence where an oath should have been. The cup swallowed his features and returned them wrong: an eye, a mouth, a cheekbone, then blankness.
The whisper spoke.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless, a member of House Morvain.”
Ossric made a small sound.
Malchior’s hand moved toward the chain beneath their robe, where some private token lay hidden. They stopped before touching it.
Isolde watched the image of Ignatz approach the gate.
“You know him,” they said.
“Everyone who has served long enough knows the name.”
“That was not my question.”
“It was the only answer you are entitled to.”
The man in the cup lifted one hand. The gate opened before him. No sentry challenged him. No horn sounded. The road beyond was empty, but the darkness gathered on either side as though waiting to be given orders.
The cup whispered again, softer now.
“House Morvain.”
The words slid beneath Isolde’s skin.
House Morvain had old walls, old claims, old appetites. It could lend a name to a sword and call the wound lawful. It could turn a private grievance into a public necessity, then mourn the dead with a dry eye. Isolde had learned that power did not require innocence. It only required witnesses willing to forget what they had seen.
The image shifted.
A hand rested on a map.
No border could be made out. No banners. Only roads, coastlines, and black marks spreading like mold beneath the skin of parchment. One mark pulsed near the sea. Another answered from inland. The fingers moved between them with deliberate care.
Malchior leaned over the cup.
“Stop this.”
Isolde looked at them. “You are afraid of a map?”
“I am afraid of people who mistake symbols for commands.”
“Then you are safe. I mistake nothing.”
The cup’s red eye widened. A filament of Isolde’s blood pulled from the wound and stretched toward the image. It trembled, thin as spider silk, before sinking into the painted roads.
The room filled with the smell of wet iron.
Ossric shoved backward from the table. His stool struck the wall and fell. “This is forbidden.”
“You brought the cup.”
“I brought a sealed vessel for a sealed inquiry.”
“You brought a witness.”
His face had gone gray. In the candlelight, the quartermaster looked younger than his office, almost painfully so. The fear in him was not theatrical. Isolde could smell it beneath the wool of his coat, sharp and sour.
Malchior turned on him. “You said the water came from the eastern cistern.”
“It did.”
“Who touched it?”
“No one.”
“Nothing is touched by no one.”
Ossric swallowed. “It was taken under guard.”
“Whose guard?”
His mouth closed.
There it was—the little door in him, the place where an answer had been locked away. Isolde felt the blood in the cup stir in recognition. Not guilt, precisely. Guilt was too warm a word. This was calculation cooling into terror.
“Name the guard,” Isolde said.
“I cannot.”
“You can.”
“I was ordered not to.”
“By whom?”
The whisper in the cup began to laugh.
It was not a human laugh. It had no mirth in it, only the grinding rhythm of stones forced together beneath deep water. The tower of Fenspire blurred. The road vanished. Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood again in the red-black depths, though now his face was clear enough to reveal a scar at the mouth.
Isolde had not seen that scar before.
The blood-mage’s own reflection stared back at them from the water beside his.
Their faces touched.
For an instant, Isolde felt another will enter the cut in their thumb. It did not push. It waited. That was worse. A hand upon a door, patient because it knew the door would open.
A memory rose that was not theirs.
A chamber with no windows.
The taste of ash.
A voice reciting terms.
Ignatz standing before someone seated beyond the reach of the light. The seated figure was only a shape. No face. No title. The air between them seemed stretched taut by obligation.
Isolde heard the last words clearly.
“Tell House Morvain the coast is not dead.”
The memory snapped.
The cup burst.
Not shattered—burst. Its water leapt upward in a dark column, striking the ceiling, then fell in a rain of cold droplets. The blood on Isolde’s thumb burned black. Ossric cried out and shielded his face. Malchior seized the edge of the table as the stone beneath it groaned.
For a heartbeat, the room held the smell of salt and rot.
Then every candle went out.
Darkness closed around them.
Ossric was breathing too quickly. Malchior’s robe rustled. Somewhere beyond the door, a boot scraped across stone and halted.
Isolde felt the shape of the knife beneath their sleeve. Their thumb throbbed. The cut had sealed itself, though the skin around it had gone numb.
“Who is outside?” Ossric whispered.
“No one,” Malchior said.
The boot scraped again.
Isolde smiled without warmth. “You are both becoming careless with that word.”
They moved toward the door. The dark seemed reluctant to release them. It clung to their clothing, tugged at their hair, pressed its damp mouth against the back of their neck. Behind them, the cup lay intact on the table. Empty now. Its inner surface was filmed with a red residue that formed no pattern Isolde could read.
The latch lifted.
Malchior said, “Do not open it.”
“Why?”
“Because you have not asked who sent the guard.”
“Neither have you.”
“I am asking you not to open it.”
Their hand rested on the latch.
The voice from the cup returned, not from the table this time, but from the other side of the door.
“Isolde.”
Ossric whimpered.
Malchior’s breath stopped.
Isolde knew the voice. It had no name in the room, but it carried the authority of a command that had once been obeyed. Their fingers tightened around the iron until the metal bit the palm.
“Say it again,” Isolde whispered.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven.”
The title entered them like a hook.
There were many ways to pronounce Unforgiven. Some made it an accusation. Some made it a prayer. Some made it a warning offered too late. This voice gave the word its oldest meaning: not the one who had been denied pardon, but the one who had ceased to seek it.
Behind Isolde, Malchior spoke in a low, controlled voice. “You will not answer.”
“Why?”
“Because a name can be a summons.”
“And if I have already been summoned?”
“Then you are standing at the wrong door.”
The corridor beyond fell silent.
Isolde pictured the dark outside: the narrow passage, the damp stones, the guards who would have been told to wait somewhere else. They pictured the door opening inward, the space beyond empty, and the waiting thing occupying the blind angle beside the hinge.
Their blood knew before their mind did.
Someone had been admitted.
Not into the chamber.
Into the bargain.
Isolde opened the door.
The door opened on Ossric Ashgrove.
He stood with one hand lifted, as though the wood had interrupted a knock he had not yet decided to give. Rain silvered his shoulders. He wore the plain dark coat of a quartermaster, its hem stained with road-mud, and held a narrow iron case against his ribs.
Behind him, the passage was empty.
Isolde looked first at the floor. No wet footprints but Ossric’s. No shadow laid wrong beneath the lamps. No breath steaming in the cold.
Then they looked into his face.
“Who admitted you?”
Ossric swallowed. “No one.”
Malchior came to stand at Isolde’s shoulder. The Arch-Prelate’s presence seemed to draw the darkness into order. Candlelight struck the scorched planes of their skin and made a saint of every scar.
“That is not an answer,” Malchior said.
“It is the only one I have.”
“Then you have come carrying an answer you do not understand.”
Ossric glanced at Isolde. He had the anxious eyes of a man who counted things because numbers did not change their minds. “I was told to bring this to the commander of Gloammarch.”
“You were told by whom?”
His gaze fell to the iron case.
The latch was sealed in black wax. Not with a crest. With a fingerprint.
Isolde felt the old pressure behind their eyes, the blood in their skull tightening as if some invisible hand had closed around it. A summons could be written in ink. A bargain could be written in blood. This was neither. It was a door pretending to be a message.
“Give it to me,” Isolde said.
Ossric did not move.
Malchior’s fingers brushed the sleeve of Isolde’s coat. A warning, light as ash.
“Quartermaster,” Malchior said, “you were born in 333 AS. You have survived by remembering who ordered what, and when. Remember this moment carefully.”
Ossric’s mouth tightened. “I remember.”
“Then remember obedience.”
“I remember that men who obeyed at Blackport were buried beside men who refused.”
The name changed the room.
Blackport came back in the smell of the rain: brine, rot, and the bitter mineral taste that had clung to every well after the Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS. It had ended in 321 AS with 70,907 casualties and the total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel had emerged as victor.
The official accounts called it a triumph of discipline.
The wells had called it something else.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Isolde remembered a boy with blue lips trying to drink from a cup that had already killed his mother. They had been younger then, though not innocent. Innocence was only ignorance that had not yet been punished.
“Bring the case inside,” Isolde said.
Ossric crossed the threshold.
The door shut behind him with a soft, final click.
Malchior looked at the iron seal. “Where did you find it?”
“In the stores beneath the western armory.”
“You were searching the stores?”
“I was inventorying them.”
“And this was inventory?”
“No.” Ossric placed the case on the table. “This was hidden beneath a false bottom in a crate marked lamp oil.”
Isolde remained standing. Their reflection trembled in the polished iron: a pale face, dark eyes, the signs of the Blood-Mage written not on the skin but in the way the air seemed to recoil from their hands.
“Who has access to that armory?”
Ossric’s eyes flicked once toward Malchior.
The Arch-Prelate smiled without warmth. “Say it.”
“Warden-Commander Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The name settled between them.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless served House Morvain. His authority had always carried the blunt weight of a locked gate, but Isolde had learned that gates were most useful to those who knew which side of them held the keys.
Malchior’s face did not change.
“Open it,” they said.
Ossric shook his head. “The seal is not mine to break.”
“Nor mine,” Malchior said.
Isolde reached for the case.
Blood stirred beneath their fingernails.
The wax softened before their touch. Its black surface shivered, then split with a wet whisper. A thin line of red appeared along the seam—not their blood, not Ossric’s. It smelled of iron left in rain.
The case opened.
Inside lay three folded sheets, a brass token, and a strip of parchment so narrow it looked like a dead moth.
The top sheet bore a list of places.
Fenspire. Gloamreach.
Beneath each name, figures had been written in a precise military hand.
Fenspire: garrison 3,742.
Gloamreach: garrison 2,483.
Isolde’s fingers went cold.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire raised above the dim land like a finger held to the mouth of the world. Gloamreach was quarantined, sealed away from the coast by suspicion and orders no sane person questioned aloud.
The figures were not estimates. They were not the sort of numbers a quartermaster copied for comfort. They were the counts of bodies that could be fed, armed, moved, or killed.
Malchior leaned over the table. “That inventory is current?”
Ossric nodded. “The figures were corrected three times.”
“By whom?”
“I do not know.”
“You do.”
“I know whose hand wrote them.”
“Whose?”
Ossric looked again at Isolde. “Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The second sheet contained roads. Not roads as they appeared on maps, but roads as they existed beneath weather: dry crossings, collapsed bridges, stretches where patrols were thin. Beside each route were small marks, each one shaped like a ring cut through by a blade.
The Iron-Ring Cartel’s sign.
Isolde read without touching the page.
“Why would a Warden-Commander keep Cartel marks in a sealed armory?” they asked.
Ossric’s answer came too quickly. “He would not.”
“Then why are they here?”
“I said I do not know.”
“You said the writing was his.”
“I said the hand was his.”
“Do you believe those are different things?”
The quartermaster’s face had gone gray. “I believe a man may write what another man commands.”
Malchior lifted the brass token.
One side showed the five-pointed device of the Iron-Ring Cartel. The other was blank except for a shallow depression, round and dark, as if something had been pressed into it and removed.
“A payment token,” Malchior murmured.
“No,” Isolde said.
Their blood had begun to listen.
They placed one fingertip against the brass. A pulse moved through it. Not warmth. Memory.
A gloved hand.
A table.
A ring of iron sliding across wood.
A voice speaking behind a closed door.
The impression vanished before the words became clear.
Isolde withdrew their hand.
Malchior watched them. “What did you see?”
“Enough.”
“That is not a quantity.”
“It is the only one you are getting.”
The Arch-Prelate’s eyes narrowed. In the candlelight, the forged lineage papers hidden beneath their robes seemed to weigh upon them more heavily than any holy relic.
