Sabelle’s expression did not change, but the room seemed to acquire a colder center.
“Voltaire Hollowmere fought in The Leaden Accord, fighting for The Ashen Vanguard,” they said. “That is what Caedmon Fellgard wrote.”
“Then why ask me?”
“Because Caedmon records what is placed before him. You record what people intend.”
The accusation was accurate enough to be dangerous.
Morwenna thought of letters folded inside oilskin, of sealed packets hidden behind charts, of instructions sent without signatures. She thought of the Iron-Ring Cartel’s payments—not coin alone, never merely coin, but access, forewarning, absences arranged where absences could be mistaken for weather or incompetence.
She had told herself that intelligence was a current. It moved regardless of who opened the sluice. She had only chosen where to stand.
Below, the thing struck the stone.
The floor jumped. The basin tipped and spilled a black fan across the cloth. Sabelle caught the plate before it slid away.
From the corridor came a muffled cry.
Morwenna turned toward the door.
“Scribe,” Sabelle called.
No answer.
“Caedmon Fellgard.”
A heavier impact shook dust from the lintel.
Then Caedmon’s voice came through the wood, strained but controlled. “The outer stair is sealed.”
“By what?”
“Stone.”
“Can you open it?”
“I can hear something on the other side.”
Sabelle glanced at Morwenna. “And?”
Caedmon’s breathing touched the door like a hand. “It is breathing back.”
The sound beneath them ceased.
That was worse than the screaming.
Morwenna’s fingers found the hilt at her belt. The gesture was habitual, almost ceremonial. Her weapon waited where it always waited, obedient to the last order she had given it. A blade was a simple thing. It did not conceal its appetite.
Sabelle folded the stained cloth around the plate.
“Where does the route end?” they asked.
Morwenna did not speak.
“Fleet Admiral.”
The title landed with the old authority of a command barked across a storm-tossed deck. For one instant she was back among rigging and salt, with men waiting for her to point toward danger and call it necessary.
The route ended nowhere marked on any chart.
That was why it had been useful.
“The destination was erased,” she said.
“By you?”
“Not by me.”
“But you know it.”
“I know what it avoids.”
Sabelle’s hand closed around the bundle. “What does it avoid?”
Morwenna stared at the black water soaking into the cloth.
“The sea.”
A pause.
Then Caedmon shouted from the corridor.
The door bowed inward.
Once.
The hinges screamed.
Morwenna drew her blade. Candlelight ran along its edge, thin and bloodless. Sabelle did not draw a weapon. They placed the wrapped plate inside their coat and raised one hand toward the door.
A second blow struck.
This time the wood split.
Through the widening crack came a breath of marsh rot, cold water, and the faintest trace of ash.
Morwenna saw a shape beyond the threshold—not a face, not yet, but a pallid height stooping beneath the lintel. Something dragged itself across the stones with the patient labor of a creature that had all the time in the world.
Sabelle spoke a word Morwenna did not know.
The candles went out.
In the dark, Caedmon Fellgard began to pray.
The thing outside answered him in Voltaire Hollowmere’s voice.
The voice came from the threshold.
“Morwenna.”
It was Voltaire Hollowmere’s voice, worn thin by distance and water. It carried the old iron of command, the habit of being obeyed even when no one wished to obey.
Morwenna’s hand found the hilt at her side. The blade was a comfort only because it was solid. The darkness had made the room uncertain; the walls seemed to breathe around her, and the floor gave a faint, wet complaint beneath the thing’s weight.
Caedmon Fellgard’s prayer faltered.
“Do not answer it,” Sabelle said.
Their voice was near. Too near. Morwenna heard the whisper of cloth, the careful movement of someone who had not panicked and therefore was more dangerous than anyone who had.
“What is it?” Caedmon asked.
“A debt.”
The thing beyond the door scraped one long nail—or bone, or iron—across the broken wood.
“Morwenna,” it said again. “You sold the tide.”
Her mouth went dry.
In the dark, memory rose with the precision of an opened ledger: sealed charts, altered patrol routes, harbor depths written in a cipher no court clerk could read. Information passed through hands that never touched one another. A coin purse left beneath a loose flagstone. A message burned after its contents had been learned.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had never asked her to betray a fleet. That would have been vulgar. They had asked for smaller things—the hour a convoy departed, the strength of a watch, the name of a captain who might be bought. Small things became channels. Channels became rivers. Rivers carried kingdoms into ruin.
She had told herself the realm survived because of it.
She had told herself survival was a kind of innocence.
“Your silence answers,” said the voice.
A pale hand entered through the split in the door.
It was not pale like flesh. It was the color of drowned wax, ridged and gleaming with marsh water. The fingers curled over the timber. Mud fell from them in black beads.
Morwenna stepped backward, and her heel struck Caedmon’s boot.
The scribe sucked in a breath. His body was rigid beneath her touch, his fear held in the same disciplined posture he gave to ink and parchment. She remembered seeing him at tables crowded with petitions, inventories, and death rolls, his hand moving without tremor while men outside begged for bread. A keeper of records. A servant to what had happened, rather than to what anyone wished had happened.
“Caedmon,” she whispered. “The lamp.”
“It is extinguished.”
“Then relight it.”
“With what?”
She almost laughed. The sound would have been hysterical and therefore useful to nothing.
The thing pulled itself farther into the room.
Sabelle moved first. A shape crossed the darkness; then something struck with a wet, heavy force. The creature made no cry. The impact shook the doorframe.
Morwenna drew her weapon.
The blade came free with a whisper.
For an instant, the dark opened around the edge. A weak red line crawled along the steel—not reflected light, but a dull inner glow, as though the metal remembered a furnace.
The creature turned toward her.
She saw its head.
It had no face. Water streamed from a hollow where features should have been, and beneath the dripping veil something pale shifted, searching. Its neck bent at an angle that belonged to a broken doll. Around its throat hung scraps of blackened cloth, perhaps a uniform, perhaps a burial shroud. The stench of marsh and old ash thickened until Morwenna tasted it at the back of her tongue.
“Morwenna Ashgrove,” it murmured.
The use of her full name struck harder than any blow.
Sabelle’s weapon—or perhaps only their hand—caught the creature across the chest. A flash burst in the dark, white and soundless. The revenant recoiled, its arms flinging wide.
Revenant.
The word settled into Morwenna’s mind with a coldness deeper than fear.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned had a bound revenant in their cellar.
The secret had been spoken in whispers by those who believed themselves too cautious to be overheard. Morwenna had dismissed it as court venom, the sort of tale bred wherever power was hidden behind stone. Yet the thing stood before her now, wet with the grave, and Sabelle’s movements possessed the weary familiarity of a jailer dealing with a prisoner who had escaped before.
“You keep this below us,” Morwenna said.
“Not now.”
“Where is its chain?”
“Not now.”
The revenant lurched forward.
Sabelle caught it by the wrist. The creature’s other hand struck their shoulder and drove them into the wall. Stone groaned. Their crown—one of them, Morwenna could not tell which—rang against the masonry.
Caedmon shouted a line from his prayer and threw something. It shattered against the revenant’s back. The smell of vinegar and bitter herbs flooded the room.
The creature paused.
“Records,” it said.
Its voice had changed. For a breath it spoke in Voltaire Hollowmere’s voice, then in Caedmon’s, then in a child’s voice that made Morwenna think of no one she knew.
“Records burn. Names remain.”
Caedmon crouched beside the table. Papers whispered beneath his hands.
“What are you doing?” Morwenna demanded.
“Finding what it wants.”
“Everything wants something.”
His fingers closed around a small leather folio. He rose with it pressed against his chest. The faint outline of his face emerged as the red glow from Morwenna’s blade found him.
The revenant looked at the folio.
Sabelle drove their elbow into its throat.
The creature folded, but its fingers remained locked around Sabelle’s arm. The skin beneath its grasp blackened at once, spreading in thin veins.
Morwenna moved before thought could stop her. She struck the revenant across the knuckles.
The blade bit.
No blood came. A sound like splitting ice passed through the room, and the hand released Sabelle. The creature staggered away, its head snapping toward Morwenna.
“You opened the way,” it said.
She knew, then, what it meant.
The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties. The Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor. Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm, and the world accepted that judgment because the dead could not contradict it.
But an artifact had survived.
Supposedly destroyed, it had been spirited away while the armies vanished beneath the storm. Morwenna had learned that truth in fragments, each fragment purchased by treachery. The artifact was not a weapon in any simple sense. It was a key, or a vessel, or a wound made portable. The Cartel had wanted its location.
She had sold them pieces of the truth.
The revenant knew.
“Where is it?” it asked.
Morwenna’s grip tightened until the hilt cut into her palm.
Sabelle turned their head toward her. Whatever pain the revenant had caused, they concealed it behind that severe stillness. “You know what it means?”
“I know what it wants.”
“That was not my question.”
“No,” Morwenna said. “It was not.”
The creature crossed the room in a blur of wet limbs. Sabelle raised an arm, but the revenant passed them, reaching for Morwenna. Caedmon flung himself between them.
He did not look brave. He looked terrified, which made the act worse.
The revenant’s hand closed around his throat.
The folio fell.
Caedmon clawed at the wrist, his boots scraping uselessly over the stone. His other hand opened and closed, still trying to write.
Morwenna saw the page that had slipped from the folio. A dispatch, marked with the seal of Palewell Abbey.
She knew the place from naval reports. Palewell Abbey stands in The Pale Coast. It was founded in 244 AS, rebuilt, and maintains a garrison of 5998. It is not a core holding. The words had been copied in Caedmon’s careful hand, without comment.
Below them, in a second column, another notation:
Greyfell Citadel.
No explanation. No destination. Only the name, surrounded by corrections and ink so dark it had nearly eaten through the page.
The revenant tightened its grip.
Caedmon’s eyes bulged. A small, humiliating sound escaped him.
Morwenna lunged.
Her blade entered beneath the creature’s ribs. The point emerged from its back, trailing strands of dark water that writhed like worms in moonlight. The revenant bent around the steel. Its face came close to hers.
The hollow beneath its dripping veil contained a glimmer.
Not an eye.
A shard of light trapped in a depthless socket.
The Ley-storm lived there.
Morwenna tried to wrench the blade free. The creature leaned into it instead, bringing its mouth—or the place where a mouth had once been—against her ear.
“Palewell Abbey is a door,” it whispered. “The artifact is not dead.”
Sabelle seized the revenant from behind. Their uninjured hand closed around its throat, and they spoke the unknown word again.
This time, the word had weight.
The room buckled.
Morwenna fell to one knee. Caedmon collapsed beside her, coughing, while the revenant convulsed between Sabelle’s arms. From somewhere below the floor came a sound of chains dragged across stone.
A second sound answered it.
Then a third.
Morwenna looked at Sabelle.
Their face was bloodless in the returning dark. They had not merely kept a bound revenant in their cellar. They had kept something beneath it, something that recognized the command and strained against it.
“You brought us here for this,” Morwenna said.
Sabelle’s gaze dropped to the fallen dispatch.
“I brought you here because you were already involved.”
“With what?”
The revenant’s body began to come apart.
Not decay. Unmaking.
Its limbs thinned into streamers of marsh mist. The cloth around its throat burned without flame. Beneath the dissolving flesh, lines of white fire appeared, forming a pattern Morwenna recognized from the sealed reports of the Leaden Accord.
A circle split by a descending stroke.
The mark that had been found on the artifact’s empty reliquary.
Caedmon saw it too. His hand crept toward the folio.
“Do not touch that,” Sabelle said.
The scribe froze.
The revenant’s remaining shape bent toward Morwenna one last time.
“Tell the Iron-Ring Cartel,” it said.
The floor opened.
Not cracked—opened, as if a black mouth had been waiting beneath the stones. Cold air rushed upward, carrying the smell of wet earth, old blood, and extinguished candles. Sabelle vanished to the waist. Their hand caught the edge, fingers clawing into the mortar.
Morwenna seized their wrist.
For one moment they hung together above the dark: High Inquisitor and Fleet Admiral, jailer and accomplice, each holding the other above whatever waited below.
Sabelle looked up at her.
“Let go,” they said.
The chains beneath them began to climb.
Morwenna felt the wrapped plate beneath her coat grow warm.
Far below, in the dark under Greyfell Citadel, something struck stone once.
Then again.
Then, in a voice that was neither Voltaire Hollowmere’s nor the revenant’s, it spoke her name.
Chapter 11
The quarantine bells of Gloamreach did not ring so much as shudder.
Their iron voices rolled through the fog and struck the walls of the old chapel, where Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched stood with one palm pressed to the altar stone. The rock was cold beneath the glove. Cold enough to feel like judgment.
Beyond the shuttered windows, the Pale Coast had vanished into white murk. Gloamreach lay sealed inside it, its gates barred, its roads watched, its breath held. The garrison numbered 2,483, and every one of those soldiers had been ordered to treat the town as though it were already dead.
Malchior had delivered the order themselves.
“By sanctified authority,” they had said, their voice carrying over the wind, “Gloamreach is quarantined.”
The words had pleased the guards. Authority always pleased those who did not possess it.
Now the chapel smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the faint mineral tang that rose from the sea. Malchior lifted their hand from the altar. A pale smear of salt clung to the black glove.
Behind them, the door opened.
Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven entered without asking leave.
They wore no visible insignia of rank. They needed none. The Blood-Mage carried their reputation like a second skin, and the silence that followed them through the chapel was its proper herald. Isolde had been born in 286 AS, though Malchior had never understood why anyone would record such a thing. Birth was an accident. What a person chose afterward was the only date that mattered.
Isolde’s gaze passed over the altar, the icon fractured by the Sundering, the candles burning low in their cups.
“You closed the town,” they said.
“I did.”
“On what evidence?”
“On the evidence of the bells.”
“The bells were rung by frightened men.”
“Frightened men still have hands.”
Isolde smiled without warmth. “And frightened Arch-Prelates still have throats.”
Malchior turned toward them. The firelight caught the faint red veining at their temples, the mark that had earned them the name Flame-Touched before they had earned the vestments. The title had proved easier to carry than the truth beneath it.
The truth had been written in their own hand.
They had forged their lineage papers.
Not altered them. Not embellished some ancient record with a flattering flourish. Forged them. Ink, seals, dead signatures, a chain of descent that led nowhere except toward the office they now occupied. The papers had survived scrutiny because Malchior had understood what the examiners wished to find: not truth, but permission to believe.
A lie, carefully sanctified, became history.
“You came to challenge the quarantine?” Malchior asked.
“I came to challenge you.”
“Then you have mistaken the chapel for a battlefield.”
“I have mistaken nothing.”
The bells shuddered again. Dust whispered from the rafters.
At the far end of the chapel, Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood in the doorway he had left open. The Warden-Commander had been born in 258 AS, and the years had made his authority seem less like a garment than a scar. No canonical feature distinguished him from any other hard-bitten officer; his epithet did the work. The Oathless. A title bestowed by enemies, perhaps, or friends who had lived long enough to become enemies.
His hand rested near the hilt at his side.
Isolde’s eyes narrowed.
“Still following me?” they asked.
“I was here first.”
“That has never stopped you.”
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” Malchior said, “you were ordered to remain outside the inner chapel.”
“I remained outside until the Blood-Mage entered.”
“Then your obedience is as selective as your memory.”
Ignatz looked at Malchior, and something passed between them that had no name fit for the chapel. Suspicion, perhaps. Or recognition. Ignatz secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel, though no confession had crossed his lips. Malchior had seen the signs in the ledgers: patrols redirected, warnings arriving too late, sealed routes known to hands that should never have touched them.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had learned how to purchase silence. Ignatz had learned how to sell it.
Isolde stepped nearer the altar.
“Ask him where the report came from,” they said.
Malchior kept their face still. “Which report?”
“The one naming the wells.”
Ignatz’s expression hardened. “There are no wells named in my report.”
“Then it is fortunate that I did not mention a report.”
“You mentioned one now.”
“I mentioned wells.”
The chapel seemed to contract around them. Outside, the fog pressed its blind face to the shutters.
Malchior had read the records in the dead hours before dawn. They had read them beneath a single candle while the quarantine seals dried on the gates. The records concerned the Purge of Blackport, which began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. They recorded 70,907 casualties and the total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Those were the approved words.
Approved words were bones laid in orderly rows. They made a clean grave for whatever had truly happened.
The secret truth of the Purge of Blackport was that the victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Malchior had found the sentence hidden beneath a scraped layer of ink, pressed into the parchment so deeply that the fibers still remembered it. The Iron-Ring Cartel had not merely defeated its enemies. It had murdered its own allies and let the slaughter wear the mask of war.
The wells had carried the betrayal farther than any blade.
“Blackport,” Malchior said.
Ignatz’s eyes flickered.
Isolde’s smile returned.
“The Purge of Blackport,” Malchior continued, “began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. It caused 70,907 casualties and ended with the total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.”
“Everyone knows that,” Ignatz said.
“Everyone knows the record.”
“And the record is sufficient.”
“No,” Isolde said. “It is convenient.”
Malchior watched Ignatz. “The secret truth of the Purge of Blackport is that the victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.”
For a moment, the only sound was the trembling of the bells.
Ignatz did not move. That was the movement. His stillness became too deliberate, too complete. A man innocent of a thing might recoil from it. A man guilty of nothing might laugh. Ignatz merely stood there, measuring what the words would cost.
Isolde looked pleased, but not surprised.
“You knew,” Malchior said.
“I knew rumors.”
“You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The Warden-Commander’s hand left the hilt and fell open at his side.
Isolde turned their head slightly. “There. That is the first honest sentence spoken in this room.”
“I have never sold anything to the Cartel.”
“Then you have given it away,” Malchior said.
Ignatz’s gaze sharpened. “Careful, Arch-Prelate.”
The title entered the air between them like a drawn knife.
Malchior felt the old pressure behind their ribs, the pressure that came whenever someone spoke of blood, inheritance, right. Their claimed lineage was suspect. They knew it. Isolde might know it. Ignatz might know it. The forged papers lay somewhere beyond the chapel walls, protected by locks and prayers that could not withstand a patient hand.
Their sanctified authority strained against the concealed fabrication beneath it. Every order they issued had to be louder than the doubt.
“Do not mistake caution for fear,” Malchior said.
“I mistake nothing.”
“That is your favorite lie.”
Ignatz took one step into the chapel. “You shut Gloamreach because of a phrase on a damaged page. You accuse me because a Blood-Mage wants my throat opened. You stand there in stolen robes and call it judgment.”
Isolde’s eyes flashed.
“Say that again.”
“You heard me.”
The Blood-Mage moved before Malchior could speak. Not quickly. Quickly would have been mercy. Isolde crossed the distance with the cold grace of a drawn thread, and the blood beneath Ignatz’s skin rose in dark lines along his throat.
Ignatz staggered.
Malchior felt the chapel’s old wards wake underfoot. The altar gave a low, grinding sound. Flame stirred in the lamps, bending toward Isolde as though compelled by a wind no one else could feel.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” Malchior said.
The Blood-Mage did not look away from Ignatz.
“You are a guest here.”
“I am his rival,” Isolde said. “That is not the same as his executioner.”
The words settled with the weight of a formal declaration: Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven rival of Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.
Ignatz’s face had gone gray. “You plotted the death of your own liege,” he rasped. “Do not dress yourself as a judge.”
The blood at his throat tightened.
Malchior raised their hand.
“Enough.”
The command struck the room with less force than the bells, but the old authority in it was deeper. The blood withdrew beneath Ignatz’s skin. He dropped to one knee, coughing, one fist pressed against the stone.
Isolde’s fingers remained slightly curled.
“You should thank me,” they said.
“I thank no one who comes armed with grievance.”
“Then you will die without gratitude.”
Malchior looked from one to the other. Isolde carried grievance like a lit coal, ambition like a hidden blade, and concealed betrayal like a prayer learned in childhood. Ignatz projected command undermined by secrecy. The two of them were made for conflict, and the powers beyond the chapel would feed upon it.
The Ashen Vanguard would call for discipline. House Morvain would call for leverage. The Silent Choir would call for silence and mean obedience. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call for nothing at all until it knew which throat to purchase. Somewhere in the dark, the Bleeding Crown would count the bodies before they fell.
Five powers contended over the ruins, and every ruin had a door.
A bell began to ring below them.
Not the quarantine bell. This one was smaller, sharper. An alarm from the gatehouse.
Ignatz rose.
“What now?” Isolde asked.
Malchior turned toward the shuttered window. Through a seam in the wood, the fog showed itself as a blank, shifting wall. No torchlight pierced it. No rider could have reached the gate unseen.
“Someone is at the outer road,” Ignatz said.
“Gloamreach is sealed,” Malchior replied.
“Yes.”
The alarm rang again.
Once.
Twice.
Then a third time, followed by a silence so sudden that Malchior felt the whole quarantined town listening.
A strip of paper slid beneath the chapel door.
No hand remained on the other side.
Isolde looked down at it. Ignatz looked at Malchior.
The paper bore a seal pressed in iron-red wax.
Malchior recognized the mark of the Iron-Ring Cartel.
They bent to pick it up, and the moment their fingers touched the seal, the wax split like a wound—
The seal opened onto a second strip of paper, folded three times and blackened at the edges as though it had been held too near a brazier.
No script showed on its surface.
Then the ink rose.
It did not seep into the fibers. It gathered there in glossy beads, crawling against the grain, joining itself into letters with the patient obscenity of insects.
ARCH-PRELATE MALCHIOR CINDERVALE THE FLAME-TOUCHED,
Malchior’s thumb tightened around the paper.
Isolde leaned close enough that a strand of her hair brushed their sleeve. Ignatz did not move. His silence had weight now. It stood between them like a drawn blade.
The message continued.
THE OUTER ROAD IS NOT EMPTY. THE TOWN IS NOT SEALED. YOUR GARRISON IS NOT YOURS.
Beyond the chapel, the alarm bell gave a single muted clapper-stroke, as if a hand had tested its throat and found it full of blood.
Malchior read on.
YOU HAVE THREE HOURS BEFORE THE WEEPING LURKER IS UNLEASHED IN THE PURGE OF BLACKPORT.
Isolde’s breath stopped.
The ink shivered. For one moment, the letters blurred into dark wet veins.
Then more words formed beneath them.
MAELIS GREYFEN FOUGHT IN THE PURGE OF BLACKPORT, FIGHTING FOR HOUSE MORVAIN. ASK WHAT MAELIS GREYFEN SAW BENEATH BLACKPORT. ASK WHO OPENED THE WATER.
Ignatz’s face remained composed, but something in his posture altered. A small withdrawal. A commander’s instinctive step backward from a fire not yet visible.
Malchior looked at him.
“Do you know the name?”
“I know many names.”
“That was not an answer.”
“It was the only one I chose to give.”
Isolde laughed softly. There was no mirth in it. “You hear that, Arch-Prelate? The truth has arrived with conditions.”
The paper grew colder beneath Malchior’s fingers. Cold enough to ache.
A final line surfaced.
THE PURGE OF BLACKPORT BEGAN IN 311 AS AND ENDED IN 321 AS. 70,907 CASUALTIES WERE COUNTED. THE AGGRESSORS WERE ROUTED. REMEMBER THE WEEPING LURKER.
The ink ceased its crawling.
For a breath, nobody spoke.
Malchior had heard the numbers spoken in sanctuaries where the walls were painted with ash. Seventy thousand and nine hundred and seven dead, set down in ledgers by hands that had trembled, then been replaced by hands that did not. The number had become a prayer without a god. The Purge of Blackport had begun in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS, and every telling of it had a different wound at its center.
But no sanctioned account spoke of a Weeping Lurker.
Not in the sermons. Not in the sealed records beneath the prelatical vaults. Not in the lineage papers Malchior had forged with their own hand, copying the flourishes of dead witnesses and staining the margins until the lies looked old enough to be holy.
Their pulse beat against the paper.
Isolde watched them.
“You know it,” she said.
“I know the phrase.”
“That is not what I asked.”
Ignatz’s gaze shifted to the chapel doors. “The outer road.”
“You think the message is a diversion?” Isolde asked.
“I think the Iron-Ring Cartel does not spend wax and paper to frighten children.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel spends everything to frighten everyone.”
“And yet you are frightened.”
Her eyes turned upon him. The pale hollows beneath them seemed darker in the candlelight. “I am interested.”
“You plotted the death of your own liege,” Ignatz said. “You call that interest?”
The chapel changed around them.
The candles guttered, though no wind moved through the room. Malchior heard the faint scrape of Isolde’s glove against the hilt at her hip. Blood-Mage, Unforgiven—both names had been laid upon her like iron brands, and neither had made her smaller.
“Say it again,” she whispered.
Ignatz did not.
That restraint was more dangerous than an insult. Malchior had seen men pray before executioners with less terror than Ignatz showed when Isolde smiled.
The alarm rang from the gate.
Once.
Then the bell cracked into a frantic peal.
Boots hammered across the yard outside. A voice shouted, but the words were swallowed by the fog. Another voice answered from nearer the walls. Then came the sound of something heavy striking stone.
Malchior folded the message. The paper resisted, stiffening like cured hide.
“Who has access to the garrison signal?” they asked.
Ignatz’s eyes stayed on the door. “The Warden-Commanders.”
“Who else?”
“Those permitted to stand beside them.”
“Name them.”
His jaw tightened.
Isolde stepped between them. “Do not waste the night making him confess to every sin he has committed. We may not have the leisure.”
“I have committed no sin that concerns you.”
“Then you have been unusually idle.”
Another impact sounded outside. The chapel’s iron-bound door trembled in its frame.
Malchior felt heat stir beneath their skin. It began at the sternum, a coal kindled in the hidden furnace of their body. Flame-Touched, the faithful called them, as if the fire were a blessing and not a thing that had never once asked permission before entering their blood.
They rose.
“Open the reliquary.”
Ignatz looked at them sharply. “The quarantine orders forbid—”
“I did not ask what they forbid.”
“The reliquary holds nothing suited to a breach.”
“You have not seen what I brought into Gloamreach.”
“No,” Ignatz said. “You made certain of that.”
Isolde’s attention flicked toward him. “That sounded almost like suspicion.”
“It sounded like observation.”
“It sounded like the beginning of courage.”
Ignatz turned on her. “You mistake defiance for courage because defiance is the only virtue you have managed to keep.”
Her hand moved.
Malchior caught her wrist before the blood-magic could answer. Beneath their fingers, her pulse was quick and strong. A thin red line appeared along the crease of her palm, rising without a wound.
“Not here,” Malchior said.
Isolde looked down at their hand on her. “You give orders as though the walls still belong to you.”
“The walls belong to whoever survives the night.”
For the first time, the words silenced them all.
Something dragged itself across the far side of the chapel door.
Not boots. Not claws. A wet, intermittent pull, followed by a faint sound like a child weeping into cloth.
The Warden-Commander went utterly still.
Isolde’s blood withdrew beneath her skin.
Malchior released her wrist.
The sound came again.
A slow drag.
A soft sob.
A pause.
Then a delicate tapping began against the door.
Three taps.
A pause.
Three more.
Ignatz whispered, “That is not the Weeping Lurker.”
“Then what is it?” Isolde asked.
“I don’t know.”
His admission fell into the chapel with the force of a stone dropped down a well.
Malchior approached the door. The fog pressed against the narrow windows, pale and shapeless. Beyond it, Gloamreach had vanished. No battlements. No courtyard. No watchfires. Only the blank wall of mist, breathing against the glass.
Something tapped again.
Malchior raised one hand. Fire moved beneath the skin of their palm, illuminating the fine scars across it. The light was not golden. It was the color of a furnace seen through bone.
A voice spoke from beyond the door.
“Arch-Prelate.”
The voice belonged to no age. It was gentle, hoarse, and wet with grief.
Isolde came to stand beside Malchior. “Who are you?”
The answer came after a long silence.
“Maelis Greyfen.”
Ignatz swore.
It was a small sound, almost private, but Malchior heard it. So did Isolde.
The tapping stopped.
Malchior stared at the door. The name in the message seemed to pulse inside their folded hand.
“Maelis Greyfen,” they said. “You fought in The Purge of Blackport, fighting for House Morvain.”
“Yes.”
The voice drew nearer to the wood, though nothing scraped or stepped.
“What did you see beneath Blackport?” Malchior asked.
A wet breath passed through the cracks.
“Water.”
The chapel candles bent toward the door.
“Whose water?” Isolde demanded.
“Everyone’s.”
Ignatz backed away. His heel struck the first step of the dais.
The mist behind the windows thickened until it blotted out even the faintest suggestion of the outside world. Something began to trickle beneath the door. It spread over the flagstones in a thin black sheet, carrying the sour smell of stagnant wells and old iron.
Malchior’s fire recoiled from it.
That frightened them more than the voice.
“The Weeping Lurker was unleashed in The Purge of Blackport,” Maelis Greyfen said. “And now it has found the road to Gloamreach.”
Isolde crouched and touched one gloved finger to the black water.
The leather hissed.
She pulled back. A dark stain had eaten through the fingertip.
“Open the door,” she said.
Ignatz stared at her. “Have you lost what little mind you possess?”
“It knows us already.”
“It knows the Arch-Prelate.”
“It knows the Cartel’s message. That is not the same thing.”
Malchior looked at the spreading water. It had reached the hem of their robe. The fabric drank it, and beneath the cloth something cold moved across their ankle.
Their forged lineage papers rested inside their vestment, close to the heart.
The old seal. The invented names. The dead bloodlines made obedient with ink.
A thought came to them, sudden and poisonous: if the thing outside could smell lies, it would not need to break the door.
“Why are you here?” Malchior asked.
Maelis answered at once.
“To ask which of you is still human.”
Isolde’s eyes narrowed.
Ignatz’s hand went to his sword.
Malchior heard the lock turn.
Not by any hand they could see.
The bar lifted inside its brackets with a slow metallic groan.
From the other side, the voice began to weep.
The door opened inward.
No wind entered. No rain. Only a pallid shape folded beneath the lintel, its head bowed as though it had forgotten the use of a neck.
The weeping continued.
It came from the shape, from the walls, from somewhere beneath the floorboards. Malchior felt each sob press against their teeth. Their tongue tasted of iron.
“Stand aside,” Maelis said.
The shape lifted its face.
There was no face.
A smear of wet darkness occupied the hood, and within it pale motes trembled like drowned stars. One of them drifted forward. It touched the threshold. The stone blackened.
Ignatz drew his sword.
The blade made a small, almost courteous sound.
“Do not,” Isolde whispered.
“Do not what?”
“Give it a thing with which to remember us.”
Ignatz’s grip tightened. “It already remembers.”
The shape turned toward him.
For one heartbeat, the weeping stopped.
Then Ignatz staggered.
Malchior saw what he saw: a road under a colourless sky, a ring of bodies around a well, hands crawling at the water’s edge. Ignatz stood among them, younger only in the way a blade was young before its first killing. His mouth moved. Words passed from him into unseen hands. Intelligence, bought and sold. A seal pressed into wax. The Iron-Ring Cartel waiting beyond the frame.
Ignatz struck at the vision.
His sword passed through the shape and buried itself in the door.
The weeping began again.
“Get out of my head,” he snarled.
The thing did not answer. It reached for him.
Isolde stepped between them.
Blood welled from the tips of her fingers. Not spilled—summoned. It gathered in red beads, shining with an inner heat, then strung itself between her hands in fine, trembling threads.
The shape paused.
“Blood-Mage,” Maelis said.
Isolde’s mouth curved without humour. “You sound surprised.”
“I am surprised you have any left to spend.”
“You should be more surprised by your own.”
The threads snapped outward.
They struck the darkness beneath the hood and sank into it. Isolde pulled. The thing bent toward her, its limbs lengthening like wet cloth caught on thorns. The room filled with the smell of opened veins.
Malchior’s heart began to beat too hard.
Their forged lineage papers lay beneath their vestment. They could feel the old seal through the layers of cloth, its raised edge pressed against the skin. A false descent. Invented names. Dead bloodlines made obedient by ink.
The thing’s faceless head turned.
Not toward Isolde.
Toward Malchior.
They raised one hand, and the brand beneath their palm answered. Flame appeared without light: a coal-red line circling the wrist, then a crown of thin fire over the knuckles. The shape recoiled.
For an instant, Malchior believed sanctity had saved them.
Then the thing wept in their own voice.
“I was born in 289 AS,” it said.
Their hand faltered.
The fire crawled backward beneath their skin.
“I serve as Arch-Prelate,” it continued. “I am Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched. My blood is old. My claim is clean.”
The words were not spoken aloud. They came from the papers.
The seal grew hot against Malchior’s chest.
“Enough,” they said.
The shape leaned closer.
“Forged.”
The door slammed shut.
The iron bar dropped into place with a crack that shook dust from the rafters. Isolde’s blood-threads snapped, whipping back across her wrists. She hissed and clutched one arm.
Ignatz tore his sword free.
Malchior stood motionless, staring at the wood.
Behind it, something dragged its fingers downward.
One stroke.
Two.
Three.
The marks remained after the sound ceased.
Maelis watched Malchior instead of the door. “It knows.”
“It knows many things.”
“It knew the word forged.”
“So did you.”
“I knew the look of the papers.”
Malchior turned. “You have not seen them.”
“No.” Maelis’s eyes were pale in the dimness. “But I have seen what people become when they wear a name that does not belong to them.”
Ignatz laughed once. There was no amusement in it.
“Listen to the priest,” he said. “The Arch-Prelate will burn us all for the comfort of a genealogy.”
Malchior faced him. “You have no right to speak of comfort.”
The Warden-Commander’s sword remained bare in his hand. “And yet I am still speaking.”
“You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The silence that followed seemed deeper than the sealed room.
Isolde looked from one to the other. Her expression sharpened, grievance finding a new edge.
Ignatz did not deny it.
He lowered the sword point until it rested against the floor.
“Who told you?”
“The same thing that told you to fear the door.”
A muscle moved in his jaw. “You think it shows truth.”
“I think it shows what will wound us.”
“Then you should pray it does not learn the difference.”
Malchior felt the papers shifting beneath their vestment, though they lay still. The parchment seemed to breathe against their ribs. Their false ancestors pressed close, patient as worms.
Isolde laughed softly.
“How solemn you both are,” she said. “As if confession makes any of this cleaner.”
“Your turn,” Ignatz said.
Her gaze slid to him. Whatever lay between them had the old, settled shape of hatred. Not sudden, not theatrical. It had been carried, polished, and kept sharp.
“You want my sin?”
“I want to know what it saw.”
“It saw nothing you did not already suspect.”
“That you plotted the death of your own liege?”
The blood around her fingers thickened.
Maelis took one step back.
Isolde did not look ashamed. That, more than the accusation, unsettled Malchior. Shame was a leash. Without it, ambition became a creature with no throat to seize.
“My liege mistook obedience for ownership,” Isolde said. “I corrected the error.”
“Did you kill them?”
“No.”
“Did you plot it?”
“I plotted.”
The answer landed with the weight of a stone.
Beyond the walls, the dark pressed close. Somewhere in the building, a hinge creaked. No one moved toward the sound.
Malchior reached beneath their vestment and drew out the papers.
The parchment was damp.
Not with rain. With a thin, clear fluid that gathered along the folded edges and fell in slow drops to the floor.
Isolde stared at it. Ignatz’s face hardened.
Maelis said, “Do not open them.”
“If I do not, it will.”
“Then let it come.”
Malchior unfolded the first sheet.
The old seal had softened. Its stamped emblem had blurred into a black ring, and the invented names beneath it were bleeding into one another. The ink ran in narrow rivulets. At the bottom, where the lineage ended, a second hand had appeared.
Not written.
Carved.
MALCHIOR CINDERVALE THE FLAME-TOUCHED
The letters deepened while they watched.
The fire beneath Malchior’s skin flared. Pain climbed their arm, hot and intimate. Their knees weakened.
“I was born in 289 AS,” they said, because the words were expected of them.
The room listened.
“I serve as Arch-Prelate.”
The carved letters shuddered.
“My lineage is—”
They stopped.
The door began to weep again.
Not the creature’s voice this time. A woman’s voice. Then a child’s. Then the hoarse, exhausted sobbing of someone who had cried until crying became the only proof they remained alive.
Maelis approached the door.
“Do you hear that?”
“I hear enough,” Ignatz said.
“No. Listen.”
Malchior did.
Under the weeping lay another sound: distant horns, muffled by walls and years. The grind of wagons over ash. Men shouting. Water being drawn from a well. Then silence, broken by the brittle laughter of those who had survived.
The Purge of Blackport had left voices in the world that no prayer could bury.
Malchior saw the wells.
They saw the Iron-Ring Cartel standing among the victors while their own allies drank poison, and they understood that betrayal did not require hatred. It required only a hand steady enough to pour.
The image passed.
A map lay across the floor where no map had been before.
Its parchment was grey and stiff. Two places had been marked in red.
Gloamreach.
Fenspire.
Malchior crouched.
“Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast,” they read. “Quarantined. Garrison: 2,483.”
The ink trembled beneath their finger.
A second notation had been written beside it.
“Garrisoned Fenspire,” Malchior continued. “Founded in 57 AS. Garrison: 3,742. Gloaming Reach.”
Ignatz leaned over the map. “Those numbers are current?”
“They are written as fact.”
“By what?”
Malchior looked toward the closed door.
The weeping had stopped.
Isolde crouched on the opposite side of the map. Her blood had ceased flowing, but the skin at her wrists remained red and raw.
“Why those places?” she asked.
Maelis did not answer.
Malchior studied the red marks. Gloamreach sat at the edge of the Pale Coast, isolated by quarantine and sea-mist. Fenspire rose in the Gloaming Reach, disciplined and watchful beneath its stark silhouette. Two garrisons. Two locked jaws.
The map’s red lines connected them.
Then a third line appeared.
It ran from the map’s centre to the papers in Malchior’s hand.
Ignatz saw it too.
His sword came up.
“Burn it.”
Malchior’s fingers closed around the parchment. “It may be a warning.”
“It may be a summons.”
“Those are not always different.”
The line brightened.
The old seal cracked.
From beyond the door came a single knock.
Not loud.
Not urgent.
A knuckle against wood.
Then another.
A third.
The voice spoke through the grain, and this time it used no borrowed sorrow.
It spoke with Malchior’s voice.
“Open.”
Malchior felt the forged lineage papers unfold by themselves beneath their hand.
On the final page, beneath the carved name, fresh ink began to write.
Not a bloodline.
A date.
Chapter 12
The sea had gnawed the lower steps of Palewell Abbey to a lacework of stone.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood above the tide and watched the black water work at what remained. Spray reached her boots in cold, needling bursts. Behind her, the rebuilt abbey kept its pale walls turned toward the coast, every narrow window dark beneath its battlements. Sanctuary had been scoured from the place. What remained was a garrison with prayers painted over its murder-holes.
A bell sounded once.
Not an alarm. A summons.
Morwenna did not move until the echo had gone out over the water.
“Fleet Admiral.”
Caedmon Fellgard waited at the stairhead with a ledger held against his chest. His posture had the rigid patience of a man who trusted ink more than flesh. A smear of black marked one finger. The wind worried at his sleeves.
“Who rang it?” Morwenna asked.
“Corvus Hollowmere the Pale.”
“Then he has learned to count.”
Caedmon lowered his eyes. “He commands Palewell Abbey (since 374 AS).”
The sentence had the sound of a copied line, and perhaps it was. Caedmon carried facts as other men carried knives: close, sharpened, and never shown without purpose.
Morwenna looked back at the surf. The abbey had been founded in 244 AS. Its stones had been broken, its bones rearranged, and its garrison raised to 5998. The number had been entered three times in the fleet’s accounts, each time in a different hand, as though repetition might make the walls safer. Palewell Abbey was not a core holding. That distinction had been spoken in council with the calm of a verdict. Not core. Not essential. Not worth the ships required to relieve it.
Yet Corvus had rung for her.
“Take me to him.”
Caedmon turned.
Morwenna followed him inside.
The passage smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and salt trapped beneath old mortar. Rebuilt walls did not settle like ancient ones. They cracked with small, private noises. Beyond the slit windows, the Pale Coast heaved under a sky the color of beaten pewter.
“Is the High Inquisitor here?” Morwenna asked.
Caedmon’s step faltered. It was almost nothing. Morwenna had spent her life learning the weight of almost nothing.
“Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned arrived before dawn.”
“Arrived for what?”
“I was not told.”
“That is not an answer.”
“No,” Caedmon said. “It is the answer I have.”
He led her into a chamber where the ceiling beams had been blackened by age or smoke. A map of the realm covered the central table, pinned at its corners with iron nails. The five powers had been marked in different colors: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Along the coast, a red thread ran from one salt-stained mark to another.
Corvus Hollowmere the Pale stood at the far side of the table.
Morwenna had never seen him before. She gave the fact no shape beyond that. Faces were weather. Offices were architecture. The man’s pale title was less important than the command beneath it.
Sabelle Mournvale sat beside the hearth, wearing the black severity of a High Inquisitor. The two crowns upon their seal gleamed dully at their throat. They watched Morwenna without blinking.
Caedmon placed his ledger on the table.
“Fleet Admiral,” Corvus said. “You came quickly.”
“The bell was loud.”
“It was meant to be heard.”
“Then speak loudly.”
A silence gathered. It was not fear. Fear had heat. This was the cold interval before a blade cleared its sheath.
Corvus touched the red thread with one finger. “A vessel passed the outer shoals without declaring its cargo.”
“Many vessels do.”
“This one carried no colors.”
“Then it was wise.”
His mouth tightened. “The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS. The Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor. Fourteen thousand and eleven casualties were recorded.”
Caedmon’s pen moved.
Morwenna watched the ink descend.
“14,011,” she said. “If you are going to summon me, Corvus, use the number written in the records.”
Caedmon’s pen paused, then corrected the line.
Corvus looked from the scribe to her. “Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm.”
“So the records say.”
“The records also say the artifact was destroyed.”
Morwenna felt the old wound open beneath her ribs—not pain, precisely. Recognition. The sea wind passed through the chamber’s cracks and touched the back of her neck.
“Supposedly destroyed,” she said.
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened.
Caedmon stopped writing.
Morwenna had sold the first fragment of that intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel in a room without windows, for a sum paid in sealed metal and promises. She had sold the second fragment later, when the Cartel had stopped asking whether the artifact survived and begun asking where it had gone. She had never sold the truth. Truth was too dangerous to spend all at once.
“The hidden truth,” Corvus said, “is that the supposedly destroyed artifact was spirited away.”
“By whom?”
“If I knew, I would not require a fleet admiral.”
“You require ships. That is different.”
“I require your silence.”
At the hearth, Sabelle shifted one gloved hand across the other. Their expression did not change, but something below the floor gave a muffled scrape.
Caedmon looked down.
Morwenna did not.
She had heard rumors about the High Inquisitor’s cellar. Rumors were usually the dead dressed in other people’s clothes. Yet this sound had weight. A bound revenant, if the whispers were true, kept beneath the abbey while Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned spoke of purity above it. Morwenna wondered whether the creature remembered its name. She wondered whether Sabelle feared that it did.
“Your vessel was seen from the western tower,” Corvus said.
“My vessel?”
“The fleet’s vessel.”
“Then accuse the fleet.”
“I accuse the absence of a declaration.”
“A declaration is a scrap of paper. It does not make a cargo innocent.”
“Nor does silence make it guilty.”
“No,” Morwenna said. “But it makes it valuable.”
The bell sounded again.
This time it rang twice.
Corvus turned toward the shuttered window. Caedmon’s hand closed over his pen. Sabelle rose, and the movement drew another scrape from beneath the floorboards.
A soldier shouted somewhere beyond the chamber.
Then another voice answered, too distant to understand.
Morwenna crossed to the window and opened the shutter.
The coast below was a confusion of foam and black rock. Beyond the harbor mouth, a single ship labored against the swell. No colors. No lanterns. Its sails were furled, its hull dark with water. It had come in under the storm’s cover and now drifted just beyond the abbey’s reach.
On its deck, figures moved.
Not sailors, Morwenna thought.
She felt for the sealed message hidden inside the lining of her coat. The paper was dry. The Cartel’s cipher had been pressed into it with a blunt instrument: three lines, no greeting, no signature.
THEY KNOW THE ARTIFACT LIVES.
DO NOT LET SABELLE OPEN THE CELLAR.
BRING US THE SHIP.
The message had been waiting for her before she reached the coast. She had read it beneath a hooded lamp while the fleet cut through the dark. Since then, every mile had seemed to narrow around her.
Corvus came to stand beside her.
“Do you recognize it?”
“I recognize a ship.”
“Will it anchor?”
“It has no colors.”
“That was not my question.”
“It will not anchor because you command it to.”
His eyes remained on the vessel. “You were born in 288 AS, Morwenna Ashgrove.”
Caedmon’s head lifted.
Morwenna turned slowly. “You keep a curious ledger.”
“Birth records are not curious. They are useful.”
“Useful to whom?”
“To those who must know how long a person has had to become what they are.”
Sabelle spoke from behind them. “And what have you become?”
Morwenna looked at the ship.
The answer waited in the lining of her coat, pressed into paper and paid for in silence. She had become a Fleet Admiral who sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. The words felt smaller spoken within herself than they did when written. Treason required witnesses. Without them, it was merely another duty performed in darkness.
“Someone who dislikes being questioned by scribes and inquisitors,” she said.
Sabelle smiled without warmth. “You dislike being known.”
“Everyone does.”
“Not the dead.”
The scrape beneath the floor came again.
This time it was followed by a soft, wet exhalation.
Caedmon’s face lost what little color it possessed. Corvus looked toward the hearth.
Morwenna saw the calculation pass through him: the ship outside, the revenant below, the High Inquisitor at his back, and the Fleet Admiral between them. A commander could survive one threat by choosing another. A ruler could survive several by naming them law.
The ship’s bow swung in the tide.
For an instant, something pale showed beneath its forward rail—not a flag, not a lantern, but a length of cloth knotted around a human arm.
The arm lifted.
Sabelle stepped toward the hearth.
“Do not,” Morwenna said.
The High Inquisitor stopped.
The word had left Morwenna before she had chosen it. In the room, it stood naked and irreversible.
Corvus reached for the bell rope.
Morwenna’s hand went beneath her coat, closing around the message meant for the Iron-Ring Cartel, while below the floorboards the bound revenant began to whisper—and Caedmon, pale with terror, bent to hear what it said.
The rope shuddered beneath Corvus’s hand.
Not yet rung. The bell above them gave a dull, reluctant tremor, as if even iron could be made to hesitate.
Below, the revenant whispered.
Caedmon Fellgard bent nearer.
Morwenna heard only the scrape of his breath and the faint movement of his pen. He had brought the pen down without seeming to decide it, the nib poised above the page while the dead voice crawled through the floorboards. His shoulders were narrow beneath his robe. Ink had darkened the side of one finger. A scribe’s hands, made for preserving what others wished forgotten.
“What does it say?” Morwenna asked.
Caedmon did not look up. “I am not certain it uses words.”
“Then write the sounds.”
His pen touched the page.
The whisper below thickened. It moved through the stone in wet threads, a voice dragged across the underside of the world. Sabelle stood by the hearth, one hand still extended from the command Morwenna had given. Firelight trembled over the metalwork at their throat and over the shadow cast by the crown they wore—not a king’s crown, not entirely, but something fashioned to remind every witness that authority could be inherited from ruin.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned had been born in 263 AS. Morwenna knew the year because High Inquisitors were entered into the old ledgers twice: once as children and once as instruments. Sabelle’s second entry had been written in a different hand.
Their gaze remained on Morwenna.
“You have mistaken restraint for mercy,” Sabelle said.
“I have mistaken nothing.”
“No?” Their voice was quiet. “You heard a dead thing speak and reached first for the living.”
Morwenna’s hand remained beneath her coat, closed around the message intended for the Iron-Ring Cartel. The paper had warmed against her palm. Its folded edge pressed into the flesh like a blade too dull to cut cleanly.
Outside, the ship’s hull groaned against the tide.
The arm beneath the forward rail had vanished.
Corvus released the rope. “There was an arm.”
“There was cloth,” Sabelle said.
“There was an arm,” Corvus replied.
The High Inquisitor’s eyes did not leave Morwenna. “Then you should be grateful it did not wave.”
Caedmon’s pen scratched faster.
The revenant spoke again, and this time a word rose clear enough to be understood.
“Leaden.”
The fire drew inward.
Morwenna felt the room alter around her. Not visibly. The hearth remained a hearth; the black beams remained black beams. Yet some old pressure had entered the air, some weight that belonged beneath mountains and beneath oaths.
“The Leaden Accord,” Caedmon whispered.
Sabelle turned toward him. “Read what you have.”
Caedmon swallowed. His face had gone pale, though his hands stayed steady.
“The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS,” he said. “It ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties. The Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor.”
The ship struck something below with a hollow boom.
Corvus stared toward the shuttered window. “That is written in every account.”
“Not every account,” said Morwenna.
The revenant hissed beneath them.
Caedmon’s nib shivered. “Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm.”
“Yes,” Sabelle said. “That too is written.”
“And the hidden truth,” Caedmon continued, “is that a supposedly destroyed artifact was spirited away.”
No one moved.
Morwenna watched the page. The scribe had written the words in a cramped hand, forcing them together as if the truth required less space than a lie. She had seen records altered by order of admirals, abbots, princes, and merchants. Ink was obedient. Paper had no conscience. Only men pretended otherwise.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had been named victor after both hosts had been annihilated. A victory over ash. A triumph measured in the absence of survivors. Morwenna had spent years learning how much intelligence could be bought with that kind of silence.
The message beneath her coat seemed to pulse.
Sabelle approached the table.
“Who told you to stop me?”
“No one.”
“Then why did you?”
Morwenna looked at the hearth. A coal collapsed, sending a spray of sparks up the chimney. “Because you are not the only one who can hear what is beneath us.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the one you are receiving.”
For the first time, Sabelle smiled.
It had none of the warmth that preceded a smile in the living. “You were born in 288 AS, Fleet Admiral. You learned command under a realm already full of ghosts. You should know that anything which whispers from below is either hungry or useful.”
Morwenna’s fingers tightened around the message.
The title struck her as an accusation. Fleet Admiral. A station built from discipline, signal, and the public fiction that every order passed through one visible hand. Her authority had been forged in open water, where distance made people honest about fear. Here, beneath stone and sanctity, every silence had a second mouth.
“Perhaps it is neither,” she said.
“Nothing is neither.”
Caedmon looked up from his page. “It is saying there is no artifact.”
Sabelle’s attention shifted to him.
Caedmon’s throat worked. “Or—no. It says the artifact has no—” He frowned, listening. “No grave.”
The revenant’s voice ceased.
The silence afterward was worse.
Morwenna heard the tide beneath the walls, the minute settling of the timbers, the dry rasp of Corvus’s breathing. Somewhere above, a gull cried and was cut short.
Sabelle placed both hands upon the table. “Caedmon Fellgard, do not embellish what you hear.”
“I am not embellishing.”
“You are frightened.”
“Yes.”
“At least fear remains a form of honesty.”
Caedmon lowered his eyes. His pen resumed its work, though the page had begun to tremble under it.
Morwenna thought of Greyfell Citadel, founded in 62 AS in the Shattered Vale. An abandoned fortress outside the realm’s core holdings, grey stone emptied of banners and purpose. It had been raised to command the passes, then left to the weather and whatever slept in its cisterns. Every chart called it irrelevant. Every smuggler’s route bent toward it.
The ship had not come by accident.
Neither had the arm.
“Where is the vessel bound?” Morwenna asked.
Corvus’s mouth tightened. “You assume it is bound anywhere.”
“Everything afloat is bound somewhere.”
“Not wreckage.”
“Wreckage does not signal.”
“There was no signal.”
“Then why are you still watching the window?”
Corvus turned from her. His face was hard with the particular anger of a man forced to doubt his own sight. “Because Palewell Abbey is not blind.”
Morwenna let that settle.
Palewell Abbey stood in The Pale Coast. It had been founded in 244 AS, rebuilt after ruin, and maintained a garrison of 5998. It was not a core holding, but its walls had been thickened until prayer could be delivered through arrow slits. Six thousand nearly, in all but name; 5998 in the ledger, because ledgers demanded that two absences be made visible.
“Palewell’s garrison would have seen the ship,” Morwenna said.
“Palewell’s garrison sees what it is ordered to see.”
“And who ordered them?”
Corvus said nothing.
Sabelle lifted their hand from the table and touched one finger to the folded edge of Morwenna’s coat, not quite touching the hidden message. The gesture was delicate. Intimate only in the way a knife’s point was intimate with the skin.
“You carry a letter,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna did not blink. “I carry many things.”
“A letter intended for the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The fire made a soft cracking sound.
Caedmon’s pen stopped.
Corvus looked between them. “Is that true?”
Morwenna considered denying it. The denial came easily; she had worn it in councils, aboard flagships, before men who would have condemned her for less and purchased her for more. But Sabelle had not asked how they knew. Their certainty had already crossed the room and seated itself among them.
“Yes,” Morwenna said.
Corvus’s hand moved toward the weapon at his side.
Morwenna did not look at it. “If you draw, you will make the room smaller. That will benefit the dead thing beneath us.”
“Do not instruct me in rooms.”
“I instruct you in consequences.”
Sabelle’s expression had gone still. “What does the Cartel want?”
“Information.”
“They always want information.”
“They want what they are willing to pay for.”
“And what are you willing to sell?”
Morwenna felt the old, familiar division open inside her: the admiral on one side, the woman who counted coin and currents on the other. She had never mistaken the two for friends. The admiral believed in command. The other believed command was merely the most expensive form of leverage.
“Routes,” she said.
“Which routes?”
“Those not protected by your bells.”
Corvus’s hand closed around the hilt at his side.
Sabelle did not move. “You have been selling intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The words were not loud. They did not need to be.
Morwenna looked at the dead hearth, the old mortar, the ash gathered in its corners. She imagined the message burning. She imagined the Cartel’s disappointment, then its patience. Merchants could forgive betrayal when betrayal remained profitable. They did not forgive waste.
“Yes,” she said.
Caedmon made a small sound.
Morwenna turned to him. “Write that as well.”
The scribe stared at her.
“Write it,” she repeated.
His hand lowered. The nib touched the page.
Sabelle watched the confession take form. Their eyes were dark in the firelight, and beneath the severity of their face something stirred—satisfaction, perhaps, or the colder pleasure of a lock finding its key.
“You think this saves you,” they said.
“No.”
“Then what does it do?”
“Places the truth where it can be used.”
“By whom?”
Morwenna heard it then.
Not beneath the floorboards.
Outside.
A knock against the hull.
Once.
Twice.
A third time, softer than the others.
Corvus turned toward the window. Sabelle’s hand went to the bell rope again.
Morwenna caught their wrist.
The contact lasted no longer than a breath. Sabelle’s pulse was calm beneath her fingers.
Below them, the revenant began to laugh.
The laughter rose through the timbers, wet and patient, as though the thing below had learned the shape of amusement from overheard mouths.
Sabelle looked down at Morwenna’s hand.
Not at her face. At the fingers closed around their wrist.
“Release me.”
Morwenna did.
The bell rope trembled beside them. Its iron tongue gave a small, betraying chime.
Outside, the darkness pressed against the glass. No lantern showed beyond it. No pale face. Only the black water, broken by a skin of rain, and the reflection of the cabin fire shivering where the window should have opened onto night.
Corvus had not moved from the window.
“Was that the signal?” Morwenna asked.
“No,” Corvus said.
Their voice had changed. It carried none of the command with which they ruled Palewell Abbey. There was fear in it, but not fear for themselves. Morwenna knew the sound. It was the fear of a person who had trusted a wall to remain a wall.
The revenant laughed again.
This time, something struck the underside of the deck.
Wood groaned.
Sabelle’s expression remained composed. They drew a narrow blade from beneath their coat, not with haste but with the grim economy of practice. The fire found the metal and slid away.
“Stay here,” they said.
Morwenna almost smiled. “To whom?”
Sabelle glanced toward Corvus. “Both of you.”
Corvus turned from the window. “You would leave us above it?”
“I would leave you above what is already beneath you.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are owed.”
The hull gave another shudder. A cup rolled from the table and broke against the wall. Wine spread across the boards, darkening the grain. Its smell mingled with the damp and the old smoke, sweet as rot.
Morwenna felt the weight of the message hidden inside her coat.
Not a letter. Not anything so innocent.
The information had been written in a cipher that could be read as a devotional inventory if found by the wrong hands. The Iron-Ring Cartel preferred such arrangements. Truth disguised as piety. Treason dressed in a clerk’s careful ink.
She had sold them less than they wanted and more than they deserved. That was how she had survived each exchange. Give them a gate, keep the key. Give them a name, keep the reason. Yet the truth she had placed before Sabelle was different. It had not been purchased. It had been lifted from the dark and set between them like a blade.
Now someone waited outside the hull.
Or something.
The window clicked.
Morwenna turned.
A fingertip pressed against the outer pane.
It was grey through the glass, the nail blackened, the skin stretched thin enough to show the cords beneath. The finger withdrew. A palm replaced it, leaving a smear of water that did not run downward. It crawled sideways, gathering itself into a thin, trembling line.
Corvus whispered a prayer.
Sabelle watched the hand without blinking.
“Open the door,” called a voice from outside.
The sound was muffled by rain and timber, but it was unmistakably human.
Morwenna knew it.
Not the speaker. The cadence.
A voice trained to make requests sound like verdicts.
Sabelle’s blade lowered a fraction. “You should not be here.”
“Neither should you.”
The words came again, closer now, from beneath the cabin. The revenant had stopped laughing.
Morwenna looked toward the trapdoor.
It was shut. Iron-banded. A lock rested in its bracket, though she had seen Sabelle carry no key. The seams around it had been sealed with wax. Someone had pressed a mark into the wax: a circle broken by three straight strokes.
The mark of the Silent Choir.
She had seen it on intercepted cargo, on drowned reports, on the margins of ledgers bought and burned before they could reach any tribunal. The Choir left no proclamations. It left absences. A missing witness. A door found open. A page cut cleanly from a book.
“Who is below?” Corvus asked.
Sabelle did not answer.
The voice outside gave a soft, almost affectionate sigh.
“High Inquisitor.”
The title entered the room like cold air.
Sabelle’s face hardened. “You are trespassing.”
“You invited us.”
“I invited no one.”
“You invited the truth.”
Morwenna felt the room contract around that word.
The fire snapped. A coal broke free and rolled across the hearthstone. Shadows leapt over Sabelle’s crowned brow, across the severe planes of their face, and vanished into the folds of their coat. Twice-Crowned. The title had once been spoken with reverence, then with suspicion, and now with the cautious disgust reserved for things that remained powerful after they had become impossible to forgive.
Below them, the lock turned.
Corvus swore.
The sound was quiet, but it had the force of a cannon shot.
Sabelle crossed the room in three strides and seized the trapdoor’s iron ring. The wood bucked beneath their hand.
“Go to the stern,” they ordered.
Morwenna did not move. “Why?”
“Because if the door opens, you will be the first thing it sees.”
“That is not reassuring.”
“It was not meant to be.”
Corvus drew a pistol from within their coat. The weapon looked too small for the room, too delicate for whatever waited beneath the boards. They held it with both hands.
Morwenna saw then what the cold had hidden: a line of blood running from Corvus’s palm to their sleeve.
“You’re hurt.”
“I am commanded.”
“Those are not opposites.”
“No,” Corvus said. “But they are not the same.”
The lock clicked.
Sabelle planted one boot on the trapdoor. Their blade hovered at the seam.
The voice outside spoke once more.
“Morwenna Ashgrove.”
Her name sounded wrong in that mouth. Flattened. Studied.
She had heard it spoken by sailors, ministers, officers, enemies, and men who wished to become one of those things. This voice knew nothing of her rank and everything of her use.
“I know what you carry,” it said.
The message inside her coat seemed to warm against her ribs.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had taught her never to reach for concealed steel while being watched. Never to answer a threat with a confession. Never to mistake a person’s knowledge for their certainty.
She had learned those lessons before the Leaden Accord, when every harbor had been a mouth and every mouth might have been bought.
She had forgotten none of them.
Sabelle looked at her. “What did you tell them?”
“Nothing.”
The answer came too quickly.
Their gaze sharpened.
Morwenna held it. “Nothing they can prove.”
“That is a different answer.”
“It is the one that matters.”
Beneath the trapdoor, the revenant began to whisper.
The words were indistinct, but the rhythm was clear: a child’s counting song without its numbers, a melody stripped of innocence and left with only the bones. Morwenna had heard sailors hum similar tunes before storms. They always stopped before the final verse.
Sabelle’s fingers tightened around the iron ring.
“You will speak plainly,” they said.
“Not while your guest is listening.”
“My guest?”
“Your prisoner.”
The revenant fell silent.
The quiet that followed was worse than its laughter.
Corvus’s pistol swung toward the door. “You keep it below?”
Sabelle did not look at them. “I keep nothing.”
The trapdoor lifted an inch.
A breath emerged from the crack. It smelled of old soil, salt, and something medicinal burned past bitterness. Morwenna’s skin tightened along her arms.
Sabelle forced the hatch down.
Something struck from beneath.
The boards bowed upward. The wax seal split with a faint, wet sound.
A second blow.
The hinges screamed.
“Open the door,” called the voice outside.
“Get away from the window,” Morwenna said.
Corvus did not obey. Their eyes remained fixed on the black pane.
“Why?”
“Because it wants us looking out.”
The grey hand appeared again.
This time it was not alone.
A second palm pressed beside it. Then a third, each one emerging from the dark at impossible distances, as though the outer wall had become transparent to a crowd waiting on the other side. No faces. No bodies. Only hands, pale and patient against the rain.
Corvus raised the pistol.
“Do not,” Morwenna said.
The nearest fingers curled.
The window cracked.
A line of silver ran from top to bottom.
Sabelle’s head snapped toward it. “What did you bring here?”
Morwenna could have lied.
She had lied in council chambers, in war rooms, in the mouths of harbors where men watched her ships burn and waited to learn which way the wind would carry the blame. Lies were tools. A good commander kept them clean.
But below them, the revenant had begun to laugh again.
And outside, the hands were tapping against the glass in a slow, deliberate pattern.
Once.
Twice.
A third time.
Morwenna reached beneath her coat and withdrew the sealed strip of parchment.
Sabelle’s eyes dropped to it.
Corvus’s pistol wavered.
The seal bore no crest. Only a narrow ring of black wax, pressed flat.
“I did not bring this here,” Morwenna said.
The trapdoor tore free of its hinges.
Sabelle moved first, driving their blade downward as something pale surged through the opening. Steel struck flesh—or what had replaced flesh—and the cabin filled with a shriek so thin it seemed to come from inside Morwenna’s teeth.
The window shattered.
Rain blew in.
The hands vanished.
For one breath there was only fire, broken glass, and the stink of the opened cellar.
Then the thing beneath the deck spoke in Morwenna’s own voice.
“Open the message.”
Chapter 13
The bell above Fenspire had a cracked voice.
It spoke across the Gloaming Reach in a single iron note, and the sound entered Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven through the scars beneath their ribs. The tower had stood since 57 AS, a black needle thrust into the dim country, and its garrison of 3,742 kept watch from walls that had outlived every oath sworn beneath them.
Below, soldiers moved through the rain with hooded lamps. Their armor glimmered like wet bone. The garrisoned city did not sleep so much as clench itself against the dark.
Isolde stood beneath the covered walk, one gloved hand resting on the pommel of a knife they had never drawn in public. Water whispered from the roof. Beyond the parapet, the Gloaming Reach sank toward the Pale Coast, and somewhere past that pallid, wind-scoured margin lay Gloamreach: quarantined, sealed from the surrounding coast, guarded by a garrison of 2,483.
Nothing entered Gloamreach without being counted.
Nothing left without being changed.
“Your blood is on the stone.”
The voice came behind them.
Isolde looked down. A red thread had slipped from the cut in their palm and darkened the flagging between their boots. They had not felt themselves open the wound. Their body had learned to obey grievance before thought.
Ossric Ashgrove crouched beside the stain with a ledger balanced on one knee. He was a quartermaster, born in 333 AS, and every inch of him seemed made for measuring what remained after other people had taken too much. He dipped a rag into a bucket and scrubbed the stone.
“You count stains now?” Isolde asked.
“I count everything that might be blamed on me.”
“Then you are a better servant than most.”
Ossric’s fingers paused. His temperament was not recorded in any ledger Isolde had seen, but caution had a texture. It lived in the way he kept his eyes lowered, in the careful silence between each breath.
“The Warden-Commander is waiting,” he said.
“Which one?”
Ossric’s hand tightened around the rag.
There was only one Warden-Commander in Fenspire, but titles were doors, and Isolde had spent too long learning which doors were trapped.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” Ossric said.
The name moved through the covered walk like a draught from a crypt.
Ignatz had been born in 258 AS. He wore command as though it were a cloak inherited from a dead man, broad enough to hide whatever was underneath. His intelligence passed into the Iron-Ring Cartel by secret channels, though the Cartel’s agents never called it selling. They called it accounting. They called every betrayal a balance restored.
Isolde turned from the parapet.
“Did he say why?”
“He said only that the matter concerned Blackport.”
“Then it concerns a corpse.”
Ossric glanced toward the rain. “The Purge of Blackport ended with seventy thousand—”
“70,907.”
The quartermaster swallowed.
“70,907 casualties,” Isolde said. “You need not soften the number for me.”
“I had not meant to.”
“No. You meant to survive saying it.”
He looked at them then, and his eyes held the flat, sleepless terror of a man who had learned that truth was not protection. Isolde understood that terror. They carried a different kind. Their own was sharpened, banked, made useful.
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. The aggressors were totally routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Those facts had been carved into proclamations, repeated in sanctuaries, stamped upon ration chits and military dispatches until the words had worn smooth. But beneath them lay the concealed truth: the victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Isolde had tasted that truth once, in the bitterness of a report burned at the edges.
“Is the Arch-Prelate here?” they asked.
Ossric resumed scrubbing. “Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched arrived before dusk.”
“Of course they did.”
“Arch-Prelate Malchior said the meeting required witnesses.”
“Malchior says many things.”
“Those are dangerous words.”
“So is Malchior.”
The bell sounded again. Its cracked note trembled in the rain.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched had been born in 289 AS and served as Arch-Prelate with the rigid grace of someone balancing a crown upon a blade. Their lineage was displayed in every robe, seal, and prayer: ancestral ink, sanctified blood, a chain of names reaching backward into the ruin. Isolde knew the papers were forged. The knowledge had come to them folded inside a dead courier’s coat, though the courier’s name was not worth remembering.
Malchior’s authority was holy only so long as no one held it to the light.
“Go on,” Isolde said.
Ossric stood. He was younger than the walls, younger than most of the fear inside them, and yet the damp had already settled into his shoulders.
“The Warden-Commander is in the old tally chamber.”
“Did he bring soldiers?”
“Fenspire is garrisoned.”
“That was not my question.”
Ossric’s mouth thinned. “Yes.”
“Then he brought witnesses after all.”
They walked.
The old tally chamber occupied the lower spine of the tower, where the air smelled of iron, lamp oil, and the mineral damp of the Reach. Narrow windows slit the walls but admitted no view. Fenspire had been built to see without being seen. Its defenders kept their eyes on roads, marshes, and the pale distance toward the coast. Its secrets remained underground.
Two soldiers barred the chamber door. Their faces were hidden behind half-masks, and their hands rested near their weapons.
Isolde stopped before them.
“Do you know who I am?”
Neither answered.
“Good.”
The door opened from within.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood at the far end of the chamber, beneath a map pierced with black pins. No canonical feature marked him; authority had left no portrait in the records, only the title Warden-Commander and the epithet the Oathless. Isolde found the absence fitting. A man who sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel had no need of a face. A shadow could be purchased more cheaply.
Malchior stood beside the table in flame-colored vestments darkened by rain. Their hand rested upon a bundle of papers bound with red cord.
“You are late,” Ignatz said.
“I was washing blood from the floor.”
“Yours?”
“Does it matter?”
“To a quartermaster, perhaps.”
Ossric remained outside. The door closed between them with a damp wooden groan.
Malchior’s gaze settled upon Isolde’s palm. “You make a sacrament of injury.”
“You make a sacrament of paper.”
The Arch-Prelate’s expression did not move. Only the fingers upon the cord betrayed them, pressing hard enough to blanch.
Ignatz turned to the map. “Gloamreach has sent no confirmation.”
“It is quarantined,” Isolde said. “That is the meaning of the word.”
“It has a garrison of 2,483.”
“And still the dead may outnumber the living.”
“No one has said there are dead.”
“Then why is the coast silent?”
The Warden-Commander touched one of the black pins. It marked the Pale Coast, though the mapmaker had rendered the shore as a thin white scar.
“Because silence is cheaper than defense.”
“Spoken like a man who has sold both.”
The chamber tightened.
Malchior looked from one to the other. “We are not here to trade accusations.”
“No,” Isolde said. “We are here to decide which accusation will be made official.”
Ignatz’s hand remained upon the pin. “The Iron-Ring Cartel has requested an accounting of the Blackport routes.”
“They requested intelligence,” Isolde said.
“They requested an accounting.”
“And you intend to provide it.”
His head tilted slightly. “You speak with confidence.”
“I speak with memory.”
The rain struck the narrow windows. In the black glass, Isolde saw a blurred reflection: the pale planes of an Unforgiven Blood-Mage, the red at their palm, the dangerous stillness of grievance held beneath the skin. They had plotted the death of their own liege. The thought rose without remorse, not because remorse was absent, but because it had been burned away and replaced by something more durable.
No one in the chamber knew the shape of that plot.
Malchior knew many secrets, but not that one.
Perhaps.
“The Purge of Blackport was a victory,” Malchior said. “The aggressors were routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor. That is the record.”
“The record is a grave with the lid nailed shut.”
