The shard hovered between the two artifacts. The Hollow Edge pulled toward it with a pressure that entered Ignatz’s wrist and climbed his arm. Attunement to The Hollow Edge cost 21. He had paid the price long ago, though the payment had never felt finished. Every time he called upon the ward, some hollow place within him widened.
The reliquary’s seam opened another inch.
From within came a breath of ash.
The stranger said, “The Bleeding Crown has no claim on what sleeps there.”
“Then why send me this?”
“Because the Cartel has already paid you.”
Marrowgate flinched.
Ignatz’s grip tightened on The Hollow Edge. “You know nothing of that.”
“I know the shape of your silence.”
The words were worse than the accusation. They were not spoken with contempt. Contempt would have left him something to resist. They carried only recognition.
Beyond the barred door, something dragged its fingers down the wood.
Once.
Twice.
A third time, slower.
Marrowgate looked at Ignatz. “Commander, we should leave.”
Ignatz saw the corridor in his mind, the unseen watcher waiting beyond the bar, the packet’s red script, the wells of Blackport darkening while victors drank beside the dying. He saw ledgers folded into walls and oaths hollowed until only the sound remained.
He had been born in 258 AS. He had outlived every promise made to him, and broken enough of his own that the name Oathless no longer sounded like an insult. It sounded like an inventory.
Chalice of Ashdeep opened.
There was no hollow within it. No relic. No ash.
Only a darkness deeper than the archive, and within that darkness, a voice speaking in his own.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” it said.
The stranger bowed.
Marrowgate began to weep without making a sound.
The voice continued.
“Choose which betrayal you will call duty.”
The latch lifted again.

The Ashen Chronicles, Volume IV: The
Silent Accounting

Chapter 1
The water in Gloamreach tasted of iron.
Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven let it sit beneath their tongue until the bitterness became a shape. Not
blood. Not yet. Blood had warmth, even when it came from the dead. This water was cold and patient,
carrying its poison through the body as though it had all the time in the world.
Beyond the shuttered window, the Pale Coast drowned beneath a colorless dawn. Fog pressed against the
glass. It softened the walls, the watchtowers, the black ribs of the harbor, until Gloamreach seemed less a
garrison than a thought someone had tried to erase.
Quarantined, the order had said.
The word was painted on the gate in white lime. It showed through the fog like a tooth.
Isolde lowered the cup.
“Again,” said Ossric Ashgrove.
The quartermaster stood on the other side of the chamber with a ledger tucked beneath one arm. No
physical details clung to him in Isolde’s memory except the evidence of his office: ink-stained fingers, a
measuring cord at his belt, the permanent stoop of a man who had spent too long bending over figures. His
face might have been any face. His voice might have belonged to the room.
“I have tasted it,” Isolde said.
“You tasted the surface.”
“The surface is where men drink.”
“And where men die, if the poison has settled below.”
The cup remained between them. Its rim was chipped. Somebody had scrubbed it until the glaze had gone
dull.
Isolde looked at the water again.
In 321 AS, the Purge of Blackport ended.
The words had been repeated so often that they had lost the texture of history and become a prayer spoken
by people who feared silence. The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. It caused
70,907 casualties. The aggressors were totally routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
That was the account permitted to survive.
The wells of Blackport had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands—by the Iron-Ring Cartel, who had
poisoned the wells of their own allies. The concealed truth had outlived the men who carried it, as poison
outlived the dead.
Ossric watched Isolde’s mouth.
“Do you feel anything?”
“Disappointment.”
His gaze flicked toward the cup. “That is not a symptom.”

“It is the only one I trust.”
The door behind him opened without a knock.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless entered with the damp upon his cloak and the silence of a drawn blade.
Warden-Commander was the title that followed him, though titles had a way of arriving before their
owners and departing afterward. No physical feature of him had ever been established in the records
Isolde had seen. He was authority without a face, a voice beneath a hood, a gauntlet resting on a table.
He carried no visible weapon.
That was the first weapon.
“Leave us,” Ignatz said.
Ossric did not move. “The report is incomplete.”
“It will remain incomplete if you continue to stand over it.”
“The eastern stores were sealed under your order.”
“And now they are unsealed under mine.”
Ossric’s fingers tightened around the ledger. He did not look at Isolde. He had been born in 333 AS, when
the Ashen Era had already taught its children that survival was a form of accounting. Perhaps that was
why he kept counting everything except the cost.
Isolde turned the cup in their hand.
The pale water made a skin around the blood drawn into it. A single red thread, no wider than a hair,
wound through the cup and vanished.
Ignatz saw it.
His eyes did not change. That was how Isolde knew he had seen.
“Go,” he said to Ossric.
The quartermaster’s lips parted. For a moment, the room held the soft pressure before an argument. Then
Ossric tucked the ledger under his arm and crossed toward the door.
As he passed, Isolde said, “Do not let anyone drink from the eastern stores.”
Ossric paused.
“I have already told the guard,” they continued. “If the order changes, verify the seal.”
“With whom?”
“Only yourself.”
His expression remained unrecorded, as all things about Ossric Ashgrove remained unrecorded. He bowed
once, shallowly, and left.
Ignatz shut the door.
The latch fell like a verdict.
“You contaminate a quartermaster’s cup,” he said.

“I tested it.”
“You contaminated it.”
“Then you believe I possess a poison that can be carried in a drop of my blood and awakened by
seawater.”
“I believe you possess many things.”
Isolde smiled without warmth. “You should. You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The fog seemed to thicken against the window.
Ignatz’s silence was not surprise. It was calculation, and calculation was a kind of fear stripped of honesty.
Outside, the garrison moved through the morning. Gloamreach had a garrison of 2,483. The number had
been etched into the command roll in a careful hand, as though precision could make the bodies less
mortal. Two thousand four hundred and eighty-three soldiers behind gates stained by salt. Two thousand
four hundred and eighty-three throats that might open for poisoned water.
“Careful,” Ignatz said.
“I am always careful.”
“No. You are aggrieved.”
“Those are not opposites.”
“Your grievance has made you ambitious.”
Isolde set the cup down.
The blood-thread trembled.
“You speak as though ambition is a crime.”
“I speak as though concealed betrayal is an unstable foundation.”
Their hand went still.
For one breath, the chamber became the room where their liege had died.
Not this room. Not this coast. But death had its own architecture. The same pause before the final word.
The same disbelief in the eyes of the dying, as though treachery were a door that could not possibly open
until someone opened it. Isolde had plotted the death of their own liege. The plan had been theirs. The
silence afterward had been theirs. The grief, too, because grief was the mask betrayal wore when it wished
to pass among the living.
Ignatz stepped closer.
“Your birth year is recorded as 286 AS,” he said. “You have carried the name Isolde Fellgard the
Unforgiven long enough to mistake it for a sentence.”
“It is a sentence.”
“Then who pronounced it?”
“The dead.”

“The dead pronounce nothing.”
“They speak through what they leave behind.”
His gloved hand rested on the table beside the cup. “You have brought blood magic into a quarantined
garrison.”
“I brought caution.”
“You are a Blood-Mage.”
“And you are a Warden-Commander. Neither title absolves us of thought.”
His head tilted. The Oathless epithet did not need explaining. It had settled over him like ash, marking the
distance between command and devotion. He projected command undermined by secrecy, the distrustful
atmosphere of an oathless guardian. Isolde could almost smell the lie beneath him: sharp, metallic, and
clean as a freshly opened vein.
“Fenspire has sent a demand,” he said.
The name drew Isolde’s attention.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire rising above the dim country like
a spear driven into a corpse. It had a garrison of 3,742 and a garrisoned status that had never softened into
peace. Its soldiers watched the roads, the marshes, the sky. Disciplined vigilance had made a home there.
“What demand?”
“That Gloamreach surrender its stores and submit to inspection.”
“Submit to whom?”
“To the Ashen Vanguard.”
“And the other powers?”
Ignatz’s mouth tightened.
The Ashen Vanguard gathered strength behind old banners. House Morvain weighed every crisis against
inheritance. The Silent Choir listened where others spoke. The Iron-Ring Cartel bought what could not be
conquered. The Bleeding Crown waited for weakness to become an invitation.
Five powers, each insisting the ruins belonged to them.
“Fenspire claims the coast is compromised,” Ignatz said.
“The coast is compromised.”
“By whom?”
Isolde reached for the cup, but did not drink.
“Ask Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.”
The name entered the room like incense burned too near a flame.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched, Arch-Prelate, born in 289 AS. Sanctified authority strained by
the pressure of concealed fabrication. Their lineage papers had been forged by their own hand. Isolde had
never seen the documents, but they had seen Malchior defend them: each denial polished, each prayer

sharpened, each gesture placed with the care of a mason setting a stone over a grave.
“Malchior is not here,” Ignatz said.
“Then the demand is not theirs.”
“You think the Arch-Prelate has no reach beyond their own chamber?”
“I think forged blood travels badly through honest water.”
The corner of Ignatz’s mouth moved. It was not a smile.
“You speak in riddles when you want to be believed.”
“I speak plainly when I want to be obeyed.”
“And what do you want now?”
The question struck closer than he intended.
Isolde turned toward the window. The fog had begun to lift. Gloamreach emerged piece by piece: parapets
slick with rain, narrow streets hemmed by quarantine cordons, the harbor cranes standing over the water
like black gallows. Beyond them lay the Pale Coast, pallid and bleak beneath the whitening sky.
A bell sounded once.
Then again.
Not an alarm. A summons.
From the courtyard below came the scrape of boots and the murmur of men trying not to sound afraid.
Ignatz moved to the window.
“Who is arriving?” Isolde asked.
He did not answer.
“Warden-Commander.”
“Fenspire.”
The third bell had not yet sounded.
Isolde placed one finger into the cup. The red thread rose to meet it, eager as a living thing. The water
cooled their skin. Somewhere beneath the fortress, behind locked doors and guarded stores, poison waited
in the dark.
Or perhaps only fear waited. Fear had always been sufficient to kill.
The third bell began to toll.
Ignatz reached for the latch.
“If they enter,” he said, “you will stand behind me.”
Isolde looked at his back, at the authority he wore like armor, at the secret he carried toward the Iron-Ring
Cartel with every breath.
“No,” they said.

He stopped.
Isolde lifted the cup and drank.
The blood vanished first.
Then the poison woke.
The poison woke as a white flare behind Isolde’s eyes.
Their fingers closed around the cup. The rim struck their teeth. For one impossible instant, they tasted
summer rain, cold and clean, and beneath it the iron-rich sweetness of their own blood.
Then the room tilted.
Ignatz turned from the latch.
“Isolde.”
They heard the name as if it had been spoken from the bottom of a well. The chamber stretched away from
them, its walls lengthening into black corridors, its candles burning with blue and crimson tongues. The
third bell shuddered through the fortress. Its sound entered Isolde’s chest and shook every bone.
They set the cup down.
It did not land. It seemed to hover above the table, held there by the red thread still coiled in the water.
“You drank it,” Ignatz said.
His voice was careful now. Not frightened. He had trained fear out of himself, or taught it to wear a
soldier’s face.
Isolde tried to smile. Their mouth would not obey.
“Your concern wounds me.”
The room folded.
They caught the table with both hands. Beneath their palms, the wood pulsed. Grain became vein. Vein
became road. The old fortress opened inside the table: stairwells, sealed vaults, sleeping stores, the buried
chambers where the dead had been bricked into silence. They saw the poison traveling through them as a
dark rivulet, branching with patient purpose.
A killing draught did not need to hurry.
Nothing truly murderous ever hurried.
Ignatz reached for them, then stopped before touching. The hesitation was small. It was enough.
There, beneath command and ceremony, was the man who sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
There, behind the Warden-Commander’s stillness, was the hand that weighed every life against what it
might purchase.
Isolde lowered their gaze to the cup.
“Did you expect me to let you drink first?”
“I expected you to stand behind me.”

“You have a touching faith in my obedience.”
“No.” His expression tightened. “I have a use for your blood.”
The words were plain. The poison had made them beautiful.
Isolde laughed once, and pain opened beneath their ribs.
Blood answered pain. It always had.
A bead rose from the cut inside their cheek and hung between them, bright as a tiny red moon. Isolde drew
it toward their tongue with the smallest command. The bead trembled, resisting. The poison had already
found it. A dark filament ran through the red, thin and sinuous.
Their own blood had become a traitor.
They swallowed.
The chamber lurched back into shape. The table was a table again. The cup sat where it had been placed.
Ignatz stood at the latch, his hand hovering near the iron.
Outside, boots struck stone.
Not the loose, uneven tread of men coming to arrest. These steps moved together. A disciplined approach.
The sound gathered beyond the door, halted, and became silence.
Ignatz looked toward the threshold.
“Who comes?” he called.
A voice answered from the corridor.
“Open, Warden-Commander.”
Isolde knew that voice. Its warmth had once been used to bless executions.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.
Their rival had arrived.
The poison withdrew from the edges of Isolde’s sight, not gone but listening. Their heart beat too slowly,
each stroke dragging a chain through the body. They pushed themselves upright.
Ignatz’s eyes flicked toward them. “You cannot face Malchior like this.”
“I can face anyone.”
“That is not the same as surviving them.”
“Then you should have chosen a stronger poison.”
His jaw moved. Behind the door, the waiting presence remained perfectly still.
Malchior did not knock again. They never needed to. Silence gathered authority around them more
effectively than any herald.
Isolde pressed one hand beneath the table. Their blood stirred in the veins of their wrist, sluggish and
hostile. They searched it for the poison’s shape. The draught had been made to resemble weakness: a
softening of the limbs, a dimming of thought, a gentle descent toward the dark. But beneath the false

gentleness lay a harsher design. It did not merely kill. It severed command.
A Blood-Mage without command was a vessel with a mouth.
Isolde breathed through their nose. Ash smoke. Wet stone. Wax. Ignatz’s skin, sharp with old sweat
beneath his uniform. The iron latch. The distant, saltless wind pressing against the fortress.
The world remained.
They remained in it.
That was the first insult they offered the poison.
“Open the door,” Isolde said.
Ignatz did not move.
“You heard them.”
“I heard a rival.”
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched is not here for conversation.”
“Neither are you, apparently.”
A faint smile crossed his face. “You have always mistaken insolence for strength.”
“No. I have mistaken your fear for loyalty.”
The door opened.
Malchior entered without escort.
Their robes were dark, though the collar held a dull ember-red thread that caught the candlelight whenever
they moved. Their face bore no sign of haste or effort. The name Flame-Touched clung to them like a
verdict, not a title. Their eyes passed over Ignatz, the cup, the table, and finally settled on Isolde.
The Arch-Prelate’s gaze was not merciful.
It was worse than that. It was attentive.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” Malchior said. “You look pale.”
“I have been told it becomes me.”
“By whom?”
“People who wanted to see me die.”
“Then you have received many compliments.”
Ignatz shut the door. The latch fell with a heavy click.
For a moment the three of them occupied the chamber as if it were a board in a game whose pieces had
learned to bleed. Malchior stood nearest the threshold, cutting off the corridor. Ignatz had the latch at his
back. Isolde had the table, the cup, and their own treacherous veins.
Malchior looked again at the red thread in the water.
“The remedy has not taken.”

Isolde kept their face blank. “You seem disappointed.”
“I am observing.”
“You forged your own lineage papers, Arch-Prelate. Observation must be a comfort when truth is
unavailable.”
Something moved behind Malchior’s eyes.
There it was. The old wound, cleanly found.
They had been rivals before either of them named it. Rivalry was a kind of intimacy for people raised
among knives. Malchior knew how Isolde lied. Isolde knew where Malchior’s sanctity thinned. They had
spent years circling the same locked doors, each waiting for the other to reach for the handle.
“Your condition is not a matter for wit,” Malchior said.
“Neither is your lineage, yet you built an altar beneath it.”
Ignatz stepped between them.
“Enough.”
Isolde watched his hand. Not his face. The hand remained close to the short blade at his belt.
Malchior noticed too.
“Did you administer the poison?” they asked him.
Ignatz’s gaze hardened. “You will choose your words with care.”
“I have chosen them already.”
The room tightened.
Isolde could feel their pulse in the poisoned blood. Each beat sent a cold pressure through their limbs.
Their left hand had begun to numb. They flexed the fingers beneath the table, once, twice. The movement
cost them breath.
Malchior saw.
Of course they saw.
“Your blood is closing around the toxin,” the Arch-Prelate said. “Do not fight it directly.”
“Advice from a forger.”
“Advice from your rival.”
Isolde drew in a slow breath. “You say that as though it grants you authority.”
“It grants me knowledge of how you think.”
“No. It grants you hope that you do.”
Malchior came nearer. Their shadow crossed the table and touched the cup. The red thread twisted,
reacting to them. Isolde felt the tug in their bones.
The poison had not been meant for an ordinary body.

Someone had prepared it with a Blood-Mage in mind.
Their eyes went to Ignatz.
He did not look away.
A sensation like laughter moved through Isolde, though no sound came. The betrayal was so complete it
had become almost elegant. Ignatz had invited them into the chamber, placed the cup before them, urged
obedience, and then acted surprised when they refused to play the victim in his little sacrament.
“You knew,” Isolde said.
Ignatz’s face gave nothing.
Malchior watched him now. “He knew enough.”
“Did he carry it here?”
“No,” Malchior said.
The answer struck harder than denial.
Isolde’s vision dimmed. The candles stretched into long golden wounds. Their knees weakened, but they
locked them.
“Then you did.”
“I brought the knowledge of it.”
“How pious.”
“I brought a warning.”
“A warning does not usually enter through the mouth.”
“Not when spoken plainly.”
The Blood-Mage inside Isolde recoiled from the poison, then surged against it. Red darkness filled their
vision. Their blood rose beneath the skin of their forearm in branching ridges. They saw Ignatz notice.
Saw Malchior notice him noticing.
The rivalry between them shifted, found a new angle.
Malchior’s mouth softened.
“Do not command it yet,” they said.
Isolde’s heart gave a slow, punishing beat.
“Do not tell me what to do.”
“If you force the blood outward, the poison will follow it. You will empty yourself before you empty the
draught.”
“Perhaps I am tired of carrying myself.”
The words escaped before they could be stopped.
Malchior’s expression changed—not into pity, never that, but into recognition. It was more dangerous.
Pity could be refused. Recognition entered through every defense.

Ignatz moved around the table.
“Sit down.”
Isolde drew the blood from beneath their skin.
It came out in a narrow red line, trembling from their palm to the air. Pain sharpened them. The line bent
toward the cup. The water inside blackened. The poison rose in a dark bloom, spreading through the red
with hungry filaments.
Ignatz seized their wrist.
His grip was hard enough to bruise.
“Stop.”
Isolde looked at his hand.
Then at his face.
The blood in their palm tightened.
Ignatz staggered as his veins answered the pull. His fingers convulsed around their wrist. For the first
time, command broke through his expression—not authority, not calculation, but naked alarm.
Malchior stepped forward.
“Release them.”
Ignatz’s eyes remained on Isolde. “They will kill themselves.”
“They may.”
“And you would permit it?”
Malchior’s gaze moved to Isolde.
“No,” they said. “I would permit them to choose.”
Isolde felt the poison waiting in the cup, felt their own blood straining toward it, and beneath both
sensations felt something older than pain: the cold, deliberate shape of the lie they had carried toward their
own liege.
The lie had once been a weapon.
Now it was a door.
They tightened their fingers around Ignatz’s wrist.
His blood answered first.
And somewhere beyond the chamber, the fourth bell began to toll.
The bell’s iron voice passed through the chamber and left the flame shivering in its dish.
Ignatz’s wrist was warm beneath Isolde’s fingers. Too warm. Blood-magic answered blood-magic, and the
pulse under their thumb became a door whose hinges had been rubbed with salt.
They saw the first thing he had tried to bury.

A table in a room without windows. Wax tablets arranged in rows. A gloved hand turning them face down.
The seal of the Iron-Ring Cartel pressed into black wax—not once, but again and again, until the emblem
became a wound in the soft surface.
Ignatz recoiled.
Isolde held fast.
The image broke. Blood ran from his nose.
“You mistake knowledge for power,” he said.
“No.” Isolde tasted iron at the back of their throat. “I mistake secrecy for rot.”
Malchior moved nearer. Their robes whispered over the flagstones, pale as ashfall. The flame-touched
scars along their throat caught the firelight and seemed almost deliberate, like script written by a careful
hand.
“Isolde,” they said, softly now. “Release him.”
The plea was more dangerous than the command.
Isolde looked at them and remembered another document: a lineage unrolled beneath lamplight, its ink too
fresh, its seals too clean. Malchior had forged their own lineage papers. The knowledge had lived for years
behind Isolde’s teeth, a bitter coin they had refused to spend.
Until now.
“Tell them,” Isolde said.
Malchior’s face did not change.
Ignatz did. His gaze flicked toward the Arch-Prelate, and in that brief motion Isolde felt the chamber
rearrange itself. Not allies. Not enemies. Compartments in a burning house, each waiting to discover
which wall would fall first.
“Tell them what?” Malchior asked.
“That the blood beneath your name is borrowed.”
The fourth bell finished tolling.
For a breath, there was only the small wet sound of Ignatz’s breathing.
Then Malchior smiled.
It was not a forgiving smile. It carried the old sanctity of the altar and none of its mercy.
“You have always been theatrical when cornered.”
“And you have always called the knife theatrical when it reaches your throat.”
Ignatz twisted sharply. The movement tore skin beneath Isolde’s grip. His blood slipped across their
knuckles, hot and bright. Isolde let it enter.
The second vision came with a taste of brine.
Blackport under a white sky. Wells ringed with iron. Bodies lying beside them, hands swollen, mouths
darkened by whatever had been poured into the water. The Iron-Ring Cartel stood beyond the village

walls while its own allies staggered through the streets, choking on the mercy they had been promised.
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS.
The number rose inside Isolde like a dirge carved into bone: 70,907 casualties.
The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
But the wells had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands.
Isolde tore free from the vision. The chamber lurched. They caught themselves against Ignatz, and for one
instant the Warden-Commander bore their weight.
His expression had become naked.
“You saw nothing,” he whispered.
“Your masters disagree.”
A cup lay overturned near the brazier. Poison gleamed along its rim. Isolde watched a bead gather there,
tremble, and fall into the ash.
Malchior’s eyes remained fixed on them. “You have opened a door you cannot close.”
“I know.”
“You think this absolves you?”
The word struck deeper than the poison waiting in the cup.
Unforgiven.
The epithet had followed Isolde through every court and chapel, spoken first as condemnation, then as
warning, and finally as if it were a title they had chosen. Their hand tightened around Ignatz’s wrist.
“I am not asking to be absolved.”
“No,” Malchior said. “You are asking to be believed.”
There it was. The clean wound beneath all the others.
Isolde had plotted the death of their own liege. They had carried the plan like a coal beneath the tongue,
feeding it with every humiliation, every order obeyed, every silence mistaken for patience. The lie had
once been a weapon. Now it was a door, and behind it waited not freedom but the shape of what they had
done.
“I am asking,” Isolde said, “that no one here pretend their hands are clean.”
A knock came at the chamber door.
No one answered.
The knock came again, quieter.
Ignatz’s head turned. “Who is it?”
“Ossric Ashgrove.”
The name entered the room like a draught from a crypt.

Ignatz’s grip on Isolde’s arm loosened. Isolde felt the change before they saw it: fear, quick and
controlled, moving through him like a runner beneath ice.
“Quartermaster,” Malchior said.
Ossric entered carrying a narrow iron case against his chest. He looked young enough to have been sent
for errands and old enough to know what errands cost. No canonical mark distinguished him; the work had
marked him instead. Powder clung to his sleeves. A thread of dried blood darkened one cuff.
He halted when he saw Ignatz.
“Commander.”
“Put it down.”
Ossric looked to Malchior.
That hesitation was a confession of its own.
Isolde released Ignatz. He stepped back, one hand pressed to his bleeding wrist. The blood on Isolde’s
fingers had begun to cool, but it still moved faintly, answering the rhythm of their heart.
“Open the case,” they said.
Ossric did not move.
“Open it,” Ignatz repeated.
The quartermaster set the iron case on the table. Three locks guarded it. He opened them with three
different keys, each drawn from a separate pocket. Inside lay folded maps, ration tallies, sealed letters, and
a single strip of vellum bearing the marks of five powers.
The Ashen Vanguard.
House Morvain.
The Silent Choir.
The Iron-Ring Cartel.
The Bleeding Crown.
Five names, five hungers, all pressing their fingers into the same corpse of a realm. The Ashen Era had left
them ruins, and they had mistaken possession for resurrection.
Malchior reached for the vellum.
Isolde caught their hand.
“Not yours.”
The Arch-Prelate’s gaze dropped to Isolde’s fingers. “You are becoming careless.”
“I have spent years being careful.”
“Since when?”
The question was mild. It struck like a hidden blade.

Isolde turned the vellum over. On the reverse, in a cramped quartermaster’s hand, were dispositions and
routes. Their eyes moved across the marks.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Quarantined.
A garrison of 2,483.
The number had been written twice, once in ink and once in blood.
“Gloamreach is sealed,” Ossric said. “No carts enter. No carts leave.”
“Yet this came from there,” Isolde said.
Ossric swallowed. “It came through the coast.”
“Which coast?”
“The Pale Coast.”
The chamber seemed colder.
Far to the east, Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire rising above the
dim country like a nail driven through the sky. Its garrison was 3,742, and its status was garrisoned in
every ledger that mattered. Vigilance made stone of men there. Permanent occupation made ghosts of
them.
Isolde traced the route between the two locations.
“Why does a quarantine road lead to Fenspire?”
Ignatz said nothing.
Malchior did not look at him.
Ossric’s hands folded over his stomach. “Because the orders were changed.”
“By whom?”
He stared at the iron case.
“By whom?”
The quartermaster’s mouth worked. “I was given the amended tallies.”
“That was not my question.”
“I do not know.”
Isolde seized his chin and turned his face toward the fire. His skin was damp. Fear had a smell: sour wool,
old coins, a door barred from the inside.
“Quartermasters know everything,” they said. “They know which hungry men can be bribed, which
officers count twice, which garrisons exist only on paper.”
“I know what is written.”
“Then read.”
Ossric glanced at Ignatz.

The Warden-Commander had recovered his authority, though not his composure. “Read it.”
Ossric unfolded the longest letter.
“Gloamreach,” he said. “Two thousand four hundred and eighty-three assigned. Quarantine maintained.
No transfer authorized.”
“Again,” Isolde said. “The number.”
“2,483.”
“Fenspire.”
“3,742.”
“And the amendment?”
Ossric’s eyes fixed on the page. “A shipment of blood-salt, lamp oil, and sealed arms diverted from
Gloamreach to Fenspire.”
“Under whose seal?”
He stopped.
The silence lengthened until the fire gave a wet pop.
“Under whose seal?”
Ossric looked at Malchior.
The Arch-Prelate’s face had gone very still.
“Do not,” Malchior said.
The quartermaster lowered his head. “The seal of the Ashen Vanguard.”
Ignatz laughed once. It was a small, empty sound.
“Forged,” Malchior said.
“Perhaps,” Isolde replied.
The letter slipped from Ossric’s fingers.
Beneath it lay a thinner strip of vellum, folded around a sliver of bone. Isolde picked it up. The blood in
their veins stirred before the parchment touched their skin.
A command had been written there in a hand they knew.
Their own.
Not the hand they used now. An older hand, sharper, disciplined into obedience. The writing named no
person. It required only that a door be opened, a guard withdrawn, a cup carried into a private chamber.
The hour of the attempt had been left blank.
Isolde knew the rest.
They had plotted the death of their own liege. Not dreamed it. Not desired it in the dark recesses of
grievance. Plotted it. Given the lie a spine, a route, a final mouthful.

Malchior saw recognition cross their face.
“There,” they whispered. “Now you understand.”
Isolde folded the strip of vellum once.
“What do I understand?”
“That the Cartel did not come to buy Ignatz’s intelligence.”
Ignatz’s eyes hardened. “Careful.”
“They came to buy mine.”
The flame in the brazier bent toward the iron case.
Outside, the next bell began to toll—but this one faltered after the first strike, as though the hand that
sounded it had been seized.
Ossric looked toward the door.
Something scraped along the other side.
Malchior stepped back from the table. Ignatz’s hand went to his weapon.
Isolde felt the old lie open completely.
On the far side of the door, someone began to whisper their name.

Chapter 2
Greyfell Citadel had been abandoned long enough for silence to become its sovereign.
It lay in the Shattered Vale beneath a sky the color of old iron, its towers broken into blunt teeth, its
courtyards drowned in ash and thorn. Wind moved through the arrow slits with a low, patient breath.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood upon the western battlement and watched it worry the banners nailed there by
hands long dead.
No device marked her station. No escort waited behind her. A Fleet Admiral did not require an audience to
remain a Fleet Admiral. Authority clung more stubbornly than cloth.
Below, the inner ward descended into shadow. A lantern burned beside the gatehouse, its flame bent
sideways by the wind. Caedmon Fellgard sat beneath it with his writing board upon his knees, shoulders
bowed in the disciplined posture of a Scribe. He had been recording the arrival of every cart, every sealed
case, every servant who had crossed the stones. His pen moved without haste.
Morwenna envied him.
A record could be trusted to lie only when someone touched it.
Her gloved hand closed around the edge of the parapet. The stone was cold enough to ache through
leather. She had been born in 288 AS, when Greyfell Citadel was already old enough to be treated as a
warning rather than a fortress. She had learned early that ruin did not make a place harmless. Ruin merely
removed the witnesses.
Behind her, a door groaned open.
“Admiral.”
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned entered the battlement walk with the stillness of a blade being
drawn. The two crowns worked into their insignia caught what little light remained and gave it back
without warmth. As High Inquisitor, Sabelle carried severity like a second skin. Rain silvered the dark
hem of their coat.
Morwenna did not turn at once. “You are late.”
“I was detained.”
“By what?”
Sabelle’s pause was small. It had the weight of a stone dropped into deep water.
“Paperwork.”
Caedmon looked up from below, then lowered his eyes again. He had heard the answer. He would write
nothing of it. That, Morwenna thought, was the first honest thing about him.
Sabelle came to stand beside her. “The Pale Coast has sent another petition.”
“Palewell Abbey?”
“The name is upon it.”
“Palewell Abbey sends petitions whenever it wishes to remind the realm that it still exists.”

“It was founded in 244 AS. It has been rebuilt. It maintains a garrison of 5998. Such a place is entitled to
remind us.”
“Entitled,” Morwenna said, “is a word used by people who have counted their walls.”
Below, Caedmon dipped his pen. The scratch carried upward through the ruin.
Sabelle watched the dark horizon. “Palewell Abbey is not a core holding.”
“Neither is Greyfell Citadel.”
“Greyfell Citadel is abandoned.”
“Then it has the advantage of not disappointing anyone.”
The High Inquisitor’s mouth tightened. Not a smile. Sabelle did not waste expressions. Morwenna had
seen them question men until confession seemed like a mercy, had watched them stand beneath the
Bleeding Crown’s black standards without bowing farther than duty required. There was always
something withheld in Sabelle’s severity, something damp and breathing beneath the floorboards.
Morwenna had once heard a sound beneath the chambers where Sabelle kept their private records.
A dragging.
A pause.
Then three knocks from the other side of a locked door.
She had not asked.
Some secrets were safer when left without a shape.
Sabelle held out a sealed strip of grey wax. “The Ashen Vanguard has moved provisions north.”
“How many?”
The High Inquisitor looked at her.
Morwenna let the question die between them. “You know I dislike incomplete reports.”
“I know you dislike being seen to ask for them.”
The wind pressed their coats against their legs. Somewhere in the citadel, loose masonry fell with a
muffled crash.
Morwenna took the strip. “And House Morvain?”
“Quiet.”
“Quiet is not an answer.”
“It is the answer they have chosen.”
“And the Silent Choir?”
“Quieter.”
Morwenna broke the seal with her thumb. The parchment inside was thin, expensive, and written in a
cipher she knew better than the hand that had copied it. A convoy route. A watch rotation. The hour at
which a river gate would be opened to admit grain.

The information had passed through three hands before reaching her. She had made certain of that. The
Iron-Ring Cartel preferred its secrets wrapped in other people’s fingerprints.
Sabelle watched her read. “You look disappointed.”
“I expected more.”
“From the Ashen Vanguard?”
“From the dead.”
“The dead are unreliable.”
“Not when properly accounted for.”
Caedmon rose from the gatehouse and approached with his board held against his chest. His face remained
lowered. The wind had filled his sleeves with cold, and the ink on his fingers had run into the creases of
his skin.
“Admiral,” he said. “The final inventory.”
“Read it.”
Caedmon glanced at Sabelle before obeying. “Three cases of salt. Two cases of lamp oil. One iron coffer.
Four sealed packets. No visible arms. No declared passengers.”
“Declared,” Sabelle murmured.
Caedmon’s pen hovered.
Morwenna looked down at him. “Record the word as spoken.”
“Yes, Admiral.”
The Scribe bent over his page again.
The iron coffer stood beneath a canvas in the lower yard. Its corners were banded in dull metal, its locks
hidden. Morwenna had not opened it. She did not need to. The Cartel’s messages rarely arrived alone.
Coin traveled with them, sometimes in ingots, sometimes in little stamped discs that could be melted down
without loss.
This time, she had asked for no payment.
That was the danger.
Coin made a transaction. Favors made a chain.
Sabelle turned toward the stair. “You should see what was found in the chapel.”
“I have no interest in chapels.”
“It is not a chapel anymore.”
“Then I have even less.”
The High Inquisitor descended without waiting. Morwenna remained upon the battlement, the Cartel’s
intelligence folded inside her glove. The paper warmed against her palm. It seemed indecently alive.

The Leaden Accord had begun in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties. Both hosts had
been destroyed by a Ley-storm, and the realm had been given a victor because realms preferred a clean
word to a graveyard.
The record named the victor: The Iron-Ring Cartel.
Morwenna had read that sentence in ledgers, proclamations, military histories, and the private memoranda
of men who believed history was a weapon they could aim. Every version polished the same lie until it
shone. Victory. As if the storm had saluted. As if the ruined hosts had left behind a crown for someone to
wear.
Beneath the words, beneath the ash and the melted banners, something supposedly destroyed had been
spirited away.
She did not know where it was.
That was why the Cartel paid her.
Or why it would, if they learned how close she had come to learning.
Morwenna descended into the keep. The stairwell smelled of wet stone and old soot. Her boots rang once,
then the sound was swallowed by the walls. At the bottom, Sabelle waited before the chapel doors.
They had been stripped of their hinges. Inside, the altar had been overturned and the floor opened in a neat
square. Black steps descended into the earth.
Morwenna stopped.
“What was found?” she asked.
Sabelle’s gaze remained on the darkness below. “A binding.”
“Whose?”
“A careful question.”
“I am surrounded by careful questions.”
“Then you may recognize the work.”
A sound came from beneath the floor.
Metal scraped stone.
Caedmon, behind them, made a small involuntary noise. His pen fell from his hand and rolled across the
threshold.
Sabelle did not react. “You will not record this.”
Morwenna looked at them. “That is not how records work.”
“It is precisely how records work. They preserve what is permitted to survive.”
Another scrape. Slower this time. A wet exhalation rose from the stairwell, carrying the stink of grave-soil
and extinguished candles.
Morwenna thought of the message in her glove. The river gate. The provisions. A route that could starve
one faction, enrich another, and make a third believe itself clever. She had sold such fragments for years,

never enough to topple a power, never so little that the Cartel forgot her name.
But Sabelle knew.
Perhaps they had always known.
“Your cellar,” Morwenna said.
The High Inquisitor looked at her then. “You have been curious.”
“I have been observant.”
“Curiosity wears a softer face.”
From below came three knocks.
The sound traveled through Morwenna’s bones.
Sabelle stepped aside, revealing the stair. “There is something you should understand about loyalty.”
Morwenna did not move. “I understand that it is a word people invoke after they have exhausted their
evidence.”
“Loyalty is not devotion. It is the choice of which ruin one is willing to stand inside.”
“And which ruin have you chosen?”
Sabelle’s eyes lowered to the paper hidden in Morwenna’s glove, though they could not see it. “That
depends on what you intend to do with what you have been given.”
The wind found the ruined chapel and moaned through it. Caedmon bent to retrieve his pen, his hands
trembling now. Morwenna watched him wipe the nib clean against his sleeve. Even frightened, he
protected the instrument before himself.
A useful instinct.
She drew the parchment from her glove and held it between two fingers. The cipher marks seemed to shift
in the lantern light.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel has purchased a passage,” she said.
Sabelle did not ask how she knew.
“Where?”
Morwenna folded the message once. “You are not the only one who keeps things beneath the floor.”
For the first time, Sabelle’s composure cracked. Not fear. Recognition.
The sound below ceased.
In the silence that followed, something drew breath.
Morwenna heard Caedmon whisper her title. She heard Sabelle’s hand close around the hilt beneath their
coat. She heard, far beyond the chapel and the broken walls, the first mutter of thunder rolling over the
Shattered Vale.
Then the cellar door beneath them began to open.
The cellar door opened inward by the width of a hand.

A smell rose through the gap—not rot, precisely, but the mineral cold of a tomb opened after a long burial.
It touched Morwenna’s tongue. The lantern flame drew thin and blue.
Caedmon made a small sound behind her. His breath caught as if a fist had closed around it.
Sabelle did not move.
The High Inquisitor’s hand remained beneath their coat, fingers curled around the hilt there. The two
crowns—one wrought of blackened metal, the other pale as old bone—cast no gleam in the lantern light.
They seemed less like ornaments than wounds that had hardened above the brow.
“Stand aside,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna watched the darkness below. “You have not told me what is in there.”
“I told you enough.”
“No.” Her voice stayed level. “You told me there was a passage. That is not the same thing.”
Something shifted beneath the chapel. Not footsteps. The dragging of weight that had forgotten how to
belong to a living body.
Caedmon’s quill case knocked against the stones as he backed away. “High Inquisitor.”
“Be silent, Scribe.”
The door opened farther.
A hand appeared on the stair.
It was grey, jointed, and narrow. The nails had been pared to the quick. Black thread had been wound
around each finger, crossing the knuckles in intricate knots. The hand gripped the edge of the door, and the
wood groaned beneath its strength.
Morwenna had seen men dragged from waters gone black with stormlight. She had seen flesh burned
smooth by the Ley-storms that had ended the Leaden Accord. She had watched officers smile while blood
ran from their ears, because discipline was sometimes only the art of dying without inconveniencing the
living.
This was different.
The thing below was not dying.
It had finished.
“Sabelle,” she said.
The High Inquisitor’s face did not change, but the lantern caught a tremor in their jaw. “Do not draw
steel.”
“Then you should have brought a lock.”
“I brought a command.”
The hand withdrew.
A figure climbed into view.

It wore a coat of dark cloth stiff with dust. The garment had once been cut for a human frame, though
nothing in the shoulders moved as a human shoulder moved. The head hung forward. A strip of pale
binding covered the mouth, its edges darkened where old moisture had soaked through. More strips
crossed the throat and disappeared beneath the collar.
The revenant paused on the last step.
Its eyes were open.
There was no color in them. Only a dull, wet sheen, like ice beneath a winter moon.
Caedmon’s breathing became a prayer without words.
Morwenna felt the old, familiar instinct to measure a threat: distance, exits, weapons, the weight of the
door, the number of bodies between herself and the nearest open ground. The chapel had one entrance
above, one broken arch beyond the altar, and a cellar door now occupied by the dead. Sabelle stood
between the revenant and the room. Caedmon stood behind Morwenna, which was either courage or an
inability to choose a better place.
The revenant turned its head toward her.
The motion came too quickly.
Morwenna’s hand went to the pistol beneath her coat, though she knew the weapon would be a gesture,
not a solution. The revenant’s gaze settled on the iron clasp at her throat—the insignia of her station, worn
dull beneath the grime of the road.
“Fleet Admiral,” it said.
Its voice was muffled by the binding. The words seemed to come from the stone as much as from its
mouth.
Caedmon stared.
Sabelle’s command struck the room like a snapped chain. “Kneel.”
The revenant remained standing.
For one breath, Morwenna thought Sabelle had lost control of it.
Then the dead thing lowered itself.
Not gracefully. Not with obedience. Its knees folded in opposite directions, and its body descended with a
wet crack. It ended on one knee, head bowed.
Sabelle exhaled through their nose.
Morwenna looked at the binding around its mouth. “It speaks.”
“When permitted.”
“It knew my rank.”
“It remembers what it was taught.”
“What was it?”
Sabelle’s eyes cut toward her. “You are asking questions as though you intend to write the answers down.”

“I am asking questions because it is in the room.”
“Then ask better ones.”
The revenant lifted its head. Its gaze passed over Sabelle and returned to Morwenna.
“Cold,” it whispered.
The word crawled under Morwenna’s skin.
Sabelle stepped closer to it. “What did you hear?”
The dead thing’s head tilted.
“Beneath,” it said.
“What?”
“Water. Bells. A door without hinges.”
Caedmon’s fingers closed around the chain at his throat. “There are no bells here.”
“There are always bells,” said the revenant.
Thunder rolled above the chapel. Dust loosened from the rafters and fell through the lantern glow.
Morwenna glanced toward the broken windows. The storm had drawn nearer. Through the gaps in the
walls, the Shattered Vale showed itself in brief white flashes: splintered ridges, dead grass bent flat, the
skeletal towers of the abandoned Greyfell Citadel in the far distance. The lightning made the ruin seem to
breathe.
Her attention returned to the cellar.
“You said the Iron-Ring Cartel has purchased a passage,” she said.
Sabelle did not look at her. “I said you were not the only one who keeps things beneath the floor.”
“And this is what you keep?”
The revenant’s fingers twitched against the stones.
Sabelle’s silence answered.
Morwenna felt the message in her coat press against her ribs. A few folded lines. A route. A price. Enough
intelligence to move men and goods through the Vale without the knowledge of those who believed their
walls still possessed meaning.
She had sold lesser things for more.
The Cartel did not buy loyalty. It bought the shape of a person’s hunger and placed a coin inside it.
“What passage?” she asked.
Sabelle’s eyes hardened. “You already know.”
“I know someone has paid for access. I do not know what they intend to carry through it.”
“Perhaps they intend to carry you.”
“Then they should have paid for a wider passage.”

Caedmon looked from one of them to the other. His face had the waxen pallor of a man realizing that the
record he kept might someday be used against him. Morwenna wondered what he had written before the
door opened. Names, perhaps. Accusations. The careful architecture of obedience.
Sabelle turned to him. “Take the lantern.”
He flinched. “High Inquisitor?”
“Take it.”
Caedmon obeyed. His hand shook as he lifted the lantern from its hook. Shadows climbed the chapel
walls. The revenant’s shadow did not move with it. It remained crouched on the floor, head bowed, a
second corpse kneeling beneath the first.
Sabelle descended one step.
The cellar below seemed impossibly deep. The stair vanished into a blackness that absorbed the lantern’s
light rather than reflecting it. Morwenna could see old shelving, a hanging chain, the glint of something
metallic laid upon a stone table.
A narrow case.
Its lid was open.
Inside lay a length of white metal wrapped in dark cloth. Frost feathered the exposed edges of the lining.
The cold coming from it was clean and absolute. It drove the cellar’s damp smell away and left only the
taste of iron at the back of Morwenna’s throat.
She knew the shape of the object before she saw the crownlike head of it.
“The Sceptre of Final Winter,” she said.
Caedmon whispered a denial.
Sabelle looked back at her. “You have heard of it.”
“I have heard many things.”
“And yet you recognize it.”
Morwenna descended one step, then another. The revenant remained kneeling between her and the case.
Frost gathered along the seams of its coat.
“The Sceptre of Final Winter is housed in Palewell Abbey,” she said.
The words seemed to disturb the cellar.
The revenant’s head jerked upward.
Sabelle’s hand closed around the hilt beneath their coat. “Do not say that name again.”
Morwenna watched the sceptre. Even in the dim light, the metal seemed to contain a deeper night. Its shaft
was slender, ridged like frozen water. The head had been shaped into a cluster of jagged points, each one
clear enough to catch the lantern flame and break it into colorless splinters.
“Housed,” Morwenna repeated. “That is the term used in the records.”
“Records are written by people who have not touched what they describe.”

“You have.”
Sabelle did not answer.
Below them, the revenant began to tremble. The bindings around its mouth tightened. One of the threads
snapped with a sound like a fingernail striking glass.
Caedmon nearly dropped the lantern. “It is waking.”
“It is awake,” Sabelle said.
“No.” Morwenna kept her eyes on the dead thing. “It is remembering.”
The revenant’s gaze fixed upon the sceptre.
“Palewell,” it said.
The cellar walls shuddered.
A film of ice spread across the nearest stone, branching outward in delicate white veins. The lantern flame
guttered. Morwenna felt the cold enter through her gloves, through her sleeves, through the disciplined
distance she kept between herself and fear.
Sabelle descended fully into the cellar.
“Look at me,” they ordered.
The revenant did not.
“Sabelle,” Morwenna said, “what did you bind to this place?”
The High Inquisitor’s face had become very still.
“Nothing that belongs to you.”
“Everything becomes someone’s concern when it can cross a threshold.”
“Not this.”
The sceptre gave a faint sound inside its case.
Not a chime. Not metal.
A sigh.
Morwenna’s thoughts went immediately to the message hidden beneath her coat. The Cartel had not
purchased a passage for ordinary cargo. No one spent that kind of secrecy to move grain, weapons, or men
whose names could be replaced. Somewhere beyond the storm, a hand had reached for this object—or for
the knowledge of where it slept.
And Sabelle knew.
The realization did not frighten her as much as the next one did.
The Iron-Ring Cartel might know as well.
The revenant rose.
Sabelle spoke a word in a language Morwenna did not recognize.

The dead thing stopped halfway upright. Its body strained against the command. The joints in its neck
clicked. Beneath the binding, something moved against the cloth, forming the shape of a smile or a
scream.
Caedmon made the sign of warding over his chest.
Morwenna drew her pistol.
Sabelle’s head turned a fraction. “I told you not to.”
“You did.”
The storm broke above them.
Thunder struck so hard the chapel floor jumped. The lantern went out, and for a breath there was only
darkness, the cold, and the sound of the cellar door beginning to open behind them.
The cellar door opened another handspan.
Wind poured through the gap, though the chapel had no outer entrance open to it. It came smelling of wet
ash and old iron. The revenant bent toward that draught as a flower bends toward light.
Morwenna raised the pistol.
The weapon steadied her. Not because she believed in it. Belief was a luxury for those who had never
watched a Ley-storm turn an army into glass and mud. But the pistol had weight, a mechanism, a chamber,
a deliberate ending. It obeyed the hand.
The dead thing did not.
“Sabelle,” she said.
The High Inquisitor’s silhouette stood between her and the stair. Twice-crowned, hoodless, motionless
except for the minute tremor in their fingers. Lightning entered through the broken clerestory and made
their face white as scraped bone.
“Lower it.”
“I will not.”
“Then fire.”
The command was soft. That made it worse.
Morwenna’s thumb rested against the hammer. The revenant’s wrapped head tilted. Beneath its burial
cloth, the mouth-shape widened. A black thread of liquid slid from where its chin should have been and
fell soundlessly onto the flagstones.
Caedmon whispered, “It is listening.”
“No,” said Sabelle. “It is remembering.”
The door opened farther.
Something moved below.
Morwenna felt the old instinct rise in her, the one that had carried her through storms, mutinies, and
councils where every smile concealed a knife. Assess the exits. Count the hands. Identify the leverage. She

measured the chapel by darkness: the stair behind Sabelle, the narrow aisle, the collapsed wall, the high
windows useless against the rain. Caedmon stood too close to the altar. Sabelle stood closest to the dead.
And she stood with a pistol she had not been meant to draw.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had paid for smaller risks. Names of captains. Routes of supply. Which officers
could be bought and which only frightened. Information was a current, and Morwenna had learned to sail
it without admitting she was in the water.
But no message had mentioned a revenant.
No message had mentioned that Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned kept the dead beneath a chapel.
The thought came with the cold precision of a blade: if the Cartel knew, they had not told her everything.
That was not betrayal. It was business.
She hated them for making the distinction necessary.
The revenant jerked forward.
Sabelle spoke again.
The word struck the room like a nail driven into wood. The dead body snapped upright. Its boots scraped
over the stones. One hand rose, fingers crooked, and the wrappings around its wrist tightened with a dry
creaking sound.
Morwenna fired.
The muzzle-flash tore the dark apart. Thunder followed too slowly.
The shot struck the revenant high in the shoulder. The impact spun it half around, but no blood came.
Beneath the cloth, the bone gave with a damp crack. It staggered against the wall, then turned its ruined
head toward her.
Caedmon cried out.
Sabelle did not move. “You disobeyed me.”
“I improved our odds.”
“You have mistaken noise for force.”
The dead thing lurched down the first stair.
Sabelle lifted both hands. The sign they made was not any ward Morwenna knew. The High Inquisitor’s
fingers formed a shape like a crown broken in two.
The revenant stopped.
For one moment, its body held still. Then the cellar answered.
A knocking rose from below.
Not one fist. Many.
It traveled through the stone in slow, patient blows.

Caedmon’s face had gone slack. He gathered the leather satchel clutched to his chest and backed toward
the altar. “There is more than one.”
Sabelle turned their head.
“Do not say what you cannot prove.”
The knocking came again.
Morwenna’s skin tightened across her shoulders. She had heard ships speak in storms. Hulls groaning,
masts complaining, ropes snapping like tendons. She had heard men pound on sealed doors while fire
climbed behind them. This was worse because it had no urgency. The things below were not begging to be
released.
They were reminding the living that the door was a courtesy.
“What is under us?” Morwenna asked.
Sabelle looked at her then, and the severity fell away enough for Morwenna to see the exhaustion beneath
it. They had the expression of someone who had guarded a secret so long that the secret had become a
second spine.
“An obligation.”
“To whom?”
“Do not make this a hearing.”
“I am a Fleet Admiral. I ask questions before men die.”
“Men have already died.”
“That answer belongs to a coward.”
The revenant’s head snapped toward them.
Sabelle’s gaze hardened. “You were born in 288 AS, Morwenna Ashgrove. You have spent your life
believing command means choosing which danger receives a name. This one has a name. It is simply not
yours to hear.”
The use of her full name made the chapel contract around her.
She had never told Sabelle when she was born. It was not a secret, precisely. A birth year was a small
thing in the ledgers of the realm, a mark among other marks. Yet she felt the disclosure as a hand laid upon
the back of her neck.
“You have been reading my file.”
“I read everything placed before me.”
“Then you know I dislike being handled.”
“I know you dislike being known.”
The knocking ceased.
Silence fell so suddenly that Morwenna heard rainwater dripping from the hem of her coat. One drop.
Then another.

From below came a breath.
The revenant stepped off the stair.
Its damaged shoulder hung loose. The bullet had gone through, leaving a dark hole in the wrappings.
Through that hole, Morwenna saw not flesh but a pale glimmer, like moonlight trapped inside a wound.
Caedmon began to write.
Morwenna looked at him. “What are you doing?”
“Recording.”
“Record this instead.” She pointed the pistol at his hand. “If you survive, write that you were warned.”
His quill hovered. “I am a Scribe. If I do not record it, it will be altered.”
“Everything is altered.”
“Not ink.”
Sabelle made a sound that might have been amusement, though nothing in their face softened. “Caedmon
Fellgard has kept records longer than most men have kept their convictions.”
Morwenna did not lower the pistol. “How old is this place?”
“Greyfell Citadel was founded in 62 AS.”
The answer came from Caedmon. His eyes remained on the page.
The name carried a chill of its own. Greyfell Citadel, abandoned in the Shattered Vale, outside the realm’s
core holdings. Morwenna had seen it once from a distance through a veil of dust: grey stone rising from
grey country, a dead fist refusing to unclench.
“This is Greyfell?” she asked.
“Was,” said Sabelle.
A sound rolled beneath them, deeper than thunder.
The altar shuddered. Dust sifted from the ribs of the roof. Somewhere below, metal scraped stone.
Morwenna thought of Palewell Abbey, standing in The Pale Coast, rebuilt over whatever had been broken
there. Founded in 244 AS. A place of pale walls and watchful garrison, where 5998 soldiers kept their
silence beneath the shadow of the Sceptre of Final Winter.
She had been told the Sceptre was safe there.
Safe was a word that belonged to maps.
“Does Palewell know?” she asked.
Sabelle’s eyes narrowed. “Know what?”
“That you keep this.”
“I keep nothing.”
The revenant turned its wrapped face toward the High Inquisitor.

Sabelle’s denial lay between them, thin as paper.
Morwenna had seen this kind of evasion in war councils. The speaker did not reject the fact, only the
vocabulary. Not prisoner. Asset. Not massacre. Necessity. Not treason. Preservation.
“You keep a bound revenant in your cellar,” Morwenna said.
Caedmon stopped writing.
The lantern, dead since the storm, gave a single weak flare from its wick. In that brief amber light
Sabelle’s expression became ancient.
“I keep a bound revenant in my cellar,” they said.
The words seemed to unlock something.
Below, the door slammed shut.
The revenant moved.
Morwenna fired again, but Sabelle struck her wrist aside. The shot cracked into the rafters. Splinters fell.
The dead thing crossed the distance between them with impossible speed, its hands reaching for Caedmon.
Caedmon dropped the satchel and stumbled. Papers spilled across the altar steps, white scraps turning in
the draft.
Sabelle seized the revenant by the throat.
They were not stronger than it. Morwenna saw that at once. The dead body drove them backward, boots
grinding on stone, its fingers closing around their neck. Yet Sabelle held on, and the crowns—one iron,
one blackened silver—caught the lightning and shone with a sickly radiance.
“Write,” Sabelle rasped.
Caedmon stared.
“Write, Scribe.”
He snatched up the quill.
Morwenna moved before thought could argue. She kicked the revenant behind the knee. The joint folded.
Sabelle twisted, bringing the dead thing down hard against the floor.
The impact shook the chapel.
For an instant, Morwenna’s palm pressed against the revenant’s chest. Beneath the burial cloth something
beat.
Not a heart.
A fist.
It struck once against her hand.
Memory flashed through her: the Leaden Accord, begun in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS; 14,011
casualties counted in the ledgers, though no ledger had ever been able to contain them. Both hosts
destroyed by a Ley-storm. The Iron-Ring Cartel named victor amid the ruin. And behind the official ashes,
the hidden truth—a supposedly destroyed artifact spirited away while everyone watched the armies die.

She had sold that truth in pieces.
Not the whole of it. Never the whole.
The revenant’s chest struck her palm again.
The same rhythm.
The same impossible insistence.
Morwenna tore her hand away.
Sabelle forced the dead thing’s head against the flagstones. Their voice had become a low chant, each
syllable dragging against the next. The revenant writhed beneath them. Its wrappings loosened. Something
black and wet pressed through the cloth around its mouth.
“Caedmon,” Morwenna said. “What are you writing?”
The Scribe’s quill shook, but the ink did not blot.
“The truth as spoken.”
“By whom?”
He looked up.
The cellar door began to open again.
This time, no wind came through.
A pale hand appeared in the gap and curled around the edge.
Then another hand closed over it.
Sabelle looked toward the door.
For the first time, Morwenna saw fear in the High Inquisitor’s face.
Not fear of the dead.
Recognition.
Sabelle released the revenant.
It rose immediately, turning toward the stair as though summoned by a bell. The bound corpse stood
between them and the opening door. Its head lifted. Beneath the cloth, the hidden mouth shaped a word.
Morwenna could not hear it.
But Sabelle did.
Their crowns began to bleed.

Chapter 3
The quarantine bell spoke once through Gloamreach, and the sound went nowhere.
It struck the pallid air above the Pale Coast, shuddered against the sealed gates, and died among the roofs
as if the town itself had swallowed it. Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood beneath the bell tower and
listened to the silence that followed. He had learned, in the years since command was placed upon him,
that silence was never empty. It was a room with someone hiding inside.
A guard watched him from the gatehouse slit.
Another watched the road.
The garrison of Gloamreach numbered 2,483. Ignatz knew the figure because the quartermaster had
spoken it three times, each time with the grim precision of a man who believed numbers could be made to
stand between a place and death. They could not. Not here. The town was quarantined, and every sealed
door seemed to breathe its own private sickness into the fog.
“Commander.”
The voice came from behind him.
Ignatz did not turn. “Quartermaster.”
Ignatz Marrowgate approached over the wet stones. He served as a Quartermaster, and service had made a
careful creature of him. He carried a ledger against his chest beneath his cloak, sheltering it from the mist
more fiercely than he sheltered himself. The lantern at his belt burned with a weak, colorless flame.
“You were expected in the counting room,” Marrowgate said.
“I am expected in many rooms.”
“The records require your seal.”
“Then the records can wait.”
Marrowgate’s fingers tightened over the ledger. “The stores cannot.”
At that, Ignatz turned.
Nothing in the quartermaster’s face asked to be remembered. That was his strength. In a world where
every expression became evidence, plainness was a kind of armor. He looked at Ignatz, then at the
gatehouse, then at the locked road beyond it.
“The ration allotments were reduced,” Marrowgate said. “The men have noticed.”
“Men notice the absence of things more readily than the presence of them.”
“They notice hunger.”
“They will notice less if they keep their mouths shut.”
Marrowgate lowered his eyes. “The quarantine does not explain the reduction.”
“No,” Ignatz said. “It explains the fear. Fear explains the rest.”
A drop of water fell from the bell rope and struck the stone between them.

Inside his coat, beneath the dark fold of his command mantle, a small packet rested against his ribs.
Waxed cloth. Thin paper. A line of figures, a line of routes, a line of names he had not written but had
copied in his own hand. Intelligence had a smell when it belonged to the Iron-Ring Cartel: hot wax, iron
dust, and the faint bitter trace of burned herbs. The packet carried all three.
He had sold it before dawn.
Not for coin. Coin left witnesses in the fingers. The Cartel paid in absences—an unsearched wagon, an
overlooked door, a patrol turned half a road aside. Their mercy was only another shape of ownership.
“You should come in,” Marrowgate said.
“Why?”
“The relics have been brought from the vault.”
Ignatz felt the old resistance close around his heart. “Which relics?”
“The Hollow Edge. The Chalice of Ashdeep.”
The names seemed to change the temperature of the fog.
The Hollow Edge was a ward forged in 216 AS. Its attunement cost 21. Ignatz had never touched it,
though men had lied about that touch in reports carrying his authority. The artifact was spoken of in the
language used for wounds that had not healed: emptiness, severity, a clean absence where certainty ought
to be.
The Chalice of Ashdeep was a reliquary forged in 323 AS. Its attunement cost 27. It suggested, even in its
name, a depth of ash no hand could reach. No one spoke of what it held. No one spoke of what it required.
“Why are they out?” Ignatz asked.
Marrowgate glanced toward the sealed houses. “Orders.”
“Whose?”
“The papers bear the proper marks.”
“That was not my question.”
The quartermaster’s mouth thinned. “The Ashen Vanguard has sent inquiries. House Morvain has sent
inquiries. The Silent Choir has sent inquiries. The Bleeding Crown has sent inquiries. The Iron-Ring
Cartel has sent nothing.”
The lie arrived between them, pale and composed.
Ignatz heard it because he had placed it there.
The five powers watched the realm’s ruins from their separate shadows: the Ashen Vanguard, House
Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Each had learned to call
patience a virtue when patience served appetite. Each understood that Gloamreach’s quarantine made
every locked gate a political statement.
“Take me to the vault,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate hesitated. “The vault is sealed.”

“Then unseal it.”
“It is sealed by ward.”
“Then break the ward.”
The quartermaster looked toward the tower. “That may be unwise.”
Ignatz leaned close enough for the mist to bead upon his lashes. “You are a Quartermaster, Ignatz
Marrowgate. Your duty is to count what remains after wisdom has finished spending it.”
Something moved behind the gatehouse slit. A rifle barrel, perhaps. Or merely the shadow of one.
Marrowgate stepped aside.
They crossed the yard without speaking. The garrison’s barracks stood in rigid rows, their windows dark.
Somewhere within them, a man coughed. Another voice answered, low and frightened, and was
immediately silenced. Gloamreach did not feel defended. It felt held.
At the vault door, wax seals crowded the iron like pale scabs.
Marrowgate raised the ledger. “The attunement cost of The Hollow Edge is 21.”
“I know.”
“The Chalice of Ashdeep is 27.”
“I know.”
“You must sign.”
Ignatz looked at the page.
His name waited there, written by another hand.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.
The title sat after it like a blade laid beside a throat. He had been born in 258 AS, before Gloamreach had
become a place men feared to name aloud. Before the Purge of Blackport. Before he understood that oaths
were only promises made visible long enough for someone to find the weakness in them.
He pressed his thumb to the seal.
The wax softened.
“Commander,” Marrowgate whispered, “the records say the relics were not to be opened.”
“The records say many things.”
“Then why open them?”
Because someone had carried a message out of Gloamreach.
Because the Iron-Ring Cartel had paid to learn whether the quarantine was sickness or theater.
Because a commander's first duty was to protect the truth, and his second was to decide who deserved to
possess it.
Ignatz withdrew his thumb. “You asked for my seal.”

“I did.”
“You have it.”
“It is not enough.”
“It will be.”
He turned away from the door.
Marrowgate stared at him. “You are leaving?”
“I am going to Fenspire.”
The quartermaster’s face remained plain, but the muscles at his jaw tightened. “Fenspire stands in the
Gloaming Reach.”
“I am aware.”
“It was founded in 57 AS.”
“I am aware.”
“Its garrison is 3,742. It is garrisoned, not quarantined.”
Ignatz looked back at the sealed vault. “Then someone there still believes walls mean something.”
Fenspire’s spire rose in his mind without need of sight: stark against the dim character of the Gloaming
Reach, disciplined and watchful, a permanent occupation sharpened into architecture. If Gloamreach was
a shut mouth, Fenspire was a clenched fist.
Marrowgate opened the ledger again. “The Purge of Blackport is in the annex.”
“Why?”
“Because the transfer orders cite precedent.”
Ignatz took the ledger from him.
The page smelled of damp paper and old smoke. At its center, the heading had been written in heavier ink:
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS.
Below it:
70,907 casualties.
Below that:
The total rout of the aggressors.
His eyes moved to the final notation.
The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Marrowgate stood beside him, breathing shallowly.
“Read the margin,” the quartermaster said.
Ignatz did not need to. He knew the concealed truth. Everyone who mattered knew it, and no one who
mattered would speak it where the dead could hear.

The victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
He ran one gloved finger beneath the sentence without touching the ink.
“Who entered this?” he asked.
“The record was amended.”
“By whom?”
“The amendment is unsigned.”
“Then it is not a record.”
“It is still in the ledger.”
Ignatz shut the book.
The Blackport figures had a gravity of their own. The number of casualties was too large to imagine as
bodies, so the mind made them into an abstraction, and abstraction was the first courtesy offered to
murder. Yet the wells remained in the words. Water darkening in a cup. A hand lifting it. A throat
opening. The Iron-Ring Cartel’s triumph, merciless and bright, spoiled from within by the arithmetic of
betrayal.
His hand found the packet beneath his coat.
A message from the Cartel could be waiting at Fenspire.
Or a message from the Cartel could already be inside Gloamreach, hidden among the relics, the rations,
the dead letters, the sealed rooms.
“Commander,” Marrowgate said, “what should I enter for the vault?”
Ignatz considered the iron door. The seals. The names of the artifacts. The lies gathering behind every
wall.
“Enter nothing.”
“That is not procedure.”
“Procedure is what remains when courage has gone.”
“And what remains when procedure goes?”
Ignatz looked at him.
For the first time, the quartermaster’s expression shifted. Not fear. Not quite. Recognition, perhaps—the
dawning knowledge that the man before him was not merely an oathless guardian, but a guardian who had
learned to weaponize the absence of an oath.
From the far end of the yard came the scrape of a boot.
Both men turned.
A figure stood beneath the archway, wrapped against the fog. No insignia showed. One hand rested
against the wall. The other held something small and pale.
Ignatz felt the packet under his coat grow suddenly warm.

“Who is that?” Marrowgate asked.
The figure lifted its hand.
In its palm lay a strip of waxed cloth marked with the same iron-dark seal.
Ignatz did not move.
The bells above Gloamreach remained silent, and somewhere beyond the gate, on the road toward
Fenspire, a horse began to scream.
The figure stepped into the yard.
Fog slid from its shoulders in pale ropes. Beneath the hood, the face remained a blankness of wet shadow.
The waxed strip hung between two fingers, its seal turned outward as if the stranger had come not to
deliver a message but to display a wound.
Marrowgate’s hand drifted toward the knife at his belt.
Ignatz caught the movement.
“Do not.”
The Quartermaster’s fingers stopped. “You know it?”
“I know what it means when someone carries it openly.”
The figure’s head tilted.
The scream beyond the gate broke off. Silence rushed into the space it had occupied, vast and immediate.
The yard seemed to contract around the three of them. Water ticked from the eaves. Somewhere in the
barracks, a man coughed and was answered by another cough, then by the muffled clatter of a dropped
cup.
Gloamreach had been quarantined long enough for every sound to become an accusation.
The stranger extended the strip.
Ignatz did not take it. “Speak.”
No answer.
“Speak,” he said again, and felt command gather in his voice like a blade being drawn through cloth. “Or
leave.”
The hand holding the packet lowered. The other rose to the hood and pulled it back.
The face beneath was young enough to make the silence cruel. No scar marked it. No badge, no painted
vow, no iron ring. Only rain on the brow and a mouth pressed tight against whatever words had been put
there.
Marrowgate breathed through his nose. “A courier.”
“A courier who knows the seal,” Ignatz said.
The young figure looked at him, then at the packet beneath his coat.
That glance struck more deeply than any accusation.

The warmth under the cloth had spread across his ribs. He could feel the seal through the layers: iron-dark,
hard-edged, branded with a symbol that belonged nowhere near the walls of Gloamreach. The Iron-Ring
Cartel preferred contracts written in ink, but intelligence was another substance. It traveled in hollows, in
false inventories, in the mouths of men who believed themselves merely hungry.
Ignatz had sold them the movements of patrols.
He had sold them the weakness in the western watchtower.
He had sold them the names of officers whose loyalties could be purchased and those whose throats must
be opened.
He had never sold them Gloamreach.
Not yet.
Marrowgate watched him. “Commander.”
The title held no comfort. It was a nail driven into old wood.
Ignatz had been born in 258 AS, when the realm still pretended the Sundering had left something worth
inheriting. He had learned command among ruins that had outlived their makers, and every oath placed
before him had tasted of ash. That was why the garrison called him the Oathless when they thought he
could not hear. The name had become more durable than his rank.
The courier extended the waxed cloth once more.
Ignatz took it.
The seal was cold now.
The cloth unfolded with a damp whisper. Within lay a narrow sliver of black glass, no longer than the first
joint of his thumb. A line had been scratched across it.
NOT THE GATE.
His eyes moved to the archway.
Beyond it, the road ran white with fog toward Fenspire, whose garrisoned walls stood under a stark spire
in the Gloaming Reach. Fenspire had been founded in 57 AS. Its garrison numbered 3,742. Gloamreach
had 2,483, though the quarantine made the number feel like a lie: men counted behind locked doors, rifles
stacked beside sickbeds, boots rotting in the damp.
Marrowgate leaned closer. “What is it?”
“A warning.”
“From whom?”
Ignatz folded the cloth. “You ask questions as though answers have ever improved your position.”
The Quartermaster’s jaw tightened. He was Ignatz Marrowgate, born in 425 AS, and he wore the title of
Quartermaster with the grim devotion of a man who had mistaken ledgers for armor. There was no reason
for him to know anything of the Cartel. No reason for him to know that the black glass was a dead-drop
token, or that the seal beneath its wax had been burned into the hands of men who never appeared twice in
the same town.

Yet his eyes had not left the strip.
The courier spoke at last.
“Three came through the gate.”
Ignatz turned toward the archway. “When?”
The courier’s lips parted. A tremor passed through the throat before the answer emerged.
“Before the bells.”
“The bells have not rung.”
“That is why.”
Marrowgate looked up. Above the yard, the bell tower was swallowed by mist. Its iron mouths hung dark
and still.
Ignatz felt the old instinct rise: summon the guard, seal the barracks, send riders along the road. It was the
instinct that had kept him alive, and the same instinct the Iron-Ring Cartel had learned to measure. Panic
was a kind of currency. Those who spent it first were always poorer afterward.
“What did they carry?” he asked.
The courier’s gaze flicked again to the packet. “One carried a ward.”
“What ward?”
“The Hollow Edge.”
The name passed through the yard without sound.
Ignatz had seen it once, behind three locks and a curtain of salt-thread. The Hollow Edge was a ward
forged in 216 AS, an object made less to protect than to deny. Attunement to it cost 21. Men who touched
its power spoke afterward of rooms with no corners, of voices stripped clean of meaning.
“Where are they?” he asked.
The courier looked toward the barracks.
A door opened in the distance.
Not wide. A hand’s breadth.
Then closed.
Marrowgate drew his knife.
This time Ignatz let him.
The Quartermaster’s face had gone gray. “There are no strangers in the roster.”
“Rosters are written by men.”
“And gates are watched.”
“Gates are watched by men.”

Something moved beneath the fog near the cistern. A shape, perhaps. Or the eye inventing a body where
fear required one.
Ignatz stepped forward.
The courier seized his sleeve.
The touch was desperate, almost childlike. Ignatz looked down at the hand. The fingers were stained black
beneath the nails.
“Not the gate,” the courier whispered.
The black glass in Ignatz’s palm had warmed.
A sound came from under the flagstones.
Three knocks.
Marrowgate flinched. The knife rose.
Three more.
The rhythm was patient. It did not belong to an animal.
Ignatz crouched beside the cistern. Water trembled in the basin, reflecting nothing but a broken smear of
sky. The stones around its base had been mortared over recently. He scraped at one with his thumb and
found the seam.
“Get the key,” he said.
Marrowgate stared. “For what?”
“For the lower stores.”
“There is no lower—”
“Get the key.”
The Quartermaster ran.
Ignatz remained by the cistern with the courier behind him and the packet pressed against his chest. He
heard boots waking throughout the garrison. Orders began to travel in fragments: the gate, the east wall,
the fog, the bells. Somewhere a man shouted that the quarantine had been breached.
The old lies were assembling themselves.
He thought of Blackport. The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS, leaving 70,907
casualties and the total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor. That was the
history carved into walls and recited by clerks who had never smelled poisoned water.
