The concealed truth was that the victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Ignatz had read the proof in a ledger whose pages still smelled of lime.
The Cartel did not defeat its enemies. It arranged the world so that survival itself became evidence of guilt.
The knocks came again.
This time there were four.

The courier began to weep soundlessly.
“Why bring this to me?” Ignatz asked.
The answer came from beneath the stones.
“Because you are the one who opens what should remain shut.”
The voice was muffled, but not by earth. It seemed to speak from inside his own skull.
The Hollow Edge.
Ignatz’s hand went to the packet. “Who is below?”
“Ask the reliquary.”
Marrowgate returned, breathing hard, one hand closed around a ring of keys. “The lower stores are
sealed.”
Ignatz rose. “Then we have been storing something.”
He took the largest key. Its teeth were furred with rust.
The courtyard doors began to open behind them. Men emerged in coats thrown over nightclothes,
weapons clutched in uncertain hands. Their faces turned toward Ignatz, waiting for certainty. He could
feel it gathering in them, the simple hunger to be told where danger stood.
He almost gave them the gate.
Instead he faced the cistern.
“Keep the yard sealed,” he ordered. “No one leaves Gloamreach.”
Marrowgate’s eyes narrowed. “And if the danger is already inside?”
Ignatz fitted the key into the seam.
“Then the quarantine is working.”
The lock turned.
Below the stone, something drew breath.
Ignatz lifted the slab, and a breath of cold ash rose from the dark. In that darkness, a metal vessel waited
on a shelf of bone-white masonry, its surface filmed with soot.
The Chalice of Ashdeep.
A reliquary forged in 323 AS. Attunement to it cost 27.
Its rim was wet.
Ignatz stared at the black drops gathering there.
Behind him, Marrowgate whispered, “Commander, what is that?”
From the barracks came the first bell.
It rang once.
Then the chalice answered.

The second bell did not come from the barracks.
It sounded beneath their feet.
The stone shelf shuddered. Soot loosened from the ceiling and fell in a thin gray rain. Marrowgate caught
the wall with one hand, the other closing around the short blade at his belt.
Ignatz did not move.
The black drops on the Chalice of Ashdeep trembled as if something beneath the metal had begun to beat.
One gathered itself at the rim. It did not fall. It crawled upward instead, thick as oil, dragging a dark thread
behind it.
“Close the slab,” Marrowgate said.
His voice had lost the measured irritation of a Quartermaster faced with a locked door. Fear had entered it,
and fear made men honest in ways oaths never could.
Ignatz watched the drop reach the highest point of the rim.
“Do you hear it?”
“Hear what?”
The third bell rang.
This time the sound came from inside the chalice.
Not a peal. Not metal struck by a hammer. A low, submerged note, like a bell being rung beneath a
drowned city. It passed through the chamber and into Ignatz’s bones. His teeth ached. Somewhere above,
boots began to run across the barracks floor.
Marrowgate looked toward the open stair.
“Commander.”
Ignatz reached for the reliquary.
The air between his hand and the chalice tightened.
Pain entered his palm before his fingers touched the metal. It was a clean pain, precise and intimate, as if a
needle had been placed beneath each nail. His hand stopped a finger’s breadth from the vessel.
The black drop fell.
It struck the shelf and spread in a thin ring.
The masonry drank it.
A line appeared in the white stone, running outward from the shelf. Another crossed it. Then another. The
fractures joined in a pattern that resembled writing, though no alphabet Ignatz knew had ever been meant
to be read by living eyes.
Marrowgate retreated one step.
“You said the reliquary was inert.”
“I said it had not answered.”

“That is not the same thing.”
“No.”
The word left Ignatz quietly. The chamber took it and gave it back from every wall.
No.
He had seen the Chalice of Ashdeep only once before, and then from a distance, under a hood of canvas
and the watch of men who would have killed him if they had known what he had carried in his memory.
He had not been told where it came from. He had not asked. Questions were a kind of coin, and the wrong
question could purchase a grave.
Forged in 323 AS. Attunement cost 27.
Those facts had been entered in a ciphered ledger and passed through hands that did not belong to the
Ashen Vanguard. Ignatz had copied them for the Iron-Ring Cartel, then burned the page. He remembered
the heat of it. He remembered how the ink had curled before the parchment blackened.
He had told himself that information was not betrayal.
He had told himself many things.
Above them, someone shouted. A second voice answered. Then came the scrape and clatter of men
dragging the barracks doors shut.
Gloamreach was quarantined. Every gate had been barred against the Pale Coast, every road watched,
every vessel refused. The garrison numbered 2,483, enough to make a prison of a town and not enough to
make the prison safe.
The bells continued.
Marrowgate swallowed. “What does it want?”
Ignatz looked at the chalice.
“To be opened.”
“It is open.”
“No.”
The inside of the reliquary was blacker than the chamber around it. The darkness there had depth. It
seemed to recede not into the vessel but into some place beyond distance, where cold ash drifted through a
lightless current.
A shape moved in that depth.
Marrowgate made a sound through his teeth.
Ignatz caught his arm before the Quartermaster could flee. “Do not look into it.”
“I already did.”
“Then remember what you saw.”
“I saw nothing.”
“Good.”

The fourth bell rang.
The stone beneath the chalice split with a soft, wet sigh. A breath came through the crack, carrying the
stink of extinguished fires and old water. It touched Ignatz’s face. For an instant he tasted Blackport.
The taste brought no image at first. Only bitterness. Then the wells. The poisoned wells. The Iron-Ring
Cartel had emerged victorious from the Purge of Blackport, and the victory had been polished until its
surface shone. The dead had been counted—70,907 casualties—while the truth had been buried beneath
speeches, ash, and sealed reports.
The Cartel had poisoned the wells of its own allies.
Ignatz had learned that truth in a room without windows. He had been paid to learn it, though not to
understand why it mattered. The coin had been placed beneath his hand. The message had been carried
out. Since then, the Cartel had purchased other fragments from him: patrol routes, stores, weaknesses in
the coastward watch.
Small betrayals, he had called them.
Nothing that could topple a realm.
The chalice whispered.
Not in words. In the dry rasp of grains poured across stone.
Marrowgate jerked against Ignatz’s grip. “There’s something in the crack.”
Ignatz released him.
A black film rose between the stones. It gathered in the shape of a hand, but the fingers were too long and
the joints bent in the wrong places. It pressed against the edge of the shelf.
The chalice answered with a note so deep that the flame in the wall lamp went blue.
From somewhere beyond the chamber came the groan of a door being forced.
“Who knows we are here?” Marrowgate asked.
Ignatz did not answer.
The question entered him like a hook. He had sent a message three nights ago. Not from the garrison
office; that would have been watched. Not through the ordinary channels. The information had gone
folded inside a requisition tally, carried by a route he had used before.
Gloamreach’s quarantine had been the message.
The sealed roads. The closed harbor. The men rotated from the walls and the stores shifted beneath guard.
And the Chalice of Ashdeep.
He had not known whether the Cartel wanted the relic removed, destroyed, or merely understood. He had
sent what he knew. He had expected time.
Time was a luxury possessed by men who had not opened the wrong door.
“Commander,” Marrowgate said. “Answer me.”
“No one was meant to know.”

“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are getting.”
The Quartermaster stared at him. In the blue light, his face seemed carved from the same pallid stone as
the shelf. “You brought me here.”
“I needed the lock opened.”
“You knew what was beneath it.”
“I knew what had been recorded.”
“And who recorded it?”
Ignatz turned toward him.
Marrowgate’s courage failed before his suspicion did. He lowered his eyes, but not quickly enough.
A man could be forgiven for fear. Suspicion was another matter.
Above, the alarm began in earnest. Boots hammered through the barracks. Voices rose and collided.
Someone cried that the east gate had opened. Someone else shouted that no gate had opened, that the
sound was coming from below.
The fifth bell struck.
The crack beneath the shelf widened.
A pale powder spilled through and spread across the floor, though there was no wind. It moved against the
slope of the stones, creeping toward Ignatz’s boots. Where it touched his shadow, the shadow recoiled.
He took one step back.
The powder followed.
“Close the slab,” Marrowgate whispered again.
Ignatz looked up at the underside of the stone. The slab waited above the stair, its hinge groaning under a
pressure that did not come from any hand. If they sealed the chamber, whatever had woken might remain
below.
Or it might learn the shape of the prison.
He had spent his life around wards and walls. The Hollow Edge had been forged in 216 AS; its name was
spoken in garrison prayers as though emptiness itself could be made obedient. Men trusted old magic
because stone did not confess its doubts.
But every ward had an edge.
Every oath had a hollow place.
The powder reached the toe of his boot.
It stopped.
Then it formed letters.
Not the fractured signs on the shelf. These were plain enough to read.

OPEN.
Marrowgate saw them. His breath caught.
“What have you done?”
Ignatz’s hand went to the weapon at his side, though steel had never persuaded anything that lived beneath
the world.
“I have not done this.”
The letters changed.
A second word appeared beneath the first.
OATHLESS.
The chamber seemed to narrow around him.
Marrowgate turned slowly. “Commander—”
The sixth bell began to ring.
This time it rang above them, below them, and inside Ignatz’s skull.
The Chalice of Ashdeep rose from the shelf.
It did not leap or float. It simply ceased to rest upon the stone. Black liquid hung beneath it in a trembling
globe, and within that globe something pale unfolded, joint by joint, like a hand emerging from deep
water.
Ignatz drew his blade.
The sound of metal leaving its sheath was pitifully small.
The hand touched the rim.
The chalice cracked.
A line of darkness opened down its side, and from within came a voice made of many voices, each one
speaking from a different distance.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
Marrowgate stumbled backward.
The voice spoke again.
“Tell the Iron-Ring Cartel the door is open.”
The black globe burst.
Ash struck Ignatz’s face. Cold entered his eyes. The chamber vanished, replaced by a vast shore under a
colorless sky. Something stood at the waterline, veiled in drifting soot. Beyond it, bells swung from towers
with no walls beneath them.
Then the vision broke.
Ignatz was on one knee.

Marrowgate was shouting, but the words came from far away. The open slab had begun to descend.
Above, the stair was crowded with shadows and the glimmer of drawn weapons.
The powder on the floor had written one final word.
RUN.
Ignatz rose.
He seized Marrowgate by the collar and drove him toward the stairs. “Move.”
“What was that?”
“Not here.”
“Where do we go?”
The slab dropped another handspan. A boot appeared in the narrowing gap above, followed by the edge of
a blade.
Ignatz shoved Marrowgate beneath it.
The blade struck stone.
Sparks fell.
They reached the stair together. Behind them, the Chalice of Ashdeep gave a final, shivering note. The
sound traveled up through the soles of Ignatz’s boots and into the foundations of Gloamreach.
The walls answered.
Not with bells.
With breathing.
Ignatz looked up at the men trapped above the descending slab, then back into the chamber where the
darkness had begun to pour from the broken reliquary.
Somewhere beyond the sealed coast, the Ashen Vanguard waited for orders. Somewhere farther still, the
Iron-Ring Cartel waited for his message.
The slab touched the first helmet.
Ignatz put his shoulder beneath the stone.
“Pull,” he said.
Marrowgate stared at him. “Commander, what are you doing?”
Ignatz felt the weight descend, felt the dark breath rising against his back.
“Keeping the quarantine,” he said.
And beneath them, something laughed.

Chapter 4
The sea had withdrawn from Palewell Abbey by the time Morwenna Ashgrove reached its gate, leaving
the shore black and shining beneath the morning’s pallor.
Wind worried the pennants above the battlements. They cracked like small whips, each snap swallowed by
the greater breathing of the coast. Salt filmed the stones. The abbey had been rebuilt in pale blocks that did
not match: some clean and sharp-edged, some already softened by weather, some bearing the old scars
beneath their new skin. It was a place made twice and trusted neither time.
Morwenna dismounted without assistance.
The horse shied from the wind. She did not. A Fleet Admiral learned early that the world was always
attempting to make a spectacle of disobedience—animals, weather, subordinates, history. One endured it
by refusing to perform in return.
At the gate, a sentry lowered his spear.
“Admiral.”
“Open it.”
He glanced beyond her, toward the road. “Your escort?”
“Behind me.”
This was not true. Her escort waited at a distance where the sea mist could conceal them, though she had
brought no one who mattered. No one whose absence would be remarked upon. The lies required for
survival were seldom grand. Most were no larger than a hand placed over a page.
The sentry hesitated.
Morwenna looked at the spearpoint, then at him. “If you intend to challenge my authority, do it before I
enter. I dislike being interrupted once I have begun.”
The gate opened.
Inside, Palewell Abbey smelled of wet ash, old mortar, and boiled grain. The rebuilt cloister enclosed a
square of dead earth where a few winter herbs leaned beneath the rain. Along the inner wall stood racks of
pikes, their shafts darkened with oil. The place had been raised as sanctuary once. Whatever prayers had
survived its ruin had been hammered into military discipline.
A boy in a grey wool coat crossed the yard carrying a stack of ledgers against his chest. He saw
Morwenna, stopped, and nearly dropped them.
“Caedmon Fellgard,” he said, recovering himself. “Scribe.”
“I know what a scribe is.”
His mouth tightened. He had the reserved misery of a man who believed every word might someday be
entered into evidence. “I was instructed to bring you to the record room.”
“By whom?”
“By Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned.”

The wind drove rain through the archway behind them. Morwenna glanced at the boy’s ledgers. Their
bindings were swollen from damp, their corners blackened. “And the High Inquisitor is here?”
“Yes.”
“Waiting?”
Caedmon’s gaze flickered toward the chapel. “The High Inquisitor does not wait in the manner of ordinary
people.”
“Then lead me to the extraordinary one.”
He turned.
Morwenna followed through the rebuilt cloister, beneath arches that still held the pale, severe geometry of
an abbey though the inner faces had been reinforced with iron bands. Every window was narrow. Every
door had a bar within reach. The architects had remembered the enemy before they remembered the saint.
She had been born in 288 AS, into a realm that had forgotten how to distinguish between inheritance and
salvage. By the time she was old enough to understand maps, every border had been a wound someone
had named a province. By the time she wore the uniform of command, the sea had become the only road
that did not belong wholly to another power.
Her hand brushed the inside of her coat.
The message rested there, folded within oilskin.
She had written it herself. Three lines concerning the disposition of stores, the condition of patrol vessels,
and a weakness in the coastal watch. Nothing that could be called treason by a person who had not lost a
war. Everything that could be called valuable by the Iron-Ring Cartel.
The payment would arrive later, through hands that would not know her name.
That was the principle of secret commerce: ignorance was not an obstacle. It was the currency.
Caedmon opened the record room.
Shelves climbed the walls, burdened by ledgers, rolls, tablets, and sealed packets. The air was warmer
here, though it carried the damp animal scent of leather and parchment. A single brazier burned beneath a
flue. Beside it stood Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned.
The High Inquisitor wore no visible crown. The title was enough. Severity gathered around them like a
second garment, and their stillness possessed the intolerable confidence of a blade laid flat upon a table.
“Fleet Admiral,” Sabelle said.
“High Inquisitor.”
“You came quickly.”
“I came when summoned.”
“Those are not the same thing.”
“No.”

Sabelle regarded her for a long moment. Their eyes moved to the coat, the gloves, the damp at
Morwenna’s shoulders, and finally to the hand that had touched the message beneath the fabric.
Morwenna kept her breathing even.
On the table between them lay a map of the coast, its corners weighted by iron seals. Palewell Abbey had
been marked in red ink. Other marks gathered around it in careful clusters, though she did not recognize
the hands that had made them.
Caedmon placed his ledgers beside the map.
“Leave us,” Sabelle said.
The scribe stiffened. “The records—”
“Will remain records after you depart.”
Caedmon looked to Morwenna, as if authority might be contagious.
“Go,” she said.
He bowed and withdrew, closing the door with precise gentleness.
The room seemed to shrink.
Sabelle touched one of the ledgers. “The Leaden Accord ended in 342 AS.”
Morwenna looked at the map. “I remember.”
“Do you?”
“I remember enough.”
“The Accord was declared concluded. The Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor. The hosts were destroyed
by a Ley-storm.” Sabelle’s finger moved across the map without touching it. “And yet certain accounts
remain unsettled.”
“War leaves accounts. It does not leave answers.”
“Poetry from a Fleet Admiral.”
“An observation from a tired one.”
Sabelle’s expression did not alter. “You have been tired for a long time.”
There it was: not an accusation, but its shadow. Morwenna had met shadows in every port. They lurked
behind questions, beneath signatures, inside the silence after a subordinate said yes.
She removed her gloves one finger at a time and set them on the table.
“The Leaden Accord ended in 342 AS,” she said. “If you summoned me to dispute the calendar, I cannot
help you.”
“I summoned you because a supposedly destroyed artifact was not destroyed.”
The words entered the room softly.
Outside, rain hissed against the rebuilt stone.

Morwenna kept her face composed. The supposedly destroyed artifact had been a rumor when she first
heard it, a rumor repeated by men who wanted their failures to sound ordained. Then came the Ley-storm.
Then the wreckage. Then the silence in which every power claimed victory and no one claimed
responsibility.
The artifact had not been destroyed.
She knew this because the Iron-Ring Cartel had paid for the knowledge.
Not directly. Never directly.
“How certain are you?” she asked.
“Certain enough to distrust certainty.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are receiving.”
Sabelle opened a ledger. The pages had been scraped thin in places, the ink lifted and replaced. Morwenna
recognized the labor of a careful hand: not falsification, precisely, but the removal of a past that had
become inconvenient.
“Caedmon found irregularities in the coastal inventories,” Sabelle said. “Entries altered after the Accord.
Seal impressions repeated where they should not be. Cargo listed as ash, though no ash was recorded at
the point of disposal.”
“Then question Caedmon.”
“I did.”
“And?”
“He answered.”
Morwenna almost smiled. “That is generally what happens when a scribe is questioned.”
“Not always.”
The brazier gave a small pop. A coal collapsed inward, glowing beneath its crust.
Sabelle closed the ledger. “There is a movement of information through the coast. Some of it originates
with naval officers.”
“Some information originates everywhere.”
“Some of it reaches the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The room held its breath.
Morwenna felt the message beneath her coat as distinctly as if it had become a hot coin against her ribs.
She could imagine the Iron-Ring Cartel’s clerks receiving her report, breaking its seal, measuring each
omission. They would not ask whether she believed in their cause. Cartels required no faith. They required
appetite and arithmetic.
“I sell nothing,” Morwenna said.
Sabelle’s gaze rested upon her.

The lie came cleanly. That was what frightened her. Once, deception had required effort, a private twisting
of the mind. Now it rose in her like a reflex of the body.
“You have not asked me whether I sell anything,” Sabelle said.
“I assumed the shape of the conversation.”
“Assumption is a form of confession.”
“Then you should have summoned a priest.”
“The abbey has priests.”
“Does it?”
Sabelle looked toward the door.
For the first time, something beneath their severity showed—not weakness, but attention turned inward,
toward a locked chamber of the self. Morwenna had heard whispers about Sabelle Mournvale the
Twice-Crowned, about the cellar beneath their quarters and what was kept there in bonds. A revenant,
some said. A bound revenant, others insisted. The rumor possessed the stubbornness of truth because no
one had survived long enough to prove it false.
Sabelle returned their attention to the table.
“Someone has begun searching for the artifact,” they said. “Someone with ships, records, and access to old
military routes.”
“Then you have narrowed the field to half the realm.”
“I have narrowed it to you.”
The words struck more deeply than they should have.
Morwenna turned toward the map. Palewell Abbey stood at the edge of the marked coast, austere and
watchful beneath its new stone. Beyond it lay the dark sea, folding itself into distance. Somewhere out
there, vessels moved beneath low skies. Cargo changed hands. Messages crossed from mouth to mouth,
from ledger to ledger, until truth became indistinguishable from the price paid for it.
“What do you want from me?” she asked.
Sabelle placed a sealed packet on the map.
“Open it.”
Morwenna did not move.
“You believe I am compromised,” she said.
“I believe everyone is compromised by something.”
“And you?”
A pause.
Then Sabelle smiled without warmth. “Especially me.”
The sealed packet bore no crest. No name. Only a line of black wax pressed flat as a scar.

Morwenna reached for it.
Beneath the floor, something struck the stone once.
Caedmon’s voice cried out in the corridor.
Sabelle’s head turned toward the door.
A second blow rose from below, heavier than the first, and the brazier flame bent sideways as if a great
unseen breath had entered the room.
Morwenna’s hand remained upon the packet.
The third blow did not come.
Silence gathered in its place, thick and listening. Dust sifted from the seams between the stones.
Somewhere beyond the door, Caedmon made a wet, strangled sound, and then the corridor fell quiet
enough for Morwenna to hear the small metal teeth of the brazier settling in the heat.
Sabelle had not moved. Their face was turned toward the door, but their eyes had gone distant, fixed upon
something beneath the floor.
“You knew,” Morwenna said.
“I suspected.”
“You knew enough to bring me here.”
“I brought you here because the walls of this room are older than the citadel’s loyalties.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one that remains useful.”
Morwenna broke the wax.
The seal gave with a soft crack. Its black fragments clung to her glove like flecks of congealed blood.
Inside lay a single folded sheet, the paper thin and grey, its edges darkened as though it had been held too
close to a flame. No handwriting marked the outside.
She unfolded it.
At first there appeared to be nothing but a column of figures, each written with the narrow precision of a
clerk who had never mistaken neatness for innocence. Cargo weights. Mooring fees. Names reduced to
initials. Locations without descriptions. Dates without explanation.
Then her eyes found the pattern.
The figures were not payments.
They were movements.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had been buying access to the fleet’s blind places: shoals no chart admitted,
watchtowers that sent their signals late, channels where fog gathered thick enough to swallow a vessel
whole. The entries did not name captains. They named habits. A lantern extinguished. A chain left slack.
A patrol delayed by the length of a prayer.
Morwenna read to the bottom.

There, beneath the last column, someone had written a sentence in red ink.
THEY KNOW WHAT YOU HAVE SOLD.
Her pulse did not change. That was the first discipline of command: never permit the body to confess
before the mouth had chosen its lie.
Sabelle watched her.
“Is it true?” they asked.
Morwenna folded the sheet once. “Which part?”
“The part that troubles you.”
“I am troubled by your lack of specificity.”
“Then you are still yourself.”
The brazier flame shuddered. Its light withdrew from the walls, drawing inward until the room seemed to
float in a black sea. The stone beneath Morwenna’s boots gave a low, patient groan.
She looked down.
A hairline fracture had opened across the floor, running from the table’s carved foot to the threshold. It
was not wide enough for a finger. Darkness showed through it anyway.
Sabelle stepped back.
Not far. Only enough to make the movement visible.
Morwenna noticed. Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned was not a person who yielded ground without
an audience to witness the yielding. Their severity had always seemed carved rather than worn, a thing of
ceremony and sharpened belief. Yet now their shoulders had tightened beneath their robes.
“What is beneath us?” Morwenna asked.
“The old foundations.”
“Greyfell Citadel has no old foundations beneath this room.”
“You have studied the citadel?”
“I have studied every place where people pretend stone makes them safe.”
A sound came from below.
Not a blow this time. A dragging. Something pulled itself along the underside of the floor, slow enough to
make each scrape distinct.
Morwenna felt the old instinct rise in her: measure distance, count exits, mark weapons. The room had one
door. One narrow window overlooking darkness and whatever waited beyond it. Sabelle stood between
her and both. The packet rested beneath her palm, and the paper seemed warmer now.
From the corridor came a whisper.
“Admiral.”
Caedmon.

Morwenna turned toward the door. “Caedmon?”
The whisper came again, thinner. “Do not let them open it.”
Sabelle’s expression did not change.
Morwenna caught that stillness and held it between them.
“Who is them?”
Caedmon’s breath rasped on the other side of the door. “The dead.”
“Caedmon,” Sabelle said, voice hard enough to cut, “step away from the threshold.”
“I saw the records.”
“You saw nothing.”
“I saw the names.”
The dragging beneath the floor stopped.
Morwenna felt the silence press against her teeth.
Caedmon spoke again, louder now. “Caedmon Hollowmere fought in The Leaden Accord, fighting for
The Ashen Vanguard.”
The words struck the room strangely. Not as an answer. As a line torn from a ledger and forced into the
living air.
Morwenna looked at Sabelle.
“Who is Caedmon Hollowmere?”
The High Inquisitor’s mouth opened, then closed.
Beyond the door, Caedmon began to laugh. It was not a scribe’s laughter, nor the brittle release of a
frightened man. It came in measured bursts, each one ending in a wet click.
“He wrote it down,” the voice said. “He wrote it all down.”
“Open the door,” Morwenna said.
“No.”
It was the first refusal Sabelle had given her without ornament.
Morwenna slid the packet into the inner fold of her coat.
Sabelle noticed. Their gaze dropped to the motion and returned.
“You are making a mistake,” they said.
“I have made several. This one may be useful.”
“The document is bait.”
“Most intelligence is.”
“You believe it names you.”

“I believe someone wants me to believe that.”
“And if they are right?”
Morwenna placed both hands upon the edge of the table. The map between them showed the realm as a
field of old wounds: coastlines, passes, ruined holdings, roads that ended in ash. The five powers had each
laid claim to portions of it in ink, blood, or silence. The borders touched nowhere cleanly. Every boundary
was a threat pretending to be geography.
“If they are right,” she said, “then they have waited too long to kill me.”
Sabelle’s eyes narrowed.
“Perhaps they wanted you afraid first.”
“Fear is a private luxury. I have a fleet.”
“Your fleet cannot sail through a locked room.”
“No. But it can make a great deal of noise outside one.”
She crossed to the door.
Sabelle did not bar her way. That frightened her more than resistance would have.
Morwenna put her ear to the wood.
There was no sound from the corridor.
No breathing. No shifting cloth. No scrape of a boot.
She lifted the latch.
Sabelle seized her wrist.
The contact was brief, but their grip was astonishingly strong. Morwenna looked down at the fingers
around her arm, then up at the Twice-Crowned face above them.
“Let go.”
“You do not understand what is kept below this place.”
“Then enlighten me.”
“I am preventing a greater breach.”
“Of what?”
Sabelle released her.
The silence that followed was shaped like an admission.
Morwenna opened the door.
The corridor lay empty.
Caedmon was gone.
A single trail marked the flagstones, dark and shining in the brazier’s weak spill. It led away from the
room toward the stairwell. No footprints accompanied it. The trail began at the threshold and vanished

beneath the nearest wall, as though whatever had made it had been drawn through the stone.
Morwenna stepped out.
The air smelled of iron and wet earth.
Behind her, Sabelle spoke a word she had never heard them use.
Not an invocation. Not a command.
A name.
The floor split.
Stone folded inward with a roar. The room behind them dropped by the width of a hand, then another. The
map table tipped, sending ink, cups, and loose instruments sliding toward the fissure. Morwenna caught
the doorframe as the corridor pitched beneath her. Somewhere below, a vast chamber exhaled.
The sound was followed by voices.
Many voices.
Some pleaded. Some cursed. Some recited.
One voice called her by rank.
Another called her by the name she had been born with.
Sabelle caught the back of her coat and hauled her clear as the threshold collapsed into a jagged mouth.
The brazier fell through first, its coals scattering like red eyes. Then the table. Then the map, which
fluttered once in the hot dark before vanishing.
Morwenna clung to the wall.
The citadel trembled around them. Ancient dust rolled from the ceiling. A crack opened along the
corridor’s far stones, and from it came a pale gleam—not light exactly, but the suggestion of something
that remembered light.
“What have you kept here?” she demanded.
Sabelle stood at the edge of the break, staring downward.
Their face had lost its composure.
Below, in the dark, something began to climb.
A hand appeared first, grey and jointed, its nails packed with black soil. It gripped the broken stone and
pulled. A second hand joined it. The fingers trembled with effort or hunger.
Sabelle whispered, “I kept it bound.”
Morwenna reached for the knife beneath her coat.
“You said it was dead.”
“I said nothing of the sort.”
The thing hauled its shoulders above the edge.

A strip of rotted cloth hung from its neck. Beneath it, pressed into the ruin of its chest, gleamed a metal
plate stamped with a name.
Morwenna could not read it.
The hand tightened on the stone.
Sabelle moved toward the creature.
Morwenna caught their sleeve. “If that is what you keep bound, why is it climbing?”
“Because someone opened the lower door.”
“Who?”
The dead thing raised its head.
Its eyes were dark hollows, but something within those hollows turned toward Morwenna with
unmistakable attention.
From the stairwell came Caedmon’s voice, no longer frightened.
“Because the truth has been fed.”
Sabelle wrenched free.
Morwenna drew her blade.
The revenant’s mouth opened, and a spill of ancient dust poured over its tongue before it spoke.
“Admiral,” it said.
Then, from beneath the citadel, a second voice answered in Sabelle’s own voice.
The answer came from the dark below them.
“Admiral.”
Morwenna’s blade was already in her hand, its edge pale where the stairwell’s dead light touched it. She
did not look toward the second voice. To look would be to grant it shape. The ruin had learned that much
about people: attention was a kind of blood.
Sabelle stood between her and the revenant, one hand raised. The gesture had once commanded obedience
from courts, prisons, and battlefields. Here it seemed no more than a question posed to the dark.
“Come up,” Sabelle said.
Their voice echoed downward.
A heartbeat later, the voice beneath them answered in the same tone.
“Come up.”
Morwenna felt the old discipline within her draw tight. It was the discipline that had kept fleets steady
beneath stormlight, that had made her give orders while men drowned and the sea burned. It was also the
discipline that let her pass sealed intelligence into the hands of the Iron-Ring Cartel without allowing her
hand to tremble when the price was named.
No fleet was here. No signal flags. No clean horizon.

Only Greyfell Citadel, abandoned in the Shattered Vale, with its stones sweating black moisture and its
buried mouths opening one after another.
Caedmon descended three steps. His writing case hung against his side, knocking softly against the wall.
The fear had gone from him, but it had left something worse in its place: conviction.
“Do not answer it,” he said.
Sabelle’s head turned a fraction. “You answered me.”
“That was you.”
“And the voice below?”
Caedmon looked at Morwenna. His eyes had the meticulous emptiness of a scribe who had found a
discrepancy in a record and could not bear to leave it uncorrected.
“It knows what was written.”
“Then it knows lies,” Morwenna said.
“It knows what was concealed.”
The revenant made a low sound. Not a groan. Not breath. Something like parchment being slowly torn.
Sabelle moved toward it.
Morwenna caught their sleeve again. “You said it was bound.”
“It is.”
“Then bind it.”
“I did not bind its voice.”
The revenant’s fingers scraped over the stone. Its joints were swollen with old rot, but the nails were clean.
That detail struck Morwenna with peculiar force. Clean nails on a dead thing. Someone had tended it.
Someone had washed its hands, or commanded another to do so. The cellar had not been a prison
abandoned to decay. It had been maintained.
The secret beneath Sabelle’s severity had always possessed a shape. Morwenna had imagined chains,
sigils, a coffin sealed beneath a floor. She had not imagined care.
From below, her own voice whispered, “You sold the channel.”
A chill passed through her that had nothing to do with the citadel.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had never used that word. Their messages had spoken of routes, weather, shortages,
movements of men and iron. They had paid in coin, favors, silence. They had never said sold. Not where
ink might preserve it.
Sabelle looked at her.
The revenant’s hollow eyes remained fixed on Morwenna.
“Admiral,” it said again. “The Cartel knows.”
Morwenna stepped down until the point of her blade touched the revenant’s throat. The flesh there was
grey and split, but beneath it something pulsed—not blood, not life, but a faint pressure moving in time

with the voice below.
“You have the wrong woman,” she said.
Her voice beneath the stair laughed.
The laugh was hers too.
Caedmon flinched. “It is drawing from you.”
“Then it will choke.”
Morwenna pressed the blade in. A bead of dark fluid welled beneath the edge. The revenant did not recoil.
It leaned forward, inviting the steel.
Sabelle seized Morwenna’s wrist.
Their grip was not strong enough to overpower her. It did not need to be. Authority lived in the smallest
movement when one had worn it long enough.
“Do not cut it,” Sabelle said.
“You keep a dead thing in your cellar and object to cutting?”
“I object to giving it an ending.”
Something slammed against the underside of the stair.
Dust sifted from above. The wall shuddered. For one instant, Morwenna saw the citadel as it must have
appeared when it was young: grey towers unbroken, banners snapping in a wind not yet poisoned by the
Sundering, guards standing watch where the stair descended into the earth. Then the vision collapsed, and
she was back among cracked stones and the smell of wet ash.
The revenant raised one hand.
Sabelle went rigid.
The dead fingers pointed not at Morwenna, but at the writing case at Caedmon’s side.
“Open it,” said the voice below.
Caedmon wrapped both hands around the case.
“No.”
“Open it.”
The lock clicked.
Caedmon had not touched it.
He backed into the wall. The case swung once from its strap, and the leather fastenings uncoiled like small
black tongues. Papers spilled across the steps. Some were blank. Some bore lines of cramped script,
though the ink crawled and rearranged itself even as Morwenna watched.
Caedmon dropped to his knees.
“No,” he said again, more softly.
Sabelle released Morwenna and reached for the papers. Caedmon slapped their hand away.

“Do not read them.”
“I am High Inquisitor.”
“And I am the one who kept the record.”
“Of what?”
Caedmon’s mouth tightened. He looked toward the darkness beneath them.
“Of what was done when the host broke.”
The stairwell fell quiet.
Morwenna heard, far beyond the walls, the restless shifting of dead stone. She heard her own breathing.
She heard the faint creak of leather as the loose papers stirred without wind.
Caedmon gathered them with shaking hands. One sheet had landed against Morwenna’s boot.
She saw a line before she could stop herself.
The Leaden Accord.
Below it, the ink had been scraped away so violently that the parchment was nearly pierced. Beneath the
scar, another line showed through in fragments.
Both hosts—
The rest had been blackened.
Morwenna bent to seize the page.
Caedmon snatched it first.
His face had gone white.
“What did you conceal?” Sabelle asked.
“What was taken.”
“By whom?”
The voice beneath them answered.
“By all of you.”
A pressure gathered in the stairwell. It pushed against Morwenna’s ears, her teeth, the soft hollow behind
her eyes. The revenant’s mouth opened wider. Dust streamed from it in a steady veil, but its body did not
diminish. Beneath the dust, something pale moved behind the ribs.
Sabelle’s expression changed.
Not fear. Recognition.
“You know what is below,” Morwenna said.
“I know what should be below.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only answer that matters.”

Morwenna turned on them. “You brought us here.”
“I brought you to the citadel.”
“You knew the lower door was open.”
“I knew it had been closed.”
“You knew the revenant could speak.”
“I knew it had spoken before.”
The admission passed between them like a blade laid flat on a table.
Morwenna imagined the hidden reports she had sent into the Cartel’s hands: the disposition of forces, the
weaknesses of walls, the movement of supplies. She had told herself information was only information
until someone used it. She had told herself every power already possessed its own knives. The Iron-Ring
Cartel merely paid to know where the ribs were soft.
Now the dead thing knew.
Or something beneath it knew.
The five powers of the realm had made a habit of calling their hunger necessity. The Ashen Vanguard
called it duty. House Morvain called it inheritance. The Silent Choir called it silence. The Iron-Ring Cartel
called it trade. The Bleeding Crown called it law. Morwenna had served beneath each word without
kneeling to any of them.
The second voice spoke from the dark.
“Morwenna Ashgrove.”
Her full name.
The stone seemed to contract around it.
She had not heard it spoken in that voice since—No. The thought stopped before it found a memory. This
thing was not recalling. It was opening doors inside her.
Sabelle reached for the revenant’s face.
The dead thing seized their wrist.
The movement was so swift that Morwenna barely saw it. Sabelle struck the revenant across the jaw with
their free hand. The impact cracked through the stairwell. The revenant’s head snapped sideways, but its
fingers tightened.
Beneath the skin of Sabelle’s wrist, black lines surfaced.
Sabelle did not cry out. Their crown—both crowns, worn as a sign that had outlived the circumstances that
made it—seemed suddenly less like regalia than a burden hammered into the skull.
“Release me,” they said.
The revenant turned its hollow gaze upon them.
“Twice-crowned,” it whispered.
Sabelle’s face hardened.

The voice below continued, “Once for the living. Once for the dead.”
“Release me.”
“You kept what should have been destroyed.”
The words struck Sabelle more deeply than any blow. Morwenna saw it in the slight collapse of their
shoulders, in the minute delay before they pulled against the dead grip.
Caedmon stared at them.
“You said the lower door was opened,” he said. “You did not say it was opened from outside.”
Sabelle tore their wrist free. The black lines vanished beneath the skin.
“Because it was not opened from outside.”
Morwenna raised her blade again. “Then who opened it?”
Sabelle looked down.
The darkness below had begun to glow.
Not with flame. With a dim, colourless radiance that seemed to come from the bones of the citadel itself. It
climbed the walls in branching veins. The old mortar split. Somewhere beneath their feet, a mechanism
groaned awake after years without motion.
Caedmon’s papers lifted into the air.
The blank sheets filled first.
One by one, they turned toward Morwenna.
On each appeared a single sentence in her own hand.
The channel was clear.
Another.
The message was received.
Another.
No one will know.
Her stomach clenched.
The revenant released a breath that had been waiting in its corpse for centuries.
Below them, a door began to open.
Not the lower door. Something behind it.
Sabelle stepped backward. For the first time since Morwenna had known them, the High Inquisitor looked
without command.
Caedmon rose, clutching the ruined record to his chest.
“Admiral,” he said.
Morwenna did not take her eyes from the widening black beneath the stairs.

“What?”
He swallowed.
“The voice is not repeating what you said.”
The darkness opened another inch.
A pale shape pressed against the gap from the other side. It had no face, only the suggestion of one, as
though a face had been remembered by someone who had never seen a human being.
Caedmon’s voice broke.
“It is repeating what you have not said yet.”

Chapter 5
The bells of Fenspire had been silent for three nights, yet Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched still
heard them tolling beneath the stone.
They stood before the narrow window of the upper archive, one palm resting against the cold wall, while
the Gloaming Reach drowned beneath a skin of ash-colored rain. Fenspire’s stark spire rose through the
murk beyond the glass, black against black, its foundations sunk deep in the year 57 AS. The fortress had
been old when the world was young enough to remember its own wounds. Now its garrison of 3,742 kept
watch over a land that no longer knew what it guarded.
Behind Malchior, parchment whispered.
“Read it again,” they said.
The clerk swallowed. “The quarantine at Gloamreach remains in force.”
“Again.”
“The quarantine at Gloamreach remains in force.”
“And the reason?”
The clerk’s voice thinned. “Uncertainty of contagion. Uncertainty of allegiance. Uncertainty of—”
“Allegiance is not a fever.”
“No, Arch-Prelate.”
The title entered the room like a blade laid upon a table. Malchior did not turn. Their reflection hovered in
the window: the severe black of the office vestments, the pale flare of the sacred thread at the throat, the
face fashioned into calm. Flame-Touched, the old records called them. The word had been made to sound
like blessing. In the mirror-dark, it looked more like an accusation.
Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, sealed from the surrounding coast by gates, patrols, and fear. Its
garrison was 2,483. The number sat in Malchior’s mind with the weight of a stone. Too many mouths for a
sealed town. Too few hands if the gates failed.
“Who brought this?” Malchior asked.
The clerk lowered the page. “Warden-Commander Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
At last Malchior turned.
Ignatz waited beside the iron stove, still wearing the authority of command as though it were armor that
had begun to rust from within. No canonical feature marked him in the old ledgers; only the epithet
followed him, and the office. Warden-Commander. The Oathless. His silence had the distrustful shape of a
locked door.
On the far side of the chamber, Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven watched him with one hand resting against
the sleeve of her blood-red coat. She was a Blood-Mage, and the air near her seemed to remember it. Not
visibly. Not yet. But the rain tapped the window in a rhythm too close to a pulse.
Malchior knew the record of her birth: 286 AS. They knew, too, what the record did not say. Isolde had
plotted the death of her own liege. The secret had survived because secrets were more durable than kings.

“Leave us,” Malchior told the clerk.
The clerk gathered the parchment. “Arch-Prelate—”
“Leave us.”
The door shut. Its latch clicked with a finality that made Malchior’s forged lineage papers seem to rustle
beneath their robes.
They had written the papers themselves, years ago, copying the hands of dead archivists and inventing the
descent that had raised them to sanctified authority. Every seal had been warmed, pressed, and cooled
beneath their fingers. Every name in the chain had been chosen from graves no living mouth could
question. Their birth, 289 AS, had been a fact. Everything before it was architecture.
Isolde’s gaze lingered on their face.
“You look tired,” she said.
“I look consecrated.”
“You look as though consecration has teeth.”
“It does.”
Ignatz gave a short, humorless breath. “The quarantine cannot hold forever.”
“Then it will hold until it breaks,” Malchior said.
“Gloamreach is not the only concern.”
“No. It is merely the concern behind which you have chosen to hide the others.”
The Warden-Commander’s eyes hardened. “Five powers contend over the ruins. The Ashen Vanguard.
House Morvain. The Silent Choir. The Iron-Ring Cartel. The Bleeding Crown. Each claims the realm can
still be gathered into one hand. Each sends hunger dressed as doctrine.”
“And which hand gathers Gloamreach?”
Ignatz did not answer.
The stove exhaled a bitter breath. Coal-smoke threaded the room, mingling with the damp wool of their
cloaks and the mineral stink of the fortress walls. Malchior could taste iron at the back of their throat. It
was an old taste, older than office, older than the lies that had made office possible.
Isolde moved toward the table. “The report mentions Blackport.”
“The report mentions everything,” Ignatz said.
“Then mention it aloud.”
He looked at Malchior, not at her. That was a mistake. Isolde smiled without warmth.
“The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS,” Ignatz said. “It ended in 321 AS. Seventy thousand nine
hundred and seven casualties.”
“70,907,” Malchior said.
The number seemed to darken the room.

Ignatz’s jaw shifted. “The aggressors were totally routed.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor,” Isolde said. “That is what the ledgers say.”
“That is what the ledgers are permitted to say.”
The rain thickened against the glass. Fenspire’s sentries moved along the high parapets, reduced by
distance to pieces on a game board. Malchior imagined the whole Gloaming Reach laid out beneath a
hand: the spire, the sealed coast, the roads fading into ash. Somewhere beyond the rain, Gloamreach
waited behind its quarantine, and something inside it waited as well.
“The concealed truth,” Ignatz said, “is that the victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.”
The words did not echo. Stone was often more merciful than memory.
Isolde’s fingers tightened on the table’s edge. “Their own allies.”
“The wells were fouled before the final advance. Fever, thirst, panic. By the time the Cartel entered
Blackport, the surviving defenders could barely stand.”
“And you know this because?” Malchior asked.
Ignatz’s expression did not move, but something behind it withdrew.
“Because the truth has a price,” he said.
There it was: not confession, but the shape of one.
Malchior had seen the Iron-Ring Cartel’s account books once. Not the whole of them. Enough.
Intelligence traveled along hidden roads, and Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless sold intelligence to the
Iron-Ring Cartel. The fact had not yet been placed in any official record. It had not needed to be. A man’s
silences could be more legible than ink.
“You speak with unusual precision,” Malchior said.
“I speak with the precision required to keep Fenspire standing.”
“Fenspire has stood since 57 AS.”
“Stone does not stand by virtue of age.”
“No,” Isolde said. “It stands because someone keeps paying for the blood in its mortar.”
Her voice had softened. That was worse than anger. Malchior watched her hand. Blood-Mages were
taught to conceal their work in the smallest gestures: a pressure at the wrist, a fingernail drawn across a
seam, a breath held one moment too long. Isolde had plotted the death of her own liege. Such treachery did
not make her careless. It made her patient.
“You want the quarantine lifted,” Malchior said.
“I want the gates opened.”
“To what?”
“To witnesses.”
The word fell between them.

Ignatz glanced toward the window. “There are messages from the coast. People inside Gloamreach claim
the garrison has begun to ration water.”
“The garrison is 2,483,” Malchior said. “The number has not changed.”
“Numbers do not drink.”
“Nor do they lie.”
“Numbers are the first lie ever told.”
Malchior felt the forged papers beneath their robes again, though they were not there. Their skin prickled
as if a hidden flame had been brought too near. For a moment the chamber seemed to narrow around them,
the walls leaning inward to hear whether the Arch-Prelate’s blood was pure, whether the sanctity had a
foundation deeper than ink.
They reached for the report.
The parchment was wet at one corner.
Malchior looked down. A dark stain had spread through the fibers, reddish-brown, not rainwater. Isolde’s
hand remained on the table. A thin line of red had appeared beneath one of her nails.
“You have been reading this already,” Malchior said.
“I have been touching it.”
“Those are not the same.”
“They are, when the page is afraid.”
Ignatz stepped forward. “There is more.”
“There is always more.”
“The coast road from Gloamreach to Fenspire is being watched.”
“By whom?”
He hesitated.
Malchior folded the report. “You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. Do not sell me hesitation.”
The room became very still.
Isolde’s eyes gleamed, not with surprise but appetite. Ignatz’s hand drifted toward the weapon at his side
and stopped before touching it. The gesture was so small that another person might have missed it.
Malchior did not.
“I sell what keeps the realm from burning,” Ignatz said.
“The realm is already ash.”
“Then I sell the shape of the ash.”
“And the Cartel pays you?”
Ignatz’s silence answered.

Outside, one of the sentries lifted a horn but did not sound it. Along the lower wall, a gate chain groaned.
The noise traveled upward through the stone, a slow metallic shudder, as if Fenspire itself had woken
beneath them.
Isolde tilted her head.
“Someone is at the gate.”
“No one enters Fenspire without notice,” Ignatz said.
“Then someone has entered without notice.”
Malchior crossed to the window. Through the rain they saw torchlight below: three points wavering in the
courtyard, then four. A figure stood between them, hooded and motionless. No banner. No escort. The
gatehouse guards had lowered their spears, but not raised the alarm.
The Flame-Touched Arch-Prelate pressed two fingers to the glass.
Heat answered from somewhere beneath the skin.
Their claimed lineage was suspect. Their authority was strained. Their name rested upon papers forged by
their own hand. Yet the fire came when called, and that had always been the most dangerous proof.
“Open the archive door,” Malchior said.
Ignatz stared at them. “Why?”
“Because whoever waits below has come for the accounting.”
Isolde’s smile widened.
Malchior felt the old bells begin again, tolling under the stone, while from the courtyard there rose a voice
too low to distinguish and a second voice answering from within the fortress.
Then the lights went out.
The dark did not arrive all at once.
It gathered first in the corners, thickening where the lamps had burned. Then it climbed the walls in slow
black folds, swallowing the painted saints, the iron sconces, the pale square of the archive door.
Somewhere below, a hinge groaned. The voice in the courtyard ceased. The answering voice within the
fortress breathed once against the stone.
Malchior kept two fingers upon the glass.
Heat answered.
A coal-red thread opened beneath the skin of their hand and ran toward the wrist, thin as a vein seen
through ice. The old fire had never been obedient. It had only been persuaded to appear where obedience
would do the most harm.
“Ignatz,” they said.
“I am here.”
His voice came from near the door. A scrape of metal followed, then the muted click of a sword being
drawn. Warden-Commander Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless had a talent for making every silence sound

accused.
“Where is Isolde?”
“Where you left them.”
A soft laugh moved through the dark.
“Liar,” Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven said.
Their voice came from the opposite side of the chamber, close enough that Malchior felt the warmth of
another body in the cold. Blood-Mage. Born in 286 AS. The record had been copied in three hands, each
hand trembling differently. Their liege had died without a blade wound, and Isolde had mourned with such
perfect grief that even the dead might have believed it.
Malchior lifted their hand from the glass.
The thread of fire brightened.
For one breath, the chamber returned: the long archive table, the black ribs of the ceiling, Ignatz standing
with one hand upon his sword and the other hidden in his coat. Isolde stood beneath the sealed door,
smiling as if the darkness had been arranged for their pleasure.
Then the flame folded inward.
“Do not use that,” Ignatz said.
“You object to light?”
“I object to what answers it.”
The bells beneath the stone gave another toll. It was not loud. It did not need to be. The sound passed
through Malchior’s bones, finding the places where old vows had been buried and shaking them awake.
The archive door opened by itself.
Not wide. A seam first, blacker than the surrounding dark, then the slow widening of a mouth. Cold air
spilled from the stair beyond. It smelled of dust, salt, and something sweet that had gone rotten in a sealed
jar.
No one moved.
Malchior heard their own breathing and hated it for being so mortal.
On the threshold, carved into the stone, the seal of the Ashen Vanguard had been scored through. Beneath
it, five marks waited in a circle: the Vanguard’s ash-spear, House Morvain’s crowned thorn, the closed
eye of the Silent Choir, the linked rings of the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the bleeding diadem of the Bleeding
Crown.
The five powers had come to the same door without coming together. That was the shape of the realm
after the Sundering: every hand upon the same throat, each finger pretending not to feel the others.
Ignatz stepped forward.
Malchior raised a hand. “No.”
His sword stopped halfway from his body.

“Why?” he asked.
“Because the door opened for me.”
“Nothing opens for free.”
“Then we will discover the price.”
Isolde moved past him. The hem of their robe brushed the floor with a dry whisper. “You sound like a
priest.”
“I am an Arch-Prelate.”
“No.” Isolde tilted their head. “You serve as Arch-Prelate. There is a difference.”
The fire under Malchior’s skin shivered.
There it was: the little blade slipped between the ribs. Their claimed lineage was written on paper they had
forged with their own hand. The ink had been mixed with ash and a drop of blood, because desperation
had made ritual seem more convincing than truth. They had copied the names of the dead until the letters
began to look like wounds.
The documents were locked beneath this fortress.
Or they had been.
“Walk,” Malchior said.
The stair descended farther than the foundations should have allowed. Its walls sweated black moisture.
Each step had been worn shallow at the center, though the dust lay undisturbed along the edges. Someone
had used the passage recently. Someone had carried something heavy.
Ignatz came behind them, silent now.
Malchior did not turn. “You have been in the lower archive.”
“No.”
“Your boots say otherwise.”
“Your fire says too much.”
Isolde’s fingers touched the wall. They left a dark smear that glistened wetly before sinking into the stone.
“Blood remembers paths,” they murmured.
“Stone remembers weight,” Ignatz said.
“And men remember coin.”
The pause after that was small and complete.
Malchior slowed.
Behind them, Ignatz breathed in through his nose. The Oathless had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring
Cartel, though no confession had been dragged from him and no seal had broken upon his tongue.
Malchior knew because the wrong reports had reached the wrong hands, because patrols had vanished
from roads that only a handful of commanders knew existed, because Cartel agents had begun anticipating
orders before they were issued.

Ignatz’s secrecy clung to him more heavily than armor.
“Careful,” he said.
“Are you warning me?”
“I am advising restraint.”
“You advise restraint whenever your purse is threatened.”
His sword came free.
The sound ran down the stair like a drawn breath.
Isolde looked back, their smile gone now. “There it is.”
At the bottom, a corridor opened beneath the fortress. The ceiling was low enough that Ignatz had to bow
his head. Narrow shelves had been built into both walls, packed with ledgers, sealed scrolls, bone tablets,
and small clay vessels marked with dates.
Malchior’s gaze caught on one line of ink.
Fenspire. Founded in 57 AS. Garrison: 3,742. Status: garrisoned.
The figures were written in red.
Farther along, another ledger had been pulled free and left open upon the floor.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Garrison: 2,483. Status: quarantined.
The word seemed to breathe.
Beyond the shelves, a map had been nailed to the wall. The coast had been drawn in a pallid wash, the
land beyond it rendered in dim gray. Fenspire stood as a black spire in the Gloaming Reach. Gloamreach
lay farther out, sealed behind a ring of red ink.
“Who keeps these records?” Ignatz asked.
“Those who expect the realm to survive its rulers.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one we have.”
A sound came from behind the far wall.
Three taps.
Then two.
Isolde pressed their palm flat against the stone. The skin at their wrist opened in a fine red line. Blood
welled and ran downward, but did not fall. It crawled across the wall, following cracks that had been
invisible until then.
Malchior caught their arm.
The blood stopped.
Isolde looked at the hand around their wrist. “You touch me as if I belong to you.”

“I touch you as if you are about to kill us.”
“I have killed for less flattering accusations.”
Their eyes held his in the dark.
The liege, Malchior thought. The plotted death. The hidden hand behind it. The grief worn afterward like a
ceremonial veil. Isolde had never denied the shape of the crime. They denied only the shame.
“Release me,” Isolde said.
Malchior did.
The blood withdrew into the cut. The wound sealed with a wet gleam.
Another three taps came from the wall.
Then two.
Ignatz turned toward the stair. “We should leave.”
The archive door above slammed shut.
Dust fell in a soft gray veil.
No one spoke.
From the wall came a voice.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched.”
The name was pronounced with care, each syllable tested.
Malchior’s mouth dried.
The fire stirred in their hand, hungry now.
“Show yourself,” Ignatz commanded.
“Warden-Commander Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
Ignatz’s sword lifted.
The voice continued.
“Born in 258 AS.”
His silence was answer enough.
Isolde began to laugh beneath their breath.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” said the wall. “Born in 286 AS.”
The Blood-Mage’s amusement faded.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched. Born in 289 AS.”
The corridor seemed to narrow.
The voice did not mention their office. It did not call them Arch-Prelate. It named the birth and nothing
more, as though everything earned afterward were counterfeit.

Malchior placed their palm against the wall.
Heat spread through the stone. Dust leapt from the mortar. Somewhere beyond, something withdrew with
a wet scrape.
“Open,” Malchior said.
A panel shifted.
Behind it lay a chamber no larger than a cell. A single table waited within. Upon the table rested three
objects: a blackened crown, a sealed iron ring, and a ledger bound in pale leather.
The iron ring bore the mark of the Cartel.
The crown dripped no blood, yet the stone beneath it was stained as though it had bled there for years.
The ledger lay open to a page headed:
The Purge of Blackport.
Malchior stepped inside.
The ink was dark and crowded.
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. Casualties: 70,907. The aggressors were
totally routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Below that, in a hand nearly erased by scraping, another sentence remained.
The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Ignatz stood behind Malchior, very still.
Isolde read over their shoulder. “So the Cartel won by killing the people who made victory possible.”
“Not all victories are clean,” Ignatz said.
“No,” Malchior replied. “Some are merely well concealed.”
The sealed iron ring trembled on the table.
A drop of water struck the ledger.
Then another.
Malchior looked upward.
Nothing moved above them, but the ceiling had begun to darken. Water gathered in the cracks, black and
shining. It slid down the walls in thin streams, carrying the smell of salt and rot.
Gloamreach.
The quarantined coast had found a way beneath the fortress.
The voice spoke again, now from inside the chamber.
“Your papers.”
Malchior stared at the pale leather ledger.
Their pulse struck once, hard.

Isolde’s head turned toward them. Ignatz’s sword lowered by a fraction, not from mercy but attention.
“Your lineage,” the voice said. “Read it aloud.”
The forged pages were somewhere beneath the floor. They could feel them—not with sight, not with
touch, but with the old certainty by which fire recognized dry timber.
Malchior placed both hands upon the ledger.
The cover was warm.
“Open the book,” Isolde whispered.
“I am trying.”
“No.” Their voice sharpened. “You are deciding whether to lie.”
The water reached Malchior’s boots.
In the dark beyond the table, something inhaled.
And the first page began to turn beneath their hands.
The page turned without a hand.
Ink bled through the fibers in thin black veins. Malchior watched the letters gather, separate, and gather
again until they formed a line that seemed to have been written by a trembling child.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched, born in 289 AS.
The water lapped higher around their boots.
Isolde’s breath touched the side of their face. “There.”
“I can read.”
“Then read.”
Malchior found the words in their throat and held them there. The ledger’s warmth had become a fever.
Beneath the floor, the forged pages waited in darkness, their false seals softening in the damp. They had
prepared lies for courts, for altars, for frightened men who needed ancestry to make obedience seem holy.
They had not prepared a lie for a book that knew the shape of truth.
“Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched,” they said. Their voice did not break. That was something.
“Born in 289 AS.”
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless shifted behind them. Leather creaked. Steel whispered against its sheath.
The ledger turned another page.
A second line appeared.
Arch-Prelate.
The title stood alone, stark as a gallows.
Malchior felt the old pressure settle across their shoulders—not the weight of vestments or the ceremonial
chain at their throat, but the weight of every kneeling head they had blessed. They had learned, long ago,
that sanctity was often a posture held until the room believed it. Chin raised. Hands still. Eyes lowered at

precisely the proper moment.
The book had no use for posture.
“Arch-Prelate,” Isolde repeated. “That is what you claim.”
“It is what I serve as.”
“Serve,” she said, and the word came wetly, almost fond. “You make a sacrament of verbs.”
The ledger’s pages fluttered though the room was windless.
Malchior looked toward her. The dimness made a blade of her cheek. Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven stood
with one hand bare and the other stained dark to the wrist. Blood-Mage, the courts called her when they
wanted to frighten petitioners into silence. She wore the title as another person might wear mourning: not
to display grief, but to keep it near.
She had plotted the death of her own liege.
The knowledge rested between them, unspoken and sharp. Malchior had seen the evidence once, sealed
beneath a confession that had never reached its intended reader. A thread of blood drawn through a map.
A name cut out of a prayer. Isolde’s work, or work done in her manner. She had never denied it. Denial, to
her, was merely confession with better manners.
The page showed a new line.
Lineage:—
Nothing followed.
A clean emptiness.
The thing beneath the floor inhaled again.
Ignatz came around the table. The water folded away from his boots and returned with a soft, sucking
sound. He was a Warden-Commander, born in 258 AS, and the old title clung to him more stubbornly than
any oath. Oathless, they called him. A name that had begun as accusation and hardened into rank.
His gaze stayed on the ledger.
“Read the blank,” he said.
Malchior’s fingers tightened on the cover. “There is nothing to read.”
“There is always something written in a blank space.”
“You should know.” Isolde’s eyes did not leave him. “You have sold enough secrets to learn their price.”
Ignatz’s attention moved to her.
For one instant, no one breathed.
Then the water stirred around Malchior’s ankles as if something below had smiled.
Ignatz secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. The fact had reached Malchior in fragments:
patrol routes altered without orders, supply wagons diverted toward roads no Warden had marked, sealed
reports appearing in hands that had no right to possess them. Ignatz had not been careless. Carelessness
was for men who believed innocence could protect them.

“Careful,” he said.
Isolde’s stained hand lifted. A thread of red stretched from her fingers into the water, thin as spun glass. “I
am always careful.”
“You plotted the death of your own liege,” Malchior said.
The blood-thread quivered.
He had not intended to speak the words aloud. They escaped with the sour taste of truth.
Isolde smiled, but there was no warmth in it. “And you forged your own lineage papers.”
The ledger snapped shut.
The sound shook dust from the beams.
Malchior’s reflection trembled across the cover. Flame-light lived in their eyes though no flame burned in
the room. The old name—Flame-Touched—had been placed upon them by mouths that desired a miracle
and could not bear the ordinary ugliness of survival. They had let it remain. They had built around it. They
had forged the papers because the realm demanded a bloodline before it would permit a person to stand
above the altar.
Not a lie, they had told themselves.
A bridge.
A bridge was still made of false timber if the river took it.
The floorboards groaned.
From below came the unmistakable scrape of paper against stone.
Isolde’s head tilted. “Bring them up.”
“I cannot.”
“You can.”
“The water has reached the foundation.”
“Then drown with them.”
The voice beneath the table spoke through the wood.
“Blackport.”
Malchior’s hands went cold.
The ledger opened by itself.
Ink flooded the first page, running in rivulets that gathered into a heading.
The Purge of Blackport.
The letters shone with a dull, rust-colored sheen.
Ignatz swore under his breath.

Malchior had stood in Blackport after the last fires died. They remembered no faces clearly—only mouths
open in the dust, only the sour reek rising from wells whose surfaces shone with an oily rainbow. The
Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. It caused 70,907 casualties. The aggressors
were totally routed.
The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Those were the words carved into every official account.
The truth had been kept beneath the words, where water could reach it.
The victors had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Malchior read aloud.
At the final sentence, the room seemed to contract around them.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel poisoned the wells of their own allies,” they said.
Ignatz moved first.
His sword came free in a pale arc, and Isolde’s blood-thread hardened into a line of red glass. The ledger
slammed shut between them, its cover striking Malchior’s knuckles. Pain flashed bright enough to make
the room vanish.
When sight returned, the boards beneath the table had split.
The forged pages rose through the crack.
They came slowly, sodden and gray, pushing upward as though the dead were offering scraps of skin.
Wax seals floated loose from them. Malchior saw their own hand in every false stroke: the careful
imitation of a dead clerk’s script, the invented descent, the heraldic mark copied from a shield glimpsed
under rain.
Their lineage.
Their salvation.
Their sentence.
Isolde seized the top page. The blood in her hand ran across it, following the ink as if both had been made
for the same purpose.
“You made these,” she said.
Malchior did not answer.
Ignatz’s sword point rested against their ribs. “How many copies?”
“Enough.”
“That is not a number.”
“It was never meant to be counted.”
The Warden-Commander’s mouth tightened. “The Cartel will pay for the original.”
A silence followed—not surprise, but confirmation.

Malchior looked at him. “So they know.”
“They know what matters.”
“They know you sell intelligence.”
“They know I deliver it.”
“And what do they intend to purchase tonight?”
Ignatz’s sword pressed harder. Through the cloth, the cold entered Malchior’s flesh.
Isolde turned the wet page. “Perhaps they intend to purchase an Arch-Prelate with no blood behind the
title.”
“Perhaps,” Ignatz said.
“Perhaps they intend to purchase a throne.”
The word struck harder than the sword.
Beyond the chamber walls, bells began to ring.
Not the measured bells of worship. Not the warning peal used to summon wardens. These were broken,
irregular blows, as if someone had thrown a body against the bell-rope.
Malchior counted the intervals without meaning to. The sound carried through stone and water, through
the hidden corridors where servants slept beneath their blankets and armed men waited for orders they
believed came from a living world.
The five powers of the Ashen Era had learned to wait for weakness.
The Ashen Vanguard would call this a breach of sacred order. House Morvain would call it an
opportunity. The Silent Choir would call it a confession. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call it a bargain. The
Bleeding Crown would call it proof that every crown was only a wound held upright.
The ledger opened again.
This time the page held no writing.
A drop of blood fell from Isolde’s hand and struck the paper.
The blank drank it.
Words rose beneath the red stain.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Quarantined. Garrison: 2,483.
Malchior’s stomach tightened.
A second line appeared beneath it.
Fenspire. Gloaming Reach. Founded in 57 AS. Garrison: 3,742. Garrisoned.
The names seemed to possess distance. Gloamreach came with the taste of salt and ash, sealed away from
the Pale Coast by suspicion no decree had been strong enough to lift. Fenspire stood in the mind like a
single dark tooth above the Gloaming Reach, its soldiers watching through narrow windows, its vigilance
made permanent by fear.

No one in the room had spoken those places.
Yet the ledger wrote them as if they had been waiting beneath Malchior’s tongue.
Isolde leaned closer. Her voice fell to a murmur. “What connects them?”
“I don’t know.”
“That is the first honest thing you have said.”
The page shuddered.
A line formed under the locations.
The forged lineage opens the sealed road.
Malchior stared until the letters blurred.
The chamber filled with a smell of wet iron. Beneath the floor, something struck the stones once. Then
again. Patiently. It was not trying to escape.
It was knocking.
Ignatz withdrew his sword a fraction. “What sealed road?”
Malchior’s pulse beat against the blade.
In the ledger’s polished cover, their reflection changed. The face remained theirs, but the eyes showed
another light: a burning gate, a procession of figures moving beneath a sky the color of old bruises, and
beyond them a throne with no one seated upon it.
The book turned one final page.
There, in ink still shining wet, was a sentence addressed to them alone.
Read aloud the name you forged.
Malchior opened their mouth.
From beneath the floor, the hidden pages answered in their own voice.

Chapter 6
Rain worried the roofs of Hollowvale like a patient hand seeking a weakness.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood beneath the open arch of the command tower and watched the lower yards
drown by degrees. Water slid from the parapets in silver cords. It gathered in the ruts between the stores,
darkened the ash, and carried splinters of old timber toward the sluice. Below, figures moved through the
weather with their heads bowed, cloaks drawn tight, their labor reduced to gestures in the grey.
She had commanded Hollowvale since 311 AS.
The fact had been written into ledgers, proclamations, orders sealed in wax and pressed beneath rings. It
had been spoken aloud in halls where men measured a woman’s authority by the number of witnesses
willing to deny it. Since 311 AS, every wall, vessel, chain of stores, and watchfire here had answered to
her.
Yet the fortress had never felt like hers.
Ownership was a word for merchants and fools. Command was the narrower, colder thing. It meant that
when the gate opened, someone had decided it. When the bells sounded, someone had chosen the hour.
When a body was carried from the yard beneath a sheet, the silence around it belonged to the officer who
had permitted the silence to remain.
Morwenna kept her hands clasped behind her back.
The document in her sleeve had begun to soften from the damp.
Across the tower chamber, Caedmon Fellgard bent over the table with a quill in his hand. He was a Scribe,
and his posture had the disciplined misery of a man who believed disorder to be a moral offense. Ink, sand,
folded papers, and narrow tablets occupied every inch before him. He had arranged them according to a
system Morwenna had never understood and had never disturbed. Caedmon would rather lose a page than
find it in the wrong place.
“Read it again,” she said.
Caedmon’s quill paused.
“The account of the western stores?”
“The other one.”
He lowered his eyes to the sheet. “You have heard it twice.”
“I have heard your voice twice. That is not the same thing.”
The Scribe drew breath through his nose. He was reserved even in irritation, which made his irritation
more visible. “The report states that three sealed crates were received after nightfall. Their marks were
damaged. The porter who signed for them could not identify the sender. The seals were—”
“Not the crates.”
Caedmon looked up.
Morwenna turned from the arch. The chamber smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the metallic cold that
came down from the stone. “The note beneath it.”

“The private notation?”
“Read it.”
His gaze shifted toward the door.
No one stood there. No one that Morwenna could see. That did not make the room empty. Hollowvale had
more ears than windows. Servants listened because listening cost nothing. Guards listened because fear
trained them to. Clerks listened because secrets gave shape to their otherwise shapeless lives.
Caedmon folded his hands over the report. “It is not entered into the register.”
“Then you may read it without entering it.”
“That is contrary to my office.”
“Your office is to keep records. Mine is to decide which records deserve to survive.”
The rain thickened against the archway. A gust drove mist into the chamber, feathering the nearest
candles. Caedmon placed one hand over the papers until the corners settled.
“‘The Iron-Ring Cartel has moved agents along the coast,’” he read. “‘Their interest remains fixed upon
the disposition of the old—’”
He stopped.
“Continue.”
“The last word is illegible.”
Morwenna almost smiled. “How convenient.”
“I did not make the weather.”
“No. You merely make certain it is remembered.”
A shadow passed across Caedmon’s face. He bent again over the paper. “The note concludes that the
Cartel believes the command at Hollowvale has received no intelligence regarding their movements.”
“And has it?”
Caedmon’s fingers tightened on the page. “I am not the commander.”
“No. You are a Scribe.”
“I know what I am.”
“Then record the answer.”
He raised the quill, though there was no ink on its nib. “What answer?”
Morwenna looked toward the rain.
For nine years she had worn Hollowvale’s authority. Since 311 AS, the fortress had spoken through her
orders. It had spoken of shortages, patrols, quarrels, disappearances, and the small humiliations by which a
garrison was kept obedient. But another voice had traveled out from these walls, hidden beneath official
dispatches and carried by hands that never knew what they carried.
The Iron-Ring Cartel paid for certainty.

Morwenna sold them intelligence.
Not allegiance. Allegiance was too tender a word for what passed between them. She sold them
movements, dispositions, weaknesses in the chain. She sold them the shape of danger before danger
acquired a face. Each piece left her in a different form: a correction in a cargo manifest, a delayed order, a
sentence altered by one word. No confession survived the transaction. No signature bound her to it.
Only the consequences remained.
“The answer,” she said, “is that Hollowvale has received nothing.”
Caedmon’s expression did not change, but his silence sharpened.
“Nothing?” he asked.
“Write it.”
“If that is false—”
“It is an official answer.”
“That was not my question.”
Morwenna approached the table. The floor was cold through her boots. “You are becoming bold,
Caedmon Fellgard.”
“I am becoming tired.”
“Tired men make errors.”
“Errors are entered into the record. Tired men are not.”
His voice remained quiet. That was the danger in him. A louder man could be dismissed, punished,
frightened into obedience. Caedmon offered no surface to strike. He simply remained, meticulous and pale
beneath the lamplight, asking the question again by refusing to pretend he had not asked it.
Morwenna placed two fingers on the edge of the private notation.
“Write,” she said.
He dipped the quill.
Before its point touched the page, the bell below began to toll.
Once.
The sound crossed the rain and entered the chamber as a pressure rather than a note. Caedmon froze. The
second toll came lower, swallowed by the walls. On the third, voices rose in the yard.
Morwenna did not move toward the stair.
“Who is arriving?” Caedmon asked.
“If the bell knew, it would not be ringing.”
A fourth toll. Then a fifth.
Not an alarm. The measured summons reserved for someone who carried authority enough to make delay
dangerous.
