Caedmon sanded the wet ink and closed the report. “Should I prepare the receiving register?”
“No.”
“Then what should I prepare?”
“Nothing that can be found.”
He looked at her, and for the first time she saw fear beneath the reserve. It was not fear for himself. That
would have been simpler. It was fear of being forced to write what he understood.
The tower door opened without a knock.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned entered with rain darkening the shoulders of their coat. They
brought the weather in with them: the smell of wet stone, extinguished ash, and the bitter herbs burned in
sanctuaries when prayers had failed. Their office seemed to arrive before them. High Inquisitor. The
words needed no announcement.
Their gaze passed over Caedmon, the table, the papers, and came to rest on Morwenna.
“Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned,” Morwenna said.
“Fleet Admiral.”
The title sounded like a judgment when Sabelle spoke it.
Morwenna inclined her head. “You have traveled through unpleasant weather.”
“I have traveled through worse.”
There were many answers to that. Morwenna selected none.
Sabelle removed one glove finger by finger. “I require the Cartel’s latest movements.”
Caedmon lowered his eyes.
Morwenna watched the glove come free. Sabelle’s hands were steady. Their severity was not theatrical. It
lived in the economy of every gesture, in the refusal to waste motion on reassurance.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel is declared victor of The Leaden Accord,” Sabelle said. “That declaration has given
them appetites.”
“Victors often develop appetites.”
“The Leaden Accord ended in ruin.”
“Most accords do.”
“Fourteen thousand and eleven dead.”
The number settled between them with the weight of a stone dropped into deep water.
Morwenna’s attention flicked toward Caedmon. His quill remained poised above the register.
Sabelle continued, “Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm. Yet the Cartel behaves as if it inherited
more than a title.”
The hidden artifact.

Morwenna felt the thought move through her like a blade drawn beneath cloth. Supposedly destroyed.
Spirited away. The truth had never appeared in any report she had signed, yet absence had its own
grammar. A missing line. An empty vault. A convoy that existed only in the records of those who
expected it not to exist.
“Victories breed rumors,” Morwenna said.
“Rumors breed corpses.”
“Then you should ask the dead what they heard.”
Sabelle’s eyes narrowed. “I am asking you.”
The lamps fluttered. Somewhere below, the gate chains groaned.
Morwenna had faced storms at sea, mutinies in narrow waters, and councils where every smiling mouth
concealed a knife. She knew how authority behaved when it met resistance. It did not always strike.
Sometimes it waited. Sometimes it invited the other person to condemn themselves by filling the silence.
She let the silence remain.
Sabelle turned to Caedmon. “Scribe.”
Caedmon straightened. “High Inquisitor.”
“Are the fleet records complete?”
“Which records?”
“The ones that concern the Cartel.”
A bead of water slid from Sabelle’s sleeve and fell onto the floor.
Caedmon’s gaze moved to Morwenna. It was not an appeal. He knew better than to appeal. It was a final
measurement of the distance between duty and survival.
Morwenna heard, with terrible clarity, the scratch of his quill if he answered wrongly.
“Caedmon,” she said.
“Yes, Fleet Admiral.”
“Bring me the coastal dispositions.”
Sabelle’s attention returned to her. “And the private accounts.”
“There are no private accounts.”
“There are always private accounts.”
“Not in my command.”
“You have commanded Hollowvale since 311 AS.”
Morwenna’s pulse did not change. The words had been spoken plainly, but they struck with the precision
of a key finding its lock.
“Yes,” she said.
“Then you will know what passes through its hands.”

“I know what I permit to pass.”
“And what do you permit now?”
From the yard came a cry, abruptly cut short. The bell ceased. Rain filled the silence after it.
Caedmon gathered the papers. One sheet slipped from the stack and struck the wet stone. He bent to
retrieve it, but Sabelle moved first.
Their gloved hand closed over the page.
Morwenna saw the broken seal.
Not the report.
The private notation.
Sabelle unfolded it.
For one breath, no one spoke. Then Sabelle’s eyes moved across the writing, and the chamber seemed to
narrow around the three of them.
Morwenna reached for the pistol beneath her coat—not drawing it, merely feeling the familiar
weight—and said, “Give me that page.”
Sabelle did not surrender it.
The page remained between their fingers, its wet edge curling as though the rain had found a way inside
the chamber. Caedmon’s hand hovered near the papers, careful and useless. He looked at Morwenna, then
at Sabelle, and in that brief movement she saw the scribe choose survival over loyalty.
“Give me that page,” she repeated.
Sabelle raised their eyes.
The crowns upon their brow—one dark metal, one pale as old bone—caught what little light the room
possessed. Rain threaded down the high windows. Beyond the glass, the yard had become a smear of grey
cloaks and black water.
“You have a pistol beneath your coat,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna’s hand remained still. “You have an observation.”
“I have a habit of observing what others conceal.”
“And I have a habit of removing obstacles.”
Caedmon swallowed. The sound was small, but in the narrowed chamber it seemed to strike the walls.
Sabelle folded the page once. The broken seal flaked beneath their thumb.
“What does this mean?” they asked.
Morwenna felt the old discipline settle over her like armor. No breath wasted. No glance offered without
purpose. The instinct had carried her through decks burning under ley-fire, through councils where men
smiled while measuring the distance to her throat, through every order she had given from Hollowvale
since 311 AS.
“It means you have read a private notation.”

“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only answer you are entitled to.”
Sabelle’s mouth moved without becoming a smile. “Entitlement is a word used by those who have
mistaken access for authority.”
“Then you should understand it well.”
Caedmon bent over the table and began gathering the scattered sheets. His fingers trembled now. A blot of
ink had spread across one report, turning a column of disciplined marks into a dark bruise.
Morwenna watched him. “Leave them.”
He stopped.
“If a single page disappears,” she said, “I will know.”
“Yes, Fleet Admiral.”
His voice had the dry, abraded sound of a man trying not to be heard.
Sabelle looked down at the notation again. The page had been written in a tighter hand than the report,
with no heading and no destination. A line of cipher marked the upper margin. Beneath it, in plain script,
were the words that had tightened the chamber around them.
Gauntlet of Sorrowfell housed in Greyfell Citadel.
Morwenna had seen the sentence before. She had paid for it before she had seen it. That was the
distinction she had built her life upon: the hand that carried knowledge and the hand that spent it were not
always the same.
Sabelle read the line aloud.
The rain seemed to draw nearer.
“Gauntlet of Sorrowfell housed in Greyfell Citadel.”
Caedmon made a faint sound.
Morwenna turned on him. “Did you write that?”
“No.”
“Did you copy it?”
His eyes dropped to the table. “I copied what was placed before me.”
“By whom?”
The silence after the question was not empty. It had weight. It had teeth.
Sabelle slid the page across the table, but not toward her. Their palm remained on it.
“You see?” they said. “The scribe has no answer.”
“The scribe has the answer. He lacks the courage to speak it.”
Caedmon flinched.

Morwenna regretted the cruelty only because it had been visible. Cruelty was useful when kept clean.
Publicly, it bred witnesses. Privately, it bred obedience.
She stepped closer to the table. The rain had soaked the hem of her coat. Cold water touched her boot
through the leather. Somewhere below, a door slammed, followed by the muffled rush of feet. The fortress
was awake in the manner of a wounded animal: every sound a warning, every silence a held breath.
“Where did you find this?” she asked.
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened. “You know the location.”
“I know a line on a page.”
“You know more than that.”
“Then why ask me?”
“Because I want to hear what you will deny.”
Morwenna looked at the crowns. The title was not decoration. High Inquisitor was a blade with a human
hand around its hilt, and Sabelle had never been shy about showing the edge. Yet there was something
beneath the severity tonight. An impatience, perhaps. Or fear, buried deep enough that another person
might have mistaken it for composure.
Morwenna did not mistake it.
Greyfell Citadel lay abandoned in the Shattered Vale, outside the realm’s core holdings. A place of grey
stone and older silences. A stronghold emptied of its purpose, left to weather and thorn and the patient
work of collapse. That was what official records said. Official records were doors built to keep the curious
from seeing the hinges.
“You have no warrant,” Morwenna said.
“I require none to question a scribe.”
“To seize naval papers?”
“I have not seized them.”
“To interrogate an admiral?”
Sabelle’s fingers tightened on the page. “You came here armed.”
“I go everywhere armed.”
“That is not innocence.”
“No. It is prudence.”
Caedmon’s breathing had become shallow. Morwenna could hear the scratch of rain against stone, the
creak of the table, the small metal click of something beneath Sabelle’s sleeve. A chain, perhaps. Or a
clasp. She wondered what they carried under the black layers of their office. Relics. Instruments. Keys.
The thought came unbidden of a cellar beneath some sanctified floor, and of something bound there,
breathing without lungs.
She dismissed it. Imagination was another form of carelessness.

Sabelle leaned across the table. “The Gauntlet of Sorrowfell was housed in Greyfell Citadel.”
The words were deliberate now—not read, but declared.
Morwenna let her face remain unchanged.
“Was?” she said.
A glimmer passed through Sabelle’s eyes.
“There,” they murmured.
“Where?”
“You corrected the tense.”
“I corrected nothing.”
“You asked whether it was housed there. Not whether the statement was true.”
“I asked what you meant.”
“You asked whether it was still there.”
Morwenna felt the pistol’s weight beneath her coat, reassuring in its simplicity. A weapon never lied about
what it wanted. A weapon wanted a body opened. Men and women wanted reasons.
She turned from Sabelle to the window.
The yard below was crowded with movement. Lanterns shuddered in the rain. A line of figures crossed
between the buildings, their heads bowed beneath hoods. The citadel had been built to make every person
feel watched, and the architecture had succeeded long after the builders were dust.
“Greyfell Citadel is abandoned,” she said.
“Yes.”
“It lies outside the realm’s core holdings.”
“Yes.”
“Then the notation is either stale or false.”
“Or accurate.”
“Those are not the only options.”
“They are the only options that matter.”
Morwenna saw the reflection of Sabelle in the black window: two crowns, a pale face, the dark hand
resting over the page. Behind that reflection, Morwenna saw herself only as a shape. No features, no
history. The station spoke more clearly than a face ever could. Fleet Admiral. Command. Discipline.
Authority.
And beneath all of it, the quiet arithmetic of betrayal.
The Iron-Ring Cartel did not need every secret. It needed the right ones. A passage left unwatched. A
convoy delayed. A garrison supplied with the wrong certainty. Information was not a coin, though men
who lacked imagination treated it as one. It was a current. It moved beneath every border and carried

kingdoms toward whatever shore had paid to summon it.
This page had not been meant for Sabelle.
That was the danger.
“Who else has read this?” Morwenna asked.
Sabelle’s expression did not shift. “You are concerned.”
“I am assessing the breach.”
“Of what?”
“Security.”
“Not possession?”
Morwenna turned back to them. “Possession of what?”
The question hung between them.
Caedmon’s hand went to the edge of the table. “High Inquisitor,” he said quietly, “the notation was among
the sealed records. I did not place it there.”
“No one accused you,” Sabelle said.
“You did not need to.”
“Then you understand the benefit of silence.”
Morwenna watched Sabelle’s face. There were many forms of control. Some were built from fear, some
from devotion, some from the knowledge that the person across the room possessed a secret capable of
ending you. Sabelle wielded all three, but not evenly. The page had unsettled them.
That made it valuable.
“Give it back,” Morwenna said.
Sabelle folded it again, smaller this time. “You will tell me what it concerns.”
“I will not.”
“You will tell me who sent it.”
“I will not.”
“You will tell me whether the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell remains in Greyfell Citadel.”
Morwenna held their gaze.
“No.”
The answer was clean. It satisfied none of them.
Sabelle slipped the folded page into the inner pocket of their robes.
Morwenna drew the pistol.
She did not point it. The room changed regardless.

Caedmon recoiled from the table. Sabelle did not move, but the air around them seemed to harden. Rain
struck the windows in a sudden, furious burst, and somewhere in the walls a pipe groaned like a buried
thing waking.
“Take it out,” Sabelle said.
“Give it back.”
“You threaten a High Inquisitor over a scrap of writing?”
“I threaten anyone who steals from my command.”
“Your command.” Sabelle’s voice softened. “Is that what this is?”
Morwenna’s thumb rested against the pistol’s grip. The metal was cold enough to sting.
“I have no patience for riddles.”
“No. You have patience for concealment.”
“And you have patience for trespass.”
“I have patience for truth.”
“Truth is what survives examination.”
“Truth is what remains after the convenient parts have been burned.”
The words entered her more deeply than they should have. For an instant she smelled smoke—not the
damp coal stink of the chamber, but the bitter white smoke of a deck lost under stormlight. She saw no
faces. Only hands reaching through glare, and the black shape of something falling where no sea should
have been.
Then the memory closed.
Sabelle saw the change. Of course they did.
Their hand moved toward the inside of their robe.
Morwenna raised the pistol.
Caedmon gasped. “Please.”
The word was almost tender. It made him look younger, though Morwenna had no reason to know his age
and no desire to guess it.
Sabelle stopped with their fingers against the hidden pocket.
“Is that how you command Hollowvale?” they asked.
“You know how I command.”
“I know what reports claim.”
“Then read the reports.”
“I have read enough reports to know that paper is a poor witness.”
“Paper is the only witness that does not grow tired.”

“Paper can be altered.”
“So can memory.”
“So can orders.”
A knock sounded at the chamber door.
All three turned.
It came again: measured, restrained, not the urgent pounding of a guard bearing immediate news.
Morwenna kept the pistol raised. Sabelle’s hand remained inside their robe. Caedmon stood trapped
between the table and the door, his eyes flicking from one to the other.
A voice spoke through the wood.
“Fleet Admiral?”
Morwenna knew the voice, but not the speaker’s name, and did not need to invent one.
“What is it?” she called.
“The watch has found something in the lower yard.”
Sabelle looked at her.
Morwenna lowered the pistol by a fraction. “What?”
“A body.”
The rain filled the pause.
“Whose?” Sabelle asked.
The voice beyond the door hesitated.
Morwenna felt the page move inside Sabelle’s robe as they shifted their weight. A small motion. A hidden
decision.
The guard said, “We do not know.”
Sabelle’s eyes remained on Morwenna.
She understood then that the page was no longer the only breach. The notation had been carried into the
chamber by one secret, and the body had arrived with another. Somewhere below, beneath rain and stone,
someone had crossed the citadel’s defenses and paid for it.
Or been made to pay.
“Open the door,” Morwenna said.
Neither Sabelle nor Caedmon moved.
Morwenna kept her pistol trained toward the threshold and spoke more quietly.
“Open the door,” she said again, “and bring me the page before we go.”
The guard’s hand went to the latch.

Morwenna watched the iron move. The chamber seemed to contract around it: wet stone, lamp smoke, the
close stink of wool soaked through by the rain. Caedmon stood beside the table with his fingers pressed
flat against the ledger, as if the record might otherwise crawl away. Sabelle had not shifted. Their face
held the same pale severity it had worn since entering Greyfell Citadel, but something had changed behind
the eyes.
Not fear.
Recognition.
The door opened inward.
A body lay on the threshold, folded beneath a black cloak. Rainwater ran from the hem and gathered in the
grooves between the flagstones. One hand protruded from the cloth, the fingers broken back toward the
wrist. A strip of red cord had been tied around them.
Caedmon made a small sound.
Morwenna did not lower the pistol. “Bring it in.”
The guard bent, then stopped when Sabelle said, “No.”
The word struck harder than a shout.
Sabelle crossed the room. They knelt beside the body and drew back the hood. A face emerged from the
wet cloth, grey with cold and streaked with blood that the rain had diluted to pink. The mouth had been
sewn shut with black thread.
Morwenna felt the page shift beneath Sabelle’s robe.
Not a twitch. A pressure.
The page was not paper, then. Or not only paper. Something rigid rested against Sabelle’s ribs, concealed
beneath the heavy layers of their inquisitorial coat. Morwenna had seen contraband hidden in boots,
weapon grips, prayer boxes, even inside the hollow bones of dead birds. She had never liked mysteries
that moved when their owners breathed.
“Who is it?” she asked.
“The question is less useful than why they were sent here.” Sabelle touched the red cord with one gloved
finger.
Caedmon’s gaze had fixed on the corpse. “The seal—”
“Is not a seal,” Morwenna said.
He looked at her.
“Then what is it?”
“A warning.”
The guard glanced toward the stairwell. Beyond the open door, the citadel groaned in the weather.
Greyfell Citadel had been founded in 62 AS in the Shattered Vale, when the stone was still considered
defensible and the dead below it were still considered silent. Now the place stood abandoned, outside the
realm’s core holdings, its towers exposed to the rain and its lower passages open to whatever had learned

how to walk without leaving footprints.
Sabelle pulled the sewn thread from the corpse’s mouth.
The dead lips opened.
A folded scrap of waxed cloth had been packed between the teeth.
Caedmon stepped forward before Morwenna could stop him. Sabelle caught his wrist.
“You are a Scribe,” they said. “You produce and keep written records. You do not put your hands into
messages concealed in corpses.”
Caedmon flushed. “If it concerns the fleet—”
“It concerns everyone who can read.”
Sabelle removed the cloth and laid it on the table. The lamp flame bent toward it, thin and blue at the
edges.
Morwenna’s pistol remained trained on Sabelle’s heart.
“Open it,” she said.
Sabelle gave her a dry look. “You issue commands as if this were Hollowvale.”
“It is not Hollowvale. That is why I am asking.”
A faint smile touched Sabelle’s mouth. It carried no warmth. “You were born in 288 AS, Morwenna
Ashgrove, and still you mistake permission for authority.”
Morwenna’s finger rested along the pistol’s frame. “You were born in 263 AS, Sabelle Mournvale the
Twice-Crowned, and still you mistake secrecy for power.”
Caedmon looked between them. The guard did not move at all.
The rain battered the shutters.
Sabelle unfolded the cloth.
Inside lay a narrow strip of treated skin covered in cramped notation. Caedmon leaned toward it, then
recoiled as though the ink had breathed.
Morwenna saw columns, marks, interrupted circles. A cartographer’s language, perhaps. Or a cipher
designed by someone who believed ordinary letters were a kind of confession.
At the bottom, written larger than the rest, were three entries:
The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS.
The Leaden Accord ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties.
Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm.
Caedmon whispered, “That is the accepted account.”
“Accepted accounts are graves with their names removed,” Sabelle said.
Their finger moved lower.

A supposedly destroyed artifact was spirited away.
Morwenna felt the room lose its warmth.
For a moment she saw another chamber—not this one, not any chamber she had ever entered willingly.
She saw ledgers passed under tablecloths, coded manifests hidden among powder inventories, quiet
payments made in iron weights. The Iron-Ring Cartel had paid for scraps no one else thought worth
stealing: routes, shortages, patrol changes, the moods of commanders. Morwenna had sold them
intelligence because information was lighter than gold and easier to bury.
She had never sold them this.
The line seemed to darken under her gaze.
Sabelle watched her watching it.
“You know something,” they said.
“I know that ink is not proof.”
“You know the Cartel would bleed for the artifact.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel bleeds for anything it can weigh.”
“And you would know what they are willing to weigh.”
The accusation did not need to be spoken plainly. It entered her like cold water through a split seam.
Caedmon’s hand hovered over the strip. “There is more.”
Morwenna turned to him. “Read it.”
He swallowed. “The lower notation refers to a transfer. No destination. No carrier. Only a mark that
resembles—”
His voice broke off.
“What?” Morwenna asked.
Caedmon looked toward the corpse.
The dead hand had curled inward. The fingers were no longer broken back.
The guard saw it too and drew his sword.
Sabelle rose.
The body’s chest gave a wet, shallow shudder.
Morwenna fired.
The pistol’s report tore through the chamber. Smoke flashed white in the muzzle. The corpse struck the
stones as the shot entered its throat, scattering black thread and blood across the threshold.
The guard swore. Caedmon stumbled into the table.
Sabelle did not flinch.
“You might have waited,” they said.

“I did.”
The corpse’s fingers scraped once against the floor.
Then again.
Morwenna’s pistol came up for a second shot, but Sabelle had already taken the guard’s blade. They drove
it down through the body’s sternum with both hands. The point struck stone beneath, and the corpse
bucked around the steel.
A sound came from it—not speech, not breath, but a congested moan that seemed to rise from beneath the
floor.
Caedmon backed away. “That cannot be.”
Sabelle’s face had become empty.
“Everything can be,” they said. “Given a cellar.”
Morwenna stared at them.
The secret revealed itself not in the words but in their calm. Sabelle did not react as a person confronted
with an impossible thing. They reacted as a keeper whose property had escaped its chain.
Somewhere beneath the citadel, a revenant waited in Sabelle’s cellar.
The thought arrived whole and obscene.
Sabelle looked at her, and Morwenna knew they had seen understanding take shape.
“Do not,” Sabelle said.
“Do not what?”
“Make a decision with that knowledge.”
Morwenna considered the pistol, the page, the dead thing nailed to the floor. “You are in no position to
dictate my decisions.”
“Neither are you.”
The corpse’s mouth opened. The gums were packed with grey ash. Its eyes rolled toward the dark beyond
the door.
There came a knock from below.
Not at the door.
From under the flagstones.
Caedmon’s face emptied of color.
A second knock followed, slower than the first.
Sabelle withdrew the sword from the corpse. “We leave now.”
Morwenna seized the waxed strip before they could fold it away. “We leave with the page.”
Sabelle’s gaze dropped to the place beneath their robe where the rigid shape pressed against their side.

“You have not earned it.”
“I command Hollowvale.”
“Since 311 AS.”
The words were quiet, almost courteous. “And yet Hollowvale is not here.”
Another knock sounded beneath them.
The guard crossed himself in the old manner. Morwenna did not. She had learned young that gestures
meant to ward off darkness often served only to announce where one hoped it would not look.
Her first memory of command was not of victory. It was of a sealed room and men waiting for her to
speak while smoke crawled along the ceiling. She had been born in 288 AS, and the world had spent every
year since teaching her that authority was merely fear with a uniform on it.
She extended her free hand.
“Give me the page.”
Sabelle held her stare.
“Ask properly.”
Morwenna heard Caedmon breathing behind her. The guard’s sword dripped onto the stones. Beneath
their feet, something dragged its nails across the underside of the floor.
She lowered the pistol by a fraction.
“Please,” she said.
Sabelle smiled then—not with triumph, but with the tired satisfaction of someone watching a lock yield.
They drew the page from beneath their robe.
It was not paper. It was a thin, translucent membrane, yellowed at the edges, with writing that seemed to
have been burned into it from the reverse. As Sabelle held it out, the ink rearranged itself.
Caedmon whispered, “It is changing.”
Morwenna took the page.
The surface was warm.
A line appeared beneath the others.
Palewell Abbey stands in The Pale Coast. It was founded in 244 AS, rebuilt, and maintains a
garrison of 5998. It is not a core holding.
Below that, new marks gathered like insects around a wound.
A route. A tide chart. A sequence of symbols that ended at the abbey.
Palewell Abbey: austere, pale stone above the coast, rebuilt into a fortress and left watchful beneath the
realm’s indifference. A garrison of 5998, enough to make the place seem guarded, not enough to make it
safe. The page had named its weakness with the same cold precision it used for the dead.
The Iron-Ring Cartel would pay dearly for this.

Morwenna felt the old calculation rise in her—the weight of disclosure, the hidden recipient, the price that
could be demanded. She had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel before. She would sell it again if
survival required it.
But the page was warm against her palm, and something below the floor had begun to whisper.
Not words.
A name.
Sabelle’s name.
The flagstones split.
A black finger emerged between them, slick with cellar mud.
Sabelle seized Morwenna’s arm. “Run.”
Morwenna tore free and fired into the crack.
The shot vanished downward.
For one breath, there was silence.
Then the citadel answered from every floor below them, and the whisper became a scream.

Chapter 7
The water in Gloamreach tasted of iron.
Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven held the cup beneath her nose and breathed through the sourness. The
liquid trembled against the black glaze, reflecting the narrow window and the pale smear of the coast
beyond it. Gloamreach lay on the Pale Coast, where the sea had gnawed the land into white shelves and
drowned the roads in salt. Even behind shuttered stone, the place smelled of wet ash.
They did not drink.
“Set it down,” Isolde said.
Ossric Ashgrove obeyed. He placed the cup beside the ledger with both hands, as though the vessel might
accuse him if he touched it carelessly. Quartermaster was his office, and every movement bore the timid
precision of a man accustomed to counting what other people wasted.
“The seal is unbroken,” Ossric said.
“Seals are mouths with wax over them.”
His eyes flicked toward the cup. “The water was drawn from the inner cistern.”
“Then the inner cistern has learned deceit.”
A gust pressed against the shutters. Somewhere below, a bell gave a single muffled note. The quarantine
had been proclaimed over Gloamreach for so long that the bell no longer summoned anyone. It merely
reminded the living that the dead still possessed a voice.
Isolde turned from the window.
The room had been built for command and made suitable for suspicion. A table. A brazier low on coals. A
rack of weapons that no hand had polished since the last rain. On the wall, a map of the Pale Coast had
curled away from its pins, its edges gray with damp. Gloamreach was marked in faded black. Beyond it,
the ink roads dwindled toward Fenspire, whose stark spire rose in the Gloaming Reach like a spear driven
through the earth.
“Read it again,” Isolde said.
Ossric lowered his head over the ledger. “The stores received from Fenspire are short by—”
“Not that part.”
His finger remained between the columns. “The notation concerning the sealed wagons?”
“Read it.”
He swallowed. “The wagons were admitted under Warden-Commander authority. The accompanying
order bears the mark of Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The name remained in the room after Ossric stopped speaking.
Isolde felt the old appetite stir beneath their ribs. Blood answered blood, though it had no right to answer
the blood of strangers. Their fingers tightened against the table. The wood complained.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” they said softly. “A guardian who sends sealed water into a quarantined
hold.”

“Perhaps the wagons contained grain.”
“Perhaps.”
“They were not opened.”
“Then you know what they contained?”
“No.”
“Good. You are still capable of fear.”
Ossric’s face did not change. No canonical face had ever been granted him; he wore only the expression
the room demanded. At present, it demanded obedience.
The door opened without a knock.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched entered beneath the lintel, robes gathered in one hand to keep
them from the wet floor. The other hand rested upon the silver chain of office at their throat. Their
authority arrived before them, sanctified and strained, like a hymn sung through clenched teeth.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” Malchior said.
“Arch-Prelate.”
“Do not make that title sound like a wound.”
“Then stop wearing it as armor.”
Malchior’s gaze moved to the cup. “You have not drunk.”
“I have not become careless.”
“The quarantine ordinances require all provisions to be tested.”
“By whom?”
“By the appointed hands.”
“Whose hands?”
Malchior’s mouth thinned. Their claimed lineage was a thing of papers and seals, a tower built upon ink.
Isolde had seen how fiercely they defended it. A person who forged their own lineage papers understood
better than most that authority was not inherited; it was manufactured, then guarded until the witnesses
died.
“Do you intend to challenge the appointment?” Malchior asked.
“I intend to challenge the water.”
“You command Gloammarch since 310 AS. You do not command every throat in Gloamreach.”
“No,” Isolde said. “Only the throats that remain attached.”
Ossric looked down.
Malchior stepped nearer the table. Their shadow crossed the ledger, blotting out the columns. “The
Iron-Ring Cartel has sent assurances.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel sent assurances during the Purge of Blackport.”

Malchior’s fingers closed around the silver chain.
“The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS,” Isolde continued. “It caused 70,907
casualties. The aggressors were totally routed. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.”
“And what does that have to do with a shipment?”
“Ask the wells.”
Silence took the room.
There were old stories of Blackport, though stories were only corpses that had learned to travel. The wells
had been poisoned by the victors’ own hands, so the allies would die with the enemies. The Iron-Ring
Cartel had called it necessity. The dead had called it thirst.
Malchior’s voice fell low. “You accuse them without proof.”
“I accuse them with memory.”
“Memory is not evidence.”
“It is when the evidence has been buried in a well.”
Ossric shifted beside the ledger. “There is another matter.”
Isolde looked at him.
He drew a second sheet from inside his coat. The paper was stiff with damp, and a dark thumbprint stained
its lower corner.
“Speak.”
“The order for the wagons was countersigned by the Choir.”
“The Silent Choir?”
“Yes.”
“Which voice?”
Ossric hesitated.
“Which voice?”
“No voice is given.”
The brazier released a coal with a soft collapse. Red light breathed through the ash.
Malchior reached for the sheet. Isolde placed one hand over it.
The pressure was slight. It was enough.
Blood-magic did not require spectacle. The old teachings had made it vulgar, dressing it in knives and
bowls, in red rivers poured across altars. The true work was quieter. A pulse beneath the skin. A thread of
warmth drawn unwillingly toward the fingertips. A command whispered into the wet machinery of the
body.
Ossric stiffened.
Isolde felt the rhythm in his wrist. Quick. Quick. Slower.

“You will not touch him,” Malchior said.
“I have not.”
“You are touching him now.”
“Then he should give me a reason to stop.”
Ossric’s breathing became shallow. “The order is genuine.”
“Did I ask whether the mark was genuine?”
“No.”
“Did you verify the cargo?”
“No.”
“Did you drink from the cistern?”
“No.”
“Why not?”
Ossric’s eyes rose to theirs. For an instant, there was something there beyond timidity. Not courage.
Calculation, perhaps. A small animal deciding whether the trap had sprung.
“I was told the quarantine made inspection unnecessary,” he said.
“By whom?”
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The blood in Ossric’s wrist faltered.
Isolde released him.
He drew a breath that sounded like a blade being pulled free.
Malchior unfolded their sleeve. “This performance is beneath you.”
“Then tell me why a Warden-Commander would forbid a quartermaster from inspecting provisions
entering Gloamreach.”
“Because the order carried authority.”
“Authority is not an answer.”
“It is the answer by which the realm survives.”
“No. It is the answer by which cowards sleep.”
The Arch-Prelate’s eyes hardened. Firelight laid a false gold along their cheek. “You have always
mistaken defiance for discernment.”
“And you have mistaken forged paper for blood.”
Malchior went still.
The insult had found its mark, though Isolde felt no satisfaction. Satisfaction was a soft thing. It made a
person linger where they ought to leave.

At the window, the shutter rattled again. Beyond it, the quarantine cordons cut the streets into empty
passages. No faces appeared between the buildings. No carts moved. Gloamreach had become a sealed
vessel, and every seal invited the question of who had filled it.
“Open the wagons,” Isolde said.
Malchior turned toward the door. “I will not permit this.”
“You have no permit to withhold.”
“I speak for the sanctified authority of the realm.”
“You speak for yourself.”
“I speak for the Crown.”
“The Bleeding Crown?”
Malchior’s expression did not break, but the skin beneath their eyes tightened.
Isolde leaned close enough to smell the smoke clinging to their robes. “Then let the Bleeding Crown come
here and drink first.”
The Arch-Prelate raised one hand.
The air changed.
Not visibly. Not yet. But the room filled with the pressure of an invoked rite, with the dry taste of old
words gathering behind the teeth. Isolde felt their own blood answer, eager and treacherous. It wanted to
rise. It wanted to show Malchior what grievance could do when given a vein.
Instead, Isolde smiled.
“Do it,” they whispered.
Malchior’s hand trembled once.
The door opened again.
This time the guard outside did not enter. A voice came through the gap, muffled by the rain.
“Command.”
Isolde kept their eyes upon Malchior. “What?”
“The western gate has been opened.”
Ossric made a sound under his breath.
“No gate opens in quarantine,” Malchior said.
“Who opened it?” Isolde asked.
The voice faltered. “The order bears the mark of Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
There it was: the clean stroke of the knife.
Isolde looked toward the window. Across the pale, drowned streets, a horn began to call from the western
quarter. Once. Twice. A third time, answered by another horn farther inland.

The garrison of Gloamreach numbered 2,483, and every one of those throats could now be summoned into
the dark.
Malchior stepped back from the table. “You cannot move the garrison without authorization.”
“I command Gloammarch since 310 AS.”
“That is not the same as command of Gloamreach.”
“No,” Isolde said. “It is worse.”
They took the cup from the table.
The water inside had gone perfectly still.
Isolde drew a small knife from beneath their sleeve and cut across the pad of their thumb. One red bead
gathered, bright as a coal. Ossric watched it with horror. Malchior watched it with calculation.
Isolde let the blood fall.
The bead struck the water.
For a breath, nothing happened.
Then the cup began to whisper.
The whisper thickened until it seemed to have weight.
It crawled over the rim of the cup and fell into the room in threads, brushing the stone walls, the shuttered
window, the iron hinges of the door. Ossric flinched as though something wet had touched his neck.
Malchior did not move. The flame-touched planes of their face remained composed, but a pulse worked
beneath the skin at their temple.
Isolde kept their bleeding thumb above the water.
The blood did not disperse. It opened like a red eye.
“Speak,” Isolde said.
The cup answered in a voice made from several voices, none of them wholly human. It breathed through
the syllables. It dragged them over the table as if they were bones.
“Gloamreach…”
Ossric’s hands closed around the edge of the table. “You said this would show the command.”
“It shows what the command fears.”
“I have no fear of command.”
“That,” Malchior murmured, “is the first lie you have told tonight.”
The water shuddered.
A pale shape rose beneath its surface: not a face, not yet, but the suggestion of one pressed against ice.
Isolde leaned closer. The chill from the cup entered their cut thumb and climbed the arm, seeking the
heart. They welcomed it. Pain was a language they trusted because it had no patience for invention.
The shape altered.

A tower appeared in the water, narrow and black against a colorless sky. Its uppermost point vanished into
mist. Below it, walls bristled with watchfires. The lights did not burn yellow. They burned the dull blue of
old bruises.
Fenspire.
The image trembled, and the spire’s shadow spread across the table. It touched the sleeve of Malchior’s
robe. The Arch-Prelate glanced down at it, and for the first time their composure cracked.
“Why Fenspire?” Ossric asked.
Isolde said nothing.
They had never seen the place, but the cup had no need of eyes. It showed not what was known, but what
had been bound beneath the known. The tower stood in the Gloaming Reach, disciplined and watchful, a
blade driven into the dimness. The garrisoned walls seemed to listen for footsteps beyond their reach.
Then the image darkened.
A road emerged, pale with ash. On it moved a line of men and beasts beneath covered standards. No sigils
showed. The cloth was soaked too heavily with rain—or something darker—for its pattern to be read. The
procession halted before a gate.
A man stepped from beneath the foremost canopy.
His face refused to settle.
Isolde saw the cut of a commander’s coat, the posture of someone accustomed to being obeyed, the
stillness of a person who had learned to place silence where an oath should have been. The cup swallowed
his features and returned them wrong: an eye, a mouth, a cheekbone, then blankness.
The whisper spoke.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless, a member of House Morvain.”
Ossric made a small sound.
Malchior’s hand moved toward the chain beneath their robe, where some private token lay hidden. They
stopped before touching it.
Isolde watched the image of Ignatz approach the gate.
“You know him,” they said.
“Everyone who has served long enough knows the name.”
“That was not my question.”
“It was the only answer you are entitled to.”
The man in the cup lifted one hand. The gate opened before him. No sentry challenged him. No horn
sounded. The road beyond was empty, but the darkness gathered on either side as though waiting to be
given orders.
The cup whispered again, softer now.
“House Morvain.”

The words slid beneath Isolde’s skin.
House Morvain had old walls, old claims, old appetites. It could lend a name to a sword and call the
wound lawful. It could turn a private grievance into a public necessity, then mourn the dead with a dry
eye. Isolde had learned that power did not require innocence. It only required witnesses willing to forget
what they had seen.
The image shifted.
A hand rested on a map.
No border could be made out. No banners. Only roads, coastlines, and black marks spreading like mold
beneath the skin of parchment. One mark pulsed near the sea. Another answered from inland. The fingers
moved between them with deliberate care.
Malchior leaned over the cup.
“Stop this.”
Isolde looked at them. “You are afraid of a map?”
“I am afraid of people who mistake symbols for commands.”
“Then you are safe. I mistake nothing.”
The cup’s red eye widened. A filament of Isolde’s blood pulled from the wound and stretched toward the
image. It trembled, thin as spider silk, before sinking into the painted roads.
The room filled with the smell of wet iron.
Ossric shoved backward from the table. His stool struck the wall and fell. “This is forbidden.”
“You brought the cup.”
“I brought a sealed vessel for a sealed inquiry.”
“You brought a witness.”
His face had gone gray. In the candlelight, the quartermaster looked younger than his office, almost
painfully so. The fear in him was not theatrical. Isolde could smell it beneath the wool of his coat, sharp
and sour.
Malchior turned on him. “You said the water came from the eastern cistern.”
“It did.”
“Who touched it?”
“No one.”
“Nothing is touched by no one.”
Ossric swallowed. “It was taken under guard.”
“Whose guard?”
His mouth closed.

There it was—the little door in him, the place where an answer had been locked away. Isolde felt the
blood in the cup stir in recognition. Not guilt, precisely. Guilt was too warm a word. This was calculation
cooling into terror.
“Name the guard,” Isolde said.
“I cannot.”
“You can.”
“I was ordered not to.”
“By whom?”
The whisper in the cup began to laugh.
It was not a human laugh. It had no mirth in it, only the grinding rhythm of stones forced together beneath
deep water. The tower of Fenspire blurred. The road vanished. Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood again
in the red-black depths, though now his face was clear enough to reveal a scar at the mouth.
Isolde had not seen that scar before.
The blood-mage’s own reflection stared back at them from the water beside his.
Their faces touched.
For an instant, Isolde felt another will enter the cut in their thumb. It did not push. It waited. That was
worse. A hand upon a door, patient because it knew the door would open.
A memory rose that was not theirs.
A chamber with no windows.
The taste of ash.
A voice reciting terms.
Ignatz standing before someone seated beyond the reach of the light. The seated figure was only a shape.
No face. No title. The air between them seemed stretched taut by obligation.
Isolde heard the last words clearly.
“Tell House Morvain the coast is not dead.”
The memory snapped.
The cup burst.
Not shattered—burst. Its water leapt upward in a dark column, striking the ceiling, then fell in a rain of
cold droplets. The blood on Isolde’s thumb burned black. Ossric cried out and shielded his face. Malchior
seized the edge of the table as the stone beneath it groaned.
For a heartbeat, the room held the smell of salt and rot.
Then every candle went out.
Darkness closed around them.

Ossric was breathing too quickly. Malchior’s robe rustled. Somewhere beyond the door, a boot scraped
across stone and halted.
Isolde felt the shape of the knife beneath their sleeve. Their thumb throbbed. The cut had sealed itself,
though the skin around it had gone numb.
“Who is outside?” Ossric whispered.
“No one,” Malchior said.
The boot scraped again.
Isolde smiled without warmth. “You are both becoming careless with that word.”
They moved toward the door. The dark seemed reluctant to release them. It clung to their clothing, tugged
at their hair, pressed its damp mouth against the back of their neck. Behind them, the cup lay intact on the
table. Empty now. Its inner surface was filmed with a red residue that formed no pattern Isolde could read.
The latch lifted.
Malchior said, “Do not open it.”
“Why?”
“Because you have not asked who sent the guard.”
“Neither have you.”
“I am asking you not to open it.”
Their hand rested on the latch.
The voice from the cup returned, not from the table this time, but from the other side of the door.
“Isolde.”
Ossric whimpered.
Malchior’s breath stopped.
Isolde knew the voice. It had no name in the room, but it carried the authority of a command that had once
been obeyed. Their fingers tightened around the iron until the metal bit the palm.
“Say it again,” Isolde whispered.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven.”
The title entered them like a hook.
There were many ways to pronounce Unforgiven. Some made it an accusation. Some made it a prayer.
Some made it a warning offered too late. This voice gave the word its oldest meaning: not the one who
had been denied pardon, but the one who had ceased to seek it.
Behind Isolde, Malchior spoke in a low, controlled voice. “You will not answer.”
“Why?”
“Because a name can be a summons.”
“And if I have already been summoned?”

“Then you are standing at the wrong door.”
The corridor beyond fell silent.
Isolde pictured the dark outside: the narrow passage, the damp stones, the guards who would have been
told to wait somewhere else. They pictured the door opening inward, the space beyond empty, and the
waiting thing occupying the blind angle beside the hinge.
Their blood knew before their mind did.
Someone had been admitted.
Not into the chamber.
Into the bargain.
Isolde opened the door.
The door opened on Ossric Ashgrove.
He stood with one hand lifted, as though the wood had interrupted a knock he had not yet decided to give.
Rain silvered his shoulders. He wore the plain dark coat of a quartermaster, its hem stained with
road-mud, and held a narrow iron case against his ribs.
Behind him, the passage was empty.
Isolde looked first at the floor. No wet footprints but Ossric’s. No shadow laid wrong beneath the lamps.
No breath steaming in the cold.
Then they looked into his face.
“Who admitted you?”
Ossric swallowed. “No one.”
Malchior came to stand at Isolde’s shoulder. The Arch-Prelate’s presence seemed to draw the darkness
into order. Candlelight struck the scorched planes of their skin and made a saint of every scar.
“That is not an answer,” Malchior said.
“It is the only one I have.”
“Then you have come carrying an answer you do not understand.”
Ossric glanced at Isolde. He had the anxious eyes of a man who counted things because numbers did not
change their minds. “I was told to bring this to the commander of Gloammarch.”
“You were told by whom?”
His gaze fell to the iron case.
The latch was sealed in black wax. Not with a crest. With a fingerprint.
Isolde felt the old pressure behind their eyes, the blood in their skull tightening as if some invisible hand
had closed around it. A summons could be written in ink. A bargain could be written in blood. This was
neither. It was a door pretending to be a message.
“Give it to me,” Isolde said.

Ossric did not move.
Malchior’s fingers brushed the sleeve of Isolde’s coat. A warning, light as ash.
“Quartermaster,” Malchior said, “you were born in 333 AS. You have survived by remembering who
ordered what, and when. Remember this moment carefully.”
Ossric’s mouth tightened. “I remember.”
“Then remember obedience.”
“I remember that men who obeyed at Blackport were buried beside men who refused.”
The name changed the room.
Blackport came back in the smell of the rain: brine, rot, and the bitter mineral taste that had clung to every
well after the Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS. It had ended in 321 AS with 70,907 casualties and the
total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel had emerged as victor.
The official accounts called it a triumph of discipline.
The wells had called it something else.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Isolde remembered a boy with blue lips trying to drink from a cup that had already killed his mother. They
had been younger then, though not innocent. Innocence was only ignorance that had not yet been
punished.
“Bring the case inside,” Isolde said.
Ossric crossed the threshold.
The door shut behind him with a soft, final click.
Malchior looked at the iron seal. “Where did you find it?”
“In the stores beneath the western armory.”
“You were searching the stores?”
“I was inventorying them.”
“And this was inventory?”
“No.” Ossric placed the case on the table. “This was hidden beneath a false bottom in a crate marked lamp
oil.”
Isolde remained standing. Their reflection trembled in the polished iron: a pale face, dark eyes, the signs
of the Blood-Mage written not on the skin but in the way the air seemed to recoil from their hands.
“Who has access to that armory?”
Ossric’s eyes flicked once toward Malchior.
The Arch-Prelate smiled without warmth. “Say it.”
“Warden-Commander Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The name settled between them.

Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless served House Morvain. His authority had always carried the blunt weight of
a locked gate, but Isolde had learned that gates were most useful to those who knew which side of them
held the keys.
Malchior’s face did not change.
“Open it,” they said.
Ossric shook his head. “The seal is not mine to break.”
“Nor mine,” Malchior said.
Isolde reached for the case.
Blood stirred beneath their fingernails.
The wax softened before their touch. Its black surface shivered, then split with a wet whisper. A thin line
of red appeared along the seam—not their blood, not Ossric’s. It smelled of iron left in rain.
The case opened.
Inside lay three folded sheets, a brass token, and a strip of parchment so narrow it looked like a dead moth.
The top sheet bore a list of places.
Fenspire. Gloamreach.
Beneath each name, figures had been written in a precise military hand.
Fenspire: garrison 3,742.
Gloamreach: garrison 2,483.
Isolde’s fingers went cold.
Fenspire stood in the Gloaming Reach, founded in 57 AS, its stark spire raised above the dim land like a
finger held to the mouth of the world. Gloamreach was quarantined, sealed away from the coast by
suspicion and orders no sane person questioned aloud.
The figures were not estimates. They were not the sort of numbers a quartermaster copied for comfort.
They were the counts of bodies that could be fed, armed, moved, or killed.
Malchior leaned over the table. “That inventory is current?”
Ossric nodded. “The figures were corrected three times.”
“By whom?”
“I do not know.”
“You do.”
“I know whose hand wrote them.”
“Whose?”
Ossric looked again at Isolde. “Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless.”
The second sheet contained roads. Not roads as they appeared on maps, but roads as they existed beneath
weather: dry crossings, collapsed bridges, stretches where patrols were thin. Beside each route were small

marks, each one shaped like a ring cut through by a blade.
The Iron-Ring Cartel’s sign.
Isolde read without touching the page.
“Why would a Warden-Commander keep Cartel marks in a sealed armory?” they asked.
Ossric’s answer came too quickly. “He would not.”
“Then why are they here?”
“I said I do not know.”
“You said the writing was his.”
“I said the hand was his.”
“Do you believe those are different things?”
The quartermaster’s face had gone gray. “I believe a man may write what another man commands.”
Malchior lifted the brass token.
One side showed the five-pointed device of the Iron-Ring Cartel. The other was blank except for a shallow
depression, round and dark, as if something had been pressed into it and removed.
“A payment token,” Malchior murmured.
“No,” Isolde said.
Their blood had begun to listen.
They placed one fingertip against the brass. A pulse moved through it. Not warmth. Memory.
A gloved hand.
A table.
A ring of iron sliding across wood.
A voice speaking behind a closed door.
The impression vanished before the words became clear.
Isolde withdrew their hand.
Malchior watched them. “What did you see?”
“Enough.”
“That is not a quantity.”
“It is the only one you are getting.”
The Arch-Prelate’s eyes narrowed. In the candlelight, the forged lineage papers hidden beneath their robes
seemed to weigh upon them more heavily than any holy relic. Isolde had seen those papers once: seals too
old, witness marks belonging to the dead, a family line assembled with the patient desperation of a thief
building a staircase from stolen wood.
Malchior had made a life from documents no blade could test.

Now they looked at the Cartel token as though it had the power to expose every lie ever written.
“Read the last sheet,” they said.
The parchment strip was blank.
Isolde held it above the candle.
Letters rose from the fibers, darkening one stroke at a time.
The door is open.
Ossric made a sound in his throat.
More words surfaced.
The command is divided.
Then:
The blood remembers its debt.
The flame bent sideways.
Somewhere beyond the chamber, a bell rang once.
Not the hour bell. Not the alarm.
A single note, struck with the hesitation of a hand testing whether the metal was alive.
Malchior turned toward the door.
“Did you tell anyone you were coming here?” Isolde asked Ossric.
“No.”
“Did anyone see you take the case?”
“No.”
“Then why is the bell ringing?”
Ossric stared at the parchment. “I don’t know.”
Isolde looked down at the final line as it emerged from the blankness.
The ink was not black now. It was red.
Bring the Unforgiven to the one who killed their liege.
For one breath, the chamber held no sound but rain.
Their liege’s death had been plotted in rooms just like this: under lamplight, with maps weighted by iron,
with voices lowered whenever servants passed. Isolde had told themselves it had been necessary. They
had called it justice when no one else was listening.
The body had fallen.
The crown had remained.
They had thought the bargain ended there.

Malchior reached for the parchment.
Isolde caught their wrist.
The Arch-Prelate looked at them. “You know who this means.”
“No.”
“You do.”
“No.”
A second bell rang.
This time, something answered from the corridor.
Three slow knocks.
Ossric backed away from the door. The iron case slipped from his hand and struck the floor. The brass
token rolled in a small circle before coming to rest at Isolde’s boot.
The blank side faced upward.
In its shallow depression, blood began to gather.
Not from any wound.
From the air.
Malchior’s voice became very quiet. “Do not open it.”
Isolde stared at the door.
The knocking came again.
Three times.
Their blood moved toward it.

Chapter 8
The rain came sideways across the battlements, needling the black flags until their cloth shone like wet
wounds.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood beneath the broken arch of the old observatory and watched the Shattered Vale
drown. Greyfell Citadel had been founded in 62 AS, when the stone beneath her boots had still been new
enough to bear a mason’s pride. Now the towers were hollow teeth, the courtyards choked with rainwater
and pale weeds. It was abandoned, outside the realm’s core holdings, yet the old records still gave it a
master in a hand so certain that certainty became a kind of mockery.
Greyfell Citadel ruled by House Morvain.
The line had been copied three times on the parchment before her.
Caedmon Fellgard held the ledger open with both hands. He was a Scribe, and every inch of him seemed
bent toward the sanctity of written things: shoulders drawn inward, fingers stained dark with ink, posture
disciplined even while the storm worried at the stones around him.
“Read it aloud,” Morwenna said.
Caedmon lifted his eyes. “The Leaden Accord.”
“The whole entry.”
His mouth tightened. He did not like the request. Scribes disliked being made to turn records into
weapons.
“The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS,” he read. “It ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties. The
Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor.”
The rain struck the archway with the hard hiss of thrown grain.
Morwenna looked beyond him, toward the drowned road winding down from the citadel. Somewhere
beneath the clouds, patrols moved through the ravines. Somewhere farther still, the Cartel waited for the
intelligence she had promised to sell.
Not promised, she corrected herself.
Sold.
The word had a clean edge. It did not ask to be forgiven.
“And the cause of the ending?” she asked.
Caedmon lowered his gaze to the page. “The Leaden Accord ended when both hosts were destroyed by a
Ley-storm.”
“Both hosts.”
“The Ashen Vanguard was a belligerent in The Leaden Accord.”
His voice had the weight of a man reciting a sentence he had been taught not to understand.
Morwenna reached for the ledger. “Give it here.”

Caedmon surrendered it reluctantly. The pages were swollen with damp, and the ink had feathered at the
margins. She traced the old notation with one gloved finger.
Both hosts destroyed.
The declared victory belonged to the Iron-Ring Cartel. Victory required survivors, witnesses, banners
hauled from the mud. Yet the pages spoke of annihilation. The dead had been counted, named, arranged
into columns, and then made to serve the living.
The hidden truth lay beneath the entry in a cramped hand: a supposedly destroyed artifact had been
spirited away.
No name. No description. No destination.
The omission was deliberate. Morwenna knew the shape of deliberate omissions. They resembled doors in
a corridor where there should have been stone.
“Who altered this?” she asked.
Caedmon’s face became still. “The record does not say.”
“Records do not alter themselves.”
“No.”
“Then someone altered it.”
“Yes.”
The answer pleased her less than defiance would have. Defiance had a spine. Fear merely bent.
She closed the ledger. The clasp clicked softly, almost tenderly.
At the far end of the observatory, a lamp guttered behind a shield of horn. Its flame painted the wet stones
copper. A figure stood beside it, draped in dark robes whose hem was clean despite the mud outside.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned had arrived without escort.
Their crowns were not worn upon their head. One rested at their throat as a circlet of black metal; the other
had been worked into the clasp of their mantle. Both were narrow, severe things. They marked Sabelle as
High Inquisitor more effectively than any proclamation could have done.
Morwenna had never asked why the crowns were called twice-earned. Questions were another form of
currency, and she spent only when the return was certain.
Sabelle’s eyes moved from the ledger to Caedmon, then to Morwenna.
“You have found the wound,” they said.
“I have found an inconsistency.”
“That is what wounds are called by people who intend to survive them.”
Caedmon swallowed. His hands hovered at his sides, empty and miserable.
Morwenna turned toward the storm. “The Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor, though both hosts were
destroyed by a Ley-storm. The hidden truth says an artifact was spirited away. That is not an
inconsistency. It is a verdict written over a crime.”

Sabelle came closer. Their boots made no sound upon the stone.
“And you object to crimes?”
“I object to untidy accounts.”
“Because you are a Fleet Admiral?”
“Because untidy accounts sink ships.”
The lie came easily. Morwenna had worn authority for so long that falsehood entered it like breath
entering a bellows. She had been born in 288 AS, and the years since had taught her that every command
carried two meanings: the one given aloud, and the one purchased in secret.
The Iron-Ring Cartel paid for the second.
Not with coin. Coin was too visible. They paid with safe passage, with sealed reports, with the knowledge
that certain vessels would not be waiting where the charts said they waited. They paid by making silence
profitable.
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened. “The Ashen Vanguard will not forgive the old account.”
“The Ashen Vanguard has survived worse than forgiveness.”
“House Morvain will claim Greyfell Citadel by right.”
Morwenna glanced back at the ruined walls. “House Morvain has already ruled Greyfell Citadel.”
“Ruled,” Sabelle said, tasting the word. “The stone remains. The rule does not.”
Caedmon made a small sound. He had turned toward the stairs, listening.
“What is it?” Morwenna asked.
“Nothing.”
“Nothing does not make a Scribe listen.”
He looked ashamed of the truth before speaking it. “There are noises below.”
The storm pressed against the citadel. Water streamed through cracks in the ceiling and ran in silver
threads along the floor.
Sabelle smiled without warmth.
“Below,” they repeated.
Morwenna watched them. “You have brought something.”
“I have brought a matter requiring privacy.”
“You have brought a matter requiring a cellar.”
The smile vanished.
For one instant, Morwenna saw the High Inquisitor’s severity split open, revealing the dark chamber
beneath. She had heard whispers of Sabelle’s secret, though never the details: in the cellar below their
quarters, a bound revenant was kept in custody. A dead thing tethered to obedience. A corpse made into an
instrument by someone who wore sanctity like armor.

Caedmon looked between them, pale.
Sabelle spoke gently. “You hear too much.”
“I command a fleet.”
“You command what remains of one.”
Morwenna let the insult pass. The storm had begun to lessen, but the wind still worried at the flags. Their
wet snapping sounded like applause from a distant crowd.
She opened the ledger again and held it toward Sabelle.
“Here. Read the hand beneath the official account.”
“I have read it.”
“Then you know why the Cartel wants this.”
“I know why everyone wants it.”
“Everyone?”
“The Ashen Vanguard wants the dead avenged. House Morvain wants the citadel restored to its old
obedience. The Silent Choir wants the truth buried beneath a holier lie. The Iron-Ring Cartel wants
whatever was spirited away. And the Bleeding Crown wants all four to believe they are acting alone.”
Morwenna studied their face. “You left yourself out.”
“I am not a power.”
“No?”
“I am an instrument.”
That answer had the flatness of a blade.
Caedmon stepped toward the stairwell. “The noise is louder.”
A dull knock rose from below.
Once.
Then again.
Something struck wood with patient force.
Sabelle did not move, but their hand settled upon the clasp at their throat. Beneath the black metal, one
crown caught the lamplight; the other remained in shadow.
Morwenna felt the old instinct awaken in her, colder than fear and more useful: measure the exits, count
the hands, decide who would drown first.
The cellar lay beneath the observatory. The stairs were narrow. The rain had made the stones slick.
Caedmon carried no weapon that she could see. Sabelle carried secrets. Morwenna carried the ledger, and
within it a sentence that could purchase the Cartel’s favor or condemn her to its displeasure.
Another knock sounded below.
Caedmon whispered, “It knows we are here.”

Sabelle turned to him. “It knows nothing.”
The wood groaned.
Morwenna closed the ledger and tucked it beneath her arm.
“Open the cellar,” she said.
Sabelle’s eyes found hers. “You are giving an order?”
“I am asking to see what threatens my command.”
“Your command is not here.”
“No,” Morwenna said. “But my choices are.”
For a moment, the three of them stood within the ruined observatory while the last of the rain slid from the
battlements. Greyfell Citadel held its silence around them, old and abandoned, yet still bearing the name
of House Morvain like a curse carved into bone.
Then Sabelle drew a key from beneath their mantle.
From below came a third knock.
This time, something on the other side of the door whispered Morwenna’s name.
Sabelle turned the key.
The lock yielded with a wet, internal click. The cellar door opened inward on darkness thick as old blood.
A breath came up from below—not the ordinary chill of buried stone, but a damp exhalation that touched
Morwenna’s face and seemed to search for a place beneath her skin.
The whisper came again.
“Morwenna.”
Her name had no mouth behind it. Or too many.
She placed one hand on the hilt at her hip, though steel had never been much use against the things that
survived the Sundering. “You said the cellar was sealed.”
“It was.”
“By whom?”
Sabelle’s gaze did not leave the stair. “By those who understood the virtue of silence.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are owed.”
Morwenna looked at them. The Twice-Crowned High Inquisitor stood with one hand upon the open door,
the other hidden within their mantle. Their severity had always seemed like a kind of architecture: a clean
wall raised against the weather of the soul. Now a hairline fracture ran through it.
Below, something shifted.
Not footsteps. Not yet.
A soft dragging, followed by the delicate chime of metal against metal.

The stair descended through the citadel’s foundations, each step worn at its center by feet that had ceased
to come. Water glimmered in the joints. The walls were grey, the same dead grey as the towers above, but
darker where the rain had found a path through the masonry. Morwenna followed Sabelle down.
Behind her, the observatory remained open to the storm. The wind pushed through the broken dome and
worried at loose pages. She imagined the ledger lying beneath her arm, its columns of provisions and
deployments, its omissions more eloquent than any entry. The figures had been copied by Caedmon
Fellgard’s careful hand. Caedmon Fellgard member of The Iron-Ring Cartel. The knowledge sat inside her
like a swallowed hook.
She had sold intelligence before. She had sold routes, weaknesses, names of men who believed themselves
beyond purchase. She had never sold a voice.
At the bottom of the stairs, Sabelle lifted a shuttered lamp from a niche in the wall. The flame inside was
small and blue. It cast no warmth.
Morwenna’s eyes adjusted to the chamber.
There were no barrels. No racks of preserved meat or casks of wine. No stores for a garrison, nor any
evidence that Greyfell Citadel had been provisioned since House Morvain abandoned its claim to the
place. The cellar was a low vault of bare stone. At its center stood an iron cage sunk into the floor, its bars
blackened and carved with narrow lines of script.
Something was crouched inside.
Morwenna had seen men after a Ley-storm had taken their skin. She had seen sailors opened by winds that
shone like molten glass, heard them beg for knives, for fire, for the mercy of being made singular again.
The thing in the cage did not resemble any of them.
It wore a shape as a prisoner wore a uniform: without belonging to it.
A length of pale cloth covered its body from throat to ankle. Its head hung forward. Where its hands rested
on the floor, the fingers were too still, each joint arranged with the patience of a corpse displayed for
burial. A chain passed through the cage and disappeared into the stone beneath it.
Morwenna’s breath shortened.
The thing raised its head.
No eyes showed beneath the cloth. Yet she felt its attention settle upon her with intimate precision.
“Not a revenant,” Morwenna said.
Sabelle’s silence answered.
“You keep this here.”
“I contain it here.”
“Why?”
“Because it cannot be allowed above.”
“Then why did it call my name?”

The revenant’s covered face tilted. Its voice came from somewhere behind Morwenna now, though the
stairwell behind them was empty.
“Because you came carrying a door.”
Morwenna did not turn.
The iron cage groaned. One of the bars bent inward, not far, but enough to make the sound of complaint.
Sabelle stepped between them. “You will not address her.”
The revenant laughed.
The sound was faint. It had the dry rhythm of paper burning.
“You gave me a tongue,” it said. “Do not be offended when I use it.”
Morwenna’s hand tightened around her sword. She studied the cage instead of the thing within it. The
carved lines were not prayers. They had the repetition of instructions, though no script she knew had ever
been written with such narrow, cruel strokes.
“Who else knows it is here?”
“No one who matters.”
“That answer has killed better commanders than you.”
Sabelle’s face remained composed, but the blue flame sharpened the hollows around their eyes. “You
mistake secrecy for weakness.”
“I mistake nothing. Greyfell Citadel is abandoned. It lies outside the realm’s core holdings. Yet two men
serve here.”
At that, the revenant stirred.
Sabelle’s attention flicked toward her. “Who told you?”
“Caedmon’s records.”
“Caedmon Fellgard keeps records. He does not understand them.”
“He understood enough to write that Brannoc Palefroth serves at Greyfell Citadel.”
The revenant’s fingers drew a slow line through the dust.
“And Ederon Coldwater serves at Greyfell Citadel,” Morwenna continued. “Two servants in a dead
stronghold. Two living hands to carry food, messages, keys.”
“Brannoc Palefroth tends the outer walls,” Sabelle said. “Ederon Coldwater tends the lower passages.”
“Which includes this chamber.”
“Which includes the doors before this chamber.”
“Then one of them opened it.”
Sabelle’s mouth hardened. “Neither has the courage.”
“Courage is not required for treachery.”

“No,” said the revenant. “Only hunger.”
Its head turned toward the eastern wall. Beneath the stone came a muted impact. Once. Then again.
Someone was moving in the passage beyond.
Morwenna heard the discipline in it: weight placed carefully, pause held deliberately, breath controlled.
Not a servant carrying a lantern. Not a man lost in the dark.
Sabelle lowered the lamp shutter. The chamber dimmed until only the blue coal of flame remained.
“Stand behind me,” they whispered.
Morwenna almost smiled. “You did not bring me here to protect me.”
“I brought you here because the thing wanted you.”
That was the first honest sentence Sabelle had given her.
Another impact struck the wall. Dust sifted from the ceiling.
Morwenna reached beneath her coat and drew a narrow packet sealed in wax. The wax had been
impressed with no crest. Inside were three strips of treated cloth, each bearing a pattern of knots and
punctures. To a stranger, they meant nothing. To the Iron-Ring Cartel, they marked a channel, a warning, a
price.
She had received the packet before entering Greyfell. The instruction had been simple: confirm the
presence of the hidden asset. Do not remove it. Do not allow the Inquisitor to know you have been sent.
She had assumed “asset” meant a document, a weapon, perhaps some remnant of the artifact said to have
been destroyed in the Leaden Accord. She had not imagined a bound dead thing beneath a ruined citadel,
speaking with borrowed voices.
Sabelle noticed the packet.
Their eyes fell upon it.
“You carry Cartel cipher.”
Morwenna felt the moment narrow around them.
The revenant whispered, “There is the door.”
Sabelle’s hand moved beneath the mantle. “You have been selling secrets.”
Morwenna did not deny it. Denial was a poor tactic when the enemy had already opened the correct book.
“Caedmon Fellgard is a member of The Iron-Ring Cartel,” she said. “His records travel farther than he
does.”
“Do not make a confession sound like an accusation.”
“I am not confessing.”
“What are you doing?”
“Measuring how much you knew before tonight.”
The wall gave a third time.

A crack appeared between the stones. Blackness showed through it—not the absence of light, but a depth
that seemed to lean toward the chamber. The revenant rose inside its cage.
It unfolded slowly. Cloth whispered against cloth. The iron chain pulled taut, and the stone beneath the
cage answered with a low vibration that Morwenna felt in her teeth.
Sabelle raised the lamp.
For the first time, Morwenna saw beneath the cloth.
There was no face. Only a hollow filled with ash, and in that ash two pinpoints of wet red light.
“Open the eastern passage,” the revenant said.
Sabelle spoke a word in a language Morwenna did not know.
The cage flared. Lines of pale fire raced over the bars. The revenant convulsed, its hands closing into fists.
From somewhere above came a cry, brief and human, followed by the scrape of a body falling down stone.
Morwenna turned toward the stair.
“Brannoc,” Sabelle said.
The name did not sound like an answer. It sounded like a verdict.
A second body struck the steps.
Then Ederon Coldwater appeared at the bottom of the stairwell, dragging Brannoc Palefroth by one arm.
Blood ran from Ederon’s temple. Brannoc’s boots carved twin trails through the water, and his head lolled
at an angle no living neck would tolerate.
Ederon looked at Morwenna first.
His expression held no surprise.
That frightened her more than the corpse.
“High Inquisitor,” he said, breathless. “The outer door is gone.”
Sabelle did not move. “Who opened it?”
Ederon glanced toward the cage.
The revenant had stopped struggling. Its red lights fixed upon him.
“Not me,” Ederon said.
Brannoc’s fingers twitched against the floor.
Morwenna stepped backward, placing herself where she could see the stair, the cage, and Sabelle’s hands.
The packet of cipher cloth was still between her fingers. Its wax seal pressed into her palm.
From the wall came a slow, deliberate knocking.
Three times.
Then a voice spoke through the crack.
“Admiral.”

The title was spoken by someone outside.
Someone alive.
Morwenna knew that voice. She had heard it in war rooms and rain-swept yards, across tables where men
lied with maps laid flat between them.
Sabelle turned on her.
“You know who that is.”
Morwenna’s mouth went dry.
The revenant lifted one hand toward the failing wall, and the chain beneath the cage began to unwind.
“I know,” Morwenna said.
The stones shifted.
Beyond them, the unseen speaker laughed softly.
And Morwenna realized the voice was not calling her in. It was calling the thing out.
The chain gave a final metallic sigh.
Morwenna drew her sword, though the blade was no more useful here than a mast in a grave. The chamber
had narrowed around them. Dust sifted from the ceiling. Somewhere beyond the failing wall, stone
scraped against stone with the patient hunger of a thing opening its own tomb.
Sabelle did not look at her.
“Say the name,” the High Inquisitor commanded.
The voice beyond the wall answered with another soft laugh.
“Still issuing orders, Twice-Crowned?”
Sabelle’s hand closed around the hilt at their side. The two crowns upon their brow were not visible in the
dark, but Morwenna felt their weight in every word. Severity had always been Sabelle’s chosen armor.
Tonight it had cracked, and beneath it lay something colder than fear.
“Caedmon,” Morwenna said.
The name passed through the room like a spark through oil.
Sabelle turned then. “You knew.”
“I knew the voice.”
“You knew he was here.”
“I knew he was not where he claimed to be.”
“Those are not the same thing.”
“No.” Morwenna kept her sword low. “They are not.”
The wall buckled. A seam opened from floor to lintel, black as a cut throat. Wind came through it,
carrying the smell of wet ash and old iron. The revenant stirred in its cage. Its fingers tightened around the
bars, each knuckle pale beneath skin that seemed stretched over a memory of flesh.

Sabelle stepped between Morwenna and the cage.
The revenant tilted its head.
Not toward Sabelle.
Toward Morwenna.
There was recognition in that ruined face. Not the simple recognition of a servant who had been ordered,
or a prisoner who had been named. It knew her as a vessel knows the hand that once filled it. It knew the
shape of her treason before she had given it a name.
Morwenna felt the folded paper in her palm grow warm.
The letter had no seal. That was the first insult. Caedmon Fellgard had always trusted ink more than wax,
records more than oaths. A scribe could erase a king with a line drawn through his name. He could make a
fleet vanish between one ledger and the next.
She unfolded the paper.
A few words had been written in the narrow, disciplined hand she knew from manifests and casualty rolls.
IRON-RING CARTEL.
Below it, a list.
Palewell Abbey.
The Pale Coast.
Greyfell Citadel.
The page trembled once between her fingers. She made it still.
Caedmon spoke through the widening breach. “You have carried my messages well, Admiral.”
Sabelle’s eyes moved to the paper.
Morwenna folded it again.
The lie arrived easily. It had been bred in her for years, fed on silence and polished by necessity.
“I carry no messages for you.”
“Not for me.”
The wall broke inward.
Caedmon Fellgard stood beyond the rubble with a lantern in one hand and a slim case of black wood
beneath the other arm. Dust lay across his shoulders. His face remained composed, reserved, almost
apologetic, as if he had interrupted a meal to correct a figure in a ledger.
He wore a scribe’s gloves. Their fingertips were dark with ink.
Behind him, the passage climbed into darkness.
Sabelle raised a hand. The runes cut into the stone around the cage flared weakly, then guttered. “You
have entered a sealed chamber.”
“I have entered a room whose seal was purchased.”

“By whom?”
Caedmon looked at Morwenna.
The old instinct took her by the throat: deny, command, make the accusation smaller than the authority
that spoke it. She had been Fleet Admiral since before the Ashen Vanguard learned to fear the sound of
her ships. Command had taught her that hesitation was a kind of confession.
But Caedmon had not come to accuse her.
He had come to collect.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel does not purchase seals,” Morwenna said. “It purchases people.”
“Then you understand the arrangement.”
Sabelle moved with sudden violence.
Their blade struck Caedmon’s lantern. Flame burst across the chamber. The scribe dropped the lamp, and
the darkness swallowed him before the metal had finished ringing.
The revenant shrieked.
It was not a human sound. It had once been human, perhaps, but whatever had survived in the cellar had
been stripped of every gentleness that made a voice worth hearing. The cage jumped on its chain. Iron
shrilled against iron.
Morwenna saw Sabelle hesitate.
That was all Caedmon needed.
He emerged at the edge of the chamber, close enough that Morwenna saw ink beneath one fingernail. His
hand came up—not with a weapon, but with a small square of parchment.
“Read it,” he said.
Morwenna did not take it.
“Read it.”
Sabelle’s blade turned toward his throat. “You will leave.”
Caedmon’s expression barely changed. “If I leave, the chamber opens.”
The chain above them snapped taut.
The cage rose a handspan from the floor.
Sabelle looked upward.
Morwenna looked at Caedmon.
“You bound it to the chain,” she said.
“No. The chain is bound to it.”
The revenant pressed its face between the bars. Its mouth opened, and a thread of black fluid ran from its
tongue.
Sabelle’s composure returned in pieces. “You have no understanding of what you are touching.”

“I understand records. I understand custody. I understand that the High Inquisitor Sabelle Mournvale the
Twice-Crowned keeps a bound revenant in their cellar, despite every decree written against such
practices.”
The words did not echo. The room seemed to swallow them.
Morwenna watched Sabelle’s face.
Sabelle had been born in 263 AS, and there were moments when that fact showed—not in weakness, but
in the depth of what they had survived. They had spent too long among tribunals, relics, and the
confessions of frightened people. They had learned how to make terror kneel.
Now terror had found a chair at their table.
“You mistake secrecy for leverage,” Sabelle said.
“No.” Caedmon opened the black case. “I mistake nothing.”
Inside lay papers, folded and tied. One bore Morwenna’s private cipher. Another carried the mark of the
Iron-Ring Cartel, pressed so faintly into the page that it might have been an accident.
Her blood cooled.
The passage behind Caedmon filled with a low groan. Far below, something answered the revenant. The
sound travelled through the foundations of the citadel, through old mortar and buried chambers, until the
floor beneath Morwenna’s boots shivered.
“What is in the case?” she asked.
“Copies.”
“Of what?”
“Your intelligence.”
