Sabelle’s blade shifted toward her.
Morwenna did not turn. “You are lying.”
“I am a scribe.”
“That is not a denial.”
“No.”
Caedmon withdrew a packet and let it fall open. The pages slid against one another, whispering.
He had copied the movements of ships. Supply routes. Names of commanders. Signals used by the Ashen
Vanguard. Places where patrols changed and where watchfires were permitted to die. Nothing in the pages
was marked with her hand, yet she knew each secret as a captain knows the hidden damage in her hull.
She had sold them to the Iron-Ring Cartel one piece at a time.
Not for gold. Gold was too visible. The Cartel had paid in silence, in altered orders, in doors left unbarred
when she needed them open. It had paid by ensuring that certain questions died before they reached her.
Morwenna’s gaze touched the papers and moved away.
Sabelle saw.

The High Inquisitor’s voice was almost gentle. “How long?”
Morwenna felt the old rooms of her mind close their doors.
Caedmon answered for her. “Long enough that the first account predates the present arrangement of this
citadel.”
“Do not speak of arrangements,” Sabelle said.
“Then speak of guilt.”
The revenant struck the bars.
A crack ran through the nearest rune.
Morwenna moved before either of them could stop her. She seized the black case and drove her shoulder
into Caedmon’s chest. The scribe stumbled against the wall. Papers spilled into the dust.
Sabelle’s blade came down.
Caedmon caught the wrist.
For a man made of ledgers and quiet posture, he possessed startling strength. His fingers closed around
Sabelle’s arm, and the High Inquisitor’s crown of authority became irrelevant in the grip of bone and ink.
Morwenna saw the parchment square beneath Caedmon’s coat.
She took it.
He released Sabelle at once.
The paper was heavier than it looked. A seal had been impressed into its corner—not wax, but a dark
metallic compound that seemed to drink the lanternless gloom.
She opened it.
There was one sentence.
Morwenna Ashgrove was born in 288 AS.
Below that, in a different hand:
Every admiral has a first harbor.
Her breath stopped.
The date was not secret. It belonged to records, to birth rolls, to the orderly procession of facts that could
not be killed by denial. Yet seeing it there made it intimate. A marker driven into the earth of her life.
Caedmon bent to retrieve the fallen pages.
Sabelle stared at Morwenna. “What does it say?”
Morwenna crumpled the parchment.
The revenant began to laugh.
“Do not let it out,” she said.
Sabelle’s eyes remained on her. “You think I am the danger?”

“I think you have kept a dead thing in a cage beneath the feet of everyone who trusts you.”
“And you have fed an enemy the names of those people.”
The accusation landed cleanly. Morwenna felt no wound, only the terrible precision of it.
Caedmon gathered the last page.
“Enough,” he said.
Neither listened.
The crack in the rune widened. A thread of pale light entered the chamber from nowhere, passing through
the revenant’s ribs. For an instant Morwenna saw what lay inside the cage—not organs, not bones, but a
cramped architecture of shadows, all of them turning toward the same unseen door.
Sabelle lifted both hands.
The crowns—whatever metal or sanctity they possessed—seemed to answer. The air thickened.
Morwenna’s ears filled with a distant ringing.
“Stand back,” Sabelle commanded.
Caedmon went still.
Morwenna did not.
The revenant’s hand emerged through the bars.
Its fingers reached for her.
Not Sabelle. Not Caedmon.
Her.
The chain overhead began to unwind again, links dropping through the dark with deliberate, measured
clanks.
Morwenna understood then what the voice had meant.
It had not called the revenant out of the cellar.
It had called the cellar out of the world.
The floor opened beneath the cage.
Sabelle seized Morwenna by the arm. Caedmon seized the other.
For one absurd moment they stood joined together, High Inquisitor, Fleet Admiral, and scribe, bound by a
danger none of them could command.
Below them, darkness breathed.
And from that darkness came a voice that was not Caedmon’s, not the revenant’s, not any living voice at
all.
“Admiral.”
The chain fell.

Morwenna looked down.
Something below had opened its eyes.

Chapter 9
The rain had the color of old iron when Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless entered the records chamber.
It slid from the eaves of Fenspire and hissed against the shutters, turning the fortress into a sealed thing of
stone, smoke, and listening dark. Beyond the narrow windows, the Gloaming Reach lay drowned beneath
a low sky. The spire’s shadow reached across the yard, where men moved without speaking beneath
hooded cloaks. Their boots struck the flagstones in a rhythm too orderly to be prayer.
Ignatz did not look at them.
He carried no papers in his hands. That was why the sentries watched him as he passed.
At the end of the chamber, a brazier burned without warmth. A table stood before it, black wood scarred
by old blades and older decisions. Upon the table rested a sealed packet, a cup gone cold, and a strip of
pale metal bearing the ward-mark of The Hollow Edge.
The mark had been cut into the metal before Ignatz was born, in 216 AS, when the ward was forged. He
had touched it once and felt emptiness open beneath his skin. Attunement to The Hollow Edge costs 21.
The knowledge sat in his mind like a buried nail.
He left it untouched.
“Warden-Commander.”
The voice came from the darkness beside the brazier.
Ignatz stopped.
The quartermaster stepped forward, holding a lantern low. His face remained indistinct in the weak light,
his authority expressed in ledgers, keys, and the habit of being obeyed. The registry named him Ignatz
Marrowgate, Quartermaster. The shared name had amused other men. Ignatz Ashgrove had never found it
amusing.
“Quartermaster,” he said.
Marrowgate placed the lantern upon the table. “The seal was broken before it reached me.”
“Then it did not reach you sealed.”
“It reached me with the appearance of being sealed.”
“Appearances are a poor defense.”
“They are the defense that remains when the truth has been removed.”
The quartermaster’s gaze dropped to the packet. Wax gleamed along its edge, blackened by handling.
“You requested the Blackport rolls.”
“I requested every surviving account of the purge.”
“You have the rolls.”
“I have a packet.”
“Would you prefer I call it a miracle?”

Ignatz moved to the table. Rain trembled against the shutters. Somewhere within the walls, a chain
dragged across stone, then fell silent.
“Where are the casualty ledgers?”
Marrowgate’s fingers tightened around the lantern handle. “There are no complete ledgers.”
“There is a figure.”
“There is always a figure.”
“Say it.”
The quartermaster’s expression did not change, but the flame bent in the draft and threw a thin blade of
light across his mouth.
“70907.”
The number entered the room and seemed to remain there.
Ignatz heard, behind it, the old noise: gates splitting under fire; water ladled from poisoned wells; boots
moving through streets where no one had the strength to bar a door. He had not been at Blackport.
Memory did not require witness. Men carried it in their silences. They carried it in the way they refused
water offered by a stranger.
“The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate watched him.
“Say the rest.”
“It ended in 321 AS.”
“And the casualty figure?”
“70907.”
“Again.”
“70907.”
Ignatz laid two fingers on the packet. The paper beneath the seal had softened with damp. “The rolls say
the same?”
“The rolls say many things.”
“Do not answer with fog.”
“I answer with what was written.”
“Who wrote them?”
“Hands.”
“Whose hands?”
“Dead hands, mostly.”
Ignatz looked toward the shutters. The rain pressed against them like a crowd trying to overhear.

Blackport had been spoken of as a victory until victory lost its shape. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as
victor. That sentence appeared in every account with the stubbornness of a grave marker. The aggressors
had been routed. Total rout, the military register called it, as though a neat phrase could cleanse the earth.
But the wells had been poisoned.
Not by the defeated. By the victors.
Ignatz knew this because the intelligence had passed through him in fragments: a shipment diverted, a seal
copied, an order altered after it had already been obeyed. The pieces had come from mouths that believed
themselves safe. He had gathered them, weighed them, and sold them.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless secretly sells intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.
There was no gentler way to name it.
Marrowgate drew back from the table. “You are not reading the rolls.”
“I am reading the room.”
“The room has no testimony.”
“Rooms keep what men spill in them.”
“Then this one is full.”
Ignatz broke the packet’s seal.
The sound was small. Marrowgate flinched as if it had been a shot.
Inside lay sheets of grey paper, a few brittle, a few fresh enough to carry the bitter scent of ink. Ignatz
lifted the first. The writing had been copied by several hands. Some lines were cramped, others
ceremonious. Names had been scraped away. Locations had been replaced with marks. Certain passages
were nothing but black bars.
He read without moving his lips.
A convoy had arrived at Blackport carrying grain, salt, and sealed casks. The casks had been opened under
guard. The wells had been declared unsafe after the sickness began. An order had gone out to preserve the
city’s remaining stores for military use.
No signature.
No date beyond the one already burned into every account.
“The Cartel’s wells,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate’s lantern flame guttered. “The packet does not say that.”
“It says enough.”
“It says poison was found in the water.”
“Water does not poison itself.”
“Sometimes it does.”
“Not in patterns.”

Marrowgate came around the table. “You speak as though you were there.”
“I speak as though I can read.”
“No. You speak as though you know what the Iron-Ring Cartel intended.”
Ignatz raised his eyes.
The quartermaster had not meant to say it. That was the dangerous part. Truth often escaped through the
mouth wearing the mask of accusation.
The chamber seemed to contract around them. The brazier breathed red beneath its ash. Ignatz felt the old
instinct rise in him—not fear, exactly, but the calculation fear left behind after command had beaten it into
discipline.
He could kill Marrowgate.
The thought arrived without heat. The room offered opportunities: the lantern, the packet knife, the
unguarded throat. But murder would turn suspicion into shape. It would also waste a man who might still
be useful.
“You believe the Cartel poisoned its own allies,” Ignatz said.
“I believe the records are inconsistent.”
“You believe the wells were poisoned.”
“I believe people died after drinking from them.”
“You believe the Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.”
“That is what the accounts state.”
“Then you believe nothing.”
Marrowgate’s hand moved toward his belt and stopped before reaching it. “You ask questions that do not
belong to a Warden-Commander.”
“Questions belong to whoever survives the answers.”
The quartermaster leaned close. His breath smelled of bitterroot and stale smoke. “There are messages
leaving Fenspire.”
Ignatz let the silence answer.
“From this chamber,” Marrowgate continued. “From the garrison stores. From the quarantine dispatches.
Someone is selling the Cartel what it cannot take by force.”
Rain thrummed harder against the shutters.
“Someone,” Ignatz said.
“Someone who knows the routes. The watch rotations. The weakness in the western wall.”
“Those are many someones.”
“Not many can command men to look elsewhere.”
Ignatz folded the page and placed it atop the packet. “Are you accusing me?”

“I am warning you.”
“Warnings are accusations that fear to stand upright.”
Marrowgate’s mouth hardened. “You were born in 258 AS. You have worn command long enough to
understand what a breach costs.”
The use of his birth year struck him more sharply than the accusation. Not because it mattered, but
because Marrowgate had chosen it. Facts could be made into knives if held at the right angle.
Ignatz turned back to the table. “Do not use my birth as a summons to obedience.”
“I use it to remind you that you have been here longer than some men have been alive.”
The statement was too broad, too careless. Ignatz disregarded it. He touched the edge of the packet
instead.
A second object lay beneath the papers, wrapped in dark cloth. He drew it free.
The reliquary was smaller than his palm, its surface powdered with ash that did not fall when he tilted it.
Chalice of Ashdeep had been forged in 323 AS. Attunement to it costs 27. The name was not engraved. It
seemed to exist in the metal’s severe silence.
Marrowgate took a step back.
“That was not listed.”
“Many things are not listed.”
“Put it down.”
Ignatz studied the wrapped reliquary. It held no visible lock, no hinge, no seam. Yet the ash upon it stirred
toward his skin.
“Why was this in the Blackport packet?”
“I do not know.”
“Who sent it?”
“I do not know.”
“Why are you afraid of it?”
“I am not.”
The ash crawled against the metal.
Marrowgate seized the lantern and lifted it. “Warden-Commander.”
Ignatz felt the reliquary’s weight change. For an instant it seemed filled with water. Then with teeth. A
pressure gathered behind his eyes, and with it came the impression of a chamber beneath Blackport: stone
walls sweating darkly, a row of empty vessels, a hand lowering something into a well.
Not a vision. Not precisely.
A memory that did not belong to him.
He closed his fingers around the reliquary.

The pressure vanished.
Marrowgate whispered, “What did you see?”
Ignatz slipped the object into his coat. “Nothing.”
“That is a lie.”
“Yes.”
The quartermaster stared at him, and in that stare Ignatz saw the shape of every oath he had once been
expected to keep. Duty. Protection. Obedience. Words carved into men until they mistook the scars for
virtue.
He had broken them all quietly.
He sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel because information traveled farther than armies and left
fewer bodies in the road. That was the argument he had given himself. He had repeated it through
sleepless nights, in command tents, beneath the pale sky above Gloamreach, while sealed messages passed
from his hands into darker hands.
The argument had never mentioned poisoned wells.
It had never mentioned 70907.
A knock sounded at the outer door.
Marrowgate turned.
Ignatz did not.
The knock came again, careful and formal.
A voice spoke from beyond the wood. “Warden-Commander. A dispatch from the coast.”
Gloamreach lay along the Pale Coast, quarantined behind its own silence. Nothing entered without
scrutiny. Nothing left without record. Yet the messenger had arrived in the rain, bearing a dispatch that
had not passed through the chamber’s registry.
Marrowgate looked at Ignatz.
Ignatz looked at the sealed door.
The reliquary pressed coldly against his ribs.
“Open it,” he said.
Marrowgate did not move. “Are you certain?”
“No.”
The quartermaster’s hand reached for the bar.
Ignatz placed his palm upon the packet, feeling the damp paper, the broken seal, the concealed lines
beneath the ink.
On the other side of the door, the messenger breathed once.
Then the voice said, “The Iron-Ring Cartel sends its regards.”

The bar lifted with a sound like a bone being drawn from flesh.
Marrowgate opened the door only as far as the chain allowed. Rain pressed through the gap in silver
threads, carrying the raw smell of the Pale Coast and something fouler beneath it—the stagnant breath of a
place sealed too long against the living world.
No face appeared beyond the door.
A gloved hand entered the gap. It held a black cylinder bound in waxed cord.
“Take it,” said the messenger.
Marrowgate did not. His fingers remained upon the bar.
Ignatz watched the packet instead. The paper was not black, though the corridor beyond seemed to make it
so. Water had darkened its edges. The seal bore no crest he recognized, only a ring pressed into red wax
until the center had split.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had never needed heraldry. Its mark was a promise made by pressure.
“Who sent you?” Marrowgate asked.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel.”
“That was not my question.”
“No,” said the voice. “It was the safer one.”
The rain ticked against the threshold. Somewhere deeper in the keep, a bell gave a single muted note and
fell silent.
Ignatz felt the reliquary beneath his coat. The Chalice of Ashdeep rested against his ribs with the patience
of buried fire. It was not heavy in the ordinary sense. Weight suggested matter. The thing carried
consequence instead.
“Open the door,” he said.
Marrowgate turned his head. “Commander—”
“Open it.”
The quartermaster undid the chain.
The messenger entered without haste. Water darkened the hem of the cloak, and droplets trembled from
the leather gloves. No insignia marked the clothing. No weapon showed. That absence was more
deliberate than any sword.
Marrowgate shut the door behind the messenger. The chamber tightened around the three of them.
Ignatz remained beside the table, one hand resting upon the packet he had brought from the registry. The
other hung loose at his side. He had trained himself to keep his hands empty when men lied to him. It
made them wonder what he had concealed elsewhere.
The messenger placed the cylinder before him.
“From the Cartel,” the voice said.
“I heard you.”

“Then you heard enough to know why it is here.”
Ignatz studied the seal. “I know only that Gloamreach is quarantined, that nothing enters without scrutiny,
and that this arrived without a registry mark.”
“Then you know the Cartel has given you a gift.”
“The Cartel does not give gifts.”
“No.” A pause. “It collects debts.”
The words entered the room and found their old places.
Marrowgate moved toward the brazier. The coals had sunk beneath a crust of ash. He stirred them, though
there was no need, and sparks climbed briefly before dying. His silence had changed. Ignatz knew that
silence. It belonged to the years before a decision, when a man measured obedience against survival and
found both wanting.
“Leave us,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate’s hand stopped upon the poker.
The messenger made no sound.
“You heard me,” Ignatz continued.
“I am the quartermaster of this garrison.”
“You are a quartermaster in a sealed keep.”
“I am also responsible for every document brought into this chamber.”
“Then you will be responsible for the door.”
Marrowgate looked at him. The firelight caught in the water pooled at the messenger’s feet, turning it the
color of old blood.
“Maelis Harrowick the Pale would not have sent me away.”
The name struck with greater force than any accusation.
Ignatz saw, not a woman, not a face—nothing so merciful—but the shape of a lesson. A hand correcting
the angle of a blade. A voice insisting that an oath was not a chain but a witness. The memory had no
room in him, yet it entered.
“Do not invoke your mentor to win an argument,” Ignatz said.
“Maelis Harrowick the Pale was my mentor,” Marrowgate answered. “If I invoke her, it is because she
taught me to know when a sealed room contains more danger than the corridor.”
“Your mentor is not here.”
“No. She is not.”
The messenger tilted the head. A drop of rain fell from the cloak and struck the floor.
Ignatz hated the Cartel for knowing how to make silence useful. He hated himself for recognizing the
workmanship.

He had sold them routes, strength reports, names that had been written in his own hand. He had told
himself each exchange was an incision, a small wound made to prevent a greater bleeding. The Cartel had
accepted his intelligence without thanks, which was how he knew they valued it.
Now it had reached into Gloamreach and placed its fingers upon the Chalice of Ashdeep.
Or it wanted him to believe that it had.
“Marrowgate,” he said, “go to the outer passage. Remain within call.”
The quartermaster did not move.
“Do it.”
The man’s jaw worked once. Then he unbarred the door and stepped through, leaving it open behind him.
Ignatz waited until the footsteps had faded into the rain.
The messenger spoke. “He is loyal.”
“Loyalty is not a defense against being used.”
“Nor is treachery.”
Ignatz cut the cord.
Inside the cylinder was a strip of thin vellum rolled around a shard of grey glass. No script showed at first.
He held it near the brazier.
Letters surfaced in the warmth, pale and wavering.
CROOKGATE KEEP.
Below it, a second line appeared.
THE CHALICE OF ASHDEEP IS HOUSED IN CROOKGATE KEEP.
Ignatz did not breathe.
The room seemed to retreat from him. The walls withdrew into their mortar, the rain into the distance, the
fire into its bed of ash. The reliquary against his ribs grew cold enough to burn.
The messenger watched him.
“Where did you get this?”
“The Cartel knows where its interests lie.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you purchased.”
The words were mild. That made them cruel.
Ignatz placed the vellum upon the table. The grey glass shard lay beside it, dull as a dead eye. He had seen
such glass in the aftermath of the Sundering, set into wards and doors and the throats of men who had died
trying to open them. It held no reflection.
“Why tell me?”

“Because Crookgate Keep is not yours.”
“Nothing in this realm is mine.”
“Your command says otherwise.”
“My command says I keep what I am ordered to keep.”
“And what are you ordered to keep?”
Ignatz looked down at the reliquary’s concealed shape. “You already know.”
The messenger’s silence confirmed too much.
The Chalice of Ashdeep had been moved under authority that had never reached his desk. The registry
held no entry. No guard had reported a transfer. No seal had been broken in the chambers where such
things were recorded.
Yet the Cartel knew.
That was the horror of it—not that the Cartel possessed spies, but that every wall had begun to behave as
though it belonged to them.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged victor of The Purge of Blackport,” Ignatz said.
“Did it?”
“The records say so.”
“Records are obedient things.”
He remembered Blackport as a word spoken in briefings, always surrounded by figures and red marks.
Victory had been declared there. Victory had been celebrated there. The Cartel had stood among the ruins
and claimed the end of the killing.
A victory could be clean only from a distance.
“Why Crookgate Keep?” Ignatz asked.
The messenger’s head turned slightly toward the packet in his hand. “Because the Cartel wants you to
understand that a fortress can be opened without a gate.”
“And if I refuse to understand?”
“Then someone else will.”
“Who?”
No answer.
Ignatz folded the vellum once. The letters began to fade at the edges, sinking back into the fibers.
He could summon Marrowgate. He could order a search. He could place every corridor under arms and
have the keep turned inside out until the stone itself confessed. But the Chalice of Ashdeep was not merely
an object to be found. It was a burden of knowledge. Whoever had housed it in Crookgate Keep had
believed concealment stronger than custody.
Or had believed Ignatz would remain ignorant.

He thought of the Cartel’s intelligence in his own reports: troop movements, provisions, patrol gaps, the
quiet arithmetic of fear. He had sold information because information was weightless. One could pass it
through a hand and pretend the hand remained clean.
The reliquary disproved that lie.
The door shifted in its frame.
Marrowgate stood beyond it, one palm against the wood. He had heard enough to know the shape of the
danger, if not its name.
“Commander,” he said.
Ignatz slid the vellum beneath the packet.
“Come in.”
Marrowgate entered. His gaze went to the grey shard, then to the cylinder, then to Ignatz’s coat. He
understood more than Ignatz wanted him to understand.
“Is it about the keep?” he asked.
“It is about Crookgate Keep.”
“That is a distinction without mercy.”
The messenger moved toward the door.
Ignatz said, “You will not leave.”
“I have delivered the message.”
“You have delivered a threat.”
“A threat is a message that expects to be remembered.”
“Then remain and watch me remember it.”
The messenger paused.
Marrowgate looked between them. The brazier breathed a low red glow. Outside, the rain thickened
against the sealed windows, and Gloamreach became a world made entirely of water and walls.
Ignatz set his palm over the reliquary.
“Tell the Cartel,” he said, “that if the Chalice of Ashdeep is housed in Crookgate Keep, then someone has
placed it there for a reason.”
“Someone has.”
“Tell them I will find that reason.”
The messenger’s voice softened.
“They know you will.”
A sound came from the outer passage: a hurried step, then another. Marrowgate turned toward it.
Ignatz felt the cold beneath his hand deepen.

The messenger reached for the door.
And from somewhere inside the keep, a second voice began to call Marrowgate’s name.
The messenger’s hand stopped on the latch.
“Marrowgate,” the voice called again.
It came from the passage beyond the door. Not loudly. Not urgently. It possessed the intimate patience of a
man speaking to someone who had only stepped into the next room.
Ignatz Marrowgate had not moved. His palm remained beneath Ignatz’s, hovering over the reliquary as if
the Quartermaster feared that even air might disturb it.
Ignatz watched him.
“Answer,” he said.
Marrowgate swallowed. “Commander?”
The voice called his name a third time.
This time it came from behind them.
The rain pressed against the windows. The red glow under the reliquary’s lid trembled, and the iron seams
of the chamber gave a faint, inward creak.
Marrowgate turned.
Ignatz caught his sleeve.
“Do not.”
“But—”
“Do not answer anything that knows your name.”
The Quartermaster looked at him then, and the fear in his face was not for himself. It was the fear of a man
who had been handed a burden too large to carry and had only now felt it breathe.
Ignatz knew that fear. He had worn it beneath armor, beneath rank, beneath the hard silence expected of a
Warden-Commander. His birth had been entered as 258 AS. The record had never asked what had been
taken from him before that year ended, nor what he had learned afterward about the uses of obedience.
The voice came once more.
“Marrowgate.”
The door shuddered.
The messenger drew his blade. Its edge was dull with old work, but his grip was steady enough.
Ignatz looked down at the reliquary. The Chalice of Ashdeep lay within its black housing, forged in 323
AS, though no metal in the chamber had the right to feel so young. It seemed to draw age from the stones.
A thread of frost had formed across the lid.
“Take your hand away,” Ignatz said.
Marrowgate obeyed.

The cold withdrew from Ignatz’s palm with a slow, reluctant pull. He imagined roots being torn from
flesh.
Outside, something scraped along the passage wall.
“Who is there?” the messenger called.
Ignatz’s fingers closed around the weapon at his hip. The Hollow Edge had been forged in 216 AS. It was
not a sword, though the hand remembered it as one. The ward rested against his side with the weight of a
sealed grave.
A reply came through the door.
“Your commander.”
The messenger glanced at Ignatz.
Ignatz felt the keep listening.
“Open it,” he said.
Marrowgate stared at him.
“Commander—”
“Open it.”
The messenger lifted the latch.
The door swung inward on a breath of wet darkness.
No one stood in the passage.
Water crawled across the flagstones in thin black rivulets. The lamps burned low, each flame bent toward
the empty corridor. Farther on, where the passage turned toward the inner stair, a pale shape seemed to
wait—then vanished when the nearest lamp guttered.
The voice spoke from the stairwell.
“Marrowgate.”
The Quartermaster stepped forward.
Ignatz seized him by the collar and pulled him back hard enough to make the man choke.
At the same instant, the Hollow Edge stirred.
It did not ring. It gave a sensation of absence: a pressure behind the eyes, a hollowing in the teeth.
Attunement to The Hollow Edge cost 21. Ignatz had paid it in a room with no witnesses, and ever since,
the ward had known the shape of his fear better than any living creature.
The corridor darkened around its edge.
There, beneath the archway, lay a footprint.
Then another.
They were wet, narrow, and pointed toward the chamber.
The messenger raised his blade.

Ignatz held up two fingers.
The footsteps continued, though nothing made them.
Marrowgate’s breath trembled against his teeth. He was born in 425 AS, and his service as a
Quartermaster had taught him the arithmetic of hunger: what could be stored, what must be spent, what
loss could be concealed beneath a clean tally. It had not taught him what to do when a dead corridor began
counting its way toward him.
From the dark beyond the stair, a woman’s voice said, “You brought the intelligence.”
Ignatz felt something inside him tighten.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had paid for intelligence before. Coin had crossed from gloved hands to hidden
compartments; messages had left Gloamreach under seals that belonged to other men. He had sold them
routes, dispositions, weaknesses in walls and in commanders. He had never sold them this.
The voice continued.
“You brought the reliquary.”
The messenger looked at Ignatz now. Suspicion came easily to men who served near sealed doors. It
needed no proof, only a direction in which to face.
Ignatz stepped into the passage.
The air smelled of rainwater, lamp oil, and old ashes.
“Show yourself.”
The dark gave a low murmur.
Then a figure emerged beneath the arch.
It wore a coat soaked black from collar to hem. No face could be seen beneath the hood. A chain of iron
rings hung across its breast, each ring pale with moisture.
The messenger cursed under his breath.
Ignatz did not.
The five powers of the Ashen Era had each learned to disguise appetite as doctrine. The Ashen Vanguard
called its hunger duty. House Morvain called it inheritance. The Silent Choir called it silence. The
Iron-Ring Cartel called it commerce. The Bleeding Crown called it rule. But the figure in the passage had
no insignia beyond those rings, and that was enough.
“You are not the Cartel,” Ignatz said.
“No.”
“Then you are a thief.”
“Is that what you call yourself?”
Marrowgate made a small sound.
The figure turned its hood toward him.
“Do you remember Maelis Harrowick the Pale?” it asked.

Marrowgate went rigid.
Ignatz saw the answer before the Quartermaster gave it. The name entered the corridor like a blade laid
flat upon a table.
“My mentor,” Marrowgate whispered.
The figure’s hood inclined.
“Your mentor knew where the ash was buried.”
“Maelis is dead,” Marrowgate said.
“Dead things keep better accounts.”
Ignatz moved before Marrowgate could speak again. He drew The Hollow Edge.
The ward appeared as a line of darkness, not black but vacant, as though the world had forgotten how to
reflect upon it. The lamps leaned away.
The figure in the hood did not retreat.
“Do you know why Gloamreach is quarantined?” it asked.
Ignatz held the ward before him.
“Because the Pale Coast has no patience for carelessness.”
“Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast. Its garrison is 2,483. Men and women behind walls, told that the
walls are the reason they live.”
The rain hissed in the sealed windows behind him.
“What has that to do with this?”
“Everything.”
The figure lifted one hand. Its fingers were bare and wet. “Fenspire stands in the Gloaming Reach. It was
founded in 57 AS. Its garrison is 3,742. A disciplined place. A vigilant place. A place that has mistaken
permanence for protection.”
The messenger shifted his footing.
Ignatz heard the movement and the fear beneath it.
“Speak plainly,” he said.
“Plain speech is for those who can afford to be understood.”
The figure looked past him, toward the chamber and the reliquary.
“The Chalice of Ashdeep was forged in 323 AS. Attunement to it costs 27.”
Marrowgate’s face had gone bloodless.
Ignatz tightened his grip on The Hollow Edge. Attunement to it cost 21. He felt the old emptiness open
within his hand, listening for the Chalice, measuring the distance between severance and surrender.
“You know too much,” he said.

“I know what the Cartel wants.”
“And what does it want?”
The hooded figure’s head turned slightly.
“To open the cup.”
The reliquary clicked behind them.
Not loudly.
A sound like a fingernail touching glass.
Marrowgate flinched. The messenger looked toward the chamber.
Ignatz did not turn. He watched the figure.
“What is inside?”
“The part of the Sundering that learned to thirst.”
No one spoke.
The statement settled into the stones. Somewhere below, water moved through hidden channels. The keep
seemed less like a fortress than a body with its organs buried beneath the floor.
Ignatz had stood at the edges of the Purge of Blackport. He had seen what victory did to men who believed
themselves cleansed by it. The Iron-Ring Cartel had emerged as victor, and the tale had been made into a
banner. Banners did not carry the smell of poisoned wells. Banners did not remember the hands of their
own allies sinking beneath black water.
He had sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel because information was lighter than blood.
He had told himself that every secret was merely a door.
The figure in the passage said, “You sent them the road to Crookgate Keep.”
“I sent them nothing.”
“You sent them enough.”
Marrowgate turned on him.
“Commander?”
There it was: the true voice. Not the corridor’s imitation. Not the wet whisper beneath the arch. A human
voice, cracked by betrayal.
Ignatz could have lied. He had done so with better faces watching.
Instead, he said, “The Cartel knew the reliquary was here.”
“You knew,” Marrowgate said.
“I knew they were searching.”
“You knew.”
The figure raised its hand.

The door behind Ignatz slammed shut.
The messenger spun and drove his blade into the wood. It struck with a flat, useless sound. The lock had
not moved. The door had become part of the wall.
In the chamber, the reliquary opened.
Red light poured through the passage.
Marrowgate cried out. The figure in the hood recoiled, and for the first time Ignatz saw beneath the
shadow where a face should have been.
There was no face.
Only a pale hollow, deep enough to contain the red glow of the Chalice.
The Hollow Edge pulled toward it.
Ignatz’s wrist twisted. Pain climbed his arm.
The figure spoke with many voices now, layered and wet.
“Choose, Warden-Commander.”
Behind him, Marrowgate began to pray.
Before him, the faceless hollow widened.
And in the red light, the first drop fell from the Chalice of Ashdeep.

Chapter 10
Greyfell Citadel rose from the Shattered Vale like a tooth left in a dead mouth.
Morwenna Ashgrove saw it first through a curtain of rain: grey walls, broken towers, and the black gaps
where banners had once strained against the wind. No fires marked the battlements. No watchman called
from the gatehouse. The road beneath her horse’s hooves had narrowed to two muddy ruts between thorn
and stone, and the silence beyond them seemed to possess weight.
Greyfell Citadel was abandoned.
The thought entered her with less force than the rain. Abandoned places had their own discipline. They
kept no sentries, made no demands, offered no testimony. They were useful because the living disliked
entering them, and more useful still because the dead did not care who listened.
She raised one gloved hand.
The small procession halted behind her. Leather creaked. A horse breathed steam into the wet air. No one
spoke. They had learned not to speak when she lifted her hand.
Fleet Admiral was a title that made silence obey.
Morwenna looked back only once. The men and women behind her wore no colors bright enough to carry
across a field. Their cloaks were rain-dark, their weapons wrapped against the weather. She had chosen
them for their obedience and for the absence of questions in their faces. Questions were a kind of hunger.
Hunger made people careless.
Then she turned toward the gate.
A chain shifted overhead.
The gatehouse had been empty when they reached it. Now a figure stood beneath the arch, pale against the
dark stone. The figure wore a long coat soaked nearly black, and over it the severe collar of an inquisitor.
Two narrow crowns had been worked into the metal at the throat.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned waited beneath the ruined arch.
Morwenna dismounted. Mud took her boots to the ankle. She felt the cold find its way through the seams
of her gloves, but kept her hands at her sides.
“High Inquisitor,” she said.
“I am Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned,” Sabelle replied. “And I am the High Inquisitor.”
Their voice was neither loud nor soft. It carried because the citadel carried it, giving the words back in
thin, fractured echoes.
Morwenna approached until the rain struck both of them equally.
“I know who you are.”
“Then you know why I asked you to come.”
“I know only that the summons bore your seal.”
Sabelle regarded her with the patient severity of an executioner examining a knot. Their face gave away
nothing that Morwenna could use. That was not the same as having nothing to hide. Morwenna had

learned the difference in rooms where men confessed before they understood they had been accused.
“The seal was sufficient,” Sabelle said.
“It was inconvenient.”
“Those are not opposing qualities.”
Behind Sabelle, the gate stood open on a courtyard drowned in weeds. The rain had made black mirrors of
the flagstones. A collapsed gallery leaned against the inner wall, its beams jutting like ribs. Somewhere
farther inside, water dripped with the stubborn rhythm of a clock that had forgotten the hour.
Morwenna glanced at the ruin.
“You chose a dead fortress.”
“I chose a place beyond the realm’s core holdings.”
“That is a careful distinction.”
“It is the distinction keeping us alive.”
The words settled between them.
Morwenna had heard versions of that sentence from lords, commanders, priests, and merchants. Every
faction made a sacrament of survival. The Ashen Vanguard called it duty. House Morvain called it
inheritance. The Silent Choir called it silence. The Iron-Ring Cartel called it profit.
She had called it a message sent through three hands and paid for in coin she had never touched.
The memory came unbidden: a scrap of oiled paper, hidden beneath a naval dispatch; a cipher she had not
needed to read twice; the knowledge that a fleet’s course could be altered by a single omission. She had
sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel because information had always been worth more than blood, and
because the Cartel understood that truth had no loyalty except to the highest bidder.
Yet here, in the rain before Greyfell Citadel, she felt the old transaction turn in her mind like a blade.
Sabelle stepped aside.
“Come in.”
Morwenna did not move.
“Do you expect my escort to remain outside?”
“I expect your escort to remain where it is.”
“They are under my command.”
“Not within these walls.”
Morwenna let the rain collect along the brim of her hat. The men behind her waited in the road, watching
without seeming to watch. If she entered alone, they would read it as confidence. If she refused, they
would read it as fear. Both readings could become dangerous in other mouths.
She looked once more into the citadel. The dark beyond the gate was not empty. The air had the stale chill
of a cellar, though the courtyard lay open to the sky.
“Keep the gate unbarred,” she said to no one in particular.

One of her escort acknowledged her with a movement of the head.
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened.
“You fear a trap?”
“I fear doors.”
“A peculiar weakness for a Fleet Admiral.”
“Ships with doors can still sink.”
For the first time, something like amusement touched Sabelle’s mouth. It vanished before Morwenna
could decide whether she had truly seen it.
She entered.
The citadel smelled of wet stone, rotting straw, and old ash. Her boots struck the courtyard flagstones with
measured force. The sound went nowhere. Rain ran from the broken crenellations in silver threads,
gathering in the cracks and spilling beneath the doors of shuttered buildings.
Greyfell Citadel had been founded in 62 AS in the Shattered Vale, though no inscription remained intact
enough to prove it. Morwenna had read the surviving records in naval archives that no longer admitted to
owning them. Founding stones, siege tallies, inventories of grain and iron, lists of men whose descendants
had forgotten the names. Every stronghold believed its records would outlive its walls. Greyfell had
disproved the belief.
Sabelle led her beneath an archway scarred by fire.
“Why here?” Morwenna asked.
“Because certain things are easier to hear where no one is speaking.”
“That sounds like the doctrine of the Silent Choir.”
“Does it?”
“You tell me.”
Sabelle did not answer. Their hands were folded behind their back. The cuffs of their coat showed no mud,
though the courtyard was thick with it. Morwenna noticed that. She noticed everything that was too clean.
They passed into a narrow hall. The ceiling had collapsed at one end, exposing a strip of rain-clouded sky.
At the other, a staircase descended into darkness.
Sabelle stopped beside it.
Morwenna felt the air change.
The cold rose from below, carrying a smell beneath the damp stone. Not rot. Not exactly. Something
sweeter, older, with the faint mineral sting of blood left too long in a sealed vessel.
She did not look down.
“You keep company beneath the earth,” she said.
Sabelle turned their head.
“Do I?”

“There is a breathing sound.”
“There are many sounds in abandoned places.”
The sound came again.
A slow drag. A wet exhalation. Then a faint scrape against stone, as if fingernails—or something
remembering fingernails—moved across the wall below.
Morwenna’s pulse remained steady. Years of command had not taught her courage. They had taught her
how to make fear wait.
“Is that why you summoned me?” she asked.
“No.”
“Then you brought me here to hear it.”
“I brought you here because I wanted to see whether you would pretend not to.”
Morwenna studied Sabelle’s face. The High Inquisitor wore severity as other people wore armor, but
armor disclosed the direction of a blow. Sabelle disclosed nothing.
“Your methods are theatrical.”
“Your reputation is theatrical.”
“My reputation was assembled by people who needed me to be seen.”
“Then you have something in common with every ruler who has survived the Ashen Era.”
The dead thing below breathed once more.
Morwenna thought of the Leaden Accord, of its hosts swallowed beneath a Ley-storm and its victory
declared over graves no victor had entered. The Iron-Ring Cartel had been named victor. Named, not
crowned. There were words that functioned as locks. If repeated often enough, they kept the truth outside.
A supposedly destroyed artifact had been spirited away.
She had not seen it. She had seen the movement of ships, the sudden silence in ledgers, the frightened
arithmetic of those who thought concealment meant safety. She had sold pieces of that knowledge to the
Cartel and kept the most dangerous pieces behind her teeth.
Sabelle watched her.
“You know why the Cartel was pleased with the Accord,” they said.
Morwenna let her gaze drift to the stairwell.
“The Iron-Ring Cartel is pleased by anything that leaves a market.”
“And you?”
“I am pleased when my fleet returns.”
“You have no fleet here.”
“No,” Morwenna said. “I have only my name.”
“Names are vessels. They carry what is put inside them.”

“And what have you put inside mine?”
Sabelle turned toward the corridor. “Not yet.”
They resumed walking.
At the end of the hall, a pair of iron doors stood open. Beyond them, the old council chamber waited
beneath a roof of patched timber. A table occupied its center, its surface covered with maps, sealed
packets, and a shallow brass basin in which rainwater trembled though no drop fell near it.
Morwenna crossed the threshold.
The doors behind her swung inward.
She heard the scrape of the bolts sliding home.
Not from her escort. From within the walls.
Sabelle moved to the table and placed two fingers against the nearest packet.
“Before we begin,” they said, “you must understand that what I am about to show you has not been
copied, recorded, or spoken aloud.”
Morwenna looked at the seals. None bore a crest she recognized.
“That is an ambitious claim.”
“It is a threat, not a claim.”
“Then make it plain.”
Sabelle’s eyes lifted to hers.
“Someone has been selling intelligence from the Admiralty.”
The room seemed to contract around the words.
Morwenna felt the rain ticking against the roof. Felt the damp leather at her wrists. Felt, beneath the floor,
the patient revenant shifting in its chains.
She placed one hand on the table, careful not to touch the packets.
“Someone?”
“The evidence is incomplete.”
“How fortunate.”
“It is not fortune. It is restraint.”
“Restraint would have been bringing evidence instead of rumor.”
“I brought both.”
Sabelle broke the seal.
Inside lay a strip of sailcloth, folded around a thin metal plate. The cloth bore a pattern of dark stains,
arranged not randomly but in lines and angles. Morwenna recognized the notation at once. It was the kind
used to mark patrol routes where ink might wash away, where a sailor’s hand could be dismissed as a
tremor.

Her own cipher.
For one heartbeat she saw a harbor that was not present: lanterns blurred by fog, hulls turning without
sound, a signal lamp shuttering twice from a darkened deck.
Then the chamber door shuddered.
The thing below the citadel began to scream.
Sabelle did not flinch. Morwenna’s hand moved toward the knife at her belt before discipline stopped it.
The scream rose through the stones, thin as a child’s voice and deep as a tomb opening. Dust sifted from
the beams. The brass basin rippled, though the air remained still.
Sabelle placed the metal plate atop the stained cloth.
“Tell me,” they said, “why does the Iron-Ring Cartel possess the route of a fleet that was never—”
The question died beneath the next convulsion of the citadel.
Morwenna felt the tremor rise through the soles of her boots and enter her bones. The table shivered. Ink
crawled in its dish. Somewhere below, iron struck stone with a slow, deliberate rhythm.
Once.
Twice.
Then the scream became a wet inhalation.
Sabelle’s hand remained upon the metal plate. Their fingers were pale in the candlelight, the knuckles
sharp beneath the skin. The crowns they wore were not visible beneath the hood, but Morwenna felt their
presence all the same: a pressure in the room, a double weight behind every word.
“Answer me,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna looked at the plate.
The cipher had been stamped into its surface, though the lines seemed to move when she stared too long.
Her own cipher. Not the formal marks used by the fleet. Not the seal reserved for orders that could
condemn a ship and every soul aboard it. This was older than those. A private hand translated into
geometry, a language of omissions and false bearings.
A language she had sold.
The knowledge sat in her throat like a fishbone.
“The route is not a fleet route,” Morwenna said.
“Then what is it?”
“A lure.”
Sabelle tilted their head. “For whom?”
The chamber groaned. Fine grit slid from the ceiling and pattered across the cloth. Morwenna heard the
distant clatter of chains, though she could not tell whether it came from below or from inside the walls.
“For anyone who still believes the war ended where the ledgers say it did.”

“The Leaden Accord.”
Morwenna did not answer.
Sabelle lifted the plate. The candle flame bent toward it. “The Iron-Ring Cartel was a belligerent in The
Leaden Accord.”
The words were spoken with the flat precision of an indictment. They did not need to be louder. Sabelle
had a talent for making silence testify.
Morwenna watched the metal tremble between their hands.
“Many powers were involved,” she said.
“That is not a denial.”
“It is a fact.”
“Facts are the bones. I am asking about the knife.”
The scream below began again.
This time Morwenna heard syllables within it. Not words. The suggestion of words, shaped by a throat
that had forgotten speech and remembered only the punishment of having one. The sound pressed at the
back of her eyes.
She had stood on decks while storms tore masts from ships. She had watched men burn in oil and watched
the sea close over them without a ripple. The thing beneath Greyfell Citadel frightened her because it did
not rage like weather. It waited between its screams.
“The route was sent to me,” she said.
“By the Iron-Ring Cartel?”
Morwenna held Sabelle’s gaze.
A poor question. Too clean. Too eager to be denied.
“No.”
The lie left her smoothly. That was the worst of it. There had been a time when lying required invention.
Now it required only selection: which truth to expose, which truth to salt, which truth to bury beneath the
first.
Sabelle set the plate down.
“Caedmon Fellgard found the mark in a confiscated register,” they said. “He copied it without
understanding it. The copy led us here.”
“Where is he?”
“Writing.”
“Still?”
“Still.”
Of course. Caedmon Fellgard would be writing while stone cracked and the dead—or whatever lived
below—screamed through the dark. He would record each tremor in his disciplined hand, preserve the

order of terror as though order itself might become a ward.
Morwenna imagined the scribe bent over his pages, ink drying at the nib, his reserve mistaken for courage
by anyone who had never watched a man use duty as a barricade.
“What did the register contain?” she asked.
Sabelle’s eyes lowered to the cloth. “Names. Stores. Provisions. Soundings.”
“For a fleet?”
“For an army.”
That struck more deeply than it should have.
The fleets of the Ashen Vanguard had always required provisions, but armies left different wounds upon
paper. Grain. Pitch. Nails. Draft animals. Burial cloth. Every campaign became a hunger list before it
became a battle.
“The Leaden Accord was not fought at sea,” Morwenna said.
“No.”
“Then the cipher was repurposed.”
“By whom?”
The chamber seemed to contract around them. Candlelight withdrew from the corners. Morwenna could
smell damp mortar, old wax, and something sweet beneath them—a stagnant sweetness like flowers left
too long in a sealed room.
She looked toward the floor.
“The marsh.”
Sabelle did not move.
Morwenna heard herself breathing. Beneath the floor, something scraped once along the underside of the
stone.
“Greyfell Citadel was used as a waystation,” she continued. “Not by the fleet. By those who survived the
field.”
“Which survivors?”
“Ask the register.”
“It has no answer.”
“Then ask the dead.”
“Do not turn piety into evasion.”
“I am not the one keeping a dead thing beneath a citadel.”
The words escaped before discipline could catch them.
The silence that followed was absolute.

Morwenna knew then that she had stepped close to the edge. She could not see it, but she felt the air
change over the drop.
Sabelle’s face remained composed. Only their thumb moved, brushing once across the rim of the plate.
“What do you know of what is beneath us?” they asked.
“Less than you think.”
“Do you know the name?”
Morwenna looked at the brass basin. The reflected flame had gone black in its water.
“The Marsh Revenant lairs in Greyfell Citadel.”
The statement seemed to unlock something.
Below them, the chains began to move.
Not rattle. Move.
One length drawing across stone. Then another. A slow gathering, as if a great body were pulling itself
upright in the dark.
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened. “You have seen it.”
“No.”
“You have heard it.”
“I have heard sailors speak.”
“Sailors speak of storms as if storms possess intent.”
“Sometimes they do.”
“And this?”
Morwenna’s mouth had gone dry. “This is older than the stories.”
Sabelle leaned across the table. The candlelight showed no fear in them. That absence disturbed her more
than fear would have.
“Tell me about Voltaire Hollowmere.”
The name opened a locked compartment in Morwenna’s memory.
A field drowned in grey light. Mud sucking at boots. Standards sagging in rain that fell sideways. A figure
standing where the lines had broken, one hand lifted, not in command but in warning.
Voltaire Hollowmere fought in The Leaden Accord, fighting for The Ashen Vanguard.
She had never met him in a room like this. She had known him at a distance: a marked presence amid ruin,
the kind of soldier whose survival became an accusation against everyone who had ordered the battle.
“He was there,” Morwenna said.
“Where?”
“On the field.”

“That answer would satisfy a priest.”
“I am not speaking to a priest.”
Sabelle’s expression did not change, but the room seemed to acquire a colder center.
“Voltaire Hollowmere fought in The Leaden Accord, fighting for The Ashen Vanguard,” they said. “That
is what Caedmon Fellgard wrote.”
“Then why ask me?”
“Because Caedmon records what is placed before him. You record what people intend.”
The accusation was accurate enough to be dangerous.
Morwenna thought of letters folded inside oilskin, of sealed packets hidden behind charts, of instructions
sent without signatures. She thought of the Iron-Ring Cartel’s payments—not coin alone, never merely
coin, but access, forewarning, absences arranged where absences could be mistaken for weather or
incompetence.
She had told herself that intelligence was a current. It moved regardless of who opened the sluice. She had
only chosen where to stand.
Below, the thing struck the stone.
The floor jumped. The basin tipped and spilled a black fan across the cloth. Sabelle caught the plate before
it slid away.
From the corridor came a muffled cry.
Morwenna turned toward the door.
“Scribe,” Sabelle called.
No answer.
“Caedmon Fellgard.”
A heavier impact shook dust from the lintel.
Then Caedmon’s voice came through the wood, strained but controlled. “The outer stair is sealed.”
“By what?”
“Stone.”
“Can you open it?”
“I can hear something on the other side.”
Sabelle glanced at Morwenna. “And?”
Caedmon’s breathing touched the door like a hand. “It is breathing back.”
The sound beneath them ceased.
That was worse than the screaming.
Morwenna’s fingers found the hilt at her belt. The gesture was habitual, almost ceremonial. Her weapon
waited where it always waited, obedient to the last order she had given it. A blade was a simple thing. It

did not conceal its appetite.
Sabelle folded the stained cloth around the plate.
“Where does the route end?” they asked.
Morwenna did not speak.
“Fleet Admiral.”
The title landed with the old authority of a command barked across a storm-tossed deck. For one instant
she was back among rigging and salt, with men waiting for her to point toward danger and call it
necessary.
The route ended nowhere marked on any chart.
That was why it had been useful.
“The destination was erased,” she said.
“By you?”
“Not by me.”
“But you know it.”
“I know what it avoids.”
Sabelle’s hand closed around the bundle. “What does it avoid?”
Morwenna stared at the black water soaking into the cloth.
“The sea.”
A pause.
Then Caedmon shouted from the corridor.
The door bowed inward.
Once.
The hinges screamed.
Morwenna drew her blade. Candlelight ran along its edge, thin and bloodless. Sabelle did not draw a
weapon. They placed the wrapped plate inside their coat and raised one hand toward the door.
A second blow struck.
This time the wood split.
Through the widening crack came a breath of marsh rot, cold water, and the faintest trace of ash.
Morwenna saw a shape beyond the threshold—not a face, not yet, but a pallid height stooping beneath the
lintel. Something dragged itself across the stones with the patient labor of a creature that had all the time in
the world.
Sabelle spoke a word Morwenna did not know.
The candles went out.

In the dark, Caedmon Fellgard began to pray.
The thing outside answered him in Voltaire Hollowmere’s voice.
The voice came from the threshold.
“Morwenna.”
It was Voltaire Hollowmere’s voice, worn thin by distance and water. It carried the old iron of command,
the habit of being obeyed even when no one wished to obey.
Morwenna’s hand found the hilt at her side. The blade was a comfort only because it was solid. The
darkness had made the room uncertain; the walls seemed to breathe around her, and the floor gave a faint,
wet complaint beneath the thing’s weight.
Caedmon Fellgard’s prayer faltered.
“Do not answer it,” Sabelle said.
Their voice was near. Too near. Morwenna heard the whisper of cloth, the careful movement of someone
who had not panicked and therefore was more dangerous than anyone who had.
“What is it?” Caedmon asked.
“A debt.”
The thing beyond the door scraped one long nail—or bone, or iron—across the broken wood.
“Morwenna,” it said again. “You sold the tide.”
Her mouth went dry.
In the dark, memory rose with the precision of an opened ledger: sealed charts, altered patrol routes,
harbor depths written in a cipher no court clerk could read. Information passed through hands that never
touched one another. A coin purse left beneath a loose flagstone. A message burned after its contents had
been learned.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had never asked her to betray a fleet. That would have been vulgar. They had asked
for smaller things—the hour a convoy departed, the strength of a watch, the name of a captain who might
be bought. Small things became channels. Channels became rivers. Rivers carried kingdoms into ruin.
She had told herself the realm survived because of it.
She had told herself survival was a kind of innocence.
“Your silence answers,” said the voice.
A pale hand entered through the split in the door.
It was not pale like flesh. It was the color of drowned wax, ridged and gleaming with marsh water. The
fingers curled over the timber. Mud fell from them in black beads.
Morwenna stepped backward, and her heel struck Caedmon’s boot.
The scribe sucked in a breath. His body was rigid beneath her touch, his fear held in the same disciplined
posture he gave to ink and parchment. She remembered seeing him at tables crowded with petitions,
inventories, and death rolls, his hand moving without tremor while men outside begged for bread. A

keeper of records. A servant to what had happened, rather than to what anyone wished had happened.
“Caedmon,” she whispered. “The lamp.”
“It is extinguished.”
“Then relight it.”
“With what?”
She almost laughed. The sound would have been hysterical and therefore useful to nothing.
The thing pulled itself farther into the room.
Sabelle moved first. A shape crossed the darkness; then something struck with a wet, heavy force. The
creature made no cry. The impact shook the doorframe.
Morwenna drew her weapon.
The blade came free with a whisper.
For an instant, the dark opened around the edge. A weak red line crawled along the steel—not reflected
light, but a dull inner glow, as though the metal remembered a furnace.
The creature turned toward her.
She saw its head.
It had no face. Water streamed from a hollow where features should have been, and beneath the dripping
veil something pale shifted, searching. Its neck bent at an angle that belonged to a broken doll. Around its
throat hung scraps of blackened cloth, perhaps a uniform, perhaps a burial shroud. The stench of marsh
and old ash thickened until Morwenna tasted it at the back of her tongue.
“Morwenna Ashgrove,” it murmured.
The use of her full name struck harder than any blow.
Sabelle’s weapon—or perhaps only their hand—caught the creature across the chest. A flash burst in the
dark, white and soundless. The revenant recoiled, its arms flinging wide.
Revenant.
The word settled into Morwenna’s mind with a coldness deeper than fear.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned had a bound revenant in their cellar.
The secret had been spoken in whispers by those who believed themselves too cautious to be overheard.
Morwenna had dismissed it as court venom, the sort of tale bred wherever power was hidden behind stone.
Yet the thing stood before her now, wet with the grave, and Sabelle’s movements possessed the weary
familiarity of a jailer dealing with a prisoner who had escaped before.
“You keep this below us,” Morwenna said.
“Not now.”
“Where is its chain?”
“Not now.”

The revenant lurched forward.
Sabelle caught it by the wrist. The creature’s other hand struck their shoulder and drove them into the
wall. Stone groaned. Their crown—one of them, Morwenna could not tell which—rang against the
masonry.
Caedmon shouted a line from his prayer and threw something. It shattered against the revenant’s back.
The smell of vinegar and bitter herbs flooded the room.
The creature paused.
“Records,” it said.
Its voice had changed. For a breath it spoke in Voltaire Hollowmere’s voice, then in Caedmon’s, then in a
child’s voice that made Morwenna think of no one she knew.
“Records burn. Names remain.”
Caedmon crouched beside the table. Papers whispered beneath his hands.
“What are you doing?” Morwenna demanded.
“Finding what it wants.”
“Everything wants something.”
His fingers closed around a small leather folio. He rose with it pressed against his chest. The faint outline
of his face emerged as the red glow from Morwenna’s blade found him.
The revenant looked at the folio.
Sabelle drove their elbow into its throat.
The creature folded, but its fingers remained locked around Sabelle’s arm. The skin beneath its grasp
blackened at once, spreading in thin veins.
Morwenna moved before thought could stop her. She struck the revenant across the knuckles.
The blade bit.
No blood came. A sound like splitting ice passed through the room, and the hand released Sabelle. The
creature staggered away, its head snapping toward Morwenna.
“You opened the way,” it said.
She knew, then, what it meant.
The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties. The Iron-Ring Cartel
was named victor. Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm, and the world accepted that judgment
because the dead could not contradict it.
But an artifact had survived.
Supposedly destroyed, it had been spirited away while the armies vanished beneath the storm. Morwenna
had learned that truth in fragments, each fragment purchased by treachery. The artifact was not a weapon
in any simple sense. It was a key, or a vessel, or a wound made portable. The Cartel had wanted its
location.

She had sold them pieces of the truth.
The revenant knew.
“Where is it?” it asked.
Morwenna’s grip tightened until the hilt cut into her palm.
Sabelle turned their head toward her. Whatever pain the revenant had caused, they concealed it behind that
severe stillness. “You know what it means?”
“I know what it wants.”
“That was not my question.”
“No,” Morwenna said. “It was not.”
The creature crossed the room in a blur of wet limbs. Sabelle raised an arm, but the revenant passed them,
reaching for Morwenna. Caedmon flung himself between them.
He did not look brave. He looked terrified, which made the act worse.
The revenant’s hand closed around his throat.
The folio fell.
Caedmon clawed at the wrist, his boots scraping uselessly over the stone. His other hand opened and
closed, still trying to write.
Morwenna saw the page that had slipped from the folio. A dispatch, marked with the seal of Palewell
Abbey.
She knew the place from naval reports. Palewell Abbey stands in The Pale Coast. It was founded in 244
AS, rebuilt, and maintains a garrison of 5998. It is not a core holding. The words had been copied in
Caedmon’s careful hand, without comment.
Below them, in a second column, another notation:
Greyfell Citadel.
No explanation. No destination. Only the name, surrounded by corrections and ink so dark it had nearly
eaten through the page.
The revenant tightened its grip.
Caedmon’s eyes bulged. A small, humiliating sound escaped him.
Morwenna lunged.
Her blade entered beneath the creature’s ribs. The point emerged from its back, trailing strands of dark
water that writhed like worms in moonlight. The revenant bent around the steel. Its face came close to
hers.
The hollow beneath its dripping veil contained a glimmer.
Not an eye.
A shard of light trapped in a depthless socket.

The Ley-storm lived there.
Morwenna tried to wrench the blade free. The creature leaned into it instead, bringing its mouth—or the
place where a mouth had once been—against her ear.
“Palewell Abbey is a door,” it whispered. “The artifact is not dead.”
Sabelle seized the revenant from behind. Their uninjured hand closed around its throat, and they spoke the
unknown word again.
This time, the word had weight.
The room buckled.
Morwenna fell to one knee. Caedmon collapsed beside her, coughing, while the revenant convulsed
between Sabelle’s arms. From somewhere below the floor came a sound of chains dragged across stone.
A second sound answered it.
Then a third.
Morwenna looked at Sabelle.
Their face was bloodless in the returning dark. They had not merely kept a bound revenant in their cellar.
They had kept something beneath it, something that recognized the command and strained against it.
“You brought us here for this,” Morwenna said.
Sabelle’s gaze dropped to the fallen dispatch.
“I brought you here because you were already involved.”
“With what?”
The revenant’s body began to come apart.
Not decay. Unmaking.
Its limbs thinned into streamers of marsh mist. The cloth around its throat burned without flame. Beneath
the dissolving flesh, lines of white fire appeared, forming a pattern Morwenna recognized from the sealed
reports of the Leaden Accord.
A circle split by a descending stroke.
The mark that had been found on the artifact’s empty reliquary.
Caedmon saw it too. His hand crept toward the folio.
“Do not touch that,” Sabelle said.
The scribe froze.
The revenant’s remaining shape bent toward Morwenna one last time.
“Tell the Iron-Ring Cartel,” it said.
The floor opened.
Not cracked—opened, as if a black mouth had been waiting beneath the stones. Cold air rushed upward,
carrying the smell of wet earth, old blood, and extinguished candles. Sabelle vanished to the waist. Their

hand caught the edge, fingers clawing into the mortar.
Morwenna seized their wrist.
For one moment they hung together above the dark: High Inquisitor and Fleet Admiral, jailer and
accomplice, each holding the other above whatever waited below.
Sabelle looked up at her.
“Let go,” they said.
The chains beneath them began to climb.
Morwenna felt the wrapped plate beneath her coat grow warm.
Far below, in the dark under Greyfell Citadel, something struck stone once.
Then again.
Then, in a voice that was neither Voltaire Hollowmere’s nor the revenant’s, it spoke her name.

Chapter 11
The quarantine bells of Gloamreach did not ring so much as shudder.
Their iron voices rolled through the fog and struck the walls of the old chapel, where Malchior Cindervale
the Flame-Touched stood with one palm pressed to the altar stone. The rock was cold beneath the glove.
Cold enough to feel like judgment.
Beyond the shuttered windows, the Pale Coast had vanished into white murk. Gloamreach lay sealed
inside it, its gates barred, its roads watched, its breath held. The garrison numbered 2,483, and every one
of those soldiers had been ordered to treat the town as though it were already dead.
Malchior had delivered the order themselves.
“By sanctified authority,” they had said, their voice carrying over the wind, “Gloamreach is quarantined.”
The words had pleased the guards. Authority always pleased those who did not possess it.
Now the chapel smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and the faint mineral tang that rose from the sea. Malchior
lifted their hand from the altar. A pale smear of salt clung to the black glove.
Behind them, the door opened.
Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven entered without asking leave.
They wore no visible insignia of rank. They needed none. The Blood-Mage carried their reputation like a
second skin, and the silence that followed them through the chapel was its proper herald. Isolde had been
born in 286 AS, though Malchior had never understood why anyone would record such a thing. Birth was
an accident. What a person chose afterward was the only date that mattered.
Isolde’s gaze passed over the altar, the icon fractured by the Sundering, the candles burning low in their
cups.
“You closed the town,” they said.
“I did.”
“On what evidence?”
“On the evidence of the bells.”
“The bells were rung by frightened men.”
“Frightened men still have hands.”
Isolde smiled without warmth. “And frightened Arch-Prelates still have throats.”
Malchior turned toward them. The firelight caught the faint red veining at their temples, the mark that had
earned them the name Flame-Touched before they had earned the vestments. The title had proved easier to
carry than the truth beneath it.
The truth had been written in their own hand.
They had forged their lineage papers.
Not altered them. Not embellished some ancient record with a flattering flourish. Forged them. Ink, seals,
dead signatures, a chain of descent that led nowhere except toward the office they now occupied. The

papers had survived scrutiny because Malchior had understood what the examiners wished to find: not
truth, but permission to believe.
A lie, carefully sanctified, became history.
“You came to challenge the quarantine?” Malchior asked.
“I came to challenge you.”
“Then you have mistaken the chapel for a battlefield.”
“I have mistaken nothing.”
The bells shuddered again. Dust whispered from the rafters.
At the far end of the chapel, Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood in the doorway he had left open. The
Warden-Commander had been born in 258 AS, and the years had made his authority seem less like a
garment than a scar. No canonical feature distinguished him from any other hard-bitten officer; his epithet
did the work. The Oathless. A title bestowed by enemies, perhaps, or friends who had lived long enough to
become enemies.
His hand rested near the hilt at his side.
Isolde’s eyes narrowed.
“Still following me?” they asked.
“I was here first.”
“That has never stopped you.”
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” Malchior said, “you were ordered to remain outside the inner chapel.”
“I remained outside until the Blood-Mage entered.”
“Then your obedience is as selective as your memory.”
Ignatz looked at Malchior, and something passed between them that had no name fit for the chapel.
Suspicion, perhaps. Or recognition. Ignatz secretly sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel, though no
confession had crossed his lips. Malchior had seen the signs in the ledgers: patrols redirected, warnings
arriving too late, sealed routes known to hands that should never have touched them.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had learned how to purchase silence. Ignatz had learned how to sell it.
Isolde stepped nearer the altar.
“Ask him where the report came from,” they said.
Malchior kept their face still. “Which report?”
“The one naming the wells.”
Ignatz’s expression hardened. “There are no wells named in my report.”
“Then it is fortunate that I did not mention a report.”
“You mentioned one now.”
“I mentioned wells.”

The chapel seemed to contract around them. Outside, the fog pressed its blind face to the shutters.
Malchior had read the records in the dead hours before dawn. They had read them beneath a single candle
while the quarantine seals dried on the gates. The records concerned the Purge of Blackport, which began
in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. They recorded 70,907 casualties and the total rout of the aggressors. The
Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Those were the approved words.
Approved words were bones laid in orderly rows. They made a clean grave for whatever had truly
happened.
The secret truth of the Purge of Blackport was that the victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Malchior had found the sentence hidden beneath a scraped layer of ink, pressed into the parchment so
deeply that the fibers still remembered it. The Iron-Ring Cartel had not merely defeated its enemies. It had
murdered its own allies and let the slaughter wear the mask of war.
The wells had carried the betrayal farther than any blade.
“Blackport,” Malchior said.
Ignatz’s eyes flickered.
Isolde’s smile returned.
“The Purge of Blackport,” Malchior continued, “began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. It caused 70,907
casualties and ended with the total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.”
“Everyone knows that,” Ignatz said.
“Everyone knows the record.”
“And the record is sufficient.”
“No,” Isolde said. “It is convenient.”
Malchior watched Ignatz. “The secret truth of the Purge of Blackport is that the victors poisoned the wells
of their own allies.”
For a moment, the only sound was the trembling of the bells.
Ignatz did not move. That was the movement. His stillness became too deliberate, too complete. A man
innocent of a thing might recoil from it. A man guilty of nothing might laugh. Ignatz merely stood there,
measuring what the words would cost.
Isolde looked pleased, but not surprised.
“You knew,” Malchior said.
“I knew rumors.”
“You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The Warden-Commander’s hand left the hilt and fell open at his side.
Isolde turned their head slightly. “There. That is the first honest sentence spoken in this room.”
“I have never sold anything to the Cartel.”

“Then you have given it away,” Malchior said.
Ignatz’s gaze sharpened. “Careful, Arch-Prelate.”
The title entered the air between them like a drawn knife.
Malchior felt the old pressure behind their ribs, the pressure that came whenever someone spoke of blood,
inheritance, right. Their claimed lineage was suspect. They knew it. Isolde might know it. Ignatz might
know it. The forged papers lay somewhere beyond the chapel walls, protected by locks and prayers that
could not withstand a patient hand.
Their sanctified authority strained against the concealed fabrication beneath it. Every order they issued
had to be louder than the doubt.
“Do not mistake caution for fear,” Malchior said.
“I mistake nothing.”
“That is your favorite lie.”
Ignatz took one step into the chapel. “You shut Gloamreach because of a phrase on a damaged page. You
accuse me because a Blood-Mage wants my throat opened. You stand there in stolen robes and call it
judgment.”
Isolde’s eyes flashed.
“Say that again.”
“You heard me.”
The Blood-Mage moved before Malchior could speak. Not quickly. Quickly would have been mercy.
Isolde crossed the distance with the cold grace of a drawn thread, and the blood beneath Ignatz’s skin rose
in dark lines along his throat.
Ignatz staggered.
Malchior felt the chapel’s old wards wake underfoot. The altar gave a low, grinding sound. Flame stirred
in the lamps, bending toward Isolde as though compelled by a wind no one else could feel.
“Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven,” Malchior said.
The Blood-Mage did not look away from Ignatz.
“You are a guest here.”
“I am his rival,” Isolde said. “That is not the same as his executioner.”
The words settled with the weight of a formal declaration: Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven rival of Ignatz
Ashgrove the Oathless.
Ignatz’s face had gone gray. “You plotted the death of your own liege,” he rasped. “Do not dress yourself
as a judge.”
The blood at his throat tightened.
Malchior raised their hand.
“Enough.”

The command struck the room with less force than the bells, but the old authority in it was deeper. The
blood withdrew beneath Ignatz’s skin. He dropped to one knee, coughing, one fist pressed against the
stone.
Isolde’s fingers remained slightly curled.
“You should thank me,” they said.
“I thank no one who comes armed with grievance.”
“Then you will die without gratitude.”
Malchior looked from one to the other. Isolde carried grievance like a lit coal, ambition like a hidden
blade, and concealed betrayal like a prayer learned in childhood. Ignatz projected command undermined
by secrecy. The two of them were made for conflict, and the powers beyond the chapel would feed upon it.
The Ashen Vanguard would call for discipline. House Morvain would call for leverage. The Silent Choir
would call for silence and mean obedience. The Iron-Ring Cartel would call for nothing at all until it knew
which throat to purchase. Somewhere in the dark, the Bleeding Crown would count the bodies before they
fell.
Five powers contended over the ruins, and every ruin had a door.
A bell began to ring below them.
Not the quarantine bell. This one was smaller, sharper. An alarm from the gatehouse.
Ignatz rose.
“What now?” Isolde asked.
Malchior turned toward the shuttered window. Through a seam in the wood, the fog showed itself as a
blank, shifting wall. No torchlight pierced it. No rider could have reached the gate unseen.
“Someone is at the outer road,” Ignatz said.
“Gloamreach is sealed,” Malchior replied.
“Yes.”
The alarm rang again.
Once.
Twice.
Then a third time, followed by a silence so sudden that Malchior felt the whole quarantined town listening.
A strip of paper slid beneath the chapel door.
No hand remained on the other side.
Isolde looked down at it. Ignatz looked at Malchior.
The paper bore a seal pressed in iron-red wax.
Malchior recognized the mark of the Iron-Ring Cartel.
They bent to pick it up, and the moment their fingers touched the seal, the wax split like a wound—

The seal opened onto a second strip of paper, folded three times and blackened at the edges as though it
had been held too near a brazier.
No script showed on its surface.
Then the ink rose.
It did not seep into the fibers. It gathered there in glossy beads, crawling against the grain, joining itself
into letters with the patient obscenity of insects.
ARCH-PRELATE MALCHIOR CINDERVALE THE FLAME-TOUCHED,
Malchior’s thumb tightened around the paper.
Isolde leaned close enough that a strand of her hair brushed their sleeve. Ignatz did not move. His silence
had weight now. It stood between them like a drawn blade.
The message continued.
THE OUTER ROAD IS NOT EMPTY. THE TOWN IS NOT SEALED. YOUR GARRISON IS
NOT YOURS.
Beyond the chapel, the alarm bell gave a single muted clapper-stroke, as if a hand had tested its throat and
found it full of blood.
Malchior read on.
YOU HAVE THREE HOURS BEFORE THE WEEPING LURKER IS UNLEASHED IN THE
PURGE OF BLACKPORT.
Isolde’s breath stopped.
The ink shivered. For one moment, the letters blurred into dark wet veins.
Then more words formed beneath them.
MAELIS GREYFEN FOUGHT IN THE PURGE OF BLACKPORT, FIGHTING FOR HOUSE
MORVAIN. ASK WHAT MAELIS GREYFEN SAW BENEATH BLACKPORT. ASK WHO
OPENED THE WATER.
Ignatz’s face remained composed, but something in his posture altered. A small withdrawal. A
commander’s instinctive step backward from a fire not yet visible.
Malchior looked at him.
“Do you know the name?”
“I know many names.”
“That was not an answer.”
“It was the only one I chose to give.”
Isolde laughed softly. There was no mirth in it. “You hear that, Arch-Prelate? The truth has arrived with
conditions.”
The paper grew colder beneath Malchior’s fingers. Cold enough to ache.
A final line surfaced.

THE PURGE OF BLACKPORT BEGAN IN 311 AS AND ENDED IN 321 AS. 70,907
CASUALTIES WERE COUNTED. THE AGGRESSORS WERE ROUTED. REMEMBER THE
WEEPING LURKER.
The ink ceased its crawling.
For a breath, nobody spoke.
Malchior had heard the numbers spoken in sanctuaries where the walls were painted with ash. Seventy
thousand and nine hundred and seven dead, set down in ledgers by hands that had trembled, then been
replaced by hands that did not. The number had become a prayer without a god. The Purge of Blackport
had begun in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS, and every telling of it had a different wound at its center.
But no sanctioned account spoke of a Weeping Lurker.
Not in the sermons. Not in the sealed records beneath the prelatical vaults. Not in the lineage papers
Malchior had forged with their own hand, copying the flourishes of dead witnesses and staining the
margins until the lies looked old enough to be holy.
Their pulse beat against the paper.
Isolde watched them.
“You know it,” she said.
“I know the phrase.”
“That is not what I asked.”
Ignatz’s gaze shifted to the chapel doors. “The outer road.”
“You think the message is a diversion?” Isolde asked.
