“I think the Iron-Ring Cartel does not spend wax and paper to frighten children.”
“The Iron-Ring Cartel spends everything to frighten everyone.”
“And yet you are frightened.”
Her eyes turned upon him. The pale hollows beneath them seemed darker in the candlelight. “I am
interested.”
“You plotted the death of your own liege,” Ignatz said. “You call that interest?”
The chapel changed around them.
The candles guttered, though no wind moved through the room. Malchior heard the faint scrape of Isolde’s
glove against the hilt at her hip. Blood-Mage, Unforgiven—both names had been laid upon her like iron
brands, and neither had made her smaller.
“Say it again,” she whispered.
Ignatz did not.
That restraint was more dangerous than an insult. Malchior had seen men pray before executioners with
less terror than Ignatz showed when Isolde smiled.
The alarm rang from the gate.

Once.
Then the bell cracked into a frantic peal.
Boots hammered across the yard outside. A voice shouted, but the words were swallowed by the fog.
Another voice answered from nearer the walls. Then came the sound of something heavy striking stone.
Malchior folded the message. The paper resisted, stiffening like cured hide.
“Who has access to the garrison signal?” they asked.
Ignatz’s eyes stayed on the door. “The Warden-Commanders.”
“Who else?”
“Those permitted to stand beside them.”
“Name them.”
His jaw tightened.
Isolde stepped between them. “Do not waste the night making him confess to every sin he has committed.
We may not have the leisure.”
“I have committed no sin that concerns you.”
“Then you have been unusually idle.”
Another impact sounded outside. The chapel’s iron-bound door trembled in its frame.
Malchior felt heat stir beneath their skin. It began at the sternum, a coal kindled in the hidden furnace of
their body. Flame-Touched, the faithful called them, as if the fire were a blessing and not a thing that had
never once asked permission before entering their blood.
They rose.
“Open the reliquary.”
Ignatz looked at them sharply. “The quarantine orders forbid—”
“I did not ask what they forbid.”
“The reliquary holds nothing suited to a breach.”
“You have not seen what I brought into Gloamreach.”
“No,” Ignatz said. “You made certain of that.”
Isolde’s attention flicked toward him. “That sounded almost like suspicion.”
“It sounded like observation.”
“It sounded like the beginning of courage.”
Ignatz turned on her. “You mistake defiance for courage because defiance is the only virtue you have
managed to keep.”
Her hand moved.

Malchior caught her wrist before the blood-magic could answer. Beneath their fingers, her pulse was
quick and strong. A thin red line appeared along the crease of her palm, rising without a wound.
“Not here,” Malchior said.
Isolde looked down at their hand on her. “You give orders as though the walls still belong to you.”
“The walls belong to whoever survives the night.”
For the first time, the words silenced them all.
Something dragged itself across the far side of the chapel door.
Not boots. Not claws. A wet, intermittent pull, followed by a faint sound like a child weeping into cloth.
The Warden-Commander went utterly still.
Isolde’s blood withdrew beneath her skin.
Malchior released her wrist.
The sound came again.
A slow drag.
A soft sob.
A pause.
Then a delicate tapping began against the door.
Three taps.
A pause.
Three more.
Ignatz whispered, “That is not the Weeping Lurker.”
“Then what is it?” Isolde asked.
“I don’t know.”
His admission fell into the chapel with the force of a stone dropped down a well.
Malchior approached the door. The fog pressed against the narrow windows, pale and shapeless. Beyond
it, Gloamreach had vanished. No battlements. No courtyard. No watchfires. Only the blank wall of mist,
breathing against the glass.
Something tapped again.
Malchior raised one hand. Fire moved beneath the skin of their palm, illuminating the fine scars across it.
The light was not golden. It was the color of a furnace seen through bone.
A voice spoke from beyond the door.
“Arch-Prelate.”
The voice belonged to no age. It was gentle, hoarse, and wet with grief.
Isolde came to stand beside Malchior. “Who are you?”

The answer came after a long silence.
“Maelis Greyfen.”
Ignatz swore.
It was a small sound, almost private, but Malchior heard it. So did Isolde.
The tapping stopped.
Malchior stared at the door. The name in the message seemed to pulse inside their folded hand.
“Maelis Greyfen,” they said. “You fought in The Purge of Blackport, fighting for House Morvain.”
“Yes.”
The voice drew nearer to the wood, though nothing scraped or stepped.
“What did you see beneath Blackport?” Malchior asked.
A wet breath passed through the cracks.
“Water.”
The chapel candles bent toward the door.
“Whose water?” Isolde demanded.
“Everyone’s.”
Ignatz backed away. His heel struck the first step of the dais.
The mist behind the windows thickened until it blotted out even the faintest suggestion of the outside
world. Something began to trickle beneath the door. It spread over the flagstones in a thin black sheet,
carrying the sour smell of stagnant wells and old iron.
Malchior’s fire recoiled from it.
That frightened them more than the voice.
“The Weeping Lurker was unleashed in The Purge of Blackport,” Maelis Greyfen said. “And now it has
found the road to Gloamreach.”
Isolde crouched and touched one gloved finger to the black water.
The leather hissed.
She pulled back. A dark stain had eaten through the fingertip.
“Open the door,” she said.
Ignatz stared at her. “Have you lost what little mind you possess?”
“It knows us already.”
“It knows the Arch-Prelate.”
“It knows the Cartel’s message. That is not the same thing.”
Malchior looked at the spreading water. It had reached the hem of their robe. The fabric drank it, and
beneath the cloth something cold moved across their ankle.

Their forged lineage papers rested inside their vestment, close to the heart.
The old seal. The invented names. The dead bloodlines made obedient with ink.
A thought came to them, sudden and poisonous: if the thing outside could smell lies, it would not need to
break the door.
“Why are you here?” Malchior asked.
Maelis answered at once.
“To ask which of you is still human.”
Isolde’s eyes narrowed.
Ignatz’s hand went to his sword.
Malchior heard the lock turn.
Not by any hand they could see.
The bar lifted inside its brackets with a slow metallic groan.
From the other side, the voice began to weep.
The door opened inward.
No wind entered. No rain. Only a pallid shape folded beneath the lintel, its head bowed as though it had
forgotten the use of a neck.
The weeping continued.
It came from the shape, from the walls, from somewhere beneath the floorboards. Malchior felt each sob
press against their teeth. Their tongue tasted of iron.
“Stand aside,” Maelis said.
The shape lifted its face.
There was no face.
A smear of wet darkness occupied the hood, and within it pale motes trembled like drowned stars. One of
them drifted forward. It touched the threshold. The stone blackened.
Ignatz drew his sword.
The blade made a small, almost courteous sound.
“Do not,” Isolde whispered.
“Do not what?”
“Give it a thing with which to remember us.”
Ignatz’s grip tightened. “It already remembers.”
The shape turned toward him.
For one heartbeat, the weeping stopped.
Then Ignatz staggered.

Malchior saw what he saw: a road under a colourless sky, a ring of bodies around a well, hands crawling at
the water’s edge. Ignatz stood among them, younger only in the way a blade was young before its first
killing. His mouth moved. Words passed from him into unseen hands. Intelligence, bought and sold. A
seal pressed into wax. The Iron-Ring Cartel waiting beyond the frame.
Ignatz struck at the vision.
His sword passed through the shape and buried itself in the door.
The weeping began again.
“Get out of my head,” he snarled.
The thing did not answer. It reached for him.
Isolde stepped between them.
Blood welled from the tips of her fingers. Not spilled—summoned. It gathered in red beads, shining with
an inner heat, then strung itself between her hands in fine, trembling threads.
The shape paused.
“Blood-Mage,” Maelis said.
Isolde’s mouth curved without humour. “You sound surprised.”
“I am surprised you have any left to spend.”
“You should be more surprised by your own.”
The threads snapped outward.
They struck the darkness beneath the hood and sank into it. Isolde pulled. The thing bent toward her, its
limbs lengthening like wet cloth caught on thorns. The room filled with the smell of opened veins.
Malchior’s heart began to beat too hard.
Their forged lineage papers lay beneath their vestment. They could feel the old seal through the layers of
cloth, its raised edge pressed against the skin. A false descent. Invented names. Dead bloodlines made
obedient by ink.
The thing’s faceless head turned.
Not toward Isolde.
Toward Malchior.
They raised one hand, and the brand beneath their palm answered. Flame appeared without light: a
coal-red line circling the wrist, then a crown of thin fire over the knuckles. The shape recoiled.
For an instant, Malchior believed sanctity had saved them.
Then the thing wept in their own voice.
“I was born in 289 AS,” it said.
Their hand faltered.
The fire crawled backward beneath their skin.

“I serve as Arch-Prelate,” it continued. “I am Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched. My blood is old.
My claim is clean.”
The words were not spoken aloud. They came from the papers.
The seal grew hot against Malchior’s chest.
“Enough,” they said.
The shape leaned closer.
“Forged.”
The door slammed shut.
The iron bar dropped into place with a crack that shook dust from the rafters. Isolde’s blood-threads
snapped, whipping back across her wrists. She hissed and clutched one arm.
Ignatz tore his sword free.
Malchior stood motionless, staring at the wood.
Behind it, something dragged its fingers downward.
One stroke.
Two.
Three.
The marks remained after the sound ceased.
Maelis watched Malchior instead of the door. “It knows.”
“It knows many things.”
“It knew the word forged.”
“So did you.”
“I knew the look of the papers.”
Malchior turned. “You have not seen them.”
“No.” Maelis’s eyes were pale in the dimness. “But I have seen what people become when they wear a
name that does not belong to them.”
Ignatz laughed once. There was no amusement in it.
“Listen to the priest,” he said. “The Arch-Prelate will burn us all for the comfort of a genealogy.”
Malchior faced him. “You have no right to speak of comfort.”
The Warden-Commander’s sword remained bare in his hand. “And yet I am still speaking.”
“You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The silence that followed seemed deeper than the sealed room.
Isolde looked from one to the other. Her expression sharpened, grievance finding a new edge.

Ignatz did not deny it.
He lowered the sword point until it rested against the floor.
“Who told you?”
“The same thing that told you to fear the door.”
A muscle moved in his jaw. “You think it shows truth.”
“I think it shows what will wound us.”
“Then you should pray it does not learn the difference.”
Malchior felt the papers shifting beneath their vestment, though they lay still. The parchment seemed to
breathe against their ribs. Their false ancestors pressed close, patient as worms.
Isolde laughed softly.
“How solemn you both are,” she said. “As if confession makes any of this cleaner.”
“Your turn,” Ignatz said.
Her gaze slid to him. Whatever lay between them had the old, settled shape of hatred. Not sudden, not
theatrical. It had been carried, polished, and kept sharp.
“You want my sin?”
“I want to know what it saw.”
“It saw nothing you did not already suspect.”
“That you plotted the death of your own liege?”
The blood around her fingers thickened.
Maelis took one step back.
Isolde did not look ashamed. That, more than the accusation, unsettled Malchior. Shame was a leash.
Without it, ambition became a creature with no throat to seize.
“My liege mistook obedience for ownership,” Isolde said. “I corrected the error.”
“Did you kill them?”
“No.”
“Did you plot it?”
“I plotted.”
The answer landed with the weight of a stone.
Beyond the walls, the dark pressed close. Somewhere in the building, a hinge creaked. No one moved
toward the sound.
Malchior reached beneath their vestment and drew out the papers.
The parchment was damp.

Not with rain. With a thin, clear fluid that gathered along the folded edges and fell in slow drops to the
floor.
Isolde stared at it. Ignatz’s face hardened.
Maelis said, “Do not open them.”
“If I do not, it will.”
“Then let it come.”
Malchior unfolded the first sheet.
The old seal had softened. Its stamped emblem had blurred into a black ring, and the invented names
beneath it were bleeding into one another. The ink ran in narrow rivulets. At the bottom, where the lineage
ended, a second hand had appeared.
Not written.
Carved.
MALCHIOR CINDERVALE THE FLAME-TOUCHED
The letters deepened while they watched.
The fire beneath Malchior’s skin flared. Pain climbed their arm, hot and intimate. Their knees weakened.
“I was born in 289 AS,” they said, because the words were expected of them.
The room listened.
“I serve as Arch-Prelate.”
The carved letters shuddered.
“My lineage is—”
They stopped.
The door began to weep again.
Not the creature’s voice this time. A woman’s voice. Then a child’s. Then the hoarse, exhausted sobbing
of someone who had cried until crying became the only proof they remained alive.
Maelis approached the door.
“Do you hear that?”
“I hear enough,” Ignatz said.
“No. Listen.”
Malchior did.
Under the weeping lay another sound: distant horns, muffled by walls and years. The grind of wagons over
ash. Men shouting. Water being drawn from a well. Then silence, broken by the brittle laughter of those
who had survived.
The Purge of Blackport had left voices in the world that no prayer could bury.

Malchior saw the wells.
They saw the Iron-Ring Cartel standing among the victors while their own allies drank poison, and they
understood that betrayal did not require hatred. It required only a hand steady enough to pour.
The image passed.
A map lay across the floor where no map had been before.
Its parchment was grey and stiff. Two places had been marked in red.
Gloamreach.
Fenspire.
Malchior crouched.
“Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast,” they read. “Quarantined. Garrison: 2,483.”
The ink trembled beneath their finger.
A second notation had been written beside it.
“Garrisoned Fenspire,” Malchior continued. “Founded in 57 AS. Garrison: 3,742. Gloaming Reach.”
Ignatz leaned over the map. “Those numbers are current?”
“They are written as fact.”
“By what?”
Malchior looked toward the closed door.
The weeping had stopped.
Isolde crouched on the opposite side of the map. Her blood had ceased flowing, but the skin at her wrists
remained red and raw.
“Why those places?” she asked.
Maelis did not answer.
Malchior studied the red marks. Gloamreach sat at the edge of the Pale Coast, isolated by quarantine and
sea-mist. Fenspire rose in the Gloaming Reach, disciplined and watchful beneath its stark silhouette. Two
garrisons. Two locked jaws.
The map’s red lines connected them.
Then a third line appeared.
It ran from the map’s centre to the papers in Malchior’s hand.
Ignatz saw it too.
His sword came up.
“Burn it.”
Malchior’s fingers closed around the parchment. “It may be a warning.”
“It may be a summons.”

“Those are not always different.”
The line brightened.
The old seal cracked.
From beyond the door came a single knock.
Not loud.
Not urgent.
A knuckle against wood.
Then another.
A third.
The voice spoke through the grain, and this time it used no borrowed sorrow.
It spoke with Malchior’s voice.
“Open.”
Malchior felt the forged lineage papers unfold by themselves beneath their hand.
On the final page, beneath the carved name, fresh ink began to write.
Not a bloodline.
A date.

Chapter 12
The sea had gnawed the lower steps of Palewell Abbey to a lacework of stone.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood above the tide and watched the black water work at what remained. Spray
reached her boots in cold, needling bursts. Behind her, the rebuilt abbey kept its pale walls turned toward
the coast, every narrow window dark beneath its battlements. Sanctuary had been scoured from the place.
What remained was a garrison with prayers painted over its murder-holes.
A bell sounded once.
Not an alarm. A summons.
Morwenna did not move until the echo had gone out over the water.
“Fleet Admiral.”
Caedmon Fellgard waited at the stairhead with a ledger held against his chest. His posture had the rigid
patience of a man who trusted ink more than flesh. A smear of black marked one finger. The wind worried
at his sleeves.
“Who rang it?” Morwenna asked.
“Corvus Hollowmere the Pale.”
“Then he has learned to count.”
Caedmon lowered his eyes. “He commands Palewell Abbey (since 374 AS).”
The sentence had the sound of a copied line, and perhaps it was. Caedmon carried facts as other men
carried knives: close, sharpened, and never shown without purpose.
Morwenna looked back at the surf. The abbey had been founded in 244 AS. Its stones had been broken, its
bones rearranged, and its garrison raised to 5998. The number had been entered three times in the fleet’s
accounts, each time in a different hand, as though repetition might make the walls safer. Palewell Abbey
was not a core holding. That distinction had been spoken in council with the calm of a verdict. Not core.
Not essential. Not worth the ships required to relieve it.
Yet Corvus had rung for her.
“Take me to him.”
Caedmon turned.
Morwenna followed him inside.
The passage smelled of wet wool, lamp oil, and salt trapped beneath old mortar. Rebuilt walls did not
settle like ancient ones. They cracked with small, private noises. Beyond the slit windows, the Pale Coast
heaved under a sky the color of beaten pewter.
“Is the High Inquisitor here?” Morwenna asked.
Caedmon’s step faltered. It was almost nothing. Morwenna had spent her life learning the weight of
almost nothing.
“Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned arrived before dawn.”

“Arrived for what?”
“I was not told.”
“That is not an answer.”
“No,” Caedmon said. “It is the answer I have.”
He led her into a chamber where the ceiling beams had been blackened by age or smoke. A map of the
realm covered the central table, pinned at its corners with iron nails. The five powers had been marked in
different colors: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the
Bleeding Crown. Along the coast, a red thread ran from one salt-stained mark to another.
Corvus Hollowmere the Pale stood at the far side of the table.
Morwenna had never seen him before. She gave the fact no shape beyond that. Faces were weather.
Offices were architecture. The man’s pale title was less important than the command beneath it.
Sabelle Mournvale sat beside the hearth, wearing the black severity of a High Inquisitor. The two crowns
upon their seal gleamed dully at their throat. They watched Morwenna without blinking.
Caedmon placed his ledger on the table.
“Fleet Admiral,” Corvus said. “You came quickly.”
“The bell was loud.”
“It was meant to be heard.”
“Then speak loudly.”
A silence gathered. It was not fear. Fear had heat. This was the cold interval before a blade cleared its
sheath.
Corvus touched the red thread with one finger. “A vessel passed the outer shoals without declaring its
cargo.”
“Many vessels do.”
“This one carried no colors.”
“Then it was wise.”
His mouth tightened. “The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS. The Iron-Ring Cartel
was named victor. Fourteen thousand and eleven casualties were recorded.”
Caedmon’s pen moved.
Morwenna watched the ink descend.
“14,011,” she said. “If you are going to summon me, Corvus, use the number written in the records.”
Caedmon’s pen paused, then corrected the line.
Corvus looked from the scribe to her. “Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm.”
“So the records say.”
“The records also say the artifact was destroyed.”

Morwenna felt the old wound open beneath her ribs—not pain, precisely. Recognition. The sea wind
passed through the chamber’s cracks and touched the back of her neck.
“Supposedly destroyed,” she said.
Sabelle’s gaze sharpened.
Caedmon stopped writing.
Morwenna had sold the first fragment of that intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel in a room without
windows, for a sum paid in sealed metal and promises. She had sold the second fragment later, when the
Cartel had stopped asking whether the artifact survived and begun asking where it had gone. She had
never sold the truth. Truth was too dangerous to spend all at once.
“The hidden truth,” Corvus said, “is that the supposedly destroyed artifact was spirited away.”
“By whom?”
“If I knew, I would not require a fleet admiral.”
“You require ships. That is different.”
“I require your silence.”
At the hearth, Sabelle shifted one gloved hand across the other. Their expression did not change, but
something below the floor gave a muffled scrape.
Caedmon looked down.
Morwenna did not.
She had heard rumors about the High Inquisitor’s cellar. Rumors were usually the dead dressed in other
people’s clothes. Yet this sound had weight. A bound revenant, if the whispers were true, kept beneath the
abbey while Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned spoke of purity above it. Morwenna wondered
whether the creature remembered its name. She wondered whether Sabelle feared that it did.
“Your vessel was seen from the western tower,” Corvus said.
“My vessel?”
“The fleet’s vessel.”
“Then accuse the fleet.”
“I accuse the absence of a declaration.”
“A declaration is a scrap of paper. It does not make a cargo innocent.”
“Nor does silence make it guilty.”
“No,” Morwenna said. “But it makes it valuable.”
The bell sounded again.
This time it rang twice.
Corvus turned toward the shuttered window. Caedmon’s hand closed over his pen. Sabelle rose, and the
movement drew another scrape from beneath the floorboards.

A soldier shouted somewhere beyond the chamber.
Then another voice answered, too distant to understand.
Morwenna crossed to the window and opened the shutter.
The coast below was a confusion of foam and black rock. Beyond the harbor mouth, a single ship labored
against the swell. No colors. No lanterns. Its sails were furled, its hull dark with water. It had come in
under the storm’s cover and now drifted just beyond the abbey’s reach.
On its deck, figures moved.
Not sailors, Morwenna thought.
She felt for the sealed message hidden inside the lining of her coat. The paper was dry. The Cartel’s cipher
had been pressed into it with a blunt instrument: three lines, no greeting, no signature.
THEY KNOW THE ARTIFACT LIVES.
DO NOT LET SABELLE OPEN THE CELLAR.
BRING US THE SHIP.
The message had been waiting for her before she reached the coast. She had read it beneath a hooded lamp
while the fleet cut through the dark. Since then, every mile had seemed to narrow around her.
Corvus came to stand beside her.
“Do you recognize it?”
“I recognize a ship.”
“Will it anchor?”
“It has no colors.”
“That was not my question.”
“It will not anchor because you command it to.”
His eyes remained on the vessel. “You were born in 288 AS, Morwenna Ashgrove.”
Caedmon’s head lifted.
Morwenna turned slowly. “You keep a curious ledger.”
“Birth records are not curious. They are useful.”
“Useful to whom?”
“To those who must know how long a person has had to become what they are.”
Sabelle spoke from behind them. “And what have you become?”
Morwenna looked at the ship.
The answer waited in the lining of her coat, pressed into paper and paid for in silence. She had become a
Fleet Admiral who sold intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. The words felt smaller spoken within herself
than they did when written. Treason required witnesses. Without them, it was merely another duty
performed in darkness.

“Someone who dislikes being questioned by scribes and inquisitors,” she said.
Sabelle smiled without warmth. “You dislike being known.”
“Everyone does.”
“Not the dead.”
The scrape beneath the floor came again.
This time it was followed by a soft, wet exhalation.
Caedmon’s face lost what little color it possessed. Corvus looked toward the hearth.
Morwenna saw the calculation pass through him: the ship outside, the revenant below, the High Inquisitor
at his back, and the Fleet Admiral between them. A commander could survive one threat by choosing
another. A ruler could survive several by naming them law.
The ship’s bow swung in the tide.
For an instant, something pale showed beneath its forward rail—not a flag, not a lantern, but a length of
cloth knotted around a human arm.
The arm lifted.
Sabelle stepped toward the hearth.
“Do not,” Morwenna said.
The High Inquisitor stopped.
The word had left Morwenna before she had chosen it. In the room, it stood naked and irreversible.
Corvus reached for the bell rope.
Morwenna’s hand went beneath her coat, closing around the message meant for the Iron-Ring Cartel,
while below the floorboards the bound revenant began to whisper—and Caedmon, pale with terror, bent to
hear what it said.
The rope shuddered beneath Corvus’s hand.
Not yet rung. The bell above them gave a dull, reluctant tremor, as if even iron could be made to hesitate.
Below, the revenant whispered.
Caedmon Fellgard bent nearer.
Morwenna heard only the scrape of his breath and the faint movement of his pen. He had brought the pen
down without seeming to decide it, the nib poised above the page while the dead voice crawled through
the floorboards. His shoulders were narrow beneath his robe. Ink had darkened the side of one finger. A
scribe’s hands, made for preserving what others wished forgotten.
“What does it say?” Morwenna asked.
Caedmon did not look up. “I am not certain it uses words.”
“Then write the sounds.”
His pen touched the page.

The whisper below thickened. It moved through the stone in wet threads, a voice dragged across the
underside of the world. Sabelle stood by the hearth, one hand still extended from the command Morwenna
had given. Firelight trembled over the metalwork at their throat and over the shadow cast by the crown
they wore—not a king’s crown, not entirely, but something fashioned to remind every witness that
authority could be inherited from ruin.
Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned had been born in 263 AS. Morwenna knew the year because High
Inquisitors were entered into the old ledgers twice: once as children and once as instruments. Sabelle’s
second entry had been written in a different hand.
Their gaze remained on Morwenna.
“You have mistaken restraint for mercy,” Sabelle said.
“I have mistaken nothing.”
“No?” Their voice was quiet. “You heard a dead thing speak and reached first for the living.”
Morwenna’s hand remained beneath her coat, closed around the message intended for the Iron-Ring
Cartel. The paper had warmed against her palm. Its folded edge pressed into the flesh like a blade too dull
to cut cleanly.
Outside, the ship’s hull groaned against the tide.
The arm beneath the forward rail had vanished.
Corvus released the rope. “There was an arm.”
“There was cloth,” Sabelle said.
“There was an arm,” Corvus replied.
The High Inquisitor’s eyes did not leave Morwenna. “Then you should be grateful it did not wave.”
Caedmon’s pen scratched faster.
The revenant spoke again, and this time a word rose clear enough to be understood.
“Leaden.”
The fire drew inward.
Morwenna felt the room alter around her. Not visibly. The hearth remained a hearth; the black beams
remained black beams. Yet some old pressure had entered the air, some weight that belonged beneath
mountains and beneath oaths.
“The Leaden Accord,” Caedmon whispered.
Sabelle turned toward him. “Read what you have.”
Caedmon swallowed. His face had gone pale, though his hands stayed steady.
“The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS,” he said. “It ended in 342 AS with 14,011 casualties. The
Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor.”
The ship struck something below with a hollow boom.
Corvus stared toward the shuttered window. “That is written in every account.”

“Not every account,” said Morwenna.
The revenant hissed beneath them.
Caedmon’s nib shivered. “Both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm.”
“Yes,” Sabelle said. “That too is written.”
“And the hidden truth,” Caedmon continued, “is that a supposedly destroyed artifact was spirited away.”
No one moved.
Morwenna watched the page. The scribe had written the words in a cramped hand, forcing them together
as if the truth required less space than a lie. She had seen records altered by order of admirals, abbots,
princes, and merchants. Ink was obedient. Paper had no conscience. Only men pretended otherwise.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had been named victor after both hosts had been annihilated. A victory over ash. A
triumph measured in the absence of survivors. Morwenna had spent years learning how much intelligence
could be bought with that kind of silence.
The message beneath her coat seemed to pulse.
Sabelle approached the table.
“Who told you to stop me?”
“No one.”
“Then why did you?”
Morwenna looked at the hearth. A coal collapsed, sending a spray of sparks up the chimney. “Because you
are not the only one who can hear what is beneath us.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the one you are receiving.”
For the first time, Sabelle smiled.
It had none of the warmth that preceded a smile in the living. “You were born in 288 AS, Fleet Admiral.
You learned command under a realm already full of ghosts. You should know that anything which
whispers from below is either hungry or useful.”
Morwenna’s fingers tightened around the message.
The title struck her as an accusation. Fleet Admiral. A station built from discipline, signal, and the public
fiction that every order passed through one visible hand. Her authority had been forged in open water,
where distance made people honest about fear. Here, beneath stone and sanctity, every silence had a
second mouth.
“Perhaps it is neither,” she said.
“Nothing is neither.”
Caedmon looked up from his page. “It is saying there is no artifact.”
Sabelle’s attention shifted to him.
Caedmon’s throat worked. “Or—no. It says the artifact has no—” He frowned, listening. “No grave.”

The revenant’s voice ceased.
The silence afterward was worse.
Morwenna heard the tide beneath the walls, the minute settling of the timbers, the dry rasp of Corvus’s
breathing. Somewhere above, a gull cried and was cut short.
Sabelle placed both hands upon the table. “Caedmon Fellgard, do not embellish what you hear.”
“I am not embellishing.”
“You are frightened.”
“Yes.”
“At least fear remains a form of honesty.”
Caedmon lowered his eyes. His pen resumed its work, though the page had begun to tremble under it.
Morwenna thought of Greyfell Citadel, founded in 62 AS in the Shattered Vale. An abandoned fortress
outside the realm’s core holdings, grey stone emptied of banners and purpose. It had been raised to
command the passes, then left to the weather and whatever slept in its cisterns. Every chart called it
irrelevant. Every smuggler’s route bent toward it.
The ship had not come by accident.
Neither had the arm.
“Where is the vessel bound?” Morwenna asked.
Corvus’s mouth tightened. “You assume it is bound anywhere.”
“Everything afloat is bound somewhere.”
“Not wreckage.”
“Wreckage does not signal.”
“There was no signal.”
“Then why are you still watching the window?”
Corvus turned from her. His face was hard with the particular anger of a man forced to doubt his own
sight. “Because Palewell Abbey is not blind.”
Morwenna let that settle.
Palewell Abbey stood in The Pale Coast. It had been founded in 244 AS, rebuilt after ruin, and maintained
a garrison of 5998. It was not a core holding, but its walls had been thickened until prayer could be
delivered through arrow slits. Six thousand nearly, in all but name; 5998 in the ledger, because ledgers
demanded that two absences be made visible.
“Palewell’s garrison would have seen the ship,” Morwenna said.
“Palewell’s garrison sees what it is ordered to see.”
“And who ordered them?”
Corvus said nothing.

Sabelle lifted their hand from the table and touched one finger to the folded edge of Morwenna’s coat, not
quite touching the hidden message. The gesture was delicate. Intimate only in the way a knife’s point was
intimate with the skin.
“You carry a letter,” Sabelle said.
Morwenna did not blink. “I carry many things.”
“A letter intended for the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The fire made a soft cracking sound.
Caedmon’s pen stopped.
Corvus looked between them. “Is that true?”
Morwenna considered denying it. The denial came easily; she had worn it in councils, aboard flagships,
before men who would have condemned her for less and purchased her for more. But Sabelle had not
asked how they knew. Their certainty had already crossed the room and seated itself among them.
“Yes,” Morwenna said.
Corvus’s hand moved toward the weapon at his side.
Morwenna did not look at it. “If you draw, you will make the room smaller. That will benefit the dead
thing beneath us.”
“Do not instruct me in rooms.”
“I instruct you in consequences.”
Sabelle’s expression had gone still. “What does the Cartel want?”
“Information.”
“They always want information.”
“They want what they are willing to pay for.”
“And what are you willing to sell?”
Morwenna felt the old, familiar division open inside her: the admiral on one side, the woman who counted
coin and currents on the other. She had never mistaken the two for friends. The admiral believed in
command. The other believed command was merely the most expensive form of leverage.
“Routes,” she said.
“Which routes?”
“Those not protected by your bells.”
Corvus’s hand closed around the hilt at his side.
Sabelle did not move. “You have been selling intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
The words were not loud. They did not need to be.
Morwenna looked at the dead hearth, the old mortar, the ash gathered in its corners. She imagined the
message burning. She imagined the Cartel’s disappointment, then its patience. Merchants could forgive

betrayal when betrayal remained profitable. They did not forgive waste.
“Yes,” she said.
Caedmon made a small sound.
Morwenna turned to him. “Write that as well.”
The scribe stared at her.
“Write it,” she repeated.
His hand lowered. The nib touched the page.
Sabelle watched the confession take form. Their eyes were dark in the firelight, and beneath the severity of
their face something stirred—satisfaction, perhaps, or the colder pleasure of a lock finding its key.
“You think this saves you,” they said.
“No.”
“Then what does it do?”
“Places the truth where it can be used.”
“By whom?”
Morwenna heard it then.
Not beneath the floorboards.
Outside.
A knock against the hull.
Once.
Twice.
A third time, softer than the others.
Corvus turned toward the window. Sabelle’s hand went to the bell rope again.
Morwenna caught their wrist.
The contact lasted no longer than a breath. Sabelle’s pulse was calm beneath her fingers.
Below them, the revenant began to laugh.
The laughter rose through the timbers, wet and patient, as though the thing below had learned the shape of
amusement from overheard mouths.
Sabelle looked down at Morwenna’s hand.
Not at her face. At the fingers closed around their wrist.
“Release me.”
Morwenna did.
The bell rope trembled beside them. Its iron tongue gave a small, betraying chime.

Outside, the darkness pressed against the glass. No lantern showed beyond it. No pale face. Only the black
water, broken by a skin of rain, and the reflection of the cabin fire shivering where the window should
have opened onto night.
Corvus had not moved from the window.
“Was that the signal?” Morwenna asked.
“No,” Corvus said.
Their voice had changed. It carried none of the command with which they ruled Palewell Abbey. There
was fear in it, but not fear for themselves. Morwenna knew the sound. It was the fear of a person who had
trusted a wall to remain a wall.
The revenant laughed again.
This time, something struck the underside of the deck.
Wood groaned.
Sabelle’s expression remained composed. They drew a narrow blade from beneath their coat, not with
haste but with the grim economy of practice. The fire found the metal and slid away.
“Stay here,” they said.
Morwenna almost smiled. “To whom?”
Sabelle glanced toward Corvus. “Both of you.”
Corvus turned from the window. “You would leave us above it?”
“I would leave you above what is already beneath you.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you are owed.”
The hull gave another shudder. A cup rolled from the table and broke against the wall. Wine spread across
the boards, darkening the grain. Its smell mingled with the damp and the old smoke, sweet as rot.
Morwenna felt the weight of the message hidden inside her coat.
Not a letter. Not anything so innocent.
The information had been written in a cipher that could be read as a devotional inventory if found by the
wrong hands. The Iron-Ring Cartel preferred such arrangements. Truth disguised as piety. Treason
dressed in a clerk’s careful ink.
She had sold them less than they wanted and more than they deserved. That was how she had survived
each exchange. Give them a gate, keep the key. Give them a name, keep the reason. Yet the truth she had
placed before Sabelle was different. It had not been purchased. It had been lifted from the dark and set
between them like a blade.
Now someone waited outside the hull.
Or something.
The window clicked.

Morwenna turned.
A fingertip pressed against the outer pane.
It was grey through the glass, the nail blackened, the skin stretched thin enough to show the cords beneath.
The finger withdrew. A palm replaced it, leaving a smear of water that did not run downward. It crawled
sideways, gathering itself into a thin, trembling line.
Corvus whispered a prayer.
Sabelle watched the hand without blinking.
“Open the door,” called a voice from outside.
The sound was muffled by rain and timber, but it was unmistakably human.
Morwenna knew it.
Not the speaker. The cadence.
A voice trained to make requests sound like verdicts.
Sabelle’s blade lowered a fraction. “You should not be here.”
“Neither should you.”
The words came again, closer now, from beneath the cabin. The revenant had stopped laughing.
Morwenna looked toward the trapdoor.
It was shut. Iron-banded. A lock rested in its bracket, though she had seen Sabelle carry no key. The seams
around it had been sealed with wax. Someone had pressed a mark into the wax: a circle broken by three
straight strokes.
The mark of the Silent Choir.
She had seen it on intercepted cargo, on drowned reports, on the margins of ledgers bought and burned
before they could reach any tribunal. The Choir left no proclamations. It left absences. A missing witness.
A door found open. A page cut cleanly from a book.
“Who is below?” Corvus asked.
Sabelle did not answer.
The voice outside gave a soft, almost affectionate sigh.
“High Inquisitor.”
The title entered the room like cold air.
Sabelle’s face hardened. “You are trespassing.”
“You invited us.”
“I invited no one.”
“You invited the truth.”
Morwenna felt the room contract around that word.

The fire snapped. A coal broke free and rolled across the hearthstone. Shadows leapt over Sabelle’s
crowned brow, across the severe planes of their face, and vanished into the folds of their coat.
Twice-Crowned. The title had once been spoken with reverence, then with suspicion, and now with the
cautious disgust reserved for things that remained powerful after they had become impossible to forgive.
Below them, the lock turned.
Corvus swore.
The sound was quiet, but it had the force of a cannon shot.
Sabelle crossed the room in three strides and seized the trapdoor’s iron ring. The wood bucked beneath
their hand.
“Go to the stern,” they ordered.
Morwenna did not move. “Why?”
“Because if the door opens, you will be the first thing it sees.”
“That is not reassuring.”
“It was not meant to be.”
Corvus drew a pistol from within their coat. The weapon looked too small for the room, too delicate for
whatever waited beneath the boards. They held it with both hands.
Morwenna saw then what the cold had hidden: a line of blood running from Corvus’s palm to their sleeve.
“You’re hurt.”
“I am commanded.”
“Those are not opposites.”
“No,” Corvus said. “But they are not the same.”
The lock clicked.
Sabelle planted one boot on the trapdoor. Their blade hovered at the seam.
The voice outside spoke once more.
“Morwenna Ashgrove.”
Her name sounded wrong in that mouth. Flattened. Studied.
She had heard it spoken by sailors, ministers, officers, enemies, and men who wished to become one of
those things. This voice knew nothing of her rank and everything of her use.
“I know what you carry,” it said.
The message inside her coat seemed to warm against her ribs.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had taught her never to reach for concealed steel while being watched. Never to
answer a threat with a confession. Never to mistake a person’s knowledge for their certainty.
She had learned those lessons before the Leaden Accord, when every harbor had been a mouth and every
mouth might have been bought.

She had forgotten none of them.
Sabelle looked at her. “What did you tell them?”
“Nothing.”
The answer came too quickly.
Their gaze sharpened.
Morwenna held it. “Nothing they can prove.”
“That is a different answer.”
“It is the one that matters.”
Beneath the trapdoor, the revenant began to whisper.
The words were indistinct, but the rhythm was clear: a child’s counting song without its numbers, a
melody stripped of innocence and left with only the bones. Morwenna had heard sailors hum similar tunes
before storms. They always stopped before the final verse.
Sabelle’s fingers tightened around the iron ring.
“You will speak plainly,” they said.
“Not while your guest is listening.”
“My guest?”
“Your prisoner.”
The revenant fell silent.
The quiet that followed was worse than its laughter.
Corvus’s pistol swung toward the door. “You keep it below?”
Sabelle did not look at them. “I keep nothing.”
The trapdoor lifted an inch.
A breath emerged from the crack. It smelled of old soil, salt, and something medicinal burned past
bitterness. Morwenna’s skin tightened along her arms.
Sabelle forced the hatch down.
Something struck from beneath.
The boards bowed upward. The wax seal split with a faint, wet sound.
A second blow.
The hinges screamed.
“Open the door,” called the voice outside.
“Get away from the window,” Morwenna said.
Corvus did not obey. Their eyes remained fixed on the black pane.

“Why?”
“Because it wants us looking out.”
The grey hand appeared again.
This time it was not alone.
A second palm pressed beside it. Then a third, each one emerging from the dark at impossible distances, as
though the outer wall had become transparent to a crowd waiting on the other side. No faces. No bodies.
Only hands, pale and patient against the rain.
Corvus raised the pistol.
“Do not,” Morwenna said.
The nearest fingers curled.
The window cracked.
A line of silver ran from top to bottom.
Sabelle’s head snapped toward it. “What did you bring here?”
Morwenna could have lied.
She had lied in council chambers, in war rooms, in the mouths of harbors where men watched her ships
burn and waited to learn which way the wind would carry the blame. Lies were tools. A good commander
kept them clean.
But below them, the revenant had begun to laugh again.
And outside, the hands were tapping against the glass in a slow, deliberate pattern.
Once.
Twice.
A third time.
Morwenna reached beneath her coat and withdrew the sealed strip of parchment.
Sabelle’s eyes dropped to it.
Corvus’s pistol wavered.
The seal bore no crest. Only a narrow ring of black wax, pressed flat.
“I did not bring this here,” Morwenna said.
The trapdoor tore free of its hinges.
Sabelle moved first, driving their blade downward as something pale surged through the opening. Steel
struck flesh—or what had replaced flesh—and the cabin filled with a shriek so thin it seemed to come
from inside Morwenna’s teeth.
The window shattered.
Rain blew in.

The hands vanished.
For one breath there was only fire, broken glass, and the stink of the opened cellar.
Then the thing beneath the deck spoke in Morwenna’s own voice.
“Open the message.”

Chapter 13
The bell above Fenspire had a cracked voice.
It spoke across the Gloaming Reach in a single iron note, and the sound entered Isolde Fellgard the
Unforgiven through the scars beneath their ribs. The tower had stood since 57 AS, a black needle thrust
into the dim country, and its garrison of 3,742 kept watch from walls that had outlived every oath sworn
beneath them.
Below, soldiers moved through the rain with hooded lamps. Their armor glimmered like wet bone. The
garrisoned city did not sleep so much as clench itself against the dark.
Isolde stood beneath the covered walk, one gloved hand resting on the pommel of a knife they had never
drawn in public. Water whispered from the roof. Beyond the parapet, the Gloaming Reach sank toward the
Pale Coast, and somewhere past that pallid, wind-scoured margin lay Gloamreach: quarantined, sealed
from the surrounding coast, guarded by a garrison of 2,483.
Nothing entered Gloamreach without being counted.
Nothing left without being changed.
“Your blood is on the stone.”
The voice came behind them.
Isolde looked down. A red thread had slipped from the cut in their palm and darkened the flagging
between their boots. They had not felt themselves open the wound. Their body had learned to obey
grievance before thought.
Ossric Ashgrove crouched beside the stain with a ledger balanced on one knee. He was a quartermaster,
born in 333 AS, and every inch of him seemed made for measuring what remained after other people had
taken too much. He dipped a rag into a bucket and scrubbed the stone.
“You count stains now?” Isolde asked.
“I count everything that might be blamed on me.”
“Then you are a better servant than most.”
Ossric’s fingers paused. His temperament was not recorded in any ledger Isolde had seen, but caution had
a texture. It lived in the way he kept his eyes lowered, in the careful silence between each breath.
“The Warden-Commander is waiting,” he said.
“Which one?”
Ossric’s hand tightened around the rag.
There was only one Warden-Commander in Fenspire, but titles were doors, and Isolde had spent too long
learning which doors were trapped.
“Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless,” Ossric said.
The name moved through the covered walk like a draught from a crypt.
Ignatz had been born in 258 AS. He wore command as though it were a cloak inherited from a dead man,
broad enough to hide whatever was underneath. His intelligence passed into the Iron-Ring Cartel by secret

channels, though the Cartel’s agents never called it selling. They called it accounting. They called every
betrayal a balance restored.
Isolde turned from the parapet.
“Did he say why?”
“He said only that the matter concerned Blackport.”
“Then it concerns a corpse.”
Ossric glanced toward the rain. “The Purge of Blackport ended with seventy thousand—”
“70,907.”
The quartermaster swallowed.
“70,907 casualties,” Isolde said. “You need not soften the number for me.”
“I had not meant to.”
“No. You meant to survive saying it.”
He looked at them then, and his eyes held the flat, sleepless terror of a man who had learned that truth was
not protection. Isolde understood that terror. They carried a different kind. Their own was sharpened,
banked, made useful.
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. The aggressors were totally routed. The
Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
Those facts had been carved into proclamations, repeated in sanctuaries, stamped upon ration chits and
military dispatches until the words had worn smooth. But beneath them lay the concealed truth: the victors
had poisoned the wells of their own allies.
Isolde had tasted that truth once, in the bitterness of a report burned at the edges.
“Is the Arch-Prelate here?” they asked.
Ossric resumed scrubbing. “Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched arrived before dusk.”
“Of course they did.”
“Arch-Prelate Malchior said the meeting required witnesses.”
“Malchior says many things.”
“Those are dangerous words.”
“So is Malchior.”
The bell sounded again. Its cracked note trembled in the rain.
Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched had been born in 289 AS and served as Arch-Prelate with the
rigid grace of someone balancing a crown upon a blade. Their lineage was displayed in every robe, seal,
and prayer: ancestral ink, sanctified blood, a chain of names reaching backward into the ruin. Isolde knew
the papers were forged. The knowledge had come to them folded inside a dead courier’s coat, though the
courier’s name was not worth remembering.
Malchior’s authority was holy only so long as no one held it to the light.

“Go on,” Isolde said.
Ossric stood. He was younger than the walls, younger than most of the fear inside them, and yet the damp
had already settled into his shoulders.
“The Warden-Commander is in the old tally chamber.”
“Did he bring soldiers?”
“Fenspire is garrisoned.”
“That was not my question.”
Ossric’s mouth thinned. “Yes.”
“Then he brought witnesses after all.”
They walked.
The old tally chamber occupied the lower spine of the tower, where the air smelled of iron, lamp oil, and
the mineral damp of the Reach. Narrow windows slit the walls but admitted no view. Fenspire had been
built to see without being seen. Its defenders kept their eyes on roads, marshes, and the pale distance
toward the coast. Its secrets remained underground.
Two soldiers barred the chamber door. Their faces were hidden behind half-masks, and their hands rested
near their weapons.
Isolde stopped before them.
“Do you know who I am?”
Neither answered.
“Good.”
The door opened from within.
Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless stood at the far end of the chamber, beneath a map pierced with black pins.
No canonical feature marked him; authority had left no portrait in the records, only the title
Warden-Commander and the epithet the Oathless. Isolde found the absence fitting. A man who sold
intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel had no need of a face. A shadow could be purchased more cheaply.
Malchior stood beside the table in flame-colored vestments darkened by rain. Their hand rested upon a
bundle of papers bound with red cord.
“You are late,” Ignatz said.
“I was washing blood from the floor.”
“Yours?”
“Does it matter?”
“To a quartermaster, perhaps.”
Ossric remained outside. The door closed between them with a damp wooden groan.
Malchior’s gaze settled upon Isolde’s palm. “You make a sacrament of injury.”

“You make a sacrament of paper.”
The Arch-Prelate’s expression did not move. Only the fingers upon the cord betrayed them, pressing hard
enough to blanch.
Ignatz turned to the map. “Gloamreach has sent no confirmation.”
“It is quarantined,” Isolde said. “That is the meaning of the word.”
“It has a garrison of 2,483.”
“And still the dead may outnumber the living.”
“No one has said there are dead.”
“Then why is the coast silent?”
The Warden-Commander touched one of the black pins. It marked the Pale Coast, though the mapmaker
had rendered the shore as a thin white scar.
“Because silence is cheaper than defense.”
“Spoken like a man who has sold both.”
The chamber tightened.
Malchior looked from one to the other. “We are not here to trade accusations.”
“No,” Isolde said. “We are here to decide which accusation will be made official.”
Ignatz’s hand remained upon the pin. “The Iron-Ring Cartel has requested an accounting of the Blackport
routes.”
“They requested intelligence,” Isolde said.
“They requested an accounting.”
“And you intend to provide it.”
His head tilted slightly. “You speak with confidence.”
“I speak with memory.”
The rain struck the narrow windows. In the black glass, Isolde saw a blurred reflection: the pale planes of
an Unforgiven Blood-Mage, the red at their palm, the dangerous stillness of grievance held beneath the
skin. They had plotted the death of their own liege. The thought rose without remorse, not because
remorse was absent, but because it had been burned away and replaced by something more durable.
No one in the chamber knew the shape of that plot.
Malchior knew many secrets, but not that one.
Perhaps.
“The Purge of Blackport was a victory,” Malchior said. “The aggressors were routed. The Iron-Ring
Cartel emerged as victor. That is the record.”
“The record is a grave with the lid nailed shut.”

“The number is 70,907 casualties,” Ignatz said. “The beginning was 311 AS. The end was 321 AS. You
cannot alter what is written.”
“I can alter what is remembered.”
Malchior’s eyes flashed. “Careful.”
“Are you warning me as Arch-Prelate, or as the heir of a lineage that never existed?”
The silence afterward was exquisite.
The forged papers lay between them, their red cord bright as opened veins.
Malchior touched the bundle. “You are reckless.”
“I am Unforgiven.”
“That is not an excuse.”
“No. It is what remains after excuses have failed.”
Ignatz moved toward the table. “Enough. The Cartel believes the poisoned wells were not an act of
desperation but a design. They believe someone within the allied command knew.”
“They are correct,” Isolde said.
Malchior’s jaw tightened. “Do not make allegations without proof.”
“Proof is for courts. Power requires only an audience.”
“And what do you require?”
Isolde looked at the map. At the pale coast. At Gloamreach, locked behind quarantine and its garrison of
2,483. At Fenspire, whose 3,742 defenders watched the Reach as if vigilance could stop rot from traveling
through water.
“I require the truth to become expensive.”
Ignatz’s eyes narrowed. “The Cartel will pay.”
“Then you have already named your price.”
For the first time, something moved behind his composure—not shame, not fear. Calculation. The
Oathless had secrets beneath secrets, and somewhere among them the names of those who bought his
intelligence. Isolde imagined the documents leaving Fenspire by hidden roads, crossing the Reach under
wax and seal, arriving in Iron-Ring hands.
Five powers contended over the ruins: the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the
Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown. Each claimed to be the last wall between the realm and
oblivion. Each fed on the rubble.
Malchior drew a knife and cut the red cord.
The papers loosened.
Isolde smelled old ink, damp parchment, and the faint metallic tang of blood.
Not theirs.

“Read,” Malchior said.
Isolde reached for the first page.
From somewhere above, the bell began to ring again, though no hand had touched it. The sound shuddered
down through the tower. Ignatz looked toward the ceiling. Malchior went still.
And on the page beneath Isolde’s fingers, a line of writing began to darken as though the ink had only just
found its vein—
The letters formed themselves in a cramped, black hand.
ISOLDE FELLGARD THE UNFORGIVEN, BORN IN 286 AS.
The blood beneath the words stirred once, as if remembering the pulse of the wrist that had written them.
Isolde did not move.
The bell above gave another hollow toll. Dust sifted from the mortar. Somewhere in the tower, something
dragged its nails across stone.
Malchior leaned over the page. Firelight caught the scarlet seams of their vestments and the faint
discoloration along their throat—the mark that had earned them the name Flame-Touched. Their face
remained composed, but one hand had closed around the edge of the table.
“Keep reading,” they said.
“You knew this was here.”
“I knew the archive kept a record of blood.”
“That is not what I asked.”
“No.” Malchior’s gaze remained on the page. “It is what I answered.”
The script continued.
BLOOD-MAGE. 
UNFORGIVEN. 
DANGEROUS 
ATMOSPHERE 
OF 
GRIEVANCE,
AMBITION, AND CONCEALED BETRAYAL. SECRET: PLOTTED THE DEATH OF THEIR
OWN LIEGE.
For a moment, Isolde heard only the rain beyond the narrow windows. It ticked against the black glass
with the patience of a thing waiting to be admitted.
Ignatz’s chair creaked.
“Convenient,” he said.
Isolde turned her head. “What is?”
“That the archive knows the shape of your treason but not the name of the dead.”
“Not dead,” she said.
The word escaped before she could stop it.
Malchior looked at her then. Their eyes were pale in the candlelight, almost colorless, and utterly awake.
Ignatz’s hand lowered toward his sword.

Isolde felt the old wound under her ribs open in memory. Not pain. Pain was honest. This was the colder
thing beneath it: the knowledge that a life could be ended with a whisper, a cup, a door left unbarred. The
knowledge that she had once placed another’s death between herself and the future, then called the choice
necessity because ambition sounded uglier when spoken aloud.
“Do not mistake an intention for an ending,” she said.
Ignatz smiled without warmth. “A distinction for priests.”
Malchior’s fingers pressed harder into the table. “The page is not finished.”
New lines bled across the parchment.
THE PURGE OF BLACKPORT BEGAN IN 311 AS AND ENDED IN 321 AS. CASUALTIES:
70,907. THE AGGRESSORS WERE TOTALLY ROUTED. THE IRON-RING CARTEL
EMERGED AS VICTOR.
The last sentence appeared slowly, each letter sinking into the fibers.
THE VICTORS POISONED THE WELLS OF THEIR OWN ALLIES.
Ignatz stood.
The chair fell backward and struck the flagstones.
Isolde’s blood answered the violence before her mind did. A red thread rose from the split skin beside her
thumb and hovered between them, trembling in the cold air. The thread was thin as a spider’s filament. It
could still find an eye. It could still enter a throat.
Ignatz stared at it.
“Sit,” she said.
The Warden-Commander did not.
Malchior read the page again, lips barely moving. “The Iron-Ring Cartel.”
“Your allies,” Isolde said to Ignatz.
His expression altered by less than a breath. That was answer enough.
The bell rang.
The blood-thread snapped toward him.
Ignatz twisted aside. It struck the stone pillar behind his shoulder and sank into the mortar with a wet hiss.
The tower shuddered. Every candle flame bent toward the wound.
“Isolde,” Malchior said.
She felt the old, exquisite pressure of command trying to settle over her. Priestly authority. Anointed
authority. The kind that expected obedience to arrive before thought.
She withdrew the thread from the wall.
“Say it,” she told Ignatz.
His gaze remained fixed on the dark red filament coiling around her wrist.

“Say what?”
“That you sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel.”
Rain whispered against the windows.
For the first time since she had known him, Ignatz looked tired.
Not afraid. Tired.
“The realm is made of hungers,” he said. “The Cartel pays for knowledge. Others pay for silence. I have
never pretended the difference mattered.”
“You are a Warden-Commander.”
“I was born in 258 AS,” he said, with a bitterness that made the number sound like a sentence. “I have
worn command long enough to know that oaths are ropes tied by other hands.”
“The Oathless,” Malchior murmured.
Ignatz’s mouth tightened. “Names are also ropes.”
The page beneath Isolde’s hand shivered. The ink spread outward, swallowing the record of Blackport,
then gathered itself into a new heading.
GLOAMREACH.
A pale map surfaced in the parchment: a coastline bleached nearly white, cliffs rising like old teeth above
a dark sea.
GLOAMREACH LIES ON THE PALE COAST. CORE LOCATION. STATUS: QUARANTINED.
GARRISON: 2,483.
The number gleamed wetly.
Beyond it, farther inland, another shape emerged: a single black spire thrust into the dimness.
FENSPIRE. FOUNDED IN 57 AS. LOCATION: THE GLOAMING REACH. CORE LOCATION.
STATUS: GARRISONED. GARRISON: 3,742.
The tower’s image seemed to rise from the paper. Isolde could almost hear the wind moving around its
heights, could almost smell the iron of disciplined men standing watch in the dark.
Malchior bent closer.
“Why show us these?”
The answer appeared beneath the map.
THE COAST IS SEALED. THE SPIRE IS WATCHING.
Then, below it:
THE ROAD BETWEEN THEM IS OPEN ONLY TO THOSE ALREADY CONDEMNED.
Ignatz gave a low laugh. “That would include us.”
“No,” said Isolde. “It would include whoever wrote this.”

She lifted the page. Beneath the map, another sheet had been hidden. Its edges were stiff with brown
residue. The writing on it was less formal, more hurried.
OSSric Ashgrove, born in 333 AS. Quartermaster.
The capital letter in his name had been scratched over twice, as though the writer’s hand had faltered.
No appearance had been recorded. No temperament. Only the occupation.
Quartermaster.
A man who counted what could be carried, what could be fed, what could be withheld. A man whose
power lived in locked stores and altered tallies. Isolde imagined a faceless figure bending over ledgers
while rain ran down the walls outside.
“Who is he?” Ignatz asked.
“Ossric Ashgrove,” Malchior said.
“That was not my question.”
“It is all the page gives us.”
The parchment darkened again.
IGNATZ ASHGROVE THE OATHLESS. BORN IN 258 AS. MAJOR WARDEN-COMMANDER.
SECRET: SELLS INTELLIGENCE TO THE IRON-RING CARTEL.
The blood on the page did not accuse him. It merely stated the fact with the calmness of a grave.
Ignatz’s face became a mask carved from old wood.
Isolde watched him and thought of all the gates he had opened, all the patrols sent toward empty ground,
all the warnings that might have arrived too late because someone had paid for them to arrive so. No
number rose from the page to measure the dead. No list gave their names.
Only the secret.
That was worse.
Malchior reached for the next sheet.
Isolde caught their wrist.
The skin beneath her fingers was hot.
“Do not,” she said.
Their eyes lowered to her hand. “You are afraid of what it will say.”
“I am afraid of what it will make you believe.”
“Those are rarely the same thing.”
She released them.
The page accepted Malchior’s touch. Ink welled under their palm and spread in branching veins.
MALCHIOR CINDERVALE THE FLAME-TOUCHED. BORN IN 289 AS. ARCH-PRELATE.

The title appeared first, crowned in elaborate strokes. Then the name. Then the secret.
FORGED THEIR OWN LINEAGE PAPERS.
The bell stopped.
Silence came down so suddenly that Isolde heard the rainwater crawling through the gutters outside.
Malchior did not look at the page.
Ignatz did.
“Arch-Prelate,” he said softly. “A title built on forged parchment.”
“Most titles are,” Malchior replied.
“Not yours?”
“You have the answer.”
The flame in the nearest candle burned blue.
Malchior’s composure had not broken, but something beneath it had shifted. The sanctified authority
remained in the set of their shoulders, in the careful angle of their chin. Yet Isolde saw the strain now—the
pressure of a structure built over emptiness, the terror that one loose stone might bring the whole edifice
down.
“You forged your own lineage papers,” Isolde said.
“I made them legible.”
“Forged.”
“A word for the sin of the powerless. When the powerful do it, they call it correction.”
“And what were you correcting?”
Malchior smiled then, but the expression held no joy. “The page does not say.”
The archive answered.
A line appeared beneath the secret.
CLAIMED BLOOD IS STILL BLOOD.
Isolde felt the tower tilt.
Not physically. The floor remained steady beneath her boots, the table did not slide, the candles stood
upright. But the world had shifted its weight. Each of them had arrived carrying a concealed blade. The
papers had only placed the blades in their hands.
Ignatz stepped toward the table.
“Burn them.”
Malchior’s gaze moved to him. “That would not erase what they know.”
“It would erase the evidence.”
“Evidence for whom?” Isolde asked. “The page has no court.”

“No,” Ignatz said. “It has witnesses.”
His eyes settled on her.
The blood around her wrist tightened like a bracelet.
She thought of the liege whose death she had plotted, of the first instruction whispered in a dark room, of
how easily loyalty became a mask worn by those waiting to inherit the face beneath it. She had told herself
she had been wronged. She had told herself the realm could not survive another season beneath a failing
hand.
She had believed both things.
That was the unforgiven part—not that she had betrayed, but that some portion of her still believed the
betrayal had been necessary.
Malchior gathered the pages. The parchment resisted, clinging to the table as though nailed there by
invisible fingers.
“Leave them,” Isolde said.
“If the Cartel finds them—”
“The Cartel already knows enough.”
Ignatz’s expression hardened. “You speak as though you understand them.”
“I understand hunger. It wears many colors.”
The first page split down the middle.
From the tear seeped a dark red line, thicker than ink, crawling across the table toward the edge. It reached
the floor and continued through the cracks between the stones.
All three watched it descend.
The bell began to ring again.
Once.
Twice.
On the third toll, something below the tower answered with a knock.
The knock came again.
Not from beneath the stones this time. From within them.
Isolde felt it in the soles of their feet, a patient pressure travelling up through bone. The red line on the
floor had stopped at the foot of the table. It trembled there, gathering itself into a dark, glossy bead.
Malchior crossed themself.
The gesture was small, almost graceful. The ring on their finger scraped against the chain of their office,
and the sound seemed horribly loud in the chamber.
“Do not,” Isolde said.
The Arch-Prelate’s hand remained against their breast. “Do not what?”

“Pray.”
“I was not praying.”
“You were asking something to listen.”
Malchior’s face was pale in the tower’s failing light. The flame-touched marks along their throat seemed
to stir beneath the skin, as though embers had been laid under flesh and were searching for air.
Ignatz reached for the sword at his hip.
“Steel will not help you,” Isolde said.
His fingers tightened around the hilt. “It has helped me before.”
“Then it will be offended by the change.”
Another knock.
Dust sifted from the ceiling. Somewhere above, the bell’s iron tongue dragged against its housing without
striking. The tower groaned around them, old stone bearing the memory of every winter it had survived.
Isolde looked down at the blood.
It was theirs.
They knew the taste of it though none had touched their tongue: iron, salt, the faint bitterness that came
when a spell was being forced through unwilling channels. Blood-magic was never a matter of command.
It was negotiation. The blood remembered every wound. It remembered the hand that opened it, the
reason, the fear. It remembered debts even when the mind had buried them.
The page lay split upon the table. Beneath its torn surface, another script had surfaced in thin red strokes.
Malchior leaned over it. “This was concealed.”
“Everything worth hiding is concealed.”
“Not from us.”
Isolde smiled without warmth. “You forged your own lineage papers, Malchior Cindervale the
Flame-Touched. Concealment is not a craft you have mastered. It is merely one you have survived.”
The Arch-Prelate turned toward them.
Ignatz’s gaze moved between their faces. Suspicion sat naturally on him, like a cloak that had never been
removed. Ignatz Ashgrove the Oathless had been born in 258 AS, and age had carved no softness into him.
He carried command as if it were a burden he intended to make everyone else share.
Malchior’s voice dropped. “You choose an interesting moment to accuse me.”
“I choose the moment the dead begin knocking.”
“Do you know what you are reading?”
“No.”
That answer unsettled them more than any lie would have.
The red script lengthened.

Fenspire. Founded in 57 AS. Garrisoned. Garrison: 3,742.
The words crawled across the parchment, each letter swelling before it dried. Isolde could hear the quill
that had written them, though no quill moved: a wet, delicate scratching, like a beetle trapped beneath a
cup.
Ignatz bent closer.
“Fenspire stands in the Gloaming Reach,” he said.
“I know where it stands.”
“Then you know what it means.”
“It means someone wishes us to believe the garrison is vulnerable.”
“Or that it is not.”
The blood-script changed.
Gloamreach. Pale Coast. Quarantined. Garrison: 2,483.
The room seemed to contract around the name.
Isolde had never seen Gloamreach, but they had seen its absence. On maps, roads bent away from it.
Orders spoke of sealed approaches and withheld supplies. The Pale Coast was often described in military
dispatches with the language of weather: pallid, difficult, unavoidable. Gloamreach was described with
silence.
Malchior’s lips parted. “Why would a dead thing list garrisons?”
“Perhaps it is not dead.”
The knock came from beneath the table.
Isolde did not move. The blood at the edge of the stone shivered, and with it came a pressure behind their
eyes. For an instant the chamber vanished.
A well.
Black water under a white sky.
Hands lowering a sealed vessel into the depths.
The vision broke before a face could form.
Isolde gripped the table until their nails bit into the wood.
Ignatz saw. “What did you see?”
“A choice.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the only one you can afford.”
The page darkened. New words bled upward from the torn seam.
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS.

Malchior drew a sharp breath.
The script continued.
The Purge of Blackport ended in 321 AS. Seventy thousand nine hundred and seven casualties.
Total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
The line beneath it remained blank for a moment.
Then the final sentence appeared.
The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.
No one spoke.
Wind pressed against the tower, carrying the smell of wet ash through the cracks in the shutters. Isolde
imagined Blackport as the blood remembered it: mouths cracked with thirst, buckets lowered into
poisoned dark, soldiers drinking because orders were stronger than instinct. The Iron-Ring Cartel had
always understood that victory was not the end of a war. It was what one did to the survivors afterward.
Ignatz’s face had become unreadable.
That was answer enough.
“You knew,” Isolde said.
“I knew the Cartel won.”
“You knew how.”
“I knew what I was told.”
“You sell intelligence to the Iron-Ring Cartel. Did they tell you the wells were theirs to poison?”
His eyes shifted—not toward the door, not toward Malchior, but toward the blood on the floor.
That movement was almost tender.
Almost.
Malchior stepped between them. “This is madness. We are standing in a tower with a page that writes old
history and accuses living people.”
“History is only accusation after the witnesses are gone.”
“And what does it accuse you of?”
The question struck deeper than it should have.
Isolde felt again the last chamber, the dying liege, the warmth of blood on their hands. They had plotted
the death of their own liege with more care than they had ever given to prayer. There had been no thunder,
no righteous revelation. Only a cup, a door left unbarred, and the knowledge that afterward the realm
would have to pretend the death had been inevitable.
The page wrote again.
Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven. Born in 286 AS. Blood-Mage.
Their name appeared last, darker than the others.

The blood at their feet began to climb.
It rose in a thin filament, stretching from the floor toward the table. Isolde watched it with the terrible calm
of recognition. Their own blood answered the page. Not obediently. Hungrily.
Malchior whispered, “What have you done?”
“Nothing.”
“That is a lie.”
“Yes.”
The filament touched the parchment.
Every candle went out.
Darkness swallowed the tower. Isolde heard Ignatz draw his sword, heard Malchior’s chain strike the
table, heard stone complain beneath the weight of something waking below.
Then a voice spoke from the floor.
It was not loud. It did not need to be.
“Name the liege.”
Isolde’s breath stopped.
The voice spoke again.
“Name the liege.”
Ignatz moved toward them. His boots scraped once against the flagstones, then halted.
“Isolde,” he said, and for the first time the Warden-Commander sounded uncertain. “Do not answer.”
Malchior murmured a prayer despite the warning. The words were old, polished smooth by generations of
mouths. The tower rejected them. Each syllable returned from the walls misshapen, stripped of sanctity.
The blood climbed higher.
It curled around Isolde’s wrist.
Cold—not wet, not warm, but cold as a blade left beneath winter water. The contact opened something
inside them. A corridor of memory stretched away, its walls lined with doors. Behind one door waited the
liege’s voice. Behind another, the rustle of forged papers. Behind another, the quiet exchange of sealed
intelligence for Cartel coin.
Ignatz made a strangled sound.
Isolde turned toward him, though they could see nothing.
“What door did it open for you?” they asked.
“Be silent.”
“So it opened one.”
“I said be silent.”

The floor cracked.
A narrow seam appeared between the stones, running from the table to the tower’s centre. Red light
seeped through it—not the dull glow of fire, but the colour of fresh wounds under moonlight.
Malchior’s voice broke. “The Silent Choir buried this.”
“No,” Isolde said.
“How could you know?”
“Because the Silent Choir would have made the silence permanent.”
The seam widened.
Below, something breathed.
A gust rose from the dark, carrying the stink of old water and iron. The papers lifted from the table and
wheeled around the chamber. Fenspire flashed past Isolde’s eyes. Gloamreach. Blackport. The Iron-Ring
Cartel. Names, numbers, years, each fragment fastening itself to the next like links in a chain.
The Ashen Vanguard. House Morvain. The Bleeding Crown.
Five powers circling the same corpse, each insisting it had not been the one to kill it.
The page struck Isolde across the face.
They caught it.
The parchment pulsed in their hand.
A final line appeared, written in their own blood.
Speak the name, Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven.
The thing below knocked once more.
This time the tower answered.
Isolde closed their fingers around the page. Somewhere in the dark, Ignatz whispered an oath he had
already broken. Malchior began to recite the lineage they had forged for themself, each invented ancestor
shaking loose from the black.
And beneath their feet, the dead waited to hear whom Isolde had murdered for the sake of the living.

Chapter 14
Greyfell Citadel had been founded in 62 AS, when the Shattered Vale was still spoken of as though it
might one day heal.
Morwenna Ashgrove stood beneath its broken gate and listened to the wind move through the stone.
It made a sound like breath drawn through old teeth. Dust sifted from the archway. Somewhere above, a
loosened slab knocked against another with a patient, hollow rhythm. The citadel was abandoned, and yet
nothing here had the decency to be dead. The walls held cold. The courtyards held the stale impressions of
feet. In the black mouths of the towers, the dark seemed to watch whoever crossed beneath it.
A major Fleet Admiral had no business in such a place.
That was why she had come.
Her coat was sealed at the throat. Her gloves were clean. She carried no lantern. The grey light of the Vale
was enough to reveal the path, and blindness was sometimes safer than illumination. The Citadel’s stones
rose around her in terraces and fractured battlements, all of them the color of ash after rain. Beyond the
walls, the Shattered Vale descended in long, barren folds beneath a sky without mercy.
Morwenna had been born in 288 AS. She had learned early that authority was a garment others placed
upon the body, and that the body beneath it could still be searched, wounded, bought.
The Iron-Ring Cartel had taught her the rest.
She crossed the outer yard. Her boots disturbed a skin of pale grit. The sound went farther than it should
have.
“Admiral.”
Caedmon Fellgard stepped from the lee of a collapsed stair.
He held a writing board against his chest, as if the dead might demand a receipt. His posture was narrow
and disciplined; his clothes smelled faintly of oil, dust, and the sour glue used for binding records. The
wind teased a strip of parchment loose from the board. He caught it without looking.
Morwenna stopped three paces away.
“Caedmon.”
His eyes moved over her shoulder.
“You came alone?”
“You counted incorrectly.”
He looked back at her. “I counted no one.”
“Then you have preserved your reputation.”
The scribe lowered his gaze to the board. His fingers rested upon its edge with the care of a man touching
a blade. “The record says the passage is empty.”
“The record has been paid to say that.”

A brief silence followed. Caedmon’s mouth tightened. He had the reserved, meticulous air of someone
who believed that ink could be a form of armor. Morwenna had seen such men endure fire by insisting that
the flames be entered in the proper column.
“Is that what you brought me?” he asked. “A correction?”
“I brought what the Iron-Ring Cartel requested.”
The wind moved between them. It carried the mineral stink of distant stone and something sweeter
beneath it, a rot sealed too long beneath a floor.
Caedmon’s eyes lifted.
Morwenna saw the fear then—not in his face, but in the way his hand closed around the board. Fear was a
record too. It merely wrote itself in muscle.
“You should not say that name here,” he murmured.
“I have said worse names in better rooms.”
“Names are not the danger.”
“No. The things that answer to them are.”
Beyond the yard stood the inner keep, its upper levels sheared away. The broken crown of it showed the
sky. At its base, a door of black wood sagged inward. Iron had been driven across it in old bands, though
several had been pried loose. The gap beneath was dark enough to possess its own temperature.
Caedmon glanced toward it.
“Vault Chitin lairs in Greyfell Citadel,” he said.
He spoke the words as though he were reading them from a sentence he had spent years trying not to
understand.
Morwenna did not move.
The name had passed through reports in fragments: sightings without witnesses, emptied storehouses,
patrols that returned with their memories frayed at the edges. The Iron-Ring Cartel wanted knowledge of
the lair. Not rumor. Not a sailor’s superstition or a frightened confession extracted in a cellar. They wanted
the routes, the entrances, the depth beneath the citadel, and whatever remained to be taken.
She had sold them the first piece before leaving the coast.
She had sold them the second beneath a seal that no court could break.
The third was written inside her coat.
“Say it again,” she told him.
Caedmon’s face went pale beneath the grey light. “Vault Chitin lairs in Greyfell Citadel.”
“Good.”
“You wanted the words witnessed.”
“I wanted to hear whether you believed them.”
“I record what is attested.”

“That is not what I asked.”
His gaze dropped to the parchment. “Belief is not a category.”
“It is the only category that survives fire.”
A tremor passed through the citadel. Not an earthquake. The stone gave a low internal groan, settling into
some older wound. From behind the black door came a soft clicking, then another, as though something
below had heard its name and tested the shape of it between its teeth.
Caedmon stepped back.
Morwenna remained where she was.
She had stood upon decks while storms tore masts from ships. She had watched crews kneel when the sea
became larger than discipline. She knew the instinct to retreat, and she knew the cost of allowing anyone
to see it. Authority was not courage. Authority was the refusal to let fear choose the next movement.
“Did it hear us?” Caedmon asked.
“Everything hears eventually.”
“That is not an answer.”
“It is the one you have.”
He swallowed. “The passage beneath the keep was sealed.”
“By whom?”
“The old record does not say.”
“Then the old record is worthless.”
“It says the vault was emptied.”
Morwenna turned her head toward him. “Was it?”
Caedmon did not answer.
The silence had changed. It no longer belonged to the wind. It gathered around the door, thickened there,
