the recorded settlement history of The Shattered Vale, though the
present ruin provides little indication of its former function beyond

the fortress designation itself. No active garrison, court, or civil
administration is presently recorded at the site.
The fortress is abandoned. Embercrag feels empty and desolate, its
abandonment hanging over the ruin like a final sentence. This condition
should not be mistaken for an absence of jurisdiction in the historical
record. Embercrag Fortress is ruled by The Silent Choir, whose
authority remains the recognized ruling association for the location.
The relationship between recorded rule and present occupation is
therefore administrative rather than demonstrably residential.
Embercrag Fortress is not a core location. It is catalogued as a
peripheral site within the Shattered Vale, relevant for regional
surveys, territorial records, and the study of abandoned strongholds.
Its designation does not diminish its inclusion in formal gazetteer
records; it indicates only that the fortress does not constitute one of
the principal locations used to define the region’s central structure.
The fortress’s appearance is inseparable from the scorched, crag-bound
impression conveyed by its name. Against the broken landscape of The
Shattered Vale, its ruin presents as a fixed remnant rather than a
functioning seat of power. The site is accordingly classified by
condition and record, not by current habitation.

beyond the realm’s core holdings, among the broken reaches that retain
the stark character of the Shattered Vale. No active civic life is
recorded there. Its structures stand empty, its approaches are
unmaintained, and its presence is defined less by habitation than by
absence.

The settlement’s visual identity is an empty habitation bearing the
stark character of the Shattered Vale. Walls, lanes, and rooflines are

The atmosphere of Emberdeep is silent and forsaken. Sound carries

observable fact of the site.

Embermarch
Embermarch is a core location of the Gloaming Reach, established in 67
AS. Its recorded condition is garrisoned. The settlement presents the
hardened visual identity expected of a garrisoned settlement in the
Gloaming Reach: severe lines, controlled access, martial signage, and
an arrangement governed by readiness rather than display.
Embermarch is ruled by The Ashen Vanguard. Its garrison strength is
4063. This figure defines the settlement’s military establishment in
the current record and marks Embermarch as a position maintained for
sustained vigilance. Personnel, stores, and defensive duties are
organized according to the requirements of a permanent garrison.

danger. Civil arrangements are consequently subordinate to ordered
defense. Movement through its approaches is controlled; routine
activity bears the imprint of inspection, watch rotation, and
readiness. Even in periods of calm, Embermarch does not present itself
as a place at ease.
Its appearance is consistent with its role. Functional structures,
hardened surfaces, and restrained ornament define the visible character
of the settlement. Fires are maintained for use rather than ceremony.
Equipment is kept accessible. Personnel are expected to remain
responsive to summons and changes in condition. These qualities are not
treated as temporary measures but as the ordinary expression of
Embermarch’s garrisoned status.
The founding date of 67 AS places Embermarch within the post-Sundering

therefore clear: Embermarch is a core location, it is garrisoned, and

disciplined, and prepared for danger.

stark spire rising above the dim character of the region. The structure
is the settlement’s principal visual mark and its most immediate
declaration of purpose. From the surrounding reaches, the spire
presents a narrow, uncompromising profile against the muted sky.
Fenspire was founded in 57 AS. Its establishment belongs to the
post-Sundering development of fortified holdings, though the
settlement’s present condition is defined less by age than by function.
Fenspire is a core location, maintained as a permanent military
position rather than a transient camp or lightly held outpost.

Fenthrone
Fenthrone is a fortified coastal seat on The Pale Coast, established in
the aftermath of the Sundering’s altered order. Its visual identity is
defined by walls, watch platforms, and pale coastal terrain. The
settlement presents as a hard-edged installation rather than an open
town: stonework and defensive structures stand against the stark pallor
of the surrounding coast.

Fenthrone was founded in 229 AS on The Pale Coast. Its position remains
outside the realm’s core holdings. No classification of the site as a
core possession supersedes this status; Fenthrone is recorded as a
separate coastal seat maintained under permanent military presence.
The settlement is garrisoned by 5805 troops. This strength governs the
character of the place. Movement is observed, access is controlled, and
ordinary activity proceeds beneath a standing discipline. The garrison
is not merely an administrative detail: it is the settlement’s most
immediate civic fact. Fenthrone feels watchful because it is watchful,
with routines shaped by patrols, fixed posts, inspections, and the
continual readiness expected of a fortified seat.
Fenthrone is ruled by The Bleeding Crown. Its allegiance is therefore
entered in the gazetteer without qualification under that power’s
authority. The designation does not alter the settlement’s geographic
classification: Fenthrone remains a location on The Pale Coast, and it
remains outside the realm’s core holdings.
Architecturally, the site favors defensive mass over ornament. Pale
light, exposed stone, and the severe coastal setting reinforce the
impression of a place built to endure scrutiny and pressure. The visual
identity of Fenthrone is consequently inseparable from its garrisoned
status. Towers, gates, and ordered approaches are read as signs of
continued vigilance rather than ceremonial grandeur.
For purposes of regional accounting, Fenthrone should be cited by its
full register: a garrisoned coastal seat of The Bleeding Crown, founded
in 229 AS, holding 5805 troops, situated in The Pale Coast, and
positioned outside the realm’s core holdings.

Gloammarch stands in The Ash Wastes, where the land’s ash-dark
austerity defines the settlement’s visible character. Its walls,
towers, and public works present a bleak, martial aspect consistent
with the name Gloammarch. Surfaces are commonly described in terms of
soot, dust, and weathered stone; illumination, where maintained, serves
practical purposes before ornamental ones. The settlement’s appearance
is therefore not merely severe but administratively severe: every
feature suggests endurance, vigilance, or the preservation of function
under hostile conditions.
Gloammarch was founded in 321 AS. Its establishment places it among the
recorded settlements of the Ashen Era, though no uncontested civic
interpretation of its foundation is recognized in this entry. The
settlement is a core location, a designation indicating strategic
importance within the present territorial order. Its position in The
Ash Wastes gives that designation particular weight, as control of the
site remains a matter of active dispute.
Gloammarch is ruled by House Morvain. This rule is recognized in the
settlement’s governing record, but the status of Gloammarch remains
contested. The distinction is material: House Morvain exercises rule,
while the wider claim to the settlement is not treated as settled.
Official descriptions should retain both statements without
substituting one for the other.
The recorded garrison strength is 2148. This force is the principal
visible expression of Gloammarch’s martial condition and supports its
continued holding as a core location. The garrison’s presence does not
alter the settlement’s listed status. Gloammarch remains contested
despite its garrison strength of 2148 and despite being ruled by House
Morvain.
In demeanor, Gloammarch is tense and embattled. Its civic atmosphere is
one of maintained readiness rather than confidence. Personnel,
officials, and inhabitants are understood to conduct ordinary affairs
under the pressure of persistent dispute. The settlement holds its
ground amid that dispute; this is its defining civic posture.

For gazetteer purposes, Gloammarch should be recorded as a fortified
core location of The Ash Wastes, founded in 321 AS, ruled by House
Morvain, defended by a garrison strength of 2148, and retaining the
status contested. Further claims regarding its jurisdiction, rivals, or
future disposition are outside the certified record.

House Morvain
Faction Classification: noble house Seat: Ironfell Citadel Doctrine: Ancient noble dynasty claiming descent from the last Sunder-Kings.
House Morvain is an ancient noble house whose authority rests upon a dynastic claim and the weight of its antiquity. It claims descent from the last Sunder-Kings, a lineage asserted as the foundation of its legitimacy. This claim is not presented as a secondary ornament to its rule; it is the central doctrine by which the house defines its station and expects recognition.

The Ashen Vanguard
The Ashen Vanguard is a knightly order sworn to contain the Ley-ruins left by the Sundering. Its doctrine is not custodial in the passive sense. It defines containment as an active military obligation, requiring militant discipline, controlled force, and uninterrupted vigilance wherever dangerous remnants persist.
The Ashen Vanguard is seated at Vharenford. This seat is the principal point from which its order is identified in surviving registers. No distinction is made in those registers between its administrative authority and its military purpose: both are subordinated to the containment of the Ley-ruins.
Its visual identity is that of a militant, knightly order marked by the grim legacy of the Ley-ruins. Equipment, bearing, and ceremony are consequently treated as instruments of warning as much as instruments of war. The order presents no softened interpretation of its charge. Its appearance communicates the hazards it confronts and the severity with which it addresses them.
The Vanguard’s demeanor is severe, disciplined, and constantly watchful. Individual conduct is expected to reflect the order’s collective doctrine. Uncertainty, negligence, and uncontrolled contact with dangerous remnants are incompatible with its stated purpose. The order therefore maintains a posture of readiness even when no engagement is recorded.
The Ashen Vanguard was belligerent in The War of Drowned Light. It was also belligerent in The Accord of Mournthrone, where The Ashen Vanguard is recorded as victor. The order was further belligerent in The Leaden Accord. These entries establish its recurring presence in the military record without altering its primary classification as a knightly order.
In all formal descriptions, the central fact remains unchanged: The Ashen Vanguard is a militant order sworn to contain the Ley-ruins left by the Sundering. Its authority derives from that oath, its appearance bears the mark of that duty, and its conduct is governed by the discipline required to enforce it. Vharenford remains the seat by which the order is located in the annals.
The Bleeding Crown
Identification
The Bleeding Crown is a royalist remnant fighting to restore the shattered monarchy. Its cause is defined by loyalty to the monarchy and opposition to the realm’s fractured condition. It does not recognize the shattered condition of the realm as a legitimate settlement. Its stated purpose is restoration rather than accommodation.
The Bleeding Crown is seated at Blackford. This seat constitutes its established center of authority and the principal location from which its royalist claim is maintained.
Doctrine and Temperament
The faction’s loyalty is directed toward the monarchy as an institution, not toward the realm’s present divisions. Its opposition to the fractured condition of the realm informs its rhetoric, recruitment, and conduct. In practice, the distinction between restoration and reprisal is frequently narrow.
The Bleeding Crown is fervent in declaration and embittered by the monarchy’s shattering. It is determined in pursuit of restoration. These qualities are not ornamental descriptions; they are recognized characteristics of the faction’s public bearing and internal discipline.
Heraldic Aspect
Its visual identity is royalist and wounded, evoking a crown that has endured the shattering of the monarchy. Crown forms, damaged regalia, and marks of fracture are consistent with this presentation. The symbolism presents survival as proof of rightful endurance. It does not depict an unbroken crown. The wound is retained as evidence, warning, and claim.
Recorded Belligerence
The Bleeding Crown was a belligerent in The War of Endless Vigil and is recorded as its victor. The record establishes both its participation and its victory; it does not diminish the faction’s character as a remnant. Its success in that war is used by the faction as confirmation that the royalist cause remains capable of prevailing.
The Bleeding Crown was also a belligerent in The Accord of Mournthrone. This designation records its presence as a party to that accord’s belligerent order. No broader conclusion is entered here regarding the accord’s settlement or subsequent force.
Assessment
The Bleeding Crown remains defined by restoration, monarchy, and resistance to fragmentation. Its authority is royalist in origin, wounded in appearance, and fervent, embittered, and determined in demeanor. Codex classification: royalist remnant.
The Iron-Ring Cartel
The Iron-Ring Cartel is a merchant cartel seated at Hollowreach. Its doctrine is recorded as follows:
> The Iron-Ring Cartel — doctrine: Mercantile league running contraband through the ruined trade roads.
The Cartel is a mercantile league organized around commerce conducted across the remnants of the realm’s trade routes. Its operations concern the movement, exchange, and concealment of contraband through roads damaged or abandoned after the Sundering. The organization’s structure is consequently commercial rather than feudal, with authority expressed through control of trade, access, and passage.
Its visual identity is mercantile and hard-edged. Iron, sealed cargo, marked ledgers, guarded wagons, and reinforced trade gear are consistent with its cartel structure and contraband trade. These signs are not ornamental. They indicate a faction whose public identity is inseparable from the practical demands of commerce conducted beyond lawful channels.
The Cartel’s demeanor is calculating and practical. It is comfortable operating beyond lawful trade and does not present illegality as a moral distinction requiring explanation. Decisions are assessed by utility, risk, access, and return. Negotiation is therefore treated as an instrument of commerce rather than a display of trust.
Recorded Belligerencies and Victories
These records establish the Cartel as a recurring participant in the armed and political contests of the Ashen Era. They do not alter its primary classification. The Iron-Ring Cartel remains a merchant cartel, and its stated doctrine remains the operation of a mercantile league running contraband through the ruined trade roads.
At Hollowreach, its seated authority is understood through this same commercial logic. The Cartel’s presence is defined by transaction, movement, and controlled access. Its hard-edged appearance and calculating demeanor are functional expressions of its organization, not separate traditions. The faction’s conduct beyond lawful trade is therefore consistent with its doctrine, its structure, and its established record as belligerent and victor.
The Leaden Accord
Classification: Conflict Beginning: 330 AS End: 342 AS Recorded casualty figure: 14011 Named victor: The Iron-Ring Cartel
The Leaden Accord was a prolonged military contest whose surviving record is defined less by conquest than by erasure. Its duration began in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS. The accepted outcome names The Iron-Ring Cartel as victor. This designation remains official despite the final destruction suffered by both opposing hosts.
The Leaden Accord ended when both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm. The event rendered the declaration of victory administratively useful but militarily hollow. The recorded casualty figure is 14011. No surviving account establishes the final disposition of every combatant, and the visible remains support only the conclusion that mutual ruin followed the last engagement.
The principal contradiction lies in the artifact associated with the conflict. Public accounts state that it was destroyed. The hidden truth is that a supposedly destroyed artifact was in fact spirited away. Its absence is therefore treated as evidence of concealment rather than confirmation of destruction. The identity and present custody of the artifact are not established in this entry.
The Leaden Accord’s visual identity is leaden, storm-riven, and haunted by the absence of a supposedly destroyed artifact. Surviving depictions favor dim metal, fractured skies, vacant reliquaries, and structures reduced to inert silhouettes. These conventions do not signify a single battlefield; they signify the conflict’s condition of incomplete closure.
Its demeanor is the bleak stillness of mutual ruin concealed beneath a declared victory. This distinction is preserved in formal annotations: victory belongs to The Iron-Ring Cartel, while the hosts themselves were destroyed by a Ley-storm. The declaration and the destruction are both canonical, but they do not describe the same kind of success.
The devastation of Greyfell Citadel in 337 AS, Palewell Abbey in 338 AS, and Cindermere Hold in 338 AS marks the conflict’s destructive record. The engagement at Vharencrag Fortress in 341 AS stands as its last specifically recorded site before the ending in 342 AS.
The Purge of Blackport
Classification: Conflict Period: 311 AS–321 AS Victor: The Iron-Ring Cartel Casualties: 70907 Outcome: Ended with the total rout of the aggressors
The Purge of Blackport began in 311 AS and ended in 321 AS. It caused 70907 casualties and ended with the total rout of the aggressors. The Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor.
The conflict’s recorded scope includes two designated theatres of devastation:
The official settlement attributes victory to The Iron-Ring Cartel and treats the rout of the aggressors as the conclusive military result. The record is therefore commonly cited as a model of merciless triumph: decisive, comprehensive, and without mitigation.
A concealed truth alters that judgment. The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies. This act is not presented as a secondary accident or an incidental contamination. It is the hidden instrument by which the apparent triumph must be understood. The same force that secured victory imposed ruin upon those aligned with it.
The Purge of Blackport has consequently retained two simultaneous classifications in the annals. Publicly, it is a victorious campaign ending in the total rout of the aggressors. In restricted accounts, it is a calculated betrayal concealed beneath the language of victory. The distinction is material: the casualty figure records the scale of the conflict, but does not by itself disclose the method used by the victors.
Appearance: Blackport under purge, marked by The Iron-Ring Cartel and poisoned water.
Demeanor: Merciless triumph soured by calculated betrayal.
The conflict’s enduring emblem is thus not the routed aggressor, nor the Cartel’s undisputed victory alone, but poisoned water within a victorious domain. Its records remain serviceable for determining dates, theatres, casualties, and outcome. They are less reliable when used to describe the moral character of the victory.
The Silent Choir
Office and Authority
The Silent Choir is a secretive priesthood whose religious authority is exercised through control of the historical record. Its doctrine assigns record, correction, suppression, and revision to a single sacred function. History is therefore not treated as a fixed inheritance. It is maintained as an instrument of order, subject to examination and alteration by the Choir.
The Silent Choir records history. It censors history. It rewrites history. These duties are not separate offices in the known account of the faction, but expressions of one doctrine. The Choir’s authority rests upon possession of the accepted version of events and upon the restriction of competing versions.
The Silent Choir is seated at Vharencrag Fortress. Its seat is associated with restrained religious practice, controlled access, and the keeping of records. The visual identity of The Silent Choir is priestly, restrained, and defined by secrecy and the keeping of records. Its appearance communicates neither pageantry nor open force. It presents the discipline of custody.
Conduct
The Choir is quiet, inscrutable, and deliberate in its handling of truth. Statements are measured. Omissions are consequential. Disclosure is treated as an act requiring the same care as inscription. The faction’s silence is therefore not an absence of policy; it is a method of policy.
Its custodians maintain a severe distinction between what may be preserved, what may be concealed, and what may be rewritten. The distinction is administered through religious authority rather than public consent. For this reason, the Choir’s records possess both archival and doctrinal weight.
War Register
The Silent Choir was belligerent in The War of Drowned Light and was victor of The War of Drowned Light. The Silent Choir was belligerent in The War of Endless Vigil. The Silent Choir was belligerent in The Winter Reckoning.
No general account of these belligerencies is entered here beyond the stated record. The Choir’s own handling of the historical record remains a material consideration in all surviving accounts. Its victory in The War of Drowned Light is therefore recorded as an established factional result, while the form and interpretation of that result remain subject to the Choir’s doctrine.
The War of Drowned Light

The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. Its duration is recorded without qualification, though the violence associated with it did not resolve into a clean termination. The War of Drowned Light collapsed into a decade of guerrilla reprisals, and its conclusion therefore signifies the end of the principal war rather than the restoration of settled order.
The conflict’s recorded casualty figure is 64617. This figure is preserved in the annals as the accepted total for the war. The surviving record does not treat the number as evidence of a decisive engagement or a single catastrophic event. Instead, it belongs to a campaign remembered for attrition, concealed operations, reprisals, and the persistence of violence after formal hostilities had ended.
The War of Drowned Light victor was The Silent Choir. This designation remains the formal outcome in the principal annalistic tradition. A separate concealed record states that the spark that started it was staged by The Silent Choir. The victory and the secret staging are therefore entered together, though the latter was not presented as public cause during the conflict.
Its visual identity is one of drowned radiance, broken banners, and a war remembered through reprisals rather than triumph. Records concerning its battlefields frequently emphasize obscured light, damaged standards, and the absence of ceremonial closure. These features are classificatory rather than decorative: they distinguish the conflict from wars whose memory is organized around conquest or formal settlement.
Its demeanor is marked by concealed treachery, attrition, and unresolved vengeance. The designation applies both to the war itself and to its aftermath. The decade of guerrilla reprisals remains the principal reason the conflict is not treated as concluded in the conventional sense of victory, surrender, or reconciliation.
The War of Endless Vigil
Classification: Conflict Period: 247 AS–251 AS Recorded victor: The Bleeding Crown Casualty figure: 81577
The War of Endless Vigil began in 247 AS and ended in 251 AS. Its recorded conclusion was the total rout of the aggressors. The Bleeding Crown is recorded as the victor.
The conflict imposed severe destruction across the contested territories. The War of Endless Vigil devastated Crookvale in 249 AS. It devastated Thorncairn in 250 AS. The War of Endless Vigil was waged at Hollowreach in 251 AS.
Operational Character
The war’s visual identity is one of blood-marked watchfulness, exhausted armies, and an enemy line breaking under prolonged vigilance. Its imagery is therefore defined less by sudden triumph than by the persistence of forces that remain at their stations until opposition fails.
The conflict feels brutal and decisive on the surface. Its recorded outcome supports that appearance: the aggressors were totally routed, and The Bleeding Crown received the formal victory. This conclusion is not, however, a complete account of the war’s conduct.
Concealed Determinant
The secret truth of the War of Endless Vigil is that the losing commander was bribed to withdraw. The withdrawal remains the concealed determinant behind the apparent final collapse. Accordingly, the war is classified as both a decisive rout and a corrupted victory.
This distinction is preserved in the annals without altering the official result. The Bleeding Crown remains the recorded victor. The total rout of the aggressors remains the recorded outcome. The hidden payment does not nullify either entry; it qualifies the means by which the conclusion was reached.
The casualty figure is recorded as 81577. The devastation of Crookvale, the devastation of Thorncairn, and the fighting at Hollowreach establish the war’s material imprint across its listed sites. Together with the concealed bribery, these records define the conflict as an episode of prolonged vigilance, exhaustion, betrayal, and final collapse.

Classification: Conflict Period: 270 AS–283 AS Victor: The Iron-Ring Cartel Casualty figure: 27987
The Winter Reckoning began in 270 AS and ended in 283 AS. Its duration is recorded without interruption in the surviving annals, though the record of its final settlement remains materially incomplete. The conflict left 27987 casualties and concluded with The Iron-Ring Cartel identified as victor.
Its outcome was decided by a betrayal at the eleventh hour. This determination is accepted by the principal accounts, despite their disagreement concerning the identity and scope of the treachery. The concealed truth is that the victors poisoned the wells of their own allies. This fact is preserved in restricted testimony and is not treated as a battlefield rumor.
The documented sites indicate a conflict marked by movement through exposed winter ground, fortified holdings, and contested sources of water. No single surviving account establishes the full sequence of engagements. The destruction of Cindermere Hold and Marrowwell Abbey is nevertheless entered as a direct consequence of the conflict’s passage.
Its visual identity is one of winter, betrayal, and the iron mark of the Iron-Ring Cartel. Frost, ash, sealed wells, and the Cartel’s iron insignia recur in surviving depictions. These motifs are conventional representations and do not alter the recorded findings.
The Winter Reckoning carries an atmosphere of calculated treachery and poisoned victory. Its conclusion is therefore classified as a strategic success with concealed internal betrayal. The Iron-Ring Cartel remains the victor in the official reckoning; the poisoning of the wells of their own allies remains the concealed truth governing later interpretation.

House Morvain
Faction Classification: noble house Seat: Ironfell Citadel Doctrine:
Ancient noble dynasty claiming descent from the last Sunder-Kings.
House Morvain is an ancient noble house whose authority rests upon a
dynastic claim and the weight of its antiquity. It claims descent from
the last Sunder-Kings, a lineage asserted as the foundation of its
legitimacy. This claim is not presented as a secondary ornament to its
rule; it is the central doctrine by which the house defines its station
and expects recognition.

The house is seated at Ironfell Citadel. Its seat, identity, and
conduct conform to an aristocratic and kingly presentation shaped by
its claimed descent from the Sunder-Kings. Ceremonial display, heraldic
emphasis, and formal address are treated as instruments of continuity
rather than mere decoration. The house’s antiquity is itself a
political resource.
House Morvain carries itself with ancestral pride and a guarded sense
of entitlement. Its representatives are characterized by restraint,
formal reserve, and an expectation that precedence should be
acknowledged. Such conduct reflects the house’s view of itself as an
enduring dynasty rather than a temporary claimant among the powers of
the Ashen Era.
The record identifies House Morvain as belligerent in The War of
Endless Vigil. The record also identifies House Morvain as belligerent
in The Purge of Blackport. These entries establish the house’s
participation as a belligerent in both conflicts; they do not, in this
entry, define the full causes, operations, or outcomes of either.
House Morvain’s standing therefore derives from three mutually
reinforcing assertions: noble status, descent from the last
Sunder-Kings, and the accumulated authority of antiquity. Its posture
remains kingly in appearance, dynastic in doctrine, and guarded in
demeanor. The house’s claim is the basis upon which it presents its
right to regard itself as a principal power.

The Ashen Vanguard
The Ashen Vanguard is a knightly order sworn to contain the Ley-ruins
left by the Sundering. Its doctrine is not custodial in the passive
sense. It defines containment as an active military obligation,
requiring militant discipline, controlled force, and uninterrupted
vigilance wherever dangerous remnants persist.

authority and its military purpose: both are subordinated to the

grim legacy of the Ley-ruins. Equipment, bearing, and ceremony are
consequently treated as instruments of warning as much as instruments
of war. The order presents no softened interpretation of its charge.

watchful. Individual conduct is expected to reflect the order’s
collective doctrine. Uncertainty, negligence, and uncontrolled contact
with dangerous remnants are incompatible with its stated purpose. The
order therefore maintains a posture of readiness even when no
engagement is recorded.
The Ashen Vanguard was belligerent in The War of Drowned Light. It was
also belligerent in The Accord of Mournthrone, where The Ashen Vanguard
is recorded as victor. The order was further belligerent in The Leaden

The Ballad of Cinder Shrike
When the last red coal is buried, When the watch-fires bow and die, When the dark lays ash on doorway, Pray you do not meet the sky— For Cinder Shrike is waiting, Where the roofless shadows lie.
No bell foretells its coming, No footmark breaks the ground; The night keeps close its counsel, And swallows every sound. A shutter stirs. A candle pales. Then silence gathers round.
The Cinder Shrike is a threat Of extreme severity; Ask the scarred and ash-faced mourners, Ask the gates that guard the dead. They will not name the hour it comes. They will not turn their head.
It bears a shrike-like silhouette, Bent black against the gloom, Marked by the blackened, ember-dusted Aspect of cinder’s doom. No hearth has made that living ash, No grave has birthed that plume.
It is silent, watchful, waiting, Where the broken alleys wind; Silent beneath the leaning stone, Watchful where the lamps grow blind. A shape may crouch beside your path And leave no trace behind.
Then violently sudden— As spark from a dying brand— It falls from darkness over you, And darkness fills its hand. Its attack is born of surprise; Its mercy is not found.
The Cinder Shrike is a nocturnal ambusher, And night is its chosen veil. It hunts where the moon is strangled, Where the warding prayers fail. The bold may bar the threshold; The prudent may still pale.
So keep no proud flame burning, Do not boast beneath the eaves. The dark has patient fingers, And ash lies under leaves. If silence answers silence, Leave the road and do not grieve.
For Cinder Shrike is watchful, And Cinder Shrike is near; Its blackened, ember-dusted form May wait beside your fear. Its coming has no herald, Its ending has no tear.
When dawn at last unfastens The iron locks of night, The rooftops show their cinder, The alleys drink the light. Yet no one sings of triumph then— They count who left the sight.
Remember, child of ruin, What the old ash-singers say: The Cinder Shrike keeps darkness, And darkness keeps its prey. When the last red coal is buried, Do not call the night away.

Come close, you who keep the watch, And hush your iron breath; I sing of roads where embers sleep, Of vigilance and death. Beyond the realm’s core holdings, Where broken heavens gape, Stands Emberdeep in the Shattered Vale, With no soul left to shape.
Its houses stare with empty eyes, Its hearths are cold and black; The dust lies thick on door and beam, And silence guards each track. No welcome burns in Emberdeep, No footstep wakes the stone; An abandoned, forsaken place, That keeps its grief alone.
From 247 AS the watch was raised, And from 247 AS To 251 AS the red years rolled, With no relief for those who passed. The War of Endless Vigil Drank 81577 lives; Blood marked the walls, the armies failed, And endurance cut like knives.

# **The Ballad of Halvard Crowhurst, Keeper of the Green Ash**

Come listen, all who shelter where the blackened rafters lean,  
And warm your hands above the coals that once were bright and clean;  
For here is sung a quiet name, half-lost beneath the dust,  
Of Halvard Crowhurst, Herbalist, whose jars outlast the rust.

In **252 AS**, beneath a veiled and bitter sky,  
Halvard Crowhurst first drew breath—so smoke-stained records cry.  
No herald marked the hour with bells, no silver trumpet pealed;  
The year alone remembers him, the rest is darkly sealed.

He was a minor character, so write the ledgers plain;  
A small ink-stroke in a realm still limping from its pain.  
Yet where the wounded sought a leaf, where fever burned the skin,  
There waited work for Halvard’s hands, and patient work began.

No physical features are recorded—none for bard or clerk;  
No color of his eyes is kept, no scar, no height, no mark.  
His visual identity is associated with the work  
Of an Herbalist: with mortar, pestle, root, and bitter murk.

Perhaps he moved through shuttered rooms with bundles at his side;  
Perhaps the doors knew only this: the sick came in, then cried.  
Perhaps the steam rose thick and green, perhaps the night was long—  
The ash keeps faith with no man’s tale, and silence guards the song.

No temperament is recorded; let no singer swear  
That Halvard laughed, or raged, or prayed, or turned away in fear.  
A gentle soul? A flint-hard hand? The pages will not say.  
His silence is the only cloak the surviving records may display.

Still sing him where the lanterns fade, where winter gnaws the door;  
Sing not of crowns or iron rings, nor wars upon the moor.  
Sing of the nameless jars that wait when brighter glories cease,  
Of roots that taste like graveyard rain, yet grant a breath of peace.

O Halvard Crowhurst, hear us not—or hearing, do not heed;  
The world forgets the lowly hand that answers mortal need.  
No statue bears your counted years, no painted face is found;  
But herbs remember every wound that touched the waiting ground.

So pass the cup, and grind the leaf, and bank the dying fire;  
Let every humble remedy rise higher, higher, higher.  
For though the chronicles leave you slight, and all your marks are few,  
The work of an Herbalist remains when songs themselves fall through.

Which hand will claim them when the dead winds blow.

Then came the moths—not soft, not pale,  
But a storm with wings and a lantern’s veil.  
The **Lantern Moth Swarm**, a siege-breaker of serious threat,  
Rose where the marsh and the ramparts met.

A dense cloud of moths, close-packed and wide,  
With eerie lantern-light burning inside;  
They crawled through arrow-slits, they veiled the gate,  
They made the surest stone hesitate.

Restless they wheeled, overwhelming the height,  
Difficult to flee from, difficult to fight.  
No wall is a wall when the dark things stream  
Like ash-bright sparks through a fortress dream.

“Hold fast,” sang the marsh, or perhaps it lied.  
“Stand firm,” cried the stones, or perhaps they cried.  
And there, in the wavering lantern-glow,  
The Falconer watched what no songs can show.

Did Ignatz raise his hand? Did he call to the air?  
Did any wing answer? No witness stands there.  
The ballad knows little; the marsh knows less—  
Both trade in echoes and emptiness.

Still, when moth-light gathers on Crookgate stone,  
When contested towers groan alone,  
The keepers whisper, and the watchmen sleep:  
“Ignatz Cindervale walks by the keep.”

Not as a lord, nor a crowned command,  
But a Falconer beneath the ash-choked land.  
A minor name, yet the night winds keep  
His tread beside old Crookgate Keep.

So sing of the swarm with its restless flight,  
Of lantern-dark day and lantern-bright night;  
Sing of the keep no realm could reap—  
And the name that remains: Crookgate Keep.

The Ballad of Three Ashen Names
Come, hush the cups and bank the flame, Let no bold tongue grow loud; I sing of three whom ruin named Beneath the ash-gray cloud. Not truth, perhaps, in every strain— Yet truth wears many faces: The road keeps Korvath Greyfen’s name, The pyre keeps other traces.
Ho, turn the wheel, let black bells ring, Let broken banners mourn; The Crown may bleed, the iron sing, Yet songs outlive the torn.
Korvath Greyfen, Smuggler, came From no proclaimed high hall; Born in 289 AS, he bears No painted mark at all. No chronicler has fixed his look, No priest has weighed his cheer; His visual sign is only this: A Smuggler passing near.
He walks where shuttered markets sleep, Where old roads lose their stones; He carries whispers, ash, and sleep— Or so the tavern drones. Ask not what lies beneath his cloak, Nor whom his silence serves. The song knows only Korvath’s trade And all the doubt it nerves.
Ho, turn the wheel, let black bells ring, Let broken banners mourn; The Crown may bleed, the iron sing, Yet songs outlive the torn.
Then Sabelle Mournvale the Twice-Crowned Steps forth in iron shade; Born in 263 AS, they bear The office they have made. High Inquisitor, stern in gaze— So speaks the kneeling crowd; Their severity is like a door That shuts upon the proud.
Yet under stone, beneath their house, A secret keeps its breath: A bound revenant in their cellar, Chained to a silence worse than death. Whether this be sin or law, No singer dares decide; For inquisitorial severity And necromantic custody abide.
Ho, turn the wheel, let black bells ring, Let broken banners mourn; The Crown may bleed, the iron sing, Yet songs outlive the torn.
Ravena Stormwell bears the cloth Where standards must be borne; A Standard-Bearer, named in dust, Born in 274 AS, forlorn. No feature has the record kept, No temper has it told; Her visual sign is duty’s staff, Her banner’s weathered fold.
She may be brave, or she may fear— The song has no sure tongue. It knows her only by the flag That rises when bells are rung. And when the ash obscures the road, When every oath is worn, Three names remain in crooked ink: The smuggler, crown, and standard borne.
Ho, turn the wheel, let black bells ring, Let broken banners mourn; The Crown may bleed, the iron sing, Yet songs outlive the torn.

The Ballad of the Ashgrove Stores
Come, hear of Lysandra Ashgrove, Whose tally-staff was plain, Who watched the sacks and counted casks Beneath the ashen rain. No jeweled blade hung at her side, No crown adorned her brow; Her tools were hooks and seals and keys, And order was her vow.
Lysandra Ashgrove is a minor figure, Yet serves as Quartermaster still; Where stores grow thin and ledgers fade, She keeps them by her will. The flour is marked, the iron bound, The lamp-oil kept from spoil; She knows what hand has drawn each cord, What chest has paid its toll.
Her bearing is the watchman’s bearing, Her silence sharp and spare; She stands among the guarded stores As though danger lingered there. The ash may sift through shuttered cracks, The dead wind claw the door, But every measure waits in line, And none may claim one more.
Sing now of Stormmarch in the Wastes, Where blackened storm-clouds crawl; Stormmarch lies in the Ash Wastes, A fortress sealed from all. It was founded in 71 AS, When ash was yet young and red; Its walls have learned the taste of years, Its stones remember dread.
Its garrison numbers 9,263, A host behind the chain; Yet Stormmarch remains quarantined, Held fast from road and reign. Outside the realm’s core holdings, It stands severe and still, With strength beneath its quarantine And silence on the hill.
No trader sings its market-song, No open banners stream; The gates keep counsel with the dust, The watch keeps back the dream. A stronghold built for iron need, A settlement of gray, Where every store and salted grain Must answer for the day.
Then raise the cup for House Morvain, Ancient beneath the sun; House Morvain claims descent from The last Sunder-Kings undone. Its authority rests upon That dynastic claim of old, And on the weight of antiquity More deep than minted gold.
Its halls bear aristocratic pride, Its speech is kingly, guarded; It carries ancestral entitlement As though the world were chartered. But crowns are ash and blood is dust, And old claims bend like reeds; The leanest hand that counts the grain May govern greater needs.
So sing no boast of Lysandra, Nor call her crowned or grand; Her place is custody and care, A ledger in her hand. Yet when the ash shuts out the road And famine tests the gate, The one who knows the stores by heart May keep the stronghold’s fate.

# **The Ballad of Emberdeep’s Empty Fire**

Hear now, beneath the ash-grey sky,  
Where broken watchfires sleep,  
Of Sabelle Blackspire, Quartermaster,  
And Isolde Mournvale, falconer,  
Whose names the dead winds keep.  

Sabelle Blackspire counts the grain,  
The nails, the cords, the thread;  
No crown is shown within her hands,  
No banners rise at her command—  
Yet stores outlive the dead.  

Her tally marks are black as soot,  
Her measures cold and plain;  
She knows what hunger leaves behind,  
What empty mouths and winters find,  
What rust consumes of chain.  

Isolde Mournvale lifts the hood,  
And listens for the wing;  
The falconer’s work is wind and sky,  
A watching eye, a waiting cry,  
A shadow without spring.  

No written temper follows her,  
No colors tell her face;  
Only the cry above the stone,  
Only the beat that is not known,  
Only the ash-dark place.  

Both were born in **341 AS**,  
So says the dust-worn page;  
The Ashen Era has no song  
For every hand that labors long  
Beneath its iron age.  

Come down, come down to Emberdeep,  
Where the Shattered Vale lies bare;  
It was founded in **34 AS**,  
When fire still kissed the roof and grass—  
I swear the year is there.  

Now Emberdeep is abandoned,  
Outside the realm’s core holdings;  
Its doors gape wide to vacant air,  
Its wells keep silence in their care,  
Its hearths remember nothing.  

An empty settlement, stark and still,  
It crouches in the Vale;  
No market bell, no footstep’s sound,  
No living boast to travel round  
The stones grown pale and frail.  

There Sabelle’s ledgers turn by themselves,  
Though no hand feeds the flame;  
The Quartermaster weighs the night,  
Sets out a ration for the light,  
And enters hunger’s name.  

There Isolde hears a distant wing  
Above the roofless square;  
She raises her hand, she waits, she knows  
The falcon circles where no bird goes—  
Then finds no creature there.  

O Sabelle Blackspire, keep the count.  
O Isolde Mournvale, hear.  
The Vale has swallowed road and gate,  
Yet Emberdeep still holds its date  
And will not yield it here.  

So sing them low, you ash-bound throats,  
Where silent chimneys lean:  
The Quartermaster, the falconer,  
The empty town beyond the core—  
And all the fires unseen.

The Pale Bell’s Ballad of Mournthrone
Come close, you ash-stained daughters, Come near, you oath-worn sons; I sing of Mournthrone’s broken
word And wars that were not done. Let no priest correct my verses— The bell remembers more Than ink
that sleeps in sealed-up books Or iron on a door.
In 297 AS, the Accord began, With banners under rain; The halls grew dark, the pledges cracked, And
mercy learned its chain. The Ashen Vanguard raised its sign, While Mournthrone cast its shade; A
broken accord beneath that gloom, A promise poorly made.
Palewell Abbey watched the coast, Pale-faced against the foam; In The Pale Coast, its rebuilt walls Made
war where prayers found home. Founded in 244 AS, It kept the salt wind near; Austere, awake, its narrow
eyes Saw every oath as fear.
O, ring the pale bell, ring it low, For victory tastes of ash; The sword may name the vanquished man, But
not the hand that paid the price. O, ring the pale bell, ring it low— The dead are slow to sleep; A settled
crown is often cast Where buried bargains creep.
In 301 AS, the Accord was ended, And the Ashen Vanguard named victor; So cried the court, so wrote
the seals, So sang each paid-up singer. Yet the losing commander withdrew— Not from courage broken
through, But because that commander was bribed To do what blades could not do.
I heard it from a shuttered mouth; I swear it was not mine. The wind may have reshaped the words, The
dark may have supplied the sign. Still, truth has teeth beneath its tongue, And secrets learn to crawl; A
victory built on purchased steps Will stagger when they fall.
Then came a decade of reprisals, Guerrilla fires in rain; The road forgot the king’s decree, The fields
recalled the slain. From abbey wall to ruined hold, The old wounds opened wide; The Accord lay dead, yet
every night Its ghost walked at our side.
So sing, you guards of Palewell, Where sanctuary wears a spear; Your garrison is 5998, And watchfulness
is prayer. Though Palewell Abbey is not a core holding, Its pale stones still endure; A garrison more than
sanctuary, With no peace to make it pure.
Remember: Mournthrone shadows all, And broken vows bear flame. The Ashen Vanguard may claim the
song— The Ashen Vanguard may claim the name. But beneath the bell, beneath the ash, Beneath the
victor’s throne, The Accord of Mournthrone still breathes In every blade drawn alone.

# The Ash-Black Ballad of The Crown of Burned Names

Hear now, if your ears have not been bought,  
And keep your tongue beneath your breath;  
For I sing of a ward from the ruin-wrought,  
A circlet that bargains with memory and death.

**O The Crown of Burned Names, black in the flame,**  
**Guard what is living, unmake what is named;**  
**A hush for the lost, a veil for the known—**  
**Who wears it keeps watch, but is never alone.**

It was forged in **266 AS**, so the old scraps say,  
Though old scraps lie sweetly when ashes are deep.  
No bell gave witness, no herald cried,  
Only sparks in the dark and a vow denied.

Its **attunement cost is 60**—  
Mark that well, and mark it twice.  
Some pay with blood, some pay with breath,  
Some pay by forgetting the shape of death.

It is a crown of blackened material,  
Scarred with names that the fire could not spare;  
Each letter is wounded, each wound is a door,  
And the brow beneath it is less than before.

Its silhouette stands stark and funerary,  
A gallows of shadow, a chapel of bone.  
No jewel adorns it, no bright metal sings;  
The dark keeps its counsel around its rings.

**O The Crown of Burned Names, black in the flame,**  
**Guard what is living, unmake what is named;**  
**A hush for the lost, a veil for the known—**  
**Who wears it keeps watch, but is never alone.**

I have seen it hung where the cold lamps fail,  
And I have seen dust settle upon its rim.  
I say it was waiting; I say it was mourned—  
But dust has a voice when the mind is worn.

It brings no thunder, no radiant sign,  
No answering choir from under the stone.  
It merely stills the room around it,  
Till every small breath sounds borrowed and owned.

Remembrance enters with a covered face;  
Loss follows softly and will not depart.  
Guarded identity sits at the table,  
With one empty place and a sealed-up heart.

That is the tension the burned names bear:  
Protection in one hand, erasure in the other.  
The ward keeps watch over what must remain,  
While the fire takes the name from the brother.

**O The Crown of Burned Names, black in the flame,**  
**Guard what is living, unmake what is named;**  
**A hush for the lost, a veil for the known—**  
**Who wears it keeps watch, but is never alone.**

So pass it not lightly from palm into palm,  
Nor call it a prize for the bold or the brave.  
A crown may defend what the world would devour,  
Yet leave only silence to mark what it saves.

And if, in the dark, you hear someone sing  
A name that the blackened scars have concealed,  
Do not answer aloud. Let the lost remain lost.  
Some doors are protection; some doors are sealed.

The Ballad of Drowned Light
Come close, you ash-faced hearers, Let no bright hearth-fire sing; I bear a song of drowned radiance, Of banners with broken wing. It is not a song of triumph, Nor a crown laid safe and whole— It is the wound that keeps on speaking When the dead have lost their toll.
O bind the lamp, and bind it thrice, Hold fast what must not flee; For light may drown in secret hands, And truth wear victory.
In 225 AS, the dark tide rose: Thus began The War of Drowned Light. Its banners broke in rain-black air, Its torches failed the night. The fields were not won by valor, Nor cleansed by trumpet-call; The hidden spark was secretly staged By The Silent Choir, through all.
They struck, then veiled their fingers; They let the ashes lie. Each road became a reckoning, Each well a watching eye. No sword was ever finished When the first red fighting ceased; The war collapsed to guerrilla reprisals, And vengeance fed the feast.
O bind the lamp, and bind it thrice, Hold fast what must not flee; For quiet hands may turn the key, Yet silence is not free.
In 235 AS, the ledgers wrote The ending of the war. They marked 64617 casualties, And nothing could restore The names beneath the water, The cries beneath the clay. The Silent Choir was recorded victor— So the sealed records say.
But victory wears a drowned veil; Its bells are choked with silt. The victor’s hand may hold the seal, Yet not escape the guilt. For every broken banner Still trembles in the rain, And every reprisal leaves a door For vengeance to return again.
In 72 AS, before those years, A ward was forged and bound: The Thrice-Bound Lantern, stern of shape, With three bindings clearly found. Its strength is not in blazing forth, Nor in a conqueror’s flame; It guards by restraint and containment, And keeps the dark in frame.
At the record-board sits Morwenna Vane, A minor figure, still and slight; She serves as a Scribe, keeping written records, With ink and writing-staves in sight. Her posture is disciplined and quiet, Her attentive eyes do not depart; She copies what the ledgers demand, And leaves no wound unmarked.
O bind the lamp, and bind it thrice, Hold fast what must not flee; Morwenna writes, the lantern waits, And drowned light remembers thee.

# The Watchman’s Ballad of Blood and Sorrow

Sing low, sing long, for the lamps burned red,  
When **The War of Endless Vigil** raised its head;  
From **247 AS** to **251 AS**,  
The weary kept their watch through the killing haze.  

Blood marked the helms and the banners’ white,  
No dawn brought rest, no grave brought night;  
The armies stood with their eyes unclosed,  
While the enemy line slowly cracked and opposed.  

**81577 casualties** lay where the black rains fell,  
And the living learned the weight of a bell.  
The watchmen’s hands were stiff with scar,  
Yet still they stared across the darkened war.  

The aggressors broke in a total rout,  
Their standards trampled, their courage cast out;  
And **The Bleeding Crown** was recorded the victor—  
So sang the herald, and none sang quicker.  

But beneath the drum and the victory cry,  
A purse passed soft where the ravens fly;  
The losing commander, bought in the shade,  
Was bribed to withdraw, and the breach was made.  

So brutal the triumph, so clean the lie,  
With betrayal hidden where proud men die;  
The crown wore blood, the watch wore blame,  
And truth went limping without a name.  

Then lift the ward with its sorrowful face,  
Forged in **119 AS** for a grief-haunted place;  
Name it aloud, though the candle flame falter:  
**The Psalter of Seven Sorrows**, ward of the altar.  

To attune to its silence, the price is **49**,  
A burden of mourning, a wound made divine;  
Its pages know weeping, its binding knows pain,  
And each sorrow returns when the bells sound again.  

Sing not too loudly, lest sorrow awake,  
Nor hold it too closely, lest old wounds break;  
For wards may endure what the watchers cannot,  
And grief keeps the shape of the hand that forgot.  

Hear now of **Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven**,  
A **Blood-Mage**, by wrath from the cradle driven;  
Born in **286 AS**, when old ashes lay,  
They entered the tale after Vigil’s last day.  

Their gaze bears grievance, their ambition burns,  
And concealed betrayal wherever it turns;  
For Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven, in secret,  
Plotted the death of their own liege—repeat it.  

The Unforgiven walks where the red standards lean,  
With a dangerous heart and a face hard to read;  
No psalter can hush them, no crown can absolve,  
No watchman can know what their silence resolves.  

Sing low, sing long, let the bitter notes fall:  
The victor may triumph, the traitor may call.  
Blood marks the watching, grief fastens the chain—  
And every kept vigil remembers the slain.

The Marrow-White Ballad of Thorn Wraith
Come, hush your cup and lower your flame, Let no bright tongue undo the same; For I sing of sleep where the black bells wait, And the abbey that watches beside the gate.
Marrowwell Abbey, marrow-white, Stands in The Gloaming Reach without delight. Rebuilt from ruin, stern in stone, It keeps its vows with a soldier’s bone.
Its founded year was 218 AS— Write that in ash, and let none contest. Though it is not a core holding, still Its walls keep watch by the shadowed hill.
6656 hold the garrisoned ground, Where boot and prayer make a single sound. Six thousand six hundred fifty-six, With iron at hand and scripture fixed.
But dreams are doors no mortar bars, Nor locks of bronze, nor watchful stars. There comes the Thorn Wraith, pale and thin, Where sleeping minds let darkness in.
A dream-feeder, bred of invasion and feast, It drinks the inward and fattens the beast. It belongs to terror’s bed and breath, Half in waking, and half in death.
Its ghostly form is threaded through With thorn-like shapes of a cruel hue; Its outline wavers, faint and dire, Like a wound drawn out in silver wire.
It does not rage. It does not run. It waits till the final candle is done. Intimate, patient, predatory, It haunts the mind with hunger’s story.
Then rise the veiled ones, robed in white— The Silent Choir, who cherish night. A secretive priesthood, quiet and restrained, With sealed-up histories carefully chained.
They record what was, then censor the page; They rewrite the past to govern the age. Their religious authority is won By ruling the record beneath the sun.
Inscrutable hands with deliberate care Make truth kneel down in the cloistered air. They keep no song that the Wraith might learn, No dream uncut, no word unturned.
“Sleep, sleep,” they murmur—though none hear sound; “Let memory lie where the dead are bound.” Yet Thorn Wraith curls in the sleeper’s eye, And drinks what the silent priests deny.
So Marrowwell stands, and the dark winds moan; The rebuilt abbey guards blood and stone. Not a core holding—so the ledgers declare— Yet its marrow-white walls hold a watchful prayer.
Remember the year. Remember the name. Forget what the Choir has crossed from the frame. For when the last record is buried from sight, The Thorn Wraith wakes in the heart of the night.

The Ballad of Thorn Wraith, Sung Beside a Banked
Hearth
O hush the latch and dim the flame, Let no bright ember climb; For there is one who walks unseen Across
the fields of time. Not flesh, nor fog, nor common shade, Nor wraith that mourns the dead— But Thorn
Wraith, with a starving heart, Where sleeping thoughts are fed.
“Sleep not deep, and wake not wide, Bar the door on either side; For what comes near and does not
speak May wear your dream upon its hide.”
It enters where the eyelids close, Where silver rivers run, Where little hopes like candles burn Before the
rising sun. It drinks the road beneath the feet, The face one longs to see; It takes the word that might have
healed And leaves the tongue to flee.
For Thorn Wraith is a dream-feeder, And draws its nature from The invasion and consumption of
dreams, Wherever sleep has come. It does not hunger as beasts do, Nor tear as wolves might tear; It waits
beside the inward door And finds the sleeper there.
A mother heard a child’s soft laugh— Or so the dark seemed kind— Then watched the laughter lose its
shape And vanish from her mind. A soldier dreamed of open skies, A beggar dreamed of bread; The Thorn
Wraith drank the shining parts And left the dreamer dread.
“Sleep not deep, and wake not wide, Bar the door on either side; For what comes near and does not
speak May wear your dream upon its hide.”
Its form is ghostly, pale and thin, Yet never wholly bare; For thorn-like shapes are threaded through Its
outline in the air. Each barb appears, then fades away, Like briars seen through rain; A cruel and
insubstantial shape, Too near to name, too plain.
It leans as close as whispered prayer, It knows the pulse, the breath; It haunts the mind with patient care, A
patience born of death. Yet death is not the name for it— The waking world knows why: It belongs as
much to terror’s bed As to the morning sky.
So if you wake with frost within And thorns behind your eyes, Do not say, “It was but dreaming,” Nor
trust the light that lies. Keep one small thought that it has missed, Guard one unbroken spark; For Thorn
Wraith feeds upon the dream That first gives shape to dark.
“Sleep not deep, and wake not wide, Bar the door on either side; For what comes near and does not
speak May wear your dream upon its hide.”

The Ballad of Vharencrag, the Hollow Edge, and the Pale Stag
Sing low, you mouths that know the snow, And hush the hearth-fire’s glare; For Vharencrag stands where the black winds grind The bones of the High Spires bare.
Founded in 84 AS, they say, Its first stones bit the sky; And still it lifts its mountain face Where the thin clouds crawl and die.
Nine thousand four hundred seventy-eight Keep watch behind its wall— A garrison vast as a winter host, Yet the fortress may still fall.
For Vharencrag is formidable, But threatened in its height; The crags remember every blow, The towers mistrust the night.
And when the watchman’s courage thins And no bird dares to sing, There comes a sound beneath the stone— A slow and hollow ringing.
Then speak not loud of The Hollow Edge, The ward forged in 216 AS; Its name is emptiness given shape, A silence sharpened vast.
To attune one’s soul to The Hollow Edge Costs 21, no less; The bold may pay with blood or breath, The wise refuse the test.
It bears no kindly flame or sign, No comfort for the hand; It waits like a door with nothing behind, Where no living soul should stand.
But deeper still, beneath the roots, Where buried cold things creep, The Pale Stag of Omens turns In caverns without sleep.
A burrowing horror of serious threat, It moves where none can see; Its pallid hide drinks up the dark, Its antlers rake the scree.
No hoofbeat heralds its rising, No cry announces doom; Only the earth grows strangely still Before it makes more room.
O Pale Stag, O Pale Stag, What future do you bear? Your antlered brow is an omen’s crown, Your breath is the taste of despair.
It does not charge with roaring rage, Nor trumpet its intent; It inspires dread through quiet foreboding, And leaves the brave unspent.
So hold the walls of Vharencrag, Though the High Spires groan; Keep far from The Hollow Edge, And let its emptiness alone.
For should the deep earth open wide Beneath the mountain’s seam, The Pale Stag will climb through stone— Or was it only a dream?
Sing low, you mouths that know the snow, And let no lantern sway; For contested walls and hollow wards Make poor guards against the day.

# **The Ash-Wall Ballad of Vharenford and Ederon Coldwater**

Sing low, ash-throats, sing low,  
Where the dead winds scrape the stone;  
For Vharenford keeps watch below,  
And the wastes have made it bone.

In **291 AS**, its first stones rose  
Beneath a sky of iron hue;  
The Ash Wastes taught its gates to close,  
And taught its bells what fear can do.

It is a **core location**, stern and scarred,  
A garrisoned hold against the grey;  
Its watchfires burn behind the guard,  
Its sentries measure night and day.

**3637** stand to keep the wall—  
So the tally-board and captains say.  
Three thousand six hundred thirty-seven, all,  
With dust in their teeth and none to pray.

Sing low, ash-throats, sing low,  
Let no bright tongue praise the town;  
Vharenford does not bend or bow,  
Nor lay its iron manner down.

Then speak of **Ederon Coldwater**,  
Whose name is carried, breath by breath;  
A **Sapper**, sworn to earth and water,  
Who reads the buried road to death.

Born in **391 AS**, so the record tells,  
Though records crack and ink runs thin;  
His name is struck where the hammer fell,  
His trade is marked, but not his skin.

No chronicler grants his face to song,  
No proven temper, fierce or mild;  
The ash may hide what the ledgers wrong,  
And silence keeps the Sapper’s child.

Yet sing him still, for a sapper’s hand  
Knows the weight beneath the ground;  
It finds the hollow under the land,  
And hears where the buried dark is bound.

Do not say he loved the fortress wall,  
Or that Vharenford knew his tread;  
The truthful page does not say it all,  
And truth is a nail in the coffin of dead.

Still, when the night wind claws the gate,  
When watchmen pale at the powder’s sigh,  
The singers join his name to the state  
Of the hard-held town beneath the sky.

“Ederon!” cries the ash-black road.  
“Vharenford!” answers the guarded stone.  
One bears a craft, one bears a load,  
And each stands grimly there alone.

Sing low, ash-throats, sing low,  
Let the cinders veil the morn;  
Where Vharenford keeps watch below,  
The Sapper’s song is never born—

Yet never wholly dies away,  
For walls remember what men omit;  
And dust will carry, day by day,  
The names that no bright histories fit.

# Contract of Ashen Custody and Account

Let this instrument be read beneath a sound roof or beneath the open ruin, and let its clauses bind the hand that signs them.

**Between:**

**The First Signatory**, hereafter called the Custodian;  
and  
**Ignatz Marrowgate**, Quartermaster, hereafter called the Account-Bearer.

The Custodian places under account the following two relics:

1. **Chalice of Ashdeep**, a reliquary forged in **323 AS**. Its visual identity is that of a reliquary bearing the name **Chalice of Ashdeep**, and it suggests a deep, ashen solemnity. Attunement to it costs **27**. No hand shall attempt such attunement without the Custodian’s written assent.

2. **The Cinder-Wrought Aegis**, regalia shaped by the legacy of the **Sundering**. Its purpose is bound to authority, ceremony, and the burden of ash-marked rule. It appears as imposing regalia worked in a cinder-dark style, its surfaces suggesting fire-scarred craftsmanship. It carries an austere atmosphere of sovereignty endured beneath ruin. Its forged year is **354 AS**.

The relics shall be conveyed, if conveyance is required, only to **Embercrag Fortress**, which stands in the **Shattered Vale**. Embercrag Fortress was founded in **207 AS**. It is not a core location and has been abandoned. Its scorched, crag-bound identity contrasts with the broken landscape of the Shattered Vale; it feels empty and desolate, its abandonment hanging over the ruin like a final sentence.

Ignatz Marrowgate shall enter the relics into his quartermaster’s account without embellishment, omission, or substitution. No physical feature is established for Ignatz Marrowgate beyond his visual identity as a Quartermaster. No canonical temperament is established for him; therefore, this contract shall judge only his recorded acts and not any supposed disposition.

The Custodian shall not demand that Embercrag Fortress yield shelter, guards, fire, or welcome, for the fortress is abandoned. The Account-Bearer shall not represent the ruin as occupied, secure, or core to any realm. Field Report: Embercrag Fortress, Ashreach
Filed for the Ashen Vanguard, from the roadward watch Condition of report: firsthand where
possible; rumor marked as rumor
Embercrag Fortress stands in the Shattered Vale, and no loyal hand can mistake what has become of it.
The place was founded in 207 AS, though the stone gives no answer as to why anyone chose that crag, or
what oath was meant to endure there. Its walls bear a scorched, crag-bound identity against the broken
landscape. Black ridges bite into the sky. Old surfaces flake beneath the fingers. The fortress seems less
built than burned into existence.
It is abandoned.
I record that plainly because the empty chambers invite invention. One hears movement in the lower
works when the wind crosses the broken masonry, and the watchfires of no garrison mark the heights.
Whether those sounds are stone, vermin, or the dead is beyond my authority. I saw no living occupants. I
found no sign that Embercrag Fortress serves as a core location. Its emptiness hangs over the ruin like a
final sentence, and even the daylight seemed unwilling to remain within its courtyards.
The place is not merely vacant. It feels concluded.
Ashreach lies in The Weeping Marshes, where ash and water make a gray country of every road and
roofline. Unlike Embercrag Fortress, Ashreach is currently contested. Its garrison numbers 2598. That
count makes it a defended but unsettled holding rather than a core stronghold; yet the number did not
make the settlement feel secure. Spears were visible. So were shuttered doors, watched crossings, and men
who stared too long at every distant shape.
Ashreach presents the bleak, marsh-bound aspect of a settlement caught between ash and water. The
ground shifts underfoot. The air carries wet rot and old smoke. Walls sweat. There is no clean boundary
between the holding and the mire surrounding it. A person may stand within the palisade and still feel the
marsh reaching through the boards.
Its atmosphere is tense, unstable, and perpetually threatened. I cannot say from which quarter the next
danger would come, and that uncertainty appears to be the only agreement among those inside. Some
called the threat near. Others called it already present. I judged both statements true, though I admit the
marsh fog may have sharpened my fear.
Assessment: Embercrag Fortress is abandoned and unsuitable as a core location. Ashreach remains
defended, but contested and unsettled. Do not mistake walls for safety, nor silence for peace.

# Field Report: On the Sealed Reach and the Crooked Vale

**Filed by:** a road-worn observer of the Ashen Vanguard  
**Condition of report:** written under poor light, with the coast still in my clothes

## I. Gloamreach

Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast, though it does not seem to belong to the coast around it. It is a core location, held behind its own silence, and its garrison numbers **2,483**. I counted the standards where I could see them. Whether every bearer still lived beneath those colors, I cannot swear.

The place is quarantined. The word is painted, nailed, and spoken through shut doors. It sets Gloamreach apart from the surrounding coast more surely than any wall. Boats keep their distance. Travelers are watched. Even the gulls appear to turn aside, though that may be only the weather or my own unease.

Gloamreach bears the pallid, bleak character of the Pale Coast. Its stone seems leeched of warmth, and the roads carry the color of old ash. Yet the name gives it another face: a shadowed identity, as if the settlement were not merely darkened but concealing something beneath the dark. I found no welcome there, nor did I expect one.

Its demeanor is sealed-off and ominous. Every gate suggested a question. Every sentry held uncertainty behind the eyes. I was permitted to observe, not to understand. That distinction may be the whole purpose of the place.

## II. Crookvale

Crookvale was founded in **295 AS** in **The High Spires**. It has been rebuilt, and the rebuilding shows in every hard seam and uneven angle. The settlement retains a garrison of **1004**, though Crookvale remains outside the core holdings.

I was told the vale had survived what should have ended it. I believe the stones more than the speaker. They stand crooked, but not weak; sharp-edged, but not careless. The structure bears an identity suited to the highland settlement, where straight lines are perhaps a luxury and softness a liability.

Crookvale feels wary and resilient. Its people watched the road as if the road had betrayed them before. Doors closed without slamming. Hands remained near tools and weapons. Survival has become its governing principle—not a banner, not a prayer, but a habit worn into the settlement until no one remembers behaving otherwise.

## Closing Judgment

Gloamreach guards its uncertainty by sealing the world out. Crookvale endures by watching the world closely. I would not call either place safe. I would call both difficult to break.

That is not the same thing. But in this age, it may be the nearest thing left.

Field Report: Lantern Moth Swarm
Filed by: a shaken observer of the outer works Condition of report: written after withdrawal; certain
passages may be imperfect
General Assessment
The Lantern Moth Swarm is a siege-breaker of serious threat. I use the term “swarm” reluctantly, for it
suggests a multitude acting without purpose. This thing has purpose enough. It does not advance like
troops, nor strike like beasts. Acting as a collective, it brings mothlike disruption against fortified positions
until walls, gates, towers, and the courage behind them are made equally uncertain.
No single moth appeared dangerous. That was the first lie the swarm told us.
Appearance
At distance, the Lantern Moth Swarm resembles a dense cloud of moths. Their wings turn and vanish
within one another, so that the cloud seems less made of bodies than of moving ash. Yet through the mass
runs an eerie visual impression of lantern-light: pale glimmers, wavering halos, and brief golden stains
upon stone.
I will not swear that any true flame burned among them. I saw no wick. I saw no oil. Still, the light was
present. It gathered along the battlements and trembled in the arrow slits. Men reached toward it, believing
it near enough to grasp. Those men were not seen clearly afterward.
Observed Behavior
The swarm was restless from its first appearance. It did not settle. It pressed, recoiled, divided, and
returned, always finding another opening through which to worry the defenders. Shutters were closed; it
found the cracks. Helmets were tightened; it filled the breathing space. Cloaks were drawn over faces; the
cloth fluttered as though something beneath it wished to be let out.
Its assault was overwhelming without being loud. The air became a constant dry whisper. Sight failed in
patches. Orders crossed one another, then ceased altogether. Some defenders abandoned their posts before
the wall was touched. Others struck at empty light until their weapons broke against stone.
I record this with shame: escape did not appear to be a matter of speed. The Lantern Moth Swarm made
every direction seem occupied. Those who fled into open ground found the cloud before them. Those who
remained behind the fortification found it within.
Conclusion
Do not mistake the Lantern Moth Swarm for vermin, smoke, or a mere nuisance of the night. It is a dense
cloud with the force of a breach. It is restless, overwhelming, and difficult to escape. Fortifications may
resist iron, fire, and ordinary assault. Against this thing, a wall becomes only a place for the lantern-light
to gather.
If the cloud is sighted, conceal the lamps and prepare to abandon any position that cannot be sealed
completely. I offer no stronger counsel because I possess none.

Chalice of Ashdeep
Chalice of Ashdeep is a reliquary forged in 323 AS. Its name is borne plainly in its identity, and its presence carries a deep, ashen solemnity. I found no warmth in the thought of it. Even when held away from shadow, it seemed made for silence, remembrance, and the keeping of what should not be exposed to common hands.
Attunement to Chalice of Ashdeep costs 27. This cost is not to be dismissed as a figure for clerks. The reliquary demands a price, and those who approach it should understand that reverence is not the same as safety.
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis
The Cinder-Wrought Aegis is regalia shaped by the legacy of the Sundering. Its forged year is 354 AS. I record this without uncertainty.
Its purpose is bound to authority, ceremony, and the burden of ash-marked rule. It appears as imposing regalia worked in a cinder-dark style, with surfaces suggesting fire-scarred craftsmanship. Nothing about it speaks of easy sovereignty. It carries an austere atmosphere: rulership endured beneath ruin, not glory raised above it.
The Aegis is worn, in spirit if not upon the body, by whoever must command while the world crumbles. That is its true menace. It does not promise triumph. It demands that its bearer remain standing when triumph has ceased to matter.

Letter from the Reed-Gate Watch, Concerning Ashreach
To the Honoured Keeper of the High Seal,
I write from Ashreach, though whether “from” means standing within its walls or merely surviving beneath their shadow is a matter the marsh itself may dispute. Ashreach lies in The Weeping Marshes and is currently contested. Every road, boardwalk, and half-drowned causeway bears the mark of one claimant or another, though the mud is quick to swallow such marks by morning.
Do not mistake the smoke upon the horizon for a settled hearth. It is usually a signal, or a roof burning, or both. The settlement presents the bleak, marsh-bound aspect of a place caught between ash and water. Its timbers sweat black moisture. Its wells taste of iron. Even the bells seem reluctant to sound, as if they fear drawing the attention of whatever listens beyond the reeds.
The garrison numbers 2598. I set the figure plainly, lest some comfortable clerk reduce it to a tidier sum. Yet numbers do not make a wall steadfast. The garrison is sufficient to hold the gates for a time, and sufficient to punish any fool who tests them openly. It is not sufficient to make Ashreach peaceful, nor to make its people certain that tomorrow belongs to them.
Thus Ashreach remains a defended but unsettled holding rather than a core stronghold. That distinction is understood by every sentry, though never spoken where the officers may hear. A core stronghold expects relief. Ashreach expects footsteps in the fog.
The atmosphere here is tense, unstable, and perpetually threatened. Men sleep with one hand upon the latch and the other upon whatever weapon they trust. The ferrymen refuse to cross after dusk. The market opens when it can and closes before anyone admits why. I have seen watchfires kindled on both sides of the same embankment, each company claiming the other had trespassed first.
We hold the walls, if walls they may be called. We hold the storehouses when they are not already empty. We hold our tongues, which is presently the most valuable duty. But I cannot swear that the ground beneath us remains loyal. The marsh shifts without proclamation, and Ashreach shifts with it.
If aid is intended, send it without banners and without promises. Banners are noticed. Promises are remembered.
Written beneath a shuttered lamp, with the water rising under the door,
Your obedient and watchful servant, The undersigned hand
