# Letter Beneath the Winter Seal

_To the keeper of the sealed records,_

I write concerning **Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven**, **The Winter Reckoning**, and **Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn**. I would have you burn this after reading, though I know well that nothing written in the Ashen Era truly burns. Ash remembers. Iron remembers. Blood remembers most of all.

The public account names **The Winter Reckoning** as a conflict that began in **270 AS** and ended in **283 AS**. It left **27,987 casualties**, and the **Iron-Ring Cartel** stood as victor. That is the clean version, fit for proclamations and carved stones. The dirtier account says its outcome was decided by a betrayal at the eleventh hour. The victors poisoned the wells of their own allies.

Mark that phrase: *their own allies*. It is not a tale of honest enemies overcoming one another beneath a hard sky. It is calculated treachery, a poisoned victory, and the iron mark of the **Iron-Ring Cartel** pressed into winter’s white face. Whoever repeats otherwise is either a fool or has been paid to forget.

Then there is **Isolde Fellgard the Unforgiven**, born in **286 AS**. The record calls Isolde a major **Blood-Mage**, bearing the visual identity of an Unforgiven Blood-Mage: grievance made visible, ambition kept close, betrayal concealed beneath every measured breath. Their secret is not merely that they distrusted their liege. They plotted the death of their own liege.

I do not say this because Isolde confessed. Confessions are luxuries for the innocent and traps for the guilty. I say it because the shape of the matter is unmistakable. Blood answers blood, and a concealed betrayal leaves a stain even when no blade is found.

As for **Halvard Vane the Grave-Sworn**, born in **338 AS**, the ledgers name Halvard a major **Seneschal**. No canonical physical features are established; remember that when some tavern liar supplies a scar, a limp, or a silver eye. The epithet **the Grave-Sworn** and the formal station of **Seneschal** are the marks by which Halvard is known.

Yet Halvard, too, plotted the death of their own liege. Their manner is grave and controlled, which is merely another way of saying that the knife is kept sheathed until witnesses grow careless.

I leave you with this warning: do not mistake winter silence for peace, iron victory for honor, or sworn service for loyalty. In this realm, the wells may already be fouled.

_Sealed without a name_

Letter Concerning Morwenna Vane, Scribe
_To the Honoured Keeper of Records,_
I set down this account concerning Morwenna Vane, though I will not pretend that my eyes have gathered more than they have. She is a minor figure, and those who hunger for banners, bloodlines, and loud deeds may pass over her without a second glance. That is their loss, if not their danger. Kingdoms have been lost through broken swords, yes, but also through a missing line, a spoiled seal, or a page left where damp could reach it.
Morwenna Vane serves as a Scribe. Her work centers on the production and keeping of written records. I have seen enough of her station to say that she treats the written word as other folk treat a drawn blade: with care, discipline, and an understanding that neglect may wound long after the hand is gone. She copies, preserves, and attends to what has been entrusted to the page. Whether every mark she keeps is worthy of keeping is not for me to judge. The record survives because she does.
Her appearance is that of a scribe. Writing materials are near her, as natural to her presence as ash is to a burnt road. Quills, ink, scraped sheets, and bound leaves seem less like possessions than the proper instruments of her calling. She carries herself with the disciplined posture of a record-keeper, straight-backed and composed, as if even the weight of silence has been measured and entered into a ledger.
Her demeanor is quiet and attentive. Do not mistake this for softness. A quiet person hears what the boasting miss, and an attentive person notices what the careless trample beneath their boots. Morwenna Vane does not fill a chamber with herself. She leaves room for others to speak, then gathers their words into order. This may make her seem lesser than those who command the room. I have found that the room often depends upon the one who remembers what was said within it.
I offer no grand praise. Grand praise breeds grand expectations, and a Scribe should not be made into a banner. Let Morwenna Vane remain what she is: a minor figure with a disciplined hand, a quiet bearing, and a duty to the records. When the powerful deny what they promised, written pages may be the only witnesses left who cannot be frightened into silence.
_By a hand that has seen too many records burned,_ —

# Letter Under Grey Seal Concerning Mournwatch

_To the one who keeps the eastern records,_

I write concerning Mournwatch, though I confess that the place is not easily held in ink. A settlement may be marked upon a map, measured by its walls, and entered into a ledger with a neat hand. Mournwatch resists such tidiness. It lies in the Gloaming Reach, beneath that dim and lingering character which makes every hour seem borrowed from the night.

Do not mistake its silence for peace.

Mournwatch is garrisoned. The fact is plain enough, and any fool who doubts it need only look upon the watchfires, the barred approaches, and the sentries who turn their faces toward every road before they turn them toward a speaker. The garrison does not parade. It waits. Even the changing of the watch is performed with the grave restraint of a burial rite.

Nor should you count it among the realm’s favored heartlands. Mournwatch stands outside the realm’s core holdings, and those who govern from nearer and warmer seats are pleased to remember this whenever provisions, coin, or relief are discussed. Yet they remember the place readily enough when danger is spoken of. Then Mournwatch becomes a shield, a warning-post, a necessary hardship borne by others.

Its appearance is that of a guarded settlement set beneath the dim character of the Gloaming Reach. The walls seem less built than braced against some approaching weight. Doors are shut early. Voices are kept low. A traveler arriving at dusk sees little welcome, but many eyes. I have heard it said that the stones themselves watch the road. I will not swear to that. I will say only that no one there behaves as though the stones are blind.

The demeanor of Mournwatch is somber and vigilant. Those words are repeated in reports because they are accurate, though they fail to convey the burden of them. There is no careless laughter in the garrison square, no idle leaning upon a spear, no confidence that tomorrow will resemble today. Men and women stand as though awaiting an alarm that has merely been delayed.

If the realm still possesses a core, Mournwatch is not within it. Perhaps that is why it sees more clearly what gathers beyond the light. Keep its name in the records, and do not soften the entry. Mournwatch lies in the Gloaming Reach. It is garrisoned. It is outside the realm’s core holdings. These are not ornaments of description, but warnings.

_Sealed by a hand that has no wish to be remembered_

# A Letter Regarding the Blackport Register

**To Isolde Mournvale, falconer,**

I send this under a shuttered lamp, though I cannot say whether secrecy still has value in an age where even water may be taught to murder.

You have asked what may be trusted concerning **The Purge of Blackport**. I will give you the figures first, before memory and fear dress them in finer garments: the conflict began in **311 AS** and ended in **321 AS**. It caused **70,907 casualties**. It ended with the **total rout of the aggressors**. The **Iron-Ring Cartel emerged as victor**.

That is the account fit for proclamations.

The other account is fit for a locked room.

The wells were poisoned by the victors themselves—by the **Iron-Ring Cartel**, though the dead who drank from them had been counted among their own allies. I do not know whether the Cartel called this necessity, arithmetic, or victory’s final price. I know only that Blackport’s water turned against the living, and that the triumph afterward tasted of iron and ash.

Thus the name *Purge* is not an ornament. It is the proper word. Streets emptied. Doors were marked. Those who survived learned to distrust the cup before the blade. The aggressors broke, yes, but the hand that claimed to cleanse the city fouled its wells. Let no herald tell you that a rout makes the righteous.

You are a minor figure in the records of the Ashen Era, which is a cruel way of saying that the record has not yet found a use for your life. It notes that you were born in **341 AS**, twenty years after The Purge of Blackport ended, and that you serve as a **falconer**. It records no canonical physical details of you. It records no canonical temperament either. Perhaps that is mercy. A blank page cannot yet be made to testify falsely.

Still, a falconer knows what the court forgets: a bird may circle above a slaughter and remain untouched by it, but it sees the whole shape of the killing. Keep that sight. If you ever speak of Blackport, speak the numbers plainly. Say **311 AS**. Say **321 AS**. Say **70,907 casualties**. Say **Iron-Ring Cartel**. Say that the wells were poisoned by those who stood among the victors.

Merciless triumph is still triumph to those who inherit it. To the buried, it is only another name for betrayal.

**Sealed without a signature,**  
**one who has read the Blackport account**

Letter on the Pale Spymaster and the Choir’s Kept Silence
_To the Keeper of the Unburned Register,_
I set down these words with a hand that will not stop trembling. Burn them after reading, or give them to the ash; I care little which, so long as they do not pass beneath the eyes of The Silent Choir.
Do not mistake that body for a gathering of quiet priests and nothing more. The Silent Choir is a secretive priesthood that records, censors, and rewrites history. Its religious authority is exercised through control of the historical record. They do not merely preserve what was. They decide what may be remembered, what must be corrected, and what was supposedly never spoken. Their visual identity is priestly, restrained, and defined by secrecy and the keeping of records. Even their demeanor is quiet, inscrutable, and deliberate in their handling of truth.
I have seen no greater example of their shadow than Corvus Hollowmere the Pale.
Corvus Hollowmere the Pale is a major character in these troubled accounts, though the Choir would sooner make the phrase itself vanish. Corvus serves as Spymaster and was born in 351 AS. Their appearance is that of a pale Spymaster bound to a hidden allegiance. That allegiance is not conjecture, though I have prayed it was: Corvus Hollowmere the Pale swore a hidden oath to The Silent Choir.
There is the terror of it. A spy may conceal a message, a guard may conceal a blade, but an oath concealed beneath the whole ordering of secrets is another creature. Corvus evokes quiet secrecy and the oppressive tension of an oath kept out of sight. One hears nothing in their presence—not because nothing is said, but because every silence seems weighed, sealed, and entered into a ledger no honest hand may open.
Perhaps I have misread the signs. Perhaps the pale face is only a pale face, the measured speech only discipline, and the Choir’s records only records. Yet when history is handled by priests who censor and rewrite it, certainty becomes a luxury reserved for those who control the ink.
Keep this letter apart from the common archives. If the Choir asks whether I wrote of Corvus Hollowmere the Pale, say that you cannot recall. If they ask whether the oath exists, say the same.
I would prefer a lie that survives to a truth that is neatly erased.
_Sealed without a name,_ _One Who Still Remembers_

warmth of the sun. Its shores carry the same drained aspect, yet the place possesses a deeper shadow, as

thresholds and veiled purpose. Even the wind there seems to approach with caution.

of the burden placed upon the surrounding coast. Let provisions be measured, passages marked, and
messages permitted under watch. Let those confined within Gloamreach not vanish from all reckoning,
and let those outside it not be treated as though their fear were guilt.

# Petition of the Pale Coast Concerning Gloamreach

**To the Ashen Vanguard, House Morvain, the Silent Choir, the Iron-Ring Cartel, and the Bleeding Crown—**

We, the undersigned hands of the coast, set down this petition beneath a sky that gives no comfort, and beg that it be received before the seal upon Gloamreach is mistaken for silence.

Gloamreach lies on the Pale Coast. It is a core location, though the word *core* brings little warmth to those who dwell within its shadow. Its garrison numbers **2,483**. Let that number be read plainly, and not softened by distance or by the mutterings of courtiers who have never watched a gate after dusk.

The status of Gloamreach is **quarantined**. This sets it apart from the surrounding coast, and the separation has grown into a wall no hand can see and no honest plea can cross. We do not petition that the danger be denied. We petition that the people, stores, watchfires, and roads of the Pale Coast not be forgotten merely because Gloamreach has been shut away.

The place bears the pallid, bleak visual character of the Pale Coast. Its stones seem drained of color; its waters offer no promise; its streets hold the look of something waiting to be buried. The name itself carries a shadowed identity, and those who speak it too loudly are thought fools—or worse. Gloamreach feels sealed-off and ominous, defined by isolation and guarded uncertainty. We know this. We have lived beneath it. We do not ask for pretty words to cover the truth.

We ask instead that the quarantine be regarded as a charge, not an excuse. Let the gates be watched without cruelty. Let provisions be counted without theft. Let messages pass where passage is permitted, and let those charged with guarding Gloamreach remember that a barred door still has people on both sides of it.

If the Ashen Vanguard claims duty, let duty reach the Pale Coast. If House Morvain claims stewardship, let stewardship endure the sight of bleak stones. If the Silent Choir claims wisdom, let silence not become abandonment. If the Iron-Ring Cartel claims order, let its ledgers record more than absence. If the Bleeding Crown claims dominion, let its crown bear the weight of this sealed place.

We place no crown upon our own heads by this plea. We ask only to be heard.

**By hands marked with salt, ash, and the dust of waiting.**

Thus Blackford must not be made a vault for convenient silence. It is watchful, strained, and caught between military defense and unresolved conflict.
We demand that the full account of The Leaden Accord be preserved and read aloud before the garrison and the people. The Leaden Accord began in 330 AS and ended in 342 AS, leaving 14,011 casualties. The Iron-Ring Cartel was named victor. Yet both hosts were destroyed by a Ley-storm, and the hidden truth is that a supposedly destroyed artifact was spirited away. Let no declared victory cover the bleak stillness of mutual ruin. Let the record bear its leaden, storm-riven character, and let the absence of that supposedly destroyed artifact remain marked rather than disguised.
We further petition that every sealed inventory, witness statement, and surviving token concerning that absence be brought under guarded examination. We do not command that rumor be crowned as proof. We command only that proof not be buried beneath a victor’s seal.
Concerning the regalia called The Thrice-Bound Edge, we ask that its record be kept separate, exact, and unaltered until its nature is established. The Thrice-Bound Edge was forged in 123 AS. Its defining record contains no attunement cost. It is regalia bearing the name The Thrice-Bound Edge, and its presence conveys a restrained, binding atmosphere. If it is held within Blackford, let its custody be declared. If it is absent, let that absence be declared also. Let no clerk add a cost where none is recorded, nor erase the name from fear of what it may bind.
We ask for a public accounting, guarded copies of the records, and a place of mourning for the 14,011 casualties. We ask that Blackford’s contested status not be used to deny its duty, nor its garrison of 3,065 used as a veil over civilian testimony.
By ash, iron, and the unquiet sky, receive this petition and answer it in writing.
The undersigned, whose names are affixed below

Petition for the Warding of the Thorn Wraith
To the Honoured Keeper of the Gate, and to all who hold authority over the night,
We, the undersigned, place this petition before you with ink, ash, and what courage remains to those who must close their eyes beneath a roof.
Let it be recorded plainly: the Thorn Wraith is a dream-feeder, drawing its nature from the invasion and consumption of dreams. It does not belong wholly to any chamber, road, field, or grave. It belongs as much to the terror of sleep as to the waking world. Thus no barred door may be trusted as a complete safeguard, nor may a shutter, watchman, or lantern be mistaken for protection against a thing whose trespass begins where the sleeper’s guard fails.
Its shape must likewise be entered into the record, lest frightened tongues soften the truth. It has a ghostly form threaded with thorn-like shapes, giving its outline a cruel and insubstantial character. Those thorns are not ornament. They are the sign by which the waking mind may know what the sleeping mind cannot name. Its substance is faint, yet its purpose is not. Its outline fades, but the dread it carries does not fade with it.
Nor is the Thorn Wraith a beast that spends its hunger in haste. It feels intimate and predatory, haunting the mind with the patience of hunger. This is why we petition you. A common predator may be driven from a threshold. A common specter may be denied a resting place. But a hunger that waits within dreams may return whenever the afflicted seek sleep, and may make a refuge of the very mercy by which the weary endure.
We therefore beseech the authority of this place to recognize the Thorn Wraith as a danger requiring watch, warning, and deliberate warding. Let those who sleep be told what kind of terror may approach them. Let no keeper dismiss a troubled dream merely because the sleeper wakes beneath an unbroken roof. Let the signs of thorn-like shapes and ghostly form be treated as a summons to vigilance, not as the fancy of the exhausted.
We do not ask for grand promises. We ask only that this petition be sealed, preserved, and read aloud where sleepers gather; that the Thorn Wraith’s nature be entered without comforting lies; and that those who fear the night not be mocked for fearing what belongs to both dream and waking.
By the hand of the fearful, and for the protection of those yet unburdened by sleep,
The Petitioners

# Petition for the Warding of Sleep and the Summoning of Castellan Fellgard

_To the hands that receive pleas when the lamps fail,_

I, whose name is better left beneath this mark, submit this petition concerning the thing called the **Thorn Wraith** and the man called **Castellan Fellgard**. I do not ask that my fear be honored as proof. Fear is a poor witness, though it speaks with a voice that will not be silenced.

The Thorn Wraith is no mere tale of the dark. It is a dream-feeder, drawing its nature from the invasion and consumption of dreams. It belongs as much to the terror of sleep as to the waking world. Those who glimpse it—if glimpse is the right word—describe a ghostly form threaded with thorn-like shapes, its outline cruel and insubstantial. It does not rage like a beast. It waits. It feels intimate and predatory, haunting the mind with the patience of hunger.

Therefore I beg that the matter be placed before **Castellan Fellgard**, for **Castellan Fellgard - role: Standard-Bearer**. Let him be summoned, questioned, and permitted to speak beneath the standard he bears. I know nothing of his temperament, and I will not dress ignorance in false certainty. I know only that **Castellan Fellgard - born: 237 AS**. If his years have taught him the reading of omens, the keeping of watches, or the burden of standing where others falter, let that knowledge be made useful before more sleepers are emptied by the Wraith.

I further petition that no person be mocked for reporting a visitation. The Thorn Wraith does not require a door, a road, or a guard-post. It enters where thought loosens its hold, and it feeds where the mind believes itself unobserved. A witness may wake with no wound upon the flesh and still have been robbed. A household may call such a one fevered, faithless, or witless; I say the household may be wrong.

Let the lamps be kept, not as a cure, but as a declaration that waking folk have not surrendered the night. Let the standard of Castellan Fellgard be seen by those who fear sleep, if he is willing to bear it before them. Let the petition be entered, even if the clerk believes the ink itself has begun to whisper.

I place my mark below and ask for judgment, protection, and a hearing before the Thorn Wraith makes a grave of another dream.

**By ash, witness, and waking,**  
*the petitioner’s mark*

The Red Hand Beneath the Spire
A Sermon Delivered in Fenspire
Attend, watchful souls of Fenspire. Let the wind worry the stones, and let the stark spire above the
Gloaming Reach remind us that height is not holiness. A tower may see far and still fail to see the truth
beneath its own shadow.
Today we speak of Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed.
He was born in 255 AS, when the wounds of the Sundering had long since hardened into custom. He
became a major Sellsword Captain, a man carrying the hard, dangerous presence of a seasoned
sellsword. No canonical physical features are established for him; no honest tongue may give him a face
that history did not grant. His visual identity is the epithet “the Red-Handed” and the martial station of a
Sellsword Captain.
Yet behind that iron station lay a concealed claim. Brannoc Ironmere the Red-Handed was the
unacknowledged heir to the Bleeding Crown. Mark this well: a claim may be hidden from the court,
denied by the throne, and still burn within the claimant. Blood does not require a herald to remember
itself.
But remember this also: concealment is not sanctity. A secret inheritance may be a burden, a temptation,
or a blade waiting in the dark. The dangerous presence of Brannoc was not proof that he was righteous.
Nor was his silence proof that he was false. We who stand beneath stone and spear must beware the easy
sermon that turns a powerful dead man into either saint or devil.
Brannoc died in 300 AS during the Accord of Mournthrone. There the account ends for the body, but
not for the warning. A man may march beneath another banner while carrying a crown inside his ribs. A
hand may serve coin, steel, or destiny—and those masters do not always know one another.

# **Sermon of the Unlifted Hand: Concerning Ignatz Fellgard and the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell**

Hear me, ash-breathed faithful, and keep your hands beneath your sleeves.

There are names that thunder from ruined towers, and names that pass quietly between the sickbed and the herb-basket. **Ignatz Fellgard** is of the latter kind. Do not despise the small office. A leaf may be small and still bitter enough to teach the tongue. A root may lie unseen beneath the ash and yet hold a fever down. Whether Ignatz Fellgard heals, merely prepares, or only knows what the green things conceal, I cannot swear beyond the record. But the record says **Herbalist**, and a true sermon must not make a larger man merely because its speaker desires a larger lesson.

**Ignatz Fellgard was born in 257 AS.**

Mark the year. **257 AS.** Let no careless mouth replace it with a prettier number, for the dead and the living are both poorly served by ornamental lies.

Now consider the **Gauntlet of Sorrowfell**. It is regalia, bearing the name **Gauntlet of Sorrowfell**, and around it clings an atmosphere of sorrow and grim authority. Its forging date is not recorded. Thus we shall not invent one, though the ignorant always prefer a false date to an honest blank.

Its attunement cost is **12**.

Twelve. Not eleven, not thirteen. Twelve is the measure demanded before the gauntlet yields itself to a bearer. Yet understand this: I do not proclaim that Ignatz Fellgard wears it. So learn the narrow mercy of the ash: name what is known, bow before what is not, and fear the hand that reaches for authority without paying its due.

The gauntlet asks **12**.

The record asks truth.

And the sorrowful hand, once lifted, may never again be mistaken for an empty one.

Believers in the Ashen Era, bow your heads—not to the strength of the wall, nor to the iron of the lock, but to the judgment that waits behind both.

Therefore, keep watch over what is entrusted to you. A gaoler may guard a body. A sellsword may pursue a crown. But judgment belongs to the darkness beyond every door, and no hand—red, iron, or empty—can bar it forever.

# **A Sermon of Ash and Sorrow, Delivered Beneath the Empty Spires**

Attend, you who still possess ears beneath your hoods. Attend, you whose hearts have become sealed jars, holding only old smoke.

I am Malchior Cindervale the Flame-Touched, Arch-Prelate, born in **289 AS**. I stand before you in sanctified authority, though the weight of that office presses hard upon the breast. Let no tongue praise my blood as proof of holiness: **I forged my own lineage papers**. The ink was mine. The claim was mine. The sin was mine. Yet the flame does not ask whether the hand that bears it was born noble. It asks only whether that hand will endure the burning.

Before us rests **The Psalter of Seven Sorrows**, a ward forged in **119 AS**. Its name is sorrow, and sorrow is its proper hymn. To attune oneself to it costs **49**. Remember this: every ward demands a price, and the coward calls the price unjust only after reaching for its power. Do not mistake grief for weakness. A wound may be a door, if one has courage to enter.

Look also toward **Cindermere Hold**, founded in **246 AS** among **The High Spires**. Once its garrison numbered **8878**. Now it is abandoned, and it is not a core holding. Its blackened silhouette remains elevated above the world, severe as cinder and hollow as a dead oath. There is your lesson, plainly carved in ruin: immense strength may stand for ages, and still become an empty shell. Walls do not preserve devotion. Numbers do not preserve souls.

And behold the regalia named **Gauntlet of Sorrowfell**. Its forged year is **360 AS**. Its attunement cost is **12**. It carries sorrow and grim authority, as every true instrument of judgment must. Wear it, if you must, but know this: regalia lends no virtue to the hand. A gauntlet may close the fist; it cannot teach the fist when to open.

Therefore, mourn without worshiping your mourning. Obey without surrendering judgment. Let the forged thing in you be confessed before it becomes a throne. Let the abandoned place in you be entered before it becomes a tomb.

I have spoken my name. I have spoken my shame. The flame has heard both.

Now carry your sorrows upright. The ash remembers every false claim—and every soul that endured it.

A Sermon of the Ink Beneath the Spire
Attend, ash-breathed faithful, and lower your voices before the page.
For the page does not shout. It does not draw steel. It does not command the gate or make the war-horn answer. Yet when the shouting is ended, when the steel is rust, and when the horn is only a memory in a dead man’s skull, the page remains to accuse the living of what they have forgotten.
Consider Morwenna Vane.
Morwenna Vane is a minor figure who serves as a Scribe. Do not despise the word minor. A small mark may turn a blessing into a curse. A single omitted line may erase a household, a debt, a warning, or the name of one who stood fast when others fled.
Her role centers on the production and keeping of written records. This is not a soft labor. It is a discipline of the hand and a burden upon the soul. She gives shape to what would otherwise scatter. She keeps the dead from being wholly swallowed. She sets witness in rows, and rows endure more faithfully than tongues.
Her visual identity is that of a scribe, associated with writing materials and the disciplined posture of a record-keeper. See her, if you can: not as a torch beneath the rain, nor as a banner upon a wall, but as the steady hand bent above its work. Her demeanor is quiet, attentive. Such quiet is not emptiness. It is the stillness required to hear what louder souls trample beneath their feet.
And now behold Fenspire.

There, the stone itself seems to keep watch. Fenspire has a garrison of 3,742 and holds garrisoned status. Its atmosphere is shaped by permanent military occupation, and it projects disciplined vigilance.

# **A Sermon for the Unfinished Voice, Preached Beneath Crookgate Keep**

Attend, if your ears have not yet hardened.

Attend not for thunder, nor for the promise that the marsh will open and yield a clean road. We are gathered beneath **Crookgate Keep**, where the stones hold their silence and the waters of the **Weeping Marshes** refuse to show what lies beneath them. This keep was founded in **294 AS**. Remember that number. Stone remembers what flesh mislays.

Crookgate Keep is contested. Crookgate Keep lies outside the realm’s core holdings. Let no tongue dress this truth in silk. We are not sheltered here by certainty. We are held here by walls, by watchfulness, and by whatever fragments of duty remain when greater powers quarrel over broken ground.

And among such fragments stands **Ravena Harrowick**.

She is a **Choir Novice**. Do not despise the word *novice*. The first note is not lesser because it is first. The hand that has only begun to learn the form may yet tremble toward obedience. The mouth that has not mastered the whole measure may still refuse the lie.

Ravena Harrowick bears the modest formal bearing of a learner in choral service. See her—not as a banner, not as a champion carved upon a gate, but as one who listens before she answers. Her atmosphere is subdued and attentive. In an age that rewards shouting, such attention is a kind of resistance. In a place where every reed may conceal a blade, to listen without surrendering the soul is no small labor.

You may ask what use there is in one minor figure amid contested stones. I tell you: the Choir is not made only from its loudest voices. A wall is not made only from its highest tower. A vigil is not made only from the hand that carries the lamp. Ravena’s beginning is itself a lesson: service starts in humility, in posture, in the discipline of hearing what others pass over.

So let Crookgate Keep teach you plainly. Uncertainty is not proof of abandonment. The bleak marsh is not absolution from duty. A novice is not empty merely because she is unfinished.

When Ravena Harrowick lowers her gaze, do not call it weakness. Perhaps she is measuring the silence. Perhaps she is learning which sound deserves to be carried onward.

And when your own voice fails, remember: the first faithful act may be to listen.

Sermon of Drowned Radiance: On Sorrow, Oaths, and
the Unburied Dead
Hear me, ash-marked faithful, and let no bright lie pass your lips.
The War of Drowned Light began in 225 AS and ended in 235 AS. 64617 casualties were counted
beneath its broken banners. Yet the counting did not end the war. The conflict collapsed into a decade of

Thus was drowned radiance made: light beneath black water, banners torn before they could proclaim
triumph. Remember this when some lord praises the clean edge of a victory. There are wars that end only
in ink. There are victories that leave the dead standing in the hearts of the living.
Look, then, upon Corvus Hollowmere the Pale, the Spymaster. Corvus was born in 351 AS, and bears
the pallor of one who serves secrets more faithfully than daylight. Their hidden oath to the Silent Choir is
not shouted from a tower. It is kept beneath the tongue, where an oath becomes a chain. I say this not to
condemn the keeping of silence—for silence may preserve a life—but because every concealed vow casts
a shadow, and shadows gather where treachery has been fed.
And consider Morwenna Vosgard, the Sapper, born in 296 AS. No physical features are recorded for her,
and no temperament is recorded either. Perhaps that is fitting. The Sapper is known by the work left
behind: earth broken, stone opened, foundations made uncertain. Let no soul imagine that only famous
faces shape an age. Hands without songs may still alter the ground beneath every throne.
Before us stands the Gauntlet of Sorrowfell, regalia of grim authority. Its attunement cost is 12. I
proclaim that it was forged in 360 AS. Wear it, if you must, as one wears judgment—not as a prize, but as
a burden. Sorrow is not weakness. Sorrow is the weight that keeps the hand from becoming eager.
So kneel, but do not kneel blindly. Mourn, but do not let mourning become permission. The drowned dead
have no mouths, yet their silence accuses every oath sworn in secret and every banner raised over ashes.
Let the Choir keep its victory. Let the Pale Spymaster keep their hidden vow. Let the Sapper’s buried
work remain beneath our feet.
We shall remember. And remembrance, though dim, is a blade that does not rust.

Sermon of the Unsealed Mind, Preached at Vharenford
Hear me, watchful souls of Vharenford.
You dwell in the Ash Wastes, where the sky is a lid of dust and every wall must remember its duty. Vharenford was founded in 291 AS, and it has endured by the virtues of stone, vigilance, and obedience. Its garrisoned status is no mere mark upon a clerk’s board. Its garrison strength of 3637 is a number set against the dark, a measured answer to all that would cross the threshold unbidden.
Yet no wall is high enough against a door opened inward.
I speak of Vault Chitin, the dream-feeder of serious threat. Do not mistake it for a beast that must crawl beneath a torch before it can harm you. Its dominion is the sleeping mind. It feeds upon dreams, and the sweetest dreams are often those we guard most poorly.
Its form is hard and chitinous, suggestive of something emerging from a vault. Consider that image, and do not soften it. A vault is made to contain. A vault is sealed against theft, plague, fire, and wandering hands. But what if the thing within has learned the shape of the door? What if the lock, the hinge, and the buried seam are parts of its body?
Vault Chitin is invasive. Vault Chitin is alien. Within the mind, it is oppressive. It does not ask permission before entering the chambers of thought. It does not kneel before the sentry. It presses itself against the inward walls until fear calls that pressure a voice.
Therefore, keep watch not only upon gates and battlements, but upon the places you seal within yourselves. Let no secret become a shrine. Let no dream become a locked room where you refuse all daylight. The mind that bars every entrance may still leave a passage below.
Do not boast that you are safe because Vharenford is fortified, watchful, and governed by military readiness. These are worthy shields, and we require them. But a shield held only against the outer dark leaves the inner flesh bare.
When sleep comes, let your thoughts be plain. When dreams rise, examine them. When the unseen knocks, do not answer with your name.
Remember: the vault is not holy merely because it is closed. And whatever emerges from the sealed dark may already have been feeding there.
Remain wakeful. Remain guarded. Keep the inward door unclaimed.

The [[Ashfall Colossus]] is a threat-rating 9 creature and a nocturnal ambusher associated with the ash-dark reaches of [[Embermarch]]. It appears as an enormous, ash-marked mass whose scale makes its approach feel like a moving ruin. Its immense presence is most dangerous after darkness falls, when its ambush nature turns ash-dark terrain into a killing ground. Patient and crushing in demeanor, the [[Ashfall Colossus]] conceals its menace beneath the night. It was unleashed in [[The Purge of Blackport]].

## History

The known history of the [[Ashfall Colossus]] is defined by two facts: it lairs in [[Embermarch]], and it was unleashed in [[The Purge of Blackport]]. These details establish both its territorial association and its appearance in a major episode of violence. The creature is not presented as a wandering beast without a fixed range. Its lair in [[Embermarch]] is central to its identification, particularly because the region’s ash-dark terrain complements its coloring, scale, and nocturnal habits.

The circumstances recorded around [[The Purge of Blackport]] identify the [[Ashfall Colossus]] as having been unleashed during that event. The wording distinguishes the creature from a threat that merely happened to be encountered there. It was unleashed, placing its arrival within the destructive action of the purge and emphasizing the deliberate or consequential release of a danger already capable of changing the character of the surrounding ground.

No further account of the creature’s origin, maker, keeper, or purpose is established in the available record. Accordingly, the [[Ashfall Colossus]] is best described through its confirmed presence, its lair, and its observed manner of attack rather than through speculation about how it came to exist. Its history remains inseparable from the image of a vast mass emerging from darkness, with the terrain itself seeming to shift as it advances.

The creature’s threat rating of 9 also places its historical appearances within the highest level of danger documented for it. This rating does not depend solely on physical size. The [[Ashfall Colossus]] combines immense scale with concealment, patience, and an ambush habit that is especially effective after darkness falls. Its historical significance therefore lies not only in where it was unleashed, but in the manner by which its presence transforms an already hostile environment into a place of immediate peril.

## Relationships & Affiliations

No affiliation is recorded for the [[Ashfall Colossus]] beyond its association with [[Embermarch]] and its unleashing in [[The Purge of Blackport]]. It is not identified as a servant, ally, mount, champion, or member of any other named power. The available account does not assign it a commander, an owner, or a recognized allegiance.

This absence of affiliation is important to the creature’s classification. The [[Ashfall Colossus]] is described as a creature and as a threat, rather than as an organized faction or political actor. Its presence is expressed through movement, concealment, and destruction. Even when it appears within the context of [[The Purge of Blackport]], the record gives no confirmed relationship between the colossus and any other named entity.

Its connection to [[Embermarch]] is likewise territorial rather than political. To state that the [[Ashfall Colossus]] lairs in [[Embermarch]] identifies the place where it keeps its lair; it does not establish that the creature serves, rules, or protects the region. The lair is a feature of its behavior and habitat, while the unleashing described in [[The Purge of Blackport]] is an event in its history. Neither fact supplies an additional affiliation.

The creature’s lack of recorded allegiance also reinforces its menace. A threat whose intentions are unknown cannot be negotiated with on the basis of known loyalties, and a nocturnal ambusher does not announce its approach through visible allegiance. The [[Ashfall Colossus]] is therefore treated as an independent danger in descriptive accounts, with its actions understood through its habit and demeanor rather than through any declared cause.

## Tactical Assessment

The principal danger posed by the [[Ashfall Colossus]] is the combination of visibility, scale, and timing. In open light, its enormous form would be difficult to mistake for an ordinary presence. Yet its habit is that of a nocturnal ambusher, and its immense presence is most dangerous after darkness falls. The creature’s threat does not come from size alone. It comes from the contradiction between its colossal body and its ability to conceal that body beneath the night.

The [[Ashfall Colossus]] appears as an enormous, ash-marked mass. This appearance allows it to merge with ash-dark terrain without becoming wholly indistinguishable from it. The result is a battlefield in which the ground, the darkness, and the creature’s own form seem to overlap. The approach of the colossus can therefore feel less like the advance of a living thing and more like the movement of a ruin. Such an approach delays recognition while increasing the terror of recognition when it finally occurs.

Its demeanor is one of patient, crushing menace concealed beneath the night. Patience is a defining element of its ambush nature. The creature is not characterized by a sudden display of rage or by a reckless charge from concealment. Instead, its danger is associated with waiting, remaining hidden, and allowing darkness to become part of the attack. The killing ground is created when the terrain no longer offers reliable warning or safe distance.

The threat rating of 9 reflects the seriousness of this combination. The [[Ashfall Colossus]] is a large-scale hazard whose physical presence can dominate its surroundings, but its assessment is heightened by the way it uses darkness. The creature’s approach feels like a moving ruin because its scale overwhelms ordinary measures of distance and shelter. Concealment makes that scale difficult to judge until the threat is already near.

After darkness falls, ash-dark terrain should be regarded as the creature’s preferred condition of engagement. The [[Ashfall Colossus]] is most dangerous under those circumstances because its appearance and habit reinforce one another. Its ash-marked mass is suited to the terrain, while its nocturnal ambush behavior limits the opportunity to identify its position. The threat is therefore environmental as well as physical: the land becomes a killing ground through the creature’s presence.

The record does not describe a separate set of powers, weapons, or affiliations for the [[Ashfall Colossus]]. Its confirmed danger rests on the qualities already attributed to it: threat rating 9, nocturnal ambush, immense scale, ash-marked appearance, and patient crushing menace. These qualities are sufficient to define its tactical identity without adding unrecorded capabilities. The creature’s most consistent advantage is the night itself, beneath which its approach becomes difficult to distinguish from the motion of the ruined landscape.

## Legacy

The [[Ashfall Colossus]] endures in the record as an image of concealed immensity. Its significance is not limited to the fact that it is large, nor to the fact that it is dangerous. It represents the moment when familiar ash-dark ground ceases to be passive terrain and becomes an accomplice to the hunt. The creature’s presence changes how darkness is understood: not as an absence of light alone, but as cover for a patient and crushing threat.

Its association with [[Embermarch]] gives that region a defining danger, while its unleashing in [[The Purge of Blackport]] fixes the creature within a remembered episode of devastation. Together, these facts shape the enduring account of the [[Ashfall Colossus]]. It is a threat-rating 9 creature that waits beneath the night, appears as a moving ruin, and turns the darkness around it into a killing ground.

No uncontested founding affiliation can be established from the available accounts. The founding of Ashreach is contested among sources, and the [[Annals/Codex]] should be consulted as the authority rather than replaced by an unsupported date or simplified origin story. The disputed character of the founding does not alter Ashreach’s present regional placement or ruling affiliation, but it does limit the certainty with which its earliest history can be described.

The marsh-bound landscape is central to this assessment. Ashreach presents the bleak aspect of a settlement caught between ash and water, and its environment contributes to an atmosphere of tension, instability, and perpetual threat. Such conditions make the settlement difficult to regard as a place of dependable rest or unquestioned control. Even where defenses are present, the surrounding character of the location reinforces the sense that security is temporary.

Ashreach’s status as contested also changes the meaning of its garrison. The number 2598 should not be read as evidence of complete control. It establishes that Ashreach is defended; it does not establish that the settlement is settled, safe, or beyond challenge. The same fact that distinguishes Ashreach from an undefended holding also separates it from a core stronghold. Its military presence is substantial enough to matter, but its status indicates that the wider struggle over the settlement remains unresolved.

For [[The Bleeding Crown]], Ashreach is consequently a holding that must be maintained rather than merely claimed. The settlement’s rule is explicit, but its contested condition means that authority remains under pressure. The marshes, the uncertain ground, and the bleak environment all contribute to the impression of a position that demands constant attention.

This combination gives Ashreach its characteristic strategic profile. It is not defined by the absence of defenses, nor by the stability associated with a central fortress. Instead, it is a defended settlement whose position remains precarious. Its garrison strength, regional setting, and current status all point toward the same conclusion: Ashreach endures, but it does not rest.

## In Popular Memory

Ashreach is remembered less as a place of triumph than as a place of endurance. Its name evokes the meeting of ash and water, while its contested status gives that image a political and military meaning. The settlement stands as a symbol of authority that is present but never entirely at ease.

The atmosphere attributed to Ashreach is tense, unstable, and perpetually threatened. These qualities are not incidental descriptions; they form the core of the settlement’s identity. Ashreach is imagined as a place where defense is visible, uncertainty is persistent, and the boundary between holding and losing ground remains dangerously narrow.

Its garrison strength of 2598 reinforces this memory. The number makes clear that Ashreach is defended, yet the settlement’s designation as a contested holding prevents that defense from becoming a symbol of permanence. In popular recollection, Ashreach therefore occupies an uneasy middle ground: stronger than an abandoned or undefended site, but less secure than a core stronghold.

The disputed founding contributes to the same impression. Without an uncontested founding year, Ashreach’s origin remains a matter for the [[Annals/Codex]] rather than a settled point of common record. Its past is consequently approached with the same caution as its present. The settlement is known, ruled, defended, and regionally defined, but never entirely beyond dispute.

Blackford’s tactical identity is shaped by three fixed conditions: its position on [[The Pale Coast]], its garrison strength of 3065, and its contested status. The visual character of the location supports this assessment. The stark and dark appearance of Blackford against the pale severity of [[The Pale Coast]] suggests a site organized around endurance. Blackford stands on [[The Pale Coast]] as a dark mark against a pale landscape, watchful and strained. Its legacy is not defined by a single resolution, but by the endurance of a position that remains important, defended, and unsettled.
